INTRODUCTORY REMARKS.—The numerous and extensive collection of
islands, which stretch circularly, but irregularly, from the north-east part of South
America, towards the Gulf of Mexico, are commonly denominated by the general
term.of the West India Islands. ‘They are, by the French, divided into the Greater
and Lesser Antilles, the former comprehending Cuba, St. Domingo, (now Haiti,)
Jamaica, and Porto Rico; while the latter, or Lesser Antilles, stretch from Porto Rico
to the Island of Trinidad; these are therefore, by them, sometimes called the Wind-
ward Islands; but by the English they are commonly known by the name of the
Caribbee Islands, and not unfrequently, though certainly very improperly, divided into
the Windward and Leeward Islands. The Windward Islands of the British naviga-
tors comprise all the islands between Grenada and Martinique, both inclusive; and
the Leeward Islands, all those from Dominica to Porto Rico, including the Virgin
Islands; while the Leeward Islands, of the Spaniards, are those lying off the Spanish
Main of South America, to the westward of the Isle of Trinidad. With respect to
the Bahama Islands, which lie to the northward of Cuba, although comprehended
under the general term of the French Antilles, they form a distinct archipelago, and
will be described in the progress of the work.

CW. Inpizs. Parr I.] B

CURRENTS.

REMARKS ON THE WINDS AND CURRENTS IN THE
NEIGHBOURHOOD OF THE ANTILLES.

From the Nautical Magazine. Vol. xxv. pp. 19, 68, 187.

Winps .—‘ The N.E. trade wind prevails, particularly over that portion of sea
called the Caribbean Sea. When approaching the shores of these isles, however,
disturbances are found in these winds which will be pointed out.

On the shores of the Great Antilles, Cuba, Jamaica, St. Domingo, and Porto
Rico, the sea breeze blows regularly during the day, and the land breeze during the
night. The land breezes are fresher than those observed near the coast, and are
favourable for making passages from west to east in this sea.

In the Lesser Antilles land-breezes are not met with, or at least they are found
at so short a distance from the shore as to be useless in navigation. In these islands
two seasons are observed,—the dry and the rainy. Their periods vary in the different
islands; but it may be stated generally, that the first lasts from October to June, and
the second from June to October. During the dry season the N.E.: trade wind
blows regularly and fresh, with a clear sky. From June to October, during the
winter season, tornados and severe hurricanes are experienced between the 15th of
July and the 15th of October. In the Antilles the hurricanes blow from west.*

Hurricanes rarely penetrate into the Gulf of Mexico; some, however, have crossed
the gulf, and continued onward beyond Vera Cruz. Amongst others, those of the
18th of August, 1810, and June 23rd, 1831.

In the Atlantic Ocean, it is shown by Redfield, that their average place of com-
mencement is in the latitude of 15° N. and long. 55° W., or about N.E. from the
Island of Trinidad; from thence they pursue a W.N.W. course, until arriving near
the coast of Florida, when they follow the course of the gulf stream to the N.E.,
sweeping past the coast of the United States, and continuing far beyond the eastern
limits of Newfoundland. Some, originating south of these, have maintained their
western course beyond the Gulf of Mexico; and others, again, north of them, have
assumed their N.E. course, passing between the Bermuda and the American coast.
But the North Atlantic hurricane mostly commences N.E. of Trinidad, within the
parallels of 10° N. and 20° N., between 50° and 60° W. longitude.

CALMs AND Srorms.—Under the wind, off the high land which forms the greater
part of the Antilles, calm is experienced, interrupted by violent and dangerous squalls,
coming down from the declivities of the mountains; and it is only at two or three
leagues off at sea that the regular breeze is again found. These tricks of the wind
announce their approach by a shrill whistling, and sometimes by an agitation of the
surface of the sea. They must not be trusted in sailing with the wind from the
islands, and great care is necessary in looking to the sails. Vessels have been dis-
masted by these breezes, and many have been capsized, even at the entrance of the
bay where they had intended to anchor.

During winter strong tide rips are found in most of the bays of the Antilles,
generally after calms, or after light airs.

LESSER ANTILLES.—The following observations made at Trinidad, and Dominica,
will give a general idea of the winds met with in the Lesser Antilles.

Porto Rico.—At Porto Rico rain falls from June to August, The trade wind
blows from N.E. The sea-breeze commences at 8 in the morning, and lasts till 4 in
the afternoon, when it is followed by the iand breeze.

CURRENTS.—The Guiana Current, which is a continuation of the equatorial
currrent, runs along the low coast of Guiana towards the Isle of Trinidad. A little
south of Trinidad the river Orinoco discharges a considerable quantity of water into
the equatorial current, mingling with it; these two directions, forming a sharp
angle, the waters easily combine with each other, and the rapidity of the current is
thus considerably augmented. It then enters the sea of Antilles by the strait formed
on one side by the Isle of Trinidad, and on the other by that of Martinique; in which
space are the islands of St. Vincent, St. Lucia, Grenada, Bardadoes, and Tobago.”

4, THE CARIBBEAN ISLANDS.

Current of the Caribbean Sea and Gulf of Mecico.—In the Caribbean Sea no
constant currents have been observed; nevertheless, in the whole of this sea, and
about the islands which bound it on the east and north, variable currents are found ;
and although usually directed towards the west, yet along the coast the general current
still prevails, following the direction of the coast at a variable distance. Thus, ity
flows from east to west from the Isle of Trinidad to Cape Agulhas; thence it proceeds
W.N.W. and N.W.., as far as Cape Catoche, crossing the Gulfs of Darien and Nica-
ragua, and the Bay of Honduras; then it takes a complete circuit of the Gulf of
Mexico. ‘Thus, after reaching Cape Catoche, it turns westward towards the shores
of Campeache, along the coast of Yucatan; it thence continues towards Vera Cruz,
changes its direction, and flows northward as far as the Rio del Norte, and even
beyond that river; it flows afterwards N.E., till it meets the waters of the Mississippi;
then takes a S.E. direction towards the Tortugas. At this point its direction becomes
east, N.E., and lastly, north, following the Florida Channel, and discharging a second
branch across the Bahama Islands, that loses itself in the Atlantic Ocean.

In the middle of the Gulf of Mexico the waters do not appear to follow any par-
ticular course, as is the case in the Caribbean Sea, and they most frequently depend
as to strength and duration on the prevailing winds.

The temperature of the seas of this archipelago has been generally found higher
than that of the open sea of the same latitude; but notwithstanding the increase of
caloric carried to its waters by the surrounding continents, it is considered that
the high temperature of the Caribbean Sea arises in a great measure from the currents
of heated water that penetrate it from the torrid zone of the North Atlantic Ocean.

The Guiana Current varies in strength during its course (which is about 590 miles)
from 10 to 21, or 86 miles a day, according to the locality. It has been sometimes
found to be 4 miles an hour, while near the coast it gradually diminishes to less

than 4 a mile an hour,—The temperature of the water of this current has been
estimated at 80°.”*

ON MAKING THE CARIBBEAN ISLANDS AND NAVIGATING
AMONG THEM.

Mariners in choosing the north or south part of any of the Caribbee Islands for
their landfall, should consider, first, the point which is nearest to the port or road to
which they are destined; and secondly, the season in which the voyage is to be
performed; for, in the dry season it should be remembered, that the winds are
generally from the north-eastward, and in the rainy season, from the south-eastward ;
thus, in the dry season, it will be advisable to make the northern side of the island,
and in the wet season the southern side.

In making the Antilles there can seldom be any doubt, on account of the eminence
or heights of the various islands; but in the case of St. Bartholomew and St.
Martin the following remarks may prevent any doubts in future.

When in the parallel of St. Bartholomew, at a distance of less than four leagues,
if the weather should -be clear, the Islands of St. Eustatius, Saba, St. Christopher's,
Nevis, and St. Martin’s will be painly seen. Here the mountain of St. Eustatius
will have a table-like appearance, with uniform declivities to the east and to the west;
the summit is level, and, at the east part of this plain a peak arises, which makes it
yery remarkable. To the west of the mountain seems to be a great strait, in con-
sequence of the lands near it being under the horizon; and to the westward of that
there appears to be another long low island, the N.W. part of which seems to be the
most elevated; but it is necessary you should not be deceived, for all that land is part

of St. Eustatius. From this situation, Saba will be seen to the N.W., not so high as
St. Eustatius, but apparently of less extent than the western part of St. Eustatius,
which seems insulated. The N.W. part of St. Kitt’s makes in great mountains, as
lofty in appearance as St. Eustatius, with low land to the eastward; and east of this
low land, the Island of Nevis will rise higher than any other land.

Bank or SounpINGs.—By the recent surveys of Captain Barnett, R.N., a bank of
soundings has been discovered to extend a considerable distance to the north, east
and south-east of the islands of St. Bartholomew, St. Martin, and Anguilla, having
from 30 to 40 fathoms near its outer edge, It is composed chiefly of coral, sand, and
shells. In the parallel of St. Bartholomew 24 fathoms will be found 5 leagues off,
but with the same island W.N.W., you will have 35 fathoms on an outer bank, full
9 leagues off. This bank extends 6 leagues eastward of St. Martin, and 8 leagues east-
ward of Anguilla, and full 7 leagues north of the latter island. Its outer edges are
very steep. In dark weather the lead, by being carefully attended to, will warn you
of your approach to this group of islands.

The Island of St. Martin is higher than St. Bartholomew, and will be visible at a
greater distance; but when clouds intervene, and St. Martin’s cannot be seen, there
will be some hesitation in making St. Bartholomew. You are therefore to observe,
that when you are on the parallel of St. Bartholomew, it will appear small, with
four peaks, trending N. and §., and occupying almost its whole extent; and, if not
more than eight leagues from it, you will perceive the appearance of an islet to the
northward, and another at a short distance to the southward, As this island has
neither trees, high mountains, nor thickets, it is not subject to fogs, and may be dis- ‘
covered more readily than either St. Martin, Nevis, St. Eustatius, or Saba; and
therefore is more likely to attract the attention of the mariner.

The Island of Nevis will be seen when you are full eight leagues to the eastward of
St. Bartholomew, appearing very high. “To the westward of Nevis the narrows will
easily be discernible, and then the land of St. Kitt’s seems to rise out of the water,

and increase in height, so that the westernmost of the two mountains, which are at
the western part of the island, becomes the highest. The hill, which is called Mount
Misery, has to the westward a gentle declivity, terminating in low land, and
cannot easily be mistaken. To the west of this you will sée the large strait, or open-
ing, between St. Kitt’s and St. Eustatius; but from this situation you will only see
the high 8.E. part of that island, or rather its mountain, in consequence of which it
will seem like a yery small island, while its mountain will appear much lower than
Mount Misery; but it may easier be distinguished, from the table which its top forms,
by the uniform declivities to the east and west, as well as by the peak on its S.E.
part. Saba, from this vicinity, appears equal in size to the visible part of St.
Eustatius; but it shows only an eminence without peaks, with uniform  declivities,
and nearly round. Should a small islet appear to the west, and very near to St.
Eustatius, let not that confuse the mariner, for it is only the N.W. extremity of the
island, and getting nearer, he will discern the land which connects it to the S.E.
part. Mount Misery, on St. Kitt’s, has a sharp and high peak on the eastern
part of its summit, and will appear, at a distance, to be the summit of St. Eustatius ;
but it will not be mistaken for such, if you attend to its surface being so much more
unequal than the table-land of St. Eustatius, and that there is another less elevated
mountain appearing to the eastward, with gentle declivities, and which shows much
land to the eastward and westward of the high peak.

Should you be about six leagues distant, and to the east of St. Bartholomew, its
north-west extremity will appear insulated, making like a large island; on the”
summit of which are four small steps, and a considerable strait, or opening, to the
southward, between it and the principal island; in the midst of this strait you will
perceive a small islet. This is one of the islets that surround the island; but the first
is only the N.W. point, to the northward of which some other islets are visible; all
these are much nearer to St. Bartholomew than to St, Martin,

6 TRINIDAD.

In order to sail from one island to another, there will frequently be more trouble
than common simple navigation requires; and it will be greater when you have
oceasion to get from leeward to windward; yet this may be reduced to a trifling
consideration, if the navigation is only made through the straits or passages to the
northward of Martinique, in which the currents are weakest; but this will not be
the case in the straits to the southward, in which the current runs with more strength
and rapidity to the westward, and in the channels, between St. Vincent, Grenada,
Tobago, and Trinidad, it would be almost impracticable, the stream there running at
the rate of 2 and 2% miles an hour.

TRINIDAD. (Great Britain.)

DESCRIPTION .—The Island of Trinidad belongs to Great Britain, and is situate
_ off the north-eastern part of South America, being separated from the mainland by
the Gulf of Paria. This island is of a square form, but has two points — one
stretching out from its south-western part, and the other from its north-western
part. Its length from north to south is about 45, miles, and its breadth from east to
west, at the middle of the island, is 30 miles; but at the northern frontier, from
Point Galera to Chaguarimas, the distance is 46 miles, and at the southward, from
Point Galeota to Point Icaque, 59 miles. It is generally esteemed the largest, most
fertile, and most beautiful of all the Windward Islands, abounding with the finest
wood for ship-building, also for cabinet-work; of these the red cedar is the most
abundant and conspicuous in all parts.

Trinidad is capable of producing every article for the West India market, equal, if
not superior, to any of the Windward Islands; its sugar is excellent ; its cocoa, coffee,
indigo, and cinnamon are abundant; tobacco is cultivated for the use of the colony,
and is of a superior quality; grapes, equal to the parent stock in the south of France;
and all other fruits, congenial to the tropics, exist here and flourish in luxuriant
prodigality, equal to their native soils. There are also great quantities of wild cattle,
horses, and mules in the extensive savannahs; with plenty of game, deer, and a species
of cuenca, or wild hog, of most excellent flavour; but the most extraordinary pheno-
menon of the island is the Brea, or Pitch Lake, a natural productivn, occupying
about 150 acres, and said to be capable of supplying all the dockyards in England ;
it is of a bituminous quality, and most eminently efficacious in preserving ships’
bottoms from worms.

Trinidad is very fortunately situate out of the parallel of hurricanes, such being
scarcely ever experienced : and the shocks of earthquakes have been rarely felt, and
are never such as to occasion the least alarm. ‘The northern side of the island is one
continued range of high mountains; those from Point Galera to Maraccas are
estimated to be from 2,000 to 2,500 feet above the surface of the sea; but from
Maraccas westward they do not exceed 2,000 feet; the measured height of Maraccas
mountain is 2,947 feet. These hills are well covered with a wood, which is said to
be incorruptible; from the sides of the hills numerous streams of most excellent
water continually issue, contributing to form the River Orapache and Caroni, and
making this latter river navigable for canoes a great way into the interior of the
island.

Another ridge of hills commences at Le Branche, and runs in a W. by S. direction
towards Monserrat; the highest part of this ridge is computed to be about 1,000 feet ;
and it is remarkable that all the streamlets which arise from these hills are of a
yellowish colour. There is also another range, denominated the Southern Hills;
these stretch along the shore from Point Galeota, westward, toward Point Icaque ;

TRINIDAD. 7

but they are much inferior in height to either of the other ridges, not being elevated
above 700 or 800 feet ; that part near Point de la Grande Calie is 760 feet high. The
coasts and bays which surround the island abound with fish, in great varieties ;
oysters, lobsters, crabs, prawns, shrimps, &c., are to be found in every part, anda
fishery might be established here with very great success.

The climate of Trinidad is considered to be less moist than Guayana, and not so
dry as Cumana; the mornings and evenings are delightful, and the nights invariably
cool and refreshing ; upon the whole it may be pronounced fully as healthy as any
part adjacent; the rainy season begins in June and ends in October; but there
seldom is much rain in June, and the hot weather invariably returns from the end of
May; with the month of November the most pleasant season commences. Population
about 45,000.

MAKING TRINIDAD.—Vessels intending to make the Island of Trinidad
from the northward, will, on approaching its eastern side, obtain soundings full 15
leagues off, which will allow time to correct the situation of any ship bound from
Kurope, and render it unnecessary to lie-to, or use other precautions, either at night
or in thick weather; this understood, the mariner may shape his course either for
Point Galera or Point Galeota, according to his intention of entering the Gulf of
Paria, either by the southern or northern channels;* the former is to be preferred in
the rainy season, or from July to December; and the latter in the dry season, or from
December to June; but the latitude well obtained, it will always be more beneficial
to make the point, to which his course is directed, from the southward than from the
northward, because the current will always favour his getting to the northward, and
retard his advancing southerly; and he will sail with much more facility and rapidity
from Point Galeota to Point Galera than from Point Galera to Point Galeota. The
above points being well ascertained, and intending to enter by the northern channels,
you may proceed from Point Galera along shore, keeping at a distance of two miles,
or even less, from the land, until you reach Point Corosol, when you may take a
course somewhat more southerly, and draw closer to the coast, in order to facilitate
your entrance to the Bocas.

Vessels in want of water can be supplied at Toco, Point Sans Souci, Rio Grande,
Petit Matelot, Rio Para, Cuevas, Maracca Bay, Chute d’Eau, and Macarite.

The Bocas, or mouths of the northern entrances to the Gulf of Paria, are four :—
Boca de Mono, or Ape’s Channel; Boca de Huevos, that is, Egg, or Umbrella
Channel; Bora de Navios, or Ship Channel; and Boca Grande, or Great Channel.
These passages are generally denominated Bocas del Drago, or the Dragon’s Mouths.

Boca de Mona, or Ape’s Channel, is that which is next to Trinidad, and formed by
that island and the Island Monos; it is narrow and somewhat dangerous, yet fair
anchorage may be found within it in 25 fathoms; but the current is generally strong
and irregular, and the wind scant; the water always sets out to the northward in
this passage, the ebb-tides running at the rate of one and two miles an hour, and the

flood somewhat less ; it is also subject to calms from the heights that enclose it, and
is by no means to be recommended, being the most crooked, longest, and narrowest
of all the channels, abounding with whirlpools, and encumbered with several shoals.
A cluster of rocks lie about 800 yards E.N.E. from the N.E. point of Mono Island,
which have 8 fathoms close to them. In this passage it is high water, full-and
change, at 50 minutes after 3 o’clock.

Boca de Huevos, or Egg Channel, but commonly called the Umbrella Channel,
from the appearance of a remarkable tree that grew upon a rock, on the lee side of
the channel, which much resembled an umbrella.t This channel is formed by the

Islands Mono and Huevos, being nearly a mile wide and more than 100 fathoms
deep, the course through being S.W. by S. and N.E. by N.; here the water generally
runs out to the northward, during the ebb-tide, but with less velocity than in the
Mono Channel, and during the flood it becomes almost imperceptible; it is, therefore,
by many, considered the shortest, clearest, and best passage to enter the gulf by;
but care must be taken to avoid a rock at the S.W. point of Mono Island. It is
advisable, in this passage, to keep closer to Huevos than to Mono Island, to avoid
being becalmed by the high land of the latter, and also because the current inclines
to the N.E. This passage should, however, never be attempted with a scant wind.

Boca de Navios, or Ship Channel, is between the Islands Huevos and Chacacha-
care; it is from three-quarters to one mile and a half wide, and steep-to on each
side, the course through being S.E. by 8. and N.W. by N. This is considered the
best passage for vessels bound out of the gulf. It is advisable to keep the eastern
land on board ; and, in endeavouring to enter from the northward, you will find the
wind favourable until you arrive within the head of the passage, when you will
experience sudden flaws from the adjacent high lands. In all cases the mariner
must be attentive, and haul his wind in time, for otherwise, with a light breeze and
northerly current, he may be whirled round by the stream and driven out again to
sea. In the Boca de Navios the water always runs out, during the flood-tide, at the
rate of a mile and a half an hour; but with the ebb, its rapidity is nearly increased
to four miles; at high water only can a vessel expect to get through it, and therefore
it becomes the best to sail out by. It is here high water at 39 minutes after 3 o’clock,
full and change.

BOCA GRANDE.—This is by far the widest channel, and is formed by the Island
of Chacachacare on the eastern side, and by the high land of Paria to the westward.
Vessels formerly were accustomed to run down the northern shores of Trinidad for
the Boca Grande, availing themselves of the advantage of both wind and tide, and
enter the gulf to the westward of the Island of Chacachacare; the passage here is
full five miles broad, the ebb-tide runs with less velocity than in any of the other
channels, and the flood is almost stationary ; it is clear of dangers, the Diamond
Rock excepted.

The Diamond Rock lies off the S.W. end of Chacachacare, and is about 40
yards in circumference, and has only 9 feet water over it. It is marked by a white
buoy, with the 8.W. point of Chacachacare E.N.E., distant about 2 of a mile; El
Pato, or Goose Island, W.S.W.; and the S.E. point of Paria W. by 8. Captain
Sughrue struck upon this rock, and at the time the ship was aground, two vessels
passed him, one on each side in deep water, not 25 fathoms distant, so that it
appears to be a very dangerous rock, with deep water all round it; the current was
then setting strong to the southward, with light variable winds. In this channel
there is abundance of room to work through, but as it is to leeward of all the other
passages, few vessels now pass through it, unless they have been unable to make
their passage through those to windward.

In all these passages there is a great depth of water, and sometimes no bottom will
be found in mid-channel with a line of 100 fathoms, so that a ship of the line may
run close to the sides of the islands, except at the projecting points, or stony reefs.
The most favourable time for entering the Bocas is about two hours after the tide
begins to flow ; and for going out, one hour after ebb commences.

CHAGUARAMAS BAY, or PORT ROYAL, is that part of the Gulf of Paria
situate under the north-western peninsula of the island, and comprehends a space of
about 70 square miles, within which vessels may conveniently anchor in a depth of
water from 5 to 20 fathoms; the northern shores being bold and steep, and the
bottom in general gravel and oaze. St. Joseph, which is the capital of the island,
stands about six miles to the eastward, being built upon the banks of a small river.

About 14 mile to the south of Mono Point is the north point of an inlet called
Mona Carenage, which runs in north-eastward more than half a mile, and has from

PORT SPAIN. 9

17 fathoms at its entrance to 3 fathoms at its farther end. In the bay a ship may be
secured to the shore and perfectly land-locked. Off the sandy shore, which forms the
east side of it, isa bank, which shoals suddenly ; it will therefore be necessary to
keep on the northern side, if you should have occasion to work up so far.

CHAGUARAMAS HARBOUR.—After passing the Mono Passage, you will per-
ceive an island, called Gaspar Grande, lying 1$ mile to the southward, being 13 mile
long, half a mile broad, and of considerable height; midway between the islet and
the peninsula lies a small islet, called Gasparillo, forming two passages into Chagua-
ramas Harbour, the northern one having 5 to 15 fathoms water, and the southern 9
to 14 fathoms. This harbour is spacious, and affords good anchorage; the shores are
bold, except off the large plantation, which is situate in the principal valley on the
north side, whence a shoal of 1 to 3 fathoms extends 600 yards off; its outer edge
bends to W.N.W., and is very steep. Vessels may anchor in this bay anywhere, but
the most convenient spot for watering is in 12 fathoms, with the east end of Gaspar
Grande bearing §. by E., and Delgada, or Taitron Point, in a line with St. Joseph’s
Point. On full and change days it is high water by the shore at three hours, the
tide rising about five feet; but at the anchorage the flood stream runs until 3h. 30m.
The flood runs to the eastward, and continues only 54 hours; the ebb runs to the
westward.

PORT SPAIN.—The principal place of trade in the Gulf of Paria is Port Spain,
or as formerly designated Port d’Espana, situate 10 miles E. by S. from the Mono
Passage. The city or town is regularly laid out, and much extended of late. In the
centre of the town is Brunswick Square, and to the northward the Queen’s Park, or
Savana. On the southern part of the town is a jetty, and just to the westward is
the Water Battery, the Commissariat Wharf, and Watering Place.

Light.—At Port Spain, on the jetty, in latitude 10° 38’ 40’, and longitude 61°
81' 0’ is an hexagonal tower, 43 feet in height, and 50 feet above the sea, exhibiting
a fixed light all night, visible between the bearings of N.E. by N. and S.E., round
by the west.

In the road of Port Spain the water is very shallow, there being only 33' fathoms
at the distance of 13 mile; the bottom there is extremely foul and muddy, and more
so nearer the shore. At about 1% mile from the shore, with a white tower on a hill
near the town, bearing N.E. by E., you will find 35 fathoms, very soft mud; but
ships may anchor anywhere, the water being always very smooth.

Directions.—In sailing for Port Spain, vessels commonly pass through one of the
western passages into the Gulf of Paria, which have been already described. Here
the currents must be particularly attended to, for the stream which comes from the
southward, and sets strongly upon the southern and eastern shores of Trinidad,
becomes particularly rapid as it passes through the south-western channels into the
Gulf of Paria; while the current, which commonly sets along the northern shore,
generally runs in a W. by S. direction, and has a tendency towards the south-eastern.
coast of Cumana and Paria; these currents meeting occasion a great accumulation
of water in the gulf, which is much increased during the rainy season, and pressing
forward to the northward through the Bocas, cause a perpetual and often violent
agitation of the sea in this part; it was most probably from this circumstance that
Colon first named these channels the Bocas del Drago, or the Dragon’s Mouth.

It will readily be seen, from what has been said of the different Bocas, or
entrances, that the Boca de Huevos will be the best to adopt in sailing into the Gulf
of Paria, and the Boca de Navios in going out. In sailing inward, it will always be
advisable to take the tide of flood, and with a breeze that will keep the ship under
command; but should the wind be such that you can run through it at one stretch,
and keep a speed of 4 knots an hour, then there will be no occasion to wait for a
tide. Of aclear night there is no danger in entering this Boca; but if calm, and
the night obscure, or the wind scant, and the tide unsuitable, so that you wish to
wait for a more favourable opportunity to enter, you can anchor about 2 of a mile

10 PORT SPAIN.

from the shore, in 22 fathoms, unless the wind be at N.E., which heaves in a heavy
sea; or you can make short tacks along the coast. From Point Toco to Point
Chupara the bottom will be found mud, and to the southward of the mud the sound-
ings will be coarse sand and fine gravel; to the westward of Point Chupara it is of a
green-coloured mud; by observing these differences in the quality of the ground, the
mariner will readily know what part of the coast his vessel is abreast of, and can
proceed accordingly.

Should the mariner enter the Gulf of Paria by the Boca Grande, it will be highly
requisite that he should remember and guard against the effect of the current already
described, for otherwise he will find himself driven too far to leeward, and have great
difficulty in beating up for the port; it will, therefore, be advisable, in taking this
passage, to haul immediately round the Island Chacachacare, giving its 8.W. part a
berth of a good mile, and having passed the Diamond Rock, make a long board to
the south-eastward, then, should the wind permit, steer north-easterly for the road of
Port Spain; or, in entering by either of the Bocas, so soon as you have passed
through, and are to the southward of them, you should haul by the wind on the port
tack, both to get away from the Bocas and to near the coast of Trinidad ; follow this
track while the flood-tide lasts, and take the starboard tack so soon as the ebb
begins; by which means you will either fetch the anchorage, or approach very near
to it.

Some persons consider it preferable, after they have entered the gulf, to work tack
and tack, especially should the port tack be not favourable ; but it should be remem-
bered that the currents always run strongest opposite and near to the straits ; there-
fore, beginning to tack too much within the vicinity of the Bocas, the ebb-tide may
endanger their being forced out again, or, to prevent that, they may be compelled to
anchor; or, should neither of these events take place, they will meet the ebb, which
will, in all probability, hinder their reaching Port Spain. But, on the contrary, by
prolonging their course well into the gulf, even to the parallel of Mount Naparima, if
necessary, they will there find the ebb-tide most advantageous for the starboard tack,
so that they may either proportion their course, so as to reach the anchorage, or may
gain it by making a short tack. Whenever it happens to be a calm, or the wind so
‘light that you are unable to gain anything, then come to with your kedge, and that
will be sufficient to hold you against the strength of the tide. You should avoid
using your large anchors if possible, because they sink so deep, and there will be
difficulty in purchasing them again.

Or, if circumstances be favourable, having safely cleared the Bocas, and got well
within the Gulf of Paria, you will perceive a white tower (in ruins), called St. David's,
standing above Port Spain, come open to the southward of the Island of Gaspar
Grande; this will be visible 4 or 5 leagues. It is built of white stone, and stands in
the interior of the fortifications upon Abercromby’s heights. In sailing up, as you
advance, with the white tower near the town about EK. by N., you will see the forts
on Gaspar Grande and Point Gorda, which protect the careenage and the anchorage
in Chaguaramas Harbour; after which, the shipping off the town will become visible.
In Port Spain you may anchor to the south-westward of the town, in 5 or 4 fathoms
water, agreeable to the size of your vessel, and moor with your bowers N.W. and
§.E., having a stream cable and anchor out astern.

This anchorage is undoubtedly the safest in the West Indies, being free from
hurricanes or tempestuous weather (beyond an occasional thunder-storm), possessing
the best of holding-ground, and not requiring a pilot. It is high water at Point
D’Espagne at 4h. 30m., full and change, and spring-tides rise 4 feet; neaps, 3.
The water is slack about 14 hour, both at high and low water. The flood comes from
the west, and the ebb from the 8.E.

Should a vessel happen to drive from her anchors, she will go on soft ground, and
receive no damage; the best place to run aground is in the N.W. part of the bay.
The town has a stone jetty, and is defended by batteries; a white half-moon battery

PORT SPAIN. 11

forms a good mark for the bay, and is visible a long way off; large ships should
bring the battery to bear N.N.E.

All the western coast of Trinidad is low, except Mount Naparima, which forms a
conspicuous object, being 602 feet above the level of the sea ; this appears round, and
may be seen in clear weather full 10 leagues off. The adjacent shores of the con-
tinent to the westward are low, swampy, and full of rivulets ; the most considerable
river is that of Guaracaro, which is navigable for the largest schooners. There are
many places on the’ western coast of Trinidad where you may obtain fresh water.

From Point Icaque, or Yeacos, to Point Brae, or Pitch Point, the flood-tide sets to
the southward and westward, and the ebb to the northward and eastward. From
Point Brae to Port Spain it follows the direction of the land, with very little
difference, the flood setting south, and ebb north.

The best anchorages on the northern shores of Trinidad are in the bays of Toco,
Rio Grande, Punta de Chupura, Las Cuevas Maraccas, and to the leeward of Mara-
baral, in which water may be obtained, there being a beach, which renders the
acquisition easy. The whole of this coast is bounded by rocky shores, and, with the
exception of a small part, with steep mountains, thickly covered with. wood down to
the sea, which breaks in a heavy surf along the whole extent, rendering landing im-
possible, except at a very few places; but the soundings extend several miles off, and
are almost regular, so that a vessel may approach to eight, seven, and six fathoms
near the shore, the bottom being everywhere good, sand and mud; it is not, however,
advisable to go into any of the bays to leeward of Maraccas, as the high mountains
there prevent the wind from blowing home, and the swell in such a case renders it
difficult to manage a ship. All along the whole coast, and for the distance of three
leagues outside, the.stream runs north-eastward, or rather east, with the ebb-tide,
and §.W. with the flood, but beyond those limits its general tendency is S.W.; and
the same direction prevails between Trinidad and Tobago, only the ebb is less rapid
than the flood. i

Although from the parallel of the middle of Tobago the island may easily be dis-
tinguished in clear weather, yet you will not be able to see Point Galera at a’distance
of more than 3 leagues, on account of its being so much lower than the coast to the
westward, and its projecting out from the mainland; but in coming from the east-
ward the mountains at the back of the point will be visible 11 or 12 leagues, All
the eastern coast southward from Salabia to Point Galeota is much lower, except
near Point Manzinilla, whence four mountains rise to the W.S.W., which may be
seen 8 or 9 leagues off; this is the beginning of the middle ridge of hills, and here
named the Barrancas of Manzanilla; here also is the entrance to the River Le
Branche.

To the southward is Guataro Point, which may be readily known by its stretching
out from the coast to seaward, and by the height of the tongue that forms it. From
hence there are many plantations of cocoa, cotton, coffee, and sugar. A little north-
ward of the point is a landing-place, and here the River Guataro, or Ortoire, empties
itself into the sea, after having sent some branches to the northward, which are
navigated by canoes and small craft. Point Galeota’ may be seen at a distance of 6
or 7 leagues. Here the hills begin to rise, and stretch along the whole southern
coast, rising 760 feet above the level of the sea ; the highest of these is situate a little
to the westward of the Punta de Caza Cruz; thence they continue as far as Point
Herin; and from Point Herin to Point Icaque they diminish in size, until the last
point becomes a low beach.

It is observable, that on all the eastern coast there is no good watering-place ;
the large rivers discharge into the bays of Maturas and Cocos, called also Man-
zanilla and Guataro, the bars of which are too shallow to allow even a canoe to
pass them. There are several places of temporary anchorages, as shown on the chart,
but they are none of them safe, being too much exposed to the eastward. The
current here sets to the north-eastward, but with much less force during the ebb than

12 THE GULF OF PARIA.

the flood; this is also accompanied by a heavy swell of the sea, especially during a
gale of wind, which renders a near approach to the shore extremely dangerous.

On the southern coast you cannot obtain fresh water, except a little to the west-
ward of the Point of Casa Cruz; here a torrent from the southern mountains pre-
cipitates itself into a hole or well near the shore ; but its attainment is always attended
with trouble and difficulty. The current along the coast is always westerly, and
commonly at the rate of 2 or 25 miles an hour. In running along the south coast. of
Trinidad it is advisable to keep 2 miles from the shore, where you will find 8 or 10
fathoms, and be clear of all risk.

To ENTER tHe GULF or PARIA sy THE SOUTHERN CHANNED, which is
generally preferred during the rainy season, or from July to December, the mariner
should direct his course for Point Galeota,* which is situate in latitude 10° 9’ 30"
north, and will easily be recognized. Point Galeota is surrounded by a rocky shoal,
named Guayara Bank, consequently should have good berth given to it. The coast is
also bordered with rocks as far to the westward as Point Cusa Cruz.

Having made and rounded this point, you may run along to the westward, keeping
about 2 miles off the land, where you will find from 8 to 12 fathoms water, free from
every danger; the bottom being generally sand and gravel. Having arrived to the
vicinity of Point Herin, you will experience a change in the colour of the sea; but
this is occasioned solely by the current, and there is no impediment whatever.}
Proceeding onward, you will pass Point Quemada, or Burnt Point; here you may
approach within 4 a mile of the shore without fear, for there is no danger, and take
whatever channel you find most convenient.

The FIRST CHANNEL is formed by and between Point Icaque and the Wolf
Rock, a shoal of 9 feet water, which lies to the westward of the point, at a distance
of about 4 a mile from the land; this shoal is 2 cables’ length from east to west, and
has a rocky bottom; but the channel between it and the point has a depth of 8 and
10 fathoms, and Point Icaque is so bold, that at $a cable’s distance from it there are
8 and 9 fathoms water. ‘he current here runs to the S.W. with the flood, at the
rate of 24 miles an hour, and with the ebb it sets N.W., with the velocity of 3 or 33
miles an hour,

To enter by this channel, you haye only to round Point Icaque, at less distance
than a cable’s length, luffing up as you double it, until you are close hauled ; or steer
on to the northward, weathering at a proper distance the Points Coral and Gallo.
This channel is not dangerous by day or night, especially with an ebb-tide, the
current of which will always assist you in passing the shoal to leeward; besides you
can anchor if necessary, and never run the least danger of getting on shore, while
you will leave the shoal at least 3 cables’ length from your vessel.

The SECOND CHANNEL is formed by the above rocky shoal, and another of
gravel and rocks to the north-westward of it, and on which there are 3 fathoms
water. This shoal lies from Point Gallos S.W. by W., distant 3 miles, and from
Point Icaque W.N.W., distant 13 mile; this passage is.a mile wide, and the currents
take the same direction as in the first channel.

To enter by the second channel, it will be advisable, after you have made Point
Quemada, and run from thence along the coast, at about 4 of a mile, to steer towards
the Soldado, or Soldier’s Island; and keep on the same course until the whole of
Point Gallos is open, of Coral Point, when you should luff up; but not higher than
to the N.N.E., until you get east and west with Point Coral, when you may haul close
to the wind, in order to near Trinidad.

The THIRD CHANNEL is formed by and between the last-mentioned shoal and
Soldado Island, with its reefs and shoals to the south-eastward. The channel is
nearly 2 miles in extent from east to west. At 25 cables’ length from the eastern
part of the Soldado’s reef you will have 7 fathom’s water; in the middle of the
passage are 9 fathoms, and near the shoal 6 fathoms.

To enter by this third channel, you should first steer for the Island of Soldado, as
directed for the second channel, and continue that course until Point Gallos bears
N.E. by E. easterly, or Cedros Point becomes shut in of outer Gallos Rocks, when
luff up north, until the south front of Point Icaque comes E.S.E. § 8., and Point
Gallos E. by N., then hau! up to fetch the coast of the island. With the flood-tide,
the stream sets W. by S., at the rate of 3 and 33 miles an hour, and with the ebb
N.W. and W.N.W., near Soldado, and in mid-channel, with the velocity of 4 and 4%
miles an hour. The above passages are commonly denominated the Serpents’ Mouths.

The FOURTH, or SOLDIER’S CHANNEL, is formed by Soldado, or Soldier’s
Island, and the coast of Columbia, or Land of Orinoco; this is about 4 miles in extent,
and the current within it, in mid-channel and near the Soldado, always runs N.W. or
W.N.W. at the rate of 44 or 5 miles an hour, but the stream slackens its velocity to
14 mile within 3 a mile of the Columbian shore, which is low and shallows to a con-
siderable distance.

To enter by the fourth channel, you should steer W. § N., so as to pass 23 miles to
the southward of the Soldado, and when you bring that islet N.E., luff up north, and

run afterwards, luffing up successively, by little and little, until you haul by the wind
to gain the coast of Trinidad ; but you should be very careful in passing to the south-
ward of the Soldado not to go nearer than 2 miles, lest the current, which sets
strongly to the north-westward, should entangle you with the rocky reefs with which
the island is encumbered.

From a consideration of what has been said, it will readily be seen that at whatever
time you may enter the Southern Bocas, or Soldier’s and Serpent’s Channels, even if
by night, the first channel is the most advantageous; not only because it lies to the
westward of all the others, but because, by luffing, especially with ebb-tides, you will
pass every danger; indeed there will be no danger whatever if you keep an anchor
ready to let go, in the event of its suddenly falling quite calm, or any other accident
should happen calculated to drift the vessel towards the shoals; and by night no
other Boca can be taken so readily as this, because you will have to pass at less
distance than a cable’s length from the point; this will render the obscurity of the
night of little importance, as you will be able to discern your passage, the shore
being at so short a distance from you.

Should, however, circumstances occur, from calms or otherwise, to hinder you
taking passage into the gulf, you can anchor in Herin Bay, or anywhere on
the south side of the Island of Trinidad until daylight; but by no means lie off
and on the land, for the current, which always runs strongly in, will insensibly
drift you towards the Soldado, and you will find the utmost difficulty in maintaining
your ground at any given point.

Cedros Bay and Esperaza Bay lie to the north-eastward of Gallos Point, in either
of which is shallow water, 10 to 12 feet. Off Cedros Point, to the W. by N., lie
to Barrel of Beef and the Loo Rocks, both of which are marked by a beacon buoy.
The outer one, on the Loo Rock, is white, and lies 1} mile from the point; and the
inner one, on the Barrel of Beef, being a bell buoy.

14 SAN FERNANDO.

Landing may be made at Cedros Point, to the eastward of which is Granville
Bay, wherein is 12 feet, where fresh water may be had.

N.E. 1 E., 22 miles from Cedros Point, and 1 mile N. by W. of Rouge Point, the
nearest land, is a shoal of 3 fathoms, and to the W.N.W., 94 miles, is a bank of 5
fathoms, with a bottom of dark sand.

Having passed either of the above channels, you will be within the Gulf of
Paria, and should shape your course so as to gain the western coast of the island,
which you may sail along at a distance of 23 or 3 miles, so far as Brae Point, and
from this Port Spain is distant 8 leagues; so that by steering N.E. $ E., you will
goon see the town; and, in case you should not be able to steer that course, tack
and beat up, never standing nearer to the shore than 3 miles, for the water along the
coast becomes shallow; but if you choose to prolong your tacks into the bay of
Naparima, then tack 4 miles from the coast, giving a wide berth to two shoals that
are within it; the one W. 4 S. from the mount, distant 2+ miles; the other
other W. 3 N. from it, distant 45 miles.

SAN FERNANDO.—Just to the north-westward of Naparima Hill, and on the
coast, a new trading-place has of late years sprang up, where a pier is run out, and
anchorage in 3 fathoms may be obtained at 15 mile from the pier.

Buoy.—Port Spain bears N. $ W., 22 miles from the above anchorage; but from
the western side of Trinidad shallow water extends a long way from the land; and
a bell buoy, with staff and globe, is laid down more than 3 miles from the land.
This buoy lies, approximately, N.N.W. 3 W., 13 miles from the pier at San Fernando;
and south, 15 miles from the light on the jetty at Port Spain. ‘

The GULF or PARIA is so abundant in fish as to be capable of amply supplying
the greater part of the West India Islands; vessels never attempt sailing out of the
Gulf by the Soldado, or Southern Channel, because of the current, which would .
render every attempt impracticable.

Regulations for the Harbour of Port d’ Espagne, or Port of Spain.

1. No boats to go on board any vessel before the Harbour-master has visited; and
no boat to go on board after the vessel has been cleared by the Harbour-master,
except the boats of Her Majesty’s vessels of the Custom-house, or such as have leave
from the Harbour-master, under a penalty of 100 dollars.

2. All vessels entering by day must show their colours, and by night a light ; and
anchor where the Harbour-master shall point out; the master to report at the
Government-house immediately on landing. If intending to remain more than 48
hours, to moor from the bows one anchor to the north-eastward; to rig in their jib,
outer jib, and main booms close, and keep their boats and lighters alongside, under
the penalty of one dollar per day for each day they shall remain without being so
moored with booms in; and be accountable for all damage any vessel or boat may
sustain by their neglect.

3. Masters of vessels must furnish the Harbour-master with a written account of
all passengers on board, and also a written account of all the crew, specifying their
situations; and on the departure of the vessel, the master must satisfactorily account
for any alterations, otherwise the vessel will be detained until security be given.

4, No foreigners or coloured persons can be landed until written permission has
been obtained from the Government-house, nor any other passenger, until reported to
the Harbour-master, under penalty of 100 dollars.

5. No stones, sand, or dirt to be thrown overboard in the harbour; but landed at
the place which the Harbour-master shall point out. No tar or pitch to be boiled on
board. Penalty in each case, 100 dollars.

TRINIDAD. 15

6. None of the crew can be discharged here without first obtaining leave from the
Governor, under penalty of 100 dollars. Sailors deserting must be reported to the
Harbour-master and to the Chief of Police within 24 hours after desertion, otherwise
they will be considered as discharged without leave.

7. Masters of vessels must give 24 hours’ written notice to the Government
Secretary, before their departure, of the port to which they are bound; neglect of
this will subject them to 24 hours detention after being cleared out.

8. No foreign vessel can lay off and on without permission from the Governor ;
British vessels can only lie off and on till 5 o’clock of the day they arrive, provided
they have no passengers. Any vessel which has passengers on board, or intends to
take off passengers, must come to an anchor,

9. All sailors found on shore, without permission from their captain, will be sent
to gaol.

10. All sealed letters must be delivered to the Harbour-master.

11. Masters of vessels are warned not to allow any of their men to enter the town,
above the junction of the wharf and Marine-square, without permission from the
Harbour-master, under the penalty of 50 dollars for each offence.

12, All persons arriving in this colony are to deliver their names to the Harbour-
master on his visit to the ship, declaring their number of servants; from that officer
they will, except in special cases, receive permission to land, when they must report
to the Government-house, where, if English, they will show their passports, which
will be endorsed by the Secretary; if foreigners, they must obtain the Governor's
license to reside in this colony.

Remarks on Passing through the Bocas of Trinidad, by Commander Gt. Daniel, of
; ALM.S. Victor. ,

“ Endeavour to make the land 6 or 7 miles to windward or eastward of the Bocas,
as, in the event of its falling light winds or calm, you have good anchorage at 13
mile off shore ; and if you should be swept to leeward of them, you must work up to
the northward of Granada before you can fetch them again. The eastern, or Boca
Monos, is intricate, nor is there any advantage to be gained by making it; for entering
the Gulf of Paria, the second, or Boca Huevos, is generally used; and the third, or
Boca Navios, for going out. If the wind should not be to the northward of E.N.E.,
you ought to run to the Boca Grande; if it is, you will find, as you approach the
Boca Huevos, that it draws round to the northward ; and, if blowing a 6-knot breeze,
you may enter at any time of tide with safety. If the wind is light, you cannot
accomplish the passage with the ebb tide; but with the flood the current is nearly
neutralized, and it may then be attempted with safety. From the mast-head you
may see whether the breeze runs through. You must keep on the starboard hand
going in, to avoid the eddies which run under the high cliffs of Monos; and also
because the wind is fresher on the Huevos side. When nearly through, the studding-
sails ought to be taken-in in time, and everything ready for bracing up on the port
tack, as the wind generally blows pretty fresh from the eastward in the gulf, and if
taken a-back, you may be driven back through the Boca before you get the sails
trimmed,

The time of high water at Boca Monos is 4h. 44m. ; at Boca Huevos, at 4h. 40m.;
and Boca Navios, 4h. 34m.

The third, or Boca Navios, is the best to go out through ; it trends to the S.E. and
N.W., and the gulf wind generally draws through it from the southward, until you
get the easterly breeze outside ; at all events, the current takes you out with sufficient

Currents near Trinidad, by Captain G. H. Columbine, R.N,

“The western tropical currents, occasioned by the trade wind being confined by
the trending of the coast of South America, and thus thrown with collected force
upon Trinidad, run there with great strength, which is still further increased along
its shores by the obstruction which itself presents against the free course of the
stream; and by the Orinoco, which, flowing through plains subject to periodical
inundations, and emptying itself near this island, greatly increases the currents in
its neighbourhood, particularly about August and September, when the river is at its
greatest height.

The vast river Amazon, sometimes called Orellana, the name of the first Spaniard
who explored it, collecting its waters from almost half the southern continent, may
perhaps, though at the remote distance of 280 leagues, contribute something to its
force.

These currents vary much in their strength, at different times, without any apparent
cause. It is said they run strongest in the declining quarters of the moon ; but iT
could not: discover any satisfactory proof of this idea. Adapting itself to the coast,
the current runs to the northward along the east side of Trinidad, and takes a
westerly direction, between Tobago and Point Galera, round which it runs with such
force that it is scarcely possible for a squave-rigged vessel to beat against it round
that point, although it is sometimes effected.

Along the north coast it runs close to the shore a few leagues, as far as Rio Grande,
but there it often quits the shore, and takes a W.N.W. course, increasing its distance
from the land till it gets to the northward of the Bocas, where it seldom prevails
within five or six leagues, being repelled by the current which runs out of these
passages. ‘There the two currents blend, and run to leeward; along the south coast
they always run to the westward, about 13 or 2 knots, near Point Galeota; but as the
opposite shore of South America contracts this channel towards Point Icaque, their
strength is much increased there, and may be reckoned generally at three knots, but
often more. From hence this body of water disperses itself over the gulf, and along
the shore is subject to the influence of the tides; but in the middle it always runs to
the northward towards the Bocas, where its course being again contracted, its velocity
is proportionably increased. Having passed these straits, the body of this water pre-
serves its northerly direction for five or six leagues before it falls into the common
course of the stream of the ocean, which is there W.N.W.; but it is to be observed,
that as soon as it has passed the Bocas, a considerable part diverges to the E.N.E.,
and either runs with some rapidity to windward, or so thoroughly destroys the effect

with ease by keeping inshore. Often this easterly current extends a considerable

stream which goes out of the Boca Grande on the west side, turns round the north-
west point of Paria, and runs down that coast with such velocity, that if a ship
bound to Trinidad falls in with the land to leeward of this point, though never s0
little, she must immediately stand to the northward, at least so far as 13° lat., out of
the greatest force of the current, and work up to Grenada, before she again attempts
the Bocas. Even then, if she cannot lie S.E. by S., at least her reaching them will
be very doubtful, and her best way will be to go through the passage between Kick
‘em Jenny and Carriaco, in order to weather Grenada before she gets into the strong
lee current which prevails between that island and Trinidad, and renders it very
difficult for ships to fetch Point Salina from the Bocas. In general they only reach
about four or five leagues to leeward of Grenada. A good ship will require from 8
to 12 days to go from Trinidad to Barbadoes.”

Captain Columbine remarks,—* Sunday, May 27th, 1804, stood from Point Salina
to the Bocas; but though the ship lay S.8.E,, and went on an average 33 knots, yet
we fetched five leagues to leeward of the Bocas. Stood to the northward again, but
owing to calms under the lee of Grenada, we were not able to get up to the Carriaco
till Thursday night, when we attempted to get through, but were driven back by the
current. On Friday morning we attempted it again, but as we lay only S.S.E., we
could not weather the island close to Grenada, although we had weathered the Island
Aux Jantes and Islet Ronde; we ran to leeward between Grenada and London
Bridge (a rock midway between Grenada and Islet Ronde). The current sets with
great rapidity here to leeward, not less than three knots. On Saturday morning,
having a smart breeze, we again attempted the Carriaco Passage, and though the
ship lay only 8.S.E. 7 E., she got through very well, weathered Grenada, about three
leagues. At midnight made Trinidad, and on Sunday morning entered the Bocas.”

TOBAGO (Great Briratrn).

The ISLAND of TOBAGO is about 26 miles long, and 64 miles broad, contain-
ing 52,058 acres of cultivated land, and having a population of about 14,500. The
principal articles of exportation are sugar, cotton, rum, coffee, and indigo.

About the centre of the island is a hill of a dark red colour, which is supposed
formerly to have been a volcano. The land is, generally speaking, high, and may be
seen in clear weather more than 15 leagues off. The distance from Barbadoes to
Tobago is about 38 leagues; to Grenada, 34 leagues; and to Trinidad, 17 miles.

Taking your departure from Barbadoes to Tobago, you should sail in the morning,
or before noon ; by which means you will reach the island in daylight the following
day. Your course should be south, a little easterly, for there isa north-westerly

‘current, which you must be guarded against ; but should you make Tobago in an

evening, and are fearful of running toward it, do not lie-to, but stand well to the
southward, under easy sail, otherwise the current above mentioned may carry you so
far from the island that you will have great difficulty in reaching it again.

Tobago has not any harbours, but there are several good bays about it, which are
secure and convenient for shipping; for which reason, vessels frequently take shelter
there, especially during the hurricane months, from which this island is free.

MAN of WAR -BAY.—The best roadstead'is Maw of War Bay, which’ lies’on
the north-west side of the island. Vessels: bound to:this or any of the bays on the
north-west side of the island, should make for its north end, off which lie a cluster
-of bold rocky islets, called Melville’s or St. Giles’s Rocks, in latitude 11° 23’ north.
The westernmost of these has a large opening in it, running in a northerly and
southerly direction, which gives it a remarkable appearance; there is deep water
close to these rocks, and you may run up to them, and coast along shore toward
Man of War Bay. The distance from St. Giles’s) Rocks to the north-east point of the
bay is not. above 2 miles. Sail boldly and round the point, you will then get the bay
open; but be careful the wind does not take you aback, for it is commonly very
wavering under the high land; thus having entered, turn in and anchor as far to
windward as youcan. You will have very deep water until you get within the bay,
when. the depth will decrease from 90 to 40, 20, and 10 fathoms. There is on the
starboard or western side of the bay a small rocky shoal, named the Cardinal, which
lies about.} of a mile from the shore; it is steep-to, and the sea constantly breaks
over it, by which you will easily know and avoid it; there is also, at the bottom of
the ‘bay, a little island, known by the name of Booby Island; the best anchorage
will be found to the north-eastward of this island; you will perceive a long sandy
beach; turn or warp in towards it, in from 16 to 12 fathoms; Booby Island will then
bear 8.W. $ W., and Point Corvo W. 4 W.; Pirate’s Bay will be right a-head, where,
in the rainy season, is the common watering-place; but anchorage may also be had
along the south side of the bay in from 10 to 18 fathoms, within + of a mile from
the shore ; good water is to be obtained there, but the surf is dangerous.

Point Corvo.is the western point of Man of War Bay, about 14 mile to the west-
ward of which are several rocky islets, called the Brothers; they are bold-to, and
have a great depth of water all round them ; in the same direction, and at the farther
distance of 14 mile, lie some other rocks, of a similar form, but more in number}
these are named the Sisters; close to these are 40 fathoms water; and the adjacent
coast is all bold and irregular. In clear weather, when you are outside and abreast
of these rocks, the S.W. end of Tobago, although low and sandy, will be visible.
It will be prudent ina large vessel always to go on the outside of the rocks, for
although there is deep water within them, there is said to be a shoal, called the
Snapper, lying midway between the Sisters and the Shore, with less than 4 fathoms
over it.

In sailing along the land from Man of War Bay, you will pass several small bays,
viz., Cheese Bay, Bloody Bay, Parlatuvier’s Bay, Englishman’s Bay, Castara Bay,
Flamingo Bay, King Peter’s Cotton, and Formagier’s Bay, all affording safe anchor-
age for vessels of 150 tons; you will then reach Courland Bay. Great part of this
shore is bold and rocky, with high land in the interior.

COURLAND BAYS.—Guana, or the northern point of Great Courland Bay, lies
about 14 miles from the western point of Man of War Bay, and has a rock, called the
Beef Barrel, almost close to its northern point; the sea, particularly at low water,
commonly breaks over it; it therefore will not be dangerous to vessels which enter
Courland Bay, from the northward, in daytime; but by night, it will require you to
give a proper berth to it ; and if you should be fearful of entering the bay, you may
find good anchorage to windward of the Bluff Cliff, with regular soundings of from
6 to 20 fathoms.

In advancing to Great Courland Bay you may know it by the appearance of Point
Guana, or Courland Point, which is low, woody, flat, and rocky, with a number of
houses, called Plymouth Town, and a flagstaff upon it. Having given the Beef
Barrel a good berth, there is no danger. You may anchor about the middle of the
bay, between Guana Point and Hawk’s Bill, where you will find good ground in 6 or
8 fathoms, bringing Courland Point to bear N.E. by N., and Hawk’s Bill south; and
good fishing in somewhat deeper water, that is, in 9 or 10 fathoms. ‘The bay is clear
of rocks, with a bottom of dark sand, which holds well; the soundings decrease
regularly, and there are 3 fathoms within a cable’s length of the beach. Two or

To the southward of Hawk’s Bill is Stone Haven, where also you may anchor in
8, 8; 10, or 12 fathoms; the ground clear and good, but the shores are in some places

Little Courland Bay lies between Rocky Point, on which stands the remains of an
old Dutch fort, and Booby Point, at the extremity of which is a small islet, and from
which extensive reefs stretch out to the westward and southward, called the Buckoo
Reefs ; various channels and passages are formed between them, but they are only
navigable by boats. There is good and safe anchorage in Little Courland Bay, and
vessels ride more smoothly here than in Great Courland Bay, being sheltered by the
Buckoo Reefs and Shoals, especially within the Windward Point, which is bold-to ;
but care must be taken in sailing from Little Courland Bay, and you must obtain a
sufficient breeze to enable you to weather the Buckoo Reefs, for these stretch full 2
miles trom the shore, and at their northern part some patches, which become dry at
low water; keep therefore at a distance of 2 cables’ length from the edges of the
reef, and you will be safe; but otherwise the current will, especially in a calm, set
you directly upon the reef. Soundings extend 3 miles outside of the reefs.

Sandy Point Bay is formed by two points of land at the S.W. part of Tobago ;
they are both low and sandy. ‘To enter this bay you should haul close round the
Buckoo Reefs, and anchor at the farther end, not far from the land, in 6 or 7 fathoms
water. Vessels sailing from this place to the northward should steer full 3 miles out,
a eM themselves of a breeze, lest they should not be able to weather the Buckoo

eefs, 5 .

EASTERN SIDE OF TOBAGO.—Ships bound to any of the eastern ports of
Tobago must guard against the N.W. current, which constantly prevails round Little
Tobago, keeping well to the south-eastward. Little Tobago is a huge rock, about 4 a
mile broad, and a mile long; it lies nearly 31 miles 8.S.E. from Melville’s Rocks,
and is encompassed with many rocky islets. Between Melville’s Rocks and Little
Tobago is Tyrrel’s Bay, fit for vessels of 150 tons; the best anchorage is near the
bottom of the bay, in 7 or 8 fathoms water; but the ground between Little and Great
Tobago is foul, and subject to strong and variable currents.

KING’S BAY.—In sailing southward, 34 miles beyond Little Tobago, you will
reach Pedro Point, and 1} mile farther on is Queen’s Island, another high and round
rock; between Pedro Point and Queen’s Island, is King’s Bay, a place of good
anchorage on every part within the windward Point, in from 6 to 20 fathoms water ;
here the high eastern shore shelters you from the trade wind ; but the swell from the
south-eastward will frequently drift your vessel to the Leeward Point. To sail from
this bay, the best time will be about the break of day, when the wind commonly
blows fresh from the land to the northward.

QUEEN’S BAY.—About % a mile to the westward of Queen’s Rock, or Island, is
Queen’s Bay, situate at the mouth of a small river of that name; in sailing for this
bay you should give the rock a good berth, sailing onward until you open a large
house with a gallery to it, standing on a rising ground in front of the quays; con-
tinue thus until you bring this house in a line with a house on the above hill, and
proceed with them on until you get about 2 cables’ length from the shore, then anchor
in 5 fathoms, abreast of the watch-house ou the beach—fine sandy ground; but should
you. have a contrary wind, you must let go your. anchor, or warp up. -In sailing out
of the bay the same marks will serve without going to windward.

ROCKLY BAYS.

To the south-westward of Queen’s Island, nearly 24 miles, is Richmond Island;
the coast between them bends circularly in, and forms Prince’s and Great Hog Bays;
the ground is all foul and rocky. Here you will see the Roxburg, a large rock above
water, lying % of a mile to the westward of Queen’s Bay. Behind Richmond Island
is a small bay, named Halifax Bay, fitted to accommodate vessels of 150 fons; but the
mariner must be careful to avoid the Shoal, which is situate in the middle of the
entrance ; from hence an extensive sand-bank extends almost as low as Smith’s Island;
this bank stretches out full 14 mile from the shore, and is called Great River Shoal,
having 3 fathoms, and perhaps less water over it. Indeed, from Queen’s Bay to the
S.W. extremity of the island, so many rocks and dangers are scattered about, that no
stranger ought to navigate its shores without a pilot; but bring Richmond Island to
bear N.N.E., and you may sail along the edge of Great River Shoal in 4 fathoms
water; or by keeping it-more to the northward, you will pass along it in 12 and 14
fathoms. Smith’s Island is small, and has Pinford Bay behind it, where, although
there may be sufficient water, the ground is foul and rocky; farther to the south-
westward is Barbadoes Bay, which can accommodate vessels of 150 tons or upwards.
To sail for this bay, you should bring Smith’s Island to bear about N.W., and having
so done, luff up, and take care to avoid the coral reef which surrounds Granby Fort
Point, and is on the windward side. Advance until you get abreast of Georgetown,
where you will find tolerable anchorage in from 6 to 12 fathoms; the common and
best mark for anchoring is the Cotton Tree on the beach in one with the flagstaff on
the hill. About a mile to the westward of Barbadoes Bay is Hillsborough Bay and
River, two branches of which here empty themselves into the sea. From the mouth
of the western branch the shore winds nearly S. by W.; and directly south of this
river, distant 14 mile, is a dangerous sunken rock, called the Chesterfield Rock, with
only 8 or 9 feet water over it, while very near it are 15 and 16 fathoms; there is a
passage between it and the shore, with 11 fathoms in it, but too hazardous for
strangers to attempt. Minster’s Bay is to the westward; the ground throughout is
rocky and foul; but having passed the South Western, or Red Point, you will open
Rockly Great Bay.

ROCKLY BAYS, SCARBOROUGH.—Great Rockly Bay is formed between two
red points of land, and has two bold rocky islets at its entrance. It runs in to the
northward a considerable way, and those who are acquainted with it find a deep and
safe harbour; but like all the others on this side of the island, its entrances are
dangerous. Vessels bound for this bay from the northward should be careful to give
the shores a good berth, to avoid the dangers already mentioned; and having passed
the Great River Shoal and the Nine-feet Rock, on which the Chesterfield struck, the
sea frequently breaking over it, haul in for Scarborough Point, a bold bluff promon-
tory, within which the town of Scarborough is situate; keep the weather shore well
on board, and you will pass clear of danger, and when you get the main street well
open, you may anchor in from 7 to 26 fathoms; but the only clean part of the bay is
from 7 to 9 fathoms. Do not attempt to sail out of this bay without a pilot, for the
channel between Scarborough Point and a reef to the westward is not more than $ of
amile broad, and to astranger the passage will be almost impracticable. Little
Rockly Bay lies to the south-westward, and is covered with foul ground, the sound-
ings being extremely irregular, and in some parts shallow and dangerous.

Light.—A Lighthouse has been erected on Bacolet Point, for the purpose of
rendering the access more safe during the night, to the Port of Scarborough, in this
island. ‘The building is 46 feet in height, and 116 feet above the sea, and exhibits a
fixed light, visible between the bearings of E.N.E. and 8.W. by W. by the south.
The tower is pentagon, and coloured red and white.

Bearings of the Light-house at Bacolet Point, with Directions for making the Port
of Scarborough.—Vessels approaching Scarborough from windward, and running
down the coast on a south-west course, will not open the light until it is brought to
bear W. by S. When the light bears W. by N., the Minster Rock is in a direct line
with it. The Minster Rock lies E, by S. from the light, distant 13 mile. Continue

the same course—W.S.W.—until the light bears N.W.; then haul in W.N.W. until
the light bears north, when the ship will be abreast of the lighthouse, and should
haul in N.W. for the harbour, paying due attention to the distance from the shore.
Having got well inside the lighthouse, and lost sight of the light, vessels can go by
the lead, as the water lessens gradually, and may anchor when they get into 6 or 7
fathoms. But after losing sight of the light, coming into the harbour, you must be
guided by the eye and the lead.

The eastern point of the reef off Scarborough bears from the lighthouse W.8.W.,
distant about 14 mile.

From hence to the south-west, or Sandy Point, the shore is all rocky, and must
carefully be avoided ; the soundings are variable, and in many places very shoal.

In the channel, between Tobago and Trinidad, there is a bank, on which 3 fathoms
water have been discovered, and it is asserted some parts are still shallower; but
although it has been examined with great care, and no less water found, yet the
mariner should run over it with great caution, keeping his lead going, for there may
be some rock or shallow of small extent yet undiscovered. It has already been stated
that the current here runs to the westward at the rate of 2 miles an hour; but so,
that when you are approaching Trinidad, its direction will be N.W., and near Tobago
towards the S.W. On the N.E. part of Tobago it runs north-westerly with still
greater velocity.

The above bank was surveyed in 1843, by Captain Drew, H.M. Sloop Wasp.—

BARBADOES (Great Britatn).

The ISLAND of BARBADOES is about 17 miles long and 12 miles broad, con-
taining 106,470 acres of cultivated land, and having a population of 122,000;
the principal objects of exportation are coffee, sugar, rum, and cotton. It is the
easternmost of the Caribbee Islands, is moderately high, of level appearance, and
with very few trees upon its surface; nevertheless, in clear weather, you may see it
full 12 leagues off. Vessels from the eastward, in approaching this island, should
always get into the latitude of 12° 56’ north, and make for the southern side of the
island, for the eastern side is rocky; and from the eastern to the southern point a
reef runs along nearly 1} mile off shore; it has its name from the Cobbler, a remark-
able rock, which forms one of the number; these rocks terminate in a flat spit, which
runs out S.W., 13 mile from the southern point of the island; they must always
have a proper berth given to them, more especially by night, for by day their situa-
tion and extent will be sufficiently discoverable by the white appearance of the
water, It is said, that as you approach Barbadoes, and are at the distance of 60 or
80 leagues to the eastward of the island you will perceive the sea to be discoloured
and thick, but without soundings; by this phenomenon, if met with, you may dis-
cover your situation. The east end of Barbadoes will first appear to be lower than
any other part of the land, but having brought the north end of the island to bear
W. by N. and the southern point nearly W.S.W., it will then appear to be the
highest part; between the eastern and northern points the shores are broken and
ragged, but from the eastern point towards the south it is even, and shelves down to
seaward. The south point has been mistaken in the night for Needham Point and
Fort, which in coming from the eastward do not appear until you round the spit,
when the extreme east point of the island bears N.N.E., and the south point distant
about 3 miles; Needham’s Point and Fort will then bear N.W. by W., distant about
miles, and you can then haul up for it, keeping it a little open of the starboard
