Light.—SoutH Point or BARBADOES.—The base of the tower is 55 feet above
the sea, from which it is 200 yards distant, and stands in latitude 13° 2’ 45",
and longitude 59° 33’ 10’. The tower is 90 feet high, and is painted in alternate red
and white bands, each being 74 feet in depth.

The light is thus 145 feet above the level of the sea, and revolves once in every
minute; after an eclipse of 14 seconds, it again appears, gradually increases for 24
seconds to its greatest brilliancy, and then in 24 seconds more is eclipsed.

From the light, Seawell Point bears N.E. by E. 3 E., and Needham Point W.N.W.
z W.; and except from between the opposite bearings, the light is visible in all
directions from the deck of a vessel within the distance of 18 miles.

Vessels approaching the island are recommended, when from the eastward, not to
run down their longitude to the northward of 12° 55’; and as soon as the light is
discovered to bring it to bear west; steering from thence W. by S., and not passing
it at a less distance than 2 miles.

If coming from the north-eastward, the light will not be visible until it bears to
the westward of 8.W. by W., being concealed by the high land forming Seawell
Point ; and if kept in sight, well open of that point, it will lead clear of the Cobblers
—a group of dangerous reefs, which extend some miles from the eastern side of the
island. Mariners are advised to give them a wide berth, on account of the prevailing
current to the westward.

When the light is brought to bear north-east, a course may be shaped for Needham
Point; but, in hauling up into Carlisle Bay, that point should be kept at the distance
of 4 of a mile.

CARLISLE BAY.—Having made the southern point of Barbadoes in the parallel
of 12° 56’, you may stand in towards the land, and clearing the spit, which runs
from the southern point, haul in to Oistin’s Bay, where the ground is somewhat
rocky; but tolerable good anchorage may be found by bringing the mill at the head
of the bay to bear E.N.E. or E. by N., in 7, 8, or 9 fathoms water.

Buoy:—A black beacon-buoy, placed on the shoal extending from Needham Point,
is of great advantage in approaching the anchorage. It lies in 5} fathoms, with two
flagstaffs on the point in one, and St. Mary’s Church, in Bridgetown, bearing N.N.E.
Those nearing the buoy will observe to keep it in a line with Pelican Island, and pass
it as near as they please, hauling up N.N.E. until the water deepens to 10 fathoms ;
or when the signal-post on the hill comes open of the ordnance-wharf, when the
shoal will be cleared. This buoy is liable to be frequently washed away.

Light.—A fixed light on Needham Point, at the south side of Carlisle Bay. The
light will show red to the southward of west, and as a bright light to the northward
of west. The bright light may be seen in clear weather at a distance of from 8 to
10 miles, and the red light 3 miles.

Directions.—Vessels approaching from the southward, after passing the revolving
light on the south point of the island (giving the point a berth of at least 2 miles)
may haul up W. by N.3N., for Carlisle Bay, when they will soon make the red
light. Gradually nearing it (the lead kept going), as soon as the light shows bright
they may luff into the bay and bring up.

Needham Point may be rounded within about + of a mile, in 5 fathoms water.
Vessels approaching from the northward, as soon as they see the light on Needham
Point, must bring it on an E.S.E. 4 S. bearing, which will clear the Pelican and

Kettle-bottom shoals.

If bound for Carlisle Bay, you may run along shore to the north-westward, keeping: -

at the distance of 8 miles from the land, towards Needham, Point, on which isa
stone fort, with two signal-stayes, and giving that a good berth, to avoid the reef

which always shows itself by its breakers; keeping Pelican north point on with the.

eastern edge of Pelican Island will clear it in 8 fathoms. Having rounded this reef,
you should haul in towards the bay, bringing Charles Fort, which stands on Need-
ham’s Point, to bear S.E., and the steeple N.N.E. Or bring Needham’s Point
S.E. 3 8., the N.W. point of the bay N.N.W., and the Church N.N.E., and here you
will have 23 fathoms, sandy ground. When a house, standing upon a hill, above the
north end of the town, is open to the northward of the Church, the ground is foul,
but to the southward you will find it more clean ; and when the ‘house is open to the
southward of the church, you will find anchorage in about 12 fathoms, or in 7 or 8
fathoms, with Willoughby Fort N. by W. % W., and Charles Fort 8. by E.3E.
There is a bank with 4 fathoms on it, having tolerable anchorage; the marks for it
are—the Church bearing N.E., on with a house having a large tree to the right of it,
on the south side of the entrance into the Carenage, and the flagstaff of St. Ann’s
Barracks, about S.E., on with a wooden house of two stories, in the naval yard, to
the right of the naval wharf. Should you be bound to Carlisle Bay from the N.W.,
or from leeward, and make the land to the eastward before night, your best way
is to beat up, under proper sail, to the southward of the latitude of the south
spit, and run into the bay in the morning; if you keep under the land, and lie-to,
you wiil be subject to light baffling winds, and perhaps be driven a considerable way
to leeward. Since the new light has been established on Needham Point a vessel may
take up an anchorage in Carlisle Bay in the night. At the north part of Carlisle
Bay stands Bridgetown, the principal town in Barbadoes; it is situate at the
entrance of a small rivulet, and lies latitude 13° 5’ 30’. Water here is good and
plentiful, but wood is very scarce; and the tide is hardly perceptible.

N.N.W. from the northern part of Carlisle Bay are several detached banks and
reefs, called the Pelican and Half Acre Shoals. Vessels passing by the leeward side
of the island, on their passage to the northward, must give this part a good berth to
avoid them, for the outermost shoal is said to lie almost a mile from the shore. The
mark to clear Pelican Reefs and Shoals is the tower of St. Ann’s Castle, on with the
centre of the dockyard storehouses, bearing 8. 52° E.; this will lead over the outer
end of it in 5 or 6 fathoms.

About 5 miles from Pelican Point, the northern point of Carlisle Bay, is Hole
Town, and 31 miles beyond that is Speight’s Town, which is defended by three forts;
there are also several other forts situate along the coast. Vessels may occasionally
ride before Speight’s Town. About 3 miles to the northward of Speight’s Town is
Great Head, off which a rocky sand-bank stretches to the westward full 2 of a mile,
on which a vessel was wrecked in 1846. The northern and eastern shores of Bar-
badoes are rocky, and should be approached with caution, for there is no place of
shelter whatever. Vessels, therefore, commonly make for its southern point, as
before directed.

GRENADA (Great Brirarn).

The ISLAND of GRENADA is 18 miles in length, and about 8 in breadth ; the
population is 28,000, and its principal exports are coffee, sugar, rum, tobacco, cotton,
cocoa, and indigo. It is very mountainous, and has a broken appearance, but its
valleys are fertile ; the climate is naturally hot, but the heat is greatly tempered by
the sea breezes, and the dry and rainy seasons are very regular. There are 26 rivers,
all capable of working sugar-mills, besides other small rivulets; the eastern part of
the island is the lowest, but the ridge of mountains which extends from the northern
to the southern parts, may be seen, in clear weather, full 8 leagues off; and you may
approach any part of Grenada to the distance of 2 miles. It is not much subject to
hurricanes. ‘There are no venomous reptiles, excepting a few scorpions and centipedes;

24 ST. GEORGE’S BAY.

hot springs are numerous, and there are the remains of several volcanoes; the natural
magnet is found in various parts of the island, and the rivers abound with fish.

Vessels bound from Tobago to Grenada should weigh in the evening, and steer
under easy sail N.N.W., or N.W. by N., on account of the currents, by which
they will get near to Grenada in day-time; they may then proceed to the eastward of
the island, rounding its northern end, or sail for Point Salines at their pleasure.
There are several bays and creeks on both sides of the island, affording good and safe
anchorage, but the following are those most commonly frequented :—St. George’s
Bay, is the principal one of the island, and lies. on its western side; Caliveny
and Egmont Harbour, which is on its southern side; and Grenville Bay, which is on
ts eastern side.

ST. GEORGE'S BAY lies near the S.W. part of the island; it is bounded by
Cabrit, or Goat’s Point, to the southward, and Maliniere’s Point to the northward ;
Point St. Eloy, which is more than a mile to the southward of Maliniere’s Point, is
encumberéd with a rocky shoal, which extends a considerable way into the sea, and
must be avoided. Off the entrance of St. George's Harbour, at the distance of 5 a
mile, lie the Three Fathom Banks and the Amas Shoal. The former is said to have
several spots of coral upon it, and towards its middle has only 19 feet, but in other
parts 3! fathoms, increasing in depth towards its edges, so that to the southward
there are 8, 9, and 10 fathoms. The centre lies W. + N. from the Harbour-master’s
house at the south side of entrance, and 8.W. by W. 3 W. from St. George’s Fort at
the northern side of entrance. The Anna’s Shoal, of similar depth, lies W. by N.
1 N. from the Harbour-master’s house, and W. by 8. 7 S. from Fort George, distant
4a mile from Fort George Point. The channel into the harbour is to the northward
of these shoals. There is also a coral reef lying 4 a mile due west of Long Point,
the shoalest water on which is 13 foot, surrounded by 9, 12, and 18 feet. Between
this shoal and the point there is a passage of 6, 9, and 12 fathoms’ depth; but sur-
rounding the point there is a reef.

Directions.—Vessels making for St. George’s Bay from the southward round
Point Salines (the §.W. extremity of the island) will observe an islet, called Glover
Island, lying full $ of a mile from the land ; they should not attempt to pass between
it and the land, unless very small vessels, because it is shallow; give it a good outside
berth, and pass Point Salines at the distance of 13 mile; your water will then be 12
or 16 fathoms; farther off you deepen to 17 or 20 fathoms. So soon as you have
cleared the point, when St. George’s Bay-will open, proceed in a N.E. by N, direc-
tion, and take care not to make your course more easterly than to bring Rocky Point
of St. Elvy in line with Mount Moritz, which will clear the shoals between the town
and Salines Point. When Fort George Point comes in line with Government-house,
you will have cleared the Long Point Shoal to the north-westward. Run on with
the former mark towards St. George’s Fort, leaving St. Anna’s Shoal on the star-
board hand, and, if necessary, come close under the fort, for it is bold-to; then warp
up. You will commonly be obliged to work up into the bay, as the trade-wind will
be against you; but the ground is all clear, and the harbour capable of holding a
fleet of large ships with much convenience.

To enter the harbour, having by the before-mentioned marks reached to the north-
ward of Anna’s Shoal, you should get Fort George Point of land in line with the
south side of Military Hospital E. 3 8.; run with this mark until within 3 cables’
length of the point, or until the square town of the Scotch Kirk and Episcopal spire
are in line bearing N.E. ‘by E. 3 E.; then steer S.E. 3 8. two cables towards some
buildings in the lower bight of St. Martin’s Bay, or until the end of Martin’s Wharf
comes in line with the end of Ballast Cliff; with this, steer east, and round N.E.
towards the Carenage.

George Town possesses one of the best harbours in the West Indies, called the
Carenage, where vessels may lie land-locked in deep water, close to the wharves. The
town is handsomely built, and divided into two parts, one being called the Bay

GLOVER ISLAND. 25

Town, the other the Carenage. In entering the Carenage, you should endeavour to
keep mid-channel in 10, 12, and 14 fathoms water; for should you get near the land
on either side, it shallows to 4, 3, and 24 fathoms; on the starboard side also, farther
in, you will meet with a coral bank, which nearly dries; do not go to the eastward of
this bank, but borrow somewhat towards Fort George’s Point, and steer up the
Carenage N.E. by N. You may meet with some small spots of 3 and 4 fathoms on
each side; but in the middle of the passage there are 8, 9, and 10 fathoms, until you
approach the farther end, where it becomes shallower.

Remarks on sailing round the south end of Grenada, by Mr. H. Davey, H..S.
Cornwallis, in December.—* We ran down skirting the eastern coast; rounded the
south-eastern point, and stood along the south shore at the distance of about 3 miles,
thus clearing the Grampus Shoal, or the Porpoises, and Glover Island. There was a
fine moonlight, with a pleasant trade. At 7h. rounded Ramier Islet, giving a berth
of 1 mile to its southern point. Hauled up N.W., and when Point Salines, the 8.W.
point of Grenada, bore north, steered N.N.W., kept the lead going, first cast 9
fathoms, altered course to west and S.W. Had 8, 7, 6, 7, 8, 19, and 13 fathoms.
Hauled up to the N.W., and with Point Salines E.N.E., 14 mile, rounded to and
anchored on hard sand.

At 8 o’clock a tide set past the ship to the S.S.W. at the rate of 2 miles per hour;
at midnight the ship tended, and the tide set through to the eastward at the same
rate. At 8h. A.M. on the following day, it again set to the S.S.W., and by 10h. its
rate was 3 miles. ‘With this set of tide how valuable is Point Salines as a temporary
anchorage.

From the information of the Harbour-master, it appears that spring-tides obtain
a rate of 4 or 5 knots, that they were strong among the Grenadines, at St. Vincent,
and extended to the southward of Grenada towards Trinidad. He was also of
opinion, that throughout the range of the Caribbean Islands, the tides were of
more consequence than hitherto considered; and it appears probable that many of
the accounts that reach us respecting the currents in opposite directions, often in the
same place, may be the effect of tides. This ought to be particularly interesting to
navigators, and I think may be worthy of further investigation. We had light winds
with calms during the night.

Having waited 3 hours until the tide slackened, the ship worked up to St. George's
Roadstead; anchored in 9 fathoms, sandy bottom, Fort George flag-staff bearing
FE. 3 8.; Point Maliniere, N. 1 W. ; Point Salines, S.W. by W.”—Extracts from the
Naut. Mag., July, 1838.

Vessels from the northward, making St. George’s Bay, should give Maliniere Point
a small berth; there are 8 and 9 fathoms within a cable’s length of it. It first will
appear somewhat like an island, low, and with some straggling trees ; when you are
near it St. George’s Fort will be seen to bear §.S.E. Keep your luff for the fort,
and endeavour to bring it to bear east; but beware of the 3-fathoms shoal, already
described; and, in passing Point St. Eloy, give it a berth of 4 a mile at least, to avoid
the rocky reef that runs off it. The soundings, as you advance from Maliniere Point,
will be found regular, from 20 to 9 fathoms, and when inshore near the fort, from 9
to 5 fathoms, but the ground is foul.

Glover Island.—At 17 mile S.E. from Saline Point, the S.W. extreme of Grenada,
and § of a mile from the shore, is Glover Island, 41 feet high, and at a distance
appears like a sail. Small vessels find convenient anchorage under its lee, in waiting
for tide, when working to windward along shore.

Seringapatam Shoal, with 21 feet water on it, on which H.MS. of that name
struck in 1839, lies §.W. i W., 33 cables from Salines Point. This shoal is about
4 of a mile in extent, with 6 and 7 fathoms water round it. The sea over it is always
in a disturbed state. Vessels of 16 feet draught may pass Salines Point at the
distance of a cable. To the westward of Seringapatam Shoal, at 113 miles W. by S.

[W. Inpies. Parr I.] E

26 CLARKE’S COURT BAY.

2 §. from Salines Point, are some shallow patches, and on one of them only 29 feet
water.

The Porpoises, or Grampuses, are rocky reefs, which lie S.E. by E. ? E.,
distant 3 miles from Point Salines. They are about a cable’s length in extent, 3 feet
above water, and steep-to. The sea constantly breaks over them; and, although
there is a passage between them and the land, it will always be prudent to go to the
southward of them; and at night it is necessary you should be certain how you run,
that you may go clear of them. About § of a mile E. by S. of them is a shoal spot,
with 3% fathoms water upon it.

CLARKE’S COURT BAY.—The entrance to this bay is formed by Caliveney
and Hog Islands, and the shoals and reefs extending from them. It is larger than
Port Egmont (to the eastward), capable of holding a large number of vessels; and,
were buoys placed upon the shallows, it would present no difficulty in entering under
steam. The anchoring-ground is about a mile in length and 3 cables in breadth, in 7
and 8 fathoms water, muddy bottom. The passage is through a narrow vein of deep
water, between the banks on either side, with 2 to 4 fathoms on them. Here vessels
may find security, even from a hurricane; but there are 3 shoals in the bay to be
avoided—one in the N.E., and one in the S.W., both nearly dry ; and one with only
6 feet water upon it, in the northern part of the bay. To enter the bay, bring the
two eastern points of Hog Island in line, bearing N.N.W. 4 W., and nothing to lee-
ward of this mark. When the south extreme of Caliveney Island is in line with
Fort Jeudy Point, haul up midway between the reefs, or close with the weather shore,
and anchor where convenient.

PORT EGMONT, eastward of Clarke’s Court and westward of Fort Jeudy
Point, is an inlet 1 mile in length and 13 cable wide, carrying 8 fathoms water to
the upper part, where there is a narrow passage to an inner harbour (landlocked) 4
and 52 fathoms deep, with 21 feet water at the entrance, and where vessels may lie
hidden from seaward.

To enter this port, bring the east extreme of Gary Islet north of Adam Islet, on
with the extreme point of the west side of the harbour, and a hill to the northward
of it, bearing about N. by W. 2 W., which will lead to the entrance of the harbour.
When the land to the eastward of Fort Jeudy Point is shut in, steer more to the
northward, skirting the bank; and should the wind be so far to the northward as
N.E., be prepared to anchor quickly, and afterwards warp farther in. A vessel
may sail in with the wind to the southward of east, and out with the wind to the
northward of it.

CALIVENEY HARBOUR is a small basin extending east and west about 5 a
mile in extent to the westward of Bacaye, and separated from it by a narrow neck
of land. The entrance will be known by Westerhall Point trending to the eastward,
with light-coloured cliffs on the 8.E. side, and having three separate hills on it.
Fort Jeudy Point, 70 feet high, to the westward, stretches well to the southward,
and has a detached rock off it. This is one of the many bays on the southern coast
of Grenada; it lies E. by S.3S., 12 mile from Glover Island, and W.S.W. 4 W.
from Fort Jeudy Point, distant 3 miles to the eastward of Point Salines, and may be
said to form two harbours—the inner and outer; the latter is about § a mile long.
The former, or inner harbour, runs a considerable way up the island, and could safely
accommodate 60 sail of the line; it is narrow, the depth of water being 4 and 43
fathoms; the bottom is soft and oazy, and holds well. Here vessels may lie along-
side the warehouses, and obtain their cargoes with much convenience; and having
done so, they can be easily towed into the outer harbour, into and out of which they
can sail with the common trade wind.

In making for these places from the eastward, you will experience little danger
until past Fort Jeudy Point; but coming from the westward, be careful to avoid the
Grampuses, and not go too near the shore, for though the coast is bold, the approach
to it is foul and rocky.

GRENVILLE BAY. 27

GRENVILLE BAY lies on the eastern side of the island, and hasa separate
custom-house. The bay is open, and to those who are well acquainted with its navi-
gation, it is both safe, commodious, and well sheltered from all winds; but toa
stranger it will be difficult, dangerous, and almost impracticable, for the lead is no
certain guide; and should you get too near the rocks, you will be unable to stem the
current, which will drive you upon them, consequently the bay should not be entered
without the aid of a pilot.

Caution.—Vessels sailing for Grenville Bay must be very careful that they do
not run to leeward of it ; should they once do so, they will be under the necessity of
going round Point Salines; then turning to windward on the other side of the island,
and passing its northern point, proceed again for their destination ; for the fastest
sailing ship will be unable to make head against the southerly current, which sets
along its eastern shores. In order to avoid this mistake, it will be advisable to heave-
to a little to windward of the Telescope Rock, which lies a little to the northward of
east from Telescope Point, and is a remarkable rock, 65 feet high, rouad, and steep
on all sides. Here make a signal by firing a gun, and a pilot will directly come off
and assist you to enter. :

The bay is formed between Telescope Point and Marquis Island, which are 13 mile
apart; it is of a circular form, and throughout encumbered with dangerous reefs ;
the channel in is near Telescope Point, and there are two beacons erected on shore to
the southward of the town, and at the head of the bay; they are white, and formed
like a diamond ; these must be brought in a line, and keeping them in this direction,
you may proceed directly in, under easy sail; the channel in is between the rocks,
and not above a ship’s length wide; you must therefore steer in very steadily, and
after you get through the narrows, if your vessel should draw more than 13 feet
water, you must come-to at the mooring-chain and lighten.

Off the northerr shores of Grenada are several islets, bold-to, with passages
between and also between them and Grenada; among these is a remarkable one,
called London Bridge, with a chasm or archway perforated through it by the
waves of the sea, and from which extends a reef to the southward; this will
readily be avoided by keeping over to the north side of the channel. The northern
and western shores of Grenada are bold in general so far as Point St. Eloy, at the
harbour of St. George, where a reef runs off, which has been described before. ‘The
stream in the strait between Grenada and Tobago sets 8. 70° W., at the rate of 14
mile an hour.

THE GRENADILLAS, orn GRENADINES (Great Britatrn).

The GRENADILLAS, or GRENADINES, are a chain of small islands and
rocks, comprehended in the space between Grenada and St. Vincent. The jurisdic-
tion of these islands is divided between Grenada and St. Vincent. Cariacou, Redondo,
or Round Island, the Diamond, Levara, &c., belong to Grenada; and Bequia, or
Becouya, Great Mosquito, Bird Island, Ballesso, Canquan, Mayera, Union, Frigate
Island, Little Martinique, &c., appertain to the latter. The two principal islands are
Cariacou and Becouya; these are inhabited, and haye plantations of coffee, indigo,
and cotton, and some sugar; but are totally without rivers, and fresh water is
obtained from a few springs.

CARIACOU is the largest of these islands, and is distant about 16 miles from the
northern part of Grenada; in the space between them lie Redondo and several other
lesser islands, having channels of deep water between them, Cariacou is of an
irregular form, and has two bays on its northern side; but its southern and western

28

sides are frequented by small craft only ; for there are so many rocks, islands, and
shoals about it, that it would be extremely hazardous for ships of great draught of
water to attempt approaching that side. Cariacou is about 7 leagues in circumference,
and has a town named Hillsborough upon it. Tyrrel’s Bay is commodious, and easy
to sail into, being bold from side to side, until you reach a small point, the extremity
of the high land on the south side of the bay, from which runs a reef; all within is a
flat bight of coral and sand, with shallow water. Shut in the points of land without
the bay, and nearly in its centre you will lie secure in 14 fathoms, sandy ground.
In this bay there is a small Carenage, where by warping in, you will ride safely with
all winds, the most water being 43 fathoms. The Diamond, half in sight off the south
point of the bay, bearing 8.E. by S., is the mark for going in; the breadth at the
entrance to the Carenage is 26 fathoms; it is surrounded with mangroves, among
which are quantities of oysters.

Hillsborough Bay is about a mile to the northward of this. You may pass between
the Sister Rocks and the island, in 17 and 18 fathoms water, without the smallest
danger. The Sister Rocks lie 4 a mile from the shore; they are bold-to, but the
point from which they stretch has a reef running from it, about a cable’s length; take
care to clear this, and there is no other danger. Northward of this rocky point lies
a small island, which you should leave at a convenient distance to the starboard ; you
will then open a low rock, and afterwards the town; if bound inward, endeavour to
fetch this rock; tack and stand in to leeward a full cable and a half, then anchor;
your depth will be 14 fathoms, on a ground of sand mixed with pieces of coral.

Two miles to the northward of Cariacou is Union Island, appearing somewhat
remarkable, with high pointed hills; it is bold-to. Directly east from the northern
point of Cariacou, distant 3 miles, is the small island of Little Martinique. Seven

BECOUYA.

miles to the northward of Little Martinique, 9 miles from Cariacou, and 6 miles N.E. ,

from Union Island, is Canaguan, on the western side of which is a small sandy bay,
where you may anchor in from 18 to 25 fathoms. A reef of rocks stretches along
the southern side of this island, extending nearly a mile from shore ; but the northern
shores are bold and clear from danger. It will, therefore, be proper to keep those on
board. The marks for anchorage in this sandy bay are, to keep the north point of
the island to bear north, the south point S.W. by S., and a house on the hill 8.E. by
E. 4 E.; you will then ride in 17 fathoms, clear ground. There are several rocky
islets between Union Island and Canaguan Island, one of which is named Mayera,
and wears a cultivated appearance; they are all bold and steep-to ; but about 6 miles
to the south-eastward of Canaguan is a small rock, called the Sail Rock, which lies
out of the way, and should be avoided. Great Mosquito is full 18 miles to the north-
eastward of Canaguan. Between these are numerous smaller islands, but without
any known danger about them. About 2 leagues eastward of Great Mosquito are
Balleso and Ballewya, the former being much the larger of the two; and to the
north-westward of these, about 5 miles distant, is Becouya.

BECOUYA, or BEQUIA, or Crab Island, contains 3,700 acres of land, is 6 miles
in length, and 18 mile wide in its broadest part; its shape is very irregular. On its
western side is Admiralty Bay, where vessels may occasionally find good anchorage ;
it lies directly to the southward of Kingston Bay, St. Vincent, from which it is
distant 2 leagues. In proceeding for Admiralty Bay, you will perceive a bluff point,
round and high; give this northern point a small berth, and luff up to the eastward,
and when you get St. Vincent shut in with this bluff point, you may anchor on
coarse sand in 17 or 18 fathoms; but it will require you to be cautious, should an
easterly wind prevail, as you will then be obliged to tack, in standing to the south-
ward, for it shoals very suddenly from 17 to 3 and 2 fathoms off both sides of these
sandy bays. Wood and fish may be obtained here, but there are no rivers.

Captain Dowers, who surveyed this bay in 1811, says,—‘ This is a secure bay, in
which a wharf, capable of receiving vessels of any class alongside of it, may be con-
structed at a small expense. Fresh water, of very good quality, may be obtained at
all times by digging wells in the sand, at the distance of 50 yards from the shore.

There is a sort of wharf, built by the Rengdove, for heaving that vessel down, where
she was coppered with great facility; and farther north are the remains of an old
wharf. The tides are uncertain, but they never flow or ebb above 3 feet.” The
town is situate at the head of the bay, having numerous houses in its vicinity. On
the northern side of the bay stands a windmill, and at the point of the bay is a
small battery of three guns. Directly opposite, and in the fairway of the entrance
of the bay is a bank of sand and fine coral, with not less than 14 feet water over it,
while round it, and in the middle of the bay, are 8, 10, and 7 fathoms; within this
bank are 7 and 8 fathoms water, fine sandy ground. In sailing in, you should steer
equi-distant from the land, for there is a coral and sandy shelf, of from 9 to 15 feet,
stretching along each shore leading to the bay ; having passed these, you will enter
the bay or basin, which is very commodious, directly opposite to the town, and has
5, 6, and 7 fathoms all over it.

ST. VINCENT (Grear Britain).

The ISLAND of ST. VINCENT appears very rugged and mountainous, the
highest part being towards the northern end; for here, near Point Tarrati, stands a
volcano, called La Souffriere, or the Sulphur Mountain, which was calculated to haye
been 3,000 feet above the level of the sea; but the eruption which took place in
April, 1812, is said to have reduced its height considerably. St. Vincent is about 13
miles long, and 9 wide, at its broadest part. It contains 84,000 acres of land; but a
moiety of this is not capable of cultivation. There are at least twenty rivers sufficient
to turn sugar-mills. The population of St. Vincent’s Island, including the Grenadines,
is estimated at 28,000. Its exports are coffee, cotton, sugar, rum, cocoa, and indigo.

KINGSTOWN BAY.—The western side of St. Vincent is bold, and has several
bays, with rivulets of fresh water running into them, but the only one of note is
toward the southern part of the island, and is named Kingstown Bay ; here stands
the principal town in the island; but the best bay for shipping is at the southern part
of the island, and called Tyrrel’s Bay. St. Vincent’s Island is visible from Barbadoes,
and vessels from the eastward commonly make for the channel between Becouya and
St. Vincent, more especially when bound towards the Spanish Main, this passage
being clear, good, and convenient. If bound from St. George’s Bay, in Grenada, to
Kingstown, you will steer a north and N.N.E. course; if from Barbadoes, about
west. In running up between St. Vincent and Becouya, you will see a small high-
peaked island, called Young’s Sugar Loaf; this lies to leeward of Tyrrel’s Bay ; you
must pass this bay and get beyond the Sugar Loaf, then round the 8.E. point, which
is long and sloping, .and forms the south-eastern boundary of Kingstown Bay.

Kingstown stands at the head of the bay, close to the water-side, the soundings
are regular, on a bottom of dark sand, apparently clear, and forming a good holding-
ground ; the water on each side of the bay is deep, and you may round the eastern
point as close as you please, for there are 20 fathoms at the distance of 200 feet from
the shore. The best anchorage is in the east side of the bay; the west side is bad
ground. The best anchorage for a frigate is with the Court House bearing north, in
20 fathoms, not 4 a mile from the beach; fresh water is easily obtained. The tides
rise about 4 feet, and there generally is a slight current setting along the bay.

TYRREL’S BAY, or CARIAQUA, is situate to the southward, and may be
known by a high bluff, which in turning between Becouya and St. Vincent, you will
not fail to observe ; ‘it lies toleeward. Leaye Young’s Sugar Loaf to your port, and
proceeding in a north-easterly direction for the bay, you will find both sides bold;

30 CARENAGE, OR PORT CASTRIES.

run on in 20, 18, and 15 fathoms, and anchor wherever most convenient. Two fresh-
water rivulets empty themselves into this bay.

There are also several good bays and places of anchorage for small vessels along
the western shores of this island, and the whole coast is bold.

PRINCE'S, or BARAWALLY BAY.—At 54 miles to the north-westward of
Kingstown Bay is Barawally, or Prince’s Bay; on its northern side are some rocky
islets, called the Bottle and Glass Rocks; within them there is a small passage for
boats. Vessels coming here from the northward may haul round these rocks as close
as they think proper; and having rounded them, they may luff up as much as they
can; they will then see the Town Barracks bearing N.E. by E. 3 E.; keep on in this
direction until Bottle and Glass Point comes to bear N.W., you will then have 20 or
22 fathoms, sandy ground, If you moor in and out you may warp in and lay your
inner anchor in 12 or 13 fathoms water, while your outer one will be in 30 or 32
fathoms; moor a cable each way, and observe that all along the Bottle and Glass
side the ground is rocky, but the bottom of the bay is good sandy ground.

ST. LUCIA (Great Brirary).

The ISLAND of ST. LUCIA is 84 leagues in length, and nearly 4 in breadth;
its population is estimated by Humboldt to be about 17,000. Its exports are
sugar, cotton, coffee, cocoa, and indigo. St. Lucia lies to the north-eastward of St.
Vincent, from which it is distant about 7 leagues; the mountains are extremely
high, rising in sharp conical points, two of which are called the Pin-heads, and
covered with immense forests; the former no animal can climb; and the latter, man
is scarce able to ascend. These hills are of volcanic origin, and of this description is
one near the S.W. end of the island, called La Souffriere, or the Sulphur Hill, the
crater of which is situate on an eminence between two high mountains, whose con-
vulsions have frequently shaken the whole island. The land is nevertheless generally
fertile and well watered; but its eastern shores do not afford any good or secure
harbour or place of anchorage. The air of the interior of this island is considered
impure and unhealthy, except in those places which are cleared of wood. On several
parts of the leeward coast are small sluggish rivulets, whose declivities are insuffi-
cient to carry their waters off; these become stagnant and create marshes, the country
adjacent to which becomes pernicious.

CARENAGE, or PORT CASTRIES.—The chief place in the Island of St.
Lucia is the Carenage, which is situate on its western side, at the distance of 8 or 9
miles from its northern point. Here the water is deep, and the ground good, with
excellent shelter from all winds. There are three places for careening vessels, formed
by nature, requiring no wharves, and only a capstan to turn the keel above water.
Here a fleet of men-of-war may ride securely, unmoored, during the strongest hurri-
cane. It will certainly be impossible to enter without warping in, but you are always
sure of a breeze to carry you out, and in less than an hour a whole fleet may gain the
offing. Both sides of the bay are steep-to and bold, so that the largest ship may
come within 4 or 5 fathoms either way, there being no danger but what is visible ;
but in the plan there is placed a rocky shoal, directly in the centre of the entrance,
with 6 or 7 fathoms round. If this shoal really exists, the passage is divided into
two channels, and great care is requisite to avoid it.

Lights at Port Castries.—At the Tapion Battery, south entrance of Castries

harbour, in latitude 14° 0’, longitude 61° 5’, two lights are exhibited, placed hori-
zontally, for the mail steamers only, visible 3 miles.

There is also a single light shown on the wharf, visible 3 miles; these lights are
shown all night.

GROS ISLET BAY. 31

There are two other bays forming excellent roadsteads on this side of the island,
both to the northward of the Carenage; the northernmost is named Gros Islet Bay,
or Road of St. Croix; the other is called Du Choc Bay, and lies between Gros Islet
Bay and the Carenage.

Vessels may anchor off the south coast in Old Fort Bay, under the S.E. bluff; to
do this, you must round Point Moulaciques, the southern point of the island, which
stretches out in a narrow peninsula a full league into the sea, and having brought its
extremity to bear 8.S.E., you may anchor in 10, 8, or 7 fathoms, the ground good and
holding. Point Moulacique is in latitude 13° 41’. At the northern part of Old
Fort Bay there is a river, but the watering is somewhat troublesome, for unless there
have been heavy falls of rain, you must send your boat full $ a mile up the river to
obtain it.

At 12 or 13 miles to the north-westward of Old Fort Bay are two remarkable high
peaks, near the sea shore, called by the French the Pitons, and by the English the
Sugar Loaves, which they somewhat resemble ; they stand very near each other, but
as you advance from the southward, they will divide, and you will plainly distinguish
both; having rounded these, you may proceed along shore in about a N. by E. direc-
tion to the Carenage, there being no danger whatever. But if bound for the Carenage,
and you have sailed round from the north end of the island, you will see, as you
advance, a high bluff, called Point d’Estrees, 2 leagues to leeward; this you should
boldly run up to, and haul close in for the harbour; stand in as far as you con-
veniently can, and warp up; there are no dangers except the shoal laid down in the
plan, which by daylight you will easily avoid. On the north point is a hill higher
than those about it; there is also a small battery on this side of the harbour. In the
Carenage you will obtain red mullet and various other sorts of fish, which are caught
by hook and line.

GROS ISLET BAY is mostly frequented by men-of-war, and is a most excellent
anchorage. Gros Islet, or Pigeon Island, is a small fortified island, separated from
St. Lucia by a shallow channel, about § a mile broad, and full of rocks.

In coming into the bay from the eastward, after rounding the north point of St.
Lucia at a convenient distance, steer to the westward, and you will soon see Pigeon
Island, but do not haul up for it until it is nearly in one with the south-western
extremity of the land in sight; keep it a little open on the port bow, and pass to the
westward of it at a sufficient distance to work your ship, in case of being taken aback
by the eddy wind. There are 6 and 7 fathoms close to the island, deepening to 15
and 18 fathoms N.N.W., nearly 2 miles. In coming in, unless the wind is well to
the northward of east, you will have to work up into the bay. Observe, in standing
to the south shore, a rock, or islet, which is always above water, called the Fourieur,
or Barrel of Beef, with only 2 fathoms between it and the shore. To the eastward of
this rock, and on both sides of the bay, you require a berth of 3 of a mile, at which
distance you will have 4 fathoms water, and then suddenly shoal into 2 and 3 fathoms.
Large ships must not go higher up the bay than to bring the two high points to the
northward of the bay in one; the points lie to the eastward of Pigeon Island, and
are easily known. Small vessels may anchor about § a mile from the village, at the
eastern part of the bay, in 4 fathoms, sandy ground.*

In the channel between St. Lucia and St. Vincent, tornadoes are frequent, and
strong currents trend to the W.N. westward, but as Port Castries and Gros Islet Bay
lie at the northern part of the island, it will be advisable always to make the north
end of the island, passing between St. Lucia and Martinique, especially when bound
to either of the above ports.

MARTINIQUE.

MARTINIQUE (France).

The ISLAND of MARTINIQUE is of an irregular form, high, and rocky,
visible full 15 leagues off, extending about 35 miles in length, and of very unequal
breadth ; its population is about 99,000; its exports are sugar, cotton, coffee, and
indigo; but though the coffee is considered to be the best the West India Islands
produce, the sugar is inferior to that of several ethors. The southern part of
Martinique is distant from the northern point of St. Lucia 6 leagues, and from the
- northern part of Barbadoes 324 leagues; the direct course from the latter being
N.W., but allowance must always be made for the lee current. The channel be-
tween St. Lucia and Martinique is clear of all danger, and the breeze within it is
steady, while the stream is scarcely perceptible.

It is, says the Derrotero de las Antillas, almost a matter of indifference what part
of Martinique you make, only in case of the winds being free from the N.E., the
northern side will be preferable. In approaching Martinique on the northern side,
and intending to anchor in the road of St, Pierre, haul in close to Point Macouba,
and run along the coast, so as to pass outside of the Islets de Seron; you may then
round Point Precheur within 3 a cable’s length, and steer for the anchorage; re-
member, the shore is so steep that you will have 4 and 5 fathoms water } a cable's
length from it, and 35 and 40 fathoms at 8 cables’ length. Vessels commonly moor
with two anchors, one to the westward, in 35 or 40 fathoms, and one to the eastward,
in 4 or 5 fathoms; but it will always be better to have a cable on shore, instead of
the anchor to the eastward, to prevent your dragging with the gusts of wind that
frequently come off the high land,

Vessels approaching Martinique from the southward should pass close to the
Diamond Rock, and round Point Solomon (d’Arlet), then take a northerly course, but
without any easting, until Point Negro comes east, then you must haul by the wind,
to enable you to take Flamingo Bay, or enter the harbour. You can anchor in any
part of the great bay. But if you are bound to St. Pierre, you should steer from
Point Solomon to Morne aux Booufs, and then haul in for the anchorage. From the
south point, or Point Salines, to the northern point, or Point Macouba, you may
approach within a mile of the western shores with safety.

The air of Martinique is hot, but not unwholesome, being refreshed by regular
breezes. The months of July, August, September, and October is the winter season,
and then the winds become irregular and squally, the sea turbulent, and sometimes
hurricanes and earthquakes will occur, and shake the whole island.

The surface of Martinique is very uneven, and consists of high mountains, with
peaked tops, conical and sharp pointed ; among these there are three higher than the
rest, and visible at a great distance, their summits being enveloped in clouds; of these
Mount Pelée is by far the highest, appearing barren, and something like the crown
ofa hat. It is situate toward the N.W. part of the island; was once a volcano, and
may be plainly seen as you advance toward the island on every side. Mount Vauclain
is near the south-eastern part of the island, and is much inferior to Mount Pelée in
height, but almost covered with plantations. There are numerous bays and rivers on
all sides of the island, fit for large and small vessels to anchor in; but as Martinique
is subject to hurricanes, most of these bays do not afford protection during their
prevalence.

SOUTH-WESTERN SIDE.—In advancing toward the south side of the island,
you will observe Point Salines, which is low, and has three rocky islands lying off it,
with shoal water full 14 mile to the southward of them. As you proceed to the
westward, you will see a space between them and the point; here are two good coves,
called the Cul de Sac de Marin and Anse de St. Luce; the former affords good
anchorage, but the entrance is too narrow to be navigated without a pilot. Anse de

PORT ROYAL BAY. 33.

St. Luce has good anchorage in from 23 to 16 fathoms, muddy ground; the town of
St. Luce bearing N.W. 3 W.., distant 4 of a mile. To the westward of Point Salines,
about 10 miles, is a ]xrge rock, called the Diamond Rock, or Devil’s Island, and by
the French the Isle d2 Barque; it is 600 feet high, and about one mile in circum-
ference, appearing like a nine-pin with its top broken off, its south, 8.W., and east
sides are inaccessible, rising almost perpendicularly from the sea, but on its western
side there is a landing-place, lined with breakers. “Three batteries were in 1804 con-
structed upon it, which command the whole bay. It lies 2 of a mile off a point
of land, and there isa small passage between them fitted for boats only. To the
north-eastward of this rock is the Great Diamond Cove.

FORT ROYAL BAY.—Vessels having made the Diamond Rock, may, after
passing it, assume a N.N.W. course towards Point Arlet for 2 or 3 leagues, the shore
being bold and free from danger ; they will then open the bay, and may readily see
Fort Royal, which lies in a valley, and has Fort St. Louis (or Edward) to the east,
the ruins of Fort Bourbon to the north, and Vittoria House to the west. This house
is built of whitestone, and has a battery with a flagstaff to the south of it, and a few
small houses with red-tiled roofs to the northward. In working in, you should keep
the lead going, and you will observe a small green island, with fortifications upon it,
on the starboard side of the entrance; it is called Ramier, or Pigeon Island; having
passed this, haul up, and bring Fort Royal to bear N.E. by N. or N.N.E., but not
more to the northward, on account of the bank which runs off above 2 a mile from
Fort St. Louis; you may then anchor in from 10 to 20 fathoms; but if you wish to
go into the Carenage, on the east side of Fort St. Louis, round the Fort at the
distance of 5 a mile, and bringing the Fort on the hill to bear N. by W., steer
directly in.

Although this harbour is among the best in the Caribbees, yet it is so impeded by
several shoals, composed of hard gravel, limestone, and coral, that no stranger should
attempt to sail among them in a large ship.

FORT ROYAL Bights.—At Fort Royal, in the S.W. part of the fortress, in
latitude 14° 36° 7’, and longitude 61° 4’ 12’, two horizontal lights are exhibited,
elevated 131 feet, and visible about 6 miles.

At Point des Negres is exhibited, on a red mast, a single light of a red colour,
visible 6 miles.

S.W.35S., 1 mile from the south end of Fort St. Louis, is a small rocky bank,
called Miton, over which are 4 or 5 fathoms; the marks for which are Point Negro,
on with the outer N.W. bluff, in sight, and the outhouses with the red roofs behind
Vittoria House just shut in. §.S.W.1W., nearly a mile distant from Miton, is
another, called Bane du Gros Island, with from 3% to 5 fathoms over if. A similar
shoal lies §.S.E., distant about 3 a mile from the latter bank. Fresh water may be .
had at River Monsieur, to the eastward of the Carenage.

There is good anchorage on the north side of the bay, with Vittoria House N. 2 W.,
and Fort Edward E.N.E., in 20 fathoms, muddy bottom. Should you wish to go
higher up the bay, do not stand farther to the S.E. than to shut in half of the red-
roofed houses behind Vittoria House, when it will be time to tack to the northward.
The Guard-house and Fort on Point Negro, seen open to the southward of’ the N.W.
bluff in sight, will carry you to the northward of all the shoals lying to the south-
westward of Vittoria House; with these marks the least water will be 6 fathoms.
You will also find good anchorage with the south point of Fort Edward N. by E.iE.,
and Point Negro N.W. 3 W., in 20 fathoms, soft muddy bottom, most excellent hold-
ing ground, and to the eastward of all the outer shoals. The tides are not regular ;
but they never rise above 17 inches.

There is a little roadstead for small ships to the southward of Ramier, or Pigeon
Island. Those who are well acquainted with this place work round the N.E. point of
the island; the anchorage lies with the western part of the island brought to bear

ST. PIERRE.

north, or N. by W., or even N.N.W., in 9 feet, clear ground. The southern shore is
steep; but you must not approach too near the eastern shore, for there a bank
stretches off, over which the sea commonly breaks with a heavy swell.

To sail for St. Pierre (which is a town of some commercial importance), you will
pass Point Negro, the north-western point of Fort Royal Harbour. This is low, but
bold-to, and has a battery upon it. Two miles to the westward is the village of Case
de Navire, where there is good anchorage from opposite the battery to abreast of the
westernmost houses, but the anchorage-ground does not reach beyond 13 cables’ length
from the shore, it then sinks down into very deep water; within the distance of 3 a
cable’s length from the beach the water is shallow, but it gradually deepens to its
outer part from 5 to 25 fathoms, the latter depth being found about a cable’s length
from the shore ; beyond this depth the ground becomes hard and gravelly. Off the
battery the ground is clean, and from thence to the westward it becomes soft and
muddy. To anchor here, it is requisite you should turn to windward, before you
stand in, until the easternmost cluster of houses comes on with the valley behind
them; steer in thus, and when the point between Case de Navire and the next
village, called Case Pilote, opens outside of the land to the N.W., then your sound-
ings of 40 fathoms or upwards will show you are just advancing upon the bank; then
endeavour to get the western house on with the middle of the valley, and having Le
Gros Point, which is on the south side of Fort Royal Harbour, shut in behind Point
Negro, you may come to anchor with a large vessel in 20 or 17 fathoms; but small
ships may stand on with the same mark until they come to the depth of 9, 8, or 7
fathoms. ‘There is a good rivulet of fresh water at this village. :

La Case Pilote is a village 24 miles to the N.W. of Navire. The roadstead here
is open, the bay semicircular, and small trading vessels frequently anchor here before
the town. It is defended by two small batteries, and the shore from hence to Morne
aux Boeufs has several others built near the water’s edge ; there are also some small
villages, and the road from Fort Royal runs along shore all the way. Morne aux
Beeufs is 16 miles from the Diamond Rock, bearing N.W. 3 N. From Case de
Navire to St. Pierre the shore is very bold.

Having passed Morne aux Booufs, off the point of which is a small islet, and upon
the point a battery, the shore takes a more northerly direction towards St. Pierre.

ST. PIERRE is in latitude 14° 44’, and taking in the sinuosities of the road
about 13 miles distant from Fort Royal; its anchorage is open and unsafe in the
hurricane months, particularly as the ships are under the necessity of bringing up at
a considerable distance from the shore. The town is built upon a narrow strip of low
land, and runs parallel to the beach of a circular bay, and the hills behind almost
overhang the houses. here are three principal streets, besides some cross ones; but
these latter are too steep to admit of carriages. The surrounding hills are furrowed
by deep ravines, through which occasional torrents descend, cleansing the streets, and
greatly alleviating the heat of the atmosphere.

The best anchorage in St. Pierre’s Road is at its southern part, where you will
perceive some steep cliffs and rocks ; bring the highest steeple church (St. Peter’s) to
bear N. 2 E., and Point Carbet south, and you will have 7 fathoms water, soft oazy
ground ; or the Fort S. by E., and the great church north, about a cable’s length from
the shore; here you will have 24 fathoms. It is customary to lay one of your anchors
in 24 or 30 fathoms, and the other in 10 or 12 fathoms ; but should your stay in this
road be long, you should lie with one anchor close to or upon the shore, to the south-
eastward, and the other tothe N.W. The French vessels never remain here after
the 15th of July; but either run for Fort Royal or Trinity Bay, where they will be
better sheltered during the hurricanes. Batteries and redoubts are upon almost every
point of land on this side of Martinique. Near Fort St. Pierre is the river, where
plenty of good fresh water may be obtained, and got on board easily, either with casks
or rafts, or filled in the boats with a long hose. To the northward is Point a la Mare,
and beyond that Point Precheur, near which is the Pearl Rock.

8ST. PIERRE, 35

NORTH-EASTERN SIDE.— Vessels advancing from the south-eastward should
be careful to give the shores of Martinique a good berth, for on the eastern side of
the island there are many banks and shallows, which they must be careful to avoid ;
and in turning to windward of Point Salines, great care must be taken to steer wide
from Cape Ferré, or they will get entangled among the shoals of Vauelin. The best
mark to avoid and keep on the outside of these will be to bring the Carvel, or La
Caravelle Rock, weli open of the land before you attempt to advance to the
northward.

The outermost of these shoals is distant from Cape Ferré nearly 4 miles, and from
Point Macauba, which is the southernmost point of the Cul de Sac de Vauelin, about
24 miles. The shoals which bar the entrance are so numerous that few vessels ever
attempt the navigation, though there are several channels for small ships to enter.
The town of Vauelin is situate at the bottom of the harbour, and near the foot of
the Mountain of Vauelin. There are also two small rivulets, which enter the harbour.
From hence, almost as far as Point Caravelle, the shore is lined with sand-banks; and
though there are within this space several well-sheltered harbours, yet they are
accessible only to the natives and those who are well acquainted with the navigation.
The Cul de Sac Sans Souci, the Cul de Sac Simon, and the Cul de Sac Fregate, are
small, and will only admit vessels of small burthen; but the Cul de Sac Frangois and
the Cul de Sac Robert are larger, and may accommodate ships of considerable draught,
particularly the latter, which has two branches of harbours, where the largest ships
may anchor; it does not, however, appear to be well frequented, owing, no doubt, to
the banks which cover the adjacent parts of the coast. In order to sail into the Cul
de Sac Robert, you may proceed to the southward or northward of the little Sandy
Island, which is the outermost of the islands at the entrance, at your pleasure; if you
intend sailing in to the southward of it, you must take care to give it a good berth,
for a bank stretches out from it a considerable way ; but if you proceed to the north-
ward you had better round the island rather sharply, and going between it and the
Middle Island, steer southerly a little, until you have well passed the Middle Island,
then the harbour will be open, and you can run in; the anchorage is in 4 fathoms,
clay ground. The town stands at the farther end of the bay, and it becomes very
shoal as you approach the landing-place. On the port side are two small creeks.
There is also another passage in, leading round the northern point between two shoals
and two islands. In the former part of this channel there are 9 fathoms, and between
the islands 4 and 5 fathoms; but these channels require a pilot.

To the northward is Cul de Sac de Galion, another extensive harbour, but blocked
up by the shoals at the entrance; it is, however, known and frequented by the French
and natives. On the northern side of this harbour, and beyond all the banks, there
is a narrow arm of the sea, called Cul de Sac de la Tartane, the entrance to which is
clear and unencumbered; here small vessels may find good shelter.

Point Carvel, or Caravelle, lies about a mile to the southward of Caravelle Rock,
and is the extremity of a kind of peninsula or isthmus, which extends towards Trinity
Bay. Carvel, or Caravelle Rock, lies in latitude 14° 48’. It is a very remarkable
object, and ships making for the north of Martinique geverally take their departure
from it. In running along shore, a N.W. by W. course will carry you to Trinity
Bay, a place of considerable safety during the hurricane months. ‘The town here
is a place of great traffic, but there are several sand-banks which much obstruct
the entrance; you will also be inconvenienced by the sudden and variable flaws of
wind which frequently sweep down from the openings of the mountains, which is
always the case when the hills intercept the regular course of the trade winds.

The northern part of Martinique is all along well cultivated ; numerous towns are
scattered along the coast, and the mountains are covered to their summits With
plantations; all except the highest (Mount Pelée), which is barren, as has been before
observed.

Having reached the northernmost point of the island, which is called Point
Macoubas, and known by a waterfall, or torrent, falling from the top of the high

36

rocky coast into the sea, you will find the land bend more to the southward. About
5 miles W.S.W. from this point is a large rock, called the Pearl Rock, to the south-
ward of which are some little islands, named the Precheurs ; small vessels frequently

DOMINICA.

run in between these islands and the main and anchor. When you get abreast of the’

islands you will perceive to the southward Point Precheur, ending in a flat hummock,
with a plantation upon it; beyond this is the town of Precheur, which you may
know by the steeple of St. Joseph’s Church. Sailing on, you will discover two other
points, nearly, and sometimes appearing quite, in a line with one another; these are
the Morne aux Booufs and the Diamond Rock, both described before. Having doubled
Point Precheur, you will see the ships at anchor in the Road of St. Pierre ; they will
first appear to you like so many white houses, with terrace-like roofs ; but these are
the awnings commonly placed to keep off the sun. Between the north end of
Martinique and St. Pierre there are several villages and batteries ; the shore is steep,
and clear of every sort of danger. Having arrived off the Road of St. Pierre, you
will be compelled to traverse up to the road, on account of the prevailing east and
E.N.E. winds.

Sr. Esprit Reer.—It is stated that this dangerous reef is situate in the track
of vessels bound to Martinique, in about the latitude of 14° 37’, and longitude
58° 59’; this is said to have only 8 feet over it, and to be shaped like a half-moon,
being about 500 fathoms long from north to south, and 100 fathoms broad. The
existence of this reef is now, however, much doubted ; several of H.M. ships having
passed oyer the spot assigned to it without finding any soundings. Mariners will,
notwithstanding, do well to keep a good look out for this danger, which, if existing,
must be of recent formation.*

Sounpines or H.M.S. “ WoLyERINE” 1866,—In latitude 14° 38’, and longitude
59° 52’, soundings in 66 fathoms, and nearly in a N.W. direction for 10 miles, 44, 50,
and 68 fathoms, all rocky bottom.

DOMINICA (Great Briratn).

The ISLAND of DOMINICA is 26 miles in length, and may be reckoned 12
miles in breadth. It contains 186,436 acres of land, and is divided into 10 districts,
or parishes; the population is about 20,000; its exports being rum, coffee, cotton,
sugar, wool, &c. The situation of this island is of considerable importance to
Great Britain. In appearance it is rugged, and very mountainous; but the valleys
are fertile, though the soil is somewhat stony, and better calculated for the
production of coffee than sugar. Many of the mountains are unextinguished
volcanoes, which still continue to discharge large quantities of sulphur; and they
abound with hot springs, some of which are said to be capable of coagulating
an egg; these springs are supposed to possess great medical virtues. There are full
thirty rivers, besides numerous rivulets; the forests abound with rosewood, and the
European bee (transported to this island) swarms in the interior in prodigious num-
bers, producing in the clefts of the trees great quantities of honey and wax. The
Island of Dominica has no harbours; but the western side contains several good
anchorages and bays, the coast being all along bold and clear of danger. The prin-
cipal towns are Roseau, or Charlotte Town, situate on the S.W. side, and composed of
about 500 houses; and Portsmouth, or Prince Rupert’s Town, considerably to the
northward of Roseau. ‘

Light.—At Fort Young, in latitude 16° 18’, longitude 61° 28’, a fixed light is
exhibited from a flagstaff, visible 9 miles.

Antigua to Demerara, under the command of Captain Lord William Paget, struck sound-
ings in 7 fathoms water, in latitude 14° 28’, longitude 58° 57’. Commanders of vessels
