PRINCE RUPERT'S. BAY. 37

PRINCE RUPERT'S BAY.—Vessels bound from Barbadoes to Dominica com-
monly steer a N.N.W. course, until they have passed Martinique, then N.W., by
which they will be carried towards the north part of Dominica, and may readily
proceed between them and the Mariegalante, hauling close up to Cape Melville, the
north; point of Dominica; having rounded that, they will perceive a circular bluff,
looking like an island; this is Prince Rupert's Head, and forms the north point of
the bay. Make for this point, and having rounded it, you will open the bay, and
may turn in and anchor in 7, 8, or 10 fathoms; when standing in, you will see a low
point, with a remarkable high hill over it, distinguished by the appelation of Rollo’s
Head, or the Barber’s Block; this is the southern point of the roadstead. The
northern point, or Prince Rupert’s Head, has two fortified hills upon it, called the
Cabrits; they are connected to the main land by a low swamp.

Prince Rupert’s Bay is 13 mile deep; at its farther end stands the town of Ports-
mouth ; to the westward of the town, on the rising ground, at the inner part of the
swamp, which joins the Cabrits to the main, are a few houses, and a small plantation,
called the Cotton Hill; over the town appear two high conical hills, and to the south-
ward of them isa high mountain, whose summit seems to -penetrate the clouds.
About 14 mile to the southward of Portsmouth is the Picarde Estate Plantation ; it
is low, and near the beach. Half-way between this estate and Rollo’s Head is Mount
Allen, a fine plantation. You will also see the Indian River, which falls into the bay
about midway between the town and Picarde Plantation, in the valley which appears
to the southward of the conical hills.

Vessels when working into Prince Rupert’s Bay may stand boldly over from side
to side, a space of nearly 3 miles, for Prince Rupert’s Head is steep-to, and may be
approached. to within a ship’s length; but off Rollo’s Head are a few rocks, close in
shore. When you are off Mount Allen, you may stand towards it so as to bring a
single tamarind tree, situate near the middle of Portsmouth, in one with the highest
land behind it, bearing east ; and you may stand toward the Picarde Plantation until
a little hill to the westward begins to open with the cultivated part of the Mount
‘Allen Estate, without the western edge of Rollo’s Hill. When standing towards the
swamp, you should tack about in, 7, 8, and 9 fathoms, according as the draught of
your vessel may require. There is a shelf which stretches round the bay, from the
inner part of the Cabrits to the western side of the Mount Allen Estate, being about
a cable’s length wide; off India River it becomes:somewhat broader, and you will at
14 cable’s length from shore find 3 fathoms water ; farther out it deepens to 5, 7, and
10 fathoms; it then suddenly sinks to 15, 20, and 30 fathoms. Outside the shoalest
part the ground is the clearest, but inside of 10 fathoms it becomes rocky. The best
anchorage will be found off the Tamarind Tree, with the foregoing mark, and the
coast seen over the low land within the Cabrits, in one with the western part of the
Cotton Hill, or on with the drain at the west end of it; but should you be to the
southward of the tree, run in until the highest ground on the western side of the
cultivated part of Mount Allen Plantation comes open without the western side of
Rollo’s Hill. With either of these marks, you may anchor in 7, 8, or 9 fathoms,
muddy ground. ‘This bay is much resorted to for its safety, convenience, magnitude,
and depth of water, it having also three rivulets of fresh water running into it, and.
affording plenty of wood. Fresh water may be had at any of the rivers, but the
smaller ones are commonly the best; and plenty of fish may be caught in the bay.

ROSEAU is on the S.W. part of the island, and is the chief town. Vessels taking
their departure from the Pearl Rock, near Martinique, towards Scot’s Head, the
southern point of Dominica, should steer N. by W., making allowance for the lee
current, the distance between them being 23 miles. Scot's Head first wears the
appearance of an island, being a high rock, with aflagstaff upon it. About a cable’s
length W. by N. from the flagstaff is a rock, on which the sea sometimes breaks,
Having rounded the point there is a small bay or anchorage, called Soufiriere Bay,

where vessels may lie in from 6 to 15 fathoms. Four miles and a half to the north-
ward of Scot’s Head is the town of Roseau, which will be readily seen as you sail

38
along shore. Merchant-vessels commonly anchor off the southern part of the town,

within 4 a cable’s length of the beach ; but the ground is not good, being very steep
and rocky. To do this, it is only requisite that you should run in under easy sail,

GOUDALOUPE,

and when in proper soundings, let go your anchor. This road is better than St.”

Pierre, in Martinique, the soundings being more regular, and you may anchor in from
6 to 40 fathoms, but the latter depth is rocky ground. One mark for the anchorage
is to bring the fort to bear N.E. Heavy ships and men-of-war generally proceed
farther north to Woodbridge Bay, and, advancing to a sufficient distance from shore
and a proper depth of water, anchor.

From Roseau to Prince Rupert’s Bay the course is nearly N.N.W. $ W., the
distance being 17 miles. The whole coast is bold, but there are several anchorages
as you pass along; these anchorages are all open to westerly gales, but such only
happen during the winter.

This island is considered to be the highest of all the Antillas; its shores are all
clean, and you may approach within a mile of them. The west coast often experiences
calms, which sometimes extend full 6 miles out to seaward, on which account little
sail should be carried, and great caution observed, because of the heavy gusts that
abruptly proceed from the valleys; the best way to avoid these will be for those
bound to Rupert’s Bay to make for the northern part of the island, and for those
bound to Roseau, to make the southern part. The channel between Dominica and
Martinique offers no danger, but the weather is generally boisterous and subject to
heavy squalls, and the current runs strong to the westward.

GUADALOUPE, THE SAINTES, MARIEGALANTE,
DESIRADE, on DESEADA, &c. (FRANCE).

The ISLAND of GUADALOUPE is the largest and most important of all the
French Caribbee Islands, though the seat of government is at Martinique. It is very
irregular in form, and may properly be considered as two islands, since it is com-
pletely divided by a small branch of the sea, called Riviere Salée, or Salt River.
This strait is from 15 to 50 fathoms wide, and is capable of being navigated in some
parts by a vessel of 500 tons, but in others not even of 50 tons ; its breadth is con-
fined by mangoe trees, but the stream is clear and smooth as a mirror, and its length
is about 2 leagues. The north-eastern island is named the Grand Terre, being about
8 leagues in length and 7 leagues in breadth. This part of Guadaloupe is very
deficient in fresh water, not having a single river, and but few springs.

The western division of the island, or Guadaloupe proper, is 8 leagues long, and 5
leagues broad. A chain of mountains, extending north and south, occupy the centre
of this island; they are of amazing height, and apparently of volcanic origin. To-
wards the southern part of this ridge is La Souffriere, which still emits a thin black
smoke, mixed with frequent sparks of fire, often very visible at night. This moun-
tain was in a state of eruption in 1815; its summit forms a level plain, covered with
calcined stones; the earth being perforated in various holes and openings through
which the smoke continually issues. From the sides of this and the other mountains
numerous rivulets descend, so that this division of the island is said not to have less
than 50 rivers, contributing greatly to cool and fertilize this otherwise burning island.
This western portion of Guadaloupe, thus subdivided by the mountains, is named
Cape Terre and Basse Terre, the former being to the eastward, the latter to the west-
ward. The population of these islands, with their dependencies, the Saintes, Marie-
galante, Desirade (or Deseada), &c., is computed to be 120,000 The exports are
principally sugar (which is not- considered to be equal to that produced at Mar-

GRAND TERRE. 39

tinique), coffee (superior to that of St. Domingo), cotton, cocoa, indigo, ginger,
campeachy wood, liqueurs, &c.

GRAND TERRE has several towns, before which vessels commonly ride ; the
principal of these is called St. Louis, or Port-a-Pitre, and carries on a very con-
siderable commerce. The entrance to this port is between the little Island Cochon
and the main; the passage is well fortified on each side, there being a battery on the
island, and several on the starboard shore; there is also Fort Louis, which completely
commands the channel. On this coast are two roadsteads ; the easternmost is called
St. Francois, the other St. Anne’s, both having towns or villages adjacent; there is
also another, named Le Gozier, situate between St. Anne’s and Fort Louis, and nearly
north of an islet of the same name, from which to the westward, for about two miles
on the coast, are 6 and 8 fathoms water; here you may anchor, in the Passe de la
Port Pitre.

The western island, or Guadaloupe proper, has several towns along its shores; but
the principal one lies on the south-western side, in latitude 16° 0’ north, and is called
Basse Terre ; here a great trade is carried on in liquor, coffee, cotton, sugar, and
cocoa, &c. Vessels anchor opposite the town, to the eastward of which is Fort
Matilda, and to the westward a redoubt, both of which are well calculated for the
defence of the roadstead. Being at anchor here, you will have the western part of
the Saintes, in one with the western part of Dominica, bearing 8.E. by 8., Montserrat,
N.W., a little northerly, and the western part of Basse Terre Bay, N.W. by N.,
distant 1 mile. The Flore frigate, being moored N.N.E. and §.S8.W., had one anchor
in 7 fathoms, sandy ground, and the other in 37 fathems; Matilda Fort bearing
S.E. by E., the church N.E., the west end of the town N. by W., Point Irois N.N.W.,
and the southern point of Dominica 8.E. by 8S. The anchorage is not commodious
nor well sheltered, there being a constant ground-swell; and the bottom at the edge
is steep, that at 2 cables’ length from the shore you will find 80 and 100 fathoms; the
ground also is not good ; and to anchor, you must keep close to the shore, letting go
one anchor in 20 or 30 fathoms, on clay, and hang to it, without letting go another,
that you may be able and ready to make sail the moment south-easterly winds
come on.

From’ the anchorage of Basse Terre you may sail along the west shore as close as
you please, so far to the northward as the Hill of Le Gros Morne, which is the N.W.
extremity of this part of the island.

When bound to Basse Terre, you should direct your course so as to approach Capes
Terre, about Point St. Sauveur, then follow the coast, keeping it about a mile distant,
and pass 3 a cable’s length outside of Old Fort Point, which is the southernmost land
of Guadaloupe, and having rounded it, luff up immediately, keeping the coast at
the same distance from you, until you get opposite to the town, where you should
anchor.

In sailing either to the northward or southward, to leeward of Guadaloupe, you
ought to keep about 2 miles from the shore, for by so doing, you may get the advan-
tage of a land-breeze, which will nearly enable you to pass it before day; but by
getting farther off, you will run the hazard of being becalmed, and therefore those
who find themselves unable to come within the distance of 2 miles should run at least
7 or 8 leagues from it, by which only they will avoid the calms.

Vessels sailing from Prince Rupert’s Bay, in Dominica, for Basse Terre Road,
should steer N.N.W. 34 W., making allowance for the current; the distance being 29
miles. .

To the north-westward of Basse Terre, distant about 8 miles, is the town of Bouil-
lantes, before which ships frequently anchor, and under the shelter of the Island
Goyave to the northward, between which and Point Mallendure there is a passage ;
this point is defended by a battery. ‘Three leagues farther is Les Hayes, having an
inlet, or cove, containing a good anchorage, protected to the northward by Le Gros
Morne (a remarkable headland), by which this part of the coast may be known ; but

40 THE SAINTES.

what particularly distinguishes this part, is the Englishman’s Head, or Tete-a-
Anglais, a high grey rock, lying 1; mile from Point St. Pierre.

About 3 or 4 miles N.N.E. from Le Gros Morne is the small island Kahouane, .
within a mile of the shore; between this island and Le Gros Morne is an extensive
anchorage, running out a considerable distance from the land; but between the
island and Englishman’s Head, and between the latter and the shore, there are only
12 feet water, the sea breaking in strong winds all across the passage.

There is a good channel to the northward of Englishman’s Head, leading to the
ports on the northern side of Guadaloupe; but there are many islets, joined by reefs,
wwhich environ this coast, through or between which the barques of the natives sail ;
the navigation of these passages we are but little acquainted with.

Vessels bound from Basse Terre towards Antigua should weigh at night, keeping
only at such a distanee from the shore as to obtain the land-wind, which will assist
in getting as far as the northern part of Guadaloupe by the morning, by which means
you will have the benefit of the sea-wind to carry you across ; otherwise you may be
detained by the baffling winds which frequently issue from under the high lands.

Every ship bound to Guadaloupe ought to make for its southern part, on account
of the situation of its principal ports; if bound to Point-a-Pitre, they may approach
within 2 miles of the southern part of Grand Terre, and continue along at that
distance to the Point and Bay of Fergeaut, on which stands the town and fort of St.
Louis, where you should get a pilot for Point-a-Pitre.

The SAIN'TES are the cluster of Islands, so called from being first discovered on
All Saints’ Day; they are bold-to, and form an admirable road for shipping. The
two largest islands are called Terre d’en Haut and Terre d’en Bas, or the Upper and
Lower Land. The first, or easternmost, is about 4 miles in circumference, and con-
tains a town or village, which is situate on its western side, to the northward of
which is Fort Charlotte; between this village and a small island to the N.W., called
Fort George Island, or Cabrit, is the anchorage, which is a space about 3 a mile broad,
and has from 16 to 6 fathoms within it. On Terre d’en Bas, or the Lower Land,
stands a wooden church, and near to it are two creeks, convenient for anchorage and
landing. Here, let the wind blow from whatever quarter, there is a constant fresh
breeze. The inhabitants are poor, and chiefly subsist upon fish and vegetables. On
the 8.W. side of Terre d’en Haut is a hill, called Mont de Filles, the top of which is
813 feet above the level of the sea;.and to the N.W. of this hill is a remarkable pro-
montory called the Sugar Loaf, which is a good object for guiding ships coming from
the northward ; for when you bring it to bear S$.W. by S., it will lead you between
the Whale, or Black Rock, and a rocky bank, lying more to the westward, at the
entrance of the channel, within which vessels may haul round to the road, or, for the
game purpose, keep it open to the eastward of the south point of Fort George Island.
In sailing from the road to the westward, you must keep towards the south shore,
in order to avoid a shoal, which lies at the distance of a cable’s length from the south
point of Fort George Island. To the southward of Terre d’en Haut are several
rocky islets; but in the channel, between Terre d’en Haut and Terre d’en Bas, there
is no danger but what is visible.

The outer road is situate between the town on Terre d’en Haut:on one side, and
Fort George Island on the other. The Inner road is to the southward of Fort George
Island, and between it and the western part of Terre d’en Haut.

To enter the Outer Road, you may haul in close for the eastern end of George
Island, standing directly in for the harbour, for the-passage is quite clear; in this
channel, when the sea does not break over the sunken rocks, you should endeavour
to keep the trees, which are to the westward of the Sugar Loaf, open of the 8.K. end
of Fort George Island, until you get abreast of the island, then you may haul up for
the Inner Road. But if bound for the anchorage in the Inner Road, keep the great
bluff, or Sugar Loaf Hill, of Terre d’en Haut, shut in with the houses in the hollow,
until you bring Pic Island shut in with the northern end of Terre den Bas, when

MARIEGALANTE. 4]

you may bear up and anchor, or run through to the westward without danger. To
go through between the Whale and sunk rocks, you should haul up for the northern
end of Terre d’en Haat, 1nd give the Whale Rock a berth of a good ship’s length,
leaving it on your port side, or attend to the above marks; this will lead you to the
outer anchorage, opposite to the town. The passage between the Whale Rock and
Terre d’en Haut should not be attempted.

Tt has been ascertained that the S.W. point of the westernmost Sainte, or Terre
d’en Bas, lies S. 27° 30’ E. from the southern point of Guadaloupe, and in latitude
15° 51’, and longitude 61° 38’, the variation being about 1° east. The whole of
these islands are subject to Guadaloupe, and contain a population of about 1300;
their exports are cotton and coffee.

MARIEGALANTE is 9 miles long and § miles broad, and contains a popula-
tion of about 22,000; its produce consists of a superior quality of coffee, cotton,
alittle sugar, rum, and stock; it abounds in wood, particularly the wild cinna-
mon tree. This island is about the height of Barbadoes, and rises gradually toward
the northern part, but does not there acquire any great elevation; its southern
and eastern sides are encumbered with many rocks, some of which extend 2
and 8 miles into the sea; these are dangerous, and are the resort of innumerable
flights of tropical and other birds; the western side of the island is level and
clean, affording good anchorage in several places. Here are several caves, abounding
with crabs, and on shore are many ponds and small rivulets of fresh water; but these
sometimes become dry. Its principal town (Grand Bourg, or Basse Terre) stands near
the south-western point, where a fortress is built; from the south point to this town,
a shoal, steep-to, and always covered, trends away to the westward nearly 2 miles,
and then runs to the N. and N.E. until it ends at Point Sable. To the northward of
Point Sable is St. Louis Bay, where there is good anchorage for a fleet. The north
point of the bay, called Point May, is bluff, but not very high, to the eastward of
which is Frigate Island. When bound into St. Louis Bay from the north-eastward,
give Frigate Island a good berth, on account of the shoal water lying to the west-
ward of it; keep the island shut in with the N.E. land of Mariegalante until you
open the whole of St. Louis Bay; you may then haul up for an anchorage about
half way between Point Sable or Folence and the village which lies in the bight of
the bay.

If you are bound from this place to Grand Bourg, give Point Sable or Folence a
berth by your lead, keeping Point May open to the northward of Point Sable, and
when you deepen your water, haul up by your lead, which must be kept constantly
going on the west coast of the island. You have then to work up to Grand Bourg,
taking care not to stand to the northward of the town, when standing in shore on
the starboard tack with the usual easterly trade wind.

DESEADA, or Desirade (which means the desired island), was so named b
Columbus; it is a long, narrow, rocky island, destitute of both wood and water. It
lies 14 league from Point Chateaux, the eastern point of Grand Terre, and runs in an
E.N.E. and W.S.W. direction, being 63 miles long, and 2 miles broad; it is dependent
upon Guadaloupe. The soil is mostly sandy, and produces coffee and cotton in small
quantities. In approaching this island from the northward, you will perceive several
white patches, broken with reddish streaks; but when you are to the south-eastward,
it will at a distance appear like a galley, its eastern end forming the prow, and its
western point the tilt; at its northern end are several rocks unde: water. There is
anchorage off its S.W. part, at the distance of 14 mile from some houses which stand
on.the shore; the ground is in some parts rocky, but you must look out for a clear
spot, and anchor in 5, 7, or 9 fathoms, by bringing Petite Terre to bear south, some-
what westerly, and Point Chateaux W.S.W., which point may be1ecognized by the
hummock upon it. The water deepens farther out, and at a mile distant from the
shore there are 42 and 45 fathoms, and a little beyond that 103 fathoms.

[W. Inpizs. Parr I.] G

42 PETITE TERRE.

PETITE TERRE lies nearly S.E. 4S. from Point Chateaux, distant 5 miles;
it is a little sandy island, and appears cut into two parts by a small channel. There
is a good passage between Point Chateaux and Petite Terre ; but that between Petite
Terre and Mariegalante is most commonly used, and is considerably deeper and wider.
Tt is said good anchorage may be found, if necessary, on the western side of Petite
Terre, with 6, 7, and 10 fathoms water, distant 2 miles from the shore.

Terre de Bas Light.—A fixed light on the islet called Terre de Bas, Guadaloupe,
in latitude 16° 10’ 29", at 604 feet from its eastern extreme. The light is 75 feet
above the ground, and 108 feet above the high-water level of the sea; it is visible
from all points of the compass, and may be seen at the distance of 5 leagues.

The light bears from the extremity of Point de Chateaux 8.E. ? S.; from Morna
a Fregate de la Desiderata, S. } W.; and from the eastern point, called Double de la
Desiderata, S.W. by S. ‘The rock called the Baleine du Sud, off the Petite Terre,
bears S. by W. 2 W., 2,920 feet from the light. Ships coming from the eastward
will find from 13 to 20 fathoms water at the distance of 2 miles north or south of the
light, and should not approach it within those limits.

The channel between Point Chateaux and Deseada is good, and has from 20 to 23
fathoms water in it; while that between Point Chateaux and Petite Terre is not quite
so deep, but equally free from danger.

There is said to be a shoal, of 7 fathoms, at about 7 miles distant from Point May,
the north-western point of Mariegalante; and also a rock, under water, and dangerous,
somewhere about 1} mile to northward of the Saintes, the particulars of which are at
present not well ascertained.* ;

‘ANTIGUA (Great BriTAtn).

The ISLAND of ANTIGUA is of an irregular form, about 13 miles in length,
and 10 in breadth; its circumference is computed to be 50 miles ; it contains 59,838
acres of land, capable of cultivation ; and a population of 36,412. The-exports are
coffee, rum, sugar, cotton, wool, tobacco, &c.

* Martin’s Rue, eastward of Guadaloupe.—A letter received at Lloyd’s, from their
agent at Antigua, dated June 7th, 1842, contains the following :—“ Captain Newbold, of
the brig Transit, on her passage from Halifax to St. Vincent, in February last, discovered
a shoal to windward of this island, in latitude 16° 42’ north, longitude 59° 6’ west. He
examined it as carefully as circumstances would permit, and describes it to be about 200
feet long, and 80 feet wide, with 8 fathoms water in the centre, and much shallower on .
the edges.” “

“This shoal was seen in July, 1816, by Captain Martin, of the ship John Manning. The
shoal seemed to consist of yellow sand with seaweed upon it, and to be about 2 a mile in
length from east to west, and 4 of a mile in breadth, from north to south ; position, about
latitude 16° 42’ N., longitude 58° 45’ W.

And also seen again by the ship Cecilia, of Glasgow, 19th of July, 1823, by which the
position assigned was 16° 44’ N., longitude 58° 50’ W. ‘To the commander of this ship it
appeared to be about 13 or 2 miles long, and only about 30 feet wide ; the western part,
shaped like the bulb of a thermometer, seemed dangerous.

But by taking the longitudes 58° 45’, 58° 50’, and 57° 6’, given as estimated by the

three mercantile commanders, we gain a mean of about 58° 54’ West.”— Nautical Maga-
zine, Vol. II. p. 575.

THE ISLAND OF ANTIQUA. . 43

This island is flat, with a few brackish springs, and no navigable rivers; the inha-
bitants are wholly dependent upon the rain for water, which they preserve in cisterns ;
nevertheless it has the advantage of several fine harbours, capable of affording accom-
modation and shelter for fleets of the largest ships. Of these the principal ones are
English Harbour, Falmouth Harbour, and Willoughby Bay, on the southern side of
the island; Nnosuch Harbour on its east side; Parham Bay to the northward; and
Five Islands’ Harbour, with that of St. John’s, on the western side; the Town of
St. John being the capital of the island.

GENERAL DIRECTIONS.—On approaching Willoughby Bay, on the S.E. coast,
great caution will be requisite, in order to avoid its numerous rocky shoals, and to
enter it a pilot becomes indispensably necessary. From Willoughby Bay the shores
to the westward continue clear, and you will have no difficulty in discovering English
Harbour, an excellent port, having a dockyard and careening place for vessels of
every, size, The channel of this harbour is about a cable’s length wide, having 4
fathoms mid-channel, and 3 fathoms at + of a cable’s length from the points. Be-
yond English Harbour is Falmouth Harbour, from whence the coast becomes foul,
sending out many very dangerous rocky reefs, and thus it continues so far as Carlisle

Bay.

From Carlisle Bay to Johnson’s Point, which is the south-western part of the island,
the shore runs westerly, having a rocky shoal, 25 miles long, the southernmost edge
being distant 13 mile from the coast; between this and the land there is a channel
fit for any vessel, but this passage should never be attempted without a pilot. From
Johnson’s Point the shore continues northerly to the Five Islands, which lie on the
south side of a harbour of the same name. Between these points is a rocky shoal,
the eastern edge of which lies about 13 mile from the land; the depths on this shoal
are very unequal, and therefore it is exceedingly dangerous. To the northward of
this shoal is formed a large bay, called Five Islands’ Harbour, the northern point of
which is named Pelican Point. About 2 miles N.N.E. from this is a small island,
called the Ship’s Stern, which is on the southern point of St. John’s Harbour; between
these two points lie the Hurst Shoals, extending out above a mile from the land, the
western edge of which is nearly south of Sandy Island ; this island lies nearly 2 miles
W. by N. of the Ship’s Stern. There is a rocky reef which runs out to the south-
westward of Sandy Island nearly a mile.

About 21 miles N.E. by N. from the Ship’s Stern are the Sisters, two little islets,
lying N.W. by W. 4 W. from Corbizon’s Point, distant 3 a mile; and on Corbizon’s
Point is a fort. Between the Two Sisters and Sandy Island is the Warrington rocky
shoal, which has only 5 feet water over it.

Off the northern shores of Antigua are scattered numerous rocky patches, both
above and under water, having passages between them with deep water ; they extend
from the Diamond, a dangerous shoal, the western extremity of which lies N.N.W.
2 W., distant 24 miles from the Great Sister, to abreast of Parham Bay. Over the
Diamond are {, 2, and 3 feet water; half a mile to the eastward of the Diamond are
several patches, having from 4 to 10 feet, and perhaps less, water over them; between
these and the Diamond is a passage, which small vessels sometimes venture to sail
through, the leading mark being the Great Sister in one with Fort James, at the
entrance to St. John’s Harbour; or Hutchinson’s old mill in one with the Great Sister
§. 1. leads also through the Diamond Channel; least water 45 fathoms. ‘Three-
quarters of a mile to the southward of the Diamond is Bannister Shoal, of 2%
fathoms. To go clear to the southward of this shoal, you must bring Boon’s Mill in
one with the north part of Hodge’s Bluff. There are other passages through these
rocks, such as Boon’s, Hodge’s, and the Horse Shoe Channels, with which the natives
are acquainted, but which no stranger should attempt. ‘To describe them will there-
fore be of no use to the mariner. The bottom on and about all these ledges is coral,

and totally unfit for anchorage.

44 PARHAM HARBOUR.

We shall now proceed to give directions for entering the various harbours in
Antigua :—

NONSUCH HARBOUR is at the eastern side of Antigua, and has Green Island
at its entrance; this divides it into two channels, but this place is so encumbered
with shoals, that few ships, and those only of the natives, frequent it. The best -
channel is to the southward of Green Island, where the water is deep, and no danger
but what is visible.

PARHAM HARBOUR is to the north-westward of Nonsuch Harbour ; it is
extensive, but shallow, and abounds with numerous dangers; only small vessels
therefore frequent it, and these run in to the southern part of the bay, where the
town of Parham stands; here they ride safely in 2 or 3 fathoms water, and are pro-
tected by Fort Byam on the west, and Old Fort on the eastern side. There are
several entrances to this bay; that between Guana Island and Crump’s Island, and
through the narrows, is intricate and dangerous, being hardly practicable by those
not well acquainted with it. The Bird Channel, or that between the Birds and Long
Islands Reefs, is still more difficult; but that between Fort Byam and Long Island
may, in case of necessity, be navigated. In advancing from the north-westward, be
careful not to get entangled among the numerous rocks and shoals which line the
northern shores of Antigua. You will see a small island, called the Prickly Pear,
lying on the western side; give both that and Long Island a good berth. Fort
Byam flagstaff, in one with Pointed-hill S. by E. 3 E., leads into Parham Sound ;
when within ¢ of a mile of Fort Byam you may anchor in 4 to 45 fathoms, the fort
bearing S. by E. A stranger proceeding to Parham should always take a pilot.

WILLOUGHBY BAY lies on the eastern part of the south coast of the island ;
its entrance is very wide, but much encumbered with shoals ; it is therefore not much
resorted to by European vessels, and should never be entered by a stranger without
a pilot. There are two channels leading into the bay, it being divided by a sand-
bank, called the Middle Spit ; this bank has only 9 feet water over it. In the eastern
passage are 7 fathoms, and in the western one about 35 fathoms; the course in is
N.W. 4 W. There are two forts to protect the anchorage—one on the port shore,
called Fort Isaac, and one on the starboard side, near Bridgetown, called Fort
William. The water gradually lessens as you advance up the bay, and you may
anchor in 6, 5, 4, or 8 fathoms or less water. It is advisable to keep to the port side
_ of the bay.

ENGLISH HARBOUR.—This is a fine, safe, and most commodious harbour, well
sheltered, and capable of receiving the largest ships of war; it has a good dockyard,
supplied with every necessary for heaving down and repairing. This port, being
entirely allotted for the Queen’s service by the legislature of the island, no merchant-
yessels are allowed to discharge or take in cargo here. Vessels bound to this harbour
should, in leaving Englishman’s Head, in Guadaloupe, steer nearly north, or a little
inclined to the eastward, allowing for the current. The distance is about 37 miles.
Vessels may anchor outside the harbour, with Fort Barclay, on the north-west side of
the entrance, bearing N.N.E., and the extreme south point E. § §.,in 13 fathoms; or
they may warp in. Endeavour to lie N.N.E., or the fluttering winds which come
from the high land will much incommode you. In entering the harbour, you should
give the Charlotte Reef a berth on the starboard hand, off which a buoy is placed.
The leading mark in is Freeman’s Point in one with the western angle of Governor’s
Garden Wall, N. by E. 3 E.; this clears Charlotte Reef, in 33 fathoms; steering in
mid-channel until you reach Freeman’s Bay. In Freeman’s Bay, which is the south-
ernmost part of English Harbour, you will have good anchorage as far up as the
storehouses in 3, 4, 5, and 6 fathoms; there are four moorings in this bay, where the
larger ships ride just within the harbour’s mouth, the best harbour being to the west-
ward, and the moorings on the shore to the eastward; smaller vessels commonly lie
with one anchor to the E.S.E., and the other astern made fast on shore. The water
in the harbour is commonly smooth, but it is considered advisable to let a pilot con-
duct you in, for the entrance is narrow and somewhat shoal. Neither wood nor

FIVE ISLANDS’ HARBOUR. 45 -

water can be obtained here; for the latter you must resort to Falmouth, and even
there it is not very good.

Lights.—When the mail steamers are expected, three fixed lights, triangularly
placed, are exhibited from the flagstaff at Fort Barclay. The lights are 16 feet
apart ; the upper one, which is red, is 62 feet above the level of the sea, and they
may be seen at the distance of 8 miles.

FALMOUTH HARBOUR.—The entrance to this harbour lies about 1$ mile to
the westward of English Harbour, but is much larger, and its entrance wider.

To sail into this place, you must go close to the western, or Proctor’s Point, for on
the starboard side a ledge of rocks runs off, terminating full 3 over the passage; these
are called the Bishops. There is no entrance between these rocks and the starboard
point; but the channel in is to the westward of them, and when you have passed
them, there is good anchorage in from 3 to 43 fathoms water, On the western side
of the harbour stands a fort, or battery, on an islet ; behind which there is a spring
of indifferent water. The leading mark into the outer harbour to clear the Bishops
is the east angle of Blake Fort in one with the house on the slope of Monk Hill,
N. by W. The inner harbour lies to the eastward, and sailing-vessels must warp in.

CARLISLE BAY is a small harbour, lying 33 miles to the westward of Falmouth,
at the entrance of which a vessel may occasionally ride in 2, 3, or 4 fathoms water ;
there is a fort on the port side, and an eminence called Winter Hill on the starboard.
The town of Carlisle and St. Mary’s Church is a little way up the bay.

FIVE ISLANDS’ HARBOUR is so denominated from that number of islands
which lie off the southern point; these are connected with the point by a sandy reef.
The entrance to the harbour is = of a mile wide, and the water gradually decreases in
depth as you advance within it. A small island, called the Maiden, lies about the
middle of the bay, and beyond that to the north-eastward, a sort of creek runs up
and almost joins St. John’s Harbour. The northern point of Five Islands’ Harbour
is named Pelican Point, and has several rocks about it. Nearly W. by 8. § S., a mile
from Old Fort Point, is the Pelican Shoal, of 2% fathoms; and one mile to the east-
ward of this is Cook’s Shoal, of 9 feet. The mark to clear both these shoals on the
north side is the south extreme of Maiden Island in one with Seaforth Bluff, bearing
east; when 3 of a mile from Maiden Island you may anchor in 3 fathoms. Directly
to the westward of the Hawk’s Bill, which is a small islet near the coast, about 1
mile to the northward of Pelican Point, are several shoal patches, some not having
more than 8 feet over them. ‘T'o avoid these shoals to the southward, bring Fry’s
Mill of the Five Islands ; and by bringing Mackinnon Mill on with the Ship’s Stern,
or a remarkable tree, shaped like a camel, open of Ship’s Stern, you will clear them
to the northward.

ST, JOHN’S ROAD and HARBOUR are situate to the north-eastward of
Five Islands’ Harbour, distant about 3 miles. In the harbour there is sufficient water
for merchant vessels, and good security in all weather. The town of St. John’s is
situate at the bottom of the harbour, being the capital of the island, and the centre
of its commerce.

The roadstead lies about 3 miles east, a little northerly, from Sandy Island, in
latitude 17° 8’, or thereabout ; it lies between the Ship’s Stern to the southward, and
Corbizon’s Fort to the northward, the distance being 23 miles. At about a mile
north from the former is a dangerous ledge of rocks, called the Warrington, with
not more than 5 feet water over it, with breakers in rough weather. The mark to
clear the Warrington on the south side is Fort James in one with Drew Hill
S.E, by E., and to clear it on the north side keep Scott Hill, north of the Kirk
S.E. 2 E.

Just within the Warrington is a smail middle ground of 34 fathoms water; between
it and the Warrington are 43 fathoms. To go clear on the east side of the Warrington,
shut Hawk’s Bill in by the Ship’s Stern; and to clear it on the west side, shut in

THE ISLAND OF ANTIGUA.

Hawk's Bill with the land to the southward. At the entrance to the harbour there
is a bar, which stretches from one side to the other; in the southern or deepest part
are 16 feet, and on the northern side are 12 feet. The depths within the harbour are
from 13 to 33 fathoms, muddy ground.

Being bound for this harbour, vessels should always endeavour to make the southern
part of the island, the northern side being encumbered with dangerous rocks and
shoals, extending from the shore 2 or 3 miles. Run along the southern coast W. by N.,
at a distance of between 2 or 8 miles from the southernmost points, and you will clear
all dangers, observing particularly the reefs which lie about 2 miles from the shore in
the §.W. quarter of the island ;* continue thus until you have brought the western-
most of the Five Islands to bear north, and Johnson’s Point N.f&.; you may then haul
up N.N.W. westerly, and continue steering so until the Five Islands bear east, about
2 miles, by which course you will avoid the rocky shoals lying between Johnson’s
Point and the Five Islands; you may then steer for Sandy Island, keeping it on the
starboard bow till you are past the shoal lying off Hawk’s Bill. Having weathered
Sandy Island, should the wind not allow your approach to the Ship’s Stern Point,
you may then continue on the same tack, until Fort Hamilton, which is the middle
one of three standing on the coast to the north of the town, bears east; then go about,
and stand towards the shore of the Ship’s Stern, which you may approach within a
cable’s length, and thus gain the roadstead in a depth of 6 to 10 fathoms, with Ship’s
Stern bearing S.W. by W.; Fort James, on the north point of the entrance to the
harbour, E.S.E.; and the Warrington Shoal.N. by W.; or with the flagstaff of Fort
James on with the north side of Rat Island, in the harbour, in 6 or 7 fathoms, good
holding ground.

Should you not be able to weather Sandy Island on the 8.E. side, you must go to
leeward of it, taking care to avoid the ledge of rocks that runs out nearly 3 a mile to
the south-westward, and continue to the northward until the north point of Sandy
Island bears east, southerly ; you may then haul by the wind until you can weather
jt on the other tack.

But should you, to approach St. John’s Harbour, be obliged to take the north side
of the island, give the coast a berth of about 4 miles, steering at that distance due
west, until Sandy Island bears south, when you may run for it, until you are due
west of the northernmost coast of Antigua, then steer for Ship’s Stern Point until
rather to the southward of Fort Hamilton, then haul by the wind for the anchorage
in St. John’s: Road.

In proceeding to the northward from St. John’s Road, be careful to give a good
berth to the Diamond, and other rocky shoals which extend westerly to the meridian
of the Warrington, and north, nearly 5 miles from the Ship’s Stern. To do this you
should steer from the anchorage about N.W. by W., but not to the northward of that
course, until Sandy Island bears south, or the Ship’s Stern 8.S.E. The leading mark
to clear the Diamond Shoal is Mount Thomas and Fort Barrington in one, 8. 2 E.;
this mark also clears the Warrington. ae

The channel between Antigua and Guadaloupe is good, and offers no danger; but
that between Antigua and Barbuda is at times very dangerous; during the months

THE ISLAND OF ANTIGUA, 47

from May to November no vessel should attempt it, because of the alternate calms
and squalls they are subject to; and as the bottom is so rocky, and the depth of
water so unequal, you cannot safely let go your anchor during the calms, but may be
drifted on the rocks by the irregular currents which often prevail.

The following Description and Directions for the Island of Antigua are by
Captain E. Barnett, R.N., late of H.M.S. Thunder :—*

“ ANTIGUA, compared with other of the Antilles, is of moderate elevation, its
highest point being 1,389 feet above the level of the sea, and which is seldom
obscured. It is 13{ miles long from east to west, and 9% miles broad from north to
south, and is nearly square, but deeply indented on all sides, particularly on its north
and east, where there are many creeks and bays, navigated by droghers ; its north-
east and east ends are low, its south-west and west sides of irregular height; several
of the hills, however, are very remarkable, and highly valuable to safe navigation,
for the whole island is fringed with shoals, with the exception of the small space on
the south side, between the west side of Willoughby Bay and Old Road.

Commencing our description from the S.E. end of the island, the east end is
formed by Green Island, which terminates at Man-of-War Point, a bold rocky head-
land, and 170 feet in height; it is steep and bold-to, and may be rounded within a
mile.

Nearly } a mile to the S.W. of the Point is Ten Pound Bay, unnavigable on
account of the heavy swell always at the entrance of the cut.

Ricket’s Harbour, at the §.W. end of the island, affords shelter to droghers.
York IsLAND (a small round rocky islet) is 1,2, of a mile to the S.W. of Man-of-

0

War's Point, and which may be said to form the outer part of the eastern entrance to
Nonsuch Harbour. York Island is nearly connected by dry reefs to the shore of
Antigua, which takes a S.W. direction for the distance of 15 mile, where it termi-
nates in two bold, precipitous, rocky headlands, 215 feet high, which are very
remarkable, especially when the sun shines on the white cliffs in the morning. In
this space are the two small bays Mariegalante and Exchange. The shore is fringed
with coral, but it may be approached within a mile in favourable weather.

From Hudson Point, the southernmost of the headlands, before mentioned, the
coast takes a sudden turn to the W. by N., for 22 miles, forming the north side of
Willoughby Bay, which is a remarkable, flat, wooded table land, 350 feet in height,
the coast taking again a sudden turn to the S.8.E., for 25 miles from the head of the
bay, which is very low and sandy. The deep indentations readily point out the
entrance to this harbour, more particularly as the §.W. side is formed of irregular
hill of. much greater elevation.

WILLovucuBy Bay.—Willoughby Bay, although capable of affording safe anchor-
age to ships of large class, is so difficult and dangerous of access, that it is seldom or
never frequented, the produce of that part of the country being sent by droghers to
St. John’s. Its S.E. side is protected by a coral ledge, dry in many parts, through
which there are two narrow cuts leading into the bay. The N.E. cut is only 220 feet
wide, but has a depth of 29 feet; the S.E. one is nearly a cable’s length in width,
but so tortuous and intricate that no line of direction can be given for its navigation.
To enter the N.E. channel, run down about a mile distant from the reef, until the
chimney of Lyon’s steam-mill, on the north shore, is in one with a bush on Delep’s
Hill; steer in on that line till the leading mark is visible, viz., Cochrane’s Mill,
situate on the low land at the head of the bay, in one with the rocky point, on which
there is the ruin of a fort, scarcely however visible, which forms the south side of

Christian Bay; this line will carry you through the opening, and when Fort Shirley
comes on with the south point of the inner part of the bay, you may haul gradually
up for the anchorage. With the prevailing winds, however, this mark would be
useless incoming out, asa ship would not lie out; and as we can give no safe
directions for the other channel, the anchorage is only free to steamers, and even to
them our directions are useless without the assistance of an experienced pilot, more
particularly as this bight is exposed to the full force of the sea and swell of the
ocean, which makes it very dangerous to approach in strong breezes.

SutrtEy Hricuts.—Three-and-half miles to the S.W. of Hudson’s Point, and
5 miles due west from the east end of the island, are the Shirley Heights, a bold
rocky promontory, of a mile in length, rising perpendicularly up from the surface
of the sea to the height of 545 feet, on the flat summit of which may be seen the
barracks and the buildings of the garrison, and at the western edge of the precipice,
a little more elevated, the two signal-posts of Fort Shirley, which point out the
entrance to English Harbour. Between Willoughby Bay and the heights are two
small inlets—Marmora Bay and Indian Creek—which will admit small vessels. The
entrance of the former is obstructed by a bar on which there are only 10 feet, and
the latter has a dangerous shoal near the middle of the entrance, which is little more
than a cable’s length in width; it generally, however, shows itself. From Indian
Creek to Old Road Bluff the shore is clear, and so steep that you may pass within
half a mile of almost all parts of it. :

EnciisH Harzour.—English Harbour lies at the base of the Shirley Heights ;
the west end of the promontory forming the east point of its entrance, which, between
it and Fort Barclay, isa cable’s length only in width. The greatest depth in the
narrows is 24 feet, and this only on one exact line of direction, viz., the north end of
the wall of Dow’s Hill House in one with the low rocky point which forms the north
end of Freeman’s Bay—a very doubtful mark, from the wall being so greatly elevated
above the point. In the very centre of the channel there is a small spot, on which
there are only 212 feet ; the 24-feet channel is therefore not more than 120 feet wide;
and, as no confidence can be placed in the wind, which baffles about in all directions,
immediately after you come under the heights, no stranger can attempt to follow our
directions without the assistance of a pilot. Should the wind be at N.E., or even
E.N.E., you will most probably have to anchor outside the narrows, and warp in, and
should it blow strorg, the gusts rush through the valleys with such force, and the
holding-ground is so bad, being a flat rock, that a second anchor will most likely be
required to bring you up; it is therefore attended with some danger. A small fair-
way buoy is gencrally placed on the east or weather side of the channel.

Intending to enter the harbour with the prevailing wind at east, stand boldly in
under the heights, a little to windward of Fort Charlotte Bluff (the east point of
entrance), and then keep the ship under full plain sail, trimmed by the wind; hug the
shore close, giving the bluff a berth of a cable’s length, and having rounded the buoy
close to starboard, keep the leading mark on until the dockyard-staff is on with the
end of Fort Barclay, then luff close up, take in the courses, and if you have strong
way, will most probably shoot round the point of Fort Barclay before the wind from
the high lands comes off from the northern shore. If the ship loses her way and
becomes unmanageable before this, you must anchor immediately ; if you succeed in
shooting in, be prepared to wear short round, and when in the centre of the channel
clew up, as you will most probably have sufficient way to carry you to the anchorage
off the dockyard. If you intend going no farther than the moorings in Freeman’s
Bay, you will of course keep your wind, and shoot up to windward as far as possible,
that you may be able to drop your anchor in good holding-ground, ready for warping.
Boats from the dockyard are generally in readiness with hawsers, but your own
should be also ready to assist.

FatmoutH Harpoour lies a mile to the westward of English Harbour, and affords
excellent anchorage to a few vessels of large class, there being 24 feet water in the

THE ISLAND OF ANTIGUA. 49

centre; it is, however, rather confined, the entrance between Black and Proctor’s
Points, which are bold and steep-to, is 3 cables’ length wide. . The harbour may be
said to be divided into two parts, the eastern end being separated from the western
by a spit, which extends from Blake Island to near the centre of the bay, where it
terminates in a small shoal, on which there are only 12 feet; between it and the foul
ground, off St. Ann’s Point, the channel leading to the inner anchorage is not quite a
eable’s length wide, too narrow for a sailing-vessel to pass against prevailing wind,
but affording free access to steamers. The outer anchorage occupies a square of about
2 cables’ length each way; the inner is more capacious, being about the same distance
in width, and nearly 3a mile in length from east to west. The leading mark into
the outer anchorage is the east end of Blake Island Fort, on with a remarkable house,
on the western slope of Monk Hill, and having passed the Bishop Shoal, which
always shows itself, you may anchor at pleasure according to your draught of water.
We can give no good leading mark for the inner channel.

From Falmouth to the west end is the highest part of the island, and in many
places the base of the hills rest on the shore; in the immediate vicinity of Falmouth
there are two remarkable elevations. Monk Hill, on the north side of the harbour,
is readily distinguished by the fort and signal-staff, which crowns its flat summit, the
8.E. end overlooking a rocky precipice, 695 feet above the level of the sea. The
other lies on the N.W. side of the harbour, 13 mile to the westward of Monk Hill,
and is a large, isolated, conical, wooded hill, which rises to the height of 1,058 feet ;
when seen from the N.E. or S.W., its summit terminates in a single peak, but from
the N.W. and north it appears doubled, or saddle-shaped, from which it sometimes
takes its name; but, as there is another hill so called on the west side of the island,
we have termed it the Falmouth Peak. These two hills are very conspicuous objects
from the north side of the island, where they are of great value to safe navigation.
They may both of them be seen from Barbuda, in clear weather, at a distance of 45
miles. The hills on the west side of them are more lofty, but not remarkable to
strangers, with the exception of Boggy Peak (the highest in the island) which is
slightly elevated above the neighbouring hills, and 1,339 feet above the level of the
sea, and is seldom obscured.

OLD Roap Buurr.—At 22 miles to the westward of Falmouth is a bold round
headland, 135 feet in height, rising abruptly from the shore, and readily distinguished
when seen from the east or west. We have observed before, that this part of the
shore, although skirted by a rocky ledge, in most parts may be safely approached to
within 3 a mile.

Dine-a-Dina Noox.—Midway between Proctor’s Point and the bluff is Ding-a-
Ding Nook, a small bay, in which droghers find an anchorage.

OLp Roav.—The shore on the west side of the bluff turns suddenly to the north-
ward for 3 a mile, when it forms the Bay of Carlisle. The town of Carlisle is situate
at the west end of the beach, which is backed by an extensive fish-pond, private
property. An excellent spring of water runs through the valley, but loses itself in
the swampy grounds, at some distance from the shore at the head of the pond.

There is good anchorage with the prevailing winds about midway between the
bluff and the 8.W. point of Carlisle Bay, on which there is an old fort, in 5 fathoms,
about 7 of a mile from the shore, or more. A ground swell, however, generally

sweeps in from the southward, which causes a ship to roll heavily, and landing is
sometimes difficult, for the sea breaks a considerable distance from the beach,

Goat Hitt.—A small rounded eminence, 115 feet in height, standing conspicuously
on a projecting point, 14 mile to the westward of Old Road Bluff. Between Old
Fort Point and it are three sandy beaches, skirted by a coral ledge; from Morris’s
old mill, which is a remarkable object, being the only one seen on this part of the
shore (Brock’s being hidden in the trees), to Goat Hill the ledge extends off to the
distance of upwards of a cable’s length.

50

From Goat Hill to the west end of the island the shore is very low and sandy,
with swampy ground at the back; to the foot of the islands it is still skirted by a flat
coral edge, even with the surface, in which, however, there are one or two openings
through which a boat may pass to good landing.

This part of the shore is also fringed by an outer solid reef, nearly dry in many
places, the east end of which lies nearly 3 of a mile south of Goat Hill, from thence
it extends in a westerly direction 2 miles, and at that end there is sometimes seen a
small sandy cay, which is occasionally heaped up and washed away by the action of
the rollers; its outer or southern edge is wall-sided, and therefore dangerous to
approach in the night, for the lead will give no warning whatever; and, being under
high land, no estimated distance can be depended upon. In the daytime it is avoided
by keeping Dow’s House, on the Shirley Heights, just open of Old Road Bluff;
within the outer barrier there is a second or middle reef, running parallel with the
shore, at the distance of 4-10ths of a mile, between which and the shore there is very
excellent anchorage and a good watering-place. At the eastern entrance there is not
less than 25 feet water; the western entrance is, however, obstructed by a flat rocky
bar, on which there is not more than 22 feet, over which vessels must pass on leaving
the anchorage, there not being room to beat through to the eastward.

THE ISLAND OF ANTIQUA.

Ships running for this anchorage from the eastward should haul close round Old
Road Bluff, in towards Morris’s old mill, passing Curtin Bluff, which forms the east
end of Morris’s Bay, within + of a mile; when abreast the mill you will, if ciear, see
the discoloured water at the end of the reef, and the ledge which runs off from Goat
Hill, which will enable you to direct your course in mid-channel, which is nearly + of
a mile wide. We can give no leading mark, and the above directions are not sufficient
to guide a stranger without the assistance of a pilot. If beating up for the anchorage
from the westward, outside the reef, you will perceive, over Goat Hill, a rocky fork,
branching off to the southward, from the main or highest ridge of hills, on which are
three remarkable peaks, particularly the southern one, which is the lowest. When
these peaks are in one with Morris’s old mill. you will be to the eastward of the shoal
ground off the east end of the reef, and may therefore stand on until you have reached
the middle of the channel.

The best and most convenient anchorage for watering is with Morris’s old mill in
one with the south side of Goat Hill, and the great house on Harvey’s estate, called
also Cade Bay, which lies in the vailey under Boggy Peak, bearing about N.E. by N.,
where you will be midway between the shore and middle reef. As before observed,
you must leave the anchorage by the western channel; therefore, when running down,
keep the shore on board (the edge of the ledge is in general distinctly seen), taking
care not to open Morris’s old mill to the southward of Goat Hill until the leading
mark for the bar (Fry’s mill just in sight to the westward of Crab Hill) is nearly on,
which will be known when Pearn’s Hill is on with Fry’s Point, when the sails should
be trim:med ready to enable you to haul up quickly upon the leading mark. This is
a point which requires skill and great attention, to prevent your falling on the lee
side of the bar, which is very dangerous. Should you, however, find that you have
taken too great a sweep on rounding-to, there is room to make a small hitch, provided
it is done in time; but, as we have already said, a stranger cannot navigate these
channels without: the assistance of a pilot. When Morris’s old mill is just seen to
the southward of Goat Hill, you. are between the shoals on the bar, which are distant
from each other 3 cables’ len ; having passed the bar and bound to the eastward,
do not haul up until Dow’s House comes open of Old Road Bluff.

The 8.W. end of the island terminates at Johnson’s Point, which is low and rocky ;
on the Point there is the ruin of a fort, the barrack is seen a little within it; a short
distance from it is a small rocky islet of the same name, covered with brushwood,
and 18 feet in height ; being, however, under the high land, they are not readily
distinguish:d, until on a N.W. or S.E. bearing, From hence the west side of the
island turns sharply round, and takes a northerly direction for a distance of 22 miles
to the Reed Point. In this space are Picart, Firy, and Morris Bays, separated by

THE ISLAND OF ANTIQUA. 51

bluff rocky headlands, about 100 feet in height, rising abruptly from the shore: the
highest part of the island may be said to terminate at Morris's Bay. In the vicinity,
however, there are several very remarkable heights, which are of great value to sate
navigation, and become conspicuous objects immediately after opening out this side
of the island. Six of these are situate close together, on the south side of Five
Islands’ Harbour. The Saddle, 590 feet, and Flat lop Hills, .500 feet in height, are
at once distinguished by their names, and being the westernmost of all. Leonard,
Pearn, and Mosquito Hills are ccnical, with peaked summits, thickly wooded ; the
two former are nearly of the same elevation, the latter very much lower.

Tuomas Mount, or Round Hill, situate on the north side of the same harbour, is a
large round wooded hill, 547 fect in height, when seen from all directions but the
N.N.W., when it appears more peaked at the summit; $ of a mile to the westward of
it there is a narrow irregular table ridge, of moderate elevation, but at its east end
there is a small peak, 463 feet in height, which may be seen for a long distance, and
with a little local knowledge become a valuable landmark. Reed Point is at the
foot of a wooded hill of moderate height, separated from the shore by a narrow neck
of swampy land, forming the west side of Mosquito Cove, which is 4-10ths of a mile
deep east and west, and 3-10ths of a mile wide at the base of Mosquito Hill; from
thence the shore turns to the westward, and terminates a mile distant in Pearn Point,
which is low and rocky. All this part of the coast is dangerous to approach, being
skirted by a coral ledge, studded with rocky heads, some of which have as little as
10 feet water over them. Three-quarters of a mile west of Ffry Bay there is one
which generally shows itself; the outermost shoal lies 2 miles off shore in the same
direction.

There is, however, a good channel within the shoals for vessels drawing 14 feet,
provided the prevailing wind is not to the northward of K.N.E. To navigate it,
having passed the bar as before directed, or if pursuing the route from the eastward
through Cade Bay anchorage, give Johnson Island a berth of % of a mile, and then
steer with Sandy Island on with the N.E, side of the highest of the Five Islands,
until the Hawk’s Bill Rock comes on with Pelican Point, which mark will carry you
through the Five Islands Channel, which is, however, only a cable’s length wide; if,
therefore, on your approach, you should find the wind too scant to allow you to make
certain of lying through, you had better pass out to the S.W. of the Five Islands,
taking care to avoid the north end of the lrish Bank, by not opening Flat Top Hill,
to the southward of Mosquito Hill, when near it. You may also anchor before coming
thus far in the centre of Picard Bay, in 3 fathoms, 3-10ths of a mile trom the shore,
where there is good holding-ground, and good landing on the east side of Ffry’s Bluff.
Should you have succeeded in getting through the Five Islands Channel, we can give
no farther leading mark, but you may pursue the inshore route with safety, by steer-
ing from thence direct for Pelican Island, a small rocky island, 8 feet above the level
of the sea. ‘Two cables’ length to the westward of the east point of Five Islands’
Harbour you will soon perceive a breaker, which lies a cable’s length off the west
point of the island; round this within a cable’s length, and then hug the shore close
on board, taking care not to open Fort Barrington, on Goat Hill, or Ferris Point,
until you are past the Hurst Banks, or the Table Peak is nearly in one with the
Hawk’s Bill Rock.

Ships passing outside the shoals, bound to St. John’s Harbour, should, as before
directed, not shut in Dow’s House of Old Road Bluff, until they have passed to the
westward of the leading mark for the bar, when they may haul gradually up to the
N.W., taking care to open Hawk’s Bill Kock out to the westward of the Five Islands
before Johnson’s Island comes in one with Old Road Bluff, when they may haul up
north. The soundings off the 8.W. end of the island in this track are very irregular

and rocky, varying suddenly trom 7 to 12 fathoms, and in the night this part should

not be approached within the depth of 10 or 12 fathoms.

The Five IsLanDs are a small group of low, rugged, rocky islets, scantily clothed
With brushwood, the outermost lying 4 a mile west of Pearn Point, and are easily

52

recognized from the north and south direction; from other points, being under the
hills, they are not easily distinguished, except the largest, which is 50 feet in height;
the innermost lies a cable’s length from the shore, leaving a small channel. for a
drogher. ‘The ship channei we have described is between the highest and the one
next east of it; there are really but four islets, for the N.E. point of the largest,
which is called the fifth from its appearance at a certain distance, is connected with
the island by a low coral ledge; the two outer ones are steep-to on their north and
west sides.

Rep CuirF.—Three-tenths of a mile to the N.E. of Pearn Point, at the east end
of a sandy beach, there is a remarkable red cliff, about 30 feet in height, which forms
the 8.W. point of Five Islands’ Harbour, which, forming a deep indentation to the
eastward, is 15 mile in extent in that direction, and 2 of a mile from north to south.
This is a very secure anchorage during the prevailing winds, although exposed to the
rollers, for vessels of 16 feet draught; the holding-ground is very good. ‘There is,
however, a dangerous small patch of rocks in the very middle of the harbour, on
which there are only 9 feet water; its shoalest part lies with Sandy Island in one with
Pelican Point, the N.W. point of the harbour ; to avoid it. to the northward, which is
the side on which it should be passed on entering, do not open Drew’s Hill to the
southward of Maiden Island, which is a remarkable, small, round, rocky islet, with
precipitous sides, crowned with small trees, the tops of which are 90 feet above the
level of the sea, lying in the middle or eastern part of the harbour. We are not able
to give any mark for passing it to the southward. The harbour is also obstructed at
the entrance by the Pelican Shoal, on which there are only 15 feet water. If working
in to the southward of it, do not shut Drew’s Hill in with Maiden Island; and when
the Great Sister is in one with Ferris Point, you will be close to the inner or east side ©
of it. The shoal is cleared to the northward by not opening Seaforth Head, a roeky
bluff hill at the east end of the harbour, to the southward of Maiden Island. If
approaching from the northward the better way is to keep in the inshore channel,
already described, and haul sharp round Pelican Island Rock, when, if the sea breeze
is to the northward of east, you may fetch in to windward of Cook’s Shoal.

The Hawnx’s Btu Rock lies 13 cable’s length from the shore, and midway between
Pelican and Ferris Point, which are 11 mile distant. It is asmall, barren, rocky islet,
25 feet in height; its west side, being composed of soft sand-stone, has been cut into
by the action of the sea, formerly a perpendicular cliff, to nearly the top of the rock,
where it overhangs, projecting out almost horizontally for a few feet, and then
becomes rounded to the summit, on which there is a knob of rock, and when seen clear
of the land from the northward or southward, has the appearance of a hawk’s bill,
and cannot be mistaken; there is no passage within it even for a boat, but on its
outer side it is steep-to within a cable’s length.

Goat HIL1, eight-tenths of a mile N.E. of Ferris Point, is of conical shape, 176
feet in height, and is readily distinguished by the small fort with its two signal-staffs
on its summit, more particularly from the §.W., from whence it also appears a well
defined point or headland. The hill is situate on a narrow neck of land, on the west
side of which is Deep Bay, where there is temporary anchorage for small vessels.

THE ISLAND OF ANTIGUA.

Suip’s SteRN.—Nearly a cable’s length from the point is situate a narrow flat-
topped rocky islet, slightly wooded 1-10th of a mile in length, called the Ship’s Stern,
its west side having something of that appearance. It is a bold perpendicular cliff,
60 feet in height, having several large masses of rock lying at its base, which are
very remarkable from the 8.W. or N.E. directions. From hence the shore takes an
abrupt turn to the E.S8.E. for 22 miles, forming the south side of the harbour and
Road of St. John’s,

Sr. JoHn’s.—St. John’s is the capital of the island, and lies on the side of a gentle
acclivity, which at the upper part of the town, is 80 feet above the level of the sea.
From the offing it is readily distinguished by the cathedral, a large massive white
building, with two lofty towers, the vanes of which are 157 feet above the sea. The

BARBUDA. 53

only other remarkable object is the kirk, a small square white building, with a
nipped or sloping roof, and asmall bell turret at its west end; it stands a little
above the cathedral, nearly 4 of a mile to the S.E. of it. The centre part of the city
is well built and clean, the streets running parallel and at right angles with the shore.
The commerce of the island is carried on from hence both inwards and outwards, the
produce and supplies being conveyed by the droghers to and from all other parts,
with the exception of Parham, where 3 or 4 ships load annually.

The harbour is secure against all winds except hurricanes, but confined, and not
at all convenient, for ships of only 12-feet draught cannot come within 3 of a mile of
the wharf, and those drawing over 14 feet are obliged to load in the roads; it is also
exposed to the rollers, which at times break over the jettys and do much mischief.
It is of irregular shape, nearly 2 miles in length from the bar to the head, and
between Week Point and the north end of the cove it is of a mile wide. Here,
however, it is divided by Rat Island, a small rugged rocky islet, on the summit of
which is the lunatic asylum and signal-staff, which are conspicuous objects, the wall
which surrounds the building being 137 feet above the level of the sea. The islet
has recently been connected to the shore at the west end of the town by a well-built
stone causeway, with a carriage road to the foot of the hill. That part of the harbour
situate on the south side of the island is alone occupied by shipping, and abreast of it
there are 10 feet water. The N.W. point of the harbour terminates in a small rocky
bluff, 38 feet in height, on which is situate Fort James, a mile from the nearest part
of the opposite shore, which may be termed the entrance for small vessels. The
harbour, however, is obstructed by a narrow sand-bar, 6-10ths of a mile to the west-
ward of the fort, on which there is only a depth of 153 feet at low water. As the
trade wind continually blows from almost the same direction, ships will always have
to beat in; therefore those drawing 13 feet, having passed within the middle ground
should keep Yepton Mill on with the east end of Loblolly Bay, until the westernmost
house in the city (which isa long low building with a red roof, and with a small
flagstaff near the east end of the wharf on which it stands), is in one with the
cathedral, when you may haul to the wind and cross the bar. The deepest part,
however, is only acable’s Jength wide, and to beat up from it into the harbour,
can only be effected by a good local knowledge, with the assistance of a pilot, for
we can give no safe directions. A nun-buoy has recently been placed on the west
end of the bar, which is of great use, enabling you to haul your wind more quickly
than can be done by attending solely to the leading-marks. To the north of the
channel mark, or buoy, there are 13 feet water in that direction, until Fort James’s
Bluff is in one with the north side of Rat Island, to the northward of that there
are 9 feet.”

BARBUDA. (Great Bnrirtarn.)

The ISLAND of BARBUDA is low and flat, with a rocky shore, somewhat
elevated towards the east, north, west and north-west; it is well inhabited and
fertile, producing cotton, corn, sheep, fowls, fruit, pepper, indigo, and tobacco; but

ood water is scarce. The greatest extent of Barbuda from N.W. to S.E. is said to
te about 14 miles, and its highest land is not to be discerned on any side more than
6 leagues off ; the greater part of its shores are rocky, foul, and extremely dangerous.
'To the south and south-west rocky spits extend into the sea ina S.W. and 8.W. by W.
direction, nearly 7 miles, from Spanish Point, the 8.E. point of the island. The
shoals which lie in this direction, are named the Palaster Reef, Dodington Bank,
and Codrington Shoals, haying depths of 5 to 8 fathoms between them. The

BARBUDA.

Codrington Shoals are small patches, having only 9 to 12 feet on them; the mark to
clear them to the westward is the martello tower and flagstaff bearing N. by E.
The Codrington Bank lies ina S.W. by S. direction from Spanish Point, and has
generally 7 to 9 fathoms on it, but near the extreme point only 53 fathoms, with .
Spanish Point bearing N.E. by N., distant 8 miles; and Palmetto Point N.N.W.,
10 miles. Previous to the late survey by Captain K. Barnett, R.N., the rocky reefs
which surround this island were supposed to lie at a much greater distance from it
than they have been found.

The reefs which border the east side of the island, from Spanish Point to Hog
Point, a distance of 11 miles, do not extend above a mile from the shore, with
20 fathoms near their outer edge, and 60 fathoms at 2 miles from the island; near
the middle of the east side of the island are the Hog Cliffs, considerably elevated.
This part of the island is named the Highlands, and is elevated 205 feet. Goat Point
lies 33 miles N.W. by W. from Hog Point, and is bordered by Cobb Reef, which
extends full 13 mile from the land, with 10 to 11 fathoms close to its outer edge.
Goat Reef joins the north end of Cobb Reef, and extends from thence 3 miles to the
westward, and 2 miles from the north end of the island, having 8 to 10 fathoms very
near it. Billy Point is the N.W. point of the island, and Cedar Point lies 12 mile
8.W. by S. from it. A dangerous rocky fiat lies off this part of the island, extending
23 miles from the land, and continues to run to the southward 3 the length of the
island; southward of this, as far as Palmetto Point, you will have 5 fathoms at
2 miles from the island, but you may approach Palmetto Point, within 2 of a mile
from the southward. At 2 miles eastward of Palmetto Point is the principal
landing-place, where there is a martello tower and flagstaff, and a remarkable tree
near it; from hence is a good road running northward, 3 miles, to the village and
castle of Codrington. ‘The martello-tower bears from Cocoa Point, the south point
of the island, N.W. $ W., distant 5 miles, and from Palmetto Point, E. by N.3N.,
2 miles.

The west side of the island is formed by a narrow neck of land, covered with trees,
7 miles in length, which divides the sea from a fine lagoon within it; this lagoon is
6 miles long and 1% broad, and is entered by a narrow channel at the north end, with
only 3 to 6 feet init. The castle and village of Codrington stands on the east bank
of the Lagoon. The west and S.W. part of this island may be approached by the
lead, as: shallow water extends off at a considerable distance. Twenty fathoms will
be found 11 miles west of Palmetto Point, and 100 fathoms at 14 miles west of the
same point.

On the western side of the island, abreast of the village, there is good anchorage,
in 54 to 6 fathoms, with Palmetto Point bearing 8.E., distant 3 miles. There is also
anchorage off the §.W. coast, in 53 fathoms, sandy ground, Palmetto Point bearin
N.W. by W.., distant 2 miles ; and Cocoa Point, the south point of the island, E.S.E.,
distant 4 miles; near this latter point is a small battery, and there are several others
on the shore, and a fort on Spanish Point. The present inhabitants of the island
are about 500, who are under the government of Antigua, and are chiefly employed
in raising stock for the neighbouring islands. Citrons, pomegranates, oranges, figs,
raisins, and a variety of herbs and roots are cultivated with much success, and the
island abounds with the finer sorts of wood.

The following remarks on the Island of Barbuda, published in the Nautical Maga-
gine, for February, 1835, are by Mr. James Goodlet, late Master of the Jean Stewart,
wrecked there on the 10th June, 1834 :—

“The town and castle of Barbuda are situate on the western side of the island,
on the edge of a beautiful lagoon, about 8 miles in length and 14 in breadth, abound-
ing in excellent fish of different kinds. The entrance of the lagoon is on the north-
west side of the island, about 40 fathoms broad, with from 24 to 34 feet water, sand
and mud, There are several small islets and shoals in different parts of this fine

lake.

BARBUDA. 55

The castle is in latitude 17°45’ 24”; north point of Goat Island, 17° 54’ 24’;*
south-east end (Spanish Point), 17° 32’ 30’; landing at the river, where there
is a fort and martello tower, with a flagstaff upon it, 17° 41’ 39’; the fort is in bad
condition, with a breach on its south side, mounts 9 guns; height of the tower, 56
feet. Latitude of S.E. end, where the Jean Stewart was wrecked, on the beach
opposite the vessel, 17° 34’ 48’. Wreck S.E. by E., distant 13 mile from the shore.

From the centre of the island to the north end, the land rises gradually to the
height of 170 feet above the level of the sea; this terminates the headland abruptly
into a level plain on the north, about 2 miles north and south, and about 6 miles east
and west. On this headland is the ancient residence of the Codrington family ; the
house is still standing, though in a ruinous condition, the walls white, and, being 50.
feet high, may be seen from a good distance; the out-buildings and offices are still
good. There is also a large tank, capable of holding 10 months’ water. This white
house can be seen a long way off in clear weather, but cannot be approached nearer
than 7 or 8 miles, on account of the very dangerous reef surrounding the island,
extending out on the north-west and south sides to 5 and 6 miles, and on the west
side even as far as 8 miles. The reefs extend on the east side from 23 to 3 miles,
with very deep water along the edge. From the north end of these reefs, on the east
side, to the south extremity, there is no entrance whatever, not even for boats, which
is the cause of all goods saved from wrecks having to be carted to the castle, or to
Grasmor’s Landing, to be sent to Antigua for sale. The island being overgrown
with wood, fresh roads have to be cut for every wreck.

This island is entirely surrounded by reefs of a very dangerous kind, as vessels
may in the daytime be aground before they are observed, unless a very good look-
out is kept. The outer edge of the reefs have from 3 to 8 feet water on them ; that
is, the south, west, and north sides of them.

There are several anchorages; that of Grasmor’s Landing, on the south side,
about 12 mile from the Spanish Point, has about from 12 to 14 feet water; but to
enter this channel, you must run down outside of the reefs, until Cocoa Point bears
N. by E., when you will see the western edge of the reef square with the water,
about 34 miles off shore; round this close-to, keeping a good look-out for the brown
patches as you beat up, between the outer and inner reefs. These brown patches are
all ragged coral rocks, from about 1 to 3 feet below the surface, and are so numerous,
that only small vessels, and they with difficulty, anchor in the roadstead, and must
be well acquainted to gain the anchorage.

The best anchorage is off the fort, at the south-west end of the island, called the
River, with the fort bearing north, in about 7 or 8 fathoms, sand and mud, 13 mile off
shore; this is very unsafe for large vessels, as the reefs both to windward and leeward
extend a long way out to the southward. The vessels belonging to the island run in
between the rocks, and anchor in from 10 to 12 feet, about 40 fathoms from the
beach, on a sandy bottom, close under the fort. ‘This being the principal exporting
place on the island, the road from thence to the town is very good; should a
stranger land here, and hoist a flag on the fort, horses will always be sent down
to meet him.

There is also an anchorage on the north-west side, to enter which is very dangerous,
the reefs extending so far out to sea, and many invisible, so much so that you may be
aground before any danger appears. I would advise none but those well acquainted
