On THE CURRENTS BETWEEN BARBUDA AND ANTIGUA.—The currents between
these two islands are very deceiving. After the loss of the Jean Stewart, and during
my stay with Mr. Winter there, he often informed me of the currents of this part of
the West Indies, which much surprised me, and which I saw a proof of, between the
11th and 20th. Being always on the beach after the sinking of the vessel, many of
the articles washed off the deck were, on the first day, washed to the north-east end
of the island; and, before we landed, many of the water casks were on the beach
before us, about 2 or 3 miles to the northward.

After the 20th, going and coming every other day between these islands, I
remarked, that from nearly full moon to the last quarter the current sets very strongly
to windward, sometimes at the rate of from 1 to 1 mile per hour, although the
course, from the River’s anchorage to the Sisters, going into Antigua, was south, by
compass, and generally from nearly full moon, and two or three days after, was
obliged to steer S. by W. and S.S.W.; when, after full, and towards last quarter,
§.S.E. and S.E. by S., and N.N.E. and N.E. by N., which is a proof of some regu-
larity in the motion of the sea hereabout-at the above periods of the moon. How
far this extends to the eastward of. the islands I cannot pretend to say,. but should
think it must affect vessels three or four degrees off; and should thick weather then
come on, the danger must be great ,without a knowledge of this current. My own
unfortunate case is a lamentable proof of this.”

MONTSERRAT anp REDONDA (Great Brirarn).

MONTSERRAT is an island of an oval form, about 9 miles long and 6 broad,
containing nearly 30,000 acres of land, two-thirds of which are mountainous and
barren, the remainder is well cultivated ; of this about 6,000 acres are appropriated
to sugar, 2,000 to cotton, 2,000 to provisions, and 2,000 to pasturage ; its population
in 1861 was 7,645, of which 3,447 were males. Its exports are rum, sugar, and some
cotton. The eastern side of Montserrat wears an uncultivated appearance, and the
mountains appear very high, abounding with cedar and other useful and valuable
trees; but its western side gently slopes down towards the sea, and is covered with
beautiful plantations; on the S.W. side stands the town and fort of Plymouth.
Vessels from the eastward should pass the south end of the island, and anchor off the
lower end of the town, abreast of the fort, where they will have 6 fathoms, good
anchorage, within 2 cables’ length of the shore ; but should they go to the northward
of this, the ground will be foul and rocky. To the northward of Plymouth are the
Old Road and Kerr’s Bay, where vessels may ride if occasion requires. At all these
places there is a heavy surf occasionally beating upon the shore, which renders the
loading of heavy goods peculiarly inconvenient; the natives use a sort of boat,
called a coble, which they manage very dexterously, conveying the hogshead of sugar
to the vessel in the offing. If the weather should seem to indicate the approach of a
tornado, while you are lying here, which generally happens with a 8.W. wind, it
will be advisable to get under weigh directly, as the wind will best allow.

Lights.—Two fixed lights are shown on the beach at Plymouth, on the expected
arrival of the mail steamers.

Montserrat, according to the Spanish description, lies nearly S.8.E. and N.N.W.,

NEVIS AND 8T. CHRISTOPHER. 57

and may be considered asa great rock formed by two mountains; the N.E. part is
very high and cliffy, and clean to approach; the N.W. part is also high and bluff,
and the island may be seen 15 leagues off; the coast is generally steep-to, and there
are no breakers whatever, except where the ocean breaks upon the very shore, so that
a vessel may almost touch the land without the least fear of danger. But, as before
observed, there is no bay. The S.E. part is somewhat higher than the N.W., but the
declivity is more gradual, and the beach which joins the sea is low; the south part is
clean, but with south-easterly winds, the sea breaks with much force upon it. The
road is an opening of some depth, but the shelter is only when the breeze is from the
north-eastward ; and this renders it impossible for large ships to anchor in it; there-
fore it it is only frequented by small vessels.

REDONDA is a high and barren rock, 8 miles N.W. by N. from the north end of
Montserrat. It is steep-to, and at present uninhabited. It has the appearance, at a
distance, of a haycock, being visible 30 miles off. You may approach it on any side;
but on its western side there is anchorage in 10 and 12 fathoms. At the S.E. isa
little islet, called the pinnacle, which forms a remarkable appearance, and nearly
joins the land. To the westward and to the northward of Redonda are said to be
some sand banks, abounding with fish.

NEVIS anp ST. CHRISTOPHER,
CauLeD By THE Enauisa ST. KITT’S (GREAT BriTAIN),

NEVIS and ST. CHRISTOPHER’S ISLANDS both belong to the English,
and, with Antigua, Monserrat, and the Virgin Islands, form a separate government;
the Governor resides at Antigua, and occasionally visits the other islands. Nevis and
St. Christopher’s are both high, and may be seen in clear weather full 18 leagues off ;
they are divided from each other by the Narrows, a channel about 4 a league wide,
but which should never be attempted by a stranger without a pilot.

NEVIS is a small island about 4 miles broad and 5 in length, and literally may be
deemed a high mountain, whose summit is very lofty, and of volcanic origin; at the
foot of this mountain is a border of level land, extremely fertile and highly culti-
vated ; and on its western side are two rivulets of fresh water. Here also are three
toierable roadsteads ; that most frequented and most in estimation is before Charles-
town, the principal town in the island. This island is divided into five parishes or
districts ; its population in 1861 amounted to 9,822, of which 4,526 were males. Its
exports are coffee, sugar, rum, and cotton.

In making this island either from the southward or the northward, the top of the
mountain, which frequently is enveloped in the clouds, appeurs in the form of a
saddle ; this is occasioned by the broken mouth of the ancient crater; but as the
shores of the island are very low, it will be advisable not to be led too near them at
night, for from the south and S.W. points there are some rocky reefs, which might
prove dangerous. The road of Charlestown ™ lies at the S.W. part of the island; in
approaching it from the southward, you should give the point on which the fort is

ST. KITT’S.

MonkEY SHOALS.—These are the only dangers on the N.W. coast of Nevis, and
lie N.W., 43 miles from Fort Charles, and S.W. 3 S., 25 miles from the Nag’s Head;
the 8. W. end of St, Christopher.

These shoals form two small banks of coral and sand, and lie very much in the way
of large vessels approaching the anchorage of Charlestown; they lie on the edge of
soundings, and occupy a space of about a mile long, N.N.B. and S.S.W., and 2 cables?
broad, having on them 4 fathoms water. The discoloured water over them may be
seen at some distance from aloft. ‘The soundings around are very irregular.

We have observed that the Island of Nevis is separated from St. Kitt’s by a strait
almost 2 miles broad; this strait is much encumbered with shoals, and is common]
denominated the Narrows; in it isa remarkable high rock, called Booby Island,
which lies nearly in the middle of the strait; S.W. of this rock are two others, named
the Cows; these latter are connected to Nevis by a shoal, of 1 to 5 fathoms water,
with foul ground. ‘There are other shoals annexed to the N.W. part of Nevis, which
will best be understood by inspecting the chart, and which form, as it were, the
sou'hern boundary of the channel. Off the north-eastern side of the Narrows an
extensive sand-bank stretches along, forming a kind of bar to the entrance; this shoal
lies in a N.W. and S.E. direction, being full 5 miles in length, and a mile in breadth.
E.N.E., about 14 mile from Booby Island, there is a part of it with only 10 feet over
it; and near the northern part of the bank is another patch of 3 fathoms only ; this
lies pearly E.N.E. from Windward Point, in St. Kitt’s. There is a channel between
this shoal and St. Kitt’s leading into the Narrows, having 14, 12, 9, and 8 fathoms in
it; the mark to sail through it is the eastern end of Booby Island kept well open of
the eastern part of St. Kitt’s, bearing 8.S.E. a little southerly, or the west point of
Nevis, just seen to the west part of Booby Island, will lead over the shoal in 5 or 6
fathoms, and carry you clear of the shoal water on both sides; but the common
passage is between the Island of Nevis and the southern part of the shoal; the lead+
ing mark being Booby Island W.N.W., or a remarkable house near the mill in St.
Kitt’s a little to the southward of Booby Island. In this channel you will not haye
Jess than 6 fathoms water.

The western entrance to the Narrows has also a large square shoal before it; but
over this are 5, 6, 7, 10, and 12 fathoms water. The Cows and Booby Island in one
will lead clear in to the eastward of this shoal, and the Cows bearing E.N.E. will
lead in to the westward; keep to the westward of the Cows, and pass midway
between them and the shores of St. Kitt’s; near Scotch Bonnet Head there are 2F5
8, and 4 fathoms, and near the Cows 43 and 6 fathoms; mid-channel are 53 and 6
fathoms, the bottom invariably good, but there is a kind of middle shoal of 33 and 4
fathoms, situate a little to the westward of the Cows. The Narrows is of great use
to vessels bound to Basse Terre from the northward, when not being able to weather
the east point of Nevis.

ST. KITT’S, or ST. CHRISTOPHER'S ISLAND, is called by the native
Caribs, Liaminga, or the Fertile; it is 16 or 17 miles long, and of very unequal
breadth, its southern part being about 2 miles wide, while its northern part, consti-
tuting the bulk of the island, is full 5 miles broad; these two parts are connected by
an isthmus, or narrow neck of land, not above a mile wide. ‘The whole-island con-
tains 43,729 acres of land.

The centre of St. Christopher’s presents a number of high and barren mountains,
which are intersected by rocky precipices, almost impassable, and abounding with
many hot springs. Of these Mount Misery is the highest, its summit being 3,316
feet above the sea. This is an exhausted volcano. In advancing towards St.
Christopher’s, this assemblage of hills makes the island appear to be one large
mountain covered with woods; but on nearer approach it becomes less abrupt, and

BASSE TERRE ROAD. 59

the mountains, ascending one above the other, seem cultivated as high as possible.
In sailing along the S.W. side, at the distance of 2 leagues from the land, it appears
like so many detached islands, but the N.W. part is the highest; and it has been
estimated that. one-half of this island is barren and unfit for cultivation, but the
barrenness of the mountains is well repaid by the fertility of its plains, for no part
of the West Indies possesses a soil equal to it, particularly for the production of
sugar, which, therefore, forms the staple commodity for exportation. ‘The climate is
hot, but tempered by the cool breezes which descend from the hills; the air, there-
fore, becomes pure and healthful, but it is subject to storms, hurricanes, and earth-
quakes. The population of St. Kitt’s is estimated at 24,440; and its chief exports are
coffee, sugar, rum, and cotton. It is divided into nine districts or parishes, and has
4 towns and several villages. The principal town is called Basse Terre; this is on
the south-western side of the island, and contains above 800 houses, and is defended
by three batteries. The other towns are Old Road, Sandy Point Town, and Diep ;
this latter being at the northern part of the island. There is no harbour at St.
Christopher’s, and but few landing-places, on account of the tremendous surf which
continually environs the shore.

The south end of St. Kitt’s is called the Nag’s Head, on which is a lofty hummock ;
this, in sailing along, you will particularly notice (as also the high lands about Frigate
Bay) Monkey Hill—a high mountain to the northward of Basse Terre—and Brim-
stone Hill, between Old Road Town and Sandy Point Town; this latter being ren-
dered very remarkable by the square fort on its summit. Within the Narrows are
several bays, or places of anchorage, on the southern end of St. Kitt’s; these are
Major’s Bay, Banana’s Bay, Cockleshell Bay, and Mosquito Bay; in each of these a
vessel may anchor,in fair weather or in cases of necessity, but the water shallows as
you approach the shores.

BASSE TERRE ROAD.—To sail from the south-western part of Nevis towards
Basse Terre, it will be requisite to give Fort Point, at Charlestown, a wide berth—say
1 or 13 mile; you may then steer N.N.W. or N.W. by N.; in this course you will
cross the Western Bank, of 5 and 6 fathoms water, but with experience there will be
no danger whatever, and it will carry you direct for the road ; the best anchorage is
in 9, 8, or 7 fathoms water, the bottom coarse sand, with the Half-moon battery
N.W. by W.; Basse Terre Town, N.N.W.; and Fashion Fort, N.E.; or with the
Londonderry Fort, at the east end of the town, north, distant 3 a mile, and the west
point of the bay W. by N.; or you will find good anchorage in 10 fathoms, sandy
bottom, with Nag’s Head in one with the south point of the Mountain of Nevis.
Here are no tides. Vessels from the westward, when bound for the road, may run in
with the single tree on the Green Ridge, behind the town of Basse Terre, just open
to the eastward of Monkey Hill; and when the point of the high land on each side
of Frigate Bay begins to shut one another in, the water will be found to deepen
from 7 to 10 fathoms, after having passed over a rocky ridge into clean ground. You
can neither get wood nor water here.

Light.—On the beach, at Basse Terre, a fixed light is exhibited all night, from a
wooden frame; the light is red, and is visible 12 miles. When bearing N. by W.3 W., |
leads to the anchorage.

OLD ROAD.—The town of Old Road is about 5 miles to the westward of Basse
Terre, and 3 miles to the eastward of Brimstone Hill; the coast from Bluff Point to
Palmetto Point is nearly west, from thence it turns more northerly. In sailing from
Basse Terre Road for this place, you will follow the shore at a proper distance,
running only so far to leeward as to fetch it upon a wind; then stand in, under easy
sail, for the Gully, to the eastward of the town, and when St. Thomas’s Church
comes on with the flagstaff on Brimstone Hill, you will be just on the edge of the
anchoring ground, in 17 fathoms, and may run in to within a cable’s length of the
beach, and anchor in 9 or 10 fathoms, stony ground; or.anchor a little to the east+
ward.of the Red House, abreast of the Gully ; Old Road Fort bearing N. by W.,
distant 4 a mile, and the extreme points of the land §.E. and W.N.W.; but if you

60 ST. EUSTATIUS.

go abreast of the town you will get off the bank into very deep water. Fresh water
can be obtained here very readily, but wood there is none; the surf is commonly
very great,

SANDY POINT TOWN roadstead is a full mile to the westward of Brimstone
Hill; the soundings do not extend far from the shore, and are rocky, the anchorage,
therefore, is at about a cable’s length from iand, where you will find 9, 12, and 14
fathoms ; the common mark is to bring the street, extenaing from the landing-place,
through the middle of the town, end on. In coming to this anchorage from the south-
ward, you must be careful to avoid the point where Charles’s Fort stanus, as there a
rocky reef stretches out; if coming irom the northward, you must be careful to avoid
a rocky reef which lies a little to the northward of Sandy Point; this should have a
berth of a mile. When St. Ann’s Church opens to the southward of Sandy Point
you will be to the southward of it; and when Brown’s house and Horton’s fig tree
come in a line, you will clear it to the northward.

- From hence to the town of Diep the coast is rocky, and vessels sailing along it
must keep at a proper distance. ‘lhe town of Diep is situate on the north point of
the island: from its eastern side a considerable reef runs out. There are also some
rocks, called the Dogs, lying off the channel, which render its entrance dangerous
and difficult; it is therefore not frequented by European yessels. ;

ST. EUSTATIUS anp SABA (Dutcx).

The ISLAND of ST. EUSTATIUS, or EUSTATIA, rises out of the ocean
like a huge pyramidal rock, lessening towards its summit; but as you approach it, you
will discover it to consist of two mountains, the eastern one being the higher of the
two; this is hollow at the top, and is the crater of a former volcano, but now it con-
stitutes a habitation for beasts. These mountains are highly cultivated to the very
top. The population of Eustatius and Saba is estimated at 18,000. Its exports
principally consist in tobacco, cotton, sugar, coffee, and rum; but the island produces
and abounds with hogs, poultry, rabbits, and vegetables in great abundance, but
water is very scarce. On the southern side stands the town, which is divided into
two parts, called the Upper and Lower Town; the latter is close to the water's edge;
the former is more elevated, and protected by a fortress. Each town consists of a
single street. The landing here is extremely difficult, on account of the continual
breaking of the wayes upon the shore, more especially when the wind comes
from S.E.

Vessels leaving Basse Terre Road, in St. Kitt’s, for St. Eustatius, should steer from
the west end a N.W. course, and if bound into the road, give the eastern point a
good berth, and come to anchor before the town in 12 fathoms, about 3 of a mile off
the shore, bringing the church to bear E.N.E. or N.E. by E., and the west end of the
bay N.W. by N.; but this anchorage cannot be considered good, though it is much
frequented ; the ground is coarse sand and coral rock. Vessels may anchor farther
out in deeper water; but if they should chance to be here in the hurricane months,
it will be incumbent upon them to watch the shifting of the wind attentively, for
should there appear the least indication of a squall coming on, they ought immediately
to put off to sea. The Derrotero says,— This island shows itself from the S.W., its
only hill being to the south-eastward ; it descends gradually towards the west, and
comes down te the shore, where the town and anchorage are situate; but the latter
is so bad, that when the breeze comes from the southward or eastward, the swell
becomes so great that the riding or landing becomes difficult. The Island of St.
Enstatius is clear all round, except the S.E. and S.W. points, from each of which a

SABA. 61

sandy spit stretches off. There is no landing-place but the one already noticed; its
§8.E. end is distant from the N.W. point of St. Kitt’s 13 miles. The channel between
this island and St. Kitt’s is without any danger, but the current at times runs strongly
to the northward; it is also much subject to calms and variable winds, owing to the
high land, Mount Misery and Brimstone Hill obstructing the true trade wind.”

SABA lies 13 miles N.W. by W. from the northern point of St. Eustatius, and is
another high round mountain, steep and inaccessible, except on its southern side;
here is a little creek and a landing-place, which is so intricate and narrow as to
admit only one man at atime. The island is inhabited by a few Dutch families, who
cultivate the cotton plant and manufacture stockings and ‘shoes, &c. The town
is built on a small plain, but hid from seaward by a very high hill, except to the
southward. At the landing-place, a little to the south-westward of Ladder Point, is
a small battery of two guns; the anchorage is between this point and the Diamond
Rock, in from 8 to 86 fathoms; soundings continue all the way to the northward,
round as far as Green Island. The road on the south-western side is tolerably safe
with northerly or easterly winds, but open to the southward and westward. Off its
N.W. part is a rock above water, called the Diamond, and appearing, as you approach
it from the westward, like a ship under sail, being mostly white with the excrements
of birds. Off the northern part also is a little island, called Green Island; the passage
between it and the shore has 4 fathoms water. It is asserted you may perceive
ground all round the island, but its edges are steep-to, and therefore the bottom can
be visible at a small distance only, unless on its southern side; and about 4 miles
from thence are 3 and 4 fathoms, but soundings may be traced full 7 leagues;
these consist chiefly of sand, gravel, coral, and shells, and the depth of water varies
from this spot of 3 and 4 fathoms, over which the sea commonly breaks, to 12 and 14
fathoms at 5 and 6 leagues off.

SABA BANE forms nearly a parallelogram, its longest sides lying E.N.E. and
W.S.W., about 32 miles, and its shortest about N.W. by N. and §.E. by S., 20 miles.
Its nearest part is 2? miles from the S.W. part of Saba Island. Although not
entirely a new discovery, its minute examination in 1851 added quite a new feature
to the then existing charts, which tended to remove the alarm that all navigators felt
when passing to the southward of the island. The east extreme of the bank bears
8. by E., distant about 12 miles from Saba, and the north end W. by N., 8 miles.

The eastern edge of the Saba Bank is fringed with a remarkable narrow ledge of
living coral, sand, and rock, which is nearly 30 miles in length, and varies in depth
from 63 to 10 fathoms; when on this part the bottom is distinctly seen. It com-
mences about 8.W., 4 miles from Ladder Point (Saba Island), and trends thence to
the §.8.E. for 11 miles, with a breadth of 13 to 24 miles; it then turns S.S.W. for 8
miles, and is from 1 to 2 miles broad, and terminates W. by S., 12 miles farther on,
where it is merely a ridge of 9 fathoms, not half a mile broad. To the westward, or
within this ledge, with the exception of a few small coral patches, of 9 and 10
fathoms, towards the southern edge, the bottom is clear white coral sand, with a
depth of 12 to 15 and 20 fathoms, gradually increasing to the edge, but terminating
eueety in 30 fathoms. The bottom can be distinctly seen under a depth of 10
athoms.

On the northern edge of the bank there is an excellent fishing-ground, but the
Saba fishermen have frequently found the barracouta, caught here and on the bank
between St. Christopher and St. Eustatius, poisonous.

There appears to be no tide on the Saba Bank, and very little current was observed
during the survey which was made in the winter months (Admiralty Directions).

AVES, or BIRD’S ISLAND.—This solitary island lies nearly S. 4 W. from Saba,
distant about 40 leagues; it rises from the surface of the water about 16 feet, and
appears at a distance like a sand-bank; to its east and E.N.E. sides some rocky reefs
are connected, which extend a considerable way out, and anchorage may be found at
its S.W. part, about the distance of a pistol-shot from the island; here there are said

62 ST. BARTHOLOMEW.

to be 3, 4, or 5 fathoms, white sand. Two little rocky islets lie off the N.W. and west
sides of the island, which are joined to Aves by reefs, which are visible; there are
also a few trees growing on the island, and plenty of turtle frequent its shore; no
pond nor fresh water exists, but by digging a little distance within the island, springs
may perhaps be found. Numerous birds frequent this island, and render it of a
white appearance with their dung.

This small island was visited by H.M.S. Racehorse, in March, 1835. On the 17th,
in the afternoon the Island of Aves was seen. The evening was very fine, and
although it had been well looked for, the island was first observed from the deck,
about 6 miles distant. The sandy beach of the island appeared like a white line
below the horizon, the grass, with which the top is covered, being of the same colour
Be: the water that surrounds it, renders it most difficult to be seen until close on

oard of it.

The officers of the Racehorse landed the next morning, and the meridian altitude
of the sun was observed over the sea horizon by three observers, the mean of which
give the latitude 15° 40’ 56”, and the longitude, deduced by chronometer, from Port
Royal, 63° 36’ 45".

A light had been observed upon the island the night before, and a party of Danes,
from the Island of St. Thomas, were on the island gathering the eggs of the birds
that inhabit the island. The birds were seen in such numbers that they appeared
like a cloud hanging over it. They are of two species of Sterna. The Danes collect
the eggs twice a day, and during the time we were on shore, nearly enough were
gathered by the boat’s crew to load the gig.

The form of the island is a long oval, in length about 800 paces, and in the broadest
part 120 paces; it is not quite level, the highest part is only 16 feet above the surface
of the sea. The centre of the island is covered with grass, and a verge between that
and the shingle all round, of a species of armosea, about 16 paces wide. In the
middle of the island, on the south side, is a permanent hut for the egg collectors, off
which there is good anchorage. In the centre, near the highest ground, is a tomb.
The governor, a person at the head of a party of egg collectors, having died, was
buried there.

The Racehorse did not anchor, but soundings were carried out from the hut from a
cable’s length to $ a mile, with 3, 5, 54, 6, and 7 fathoms, where there is good anchor-
age with the hut bearing north, being protected by the reefs, bearing east and west ;
then standing S.E. by E., 74, 8, 82, 83, three casts with 9, thirteen casts with 10, 11,
all fine sand, then no bottom at 15 fathoms.

It would be a great advantage if a double row, or more, of cocoa nuts were planted
or sown along the north side of the island; they would not in any way interfere
with the birds, whose eggs are an article of trade to the Danish colonists, and would
render the situation of the island visible to a far greater distance than is the case at
present.

ST. BARTHOLOMEW (Swerpesn).

The ISLAND of ST. BARTHOLOMEW.—Captain E. Barnett, R.N., who has
recently surveyed this island, says,—“ St. Bartholomew contains 2,000 inhabitants;
it is of irregular shape, and deeply indented by numerous sandy bays, separated
by bold and deep rocky acclivities of moderate height. With reference to many
of the Antilles, it may be said to be formed of irregular hills, the loftiest
summit reaching only to the height of 992 feet; it is therefore lower than St.

ST. BARTHOLOMEW, 63

Martin. Its length between the extreme east and west points is 5 miles, and it varies
in breadth from 1 to 2 miles. The island is distinguished from a distance by threé
remarkable hills, near its east end, of nearly the same elevation, forming a triangle;
therefore, when seen at a distance, on the bearing of 8.S.W., W. by S., and N.W. by
W., and of course from the opposite points, they appear as if only two hills; the east-
ernmost is 992 feet high, and more peaked than the others, the southern one 861,
and the northern one 821 feet, and is distinguished by its rounded summit. The
island is in most parts barren and sterile; the numerous little valleys, however, are
well cultivated, and vegetables are at all times to be obtained; its only exports are
cattle, and a little salt. The Harbour of Gustavia, being a free port, is supported by
commerce with the neighbouring islands; generally supplies may be obtained at
almost all periods, but firewood is scarce, and water has to be purchased.

The north and east sides of the island are fringed by a coral reef to a short

distance from the shore, which always shows itself, and off them are several islands
and islets, described hereafter.

The several islands which surround St. Bartholomew, and are dependent upon that
island, are Cocoa Island, Les Ronges, or Little Turtle Rocks, La Tortue, Toc Vers,
Fregatte and Goat Islands, and Sugar Loaf Island. These lie near the island, but
within 5 miles of the north-west end of the island are the following islands, viz :—
Table Rock, Gnooper Rock, Little Gnooper, Fourche Island, Boulanger, and Barrel
of Beef Rock.

The flood-tide about the island, at full and change, runs S.E.; it is then high water
at 10 h. 30 m., and the rise of the tide is from 1 to 2 feet; the winds, which are
sometimes of long continuance, will make some little variation. The sea is alwuys
lowest when the sun is farthest to the north of the line, and so to the contrary.”

“ Cocoa Island is the southernmost of these islets, due south, 6-10ths of a mile from
the bold high bluff which forms the east side of Anse de Grand Saline; this is a
narrow, rugged, rocky islet, slightly wooded on its summit, and about 3 of a mile in
length from north to south, with a small rock nearly connected to its north end; it
is steep-to on all sides, particularly at its south end, but it is not advisable to pass
in-shore of it.

Les Roncrs.—At ? of a mile to the eastward of this island, and nearly 13 mile
S. by W. from the east end of St. Barths, are two very small rocky heads, close
together, called the Little Turtle Rocks, or Les Ronges ; they are steep-to, but being
only 3 or 4 feet above the level of the sea, are very dangerous, if rounding the island
close in the night-time.

La TorTUE is a small flat-topped rocky islet, lying 3 a mile from the north-east
point of the island, to which it is connected by a ledge of dry and sunken rocks;
and 4 of a mile to the N.E. of it are the Granadines, a small ledge, 2 or 3 feet
above the level of the sea, steep-to on its N.E. side, and on which the sea generally
breaks heavily.

Toc Vers is a small pointed rocky islet, the northern and outermost of these we
are describing. When seen from the east or west its north point resembles a lofty
pillar, standing close by the side of the perpendicular cliff, which is about 120 feet
high, and is very remarkable. It is steep-to on its north and west sides.

FREGATTE AND BoNHOMME, or GoaT ISLANDS, are two large islands, of considerable
elevation, scantily clothed with grass and low wood, and are readily distinguished ;
the latter is separated from the N.W. side of St. Barths, by a clear channel, 3-10ths
of a mile wide, but it is not advisable to pass to the southward of either of these
islands.

64 8ST. BARTHOLOMEW.

Sucar Loar Isnanp is very remarkable, having the exact form which its name
imports, when seen from any direction. Although similar in appearance to the
Gnooper, its position and greater elevation, being 181 feet above the level of the sea,
readily points it out; it lies nearly 13 mile west of the Harbour of Gustavia, and
serves as a good guide for strangers for finding the entrance; it is clear on all sides
and steep-to, except the north, from whence a narrow ledge of dry and sunken rocks
extends in that direction nearly 2-10ths of a mile; at its extremity there are two

small rocks, about 4 or 5 feet above the level of the sea, which are steep-to.

TaBLE Rock is a small rocky islet, nearly barren, and when seen from the north-
ward or southward has somewhat the appearance of a shoe, with the heel to the
westward, where it is about 30 feet above the level of the sea; it is clear all round,
and may be approached on its west side to within + of a mile.

GNooPEeR Rock is a rocky barren islet, almost circular, and about 2-10ths of a
mile in diameter, and very much resembles in appearance the Mollybeday and Sugar
Loaf Islands. It rises on all sides abruptly, and terminates in a rounded summit,
146 feet above the level-of the sea. From its south side a coral ledge of dry and
broken rocks extends off to the distance of a cable’s length, leaving a small vein of
deep water between it and the little Gnoopers; from all other quarters it may be
approached within 4a mile. The channel between it and the able Rock may be
navigated freely. ‘

THE LiTTLE GNOOPERS are a small group of detached black barren rocks, the
southernmost lying 3 a mile S.S.W. from the Gnooper Island, and the northernmost
one 15 feet in height, the intermediate ones being much lower; they are bold-to on
all Sanh aaa Ys towards the Gnooper, to which, as before stated, they are nearly
connected.

Foucue IsLanp, or Five IsLanps, are really but one island, with five remarkable
barren, rocky, peaked elevations, which, seen from a certain distance from the N.E.
or 8.W., have somewhat the appearance of being small separate islands. The two
western hills are nearly of the same elevation, being about 350 feet above the level
of the sea, the others are a little lower; at a certain distance, therefore, it has the
appearance of being only two islands. It is elbow-shaped, its northern arm being
of a mile, and its eastern 3 a mile in length, and + of a mile broad. At the east, also
at the west end, there is a small low detached islet, lying a very short distance only
from the shore, with dry sunken rocks between. A cable’s length to the westward of
the south end of the island there is a very small detached rock just showing itself
above the level of the sea.

There is anchorage on the §.W. side with the prevailing winds, but it is edvisable
not to go further into the bight than midway between the ends of the island, with the
S.E. point bearing E. by S., where you may ride with ease; closer in, under the land,
the wind is so baffling and unsteady, that in weighing you can hardly depend upon
casting the right way, and there is no room to manceuvre. Ships, however, in case of
necessity, may haul in close under the eastern arm, passing to the westward of the
little rock we have noticed. There is good landing on the sandy bay at the N.E.
corner ; the island is clear and steep on all sides.

Sup IsLanp, or La BouLancGER, isa small, barren, rugged, black, rocky islet,
rising abruptly from the sea to the height of about 120 feet, separated 2 cables’
length from a remarkable pillar-shaped rock, 4 a mile to the eastward of it, which
from its resemblance to a vessel under sail, end on, has been called the sail rock, and
which is nearly the same height. These islands are very remarkable and cannot be
mistaken.

THE BARREL OF BEEF is a small, square, black rock, only 10 feet above the
level of the sea, and steep-to on all sides but the N.W., which is foul for a cable’s
length off.

GUSTAVIA HARBOUR.—The Harbour of Gustavia is situate on the S.W. side
of the island, 15 mile to the N.W. of the south point; the only part of it, however,
that can be termed a harbour, is the inner part, a little arm of the sea, which runs in
to the 8.E., called the Carenage, on the side of which the ‘own is situate; but it will
only admit vessels of 5 or 6 feet water, and for the want of an outlet at the inner
end, is filling up by the debris washed down from the steep heights which hound it.
The outer part is a safe and commodious anchorage during the prevailing winds, but
being exposed from the south by the west to N.W., it cannot be safe in the hurricane
season, and it will not admit vessels of greater draught than 17 feet. Ships, however,
of the largest size will find tolerable anchorage under the land, from the islet to the
west end of the island.

THE CARENAGE is 2500 feet long, 650 feet wide at its inner part, and 400 at the
narrowest part of the entrance. It is bounded on its S.W. side by a rocky ridge of
moderate elevation, terminating at its S.E. end in the little sandy bay or cove of
Anse de Gallet, the shore of which is only 300 feet from the head of the Carenage ;
and at its N.W. end by a bold abrupt headland, on the summit of which is Fort Oscar,
of 4 guns, 136 feet above the level of the sea. On the N.E. side it is backed
by a ridge of wocded hills, 266 feet in height, terminating in a precipitous acclivity,
on which is Fort Gustavus IV., 170 feet high, and which protects the entrance
and points out the locality of the harbour to a stranger ; the town is quite out of sight
even at a short distance.

Tue OurEr Harzour, or anchorage, is confined in a square space about 8 cables
in extent, which may be entered on the §.E., south, or west. The S.E. CHANNEL is
between the Saintes and the shore. The Saintes are three small, low, rugged islets,
nearly connected with each other, the two largest by a dry ridge, and the smallest, or
westernmost, by a shallow ledge, which extends from it towards the Bluff of Fort
Oscar to within 350 feet of the shore, leaving a channel of only about 200 feet, not
3 a cable’s length; too narrow and dangerous for a stranger to attempt, particularly
as when under the high land the wind is so very variable that your ship is not under
fall command, and this is also to be observed in navigating the other passages, par-
ticularly when the breeze is strong, and to the northward of east.

THE SourH CHANNEL is between the Saintes and Les Islettes, which are two
remarkable barren rugged islands, lying north and south of each other, separated
about 100 yards at their base by a coral ledge; the northern one is elevated 98 feet
above the level of the sea. From the S.E. end of the southern island, a ledge, with
two small rocky islets, extends off to the distance of $ a cable, where it terminates
by the smallest of these rocks, which is very steep-to. Between this rock and the
N.W. Saintes is the channel, which is } of a mile wide.

With the prevailing winds, to enter this way, get well to the eastward, and run
the Saintes down close on board, within a cable’s length, and haul sharp round the
end rock, against which you may almost rub your sides ; should the wind be from the
E.N.E. you will most probably not fetch the anchorage, therefore keep your ship well
under your command, so that you insure staying. You may stand towards the islets
without fear; a ledge extends off a little more than a ship’s length from the north and
east sides, which being seen by the discoloured water, is readily avoided. Should you
weather this you may stand boldly over to the shore as far as necessary to enable you
to fetch a berth. If you do not weather the islets, there is room to make a short tack
to the eastward; should, however, the wind be so far to the northward under the
shore, it is better for a stranger to enter by the western channel.

THE WESTERN CHANNEL, between the islets and the shore, is 450 fathoms wide,
and the only danger to be avoided is the foul ground off the north end of the great
islets, before noticed. If coming from the eastward, you may do this by passing
either outside the"Sugar Loaf, or between it and the islets; if you pursue the latter
route, haul close round the west, or outside the Baliene, a small dangerous rock,
awash, which lies nearly % of a mile to the westward of the islettes, and tack at your

pleasure, inshore. The Baliene is steep-to, and the channel is clear between it and

We have only again to observe, that, in navigating either of these channels, you

fringed by a reef, through which, however, in the Bay of St. John’s, there is a small
opening which will admit a small vessel.

Vessels running through between St. Bartholomew and St. Martin’s should pass
to the northward and westward of the Table Rock, and those bound to the Harbour
of Gustavia, should open the Sugar Loaf, to the southward of the island, before
passing the east end, to avoid Les Roques or Ronges.”

The Islands of St. Bartholomew, St. Martin, Anguilla, Dog Island, and the
numerous islets in their vicinity, being all upon a distinct bank of soundings, may be
considered as forming one group. ‘This bank extends only a few miles to the west-
ward of these islands, but to the eastward of Anguilla, a long spit of soundings runs
off to the eastward nearly 30 miles, about 20 to the eastward of St. Martin, and
about 14 miles to the eastward and southward of St. Bartholomew. The Anguilla
Bank stretches in a northerly direction from the body of Anguilla, about 20 miles;
near the edges of this bank are only 30 to 35 fathoms, decreasing towards the islands,
bottom chiefly coral and shells.

Captain Barnett, R.N., gives the position of Fort Oscar, Gustavia Harbour, in
latitude 17° 53’ 58” and longitude 62° 51’ 30’; and further remarks: “During the
period of our survey, between the months of November and March, we could detect
neither tidal stream nor current among these islands, except on one or two occasions
whilst at anchor in Crocus Bay, at Anguilla, we swung to a weatherly, or easterly
stream; and once only experienced a westerly current of 1 mile per hour to the
eastward of St. Bartholomew, after a lengthened period of strong breezes from the
N.E. quarter. We found no difficulty in beating up from one island to the other.”

ST. MARTIN. (France anp THE NETHERLANDS.)

The ISLAND of ST. MARTIN.*—“The general figure of St. Martin forms an
equilateral triangle ; its sides facing to the east, N.W., and S.E., each 7$ miles in
length, but it is deeply indented and cut into by bays and lagoons, some of which
afford good anchorage. In comparison with many of the Antilles, it may be called
only hilly, its highest part, which is the table land, in the centre of the island, being
1361 feet above the level of the sea. ‘There are, however, several remarkable
elevations; the Saddle Hill, on the N.W. end of the island, although only 377 feet
in height, is a conspicuous object when seen from the north side of Dog Island.
Morne Fortune forming a bold promontory and conical peak, on the east side of
Simpson Lagoon, 293 feet high; the southernmost bare rocky peak of the western
range of hills, which, when seen from the N.W. and S.E., resembles a colossal face

on its N.E. side, leaning back, 900 feet high; and the conical hill, upon which is
placed Fort William, in Great Bay, 697 feet in height. The north-west part of the
island belongs to the French, and the south-east part to the Dutch. The west end of
the island terminates in a low sandy point; the N.E. point is high and bold, and
being separated from the main ridge by a deep broad valley, has the appearance of
a separate island, when seen at a distance from W.N.W. or E.S.E. direction; the
§.E. end is lofty bluff, faced by a very remarkable perpendicular white cliff, and
from which it receives the name of Point Blanche.”

The Derrotero describes St. Martin’s Island as having many hills and valleys, but
no mountain of consequence. On the §.W. side, as before observed, vessels may
anchor more conveniently and safely there than at any other about the island. At
the southern side of Grande Bay, stands St. Peter’s Fort, and on the N.W. point is
Amsterdam Fort, which amply defends the anchorage. In a line drawn from these
points there are from 6 to 9 fathoms, sandy bottom, and large ships should not go far
within this line; but nearer the shore it shallows to 5, 4, 38, and 2 fathoms. Two
miles §. 4 W. from Amsterdam Fort, is a dangerous shoal, called the Man-of-War
Rock ; it is about 23 cables’ length in circumference, and has not more than 10 feet
water over it; but there are 6 fathoms within a few feet to the westward of the
shoalest part. Upon a conical-shaped hill, above Fort Amsterdam, there is a fort
with a flagstaff, called Fort Shipley. The flagstaff half-way between the flagstaff
and barracks on Fort Amsterdam, is the mark for the rock. If you wish to
pass to the southward of the rock, do not open the horizon between the island
of St. Bartholomew and the high round key, called the Sugar Loaf, to the southward
of it. In standing in from the southward of Grande Bay, keep Fort Shipley open on
either side of the bluff on which Fort Amsterdam stands. Between St. Bartholomew
and St. Martin are several large, high, and steep rocks with channels between them.
The small islands belonging to St. Martin, are Middleburg or Hat Key, and the four
Mangroves Islands, or Pinel, Orleans, Manibrelda, and the Bird. The French town
lies at the north-western part of the island, in a bay called Marigot, having a fort on
the east side of it, and anchorage in from 4 to 7 fathoms, sandy ground; there are
also several small coves, or places of anchorage, to the eastward of Marigot, and a
large but shallow cove, called Oyster Bay, on the eastern side of the island. The
channel between St. Martin and Anguilla is good and clear from danger except a
small sunken rock, which lies directly north of the N.E. end of St. Martin, over
which are only 3 feet water, this is named the Spanish Rock.

GRANDE Bay, on Great Bay.—Point Blanche forms the S.E. point of Great Bay,
and Point Amsterdam, a rocky promontory, on which stands the ruins of a fort and
barracks. The south-west point is a mile in breadth, and nearly the same dimension
in depth; the north side of the bay is a very low sandy ridge, upon which is the
town of PHILLIPSBURGH, and immediately at the back, or north side of it, there is an
extensive and valuable salt-pond. ‘The eastern shore of the bay is very high, with
deep valleys, through which the wind rushes with great force, and should be guarded
against after rounding Point Blanche, on entering; the heights terminate to the N.E.
in a remarkable conical peak, 633 feet in height. As you advance into the bay, the
breeze generally draws off from the town, you should therefore pass Point Blanche
within + ofa mile. From a short dista\ce to N.W. of the bluff, a narrow sand-bar
sweeps round the east and north sides of the bay, 4-10 hs of a mile from the shore,
having from 8 to 10 feet on it, and { of a mile from the western shore there is a cut,
through which 11 feet may be carried. Inside there is a narrow and deep vein having
from 12 to 15 feet; there is also a similar cut through the east end.

Large ships should anchor nearly midway between the points, in 6 fathoms
Point Blanche bearing E.8.E., and the Governor’s staff, which is near the east end of
the town, N. by E. 2 E. Vessels drawing 14 feet, may lie further in, with the Governor’s
staff in one with the highest peak of the highest bill on the east side of the bay,
above noticed, and the second, or outer bluff, to the westward of Point Amsterdam,
in one with the ruin of the fort on that joint, in 19 feet; the holding ground is

good, but generally heavy rollers make the riding here very uneasy, and cause a heavy

surf on the beach. In approaching the bay from the southward, or beating up to it

es the westward, great care should be taken to avoid the Man-of-War, or Proselyte
hoal.

PROSELYTE SHOAL.—This dangerous rock is not above 100 feet in extent, and
has from 15 to 18 feet water over it, and seldom breaks in the strongest breezes. The
marks to find it are, Fort William, in one with the ruin of the barrack on Point Am-
sterdam, bearing N. 1° W.; and the Governor’s flagstaff in one with a remarkable
house, standing on the lower part of the ridge of hills to the N.E. of the town, and
close to the highest conical peak, before noticed, on the east side of the bay; this,
however, is a difficult mark to be distinguished by a stranger. It bears S.W. from
Point Blanche 1,4, of a mile distant. On the south and west sides it lies just within
the line of 10 fathoms; to the S.E. of it a ledge runs off ¢ of a mile, with a depth of
from 6 to 9 fathoms, and warns you of your approach from that quarter. In standing
in from the southward you should not open the conical peak, on the east side of the
bay, before noticed, to the westward of Point Blanche Bluff. In working up from the
westward within it, do not open the eastern or highest hill of St. Bartholomew to the
southward of the Gnoopers Island, or Mollybeday, more than its own breadth to the
eastward of Point Blanche.

To the westward of Point Amsterdam, the shore becomes indented by small sandy
bays, separated by bold woody'‘heights as far as the low rocky point, which forms the
east end of Simpson Bay, 24 miles distant. From this point a narrow ledge, on which
there are from 2 to 4 fathoms, stretches to the southward 3 a mile.

THE PELICAN Rocxs.—A cluster ofsmall detached heads, 3 or 4 feet above the level
of the sea, lies to the N.W. of the point, 14 cable’s length from the shore.

Simpson Bay.—From hence, a low sandy shore sweeps around to the westward,
forming Simpson Bay, a mile in width, and 4 a mile in depth; there is anchorage
midway between the points, in the centre of the bay, in 43 fathoms, but not good ; at
the east end of the bay there is a boat channel into the Lagoon; from hence to the
west end ofthe island, the shore is very low—sandy beaches, separated by low, rocky,
and sandy cliffs.

Approaching the west end of the island the shore is very low; great caution
should be observed in rounding it, particularly in the night, for a very shallow spit,
which may be seen in the day-time when the water is clear, runs off to the W.S.W.,
= ofa mile; therefore, in rounding this end of the island, the Five Islands should be
kept open off St. Martin until you are certain of being to the northward of the spit;

. and then indeed a ship should be cautious not to haul up too suddenly, or come within
the depth of 10 fathoms, as the N.W. end of the island is foul nearly a mile from shore.
In working up to Marigot, it is advisable to keep the Anguilla shore on board, and
not to come within the depth of 7 fathoms on the St. Martin side, until the western
bluff of the bay of Marigot bears south.

Manicor is the chief town and pert of entry of the French part of the island, and
lies at the base of a hill in the centre of the bay, on which is seen the fort (almost in
ruins) which protects it. The bay between Bluff Point, on the west, and Hancock
Point on the east, is 13 mile wide, and a mile deep, and has very good anchorage with
the wind from all points except the N.W., in from 33 to 45 fathoms. Fort Marigot
is in latitude 18° 4° 7’, and longitude 638° 5’ 45".

MEDEE Rock.—The only danger to be avoided is the Medee Rock, recently dis-
covered by that ship striking upon it; the shoal is nearly circular, and a cable’s length
in diameter, and on its N.E. side has as little as 15 feet, with 20 to 24 feet to the S.W.
of it; it bears W. by N. nearly 4-10ths of a mile from Hancock Point, and between it
and the shore there are 4 fathoms water. In entering the bay from the eastward, the
Saddle Hill, near the N-W- point ofthe island, already noticed, should be kept open
of the north side of Bluff Point, until Round Hill, a remarkably little, woody, isolated

SAINT MARTIN. 69

eminence on the bay shore, is in one with Morne Fortune, when you may haul up and
anchor on this line, or a little to windward of it, in 4 fathoms, with Crole Rock just
open to the northward of the island.

This bay is exposed to the rollers which break on the §.W. side of the bay, $ a mile
from the shore, and send in a heavy surf on the beach. From Round fill to the town
the shore is skirted by a coral ledge, which makes landing extremely difficult, except
at a spot at the east end of the town, under the west side of Fort Hill, and here even
you must be careful of sunken rocks, which lie off a short distance.

From Hancock Point to the N.E. end of the island the shore is clear, and may be
approached by the lead to within § a mile. The most remarkable object on this part
of the coast is the Crole Rock, a small, barren, black, rocky islet, with a rounded top,
rising on its north side perpendicularly from the sea to the height of 120 feet, and
separated from an adjacent point of the island, equally remarkable from its terminating
in a detached conical peak of somewhat greater elevation.

The N.E. point of the island is skirted by a reef, which always shows itself to the
distance of 2 cables’ length, and which is bold-to. From hence the coast turns abruptly
to the south; two miles from the N.E. point is Orient Bay, 4 a mile wide at its en-
trance, and a mile deep ; its entrance is between two small islands, of moderate eleva-
tion, skirted by dry reefs ; from Penels to the northernmost one, it extends off nearly
2 a mile, being, however, exposed to the full force of the trade wind and sea, it is only
safe for droghers, or small vessels, which find shelter at both ends of it. From the
southern island the shore is foul and dangerous as far as abreast Guano Kay, 13 mile
to the northward of Point Blanche. There is, however, a small opening in the reef
leading to the Oyster Pond, a small cove with 10 feet water in it, where small vessels
find security in the hurricane months, but it is difficult to enter. This side of the
island. should not be approached within the line of the adjacent islands, Mollybeday
and Tintaman, except in cases of necessity.

Guano Kay lies 14 mile N.E. by E. § E. from Point Blanche, and 4-10ths of a
mile from the nearest point of the island. Itisa small rocky island, rising almost
abruptly from the sea toa height of 100 feet, and is slightly wooded ; it is bold-to on
its S.E. and S.W. sides, but nearly 3 a mile to the N.E. of it there are two small rocks,
a little above the surface, over which the sea breaks continually.

HEN AND CHICKENS are a cluster of small barren rocks, extending in a N.E. and
S.W. direction nearly 2-10ths of a mile. The S.W. rock is 15 feet high, the others
not more than 4 ord feet. They are steep-to on all sides, and bear H. 2 N. nearly 2
miles from Point Blanche.

MoLLEBeEDAY is similar in appearance to.Guano Cay, its rocky sides slightly wooded
rising abruptly to a height of 145 feet; it is foul on the S.E. side to the distance of
4 amile, and j of a mile H.S.E. from it there is a small ledge of rocks, a little above
the surface, which always show themselves. There isa clear channel inshore of the
island, and also between it and the Hen and Chickens, but they should be pursued
only in case of necessity.

TINTAMARRE ISLAND is 13 mile long, N.E. by E. and 8.W. by W., and % a mile
broad ; its north shore is a bold rocky cliff, which, towards the east end of the island
is almost perpendicular to the height of 157 feet, topped with trees, and when seen
from the eastward is very remarkable; the east end is also rocky but much lower ;
its south and west sides are low and sandy; the whole island is fringed by a coral
reef, except at the west end. On the north and east sides it does not extend more
than + of a mile, but on its south side it reaches to 3 a mile from the beach, and ter-
minates at the S.W. point of the island. There is landing in the sandy bay at the
west end. ‘The island is uninhabited.

The, channel between the §.W. end of the reef at Tintamarre and Penel’s Island
reef is 8 of a mile wide, but it should not be navigated unless absolutely necessary,
more particularly from the danger of falling in with the Spanish Rock.

The SPANISH Rock is a very small head of coral, just beneath the surface, over
which the sea breaks heavily in strong breezes, but in moderate weather it does not
discover itself. It lies 14, mile N.W. from the S.W. end of Tintamarre, and 11 mile
E. by N. 4 N. from the N.E. point of St. Martin. The marks to clear it are Fort ~
William, just seen over the eastern high land, in one with the highest part of Penel
Island, at its east end, S.S.W. 3 W. leads clear to the S.E. of it. The S.W. end of
Tintamarre on with the first hollow to the eastward in the high land at the west end
of St. Bartholomew (an indifferent mark) leads to the S.E. of it; and the Crole Rock
just open of the N.E. point of St. Martin leads clear to the northward ; ships, there-
fore, running or beating through Anguilla Channel have only to be careful not to
shut in the Crole Rock.

Anguilla is separated from St. Martin by a clear navigable channel, 31 miles in
width in its narrowest part, which is between Crole Rock and Blowing Point.

THE ISLAND OF ANGUILLA.

ANGUILLA (Great Brirary).

The ISLAND of ANGUILLA belongs to England, and lies to the northward of
St. Martin’s; its S.W. end bearing nearly N. by W. from the N.W. point of that
island, from which it is only distant 45 miles; it is long and narrow, its shores
irregular and much twisted about, which circumstance seems to have given it the
name of Anguilla, or the Eel. From the S.W. point it runs in a N.E. by E. direc-
tion 14-miles; the western part is very narrow, but to the north-eastward it becomes
about 3 miles wide; it is not mountainous, but low, sandy, and unproductive, being
covered with dwarf timber. ‘The chief occupation of the inhabitants is the breeding
of cattle and procuring salt. There are anchorages on the western and southern
sides, and the current very little felt. Off its N.E. point lies the islet named the
Grand Scrub, from the east end of which a reef runs out a considerable way into the
sea. Off the N.W. end of this is a large rock, above water, called the Little Scrub.
There is also a small island to the westward of Anguilla, called Sandy Island, round
which are several rocks, under water ; and off the 8.W. point are two islands, called
the Great and Little Anguilletta, the latter also being called the Blowing Rock, from
a hole through which the sea forces itself, and at a distance resembles the blowing of
a whale. Vessels may safely pass to the southward of Anguilletta, and between
Anguilla and Sandy Island, keeping mid-channel, or between Anguilla Island and
St. Martin’s; but in this latter passage care must be taken to avoid a rock, under
water, before described, which lies a little way off the N.E. point of St. Martin.

The south side of the island, from its N.E. point as far as Rendezvous Bay, is
skirted within from 1 to 2 cables’ length of the shore by a coral reef, dry in many
places, through which there are several little openings, which admit boats of a large
size into good shelter; the reef is steep-to, and may be run down within 3 a mile
without danger. This reef terminates at the 8.E. point of Rendezvous Bay, from
which it extends 2-10ths of a mile; having avoided this, a small vessel may anchor
in the bay in 4 fathoms, where wood and water may be obtained.

The Browine Rock has the appearance of a whale blowing ; it is a small rocky
islet, S.E. by E., ¢ of a mile from the S.W. point of the island, and is 6 feet above
the level of the sea; it is steep-to on the south side, but inside it there is no passage
except for boats.

ANGUILLETTA is a smali rocky cay, 20 feet in height, covered with brushwood, and
lies 4 of a mile W.S.W. from the end of the island, and to which it is almost con-
nected by coral heads, having a passage only for boats ; it is bold-to on its west side.

Having rounded the west side, the South Wager will be seen standing out about
2-10ths of a mile from the shore.

SourTH WAGER is a remarkable small barren rock, about 20 feet in height; as also
the perpendicular cliffs forming the S.W. point of Anguilla on its north side. From
hence to the east end of Long Bay beach the shore is clear and ateep-to.

Sanpy IsLAnD is a low strip of sand covered with brushwood to the height of 6
feet, and lies 1,3, mile W.N.W. from Road Bay Bluff; and on the same line of bear-
ing, 4-10ths of a mile from the island, is Bowling Cay, a very small rocky islet, about
4 feet above the level of the sea; there is no passage between the two, and shoal
ground extends from Sandy Island to the S.E. nearly 4 a mile, and to the westward
a mile, leaving a channel between the shoals and Anguilla nearly 4 a mile wide.
The remarkable peak to the south end of the high land of St. Martin, which we have

* ealled the Face Peak, in one with the rocky point which terminates the east end of

Long Bay, bearing 8.8S.E., clears the west end of the shoals; on the north side the
bank is steep-to.

From Long Bay Point, which is low and sandy, the island becomes more elevated,
and from thence to Road Bay, the face of the shore is composed of cliffs, almost
perpendicular, which are remarkable, and about 150 feet in height.

Roap Bay is nearly a mile in width, and 6-10ths in depth, and affords an excellent
anchorage for small vessels of 12 or 14 feet draught; on the low sand-bank, which
forms the inner side of the bay, there is a small settlement, the inhabitants of which
cultivate the large salt-pond immediately behind it.

From Road Bay the shore continues bold and scarped, turning gradually to the
N.E. and north, until it terminates at Flat Cap Point, forming the northern extre-
mity of Crocus Bay.

CROCUS BAY.—In the eastern corner of Crocus Bay is the principal settlement
in the island. The custom-house stands at present on the summit of the hill, which
is 213 feet above the level of the sea, and is distinguished by a flagstaff at its N.E.
end; the landing-place is on the sandy bay, directly below it, to the northward, but
there is generally a heavy surf on the beach. There is very good anchorage in the
bay with the prevailing trade winds, by bringing Flat Cap Point to bear N.N.E., and
with the custom-house S.E. 3 E., in 7 fathoms, white sand, good holding-ground, 4 a
mile off shore ; but with the wind from the westward it is not safe. This, however,
seldom happens, and gives sufficient warning to enable you to get under weigh. On
the east side of the bay there is a very remarkable perpendicular cliff, which serves
to point out the anchorage when beating up from the westward.

Near the middle of the bay there is a coral patch, nearly 2-10ths of a mile in
extent, with a depth of 5 and 6 fathoms, which should be avoided. The marks for it
are, the Jewel Rock, a very small rock, lying close to the shore, 4 a mile to the N.E.
of Flat Cap Point, just seen open of that point; and a remarkably large tamarind
tree, on the north side of the landing beach, in one with a conspicuous white house,
on the lowest part of the hill above the beach.

There are two ways by which a ship may approach the anchorage—from the west,
between Prickly Pear Cays and Reef and the island; and from the north, round the
east end of the above reef. ‘The first is by far the safest; indeed, there is no danger
whatever, for a ship may anchor for the night, if necessary, under the south side of
the reef in perfect safety ; the northern channel should not be attempted without a
pilot. This channel from Flat Cap Point to the end of the reef, which bears from it
N.N.E., is 2 miles wide; near the centre of it, however, there is a dangerous narrow
ledge, the south end of which bears N. by E. from Flat Cap Point, 8-10ths of a mile,
and extends in that direction $ a mile further, on which there is as little as 20 feet,
and which breaks heavily in fresh winds; there is a clear passage between it and the
island, and also between it and the reef, which is a mile wide. A vessel leaving the

Stock and firewood may be obtained here, but no water; yams are in abundance, .

and will keep sound on board ship by merely sprinkling over them wood ashes, for

We may notice the anchorage is exposed to heavy rollers, which frequently beset
the coast of this group of islands during the periods from November to March, and
which, striking on the broadside, renders a ship’s position exceedingly uneasy and
uncomfortable. It is difficult to account for this phenomenon in these seas, as it occurs
in calms as well as in strong breezes, and it reaches as far as Antigua. Captain
Barnett gives the position of the Custom-house, in Crocus Bay, in latitude 18° 13’ 6",
longitude 63° 4’ 39”.

To the eastward of Crocus Bay the shore becomes skirted by shoals. Two miles
from Flat Cap Point a dry reef sweeps off to the N.E., a mile from the shore; and
4 miles from the point, and nearly § a mile from the main reef, there is a dangerous
breaker, which is not seen atall periods, and is very steep-to ; the shore continues foul
to within a mile of the N.E. point of the island. A ship, however, beating up on this
side will ensure her safety by common attention to the lead, the depth suddenly
increasing on your approach to within 16 to 22 fathoms of the breaker; within the
reef, at the west end, there is a boat shelter, and through an intricate opening, near
the east end, small droghers find anchorage. :

Sorus IsLAND is separated from the N.E. point of Anguilla by a narrow channel,
8-10ths of a mile wide, through which there is a deep vein of water; but it should
not be navigated, as the point of Anguilla is skirted by a reef nearly dry, a cable’s
length off, upon which you might be thrown by the sudden flaws of wind which come
off the ends of all these islands.

Scrub Island takes the same line of bearing as Anguilla, and is 2 miles long and
4 a mile broad, and is covered with brushwood and small trees, which rise to the height
of 50 feet, near the west end; its east end is very low, and from it there extends a
narrow strip of rocks, which become detached near the extremity to the distance of
2 a mile ; they are bold-to, but this end of the island should be carefully approached
from the N.E., as you are apt to come upon these rocks before you are aware of it,
being hidden by the high part of the island behind them, and the lead gives no warning.
In strong breezes the sea breaks over them, although they are § or 10 feet above the
level. About the centre of the north side of the island there is a little hill of white
sand-stone, which, when the sun shines onit, is very conspicuous. Three-quarters ofa
mile west of this, and nearly a mile north of the west end of the island is Little Serub,
rendered equally conspicuous by the contrast in colour, it being a barren precipitous
rock, rising abruptly on its N.E. side to the height of 40 feet ; there is no ship channel
between these Islands, but it may be approached from the northward without fear.
The south side of the Scrub is quite clear, and there is good landing on the sandy
beach, at the N.W. end of the island, where there is good shooting.”*

To sail from St. Kitt’s for the Dog Island and Prickly Pear Passage, aN.N.W. iW.
course, 45 miles, will bring you to the west of St. Martin’s; from hence a N. 3 W., 12
miles, will bring you to the passage, but from the lee side of St. Kustatius, a N. 2 W.
course, 46 miles, will take you to the passage.

Point, at Crocus Bay. It is 14 mile in extent, from east to west, and 8-10ths of a

Two-tenths of a mile from the south shore there is a remarkable little black rock,

WEST CAY.—From hence a broken ledge of rocks runs out until it reaches a
small low rocky cay, 6 feet in height, which lies $ of a mile west of the island ; it may
be passed without fear within 3 of a mile in day-time, but should be approached
very cautiously during the night, as the lead is not of much use.

Mipp.x Isuanp is nearly connected to Dog Island by a ledge of dry rocks ; this is
a remarkable barren islet, its N.E. side being a bold perpendicular black rock, 60 feet
in height.

East Cay is a low and rocky islet, covered with brushwood, and nearly connected
in the same way with Dog Island, and bold-to ; you have no bottom with 109 fathoms,
a mile to the northward of Middle Island.

The PRICKLY PEAR CAYS are divided by a small boat channel. The
westernmost is a narrow rugged rock, with brushwood on its summit to the height of
25 feet, 2 of a mile in length from E. by 8. to W. by N., upon which there is no
landing. ‘The eastern island is a little lower, 4-10ths of a mile long, and 3-10ths
broad; landing may be effected in a little bight on the 8.W. side. Between these
islands and Dog Island there is a clear channel, 25 miles wide; from the west end of

a heavy swell between the islands, and it is therefore advisable for vessels bound to

north of the easternmost, are the Great and Little Flirt Rocks, two small rocky islets ;
the Great Flirt about 20 feet high, the Little Flirt 8 or 10; the ground is foul around
them.

NortH WAGER is a very small rock, only 3 feet above the level of the sea.

From the Little Flirt commences the reef, dry in some places; it stretches to the
eastward 51 miles, and terminates at the northern entrance to Crocus Bay, already
described.

SEAL IsLAnps.—lIn the reef, 14 mile from the west end, are several narrow, low,
rocky islets, called the Seal Islands, and which are about 5 or 6 feet above the level of
the sea. To the northward of these islets, the reef is skirted by detached coral heads,
and should not be approached at least within a mile. To the southward of the Prickly
Pear Islands, and between the Seal Cay Reef and Anguilla, there is excellent anchor-
age, in from 10 to 12 fathoms, and out of the influence of the rollers. :

In approaching the islands we have described, from the northward, from their
being backed by the high lands of St. Martin, navigators are very apt to make a
wrong estimate of their distance from the shore, and which has led to fatal mistakes
on the N.E, side of Anguilla.

SOMBRERO,

SOMBRERO.

This island may be considered the northernmost of the Caribbean Islands. It
appears to be flat, rugged, and without soil, excepting a small patch near the centre,
on which grows a, little grass, some weeds, and a kind of samphire; but there is
nothing which exceeds a foot in height, excepting a few prickly pear plants. It
abounds in a vegetable substance which grows out of the rocks, in form and size like
a melon, but covered with prickles, and with a saltish taste. The island is overrun
with lizards, perfectly black, and about 16 inches long; there are also some land-
crabs and shell-fish ; multitudes of sea-fowl frequent the island, and during the
season, deposit their eggs within the cavities of the rocks. There is no fresh water
in any part, except what may occasionally be found in the hollows of the rocks
after a fall of rain, but which does not remain long, being soon evaporated. The
soundings are very regular all round the islands, with good anchorage on its western
side, in 6 or 7 fathoms, close to the rocks, and these are not more than 18 or 20
fathoms 3 miles off; but the eastern side and to the south-westward the bottom is
rocky. There is no beach of any description, nor any place where turtle can get
on shore. :

The Island of Sombrero cannot be seen more than 6 leagues off; the passages to
leeward and to windward of it are clear; there is little or no swell of the sea, and
vessels passing to the northward of it will be quite out of danger. Sombrero bears
from Dog Island N.W. by N., distant 21 miles.

Light.—On Sombrero a lighthouse is built, the position of which is 18° 35’ 48",
and longitude 63° 27’ 42’. The lighthouse structure consists of an open iron frame-
work, 132 feet high, painted red, and stands about one-third the length of the island,
from its southern extremity, and 60 yards from the cliff on the S.E. side. The light
is a revolving light, attaining its greatest brilliancy every minute. Elevation 150
feet above the sea, and visible 20 miles.

Description of Sombrero, by Captain E. Barnett, late of H.M. ship Thunder.

“ The small rocky island of Sombrero is the north-easternmost of the Antilles, and
its centre lies in latitude 18° 35’ 45", and longitude 63° 27' 46". It is % of a mile
long from N.N.E, to S.S.W., and not more than 150 fathoms wide; at its north
end it is about 20 feet above the level of the sea, and from thence is an ascent
by two distinct steps to the middle of the island, where it reaches the height of 37

several large masses of rock, of the same character as the islet, about 8 feet square,
and which, at a distance, have the appearance of huts. On all sides it is a pre-
cipitous rock, perfectly inaccessible, except at a little bight on the west side, + of

THE VIRGIN ISLANDS. 75

THE VIRGIN ISLANDS.*

These are a numerous cluster of islands situate to the westward of Dog and
Sombrero Islands, and extending from Sombrero to Porto Rico, or from about the
longitude 64° 12’ to 65° 9; their shores are rocky and have proved fatal to many,
but for the safety and accommodation of those who frequent these islands, nature
has formed an extensive basin in the middle, where vessels may ride in safety,
perfectly land-locked, and sheltered from every wind. This basin is called Sir Francis
Drake’s Bay, or Channel; it is about 15 miles long, and 33 broad.

In advancing towards these islands, they will appear to be joined together and
lofty, but they have deep and good channels between them, the seas around abounding
with great varieties of fish. We shall proceed to describe them by going regularly

from east to west, noticing them in rotation as they are situate, and not according to
their importance.

The eastern division of this group of islands belongs to England, and comprises
Anegada, Virgin Gorda, Tortola, Jost Van Dyke’s Isles, Tobago, Normand’s, Peter’s,
Salt, Cooper’s, Ginger, Beef, Camanoe, Scrub, and Guano Island, with numerous islets
in their vicinity. The western division belongs to the Danes, and comprehends
St. John’s, St. James, St. Thomas, Montalvan, Savannah, the Brass, and Hansnetic
Island, and several lesser islets adjacent. The whole group, excepting Anegada, is
bold, craggy, and high.

Tur TrpEs OF THE VIRGIN IsLANDS, by Sir Robert H. Schomburgk, Ph. D.,

“The obstacles opposed to the tidal wave between the Virgin Islands, cause great
irregularity in its set and velocity; and, though coasters reckon upon a windward-
tide from the moon’s rising to her zenith, and upon a leeward-tide from her zenith to
her setting, no dependence can be placed on this, the tides differing often one or two
hours, so that the change from ebb to flood sometimes precedes the rising or setting of
the moon, though it more commonly succeeds it. The windward-tide, or that which
sets to the south, and comes from the Atlantic, on running through these islands,
makes high water ; whilst the ebb, or lee-tide, sets to the N.W. The flood-tide very
probably does not extend far south, being there overcome by the currents existing in
the Caribbean Sea, swelled by the flow of water which issues from the large rivers,
Orinoco, Essequibo, Amazon, &c.; and the northern, or lee-tide, I conceive to be of
still more limited extent, being overcome by the general W.N.W. current so soon as
it leaves the Virgin Islands.

Through the greater part of the year an almost regular tide takes place along
shore among the Virgin Islands: but it is different in mid-channel, where the flood-
tide continues to run south, while the ebb has already commenced to set to the
north-westward, along shore. Asan example, on the western and northern shores
of ‘Tortola the flood acquires its highest level, at full and change, at 10 o’clock,* and
the same takes place, at 15 minutes later, on the southern side; but in mid-channel,
between Tortola and St. John’s, it continues to flow to the windward for an hour-
and-half or two hours longer. The pressure of the ebb-tide appears, however, to be
of minor force, perhaps from the circumstance that the flood-tide comes from the main
ocean, whilst the ebb has not so extensive a range; and, consequently, the difference
of the time between the reflux of the tidal stream near the shore and mid-channel
is not so considerable as in the former instance, seldom amounting to more than 30 to
40 minutes.

THE VIRGIN ISLANDS.

The time during which the flood-stream continues to run to windward in the
middle of the channels, (7. e. between shore and shore of the different islands, is
not everywhere the same among the Virgin Islands, but undergoes great modifications) ;
and whilst to the eastward of Mary Point (the northern angle of St. John’s) it often
amounts toan hour and a half, or two; it is scarcely more than 45 minutes to the
westward of it. Droghers or coasters, acquainted with this fact, when bound to the
westward, make short tacks along shore from Mary Point to Pelican Bay, avoiding
the shore of Tortola as much as possible, and thereby escaping much of the influence
of the north tide; whereas vessels less acquainted, using the whole sea-room afforded
by the channel, are much retarded in their progress.

The direction of the tides is also much cut up and altered in force by the winds
and various impediments which present themselves in the form of promontories,
narrow passages, reefs, shallows, &c.; and it is only with time and by experience
that a navigator may become acquainted with the different sets in the channel
and passages. During the period that I re-surveyed the Virgin Islands, I paid
particular attention to this subject, ana I must freely confess that it was full of
difficulties.

There are four great outflows for the southern or flood-tide, namely :—{. Between
the western end of Virgin Gorda and Peter’s Island, which space affords passages
to the tidal stream entering between Virgin Gorda and the islets to the east of
Tortola. The confiux of so many branches creates necessarily an eddy tide, which

‘we find to the east of Scrub Island. The chief mass of the stream directs its

course thence westerly to the passage between Salt and Peter’s Islands, a branch
escaping between Broken Jerusalem and Round Rock. 2. Between Norman’s
Island and St. John’s. The stream to the west of Road Harbour, in Tortola,
and to the east of Mary Point, at St. John’s, are directed towards this passage,
and unite to the north-east of Red Point; at St. John’s one branch flowing thence
towards Ram’s Head, and the other to the south-east. 3. Between the western
end of St. John’s and the eastern end of St. Thomas’s. The southern tide here is
of considerable strength, and causes no where between these islands so heavy a
swell, the waves becoming often mountains high, and the extent of water over
which the eye sweeps offering the aspect of a raging war between wave and wave.
After having cleared the passages, the stream of the flood-tide directs its course
towards Frenchmau’s Cap, or Bird Island, with the exception of the branch which
runs towards Reef Bay, in an eastern direction. 4. Between the western end of
St. Thomas’s and Culebra. A branch of this great outflow sets through the passage
between the western end of St. Thomas's and West Bay, running off towards

Brigantine; a stream strikes, however, to the south-east. Having cleared the
different passages, the southern tide is now acted upon by the trade wind, and
