The ebb-tide, with a few exceptions, takes a more decided north-western direction.
Its first great outflow is between Guano Island and Tortola: its second between
the western end of Tortola, and Mary Point; and its third between Green Cay
and Thatch Cay. The velocity with which the northern tide runs through these
three passages is no where surpassed, though it has a great many bye-ways for its
outflow, which the map will point out. From the harbour of Tortola a stream of
the ebb-tide sets easterly, which is again met by another coming from the passage
at Peter’s Island, and by a third from the Round Rock passage; they unite off
the southern bluff point of Beef Island, causing an eddy tide and a considerable
swell.

Frenchman’s Bay is divided from the main land of Tortola by a small and shallow
channel; generally speaking the tide sets here west. ‘This would be its natural
direction during the ebb-tide, and the reverse during flood; but at that period the
tidal stream running with great velocity through the passage between Tortola and
Thatch Island, it finds itself a second time compressed by the narrow passage between
Frenchman’s Bay and little Thatch Island; the waters on escaping this compression
extend and come in contact with the bluff at the tower, and a reflux takes place
towards the passage, which acts as an in-draught, forming consequently at flood-tide
an eddy race round the whole island.

This passage is said to have become deeper within the recollection of many of the
inhabitants; if this is really the case, it must be in consequence of the transporting
power of this local current.

The velocity of the tides between the Virgin Islands depends very much on local
circumstances. Where two streams unite, after having made their way through
different passages, the velocity is generally increased. ‘The southern tide is of con-
siderable force between St. John’s and St. Thomas’s; I have known that tide to be
so strong, that six able boatmen could make no progress or headway for hours ;
jt must then have run at the rate of five miles. The same is the case between
St. John’s and the Tortola shore. But the north-western tide is of still greater
strength than the flood-tide, though the latter comes from the Atlantic; the pre-
vailing current in the latitude of these islands setting W.N.W., the flood-tide has to
overcome its opposing force, which weakens its velocity. This is not the case with
the ebb, where the set of the tide and the current being nearly the same, the latter
adds its force to the first and increases its velocity. I have seen many vessels, on
beating through these islands during a north-western tide, fixed to one and the same
spot for a considerable time ; and others come to an anchor, relinquishing the contest
with so heavy a lee-tide.

The tides have their greatest force at springs, but especially at the day of full
and change; and the tide which happens at the time this takes place is considerably
stronger than the previous one. The velocity of the northern tide is strongest between
Beet Island and Comanoe, and it is often impossible to cross from one island to
the other during such a tide. The attempt proved nearly fatal to Mr. L., of Beef
Island ; who, on returning from Comanoe, thought himself strong enough to contend
with the opposing tide, but was soon deprived of his oars, which were instantly
swept away. Finding that the northern current set him to leeward, he used the
seats of his boat as paddles, which met, however, the same fate as the oars. Mean-
while the tide changed, and at daybreak, he found himself drifting towards the
Round Rock passage. Without fresh water or a morsel to eat, his boat became
the sport of the changing tides for the next two days, sometimes so near Beef Island
that he could not think but that the boat would be drifted ashore, and a southern

THE VIRGIN ISLANDS.

tide then sweeping him towards the Round Rock or Broken J erusalem. Nearly
overcome by hunger and thirst, and given up for lost by his relations, he was at last
discovered on the third morning by some people from Spanish Town, who hastened
to his assistance.

A very strong northerly tide runs likewise between Tortola and Thatch Island,
which but lately offered a more tragical instance of its force. An African proposing
to return from Belmont Estate, at Tortola, to Thatch Island, late in the evening, on
finding that his companion declined to set off at so late an hour, thought he could
manage the boat alone. He was never seen again; the keel and broken timbers of
the boat were found on the eastern end of the Thatch Island, and told his fate. Not
able to stem the tide, his boat was probably driven against the rocks, and split to
pieces. The oars were some time after picked up in one of the bays on the north
side of St. Thomas’s.

The tides are so powerful in some of the passages between some of the smaller
Virgin Islands, that the buoys attached to the ropes, which indicate where the fish-
pots are placed, sink so, that the fishermen cannot haul them except at slack tide,
when the buoys become again visible. The great strength of these tides is, however,
only partial; their average velocity in general does not exceed a mile and a half or
two miles, in ordinary cases in the channel, and probably decreases at some distance
out to sea.

The medium of the perpendicular rise of the tidal wave between the Virgin Islands
does not amount to more than two feet, being at spring tides 26 to 36 inches, and at
neap-tides 16 to 18 inches. These comparatively low tides tend to prove how
little tide there isin the Atlantic near the equator; and though there is no great
range of coast to produce a considerable elevation, the narrow passage and channel
of which this group is composed might have led us to expect a different result. ‘The
accumulation of water in consequence of the trade winds and the equatorial current,
may, in some respects, prevent a higher elevation; and accordingly we find, that
beyond these latitudes the tide rises to a greater height, even where the range
of coast is not so extensive, as from 8 to 10 feet at the Canaries, — from 4 to 6
at the Cape Verd Islands,—and from 5 to 6 at the Bermudas. The sandy shores
and beaches of the Virgin Islands are flat, or very gently sloping, which we may
take as a proof that the tides have never been of a greater height there, at least not
for several ages; and the progress of the tidal wave must consequently be very
trifling.

The southern tide is predominant during the summer months, 2.é., from the middle
of June to the middle of August; and two tides have been then known to follow in
succession, chiefly if the wind has been westerly. The consequence was, that the
perpendicular rise of the tidal wave was considerably increased, and, as an extra-
ordinary case, the water reached the height of three feet.

There is another circumstance which deserves to be particularly mentioned. At
the period when the southern tide becomes predominant, which is generally in the
middle of June, the tide sets for eight or ten days continually to the south, with a
force very seldom surpassed. It is called by the fishermen the St. John’s tide, the
day of this saint occurring about that period; and commenced last year (1833) on
the 12th of June, lasting to the 21st of the same month. The seine-boats could not
round fish for the whole week, nor were the fishermen able to discover their pots,
the buoys being all sunk. At other times the ebb sets to the north, for the course of
an hour or two, when the flood begins to flow again to the south.

During the months of September, November, March, and April, the northern tide
is prevailing, and of considerable force, being assisted by the current. At this period

also the highest water is generally in the morning, and there is only a half-tide in’
the evening ; the reyerse takes place during the summer months. ;

When the ground sea is not prevailing, the water in the- channels is eyen remark-

able for its clearness, and strangers are often alarmed at seeing the bottom in 8 or 9
fathoms water; the sponge at the bottom is distinctly seen at this depth.”

Sir R. H. Schomburgk concludes by adding the following observations, which may
prove of advantage to the navigation of these channels:—“The passage between
St. John’s and a small bay, lying-midway between the former and the eastern end of
St. Thomas’s, is often selected by vessels bound to St. Thomas’s, and which may have
made the Virgin Islands to the northward of them, This should not be attempted,
however, when there is a northern tide, and the wind any way to the south of east,
ag vessels will then almost certainly be set on the reef, being unable to stem the force
of the northern tide, which is so strong here that droghers have given this passage
the name of the ‘current-hole,’ This passage is especially dangerous during the
spring months, when the northern tide is stronger than at any other period, and the
instances are not few of vessels having been set upon the reef in this direction when
the danger was quite apparent. When the tide sets to leeward, vessels beating to
windward through Drake’s Channel should make short tacks along the St. John’s
shore as soon as they have reached Mary Point, or else stand over towards Jost Van
Dyke’s, and try to fetch the passage between Thatch Island and Tortola; having
reached Pelican Bay or Witch Island, the northern tide trends to the eastward, and
favours a vessel as far as the north-eastern entrance to Drake’s Channel. Should
the tide, however, have changed meanwhile, and, at her arrival off Beef Island, be
flood, the stream there branches off to the south-west, and short tacks should be made
along Beef and Scrub Islands until the cays called the Dogs are weathered. Should
the contrary be attempted, a strong southern tide is apt to set the vessel towards the
Round Rock or Broken Jerusalem, and some efforts would be necessary to make good
what has been lost. Vessels beating to windward outside of St. John’s, when there
is a southern tide, should keep the land aboard as much as possible ; it is, however,
different when the tide runs to the northward, when they ought to stand out.” —

ANEGADA, or DROWNED ISLAND, is the north-easternmost island, and is of
a circular form, extending nearly W.N.W. and E.S.E.; its length being about
10 miles, and breadth two miles; it is surrounded by a reef, which also stretches
off from the S.E. end, nearly three leagues, and from its winding form is called
the Horse Shoe; this reef in many parts has from 2 to 6 feet over it, and is
extremely dangerous, especially the eastern side, which abounds with the wrecks of
numerous vessels, and must always be approached with the greatest caution, the
Island of Anegada being so low, that the sea will frequently break over a great part
of it.* Incoming from the north-eastward, you will perceive the Hill of Virgin
Gorda over Anegada like a hummock ;-and observe, when this hill bears S. by E.,
you will be to the westward of Anegada, and may steer on S. by W. for Tortola, but
when this hill bears about §.W. by S., although you are then to the eastward of
Anegada, yet that course will infallibly lead on to the Horse Shoe, but when the
hill bears W. by S. or west, you may run in that direction, and pass at a sufficient
distance to the southward of the reef. Let not the mariner lie to, particularly in the
night, to the eastward of Anegada, for there is commonly a westerly current, which
may drift him on the rocks. Anegada now produces some cotton, and had in 1811
about 200 inhabitants; the goats, sheep, and cattle are tolerably good, and near the
southern point fresh water may be obtained. ‘The course from Saba to the eastern
part of Virgin Gorda is N.W. { W., and the distance 26 leagues.

THE VIRGIN ISLANDS,

REMARKS ON THE ISLAND OF ANEGADA,

By Sir R. H. SCHOMBURGEK, Pu. D., &c., &c,

ANEGADA is the most northern of the cluster of islands and cays known by the
name of the Virgin Islands, and is unhappily celebrated for the number of wrecks,
in many cases accompanied with a heavy loss of life, which it has occasioned.

Of its history little is known, and there is no likelihood that it was settled early.
Pére Labet, the only early writer who speaks of the lesser West India Islands,
observes, that the aborigines used it as an occasional rendezvous, where they pro-
cured great quantities of conches; and large piles of these shells are still to be seen
at the east end of the island, but nowhere else, which seems to prove decidedly that
it was not permanently occupied, but merely resorted to from time to time.

At a later period Sir R. H. Schomburgk says, the retired bays of the island served
as a lurking-place to the buccaneers. Ultimately, as the trade among the West India
Islands became more frequent, and repeated shipwrecks in this quarter held out hopes |
of advantage to those who might be in the neighbourhood to profit by them, settlers $
took up their permanent residence on the island, and were at one time more numerous
even than they are now. They found that the loose ground which covered it was
capable of bearing provision crops, and even cotton; while the rearing of stock and
sale of the underwood, which was progressively cleared away, and which, being very :
full of gum, had a preference in the St. Thomas’s market, furnished a further resource. q
The great object, however, always was, and still is, the wreck of vessels ; and the
indolence of the inhabitants is only thoroughly roused by the cry of “ A vessel on the
reef!” Then all are roused to activity ; scarcely is the news announced, than boats
of every description, shallops, and sailing-vessels are pushed off with all haste to the
scene of action; arms that have been idle for weeks are brought into exercise ; and
both skill and intrepidity are tasked to the uttermost to get first on board. The
scene, indeed, baffles description; and it is to be feared that few are attracted by ‘
motives of humanity, though some such do exist.

The soundings between Virgin Gorda and Anegada are tolerably regular, being
from 8 to 16 fathoms; and there is, therefore, no doubt that the two communicate
and form parts of one system; but their nature is quite different, primitive rocks
predominating in the former, while in the latter we find only limestone and coral.

The direct distance between the two islands is 112 nautical miles; and the appear-
ance of Anegada, when approaching it trom this side, that is, from the S.W., is
remarkable. First, single trees show themselves in the horizon ; then the most elevated {
part of the island, called Frank’s Landing, which may be distinguished in clear e
weather, about eight miles off; and last of all the lower land. The lead usually brings
up coral rock, with coarse sand and broken shells. The greatest depth of water is
near Virgin Gorda.

At eight miles distance from Anegada, there are from 8 to 11 fathoms, decreasing
as the shoals are approached to 4 fathoms. ‘The outer edge of the reef is marked in
some places by the water breaking ; in others, merely the brown heads of the rocks, ‘
contrasted with the white coiour of the bottom, where clear, indicate the danger. (
Considerable skill is requisite to pass through the openings; but inside there is good
anchorage in 23 fathoms, about a mile from the beach. Vessels drawing more water
anchor outside, in from 4 to 6 fathoms.

The greatest length of Anegada is from E.S.E to W.N.W., 10 miles, the greatest

breadth 2 miles, which is between Pearl Point and Soldier’s Wash,* thence it dimin-
ishes towards both extremities, so that the average breadth cannot be stated to be
more than 14 mile ; and the whole circumference 23 miles.

The surrounding reef approaches nearest on the north side of the island, and is at
one point connected with the shore. Generally speaking, indeed, the distance of the
reef on the northern side is but inconsiderable, and the same may be said of the western
and part of the southern side. Its greatest extent is to the S.E., and its most southern
extremity, from the S.E. end of Anegada, is nearly 72 miles. The distance of the
reef from the south side, is from 1 tu 4§ miles.

On sounding close to the reef on the southern and western sides, a depth of
4 to 6 fathoms is found; on the northern and eastern sides, from 6 to 9 fathoms : but
at a distance, 14 mile in a northern direction, I found no bottom at 100 fathoms.
Inside of the main chain of shoals, the depth varies so suddenly, that it-is only with
great skill and attention that a small sloop can be navigated from east to west, and
vice versa, and this only on the southern side; on the northern it is quite impassable,
as the reef stretches to the shore.

There extends from the west end of the Island, in a south-westerly direction,
almost to the eastern end of Jost Van Dykes, a shallow ground ; and as the bottom is
mostly whitish sand, it appears of less depth than it really is, as not less than 7

ie fathoms were found on it.

° At the distance of about two nautical miles from Man-of-War Point, the southern

reef joins the main reef; it has been called the Long Shoal, from the density of its
# ~— beds, which, for a considerable distance, form almost one entire mass. Thence the
shoals become, with the exception of the main reef, more detached ; the latter stretches
to the south-east till it reaches the elbow, or extreme south-eastern end, when it turns
gradually to the south-west, forming almost a half circle, known by the name of the
Horse Shoe. The depth of water increases from this towards the east end of Spanish
Town; but there are still some dangerous shallows in the way, with only 3 or 4,
nay, even 2 fathoms water on them.

The surface of the Island of Anegada is for the most part a dead level, with only
occasionally a turpentine or loblolly tree overlooking the underwood. However, on

- the south-eastern side, the ground does rise gradually, from north to south, about 60
feet, which is the highest point of Anegada, and commonly called Frank’s Landing.
The southern side of the island is one continued mass of shelves, loosely covered with
vegetable earth, more or less mixed with sand. This mould is, doubtless, the decom-
posed matter of algce, which through exposure to the sun, have lost their saline
property, and form a most excellent vegetable earth ; it is light, and of a dark brown }
colour, and leaves on the tongue a somewhat acid taste. It is so lightly settled on
the shelf that it often covers the ground only a few inches.

The western end of the Island has been covered with sand, forced forward by an |
immense ground sea or surf, to which it is still subjected from time to time ; and hence |

sand has formed little hillocks, 40 feet in height. Behind the first range is a second,
or even a third; all of which are now covered with a species of arunda, and the |
surianna maritima. After these little hillocks have stretched for some miles in an

easterly direction, the shoré takes a rocky appearance; and instead of sand, detached
pieces of limestone and coral are heaped up, which reach even a height of 30 feet and
more. The productive soil lies chiefly behind these rocky hillocks, and is cultivated
by the inhabitants to raise their crops. On approaching the eastern end, sand-hills
begin to rise gradually again, till on the southern side the bays become almost level
with high-water mark.

The ponds of Anegada form an important feature in a description of the island;
those towards the west are of the greatest extent; those on the south side form a
junction with the sea. The surrounding banks of the ponds are, in general, two feet
higher than the surface of the water; but sometimes it accumulates so suddenly, that
it overflows and inundates the whole southern side ; while at other times again it falls,
which seems to be caused not merely by evaporation, but by an absorption through
the lower strata. The evaporation of the ponds is, during this time, unhealthy, and
the effluvia arising from them scarcely to be borne. A long continuance of dry
weather, however, always lessens the quantity of water considerably ; and when
this takes place during the month of August, a large quantity of salt may be obtained
from some of these ponds.

Fresh water is found in abundance on almost every part of the island, frequently
even in the immediate vicinity of the sea, and surrounded by salt-ponds. On the
north side, near Loblolly Bay, are a range of shelf-holes, called the Wells, which
are filled with fresh water. ‘The formation of these shelf-holesis curious: the mouth
is usually from 10 to 25 feet wide, and they descend in the form of a funnel; the
water contained in them is said often to rise to an uncommon height, as though forced.
up by some pressure from beneath, but in general they ebb and flow with the sea.
A little inland, at the west end of the island, fresh water, which keeps well, may be
abundantly obtained ; and, as there is good anchorage in the vicinity, whole fleets
might be supplied with any quantity they required, by digging holes in the sand.

One would suppose that the climate, considering the low situation of the island
and the effluvia which escapes from the ponds, would be unhealthy, but the
examples of longevity prove almost to the contrary ; but as soon as the rainy season
sets in, and the lowest parts of the island are inundated, fevers and influenza prevail.
Fogs, equal to those which we have on the continent, rise here very suddenly ; and I
was myself witness of one which caused a considerable consternation among the
inhabitants, the cry having been raised that the sea had come over the land from the
north side. And certainly the appearance was appalling enough, large masses of
white fog rolling heavily over the land, and approaching from the north ; nor was I
surprised it had been at first mistaken for the sea.

In calm and clear weather, and chiefly at high water, objects at Virgin Gorda,
which at other periods are entirely invisible, seem to rise above the surface of the
water, leaving apparently a vacancy between, and trees, rocks, &c., appear accord-
ingly to hover in the air. In cloudy weather, or when the sea is agitated, this curious
refraction is never observed.

CURRENTS.—Vessels bound from America to the West Indies, and chiefly to
St. Thomas’s, find themselves frequently to the north of the Virgin Islands; and this
deviation from their intended course has proved but too often fatal, having brought
them on- the reefs of Anegada, when they thought themselves far to the southward

of that dangerous island. Nor can repeated occurrences like these be attributed
exclusively to errors in the observations for determining the latitude, or to false
reckoning.

Sir R. H. Schomburgk observes, that during his survey of the island and reefs of
Anegada, he had many proofs of the existence of a north-westerly current, and
adds: “1 saw, on the north side of Anegada, a great quantity of cork shavings; and
on inquiry, was told by the inhabitants that such had been drifted ashore annually
for many years, in sufficient quantity to supply them abundantly with cork to attach
to their fishing-nets. Now, the cork-tree being indigenous to the south of Europe,
and in Africa, I conjecture that this drift is first brought from the coast of Spain and
Portugal, and swept along with the south-east current which prevails there, till it
meets the grand westerly currents, through which it is carried by the branch which
takes this north-westerly direction to the low shores of Anegada; and it would be
desirable to ascertain whether like pieces of cork are drifted on other shores of the
Caribbean Islands.

There is also a remarkable current inside the reefs of Anegada, which sets along
the shore from west to east on the north side, and from east to west along the south
side of the island, till it completes the round, when it is discharged through a channel
near the west end.

On examining the list of 53 vessels wrecked on Anegada, it will be observed that
the Americans are the greatest sufferers; the next in number are those of Spain ;
with ‘few English, and still fewer of other mations; and it is certainly true, that the
Americans trade the most with St. 'Dhomas’s. But besides this, their vessels, after
having crossed the Gulf Stream, are likewise most exposed to the influence of the
north-west current; and next to them are the vessels from Spain, bound to Cuba,
which may have taken advantage of the western tropical current.—<Abridged from the
Geographical Journal, Vol. ii., p. 152.

VIRGIN GORDA.—The Island of Virgin Gorda, or Spanish Town Island, is
nearly nine miles long, and of irregular shape, being exceedingly narrow at both
ends, but somewhat broader and higher near the middle; it lies almost in a N.E.
and S.W. direction, bending a little circularly towards the north, and contains
51,900 square acres of land; the population of Virgin Gorda, Anegada, and Tortola,
is estimated by Humboldt at 8500. Virgin Gorda is divided into eight districts, and
possesses 345 plantations, Its exports are sugar, rum, tobacco, indigo, peas, and

84. THE VIRGIN ISLANDS.

some cotton, but the latter article seems not to be congenial to the soil, which is dry
and sandy; the land is mostly level, and in rainy weather is watered by several
small rivulets, but these in summer frequently dry up and disappear; the inhabitants
are supported chiefly by potatoes and fish. The island has three harbours; that on
the north-east side is called North Sound, or Gorda Sound. Mr. Lockwood says,
this is a secure port, of great capacity, and its entrance is not difficult to discover.
It is protected by several islands, between which the passages are narrow, and
encumbered with rocks; but when wit! in the Sound, you lie in great security. The
best passage is between the Prickly Pear and Moskito Is:and, but this is obstructed
by a reef on each side. To sail into this Sound, coming from the eastward, pass
Necker Island, so as to avoid the sunken rock which lies 2 of a mile to the eastward
of it; when Moskito Island is open to the north of Necker Island, you are clear of
that Canger, which at most times you may see by the water breaking on it. When
past this rock, steer about S.W. by W. for the N.W. part of Necker Island, under
which there is good anchorage in 10 and 11 fathoms, fine sandy bottom, and smooth
water with the prevailing trade wind ; the west point of Prickly Pear Island, forming
the north side of the Sound, will bear about §.W. by S. from you; steer next for this
point, taking care to avoid the reef which runs off it. The entrance into the Gorda
Sound is between this reef and one to the S.W., which stretches to the eastward from
Moskito Island, on which reef there is a high black rock. The mark to keep clear
to the westward of the reef running off Prickly Pear Island, is two trees on the top
of the ridge to the southward on Virgin Gorda kept just in sight to the eastward of a
bluff situate on the south side of the Sound. This mark, although not very distinct,
may be useful. Another mark is, a house in Virgin Gorda in one with a remarkable
tree standing a little to the southward of it; these seen over Knat Point, bearing
S.iW., lead through this norrow passage in the best water. When in the fair
channel, you will see the low neck of land in the upper or eastern part of the Sound
just in sight to the southward of Prickly Pear, then haul up to the eastward, your
sails being previously trimmed for that purpose, by which means, having fresh way
on your vessel, you will shoot to the eastward, clear of the 8.W. reef, although the
wind should be a little to the southward of east.

In the channel into the Sound there are 5 to 7 fathoms, and from 8 to 12 in the
Sound. A rock is said to he near the S.E. corner of the Sound, at no great distance
from the shore, named Oyster Rock, with only 13 foot water on it. Between Moskito
Island and Virgin Gorda, there are only 10 and 12 feet water.

West Bay, on the N.W. side of this island, is more open, and much frequented ;
but some rocks, named the Seal Dogs, above water, lie near the middle of the
entrance from the northward, and must be avoided; the anchorage is to the south-
ward of these rocks; here you will have 13 or 14 fathoms, sand and oaze, and lie
nearly midway between some islands, called the Dogs and Virgin Gorda; the ground
holding well. A better place for anchoring is to the southward, in Thomas's bay ;
here you will ride safe in 6, 7, or 8 fathoms, directly before the town; but there is a
reef in the middle of the bay, which runs north and south, and many ragged rocks at
the bottom.

The best mark to know Virgin Gorda is the hill, situate near the middle of the
istand, of moderate height, and standing alone; this is named Virgin Peak, and
is elevated 1370 feet; this in clear weather will be seen seven leagues off. The
ground is so clear under the lee of Virgin Gorda, that 300 sail may anchor in the
space between the Dogs and the valley. At 35 miles to the westward of St. Thomas’s
Bay is Scrub Island, and a little to the south-westward of that is Beef Island ;
these form passages into Sir Francis Drake’s Channel. You may sail in on
either side of the Dogs, or between the Dogs and Scrub and Beef Islands;
this latter is the widest passage, but there is a shoal of 15 feet, named the Tow
Rock, lying in mid-channel, about 1 mile to the N.N.E. of the eastern end of
Scrub Island, the marks given for it being the eastern points of Scrub and Salt
Islands open, and the great Dog Island bearing E. by 8.; you may easily ayoid it on

NORMAN'S ISLAND. 85

either side, by borrowing near to the Islands each way. The soundings in this passage:
are from 11 to 14 fathoms.

To the south-westward of Virgin Gorda is a remarkable cluster of ragged rocks
the apparent effect of some volcanic convulsion of nature; these are named Old
Jerusalem or the Fallen City, the Round Rock, and Ginger Island ; between the
two latter is the common passage into Sir Francis Drake’s Channel, and is called the
King’s Channel, or Round Rock Passage; but to the northward of the Round Rock,
is a danger under water, with only 11 feet overit. Between Round Rock and
Ginger Island the channel is clear, and has 16 fathoms water in it, both sides being
steep-to. Further west are Cooper's and Salt Islands; the passage between Ginger
and Cooper’s Island is good, and sometimes used; in it are 11, 18, and 19 fathoms;
on your port side is the Carvel Rock, above water, but the channel between
Cooper’s and Salt Island has a dangerous rock in it, just awash, and therefore
seldom frequented.

Peter’s Island is a narrow crooked island, of irregular form; one-third of a
mile off its north-east point is a remarkably rocky islet, called the Dead Chest; the
channel between Peter's Island and the Dead Chest is very clear and good, and
consequently much adopted in going to the westward; but that between the Dead
Chest and Salt Island is not so safe, on account of a sunken rock, called the Blonde
Rock, over which are only 12 feet water; this bears from the Dead Chest E. by
N. 3 N., distant about 5 a mile, and may be passed on either side; but the safest way
for strangers is to keep close to Salt Island, which is very bold close to the shore,
that not being the case with the east side of the Dead Chest.

NORMAN'S ISLAND lies about 1 mile to the south-westward of the S.W. end
of Peter’s Island; its length W.S.W. is 2 miles, and its breadth nowhere 1 mile; its
shores are irregular and much indented with coves; on its western side is Man-of-
War Bay, where vessels may ride in from 18 to 3 fathoms, the bottom clear from all
danger. To the northward of Norman’s Island is the Pelican or Witch, and near that
are four small perpendicular rocks, called the Indians; between these and the
Pelican are only 9 feet water. In passing between Peter and Norman’s Islands, you
should run in nearer to the latter, for at the S.W. point of the former is a rocky cay.
called the Carrot, 80 feet high, and a sandy shoal, stretching out a considerable way
into the channel. The Carrot Shoal, of 10 feet, lies } of a mile W.S.W. from the
cay. §S.S.W. from the south-west end of Norman’s Island, distant nearly a mile
lies a sunken rock, called Santa Monica, with only 10 feet water over it, the marks for
it being the Carrot Rock just opon to the south of Norman’s Island, or the two
extreme southern points of Norman and St. Peter’s Islandsin one. Ringdove Rock,
with only 12 feet on it, lies off the N.W. point of Norman’s Island ; the mark to
clear it on the west side is, Treasure Point on with West Hill in Norman’s Island.
Midway between Norman’s and St. John’s Island is Flanagan Island, off the southern
part of which is a rocky reef. ‘There are navigable channels on each side of Flanagan
Island, only taking care to give a good birth to the Santa Monica Rock, in the eastern
channel, and to St. John’s Island, in the western channel, for some sunken dangers
lie on that side. These are the islands from the south-western part of Virgin Gorda
to St. John’s, which enclose Sir Francis Drake’s Channel on the south-eastern side,
while St. John’s, Tortola, Beef, and Scrub Islands, form its west and N.W. boundary.

The ISLAND OF ST. JOHN is 8 miles long and 3} broad; it is said to be well
watered and cultivated. [ts exports are sugar, rum, tobacco, cotton and coffee.
There is one harbour to this island, called Coral Bay, which is situate at its S.E. end,
and is reported to be one of the best among the Virgin Islands; here you will see,
on the starboard point of the entrance, named Moor’s Point, a white-walled fortress,
which is visible a very considerable distance. ‘Toward the port is Buck Cay, off the
southern part of which are some sunken rocks. ‘The principal channel to this place
is between Buck Cay and Moor’s Point, where the soundings all the way in are
regular, gradually lessening from 12 to 5 fathoms; should the wind be anywhere to:

the northward of east, there will be good riding at the entrance of the bay, but if
the southward of E.S.E. you must anchor outside the point, and warp in. Aboutia
mile inside of Moovr’s Point, is the town and governor’s house, above which English
vessels seldom go; there are, however, large lagoons beyond that, and the harbour
opens very large, having good anchorage in various places. You will observe in
sailing in to leave one-third of the channel to windward from Moor’s Point, and two-
thirds to leeward from Buck Cay, and then you will not come into less than 5
fathoms water. The common anchorage is within 4 of a mile of the weather shore,
running your stream anchor to the S.W. on account of the land breeze, which is
usually between the S.8.E., south, and 8.W. Moor N.E. and S.W.; the ground is
good and the depth 6 fathoms. It is said a small bank lies off the gate, about a cable’s
length from the shore, with only 10 feet water over it. The watering-place is at the
south end of the town, outside the southern gate, but it is not good,

The islands and rocks dependent on St. John’s, are Layango and the Corn Islands,
the Witch, Bird’s Cay, Round Island, and the western chain of islands and rocks
enclosing Sir Francis Drake’s Channel to the southward.

The ISLAND OF TORTOLA lies on the northern side of Sir Francis Drake’s
Channel, and is about 9 miles in length, and 3 miles at its broadest part; it is the
principal island belonging to the British, and has a population of 10,520; its exports

are sugar, rum, and cotton, the latter being of excellent quality. Road Town is the _

chief place, and only good harbour in the island; in 1802 this was declared a free
port, and therefore became a place of great resort.

_ Vessels bound to Tortola, if coming from the northward, generally proceed round
Virgin Gorda, and enter Sir Francis Drake’s Channel, between Virgin Gorda and
the Island of Tortola, Here they will choose the channel most convenient, passing
either between the Dogs and Gorda, or between the Dogs and Scrub Island; in the
former passage keep mid-channel, and there is no danger whatever; but between the
Dogs and the Tortola side, there is the fifteen-feet shoal, named Tow Rock, already
described; this lies to the north-eastward of Scrub Island; butships from the south-
ward find entrance between some of the various islands to the southward. Of these

assages, that between Round and Ginger Islands, called the King’s Channel, or

ound Rock Passage, is that most commonly adopted. In proceeding for this channel
from the south-eastward, you will first make Virgin Gorda, steering W.N.W., some-
what northerly, direct towards its south-west end; and so soon as you arrive within
7 or 6 leagues of it, you will perceive the high land of Tortola, and also the rocks
and islands to the southward and eastward of Sir Francis Drake’s Channel. Having
obtained a clear sight of these, you should enter for the south side of the Round
Rock, which has a remarkable appearance, and cannot be easily mistaken; as you
near this rock, you will perceive the low cays which run out from the §8.W. end of
Virgin Gorda, called the Fallen City ; these extend to within 2 cables’ length of the
Round Rock. These reefs form a singular appearance, and resemble ruins, being a
collection of barren stones, without the least verdure upon them. Being at a distance
of 2 or 3 leagues to the eastward of these cays, endeavour to bring the Round Rock
to bear N.W,, a little westerly, and steer direct for its southern side, and as you run
through the passage, it will be proper to keep about 4 of its breadth from the Round
Rock, and go $ away from Ginger Island, by which you will guard against being,
with light winds, driven too near Ginger Island. The course through the channel is
nearly N.W. by W., and the passage + a mile wide; the rocks on both sides are com-
posed of slate, and you will find the water deep, and more than 14 or 15 fathoms
within a cable’s length of Round Rock.

Having cleared this channel, you will steer on to the westward, until you perceive
on the island of Tortola, to the W.N.W. of you, a negro town, a white house, and
fortress; then steer W. by N. and west. The eastern point of Tortola Road_ bears
from the Round Rock nearly W. 3 N., and is distant about 8 miles. You will now
see the flagstaff on Fort Burt at the western point of the harbour, but observe not to
run too near this point, for off it lies a dangerous reef. The eastern point of the

ISLAND OF ST. THOMAS. 87

harbour is a craggy bluff, having a roadway round it; but be particularly cautious
not to run to the westward of Road Harbour, for there is a small place called Sea
Cow Bay, which bears some resemblance to the entrance of Road Harbour, and the
mistaking one for the other might be productive of inconvenience and danger; there-
fore, if any way doubtful, as you approach the eastern point, look to the south-west-
ward, and bring the Indians, which are four remarkable pinnacle rocks, off the N.W.
end of Norman’s Island, to bear S.W. by S. ; having done so, and being within a
mile of the Tortola shore, you will have 'l'ortola Road open, and should bring the
leading-mark on, which is Todman Peak in one with the cocoa-nut trees on Wickham
Cays; this will lead between the Scotch Bank on the north, and Lark Bank on the
south, up to the anchorage in the harbour; observe the eastern side as you advance,
and on the third bluff point you will discern Fort Shirley, abreast of which ships of
large dimensions usually anchor. If in a small vessel, you may keep on to the west-
ward, until you open Fort George, which you will bring to bear north, a little westerly,
then haul in, and steer for the citadel, when you may anchor abreast of the point of
the first battery, the battery bearing N.E. The mark for the anchorage is the battery
flagstaff, on the west point of the bay, in one with the Guard-house which stands
behind the battery; here you will lie in 10 fathoms, only a cable’s length off the
shore; moor N.N.E., with your stream-anchor, for the ground is foul, and should
your bower part, your stream will check you into the bay, and enable you to clear
the rocks off its western point. Within Drake’s Channel, and also in the passages
to it, the tides commonly run quick over the foul ground, and cause a constant ripple.
High water at 8h. 30m. full and change, springs rise 14 foot. The lowest tides in
April and May.

The above directions for Tortola must be attended to, should you proceed through
either of the other passages; but vessels commonly, in sailing from Tortola, adopt
the southern channel, passing through between Norman’s Island and Flanagan, or
Flanagan Island and St. John’s. There is a passage to the northward of John’s and
between the S.W. end of Tortola and Frenchman’s Island on the one side, and Thatch
Islands on the other, but it is intricate and dangerous; also between the Thatch
Islands and St. John’s, but these are very little used by European vessels. The small
islands dependent on Tortola are the Thatch Islands, Frenchman’s Cay, and Van
Dyke Islands, Guano, Camanoes, Scrub, and Beef Islands.

The Van Dyke Islands lie to the northward of the western part of Tortola, distant
almost 3 miles; there isa good channel between them and a small sandy island,
which lies midway of the passage. On the south side of the larger Van Dyke are
three small harbours; that called Little Harbour appears to be a good place for small
vessels, but the other two are encumbered with rocks at their entrances.

The ISLAND of ST. THOMAS lies to the westward of those islands we have
been describing, and belongs to the Danes; the trade here is considerable, more
especially in times of peace, for there is a market for those articles which are deemed
contraband by the English, French, Dutch, &c.; and, during war, their prizes are
frequently carried to this island for sale,

St. Thomas’s is 12 miles long, and 3 miles broad. I{s exports are sugar, tobacco,
rum, cotton, and cattle. This island is traversed by a range of hills, which runs in an
east and west direction; these, like St. John’s, descend gradually towards the shore ;
they were formerly well clothed with trees, but these being destroyed, the island is
now subjected to great drought, the soil being sandy, and the rivulets chiefly dried
up; water, however, may readily be obtained three feet under the surface, but the
inhabitants chiefly rely on rain water, which they preserve in cisterns. The principal
town of St. Thomas’s, sometimes called Charlotte Amalia, lies on the southern side of
the island, with a large factory at its extremity ; here is an excellent harbour, fit for
all kinds of shipping, where whole fleets may lie secure and land-locked from all
winds, except only those coming from the S.W. to the S.E. by S., to which it is
somewhat exposed, but these winds are seldom prevalent, unless during the hurricane

months. The inhabitants are a mixture of Danes, English, French, Dutch, Germans,
and Jews, who all have their separate places of worship.*

FRENCHMAN’s Cap.—When approaching St. Thomas Harbour from the eastward,
two small islands will be observed on the south side of St. Thomas, named French-
man’s Cap and Buck Island. Frenchman’s Cap, or Bird Island, is the outer or
southernmost, and lies §.S.W. § W., 4% miles from Dog Island, at the eastern extreme
of St. Thomas. It is a remarkable islet, 14 cable long, a cable broad, and 195 feet
high, covered with long grass, and steep-to. On the north side there are 5 to 9
fathoms water at 2 cables from the islet, aud on the southern side 24 fathoms a cable
off,

Buck Isuanp is a small islet, about 120 feet high, partially covered with brush-
wood, lying about 14 mile from the nearest part of St. Thomas, and S.E. 25., 3 miles
from Mohlenfel’s Point. It is steep-to on its south side. Off the west end a shallow
ledge extends to the distance of } a cable, and on the north side the depth is 5
fathoms, at the same distance. Good landing will be found in the little bay at the

PackET Rock is a small coral shoal, about 4 a cable in extent, witha depth of only

ground inside the shoal is clear, with a depth of 8 and 9 fathoms, sand and rock,
extending from Long Point as far west as Coculus Bay, 23 cables south of which bay
there is a small head with only 9 feet on it, but it is out of the line of track, and can
be easily avoided.

When on the western end of the Packet Rock, the flagstaff on Mohlenfel’s Point
and Contant Mill will be in one, bearing N.W. by W., and the remarkable needle-
pointed rock at Patrick Point will touch the southernmost house on the northern
saddle of Great St. James Island, bearing E. by N. 4 N.

THE TRIANGLES, on the east side of entrance te St. Thomas Harbour, lie nearly
midway between Green Cay and Mohlenfel’s Point. They consist of three small
rocks, forming a triangle; the eastern rock uncovers 3 feet at low water, the northern
rock a foot, and the §.W. and outer rock 2 feet, and this latter is nearly 4 cables from
the shore. Banana Point (the north end of Water Island) just open of Cowell Point,
(the S.W. point of entrance to the harbour), bearing N.W. by W., leads close to the
S.W. of them, and northward of the 17-feet rock, south of them.

A small detached coral rock, about 35 yards in diameter, lies with the two western
rocks of the Triangles group in line, bearing north, distant nearly 12 cable. It has
17 feet least water on it, and 7 fathoms close to,

Directions.—Judge Berg’s house (the only flat-roof building above the town of

Point KNOLL is a small coral head, with 3 fathoms water over it, lying S.W.
2 W. from the lighthouse, and nearly 2 of a cable from the nearest part of Modhlen-
fel’s Point. The highest part of Rupert Rock and Kiser Tower in one, bearing
N. by W. leads over it.

RHODE Bank lies N. by W. 3 W., } of a mile from Knoll Point, and consists of 3
small coral heads lying close to each other, with from 15 to 17 feet water on them.
At the distance of nearly half a cable’s length north of the bank there are from 24

decreasing to the shore, When on the north end, the highest part of Rupert Rock

north end of Revenge Sand (Water Island) just open of Cowell Point, W. by S. 2S.
Kier Tower in one with the western part of Rupert Rock, N. by W., crosses the
western edge in 23 feet.

Buoy.—The above rock is marked by a black buoy, surmounted by a cage-work
beacon.

Rupert Rock.—This rock is situate a little more than a quarter of a mile to the
northward of Rhode Bank, on the eastern side of the harbour. This rock is 13 feet
high, and was, previously to the late hurricane, kept whitewashed, and if so at the
present time, cannot well be mistaken. It lies 4 a mile to the northward of the

Beacon.—On the westernmost of the above rocks is an iron beacon, with a lozenge
or diamond head, painted white. On the south they are steep-to at 30 yards off; on
the east, between them and Hayensight Point, there are only from 12 to 15 feet
water.

Between the above rock and Rhode Bank is the Quarantine Ground, in which the
depth gradually decreases to the shore from 5 to 8 fathoms.

The above form the whole of the dangers on the eastern side of the entrance. We
shall now notice those of mid-channel and western side.

Scorpion Rock lies immediately in the way of the entrance to the harbour,
between the lighthouse and Cowell Point. It is a small coral rock, not more than 27
yards in length and 10 yards in breadth, with 2 or 3 heads higher than the rest, on
which there are 20 feet water at the lowest springs in May. About 4 a cable west-
ward of the rock there are from 26 to 28 feet water, and nearly 4 a cable eastward
from 28 to 80 feet. When on the shallowest part, the east end of the roof of the
highest house on French Hill will be seen just over Frederik Point, bearing N.N.W.
z W.,and Cowell Point just clear of the south end of Sand Bay (Water Island), west.

Buoy.—Near to the south-eastern edge of the Scorpion Rock a red buoy, with
baloon, is moored.

Having described the dangers on each side of the entrance, there remains but one
other danger inside, and that we are informed has been deepened to 24 feet, so

Kir SHOAL is a small patch of 174 feet water, composed of sand and dead coral ;

Anchorage.—The best anchorage in St. Thomas Harbour for large ships is with
the highest part of Rupert Rock in one with the lighthouse, and Long Bay fairly
open, in 53 fathoms. This, too, is a good berth for getting under-weigh when
leaving the harbour or shifting berth.*

Directions.—In sailing for the Road of St. Thomas’s from the eastward, you will
perceive Buck Island, which lies about 4 miles outside the harbour’s mouth; 3 miles
to the south-eastward of which is a small rock, called Bird’s Cay, or Frenchman’s Cap;
between this and Buck Island the channel is safe, but that between Buck Island and
St. Thomas’s has several sunken rocks about it, especially the Packet Rock, which has
but 5 feet water over it, but 7 fathoms at a short distance round it; vessels, there-
fore, commonly leave Buck Island to the northward in proceeding for the harbour.
When, therefore,’you have passed it, and brought the mouth of the harbour open, that
is, the low fort on the west side of the entrance open to the westward of the fort
and point on the east side of the entrance, steer N. by W. or N.N.W. for the town,
taking care to give the eastern side a good berth to avoid the Triangles, which are above
water ; (Banana Point open west of Cowell Point, N.W. by W., clears them), thus you
may fun on until you are within 4 a mile of the fort, which is white, and stands on
the eastern end of the town. Here you may anchor in 6 or less fathoms, in good
holding ground, and clear from every dangerous obstruction. In the Great Carenage,
which is on the west side of the harbour, are large moorings on shore, where vessels
may be secured, and lie as safe as in any harbour in the West Indies, during the
hurricane season.

The Fatrway leading marks into the harbour are the two double lights} in the
town in one bearing N. by W., or the west point of Water Battery in one with the
east end of the Episcopal Church.’

Running inside of Buck Islands by day, and in clear weather :-—

You may bring the northern point of Water Island clear of the southerr. point of
Cowell’s Batteries, which will clear both the Packet Rock and the Triangles.

When Christian’s Fort shows well clear to the westward of the point by Méhlen-
fel’s Battery, you are to the westward of the Triangles, and can steer into the
harbour.

Light.—A lighthouse has been erected at Méhlenfel’s Battery, on the east point
of the entrance to the harbour of St. Thomas, in latitude 18° 19’ 22", longitude
64° 55'8". The elevation of the light above the level of the sea is 95 feet; it is
visible at the distance of 4 leagues. ‘he light is red, the lantern having red glass
panes at S.E., south, and 8.W., and it is easily distinguished from the lights in the
town or neighbouring houses.

This lighthouse has been erected in order that ships may with greater safety enter
this harbour in dark nights, and find the windward or eastern part of the entrance,
without being in danger of approaching too near the hidden rocks, lying outside the
harbour to the east, called the Triangles. To go clear west of these rocks, the east
angle of the lighthouse is brought to bear in a line (N. by W. 3 W.) with the 8.W.
corner of a whitewashed kitchen, lying to the north, which is the nearest the
Triangles must be approached, and about 1 cable’s length distant from them ; and
the more the kitchen is covered by the lighthouse, the greater is the distance from
the Triangles.

The kitchen, being only about 67 feet north of the tower, will, during the night
and in clear weather, be visible from the reflection of the lamp.

At the King’s Wharf, in town (west of Christiana Fort), a lamp, with red glass,
towards the harbour, will at the same time be seen west of Point Méhlenfel; this
being free, a ship may safely bear away for the harbour.

Prince Rupert’s Rock, near the middle of the entrance to the harbour, will always
be kept whitewashed, and thereby be visible at night. For further information,
reference must be made to the chart of the harbour.

REGULATIONS FOR THE PORT OF ST. THOMAS.

1.—No vessel is allowed to stand off and on, or to anchor in the out bays, without

special leave.

9.—-No vessel which has anchored outside Prince Rupert’s Rock, is allowed to
remain at anchor there longer than 24 hours, for which a special leave must be im-
mediately applied for, and which does not exempt the vessel from entering and clear-
ing at the custom-house in the usual manner.

3.—No vessel is allowed to anchor in front of the fort, so as to mask it, or prevent
it from taking a range of the whole entrance of the harbour. ‘The sterns of vessels
anchoring to the eastward of the harbour, must, in consequence thereof, not lay more
westerly than in a S.8.E. direction from the flagstaff on the fort, and the bows of
vessels anchoring to the westward in the harbour not more easterly than S. by W.
from the same. When the cargo, or part thereof, is intended to be entered for
exportation, the vessel has to anchor to the eastward of the fort, or immediately
to remove thereto. No vessel must leave the port after sunset, except with night

pass.
4,—No boats are permitted to take a rope from, or make fast to any vessel before

she has anchored. No persons are permitted to go on board or leave a yessel before

the captain of the port has been on board and given such permission. By non-
compliance herewith, the offender, after summary investigation by the police-
master, will be fined in a sum of five to twenty-five pieces of eight, according

to circumstances,

5.—To the captain of the port shall be immediately reported whether there are
any sick persons on board—if the vessel comes from a place where any contagious
disease is prevailing—if any gunpowder, arms, or warlike stores are on board—and if
there are any passengers. All, persons are considered as passengers who are not
proved to belong to the crew of the vessel.

If the captain of the port forbids a passenger to go on shore, the master of the
vessel is answerable that such passenger does not leave the ship before a permit from
the police is obtained.

6.—Ships’ papers, manifests, and other documents concerning the articles and
quantity of the cargo must be delivered to the captain of the port on demand.

7.—After the vessel is brought to anchor, the master has—

First.—Within two hours to report himself to Christian’s Fort (which again must
be done before the anchor is weighed or the vessel is removed to another place), and.
before his departure he has to present there his custom-house clearance.

Second.— Within two hours after his arrival he shall deliver to the police-office an
exact list of the passengers who have arrived with him, under a penalty of from 25
to 200 pieces of eight. ;

Third.—And within 24 hours make an entry at the custom-house. Should he com-
mence to discharge cargo before the vessel is entered at the custom-house, he will be
liable to a fine of 300 dollars.

8.—Vessels coming into the harbour after sunset must show colours the next morn-
ing at sunrise, and then immediately be reported to the fort; and, if any passenger
on board, at the police-office before 9 o’clock..

In such cases the master may, when there is no sickness on board, or at the piace
from whence he came, land passengers well known to him and entirely unsuspicious;
but he is then responsible, as well for accidents which may arise therefrom, as
for the personal appearance of the passengers at the police-office on the following
morning.

9.—None of a vessel’s crew may be discharged, or left on shore here, without the
police-master’s permission, and every change of the crew shall be noted by the proper
authority on the muster-roll, before the departure of the vessel.

Every person who may be on board when a vessel departs, shall, if belonging to
the crew, be duly entered on the muster-roll of the said vessel by the proper authority ;
and, if a passenger, be provided with a lawful passport, under a penalty of from 25
to 200 pieces of eight, to be paid by the master.

10.—All vessels shall moor immediately after having anchored ; the jib-boom shall
be rigged in, and sprit-sail yard laid fore and aft, and everything that might prevent
vessels from warping, or sailing in the harbour, taken on board, and not again rigged
out until the vessel is hauled up and ready for sailing.

No boats or stages are permitted to lay astern of any vessel.

Anchors by which the vessel is moored must be provided with buoys and shortened
buoy ropes.

11.—Except in extraordinary cases, no boats are permitted to discharge or load at
any wharf after sunset; none of the crew of vessels lying in the harbour (masters
and mates excepted) may be ashore after the evening gun has fired, unless they are
provided with a pass from the police. After sunset no boats are allowed to lie at
any other than the King’s wharf, and. must not be detained for their officers later
than 8 o’clock. ~ *

12.—It is prohibited to warm pitch, tar, turpentine, or oil on board ; to throw dead
animals overboard; to careen vessels for the purpose of scraping or cleaning the
bottom. It is also prohibited to throw ballast overboard, liable to a penalty of

ISLAND OF SANTA CRUZ. 93

150 to 300 Rdr. W. Ct., of which one-third will devolve on the informer. A place for
discharging ballast will be pointed out by the harbour-master.

13.—It is not permitted to fire guns, musquetry, pistols, or other fire-arms in the
harbour after sunset, except in cases of distress.

14.—Any one that loosens, or cuts away a buoy, will be imprisoned immediately,
and liable to the severest punishment.

15.—No porter or labourer shall be employed without being provided with a written
permission from the police-master, and his plate as ordered.

16.—When an alarm is fired, viz., two guns in quick succession, from Christian’s
Fort, the half of the crew of each vessel (or more, when demanded) shall, with the
master or mate, proceed to the King’s Wharf, and there place themselves under the
command of the captain of the port; when the alarm is fired on account of fire
breaking out in the town, the crew shall bring with them two or three small sails,
axes, buckets, boat-hooks, a running tackle, and can-hooks.

17.—Masters of vessels lying in the harbour shall, whenever any of the crew are
taken sick, make immediate report thereof to the officer of health, who is to inspect
that no other than regular physicians attend the patient. In every case where this
order is neglected, the master of the yessel will be liable to a fine of 500 pieces of
eight.

18.—Masters of vessels bound for Danish ports, or for Hamburg, shall report them-
selves at the post-office eight days before they intend to sail.

19.—All orders from the captain of the port with regard to order in the harbour,
must be immediately complied with, as those who do not conform thereto will be
punished, according to the existing laws, and have to pay all expenses thereby
incurred.

No excuse of ignorance of the existing laws, even those which may not be men-
tioned in these regulations, will be valid.

20.—Every master of a vessel entering this port is to ask for a copy of these port
regulations, for which he will pay three cents.

a sail; this may be seen several leagues off, and forms an excellent mark for vessels
coming through the Virgin’s Passage, or from the westward for St. Thomas’s
Harbour. There are seyeral rocky islands which surround St. Thomas's Island, and
the following are dependent upon it—Green Cay, Hansnetic, and Brass Islands,
St. James’s, Buck, and Water Islands, Bird’s Cay, Bergantin, Cobrito, Flamenco,
and Montalvan,

It is said that a supply of excellent water may be obtained near Black Point, on
the south side of St. ‘Chomas Island, about 3 miles from the east end, and wood from
the adjacent cays.

“The channels. between the Dog Islands, Sombrero (Scrub Island), and Virgin
Gorda, are all good, and are the passages by which vessels must pass from the north-
ward to enter Drake’s Channel. ‘The southern passages most used are between
Ginger Island, and the Round Rock, Salt Island, and the Dead Chest; Peter’s and
Norman’s Island, and Norman’s Island and Flanagan Cay. The channel between the
Dead Chest and Sait Island, when used for going out of Drake’s Channel, requires a

good breeze, steady from E.S.E. towards the south, for otherwise you may get
entangled with Peter’s Island, as the current sets strongly between it and ‘the
Dead Chest ; and the swell, when the breeze is fresh, is heavy, and will retard the
progress of the vessel, and much increase her lee way. Care also must be taken to
avoid the 12 feet rock, lying about $a mile E.N.E. of the Dead Chest, which is
dangerous.

The sea along the whole of the western coast of Virgin Gorda is tranquil during
the time of the breezes, and you may anchor along the whole length of it, assured of
having not less than 8 fathoms, nor more than 16 fathoms, at the distance of 1 mile
from the shore, the bottom being all sandy ground. Vessels sailing to the southward
of the Virgin Islands, generally run through between Buck Island, and Bird’s Cay,
commonly called Frenchman’s Cap; and those who run for St. Juan’s Head, in Porto
Rico, commonly pass between the Sail Rock and Green Island.

There is a harbour on the west coast of Norman’s Island, called Man-of-War Bay,
which is more secure and better sheltered than that of Virgin Gorda; for in it, so
far as Flanagan Islet, the sea, during the breezes, is as calm as a bath; the gusts of
wind are not felt within the harbour, and when the breeze blows fresh outside, the
air will be very lightly felt within. But as the interior of the harbour is to the
windward of its points, and its width is not above 4a mile, large ships will not
be able to beat up into it; when, therefore, these are coming from the northward,
it will be necessary they should pass close to the point and luff up, and anchor
in the middle of the harbour’s mouth, warping or towing in afterwards, as may
best suit their convenience; but if it be not the hurricane season, they will ride
very well at the entrance. In coming in from the southward, they may continue
to tack to the northward without danger, and when advanced far enough, heave
about for the south tack; but should the wind be from the northward, you may
run still further in, and lie as in a dock; your sails should be furled smartly, or
the flaws with the north winds may otherwise cause you to drive, and there is
no room for manceuyring. Off the 8.W. part of Norman’s Island there is a rock
of small extent, with only 9 and 11 feet over it, called the Monica Rock.” *

SAINTE CROIX, on SANTA CRUZ. (DENMARK.)

The ISLAND of SANTA CRUZ is by some considered to be the southernmost
of the Virgin Islands; it is situate at least 32 miles to the southward of St. Thomas’s
and St. John’s Islands; its length is 19 miles, and its western part is 5 miles broad,
containing 51,900 square acres of land ; the population in 1823 was 32,000; its chief
exports are sugar, rum, cotton and cattle. The land is not mountainous, but nearly
level, having only a few trifling elevations, two of which, on the eastern part, rise
rather higher than the rest. This island has but few trees, wood therefore is scarce,
yet the land is fertile and well cultivated, abounding in sugar-canes, oranges, citrons,
and various other fruits ; there are 15 small rivulets, but most of these become dry
occasionally, and consequently leave it badly watered ; neither is it wholesome, until
it is well settled in jars. There are two towns, Christiansted and Fredericksted ;
the former is the principal one, and lies on the northern shore, towards the eastern
part of the island; this place contains 5,000 inhabitants, and its harbour is very
difficult of access, being encumbered with many shoals, one of which stretches out
nearly 2 miles to seaward in a north-easterly direction. This shoal has 2 fathoms
over it, and in some spots not more than 6 or 7 feet ; added to which there are other

shoals to the westward, which contract the channel, and render it circuitous, narrow,
and dangerous. It is defended by the Fort of Sophia Frederica, which is built on
the little Island of Loot, in front of the town, and by the Fort of Louisa Augusta,
standing on a neck of land to the eastward; so that vessels passing to the anchorage
before the town, must obtain a pilot, and go under the guns of both forts. Nearly
2 miles eastward of Louisa Augusta’s Fort is Green Cay, and E.N.E. § N., 4 miles
from the same fort, and W.N.W., 3 miles from the east point of the island, is Goat,
or Buck Island, from which a reef extends E.S.E., about 2 miles in length, and
stretches out about 1 mile to the north-westward of the island. Under the lee of the
island there is good anchorage. The mark to avoid Buck Island and Reef to the
northward is Baron’s Bluff, and Ham Bluff in one. The shores from Green Cay to
the east end of the island, and thence along the south side of the island, are lined
with rocky reefs; small craft pass between these and the shore, but large and foreign
ships must always give this side of the island an ample berth, sailing at the distance
of 24 or 3 miles. Off the south-western point a sandy reef stretches out, which must
not be approached too near.

Fredericksted lies on the west side of the island, and is also protected by a fortress ;
the bay is open, but the anchorage is tolerably good, and extends a considerable way
to the northward of the town, although not far to the westward. The depth varies,
according to the distance from the land. A flat, with 3 or 4 fathoms water, extends
to the northward of the fort, continuing with the same depth, about 4 cables’ length
from the shore, the bottom being fine white sand, with coral rocks interspersed. The
water is so very clear, that in general you can see where to let go the anchor in a clear
spot. A good berth is with the fort bearing E.N.E., in 10 fathoms water, or with
the street to the south of the fort, when seen up and down. The anchorage is much
exposed to the westerly winds, and therefore an improper place during the hurricane
season.

A shoal has been discovered to the north-eastward of St. Croix, and lately been
explored by Mr. Lang and Captain Krieger, of the Danish Navy, by whose authority
it is placed in latitude 17° 49’ 37’, and the longitude of its eastern part is 64° 28",
and bears from Buck Island about E.N.E. 3 E.; it consists of a long ledge of coral
rock, over which the least water appears to be 54 and 6 fathoms, while immediately to
the northward you will be out of the reach of soundings; to the southward of this
bank the water deepens gradually to 10 and 15 fathoms, or more, leaving a wide
channel between the bank and that which extends easterly from the east end of St.
Croix, which Mr. Lang places in latitude 17° 45’ 30’, and in longitude 64° 34’. The
mark for the northern part of the bank is Coakly Bay Mill in one with Mr.
Lang’s Observatory; and the southern part of Buck Island in a line with Bellvue
Mill will lead off it to the northward. To avoid it, when coming from the southward
and eastward of St. Croix, and standing to the N.W., you should approach no nearer
than 4 leagues from the east end of the island, and keep fully that distance to the
eastward of the east end of Buck Island, until the northern part of Buck Island
bears from the ship W.S.W., southerly, when the vessel may be kept more westerly
if necessary.

“SIR A. LANG'S OBSERVATORY is in latitude 17° 44’ 32”, longitude
64° 410"; its height is 440 feet above the level of the sea. The latitude is true to
within one second; the longitude is the result of the labour of years, and the present
assumption of 64° 41’ 0” in are, or 4h. 18m. 44s. in time west from Greenwich, I
consider to be determined with such certainty, that I do not think the error in its
determination can exceed four seconds in time, or one minute in are, and I trust is
less. Iam induced to consider it the most accurately determined position in the West
Indies, and the situation of some other islands and places on the Spanish main have
been corrected from it. On the above data, the longitude of the other stations in the
island are accurately determined ; their latitudes are certain to one or two seconds.

The dangers running down the north side of the island commence with Buck
Island reefs ; keep to the north of this island near a league, and when at this distance
it bears south, steer down west (which carries you far to the north of the Scotch-reef,
Christiansted Harbour-reef, or the White Horse of Salt River Point,) until you bring

until you pass the north-west rounding of West End Bay, when you can haul up for

Along the greatest part of the south side of the island, a ledge of reefs, with a
few channels, practicable for small vessels, lines the coast at a distance from the shore
in some places of nearly two miles ; and although they generally break, thus showing
their danger, still shoal water extends some distance to the south or seaward of them ;
therefore they must be approached with great caution, especially as no correct survey
has ever been made of them that I know of. This object I once had in contemplation,
but it is now beyond my means. These reefs commence near the shore, at a small
distance to the westward of the east end point, gradually increasing their distance
from the shore, according to the irregularity of the projecting points of the coast.
The most dangerous part of them, and the most distant from the shore, commences in
running down to the westward with an outer ledge, when you have signal-hill
flag-staff bearing about north, and continues for eight miles, until you bring the

flag-staff on St. George’s Hill, which is about a mile and a half to the east of the

Fort Fredericksted, to bear in the same direction, say north. Running down this
space, you should keep a league off the shore, which is also deceiving from its being
so very low. You have then to give a corresponding berth to the dangerous reef
and the shoal water on its back, which runs off from Sandy Point, which you will
be clear of, when you bring the north-west rounding of West End Bay to bear N. by E.
when you can haul up under the lee of the reef and the land.

Mount Eagle is the highest point of land in the island, and is 1,162 feet above
the level of the sea. Nearly one mile to the §.E. is Blue Mountain, which is not so
high as Mount Eagle by about 60 feet. They are connected together by a lower
ridge, which runs from one to the other.”—<Abridged from Remarks in the Nautical
Magazine, April, 1841, by Andrew Lang.

THE PASSAGE ISLANDS (Sparn).

These islands are situate to the westward of the Virgin Islands, and between the
latter and Porto Rico; they consist of two large and several smaller islands; of
these the Culebra or Serpents’ Islands, called also the Passage Islands, are the north-
ernmost; they are dependencies of Porto Rico, belong to the Spaniards, and are ver
iniperfectly known. The Great Culebra is about 7 miles long and 3 broad; the Little
Culebra, or Culebrita, lies off the north-east part of the Great Culebra, and has several
rocky islets about it; they are both low, and covered with trees, and there is a narrow
passage between the Great and Little Culebra. A rocky reef commences a little to
the southward of the Little Culebra, and bends round to the westward, along the
whole extent of the Great Culebra, between which and the island there is a channel

with from 5 to 11 fathoms water in it, but too dangerous for strangers to attempt. -

Some rocks and islands also stretch off the N.W. end of the Great Culebra, almost so
far as Cape St. Juan, in Porto Rico, rendering the pi ssage along the eastern coast of
Porto Rico almost impracticable, and known only to the natives. The westernmost

VIEQUE, or CRAB ISLAND, lies directly to the southward of the Culebra; it is
a long narrow island, and is so named from the quantity of crabs it abounds with;
this island is well clothed with verdure and trees, and is reported to have a soil rich
and fertile; on its north-eastern side, towards the west end, it is low and smooth;
but towards the S.W. it becomes elevated, and even hilly. ‘The northern shore has
some dangers about it, particularly towards the west; but the passage between it and
the Culebra is at least 6 or 7 miles wide, and may be navigated with safety. It ig
said there is good anchorage off a low sandy point at the west end of the island in 4
fathoms; but this should be adopted with much caution. The southern side is free
from any known danger, and may be sailed along at the distance of 14 or 2 miles;
about the middle, on this side of the island, is anchorage off a sandy cove, in 14
fathoms. About 3 miles to the eastward of the S.W. point are two small islands or
cays, upon one cf which isa fort. From the §.W. point of Crab island to Cape de
Mala Pascua, the south-eastern extremity of Porto Rico, the course is W.S.W., and
the distance 17 miles.

“ Vieque, or Crab Island, is of moderate height, and well-wooded; the south-west
end is hilly, and to the westward it is low and uneven; on the west end is a low and
sandy point, and with it, bearing N. by E. about 14 mile, is the anchorage. In
working in, do not bring this point to the southward of east, as there are numerous
shoals between it and the east side of Porto Rico ; and, from the report of the fisher-

soundings regular, and 13 mile off shore there are 6 fathoms, The shore should
not be approached nearer, as the soundings are irregular and the ground rocky.

There are a few settlers, but chiefly on its north end. We procured a small supply

southern one has a small run of fresh water, but it is brackish close to the beach; a
small supply could be obtained by carrying breakers a little way up the stream, but
with much labour. We hauled the seine in the northern bay, but caught only a few
fish.

It should be remembered that the northernmost bay is bold, and the bottom sandy ;
you may approach it to within 2 of a mile, with 4 fathoms. ‘he southern one has a
rocky bottom—soundings irregular; and should it be necessary to anchor off it for a
small supply of water, it must be carefully approached.”——Remarks of H.ILS.

PORTO RICO.

PORTO RICO (Spary).

Variation at E, end of Porto Rico 1° 40’; in the Mona Passage 2° 15’ Easterly.

PORTO RICO is about 31 leagues in length from east to west, and 11 in breadth,
where broadest. ‘The N.E. point of the island is named Cabeza de San Juan, or Cape
St. John, whence the range of mountains named Luquillo commences; the most
elevated part of which, El Yunque (the Anvil, 3,700 feet high), may be seen at the
distance of 23 leagues, forming a useful sea mark. The range continues to the west-
ward, with several intervals or breaks, until it ends in a saddle-hill, named Silla de
Caballo, or the Horse’s Saddle, which is to the southward of Arecibo. These moun-
tains have branches diverging to the north and south, and extending to the coasts ;
the whole covered with wood; the summits of the highest are often covered with
snow. In the intervals are fertile valleys and plains, watered by many rivulets, but
subject to excessive droughts. Its air is tolerably healthy, though subject to severe
storms and hurricanes, like the rest of the islands of the West Indies. The rainy
season is from June to August, and the most violent hurricanes are generally about
midsummer or the beginning of harvest. The sea breeze commonly begins about
8 o’clock in the morning, and continues blowing until 4 in the afternoon; from 4 to
6 o’clock the heat is excessive.

The population in 1836 was estimated at 357,000. The capital, Sr. JUAN, stands
on the western part of an island, on the north side, which forms a good harbour,
defended by a citadel, called the Morro Castle, and other works. ‘This island is
about 2! miles in length, nearly E. by S. and W. by N.; and its S.H. point is con-
nected to the mainland by a bridge stretching across the narrow channel of St.
Antonio. The town is populous-and well built, the see of a bishop, and the residence
of the governor.

The north coast extends nearly east and west, and is very imperfectly known.
It is rugged and uneven, and towards the east end of the island of considerable
elevation, but affords no shelter, having many rocks and islets, on which the sea
sometimes breaks with great violence. It is recommended to give this part a good
berth of 3 miles or more, asa small rock of 14 feet water, with 5 and 6 fathoms
around, is said to exist about 20 miles eastward of Port San Juan, and about 3 miles
off shore. This at present may appear as an isolated danger on the chart, but may
possibly, when the coast is properly surveyed, be found to be a portion of other reefs
and dangers hereabout. St. Juan is about 10 leagues to the westward of Cabeza de
San Juan, the N.E. point of the island.*

EAST COAST of PORTO RICO.—The shores of Porto Rico in general are
but imperfectly known to the Europeans. The north, west, and south coasts may,
however, be approached with caution, from the instruction we are enabled to give;
but the east coast, for the most: part, is so crowded with reefs, islets, and dangers, that
no description we could at present give would enable the mariner to approach with-
out the aid of a pilot. These are to be obtained at St. Thomas’s, and sometimes at
Biéques. Nothing like a survey has as yet heen made of this part, and and it con-
trasts sadly by the beautiful surveys made by order of the British Admiralty of the
Virgin Islands and Anegada Reefs.
