THE HARBOUR OF ST. JUAN. 99

We shall, however, enumerate the several ports on this coast that are visited by
vessels for sugar, which is largely cultivated in the neighbourhood of the ports; the
first of these ports is—

PUERTO FAJARDO, 33 miles to the southward of St. Juan Head, with a depth
of 16 to 23 feet.

BAHIA HONDA, or, as some now call it, Great Harbour, lies 10 miles to the
south of St. Juan Head, and a little westward of Puelca Island. It is about a mile
in extent, and open to the southward, and is protected by reefs which contract the
channel from a mile to about 4 of a mile in breadth. Inside, the anchorage is in 5 to
8 fathoms, between the patches; but large vessels had better lie outside the reef, off
the entrance, in 6 or 8 fathoms.

PUERTO NAGUABO is 5 miles W.S.W. of Bahia Honda, and is formed by
Lima Point to the N.E., and Santiago Islet to the S.W. The depth of water is from
43 to 33 fathoms. On the right bank of the river is the village of Ucaris.

PUERTO HUMACAO is between Santiago Islet on the N.E., and Candeleros
Point to the southward. The towns of Naguabo and Humacao are a short distance
inland on the borders of the rivers of the same name. These ports require the
assistance of 9, pilot, as previously recommended; and vessels bound to either of the
two last mentioned, or to those that follow on the S.E. coast, had better take the
passage to the southward of Biéques Island.

PUERTO YABUCOA is between Guaques and Yeguas Points, in lat. 18° 4’, and
about 5 miles N.N.E. of Cape Malapascua. ‘The village stands about 2 miles in the
interior.

PUERTO MAUNABO is just to the east of Cape Malapascua, and between that
cape and Tuna Point on the north. The town is some miles in the interior, on the
border of the river.

PUERTO PATILLAS is 6 miles westward of Cape Malapascua, inside the
Gauyama Reef.

NORTH COAST. The HARBOUR of ST. JUAN is about 30 miles to the
westward of St. John’s Head, being very capacious, and the largest ships may lie
there in perfect safety, in 5 or 6 fathoms water. The entrance is along the west side
of the island, on which the town is erected, and between the Morro Point and three
islets, called the Cabras or Goat Islands. South of the latter is a smaller islet, off
the sandy point, having on it a little square fort, called Hl Canuelo, which defends the
western side of the harbour. The western side of the entrance is rocky, but in the
channel, which is generally buoyed, the ground is gravel and sand, with a depth of 5,
6, and 7 fathoms. The western and southern sides of the harbour are flat and shoal.
The low point of land on the south side of the town is also surrounded by a shoal, to
the eastward of which ships generally ride, to be out of the swell of the sea, occasioned
by the trade-wind, which generally blows directly into the harbour.

Light.—The revolving light at Fort St. Juan, on the Morro, is in latitude 18° 29’,
and longitude 66° 7’. It revolves every two minutes, and is said to be only 8 seconds
bright; is elevated 171 feet, and may been seen 18 miles in clear weather. To enter
St. Juan a pilot is indispensable.

Directions.—Nearly §.S.E from the mouth of the harbour, and in an east and
west direction, are two ranges of small uneven wooded hills, of moderate elevation,
separated by a small low plain. At the foot of the highest hill on the eastern range
there is a plantation, the cultivated grounds occupying a portion of the northern face.
The summit of the western range is almost flat, and hence it is called the Maseti or
Little Table, and is easily distinguished from the surrounding heights. On the western
extremity there is a white rock, which becomes visible on rounding the Morro. The
entrance to Port San Juan may also be readily distinguished by the Morro Castle and
Lighthouse at the N.W. end of the Morro island. In approaching the port from the

eastward, with the usual trade wind, run down the north side of the island at the
distance of about 3 miles, until Salinas Point comes a little open to the northward of
Great Cabras Island. Steer in on this line until Little Table Hill is in line with the
Morro Pcint, when haul in towards Fort Canuelo. When the highest hill on the
eastern range, described above, comes in one with the Morro Point, or, if the former
cannot be made out, the flagstaff comes in one with the northernmost watch-turret of
tie two on the N.W. battery, which is the lowest in the Morro Castle, haul in for the
Little Table.

Having rounded the buoy on the St. Helena Spit, and opened the south end of
the island, which lies close under Salinas Point, to the southward of Fort Canuelo,
the vessel may be anchored as convenient, in the Outer Port, in 5 fathoms, abreast
St. Juan Gate. The Morro Point may be passed to the N.W. at 4 a cable, and
if the buoys are on the St. Helena and St. Augustine shoals, there will not be
much difficulty or risk in following these directions thus far; but a pilot will
be absolutely necessary if wishing to proceed into the inner port. — Admiralty
Directions.

PORT OF ARECIBO.

Should you have cecasion to enter the harbour with a southerly wind, you must
tun into the channel with your upper sail set, in order to preserve your way when
you get under the lee of the Morro. You should also have your boats out with a
kedge anchor and warp, ready to run out, or to tow, both of which are frequently
necessary. With a strong wind from the northward, the sea on the bar frequently
breaks and becomes dangerous, on account of the difficulty of steadying the vessel ;
and at that time great attention to the marks given is absolutely necessary. In the
outer harbour mocr, with an open hawse, to the N.W. The inner harbour, the depth
of which is said to have considerably decreased since the survey of 1793, ought not
to be taken by ships of large draught. But, as previously observed, no person should
attempt to enter without a pilot. There is no fresh water here, except rain, which is
preserved in cisterns. It ig high water in the harbour at 8h. Ym. on the days of full
and change, and the greatest rise of the tide is about 18 inches.

The FORT of ARECIBO lies 32 miles to the westward of St. Juan. Vessels
bound to this port should make the City of Porto Rico early in the morning. This
will allow of their running their distance, so as to make the anchorage of Arecibo in
good time before night, which is very desirable, as the currents are often strong and
uncertain. In running down the coast, at about 3 or 4 miles from it, two towns will
be seen; the first, Tortuguero, about 7 leagues from the city; the next, Arecibo,
which may be kncwn by its having a civcular fort on the beach to the right, end the
ruins of a church in the middle of the town, and also by a look-out-house and flagstaff
on a steep hill to windward of the port, about a mile from the town. ;

It is the custom, on vecsels, approaching the anchorage, for a pilot to come out in a
small boat, bearing a white flag, not to board, but to pull in before the vessel by way
of leadirg in; but as the sea breeze is generally strong, it often happens that the
vessel overruns the pilot boat, and the captain has to look out, and to bring his ship
to an anchor himself. The anchorage has 4 fathoms in it; the reefs are steep-to, and
the depths gradually decrease to the mouth of the river, which is nearly dry; the
rise and fall at springs is 8 feet.

The holding-ground at Arecibo is very indifferent, end in the season of the northers
(viz., from November to February), ships ought to anchor in the offing, at least 2
miles outside the reef, and be ready to slip; but in the months of April, May, June,
and July they may anchor inside, and close to the reef in 4 or 32 fathoms.

This haibour is opcn to the N.W., and in front of the town a rocky shoals runs off
some distarce. ‘Ihe mouth of the river is on the N.E. part of the bey, and runs at
the back of the town.

The trade of Arecibo is rapidly increasing — Nautical Magazine, 1843.
To the westward of Arecibo there is nothing to attract the mariner’s notice in any

AGUADILLA BAY, 101

place of commerce or anchorage, the coast being flat, low, and sandy; it is therefore
well to avoid too near an approach to a coast so little known. Twenty-four miles
from Arecibo is the point Peiia Agujereada (Pierced Rock), where the coast turns to
the S.W. fora mile, being composed of bold rocky cliffs, terminating at Bruquen
Point, the N.W. end of the island; thence the coast stretches further to the 8.W.
about a mile, but is low and sandy, as far as Pehas Blancas, or Whitestone Point,
which is covered with trees. Within a mile of Bruquen Point are 20 to 25 fathoms,
at which distance it may be safely rounded; but Pefas Blancas must be approached
with caution, for a reef stretches off it to the distance of a mile.

AGUADILLA BAY is that portion of the west coast of Porto Rico between
Point Pefias Blancas and fan Francisco, which is about 6 miles to the southward of
that point. It is an extensive bight, but free of danger, except the sand-bars at the
entrance of the rivulets on the southern side of the bay, some of which extend off
about 2 cables; the shore is sandy and bordered by a narrow ledge of soundings
about 4 of a mile in breadth; this ledge is steep-to. The town of San Carlos is
situate on the shores of this bay, about 2 miles to the southward of Pefas Blancas,
on the shores of the river Aguadilla, where good water may be obtained, and also
other refreshments. There is good anchorage off the town of St. Carlos, from 1 to 3
cables from the shore, in a depth of 4 to 15 fathoms. With a large vessel, a good °
position will be with a large house, just beyond the 3-gun battery, at the N. end of
the town, bearing N.E. 3 F.; the church E. 4 S.; and the N. point of the bay N. by
W.; this will be in about 18 fathoms, at 4 a mile from the shore, on good holding-
ground.

Remarxs In H.M.S. ARAcHNE.—* The only danger in approaching this anchorage
is a reef running off § a mile from Point Blancas, a long, low point; it is 1 mile to
the southward of Point Bruquen, the N.W. point of the island. Between Point
Blancas and Point Jiguero, the S.W. point of the bay, the coast is perfectly clear, and
you can approach any part of it within + of a mile.

The town of Aguadilla lies on the north end of a large sandy bay, extending
from Point Jiguero. The best anchorage is with the church bearing E. by S., 3 a
mile off shore, in 14 or 15 fathoms. During the months of January and February,
when the northerly winds are prevalent, this is a very rough anchorage, as a heavy
sea rolls in, rendering it difficult, and at times impossible to land. The watering
place is in the centre of the town, through which a small river runs, rolling your
casks over the beach into the village. When the water is smooth, you can procure
it quickly, but the least northing in the wind makes a heavy surf on the beach.
Fresh provisions are cheap, also vegetables and firewood. Vessels anchoring for the
purpose of watering, it should-be mentioned, the watering place is close to the only
large yellow house situate in the centre of the town. This bay is sheltered from all
easterly winds, and from south to west. With Desecheo Island W. by S., you will
be in a fairway for the town.”

This bay is much frequented by vessels bound to Cuba, or the Gulf of Mexico, on
account of the facility with which they can procure refreshments, and because pilots
for the Old Bahama Channel may always be had here.

Directions.—In making Aguadilla Bay from the northward, be careful to avoid
the ledge off Penas Blancas; and in taking up an outer berth, be careful that the
vessel is in soundings, and do not bring the vessel up too short, or she may be apt to
drag off the bank, which is very steep-to. In proceeding towards the bay from the
southward, you will pass between the Island of Desecheo and Jigiiero Point, which is
the W. extreme of Porto Rico; and when more than 17 or 18 miles from the point
and beating up towards it, do not bring it more to the eastward than N.N.E., by
which means you will escape getting entangled with the shoal grounds off the western
side of Porto Rico. Should a vessel be riding here during the winter season, when
strong N.W. and N. winds occur, it is recommended to quit the anchorage as soon as
a change threatens ; and to any one observant, the aspect of the weather will give

102

sufficient warning to prepare for leaving. In the winter season a heavy uneasy sea
rolls into the bay, rendering a high surf on the beach even with N.E. winds.

RINCON BAY.—From Jigiiero Point the coast curves in to the eastward and
forms the small bay of Rincon, eye Point being the south extreme. The two
points bear about N.W. by N. and S.E i. by S., distant 34 miles. This bay is well
sheltered from the usual trade Tee, but i it affords no good anchorage, the water
being foul.

ANASCO BAY.—The next bay to the 8.E. is that of Anasco, bounded to the
southward by the point of Algarrobo, distant 6 miles from Cadena. -The river
Anasco empties itself into the bay, before which there is a shallow bar, stretching
out 4a mile from the shore. Large vessels may anchor outside this, and be well
sheltered from the prevailing winds.

MAVYAGUEZ BAY lies between Algarrobo and Guanajibo Points, which are
about 4 miles distant. This bay, from a line of the above points, is about 14 mile
deep, and in the northern part the depths decrease from 10 to 4 fathoms towards the
shore ; but although the anchorage affords excellent shelter from northerly winds to
vessels of moderate size, the entrance is obstructed by a line of shoals, which
requires a chart of their positions, or a good knowledge of the bay, to work-in in
safety.

MAYAGUEZ BAY.

The north point of the bay (Afgarrobo) has a house, with a red roof, built upon high ©

piles on the hill just above the point, from whence the coast trends to the §.E. for 14
mile to Puntilla, a low sandy point, on which there is a building with a chimney,
and some other buildings of a bluish colour around it, used as a sugar factory. The
shore between the two points is foul for 3 cables off, and BG) mile to, the ‘§.W. of
Algarrobo Point lie the bank of that name, the outer part of which is nearly dry
and is steep-to. Just to the southward of Puntilla, at the bottom of the bay, is the
river Mayagiiez, before which is the best anchorage, affording shelter from the
northward round by East to 8.W., and the ground good for holding. From
thence the shore is low, and bends to the S.W., with shallow. water some distance
off as far as Guanajibo Point, 13 mile N. of w hich a spit runs off nearly a mile
from the shore.

Inland, to the eastward of the bay, the land becomes elevated, where will be seen
the paps or hummocks of Cerro Gordo; and there is a remarkable peak, called the
Cerro Montuoso, on the top of which are two large trees, giving it the appearance of
a double peak. This forms a useful mark from the offing, and bears from Puntilla E.
by 8. 458. about 9 miles. The village of Mayaguez is about a mile to the H.S.E. of
the entrance to the river.

SHOALS OFF MAYAGUEZ BAY :—ia Mancha de Fuera is the first shoal
to the northward and the outermost in the bay, ty ing W.N.W., 25 miles from Algar-
robo Point. It extends in a N.N.W. and S.8.E . direction about 4 a mile, and “has
from 2 to 4 fathoms water upon it, which sometimes breaks. When approaching
this shoal, the dark discoloured water may be observed at a little distance.

La Mancha de Tierre,—This shoal lies 2 of a mile S.E. of La Mancha de
Fuera, W. ; N., 12 mile from Algarrobo Point, and about N. by W. from Guanajibo
Point. It brtends: N.W. and S.E. ., and has 14 to 3 fathoms water on it. There is a
channel between this shoal and the reef off Algarrobo Point, a mile wide, with 7
fathoms in it. This may be called the inner channel from the northward.

Allart Shoal.—This shoal was first discovered by Captain Zahrtmann, of the
Danish Navy, in 1833. Itis about 2 ofa mile in length N. and S., and 4 a mile in
breadth, with from 1§ to 2 fathoms water on it. The shallowest part lies Ws 25
miles from Puntilla; N. by W. $'W. from Guanajibo Point; and 8.W. by W. 3 W.
from Algarrobo Point. The principal channel leading to the anchorage of May aguez
is between this shoal and La Mancha de Tierra, being 7 cables in breadth, with 33 to
4% fathoms water in it.

Rodriguez Bank.—This shoal is about 14 mile to the §.8.E. of the Allart, and
just without the line of bearing from Algarrobo to Guanajibo Point, bearing from
the latter about N. by W., 1} mile. It is about 4 a mile in extent N. and 8., and
some parts of it become dry at low water. This bank is connected with the Allart
Bank by a shallow bar of from 2 to 3 fathoms upon it, and between Rodrigiiez Bank
and Guanajibo Point there are 43 and 33 fathoms, decreasing towards the shore.

BOQUERON BAY.

White Rock.—This rock, according to a French survey, wherein the above shoals
are clearly delineated, lies about midway between and just within the line of bearing
of Rodrigiiez and Allart Banks. It is a small rocky patch, having but 6 feet on its
shoalest part, and obstructs the passage between the above two banks, which would
otherwise, to small vessels, afford a good channel. It lies W. ¢8., 2 miles from the
custom-house, and W. by §S. 2S. from Puntiila Point.

Directions.—The main channel into Mayagiiez Bay is between the shoals of La
Mancha de Tierra and Allart ; and if the wind be such as will allow a vessel to lie
through either in entering or leaving the bay, the mark will be the peak of Mon-
tuoso (previously noticed) in line with the custom-house, bearing KE. by 8.38. The
custom-house stands to the southward of the river, on the shore, and is the southern-
most of four large houses with flat roofs; indeed, either of these houses will form a
mark with the peak. The church in the village (which has two turrets), in line with
the custom-house, will also lead up to the anchorage. The barracks, a large flat-
roofed building to the southward of the custom-house, ou higher ground, should not
be mistaken for it.

In turning in, a vessel may stand to the northward, towards La Mancha de Tierra,
until the custom-house and church are in one ; to the southward, in standing towards
the Allart shoal, tack before the peak of Montuoso comes in line with the church ;
but when within the two shoals, the boards may be prolonged at discretion. When
Point Guanajibo bears south, a vessel will be to the eastward of the outer banks. There
is a channel to the northward, between Las Manchas and the Algarrobo reef.
Should the wind be fair for this channel, take care not to haul round Algarrobo Point
to the eastward until the peak of Montuoso opens south of the chimney of Vigos
sugar-house, which is a conspicuous object near the shore, and of a whitish colour.

Anchorage.—H.M. steam-vessel Medea anchored in this bay in 5 fathoms, with

For large vessels there is said to be anchorage outside, to the westward of the
shoals; bat any one taking it up should be very cautious, as our information of these

The rise and fall of the tide in Mayagiiez Bay is from 2 to 3 feet, but the periods
are irregular.

PUERTO REAL DE CABO ROJO.—At the distance of 55 miles S. $ W. from
the point Guanajibo, is Puerto Real de Cabo Rojo, of almost circular form, and about
$ofa mile in diameter. It has 18 feet water at the entrance, and 16 feet in the
centre of the basin. The entrance is by a very narrow channel, and lies to the 8.
point of the harbour. From thé N. point an extensive reef runs off, which, after
doubling Cayo Fanduco, terminates at Punta de Varas.

BOQUERON BAY.—At 2 miles 8. by W. 2 W. from Puerto Real is the point
Guaniquilla, which is the northernmost point of the large bay called Boqueron.
This bay affords no safe anchorage, the approaches being obstructed by numerous
shoals, and the interior full of reefs. Punta de Melones, the southern point of the
bay is distant from Point Guaniquilla a little more than 2% miles, and nearly west
about 63 miles from Point Melones is Baxo Gallardo, or Gallardo Bank, of which we
shall speak hereafter. :

Monte de Atalaya.—This is a high mountain near the shore on the N. side of
Anasco Bay, and is the highest and northernmost peak of two which are seen on the

104 CAPE ROJO.

top of the mountain range, and is seen from the whole of the west coast. It bears
about S.E. by E. from Jigiiero Point, is very remarkable, and does not alter its
appearance when seen even from off the south end of the island Desecheo.

We have now to treat of the shoals, &c., off the west coast, and must here premise
that our information of such is very scant. They are very numerous aud imperfectly
known, and it will be well for the mariner to give this part a wide berth. One
bearing we have given previously in treating of Aguadilla Bay, that of Point
Jigiiero bearing N.N.E., which would appear, from our present knowledge of the
locality, to keep clear westward of all the dangers; but it behoves the mariner to
keep a good look-out here, for in March, 1847, the “John Brown” is said to have
struck upon a shoal 3 leagues from the nearest part of Porto Rico, and remained there
one hour and a half, thumping heavily, but ultimately came off, after throwing 5
hogsheads of sugar and some stores overboard, starting the water on deck, and the
loss of a quarter-boat. The bearings given is Desecheo island N.N.W., 9 miles; but
the position is considered doubtful.

Bank in the Mona Passage.—A bank of 4 fathoms water has lately been
discovered by Capt. W. M. Walker, United States steam-vessel “ De Soto.” From it
the Island of Desecheo bears N. 4 W., 19 miles distant ; Point Jigiiero, N.N.E. $E.,
distant 21 miles; Point Aquila, E.S.E., distant 15 miles; and is situate about 14
miles from the nearest land of Porto Rico.

Wegro Shoal.—The first of these shoals nearest the coast from the northward is
the Negro Shoal, and is of small extent and almost always breaks. It lies 34 miles
from the shore, with 6 feet water upon it, with Guanajibo Point bearing E. by N. %
N., and Jigiiero Point N. 2 W.

Las Coronas, or the Crowns, are some sand-banks about 4 miles to the south-
ward of the Negro, about $ a mile in extent, and are just covered by the sea, which
sometimes breaks. They are 33 miles from the nearest part of the shore, with
Guanajibo Point bearing N.E. 3 N., and Jigiiero Point N. } W.

Media Luna, or Half Moon, is another shoal, said to lie to the N.W. of the
Coronas, and at 5 miles from the land, and has been described as a reef of about 3 of
a mile in extent N. and S., and about 25 cables’ length in breadth, the sea always
breaking over it. About E.N.E from it, at 3 a mile, there are three rocks, which
appear above water, on which the sea always breaks. From the north end of the
shoal, Guanajibo Point is said to bear N.E. by H. 3 E., and Jigiiero Point N. } E.
The position of this shoal and the rocks is very much doubted.

Guaniquilla Shoal is a rocky ledge of about 2 cables in «xtent, and has 3
fathoms water upon it. It lies about 2 miles to the westward of Punta de Guani-
quilla with Point Guanajibo bearing N. by E.$E., and Jigiiero Point N. 2 W.
This shoal-is also considered doubtful.

The Baxo Gallardo, which is almost west from Punta de Melones, and 6 miles
distant from it, is a rocky shoal of 3 fathoms, about 3 cables’ length in extent; and
the least depth of water upon it is 2 fathoms, rocky bottom. It lies with Desecheo
Island bearing N. by W. 3 W.; Monte de Atalaya, N.N.E. ; and the south extreme of
the Morillos.(two small hills near Cape Rojo), E.S.E?

Another shoal, according to some Spanish charts, lies about 4 miles west of the
entrance to Boqueron Bay. This is said to have 23 fathoms water upon it, but it is
considered doubtful.

CAPE ROJO is the §.W. point of Porto Rico, aud slopes down from the Morillos
to a bold headland, and when first seen from the eastward or westward, appears like
two low grey islets under the high land. When seen from the southward, two
remarkable cliffs will be observed to the eastward. Cape Rojo is encompassed by a
shoal called the White Grounds, which extends 3 leagues to the S.W. At 2 or 3
leagues to the eastward and westward of the cape, there are 10, 12, and 15 fathoms.
The sand at the bottom is of such shining whiteness, that the reflection pierces

SOUTH COAST OF PORTO RICO. 105

through the water. It is a coral bank, and close to its edge no bottom is to be found,
The southern extremity bears from the point S.W. } W. about 3 leagues. Plenty of
fish may be caught here with hook and line.*

DESECHEO ISLAND.—Having described the west coast of Porto Rico and the
shoals adjacent with sufficient prolixity, it remains here to say that W. 3 N. at the
distance of 11 miles from Punta Jigiiero, is the island of Desecheo or Zacheo, of con-
siderable height and very clear. It appears like a green mountain 800 or 1,000
yards long ; several parts of it are covered with wood, and it is so high as to be seen
12 leagues off.

The SOUTH COAST of PORTO RICO.—From the Morillos in the §.W. to
Malapascua, which is the S.E. extremity of the island, the coast is of double land,
and is said to be very foul, with reefs, islets, and shoals extending in some parts a
considerable distance from it. It is therefore necessary to approach with much
caution, mote especially as very little is known of these parts in which reliance can
be placed. About equal distance between the extreme points of the south coast, is
the island called Caxa de Muertos, or Coffin Island, at 4 miles distant from the coast,
and foul at its N.E. and west parts. There are numerous rivers emptying themselves
on this coast, and various small harbours, at present only known to the natives ; of
those we have any information of, Guanica will be the first. Vessels taking the
route by the south coast of Porto Rico, and not bound to any particular port, should
keep 4 or 5 miles off the land, and not approach it without due attention to the lead.

‘PUERTO GUANICA.—This is the best port on this side of Porto Rico, and is
distant about 54 leagues eastward of the Morillos. It is about 13 mile in length, in
a N.W. and §.E. direction, and + to 3 a mile in breadth, and will accommodate large
vessels, having a depth of 6 fathoms at the entrance to 34 at the further end of the
harbour, which is more than a mile from the entrance.

The mouth of this harbour is in the middle of a great bay, formed by the point
and cliff.of Fronton de la Brea on the west, and that of Picua on the east. The
latter has contiguous to it two islets, called Cana and Cana Gorda, and from these
islets to the Punta de la Meseta, the east point of the entrance of the harbour, there
is a reef which stretches out from the coast nearly a mile, forming an arc of a circle,
united at one end with the islets, and at the other end with Punta de la Meseta.
Between Brea Point and Punta de los Pescadores, or Fisherman’s Point, the west
point of the harbour, the coast forms another harbour, which is obstructed by a reef,
which runs from Pescadores Point, and ends at the south side of the bay, about $
a mile within the point of Brea. The entrance is between the two bold headlands of
Meseta and Pescadores, and is little more than a cable’s length in width. On
approaching the entrance, it is not only necessary to give a berth to the reefs noticed
on either side of the bay, but also to a rocky shoal of only 12 feet, lying 3 cables
outside the reef, about 8 cables long, in a north and south direction. ‘The south end
of this ledge lies §.S.E. a mile from Meseta Point, and in a line between Brea and
Picua Points, with the south end of Cana Gorda E. by N., distant 2 miles.

Directions.—To take this harbour from the eastward, you must run down outside
the reefs until Meseta Point is in one with the paps of Cerro Gordo, which may be
easily recognised inland. If you run in with the point in line with the western pap,
you will pass very close to the bank, but yet in 10 fathoms water; if with the point
in line with the eastern pap, you will pass without any risk of danger. When Cana

Gorda bears E. $ N., you will have passed the rocky shoal, and may run boldly for
the entrance, and come to convenient anchorage inside. In taking the harbour from
the westward, by the Punta de la Brea, you may pass within a cable’s length, and

a cable’s length, and from thence into the harbour, observing that the south shore is
bolder than the north, and anchor where conyenient, in 5 or 4 fathoms water.

PUERTO DE GUAYANILLA.—This is a large circular bay, about 7 miles to
the eastward of Guanica, and is open to the southward. The western point is sur-
rounded by reefs, and the latter by islets. We have no further information respect-
ing it.

PUERTO DE MATANZA,.—This bay is about 3 miles eastward of Guayanilla,
somewhat similarly formed, but of which we can give nothing farther. Ata mile
8.W. by W. of Cuchara Point, which is the east point of the bay, is the small islet
of Ratones, which, when well observed, may form a mark equally for Ponce as for
this port.

PUERTO PONCE is 15 miles to the eastward of Guanica, and 7 miles to the
N.W. of the Muertos Island, or the Dead Chest. The land is low near the water,
covered with mangrove bushes and cocoa-nut trees; but the houses of the village are
also low, so that they will not become visible until you approach the harbour, which
is open to the southward. To the westward of the village there is a small fort on
the beach. On the western side of the bay, at 2 of a mile from the fort, is a small
sandy cay, named Cardona, covered with brushwood, with breakers off its east end.
This cay is connected by a reef to Cuchara Point, from which it is distant about 14
mile. ‘There appears to be no other danger near it ; but the water is discoloured for
2 or 3 miles to the southward, with irregular soundings as far out as the parallel of
Muertos Island, and south of the bay as little as 3 fathoms water will be met with.

‘Directions.—To run for this port, keep a mile from the small cay off the 8.W.
end of Muertos Island, and steer N.W. 4 N. or N.W. by N. This course will lead
up to the port, with regular soundings, on a rocky bottom, and a vessel must pass to
the eastward of the cay above mentioned, near the fort. If it blows fresh, the reef
which is passed on the starboard hand will appear to break right across the entrance;
but, as you approach, it will be observed that the breakers do not make off far from
the bushes. Pass the breakers within 2 cables’ length, and keep the southern shore
of the harbour on beard.

MUERTOS ISLAND, or DEAD CHEST, is situate 35 miles from Cape Rojo,
and 40 miles from Cape Malapascua. When first made, it appears in the form of a
wedge, the north end being high, the centre low, and the south end a sugar-loaf
mountain, which at a distance appears a detached island. The anchorage ison the
west side, off the low land, 5 a mile from shore, in 8 fathoms, in the following bear-
ings :—'S.E. point of the small island, connected by a reef above water, S.W.; the
only sandy bay, 8. by E.; the N.W. point and northern peak in one, east. There is
no danger on the west side of the island, and off the low land the soundings are
vegular; but to the northward of it the water is deeper, and there are 17 fathoms
close to the shore, to the southward of the island.

The name Dead Chest is applied to the island from its resemblance to a chest or
coffin. rom a certain point it appears like two flattened balls, separated by a broad
valley. ‘The shore towards Porto Rico is flat and sandy ; on the south side it is high
and stony. ‘There is no fresh water on it, nor trees of any kind but for fuel. It is,
however, supposed that by digging the sand a little below the mark of the highest
tides ‘and surf, fresh water may be found, as ‘on other sandy cays. Caution must be
obset'ved not to dig too deep, for at too great a depth the water is brackish. The
fresh water thus found is supposed to be rain-water, which having strained through
the sand, is kept by its specific gravity above the sea-water, which is always found
when the bottom of the hole is on a leyel with the surface ‘ofthe ocean. “This is a

good place for fish and turtle, as the latter lay their eggs in the great sandy bays,
and for this reason is much frequented by the inhabitants of Porto Rico.

Berberia Rocks.—To the E.N.E. of Muertos Island, and at the distance of 3
miles, are the Berberia Rocks, and these appear to be connected with Muertos Island
by a shelf having only 23 fathoms upon it. In the neighbourhood of these cays are
many dangerous rocks, and, like the whole of the south coast of the island, are very
imperfectly known. With Muertos Island bearing west, 3 or 4 miles distant, there
is a depth of 6 fathoms. From the hills, white water is seen a considerable distance
to the eastward; it is therefore requisite to keep the lead going. About a cable’s
length from the §.W. end of the island Muertos, and connected to it by a dry reef,
there is a small flat cay called the Hammock, which should not be rounded within
the distance of 14 mile.

Anchorage.—The western side of Muertos Island is free of danger, and affords
good anchorage in from 7 to 12 fathoms water. A good berth may be taken with
the §.E. end of the Hammock §.W.; the same cay S. by E.; and the N.W. point of
Muertos in one with the Northern Hill east, in 8 fathoms, at about 4 a mile from the
shore. Off the low land of the island the soundings are regular, but to the north-
ward of it the depth is much greater, being 17 fathoms close to the shore. Anchor-
age will also be found with the west end of the Hammock S. by EH. 3E., distant
134 mile; and the north end of Muertos N.E. 5 E.

PUERTO de JACAQUA.—This anchorage is at the entrance of the River
Jacaqua, 3 miles to the eastward of Cabullon Point, the west point of the Bay of
Ponce. Two small isiets and several reefs lie just to the westward, called the Frio
Islets. There is not much in the way reaching the anchorage, using the lead and
marking the soundings from 63 to 33 fathoms.

BOCA CHICA,.—This is a small trading port, 44 miles northward of Muertos
Island, and it is said there is no danger in approaching it. The soundings gradually
decrease from 7 to 4 fathoms as the Porto shore is approached, and the lead must be
the guide.

COAMO BAY is that portion of the coast from Coamo Point to Point Fama de la
Maria, distant 52 miles. The River Coamo empties itself into the bay, the town
being situate 8 miles up the river. Off the Point of Coama are several small islets.

PUERTO de las SALINES de COAMO is a safe harbour, about 14 miles to
the eastward of Muertos Island, which is in sight from it. Its entrance may be
known by several small cays near the shore, and a guard-house, which will be seen
when running down outside them. The channel lies between the outer or western-
most cay, which is about 4 miles to the southward of the guard-house, and a reef,
14 mile to the westward of it, which always breaks. Within the harbour there is a
rocky shoal having 163 feet water upon it, and 22 feet around. On this reef a
Spanish store-ship struck in November, 1860. It lies with the middle of the round
cay at the entrance to the channel between the coast and the islets bearing N.N.E.
4 E. and the south extreme Saso cay 8.W. 3 S.

‘Water.—There is a good watering-place in Port Salinas de Coamo, on the shore
near a lagoon, about 4 a mile to the westward of the guard-house.

Dizections.—Discoloured water extends off a considerable distance from the cays
off Port Salinas de Caomo, and 3 miles off the depth is 12 fathoms, which will decrease
to 7 fathoms, as the shore is approached. Having rounded the western cay at the
entrance within a cable’s length, steer boldly in between the eastern cays and the
reef, towards the guard-house, and anchor in 4 or 5 fathoms, with the latter bearing
N. 3 E. about a mile distant. In leaving the anchorage, if bound to the westward,
stand well out to the southward, into an offing of 2 or 3 miles from the cays, until
Muertos Island is to the northward of west, before keeping away.

To the eastward of Porto Salinas to the Cape Malapascua, the S8.E. point of Porto
Rico, there remains the Puerto de Jobos, or Boca d’Infierno, the roadstead of Guayama,

108

and the small bay of Arroya to be treated of, and in doing so, we shall introduce the
instructions from the French chart, by Captain C. B. Matenas (1853.)

Entrance to the Anchorage of GUAYAMA.—To anchor here, Cape Malapascua
must be made. At4 miles S.S.W. of this cape begins a chain of reefs, which continue,
with few interruptions, to 2 miles from Jobos, or Bouche de l’Enfer. Inside of these
reefs are the anchorages of Patillas and Guayama.* ‘i

To anchor at Guayama, after having well observed Cape Malapascua, coast along
shore 5 miles distant, until the village of Arroya bears N. } W. or north, then cross
immediately between the reefs, and anchor in 13 to 25 fathoms; the depths gradually
shallow to about 13 feet at 2 cables’ length frem the shore. The above-mentioned
reefs lie about 24 or. 8 miles from the shore. The eastern patch is almost entirely
uncovered at low water, the western seldom so, and the middle patch opposite Patillas
uncovers more on the western than on the eastern side.

ARROYA is easily known by the custom-house and houses on the beach, among
which are those of the consuls, with flagstaffs. To the westward of Arroya, at the
entrance of Jobos, or Porto de Infierno, the land abounds with sugar plantations, which
are well cultivated.

The PORTS of PATILLAS and GUAYAMA are rather dangerous during the
winter season, for it is impossible to get under-way in a lee-tide or in a gale. In other
respects the ground is sufficiently good to hold with two anchors.

JOBOS, or BOUCHE de L/INFER, is one of the best ports in Porto Rico, a true
wet dock ; vessels should not draw more than 14 to 15 feet to enter. The outlet has
a depth of 16 to 18 feet; the bottom is soft mud, with a greater depth in the western
than in the eastern part, where the landing-place is situate.

As the entrances of Jobos are difficult, a pilot is indispensable, and can be obtained
at Guayama, sometimes at St. Thomas, or in the offing, but they seldom go beyond
the reefs.

Ships sailing along the south coast of Porto Rico are exposed to sudden calms,
occasioned by the island intercepting all breezes from between north and cast. It
should not be coasted nearer than 5 miles; but the north coast, as previously observed,
may be run down at the distance of 3 or 4 miles, ;

THE MONA PASSAGE.

‘The Mona Passage, between Porto Rico and Santo Domingo, is about 66 miles wide,
and receives its name from two small islands (Mona and Monito) which lie nearly
midway across on the south side, between Cape Rojo and Saona Island.

From Cape Rojo, in Porto Ricd, to the S.E. point of Saona Island, off the S.E. part
of Santo Domingo, the bearing is W. 2 N., and the distance 26 leagues. In a direct
line between and nearly midway, but rather nearer to Saona lie the islands Mona and

Monito; the former is the largest and southernmost, and Monito is about 2 miles to
the N.W. of it. There is anchorage about 3 a league to leeward of Mona, in 7 or 8
fathoms water, sand and weeds. Desecheo, which has been described, lies nearly 10
leagues N.E. 3 E. from Mona.

Mona is an island almost level, of little elevation, and without any prominences
onit; itis not inhabited, and its surface seems covered with brushwood, without trees
of any considerable height. Its N.E. and west coasts are of white rock, perpendicular
to the water, and may be approached as close as you choose; the S. coast is consider-
ably lower, but as clean as the former. Near to the W. point, however, some vessels
anchor, in order to procure grass when engaged in carrying cattle. The island may
be seen at the distance of 6 leagues.

‘water.—Fresh water is scarce, but a little to-the right of the landing on the western
shore, there is a pathway leading to the watering-place under the southern cliffs ; and
here also firewood will be found.

Wonito is a small islet about 34 miles to the N.N.W. of Mona, and is scarcely
more than 2 cables long anda cable broad. It is much lower than Mona, and in
shape resembles a shoemaker’s last. It is quite barren, and is the resort of immense
numbers of booby birds. The pilots of these coasts state that there is a clear and
deep passage between Mena and Monito.

Tides.—It is high water, full and change, at Mona Island at 6h. 15m., and the
rise is about 2 feet. The flood sets N. by E., and the ebb S. by W., at the rate of 5 a
knot.

The following remarks are by Captain J. V. Baker, R.N., H.M. Ship, Arachne,
1834.*

Mona Istanp.—* This island is nearly level, and of moderate height. We could
not see it farther than 18 miles ona clear day. Its N.E., 8.E., and 8.W. sides are
bounded by a reef 4 of a mile off shore. At the distance of 2 miles we ran along
these sides, but saw no other danger than a reef, which extends 1} mile off the south
point.

The §.W. point (to the northward of which is the anchorage) is sand, long and low,
with brushwood and small trees on it. There is a reef off this point, about 3 of a
mile in length, to the westward.

We anchored here, with the sandy point bearing S. by W., 15 mile; Island of
Monito N. 1 E.; N. W. point of Mona (high and bluff) N.E. 4 N.

We came in from the northward, passing Monito to the westward, within 6 miles,
but had no soundings, neither could we see broken water or any danger between it
and Mona. This island is the resort of innumerable quantities of boobies ; its sides
are very white, and are inaccessible. Our anchorage was off the sandy bay formed
by the $.W. point (bearings as above mentioned), sandy bottom ; this, the N.W. side,
is also bounded by a reef about 3 cables’ length from shore ; the passage through it
is nearly in the centre of the bay, but it is narrow, and a boat must pick her way
through. The soundings are very regular ; we found 4 fathoms close to the reef, and
there would be-no danger in anchoring within { of a mile of it, bearing in mind
that it is open to all westerly winds.

We landed on the sandy beach, and found the west end of the island, which is:
low, covered with small trees, brushwood, and, at a few cleared spots, with grass, in
the latter of which were small spots of fresh water, apparently dug, but of bad
quality ; around these we found the print of the hoofs of cattle and horses, or mules,
very recently made, as was evident by the sun not having hardened the soil.. These
pools of fresh water were on the S.E. side of the sandy point, about 13 mile from

the landing. We did not find any signs of habitation or inhabitants; and, excepting
the before-mentioned fresh-water pools, we saw no possibility of obtaining water. A
small quantity of firewood might be obtained with labour.”

Directions.—Vessels coming round Cape Rojo, or from the §.E., and bound
through the Mona Passage, should, after clearing the White Grounds, endeavour to
sail in mid-channel, between Desecheo and Mona; there is no danger but what can
be seen. With the wind at E.S.E. or E., there will be no need to tack, but to sail
through with the wind quartering. It will be sufficient to steer N.W. by N. to fetch
Cape Raphael, the N.E. point of Santa Domingo, or even Cape Samana. The
currents, which generally set to the westward, must be guarded against, lest they set
you into Samana Bay, whither they frequently run with great strength.

A ship, having fetched the Island of Mona, if bound to the northern side of Santo
Domingo, may run to leeward of Mona and Monito, observing the above precaution.
With Mona E.S.E., 3 or 4 leagues, you may perceive the coast of Santo Domingo.

WINDS.—The winds around Porto Rico appear to be of the same character as
those met with in the Virgin Islands. There is no longer land breeze to take advan-
tage of, although the usual trade-wind generally slackens during the night in the
immediate vicinity of the shore. Under the W. end the wind in the daytime will
incline inward. In the winter months N. and N.W. winds sometimes occur, and blow
hard; and in the summer long calms and light S.E. airs will prevail, with terrific
squalls and heavy rains, especially on the south side. From the absence of any
remarks on the rollers, we may conclude that they are at least not so heayy or so
dangerous as at the Virgin Islands.

CURRENTS.—On the north side of Porto Rico, the current is said to incline
generally to the S.W., or toward the shore, and to run with greater velocity in the
winter than in the summer months. On the south side its course is generally
west, but its movements are here uncertain. Some navigators state that at the full
and change of the moon a strong weatherly set will occasionally be found, especially
if light winds or northers have prevailed near these periods, and consequently gives
great assistance to vessels beating to windward. In the summer months it will
Incline to the N.W. towards the shore, and round the S.W. end into the Mona
Passage with great foree. This is probably owing to the great body of water thrown
out in this direction, at this period, from the great rivers of Terra-firma,

CURRENTS AND TIDES IN THE MONA PASSAGE.
The following remarks are by Sir Robert H. Schomburgk :—

“ The wreck of the British brig Brazilian, on the eastern coast of the island of
Santo Domingo, near Punta Engano,* occurred in consequence of the strong N:W.
by W. current that sweeps the Carribean Sea, which, combining with the trade
drift, amounts probably, when not overpowered by a local current, to no less than 24
miles per day, and frequently surpasses it.

The Brazilian, Captain Power, sailed on the ist of May, 1850, from Porto
Cabello, bound for New York, laden with coffee, indigo, and hides, and made on the
7th of that month, at 10 o’clock A.M., the island of Mona bearing N.N.E., the wind
being light from E. by N., with sultry weather, the vessel carrying all sail by the
wind. At 6 o’clock p.m., Mona Island bore EH. 4 N. distant about 10 miles. The
master went about sunset on the foretop-mast-head, and enquiring from the man at
the helm how the ship’s head then was, received as answer that she held her course
north. Cape Engano bore then N.W. distant about 30 miles; and, thinking that
with a course of N. by W. he should pass about 12 miles to the east of Cape Engano,
he ordered the vessel to be kept as close to the wind as possible. She struck about

; to 5 o’clock A.M. of May 8th, on a reef near Punta Cana, about + of a mile from

THE. MONA, PASSAGE.

* Cape Engano is called by the pilots of Santo Domingo, Punta Espada; and the point
called Punta Espada in the charts is called Cabo Rafael by the pilots,

THE MONA PASSAGE. - 111

the shore ; Cape Engano bearing then N.N.E. about 43 miles distant. The current
had set, therefore, the vessel gradually from N. by E. to N.W.

Having been informed of the wreck of the vessel, I proceeded in the Dominican
man-of-war schooner Constitucion to the scene of the disaster. The passage from
the harbour of Santo Domingo to Cape Engano is usually made in two days. We
had, however, light winds, and experienced on approaching the island of Saona a
severe current, setting us N.W. by W. at a rate of 2 miles in an hour; and, on
rounding the east end of Saona and approaching Punta Espada, the current set power-
fully to the 8.S.W. at the rate of 25 miles to 3 miles in an hour, so that we found
ourselves in the morning from 20 to 30 miles further from the point of our destination
than we were the preceding evening. I could only ascribe this to the influence of the
tides, which are felt to a distance of 6 miles from the east coast of Santa Domingo;
and being much stronger than the stream current, they give an impetus to the south-
westward until the tidal wave, having gradually lost the impetus with which it swept
through the western side of Mona Passage, emerges again into the current.

In the case of the Brazilian, the vessel experienced in the first instance the N.W.
by W. current, which gradually and silently set her towards the shore; with the
change of the tide her course was retarded, and in lieu of being at midnight, as Mr.
Power expected, 12 miles to the eastward of Cape Engano, he was at that time 10
or 12 miles to the south of it, and a reef-girted shore perhaps not more than 7 or 8
miles under his lee. Cape Engano bore then probably N. by E. distant 12 miles.
The vessel had therefore been set three points to leeward, and had been retarded 20
miles in her course. Had the Brazillian tacked at that time, she would have escaped
all danger.

The Constitucion, on board of which I was, anchored on the 18th May, in the
afternoon, near Punta Cana, somewhat more than a mile off shore. The wreck of
the Brazilian was from here one mile. We found for the subsequent three days that
the tide ran with a velocity of 33 knots for nearly nine hours towards the 8.8.W.,
and merely for two hours and a half to three hours to the N.E. by N. The pilot on
board the schooner told me that he was well acquainted with the coast, and that the
tides were not always of equal strength, running sometimes six hours to the 8.S.W.
and six hours to the N.E.; at other periods the ebb tide was stronger than the flood
tide, and if such a case occurred, the north-easterly tide ran eyen with greater
velocity than the south-westerly.

The great strength of the current is to be ascribed to the swelling of the Orinoco,
which river commences to rise in April, and reaches its maximum height in August,
It pours then out its vast masses of waters through its numerous mouths, sweeping
along the southern shores of the Carribee Islands, and directing its centre towards
the promontory of Santo Domingo, called Point Mongon, (to the south of which lie
the small islands of Beata and Alta Vela), it forms there such an opposing mass of
waters to vessels, that they are known to have been detained there for weeks.*
During the inundations of the Orinoco, the velocity of the N.W. by W. current is
along the south side of Porto Rico, from 13 to 2 knots in'an hour; and the stream,
approaching the Mona Passage, sends an offset through the same, which continues its
course, assisted by the ebb-tide, until it meets the tidal wave from the broad ocean,
and, overpowered by its stronger antagonist, receives a south-western impulse, until
it reaches that distance from the shore of Santo Domingo where the tides are no longer
felt with violence. It merges afterwards in the N.W. by W. current, now combining
drift with stream, and continues its central course along the south side of Jamaica
until the Carribean current rushes into the Gulf of Mexico,

* Admiral Columbus felt this current during his second, and likewise during his last
voyage ; and Washington Irvine observes, that the currents are here so violent that
ae are often detained for months, waiting for sufficient wind to enable them to stem
the current.

112

The mass of water which this current disturbs in its course, sweeping to the N.W.,
produces, no doubt, an indraught, which causes the tidal wave that comes from the
ocean to increase its velocity, while running through the Mona Passage in a S.S, W.
direction.

From September to April the Orinoco is low; it acquires its minimum state in
February. During this period the north-westerly current is weak, and any strong
south wind that rises in the basin of the Carribean Sea will produce an accumulation
of waters, which, getting to the north, finds opposition by the configuration of the
coasts of Cuba, Santo Domingo, and Porto Rico, and are there forced in a south-
easterly direction. But this is not the only cause of a south-easterly current, which
is occasionally found in these localities. A northerly gale on the coast of the United
States, or between the parallels of 20° and 40° north, and the meridians of 40° and 60°
west, presses the masses of waters onward to the south, until they meet the barrier
which the great Antilles place to their progress. The oceanic waves rush, therefore,
through the passages of the Bahamas and Caicos Islands, the passage between Cuba
and Santo Domingo, and between the latter island and Porto Rico, &c.,* with fearful
violence, assuming an easterly direction as soon as they reach the Carribean Sea, and
hence they set frequently at that time to the south-east from Alta Vela along the coast
of Santo Domingo and Porto Rico.

The coasters are well acquainted with this fact, and it often occurs that such a
current shortens a passage from the city of Santo Domingo to St. Thomas three
days. The tidal wave recedes during such periods through the Mona Passage with
the velocity which the flood-tide usually possesses; but it sets from Mona Island
north-eastward towards the little island of Desecheo, near the north-western point of
Porto Rico.

From all these observations it results, that a vessel bound from Costa Firma to
the United States, that purposes to sail through any of the passages that the Car-
ribean Sea affords, should consider at what period the passage is made, and if between
Aprii and August, the greatest caution ought to be used in passing any of the outlets
from the Carribean Sea to the Atlantic Ocean. It will be always on the safer side in
passing by the island of Mona to consider that the stream, whether the consequence
of currents or of tides, sets to leeward, except actual observations prove to the
contrary,

I have now for more than twenty years collected data respecting the N.W. by W.
current that sweeps the Carribean Sea, and its existence is sufficiently proved and
generally acknowledged by navigators. I propose, therefore, that in lieu of the long
name which I have given to it from the point towards which it sets, it receives the
better appellation of the Carribean Current. Whatever may be the little deviations
in its direction which the configurations of the coasts give to it, its main direction ig
to the N.W.”—WNautical Magazine, 1850, pp. 585-8.

THE ISLAND OF PORTO RICO.
Variation at E. end of Porto Rico 1° 40’; in the Mona Passage 2° 15’ Easterly.

PORTO RICO is about 31 leagues in length from east to west, and 11 in breadth,
where broadest. The N.E. point of the island is named Cabeza de San Juan, or Cape
St. John, whence the range of mountains, named Luquillo, commences; the most
elevated part of which, El Yunque, (the Anvil 3,700 feet high,) may be seen at the
distance of 23 leagues, forming a useful sea mark. The range continues to the west-
ward, with several intervals or breaks, until it ends in a saddle-hill, named Silla de
Caballo, or the Horse’s Saddle, which is to the southward of Arecibo. These moun-
tains have branches diverging to the north and south, and extending to the coasts ;
the whole covered with wood: the summits of the highest are often covered with
snow. In the intervals are fertile vallies and plains, watered by many rivulets, but
subject to excessive droughts. Its air is tolerably healthy, though subject to severe
storms and hurricanes, like the rest of the islands of the West Indies. The rainy
season is from June to August, and the most violent hurricanes are generally about
mid-summer, or the beginning of harvest. The sea breeze commonly begins about
8 o’clock in the morning, and continues blowing until 4 in the afternoon; from 4
to 6 o’clock the heat is excessive.

*The year 1867 having become memorable for the severity of hurricanes and earth-
quakes in the neighbourhood of the Virgin Islands; and the recent accounts of the

together with larger portions of the surrounding plateaux may hereafter prove to have

2 EAST COAST OF PORTO RICO.

The population in 1836 was estimated at 357,000. The capital, St. JUAN, stands
on the western part of an island, on the north side, which forms a good harbour,
defended by a citadel, called the Morro Castle, and other works. This island is about
2% miles in length, nearly E. by 8. and W. by N.; and its S.E. point is connected
to the main land by a bridge stretching across the narrow channel of St. Antonio.
The town is populous and well built, the see of a bishop, and. the residence of the
governor.

The north coast extends nearly east and west, and is very imperfectly known.
It is rugged and uneven, and towards the east end of the island of considerable
elevation, but affords no shelter, having many rocks and islets, on which the sea
sometimes breaks with great violence; it is recommended to give this part a good
berth of 3 miles or more, as a small rock of 14 feet water, with 5 and 6 fathoms
around, is said to exist about 20 miles eastward of Port San Juan and about 3 miles
off shore. ‘This at present may appear as an isolated danger on the chart, but may
possibly when the coast is properly surveyed, be found to be a portion of other
reefs and dangers hereabout. St. Juan is about 10 leagues to the westward of Cabeza
de San Juan, the N.E. point of the island.+

EAST COAST of PORTO RICO.—The shores of Porto Rico in general are
but imperfectly known to the Europeans. The north, west, and south coasts may,
however, be approached. with caution, from the instruction we are enabled to give;
but the East coast, for the most part, is so crowded with reefs, islets, and dangers,
that no description we could at present give, would enable the mariner to approach
without the aid of a pilot. These are to be obtained at St. Thomas, and sometimes at
Bieques. Nothing like a survey has as yet been made of this part, and it contrasts
sadly by the beautiful surveys made by order of the British Admiralty of the Virgin
Islands and Anegada Reefs.

We shall, however, enumerate the several ports on this coast that are visited by
vessels for sugar, which is largely cultivated in the neighbourhood of the ports; the
first of these ports is

PUERTO FAJARDO, 35 miles to the southward of St. Juan Head, with a depth
of 16 to 23 feet.

BAHIA HONDA, or as some now call it, Great Harbour, lies 10 miles to the
south of St, Juan Head, and a little westward of Puelca island; it is about a mile
in extent, and open to the southward, and is protected by reefs which contract the
channel from a mile to about 4 of a mile in breadth. Inside, the anchorage is in 5 to
8 fathoms, between the patches; but large vessels had better lie outside the reef, off
the entrance in 6 or 8 fathoms.

PUERTO NAGUABO is 5 miles W.S.W. of Bahia Honda, and is formed by Lima
Point to the N.E., and Santiago Islet to the S.W.; the depth of water is from 43 to
33 fathoms. On the right bank of the river is the village of Ucaris.

PUERTO HUMACAO is between Santiago Islet. on the N.E., and Candeleros
Point to the southward. The towns of Naguabo and Humacao are a short distance
inland on the borders of the rivers of the same name. These ports require the
assistance of a pilot, as previously recommended, and vessels bound to either of the
two last-mentioned, or to those that follow on the S.E. coast, had better take the
passage to the southward of Biéques Island.

PUERTO YABUCOA is between Guaques and Yeguas Points, in lat. 18° 4’, and
about 5 miles N.N.E. of Cape Malapascua. The village stands about 2 miles in the

THE HARBOUR OF ST. JUAN. 3

PUERTO MAUNABO is just to the east of Cape Malapascua, and between that
cape and Tuna Point on the north. The town is some miles in the interior, on the
border of the river.

PUERTO PATILLAS is 6 miles westward cf Cape Malapascua, inside the
Gauyama Reef, :

NORTH COAST. The HARBOUR of ST. JUAN is about 30 miles to the
westward of St. John’s Head, being very capacious, and the largest ships may lic
there in perfect safety, in 5 or 6 fathoms water. The entrance is along the west side
of the island, on which the town is erected, and between the Morro Point and three
islets, called the Cabras or Goat Islands. South of the latter is a smaller islet, off the
sandy point, having on it a little square fort, called El Canuelo, which defends the
western side of the harbour. The western side of the entrance is rocky, but in the
channel, which is generally buoyed, the ground is gravel and sand, with a depth of 6,
6, and 7 fathoms. The western and southern sides of the harbour are flat and shoal.
The low point of land on the south side of the town is also surrounded by a shoal, to
the eastward of which ships generally ride, to be out of the swell of the sea, occasioned
by the trade-wind, which generally blows directly into the harbour.

Light.—The revolving light at Fort St. Juan, on the Morro, is in latitude 18° 29’,
and longitude 66° 7’. It revolves every two minutes, and is said to be only 8 seconds
bright; is elevated 171 feet, and may be seen 18 miles in clear weather. ‘lo enter St.
Juan a pilot is indispensable.

Directions.—Nearly 8.8.E. from the mouth of the harbour, and in an east and
west direction, are two ranges of small uneven wooded hills, of moderate elevation,
separated by a small low plain. At the foot of the highest hill on the eastern range
there is a plantation, the cultivated grounds occupying a portion of the northern face.
The summit of the western range is almost flat, and hence it is called the Maseti or
Little Table, and is easily distinguished from the surrounding heights. On the
western extremity there is a white rock, which becomes visible on rounding the
Morro. The entrance to Port San Juan may also be readily distinguished by the
Morro Castle and Lighthouse at the N.W. end of the Morro island. In approaching
the port from the eastward, with the usual trade wind, run down the north side of
the island at the distance of about 3 miles, until Salinas Point comes a little open to
the northward of Great Cabras Island. Steer in on this line until Little Table Hill
is in line with the Morro Point, when haul in towards Fort Canuelo. When the
highest hill on the eastern range, described above, comes in one with the Morro
Point, or, if the former cannot be made out, the flagstaff comes in one with the
northernmost watch-turret of the two on the N.W. battery, which is the lowest in
the Morro Castle, haul in for the Little Table.

“Having rounded the buoy on the St. Helena Spit, and opened the south end of
the island, which lies close under Salinas Point, to the southward of Fort Canuelo,
the vessel may be anchored as convenient, in the Outer Port, in 5 fathoms, abreast St.
Juan Gate. The Morro Point may be passed to the N.W. at 4 a cable, and if the
buoys are on the St. Helena and St. Augustine shoals, there will not be much diffi-
culty or risk in following these directions thus far; buta pilot will be absolutely
necessary if wishing to proceed into the inner port.”—Admiraliy Directions.

Should you have occasion to enter the harbour with a southerly wind, you must
run into the channel with your upper sail set, in order to preserve your way when

ou get under the lee of the Morro. You should also have your boats out with a

edge anchor and warp, ready to run out, or to tow, both of which are frequently
necessary. With a strong wind from the northward, the sea on the bar frequently
breaks and becomes dangerous, on account of the difficulty of steadying the vessel ;
and at that time great attention to the marks given is absolutely necessary. In the
outer harbour moor, with an open hawse, to the N.W. The inner harbour, the depth
of which is said to have considerably decreased since the survey of 17938, ought not
to be taken by ships of large draught. But, as previously observed, no person should
attempt to enter without a pilot. There is no fresh water here, except rain, which is

4 THE PORT OF ARECIBO.

preserved in cisterns. It is high water in the harbour at 8h. 2m. on the days of full
and change, and the greatest rise of the tide is about 18 inches.

The PORT of ARECIBO lies 32 miles to the westward of St. Juan. Vessels
bound to this port should make the City of Porto Rico early in the morning. This
will allow of their running their distance, so as to make the anchorage of Arecibo in
good time before night, which is very desirable, as the currents are often strong and
uncertain. In running down the coast, at about 3 or 4 miles from it, two towns will
be seen; the first, Tortuguero, about 7 leagues from the city; the next, Arecibo, which
may be known by its having a circular fort on the beach to the right, and the ruins
of a church in the middle of the town, and also by a took-out-house and flagstaff on a
steep hill to windward of the port, about a mile from the town.

It is the custom, on vessels approaching the anchorage, for a pilot to come out in a
small boat, bearing a white flag, not to board, but to pull in before the vessel by way
of leading in; but as the sea breeze is generally strong, it often happens that the
vessel overruns the pilot-boat, and the captain has to look out, and to bring his ship
to an anchor himself. The anchorage has 4 fathoms in it; the reefs are steep-to, and
the depths gradually decrease to the mouth of the river, which is nearly dry ; the rise
and fall at springs is 3 feet.

The holding-ground at Areciho is very indifferent, and in the season of the northers
(viz., from November to February), ships ought to anchor in the offing, at least 2
miles outside the reef, and be ready to slip; but in the months of April, May, June,
and July they may anchor inside, and close to the reef in 4 or 35 fathoms. :

This harbour is open to the N.W., and in front of the town a rocky shoal runs off
some distance. The mouth of the river is on the N.E. part of the bay, and runs at
the back of the town.

“The trade of Arecibo is rapidly increasing.” —Nautical Magazine, 1843.

To the westward of Arecibo there is nothing to attract the mariner’s notice in any
place of commerce or anchorage, the coast being fiat, low, and sandy; it is therefore
well to avoid too near an approach to a coast so little known. Twenty-four miles
from Arecibo is the point Pena Agujereada (Pierced Rock), where the coast turns to
the S.W. for a mile, being composed of bold rocky cliffs, terminating at Bruquen
Point, the N.W. end of the island; thence the coast stretches further to the S.W.
about a mile, but is low and sandy, as far as Pefias Blancas, or Whitestone Point,
which is covered with trees. Within a mile of Bruquen Point are 20 to 25 fathoms,
at which. distance it may be safely rounded ; but Peiias Blancas must be approached
with caution, for a reef stretches off it to the distance of a mile.

AGUADILLA BAY is that portion of the west coast of Porto Rico between
Point Pefias Blancas anl San Francisco, which is about 6 miles to the southward of
that point. It is an-extensive bight, but free of danger, except the sand-bars at the
entrance of the rivulets on the southern side of the bay, some of which extend off
about 2 cables; the shore is sandy and bordered by a narrow ledge of soundings
about 4 of a mile in breadth; this ledge is steep-to. The town of San Carlos is
situate on the shores of this bay, about 2 miles to the southward of Peas Blancas,
on the shores of the river Aguadilla, where good water may be obtained, and also
other refreshments. There is good anchorage off the town of St. Carlos, from 1 to 3
cables from the shore, in a depth of 4 to 15 fathoms. With a large vessel, a good
position will be with a large house, just beyond the 3-gun battery, at the N. end of
the town, bearing N.E. 3 K.; the church, E. 3 S.; and the N. point of the bay N. by
W..; this will be in about 18 fathoms, at 3 a mile from the shore, on good holding-
ground.

REMARKS IN H.M.S. ARAcHNE.—“ The only danger in approaching this anchorage
is a reef running off 4 a mile from Point Blancas, a long, low point; it is one mile to
the southward of Point Bruquen, the N.W. point of the island. Between Point
Blancas and Point Jiguero, the S.W. point of the bay, the coast is perfectly clear,
and you can approach any part of it within 4 of a mile.

RINCON BAY.

“The town of Aguadilla lies on the north end of a large sandy bay, extending
from Point Jiguero. The best anchorage is with the church bearing H. by S., 3 a
mile off shore, in 14 or 14 fathoms. During the months of January and February,
when the northerly winds are prevalent, this is a very rough anchorage, as a heavy
sea rolls in, rendering it difficult, and at times, impossible to land. The watering
place is in the centre of the town, through which a small river runs, rolling your
casks over the beach into the village. When the water is smooth, you can procure
it quickly, but the least northing in the wind makes a heavy surf on the beach.
Fresh provisions are cheap, also vegetables and firewood. Vessels anchoring for the
purpose of watering, it should be mentioned, the watering place is close to the only
large yellow house situate in the centre of the town. This bay is sheltered from all
easterly winds, and from south to west. With Desecheo Island W. by 8., you will
be in a fairway for the town.”

This bay is much frequented by vessels bound to Cuba, or the Gulf of Mexico, on
account of the facility with which they can procure refreshments, and because pilots
for the Old Bahama Channel may always be had here.

Dixections.—In making Aguadilla Bay from the northward, be careful to avoid
the ledge off Peitas Blancas; and in taking up an outer berth, be careful that the
vessel is in soundings, and do not bring the vessel up too short, or she may be apt to
drag off the bank, which is very steep-to. In proceeding towards the bay from the
southward, you will pass between the Island of Desecheo and Jigiiero Point, which is
the W. extreme of Porto Rico; and when more than 17 or 18 miles from the point
and beating up towards it, do not bring it more to the eastward than N.N.E., by
which means you will escape getting entangled with the shoal grounds off the western
side-of Porto Rico. Should a vessel be riding here during the winter season, when
strong N.W. and N. winds occur, it is recommended to quit the anchorage as soon as
achange threatens; and to any one observant, the aspect of the weather will give
sufficient warning to prepare for leaving. In the winter season a heavy uneasy sea
rolls into the bay, rendering a high surf on the beach even with N.E. winds.

RINCON BAY.—From Jigiiero Point the coast curves in to the eastward and
forms the small bay of Rincon, Cadena Point being the south extreme. The two
points bear about N.W. by N. and S.E. by S., distant 33 miles. This bay is well
sheltered from the usual trade winds, but it affords no good anchorage, the water
being foul.

ANASCO BAY.—The next bay to the S.E. is that of Anasco, bounded to the
southward by the point of Algarrobo, distant 6 miles from Cadena. The. river
Anasco empties itself into the bay, before which there is a shallow bar, stretching
out 2amile from the shore. Large vessels may anchor outside this, and be well
sheltered from the prevailing winds. ‘

MAYAGUEZ BAY lies between Algarrobo and Guanajibo Points, which are
about 4 miles distant. This bay, froma line of the above points, is about 13 mile
deep, and in the northern part the depths decrease from 10 to 4 fathoms towards the
shore; but although the anchorage affords excellent shelter from northerly winds to
vessels of moderate size, the entrance is obstructed by a line of shoals, which
requires a chart of their positions, or a good knowledge of the bay, to work in in
safety.

The north point of the bay (Algarrobo) has a house, with a red roof, built upon high
piles on the hill just above the point, from whence the coast trends to the S8.H. for 13
mile to Puntilla, a low sandy point, on which there is a building with a chimney
and some other buildings of a bluish colour around it, used as a sugar factory. The
shore between the two points is foul for 3 cables off, and 5 a mile to the 8.W. of
Algarrobo Point lies the bank of that name, the outer part of which is nearly dry
and is steep-to. Just to the southward of Puntilla, at the bottom of the bay, is the
river Mayagiiez, before which is the best anchorage, affording shelter from the north-
ward round by East to S.W., and the ground good for holding. From thence the
shore is low, and bends to the S.W., with shallow water some distance off as far as
Guanajibo Point, 14 mile N. of which a spit runs off nearly a mile from the shore.
