SHOALS OFF MAYAGUEZ BAY.

Inland, to the eastward of the bay, the land becomes elevated, where will be seen
the paps or hummocks of Cerro Gordo; and there is a remarkable peak called the
Cerro Montuoso, on the top of which are two large trees, giving it the appearance of
a double peak. This forms a useful mark from the offing, and bears from Puntilla E.
by 8. 3S. about 9 miles. The village of Mayagiiez is about a mile to the E.S.E. of
the entrance to the river.

_ SHOALS OFF MAYAGUEZ BAY:—a Mancha de Fuera is the first shoal
to the northward and the outermost in the bay, lying W.N.W., 24 miles from Algar-
robo Point. It extends ina N.N.W., and S.S.E. direction about 4a mile, and has
from 2 to 4 fathoms water upon it, which sometimes breaks. When approaching
this shoal, the dark discoloured water may be observed at a little distance.

La Mancha de Tierra.—This shoal lies 2 of a mile S.E. of La Mancha de
Fuera, W. } N., 12 mile from Algarrobo Point, and about N. by W. from Guanajibo
Point. It extends N.W. and S.E., and has 12 to 3 fathoms water on it. There is a
channel between this shoal and the reef off Algarrobo Point, a mile wide, with 7
fathoms in it. This may be called the inner channel from the northward.

Allart Shoal.—This shoal was first discovered by Captain Zahrtmann, of the
Danish Navy, in 1833. It is about 2 of a mile in length N. and §., and 3 2 mile in
breadth, with from 13 to 2 fathoms water on it. The shallowest part lies W., 22
miles from Puntilla; N. by W. 3 W. from Guanajibo Point; and S.W. by W. 2 W.
from Algarrobo Point. The principal channel leading to the anchorage of Mayagiiez
is between this shoal and La Mancha de ‘lierra, being 7 cables in breadth, with 32 to
45 fathoms water in it.

Rodriguez Bank.—This shoal is about 14 mile to the S.S.E. of the Allart, and
just without the line of bearing from Algarrobo to Guanajibo Point, bearing from
the latter about N. by W., 13 mile. It is about 4a mile in extent N. and 8., and
some parts of it become dry at low water. This bank is connected with the Allart
Bank by a shallow bar of from 2 to 3 fathoms upon it, and between Rodrigiiez Bank
and Guanajibo Point there are 44 and 33 fathoms, decreasing towards the shore.

White Rock.—This rock, according to a French survey, wherein the above shoals
are clearly delineated, lies about midway between and just within the line of bearing
of Rodrigiiez and Allart Banks. It is a small rocky patch, having but 6 feet on its
shoalest part, and obstructs the passage between the above two banks, which would
otherwise, to small vessels, afford a good channel. It lies W. 25., 2 miles from the
custom-house, and W. by S. 3S. from Puntilla Point.

Directions.—The main channel into Mayagiiez Bay is between the skoals of La
Mancha de Tierra and Allart; and if the wind be such as will allow a vessel to lay
through either in entering or leaving the bay, the mark will be the peak of Mon-
tuoso (previously noticed) in line with the custom-house, bearing E. by S.2 8. The
custom-house stands to the southward of the river, on the shore, and is the southern-
most of four large houses with flat roofs; indeed, either of these houses will form a
mark with the peak. The church in the village (which has two turrets), in line with
the custom-house, will also lead up to the anchorage. The barracks, a large flat-
roofed building to the southward of the custom-house, on higher ground, should not
be mistaken for it.

In turning in, a vessel may stand to the northward, towards La Mancha de Tierra
until the custom-house and church are in one; to the southward, in standing towards
the Allart Shoal, tack before the peak of Montuoso comes in line with the church ;
but when within the two shoals, the boards may be prolonged at discretion. When
Point Guanajibo bears 8., a vessel will be to the eastward of the outer banks. There
is a channel to the northward, between Las Manchas and the Algarrobo reef.
Should the wind be fair for this channel, take care not to haul round Algarrobo
Point to the eastward until the peak of Montuoso opens §. of the chimney of Vigos
sugar-house, which is a conspicuous object near the shore, and of a whitish colour.

BOQUERON BAY. 7

Anchorage.—H. M. steam-vessel Medea anchored in this bay in 5 fathoms, with
Guanajibo Point S.S.W. 7 W.; Algarrobo Point N.N.W. 2 W.; and Montuoso peak
&.2S.; the church of the village a little to the southward of the peak. Water
obtained from the river, and a good market for poultry, fruit, &c.

For large vessels there is said to be anchorage outside, to the westward of the
shoals; but any one taking it up should be very cautious, as our information of these
parts is very imperfect.

The rise and fall of the tide in Mayagiiez Bay is from 2 to 3 feet, but the periods
are irregular.

PUERTO REAL DE CABO ROJO.—At the distance of 55 miles S. 3 W. from
the point Guanajibo, is Puerto Real de Cabo Rojo, of almost circular form, and about
2 of a mile in diameter. It has 18 feet water at the entrance, and 16 feet in the
centre of the basin. The entrance is by a very narrow channel, and lies to the 8.
point of the harbour. From the N. point an extensive reef runs off, which, after
doubling Cayo Fanduco, terminates at Punta de Varas.

BOQUERON BAY.—At 2 miles S. by W. 2? W. from Puerto Real is the point
Guaniquilla, which is the northernmost point of the large bay called Boqueron.
This bay affords no safe anchorage, the approaches being obstructed by numerous
shoals, and the interior full of reefs. Punta de Melones, the southern point of the
bay is distant from Point Guaniquilla a little more than 2% miles, and nearly W.

about 63 miles from Point Melones is Baxo Gallardo, or Gallardo Bank, of which we
shall speak hereafter.

Monte de Atalaya.—This is a high mountain near the shore on the N. side of
Anasco Bay, and is the highest and northernmost peak of two which are seen on the
op of the mountain range, and is seen from the whole of the W. coast. It bears
about S.E. by E. from Jigiiero Point, is very remarkable, and does not alter its
appearance when seen eyen from off the 8. end of the island Desecheo.

We have now to treat of the shoals, &c., off the W. coast, and must here premise
that our information of such is very scant. They are very numerous and imperfectly
known, and it will be well for the mariner to give this part a wide berth. One
bearing we haye given previously in treating of Aguadilla Bay, that of Point
Jigiiero bearing N.N.E., which would appear, from our present knowledge of the
locality, to keep clear westward of all the dangers ; but it behoves the mariner to
keep a good look-out here, for in March, 1847, the “John Brown” is said to have
struck upon ashoal 3 leagues from the nearest part of Porto Rico, and remained there
one hour and a half, thumping heavily, but ultimately came off, after throwing 5
hogsheads of sugar and some stores overboard, starting the water on deck, and the
loss of a quarter-boat. The bearings given is Desecheo island N.N.W., 9 miles ; but
the position is considered doubtful.

Bank in the Mona Passage.—A bank of 4 fathoms water has lately been dis-
covered by Capt. W. M. Walker, United States steam-vessel “ De Soto.” From it
the Island of Desecheo bears N. + W., 19 miles distant; Point Jiguéro, N.N.E. 7 E.,
distant 21 miles; Point Aquila, E.S.E., distant 15 miles; and is situate about 15
miles from the nearest land of Porto Rico.

Negro Shoal.—The first of these shoals nearer the coast from the northward is
the Negro Shoal, and is of small extent and almost always breaks. It lies 3§ miles
from the shore, with 6 feet water upon it, with Guanajibo Point bearing E. by N. 2
N., and Jigiiero Point N. 2 W.

Las Coronas, ox the Crowns, are some sand-banks about 4 miles to the south-
ward of the Negro, about 4a mile in extent, and are just covered by the sea, which
sometimes breaks. They are 3% miles from the nearest part of the shore, with
Guanajibo Point bearing N.E. 2 N., and Jigiiero Point N. 3 W.

Media Luna, ox Half Moon, is another shoal, said to lie to the N.W, of the
Coronas, and at 5 miles from the land, and has been described as ayreef of about 3:of
a mile in extent N. and §., and about 24 cables’ length in breadth, the sea, always

breaking over it. About E.N.E. from it, at § a mile there are three rocks, which
appear above water, on which the sea always-breaks, From the north end of the
shoal, Guanijibo Point is said to bear N.E. by E. 3 E., and Jigitero Point N, 2 E.
The position of this shoal and the rocks is very much doubted.

Guaniquilla Shoal is a rocky ledge of about 2 cables in extent, and has 3
fathoms water upon it. It lies about 2 miles to the westward of Punta de Guani-
quilla with Point Guanajibo bearing N, by E.2E., and Jigiiero Point N, 2 W.
‘This shoal also is considered doubtful.

‘The Baxo Gallardo, which is almost W. from Punta de Melones, and 6 miles
distant from it, is a rocky shoal of 3 fathoms, about 3 cables’ length in extent ; and
the least depth of water upon it is 2 fathoms, rocky bottom. It lies with Desecheo
Island bearing N. by W. 2 W.; Monte de Atalaya, N.N.E.; and the S. extreme of
the Morillos (two small hills near Cape Rojo), E.S.E.

Another shoal, according to some Spanish charts, lies about 4 miles W. of the
entrance to Boqueron Bay. This is said to have 2% fathoms water upon it, but it is
considered doubtful.

CAPE ROJO is the S.W. point of Porto Rico, and slopes down from the Morillos
to a bold headland, and when first seen from the eastward or westward, appears like
two low grey islets under the high land. When seen from the southward, two
remarkable cliffs will be observed to the eastward. Cape Rojo is encompassed by a
shoal called the White Grounds, which extends 8 leagues to the S.W. At 2 or 3
leagues to the eastward and westward of the cape there are 10, 12, and 15 fathoms.
The sand at the bottom is of such shining whiteness, that the reflection pierces
through the water. It is a coral bank, and close to its edge no bottom is to be found.
The southern extremity bears from the point S.W. 3 W. about 3 leagues. Plenty of
fish may be caught here with hook and line.*

DESECHEO ISLAND.—Having described the west coast of Porto Rico and the
shoals adjacent with sufficient prolixity, it remains here to say that W. 3 N., at the
distance of 11 miles from Punta Jigiiero, is the island of Desecheo or Zacheo, of con-
siderable height and very clear. It appears like a green mountain 800 or 1,000
yards long ; several parts of it are covered with wood, and it is so high as to be seen
12 leagues off.

The SOUTH COAST of PORTO RICO.—From the Morillos, in the §.W. to
Malaspascua, which is the §.E. extremity of the island, the coast is of double land,
and is said to be very foul, with reefs, islets, and shoals extending in some parts a
considerable distance from it. It is therefore necessary to approach with much
caution, more especially as very little is known of these parts in which reliance can
be placed. About equal distance between the extreme points of the south coast, is
the island called Caxa de Muertos, or Coffin Island, at 4 miles distant from the coast,
and foul at its N.E. and W. parts. There are numerous rivers emptying themselves
on this coast, and various small harbours, only at present known to the natives; of
those we have any information of, Guanica will be the first. Vessels taking the
route by the south coast of Porto Rico, and not bound to any particular port, should
keep 4 or 5 miles off the land, and not approach it without due attention to the lead.

PUERTO GUANICA.—This is the best port on this side of Porto Rico, and is
distant about 53 leagues eastward of the Morillos. It is about 14 mile in length in
a N.W. and §.E. direction, and + to 2 2 mile in breadth, and will accommodate large
vessels, having a depth of 6 fathoms at the entrance to 33 at the further end of the
harbour, which is more than a mile from the entrance,

The mouth of this harbour is in the middle of a great bay, formed by the point
and cliff of Fronton de la Brea on the west, and that of Picua on the east. The

PUERTO DE GUAYANILLA. ]

latter has contiguous to it two islets called Cana and Cana Gorda, and from these
islets to the Punta de la Meseta, the east point of the entrance of the harbour, there
is a reef which stretches out from the coast nearly a mile, forming an are of a circle,
united at one end with the islets, and at the other end with Punta de la Meseta.
Between Brea Point and Punta de los Pescadores, or Fisherman’s Point, the west
point of the harbour, the coast forms another harbour, which is obstructed by a reef,
which runs from Pescadores Point and ends at the south side of the bay, about ¢
a mile within the point of Brea. The entrance is between the two bold headlands of
Meseta and Pescadores, and is little more than a cable’s length in width. On
approaching the entrance, it is not only necessary to give a berth to the reefs noticed
on either side of the bay, but also toa rocky shoal of only 12 feet, lying 3 cables
outside the reef, about 3 cables long, in a north and south direction. The south end
of this ledge lies §.S.E. a mile from. Meseta Point, and in a line between Brea and
Picua Points, with the south end of Cana Gorda E. by N., distant 2 miles.

Dixections.—To take this harbour from the eastward, you must run down outside
the reefs until Meseta Point is in one with the paps of Cerro Gordo, which may be
easily recognised inland. If you run in with the point in line with the western pap,
you will pass very close to the bank, but yet in 10 fathoms water; if with the point
in line with the eastern pap, you will pass without any risk of danger. When Cana
Gorda bears E. 3 N., you will have passed the rocky shoal, and may run boldly for
the entrance, and come to convenient anchorage inside. In taking the harbour from
the westward, by the Punta de la Brea, you may pass within a cable’s length, and
thence steer to within the Punta de la Meseta, which may be passed as close as { of
a cable’s length, and from thence into the harbour, observing that the south shore is
bolder than the north, and anchor where convenient in 5 or 4 fathoms water.

PUERTO DE GUAYANILLA.—This is a large circular bay, about 7 miles to
the eastward of Guanica, and is open to the southward. The western point is sur-
rounded by reefs, and the latter by islets. We have no further information respect-
ing it.

PVERTO DE MA TANZA.—This bay is about 3 miles eastward of Guayanilla,
somewhat similarly formed, but of which we can give nothing further. Ata mile
S.W. by W. of Cuchara Point, which is the east point of the bay, is the small islet
of Ratones, which, when well observed, may form a mark equally for Ponce as for
this port.

PUERTO PONCE is 15 miles to the eastward of Guanica, and 7 miles to the
N.W. of the Muertos Island, or the Dead Chest. The land is low near the water,
covered with mangrove bushes and cocoa-nut trees; but the houses of the village are
also low, so that thex will not become visible until you approach the harbour, which
is open to the southward. To the westward of the village there is a small fort on
the beach. On the western side of the bay, at 3 of a mile from the fort, is a small
sandy cay, named Cardona, covered with brushwood, with breakers off its east end.
This cay is connected by a reef to Cuchara Point, from which it is distant about 1}
mile. There appears to be no other danger near it; but the water is discoloured for
2 or 8 miles to the southward, with irregular soundings as far out as the parallel of
Muertos Island, and south of the bay, as little as 3 fathoms water will be met with.

Directiens.—To run for this port, keep a mile from the small cay off the S.W.
end of Muertos Island, and steer N.W. 4 N. or N.W. by N. This course will lead
up to the port, with regular soundings, on a rocky bottom, and a vessel must pass to
the eastward of the cay above mentioned, near the fort. If it blows fresh, the reef
which is passed on the starboard hand will appear to break right across the entrance,
but as you approach, it will be observed that the breakers do not make off far from

the bushes. Pass the breakers within 2 cables’ length, and keep the southern shore
of the harbour on board.

BMUERTOS ISLAND, or DEAD CHEST, is situate 35 miles from Cape Rojo,
and 40 miles from Cape Malapascua. When first made, it appears in the form of a
wedge, the north end being high, the centre low, and the south end a sugar-loaf

mountain, which at a distance appears a detached island. ‘he anchorage is on the
west side, off the low land, 3 a mile from shore, in 8 fathoms, in the following
bearings :—S.E. point of the small island, connected by a reef above water, S,W.;
the only sandy bay, S. by E.; the N.W. point and northern peak in one, BE, There
is no danger on the west side of the island, and off the low land the soundings are
regular; but to the northward of it the water is deeper, and there are 17 fathoms
close to the shore, to the southward of the island.

The name Dead Chest is applied to the island from its resemblance to a chest or
coffin. From a certain point it appears like two flattened balls, separated by a broad
valley. The shore towards Porto Rico is flat and sandy ; on the south side it is high
and stony. There is no fresh water on it, nor trees of any kind but for fuel. It is,
however, supposed, that by digging the sand a little below the mark of the highest
tides and surf, fresh water may be found, as on other sandy cays. Caution must be
observed not to dig too deep, for at too great a depth the water is brackish. The fresh
water thus found is supposed to be rain-water, which having strained through the
sand, is kept by its specific gravity above the sea water, which is always found when
the bottom of the hole is on a level with the surface of the ocean. ‘This is a good
place for fish and turtle, as the latter lay their eggs in the great sandy bays, and for
this reason is much frequented by the inhabitants of Porto Rico.

Berberia Rocks.—To the E.N.E. of Muertos Island, and at the distance of 3
miles, are the Berberia Rocks, and-these appear to be connected with Muertos
Island by a shelf having only 2% fathoms upon it. In the neighbourhood of these
cays are many dangerous rocks, and, like the whole of the south coast of the island,
are very imperfectly known, With Muertos Island bearing west, 3 or 4 miles
distant there is a depth of 6 fathoms. From the hills, white water is seen a con-
siderable distance to the eastward ; it is therefore requisite to keep the lead going.
About a cable’s length from the S.W. end of the island Muertos, and connected to it

by a dry reef, there is a small flat cay called the Hammock, which should not be
rounded within the distance of 13 mile.

Anchorage.—The western side of Muertos Island is free of danger, and affords
good anchorage in from 7 to 12 fathoms water. A good berth may be taken with the
8.E. end of the Hammock S.W.; the same cay S. by E., and the N.W. point of
Muertos in one with the Northern hill East, in 8 fathoms, at about 4 a mile from the
shore. Off the low land of the island the soundings are regular, but to the north-
ward of it the depth is much greater, being 17 fathoms close to the shore. Anchorage
will also be found with the west end of the Hammock S. by E. 3 E., distant 14 mile ;
and the north end of Muertos N.E. 4 E,

PUERTO de JACAQUA.—This anchorage is at the entrance of the River
Jacaqua, 3 miles to the eastward of Cabullon Point, the west point of the Bay of
Ponce. Two small islets and several reefs lie just to the westward, called the Prio
Islets. There is not much in the way reaching the anchorage, using the lead and
marking the soundings from 63 to 33 fathoms.

BOCA CHICA.—This is a small trading port, 44 miles northward of Muertos
Island, and it is said there is no danger in approaching it. The soundings gradually
decrease from 7 to 4 fathoms as the Porto shore is approached, and the lead must be
the guide.

COANKO BAY, is that portion of the coast from Coamo Point to Point Fama de la
Maria, distant 5{ miles. The river Coamo empties itself into the bay, the town being
situate 8 miles up the river. Off the Point of Coama are several small islets.

PUERTO de las SALINES de COAMDO isa safe harbour, about 14 miles to
the eastward of Muertos Island, which is in sight from it. Its entrance may be
known by several small cays near the shore, and a guard-house, which will be seen
when running down outside them. The channel lies between the outer or western-
most cay, which is about 4 miles to the southward of the guard-house, and a reef,
13 mile to the westward of it, which always breaks. Within the harbour there is a
rocky shoal having 165 feet water upon it, and 22 feet around. On this reef a

THE PORTS OF PATILLAS AND GUAYAMA. 11

Spanish store-ship struck in November, 1860. It lies with the middle of the round
eay at the entrance to the channel between the coast and the islets bearing N.N.E. 7 E.
and the south extreme Saso cay S.W. 3 S.

‘Water.—There is a good watering-place in Port Salinas de Coamo, on the shore
near a lagoon, about 4 a mile to the westward of the guard-house.

Directions.—Discoloured water extends off a considerable distance from the
cays off Port Salinas de Coamo, and 3 miles off the depth is 12 fathoms, which will
decrease to 7 fathoms, as the shore is approached. Having rounded the western cay
at the entrance within a cable’s length, steer boldly in between the eastern cays
and the reef, towards the guard-house, and anchor in 4 or 5 fathoms, with the latter
bearing N.4 E. about a mile distant. In leaving the anchorage, if bound to the west-
ward, stand well out to the southward, into an offing of 2 or 3 miles from the cays,
until Muertos Island is to the northward of west, before keeping away.

To the eastward of Porto Salinas to the Cape Malapascua, the S.E. point of Porto
Rico, there remains the Puerto de Jobos, or Boca d’Infierno, the roadstead of
Guayama, and the small bay of Arroya to be treated of, and in doing so, we shall
introduce the instructions from the French chart, by Captain C. B. Matenas (1853.)

Entrance to the Anchorage of GUAYAMWA.—To anchor here, Cape Malapascua
must be made. At 4 miles 8.S.W. of this cape begins a chain of reefs, which
continue, with few interruptions, to 2 miles from Jobos, or Bouche de l’Enfer. Inside
of these reefs are the anchorages of Patillas and Guayama.*

To anchor at Guayama, after having well observed Cape Malapascua, coast along
shore 5 miles distant, until the village of Arroya bears N. % W. or N., then cross
immediately between the reefs, and anchor in 13 to 25 fathoms; the depths gradually
shallow to about 13 feet at 2 cables’ length from the shore. The above-mentioned
reefs lie about 23 or 3 miles from the shore. The eastern patch is almost entirely

uncovered at low water, the western seldom so, and the middle patch opposite
Patillas uncovers more on the western than on the eastern side.

ARROYA is easily known by the custom-house and houses on the beach, among
which are those of the consuls, with flagstaffs. To the westward of Arroya, at the
entrance of Jobos, or Porto de Infierno, the land abounds with sugar plantations,
which are well cultivated.

The PORTS of PATILLAS and GUAYAMIA are rather dangerous during
the winter season, for it is impossible to get under way in a lee-tide or ina gale. In
other respects the ground is sufficiently good to hold with two anchors.

JOBOS, or BOUCHE de L’INFER is one of the best ports in Porto Rico, a true
wet dock ; vessels should not draw more than 14 to 15 feet to enter. The outlet has
a depth of 16 to 18 feet ; the bottom is soft mud, with a greater depth in the western
than in the eastern part, where the landing-place is situate.

As the entrances of Jobos are difficult, a pilot is indispensable, and can be obtained
at Guayama, sometimes at St. Thomas, or in the offing, but they seldom go beyond
the reefs.

Ships sailing along the south coast of Porto Rico are exposed to sudden calms,
occasioned by the island intercepting all breezes from between north and east. It
should not be coasted nearer than 6 miles ; but the north coast, as previously observed,
may be run down at the distance of 3 or 4 miles.

THE MONA PASSAGE.

The Mona Passage, between Porto Rico and Santo Domingo, is about 66 miles
wide, and receives its name from two small islands (Mona and Monito) which lie
nearly midway across on the south side, between Cape Rojo and Saona Tsland.

From Cape Rojo, in Porto Rico, to the S.E. point of Saona Island, off the $.E.
part of Santo Domingo, the bearing is W. 3 N., and the distance 26 leagues. Ina
direct line between and nearly midway, but rather nearer to Saona lie the islands
Mona and Monito: the former is the largest and southernmost, and Monito is about
2 miles to the N.W. of it. There is anchorage about 4 a league to leeward of Mona,
in 7 or 8 fathoms water, sand and weeds. Desecheo, which has been described, lies
nearly 10 leagues N.E. 3 E. from Mona.

WWfona is an island almost level, of little elevation, and without any prominences
on it; it is not inhabited, and its surface seems covered with brushwood, without
trees of any considerable height. Its N.E. and W. coasts are of white rock, perpen-
dicular to the water, and may be approached as close as you choose ; the 8. coast is
considerably lower, but as clean as the former. Near to the W. point, however, some
vessels anchor, in order to procure grass when engaged in carrying cattle. The
island may be seen at the distance of 6 leagues.

‘Water.—Fresh water is scarce, but a little to the right of the landing on the
western shore, there is a pathway leading to the watering-place under the southern
cliffs ; and here also firewood will be found.

Monito is a small islet about 24 miles to the N.N.W. of Mona, and is scarcely
more than 2 cables long and acable broad. It is much lower than Mona, and in
shape resembles a shoemaker’s last. It is quite barren, and is the resort of immense
numbers of booby birds. The pilots of these coasts state that there is a clear and
deep passage between Mona and Monito.

Tides.—It is high water, full and change, at Mona Island at 6h. 15m., and the
rise is about 2 feet. The flood sets N. by E., and the ebb 8. by W.., at the rate of §
a knot.

The following remarks are by Capt. J. V. Baker, R.N., H.22. Ship Arachne, 1834.*

Mona Istanp.—“ This island is nearly level, and of moderate height. We could
not see it farther than 18 miles on aclear day. Its N.E., 8.E., and S.W. sides are
bounded by arcef 4 of a mile off shore. At the distance of 2 miles we ran along
these sides, but saw no other danger than a reef, which extends 13 mile off the south
point.

“The §.W. point (to the northward of which is the anchorage) is sand, long and
low, with brushwood and small trees on it.. There is a reef off this point, about ;

“We anchored here, with the sandy point bearing 8. by W., 13 mile; Island of

“ We came in from the northward, passing Monito to the westward, within 6 miles,

but had no soundings, neither could we see broken water or any danger between it
and Mona. This island is the resort of innumerable quantities of boobies; its sides

“ We landed on the sandy beach, and found the west end of the island, which is

A small quantity of firewood might be obtained with labour.” -

Dixections.—Vessels coming round Cape Rojo, or from the S.E., and bound
through the Mona Passage, should, after clearing the White Grounds, endeavour to
sail in mid-channel, between Desecheo and Mcna; there is no danger but what can
be seen. With the wind at E.S.E. or E., there will be no need to tack, but to sail
through with the wind quartering. It will be sufficient to steer N.W. by N. to fetch
Cape Raphael, the N.E. point of Santo Domingo, or even Cape Samana. The
currents, which generally set to the westward, must be guarded against, lest they set
you into Samana Bay, whither they frequently run with great strength.

A ship, having fetched the Island of Mona, if bound to the northern side of Santo
Domingo, may run to leeward of Mona and Monito, observing the above precaution.
With Mona E.S.E,, 3 or 4 leagues, you may perceive the coast of Santo Domingo.

WINDS.—The winds around Porto Rico appear to be of the same character as
those met with in the Virgin Islands. There is no longer land breeze to take advan-
tage of, although the usual trade-wind generally slackens during the night in the
immediate vicinity of the shore. Under the W. end the wind in the daytime will
incline inward. In the winter months N. and N.W. winds sometimes occur, and blow
hard; and in the summer long calms and light 8.E. airs will prevail, with terrific
squalls and heavy rains, especially on the south side. From the absence of any
remarks on the rollers, we may conclude that they are at least not so heavy or so
dangerous as at the Virgin Islands.

CURRENTS.—On the north side of Porto Rico, the current is said to incline
generally to the S.W., or toward the shore, and to run with greater velocity in the
winter than in the summer months. On the south side its course is generally
west, but its movements are here uncertain. Some navigators state that at the full
and change of the moon a strong weatherly set will occasionally be found, especially
if light winds or northers have prevailed near these periods, and consequently gives
great assistance to vessels beating to windward. In the summer months it wiil
incline to the N.W. towards the shore, and round the S.W. end into the Mona
Passage with great force. This is probably owing to the great body of water thrown
out in this direction, at this period, from the great rivers of Terra-firma.

CURRENTS AND TIDES IN THE MONA PassaGE.
The following remarks are by Sir Robert H. Schomburgk.

“The wreck of the British brig Brazilian, on the eastern coast of the island of
Santo Domingo, near Punta Engano,* occurred in consequence of the strong N.W.

* Cape Engano is called by the pilots of Santo Domingo, Punta Espada ; and the point
called Punta Espada in the charts is called Cabo Rafael by the pilots.

14 CURRENTS AND TIDES ;

by W. current that sweeps the Carribean Sea, which, combining with the trade
drift, amounts probably, when not overpowered by a local current, to no less than 24
miles per day, and frequently surpasses it.

The Brazilian, Captain Power, sailéd on the 1st of May, 1850, from Porto
Cabello, bound for New York, laden with coffee, indigo, and hides, and made on the
7th of that month, at 10 o’clock a.m., the island of Mona bearing N.N.E., the wind
being light from E. by N., with sultry weather, the vessel carrying all sail by the
wind. At6o’clock p.m., Mona Island bore F. 3 N. distant about 10 miles. The
master went about sunset on the foretop-mast-head, and, enquiring from the man at
the helm how the ship’s head then was, received as answer, that she held her course
north. Cape Engano bore then N.W. distant about 30 miles; and, thinking that
with a course of N. by W. he should pass about 12 miles to the east of Cape Engano,
he ordered the vessel to be kept as close to the wind as possible. She struck about
% to 5 o'clock a.m. of May 8th ona reef near Punta Cana, about 4 of a mile from
the shore ; Cape Engano bearing then N.N.E. about 43 miles distant. The current
had set, therefore, the vessel gradually from N. by E. to N.W.

Having been informed of the wreck of the vessel, I proceeded in the Dominican
man-of-war schooner Constitucion to the scene of the disaster. The passage from
the harbour of Santo Domingo to Cape Engano is usually made in two days. We
had, however, light winds, and experienced on approaching the island of Saona a
severe current, setting us N.W. by W. ata rate of 2 miles in an hour; and, on
rounding the east end of Saona and approaching Punta Espada, the current set power-
fully to the 8.S.W. at the rate of 21 miles to 3 miles in an hour, so that we found
ourselves in the morning from 20 to 30 miles further from the point of our destination
than we were the preceding evening. I could only ascribe this to the influence of the
tides, which are felt to a distance of 6 miles from the east coast of Santo Domingo ;
and being much stronger than the stream current, they give an impetus to the south-
westward until the tidal wave, having gradually lost the impetus with which it swept
through the western side of the Mona Passage, emerges again into the current.

In the case of the Brazilian, the vessel experienced in the first instance the N.W.
by W. current, which gradually and silently set her towards the shore; with the
change of the tide her course was retarded, and in lieu of being at midnight, as Mr.
Power expected, 12 miles to the eastward of Cape Engano, he was at that time 10
or 12 miles to the south of it, and a reef-girted shore perhaps not more than 7 or 8
miles under his lee, Cape Engano bore then probably N. by E. distant 12 miles.
The vessel had thigiaigre been set three points to leeward, and had been retarded 20

miles in her course. Had the Brazilian tacked at that time, she would have escaped
all danger.

The Constitucion, on board of which I was, anchored on the 18th May, in the
afternoon, near Punta Cana, somewhat more than a mile off shore. The wreck of
the Brazilian was from here one mile. We found for the subsequent three days that
the tide ran with a velocity of 34 knots for nearly nine hours towards the 8.S.W.,
and merely for two hours and a half to three hours to the N.E. by N. The pilot on
board the schooner told me that he was well acquainted with the coast, and that the
tides were not always of equal strength, running sometimes six hours to the §.8.W.
and six hours to the N.E.; at other periods the ebb tide was stronger than the flood

tide, and if such a case occurred, the north-easterly tide ran even with greater
velocity than the south-westerly.

The great strength of the current is to be ascribed to the swelling of the Orinoco,
which river commences to rise in April, and reaches its maximum height in August.
It pours then out its vast masses of waters through its numerous mouths, sweeping
along the southern shores of the Carribee Islands, and directing its centre towards
the promontory of Santo Domingo, called Point Mongon, (to the south of which lie
the small islands of Beata and Alta Vela), it forms there such an opposing mass of

IN THE MONA PASSAGE. 15

waters to vessels, that they are known to have been detained there for weeks.*
During the inundations of the Orinoco, the velocity of the N.W. by W. current is,
along the south side of Porto Rico, from 15 to 2 knots in an hour; and the stream,
approaching the Mona Passage, sends an offset through the same, which continues
its course, assisted by the ebb-tide, until it meets the tidal wave from the broad
ocean, and, overpowered by its stronger antagonist, receives a south-western impulse,
until it reaches that distance from the shore of Santo Domingo where the tides are
no longer felt with violence. It merges afterwards in the N.W. by W. current, now
combining drift with stream, and continues its central course along the south side of
Jamaica until the Carribean current rushes into the Gulf of Mexico.

The mass of water which this current disturbs in its course, sweeping to the
N.W., produces, no doubt, an indraught, which causes the tidal wave that comes
from the ocean to increase its velocity, while running through the Mona Passage in a
S.S.W. direction.

From September to April the Orinoco is low; it acquires its minimum state in
February. During this period the north-westerly current is weak, and any strong
south wind that rises in the basin of the Carribean Sea will produce an accumulation
of waters, which, getting to the north, finds opposition by the configuration of the
coasts of Cuba, Santo Domingo, and Porto Rico, and are there forced in a south-
easterly direction. But this is not the only cause of a south-easterly current, which
is occasionally found in these localities. A northerly gale on the coast of the United
States, or between the parallels of 20° and 40° north, and the meridians of 40° and
60° west, presses the masses of waters onward to the south, until they meet the
barrier which the great Antilles place to their progress. The oceanic waves rush,
therefore, through the passages of the Bahamas and Caicos Islands, the passage
between Cuba and Santo Domingo, and between the latter island and Porto Rico,
&c.,+ with fearful violence, assuming an easterly direction as soon as they reach the
Carribean Sea, and hence they set frequently at that time to the south-east from
Alta Vela along the coast of Santo Domingo and Porto Rico.

The coasters are well acquainted with this fact, and it often occurs that sucha
current shortens a passage from the city of Santo Domingo to St. Thomas three
days. The tidal wave recedes during such periods through the Mona Passage with
the velocity which the flood-tide usually possesses; but it sets from Mona Island
north-eastward towards the little island of Desecheo, near the north-western point of
Porto Rico.

From all these observations it results, that a vessel bound from Uosta Firma to
the United States, that purposes to sail through any of the passages that the Car-
ribean Sea affords, should consider at what period the passage is made, and if between
April and August, the greatest caution ought to be used in passing any of the outlets
from the Carribean Sea to the Atlantic Ocean. It will be always on the safer side in
passing by the island of Mona to consider that the stream, whether the consequence
of currents or of tides, sets to the leeward, except actual observations prove to the
contrary.

THE ISLAND OF SANTO DOMINGO, OR HAITI.

Variation from 2° 40’ E, to 4° E,

This island, the second largest of the Great Antilles, is next westward of Porto
Rico, and separated from it by the Mona Passage. The island has from time to time
been under various governments, and in general been separated into two different
republics, but occasionally held under one sovereignty, and at present is con-

sidered to be in an unsettled state, so far as its political existence as an independent
nation.

Santo Domingo is 133 leagues in length from Cape Engano at the east to Cape
Trois at the west end, and from 20 to 50 leagues in width, the broadest part being
from Isabella Point on the north to Beata Point at the south side. The face of the
country is diversified with hills, vallies, and rivers. Near the centre rise the Cibao
Mountains, the highest of which are estimated at nearly 9,000 feet above the sea ;
lower ranges ramify from these, chiefly from east to west. These hills are covered
with forests of various kinds of wood, and the indigenous vegetable productions of
the island are various, beautiful, and valuable; its mahogany is unrivalled for its
texture and beauty, and there is a satinwood superior to that of other parts of the
world ; flowering shrubs are both luxuriant and fragrant; pine for ship-building and
house-carpentery is abundant. The soil is extremely fertile, producing sugar, cocoa,
coffee, cotton, indigo, &c. The climate is excessively hot and unhealthy fur Kuropeans,
but the country is continually refreshed by rains and sea breezes. ‘The total popula-
tion of the island at present is variously estimated, but may be stated at about
800,000, chiefly mulattoes ; the whites and pure negro being small in comparison.
Its principal cities are St. Domingo on the south side, and that of Cape Haitien
(formerly Cape Frangois) on the north side. The towns are Port-au-Prince, Leogane,
and the Mole of St. Nicholas on the west, and Samana on the north-east.

EASTERN COAST OF SANTO DOMINGO.—Al] the eastern end of Santo
Domingo is generally low, but the land may be seen at the distance of 10 leagues ;
and the current in the Mona Passage (as previously described), sets to the northward,
and is very perceptible. Cape Espada is the S. E. point of Santo Domingo, and that
which is nearest to Mona, being 113 leagues W.N.W. from that island. It is a low
point encompassed with a reef and a white shoal.

CAPE ENGANO.—This cape is the eastermost point of the island, and lies 42

extreme of this cape is in latitude 18° 35’ 51”, and longitude 68° 20’ 40’. It is low,
and a shoal extends from it north-easterly, between 3 and 4 miles, and has but little
water on it; therefore it requires a good berth. When the cape bears W. 3 S. at the
distance of 6 leagues, it makes as two heads ; and from it the coast of Porto Rico may
in clear weather be seen.

From Cape Engano the coast trends N.W. + W., 142 leagues to Cape Raphael; the
land is low to within 3 leagues of the latter cape, which is of middling height, and
appears at a distance like an island. Cape Raphael is known by a round mountain,
with a conical peak, like a sugar loaf, but somewhat broader at the bottom, and
situate two miles inland from it, which at a distance has the appearance of being
isolated ; it is, however, connected with the southern shore of the Bay of Samana by
low land. The shore to the eastward is foul, and should not be approached nearer
than a league, without being bound to some of the anchorages between Cape Raphael
and Engano.

This part of Santo Domingo has hitherto been very little known to Europeans, as
indeed may be said of the greater part of the island, and there are very few places
that can be taken without the aid of a pilot, as our knowledge of these parts is very
imperfect ; but most of these places and anchorages are fit only for vessels of small
draught and droghers of the country. For the information that we shall have to lay
before the mariner, we are indebted principally to the various articles by Sir Robert
H. Schomburgk which appeared in the Nautical Magazine, 1853.

PUNTA CANA.—The first anchoring place to the south of Cape Engano is
Punta Cana, in latitude 18°30’, and lougitude 68° 23’. The shore is skirted by a reef,
which obliges the vessels that have to take in cargo at this place, to lie according to
size, from 1 to 14 mile from the shore. The reef affords passages for the boats to
take off the cargo from the beach which is sandy.* Vessels (excepting small sloops
that draw not more than 6 feet), are obliged to come to an anchor outside the reef.
A vessel of from 300 to 400 tons, would not be safe closer than 14 mile from the land.
There are two breaks in the reef, which are used for taking the wood from the shore
on board. They have 6 and 63 fect water; it is, however, requisite to use caution
with the launch, as the passages are narrow, and much impeded inside by heads of
coral rocks. The swell or ground sea is sometimes very severe along this coast, and
a stiff northerly wind renders all communication with the shore impossible. The
months from May to October are the best qualified for loading here. The breeze is
ceperaly at that time to the south of east, and calms prevail more than at any other

ime.

Puntanal and Guayacanes.—These loading places are a few leagues further
towards Punta Espada, and the remarks made with regard to Punta Cuna-apply
equally to Puntanal and Guayacanes. There are some ranchos or huts on the beach,
inhabited by the labourers of the adjacent mahogany cuts. Puntanal is about 3 miles
south of Punta Cana.

Booa Yuma or Higuey.—The anchorage is good, but exposed to the breezes.
You anchor off the sandy beach called Playeta, near the windward point of the river,
in 12 fathoms water. A bar which affords only from 83 to 9 feet water, prevents
large vessels from entering the river. Within the bar there are 12 feet water. The

by ascending the river to Derumbadero. This can only be done in a small boat.

The anchorage between Cabo Falso and Punta Yuma is good; vessels may lie close
in in from 9 to 12 fathoms. The ship is, however, exposed to the north-easterly
winds. It must likewise be observed, that the tides run with great velocity, chiefly
near Punta Cuevita, where it races with a velocity of from 4 to 5 knots.

Sir Robert observes, that during my examination of these two places, I had no
boat at my command to procure soundings. The information of the depth of water
stated above, has been procured from very good sources.

According to my observations, Punta Yuma lies in lat. 18° 22’ 46’, and long.
68° 35’ 36’. From this determination [ have deduced the position of Cabo Falso as in
lat. 18° 20’ 10’, and long. 68° 35’ 24’.

The land of Cabo Falso rises in mural precipices of coraline limestone from 150 to
220 feet. The false cape is the projecting southern point of this elevation, and
presents, as seen from the north, the profile of a grotesque head.

Granchora.—This loading-place ought never tobe included in a charter-party. It
is situate about 3 miles to the S.W. of Cabo Falso. The vessel cannot approach
within several miles, and has to anchor to the lee of Catalinita, or to the lee of the
reef that stretches from Granchora towards the islets. Such a heavy sea prevails
usually along the shore, that weeks may elapse before the launch can take off a load.
The Danish brig Sympathie was, in the months of April and May, 1852, lying for
several weeks at this anchorage without being once able to communicate with the
shore. She was ultimately obliged to return without having taken off a single piece
of wood.

The same remarks apply to Punta Martel.

The following anchoring-places (Cabeza de Toro, Babaro, Los Ronchitos, and
Arena Gorda) come nearly all under one and the same category, with regard to their
practicability, as loading places. During the summer months, when the trade wind
is to the south of east and calms are prevailing, there is no danger to be apprehended,
and vessels expedite their loading in as short a time as anywhere on the coast; but
during the winter months, when north-easterly winds are frequent, the vessel is not
only endangered, but the loading is rendered difficult, as days and days may elapse
before a boat can pass from the anchorage to the land. Nevertheless, a vast quantity
of wood is loaded at the north-eastern anchoring-places, and the master who has
accepted a charter-party in which one or the other of the above-named places is
included, ought to be provided with good chains.

The first rocky point to the north of Punta Engano is Los Algodenes, which does
not afford any anchorage, probably in consequence of the configuration of the land
and contending tides. The water is always here turbulent, and the white foam or
froth has been compared to the appearance of cotton.

Cabeza de Toro,—The quantities of wood in the neighbourhood of this anchoring-
place cause it to be frequently visited by vessels. The reefs afford two passages ; the
one to leeward, called La Naybe, is even passable for schooners that draw no more
than 10 or 12 feet. Large vessels anchor outside the reef in from 10 to 12 fathoms
water, sandy and rocky bottom.

Babaro, about 6 miles from Cabeza de Toro, is considered a better anchoring-place
than the former; the sea is calmer and the reef approaches more to the land. Vessels
lie in 10 and 12 fathoms, distant 14 to 2 miles from the land. The beach sandy, and
the loading may be effected rapidly when there is no north-easterly breeze or heavy
ground-swell.

MACAO. 19

os Ranchitos is about 9 miles north-easterly from Babaro. The reef has two
passages with about 4 to 5 feet water. Vessels lie outside in 11 or 12 fathoms of
water, distant 15 to 2 miles from the land. It is a sandy beach and a good loading-
place.

Arena Gorda, about 2 miles from the former, has three passages through the
reef, which a small sloop, with 5 feet water, can safely pass to the anchorage within ;
vessels of large burden lie from 1} to 2 miles, according to their size, in 10 to 12
fathoms water.

Macao.—All the remarks respecting Babaro, Cabeza de Toro, &c., refer equally to
Macao. The anchorage is here still further off the shore than at Babaro, and the
place is much more exposed to the winds and sweepings of the sea. When I visited
Macao there was no boat to enable me to procure soundings, I learned, however,
that the vessels anchor about $a mile north of the reef (which, it seemed to me,
stretched from Cabezote Barlovento in a line towards El Infiernito), and send their
boats for the wood to the bight of the bay and to the mouth of the Anamuya. The
two rocks high out of the water, called the Cabazottes, are excellent landmarks, and
afford along them good boat passages. The passage for the bight of the bay, where
there are some ranchos for the shelter of the labourers, is between Punta Macao and
the Cabezote Barlovento; and that for the mouth of the Anamuya, close to the
Cabezote Sotavento, likewise called El Infiernito. At the mouth of the Anamuya is
a bed of excellent oysters. The nearest habitation was, at the period of my visit (in
1850) at Calado Salado, distant about 2 miles from Macao,

The position of Punta Macao, deduced from observations which I took near the
Ranchos, is in lat. 18° 48’ 0’ and long. 68° 29’ 50’.

There are anchoring-places between Punta Macao and Cape San Rafacl. The
latter, already noticed, cannot well be mistaken.

Port Jicao, ox English Harbour (Puerto de los Ingleses) lies about 11 miles
W. by S. from Cape San Rafael. Here several vessels have recently taken wood on
board. A rock, which rises above the reef that stretches from Punta Jicaco towards
the cays, is seen at a distance of 2 leagues, and serves as a mark to point out the
passages Barlovento and Sotavento. At the same time a double-peaked mountain
will be observed inland, bearing 8. by W.; keep the hummock between the two
peaks as your mark, and come to an anchor in 53 to 6 fathoms, distant + of a mile
from the land. The anchorage within the reef is safe, and has the advantage that
the vessel can leave with the trade-wind, selecting the lee pass for her passage when
standing out to sea.

It is not probable that a vessel would anchor at English Harbour without a pilot
on board; should stress of weather oblige her to do so, great precaution must be

taken when approaching the reef. The French man-of-war Scorpion was lost here in
1782.

Round Point Mangle are Los Uberos Altos. When passing from Savana de la
Mar to Hobero, in 1851, the coast from Punta del Capitan to Punta de Mangle
seemed to me more or less dangerous, and the only good port in that distance was
English Harbour. I had no opportunity to sound it, but I took observations at the
house of Senor Reyes, on the right bank of La Yeguada, which gave for the lat.
18° 58’ 50" and long. 63° 3’ 37’, The mouth of La Yeguada, or Hobero, is about 4 a
mile south from here.”

THE SOUTHERN COAST OF SANTO DOMINGO FROM
POINT ESPADA TO CAPE TIBURON.

Point Espada, as previously noticed, is the S.E. point of Santo Domingo, and from
it the S.E. point of Saona Island bears about S. by W., distant 15 miles. From
Point Espada to the S.W. the coast forms the bay called Higuey, and a smaller one
called Catalinita ; both are very foul with reefs. To the southward of the latter is
the island Saona. This island lies off the eastern part of the south coast, is about 16
miles in length from east to west, and from 8 to 4 in breadth, covered with trees, and
surrounded with a white shoal to the distance of 2 miles.

The former descriptions of the coasts of Santo Domingo were very vague, and
mostly from the Spanish Derrotero, and afforded but little assistance to the mariner ;
and at that time very little trade was carried on, and that only at two or three ports;
since then various bays and anchorages have been resorted to, but principally by
small vessels and coasters of light tonnage. Strangers should always obtain the
assistance of a pilot if not locally acquainted with the coast, for up to this time no
survey has been made of it, and, therefore, any instruction we can give must be con-
Lees very imperfect. The most reliable are from the remarks of Sir R. H. Schom-

urgk,

Saona Island.—This island extends from its eastern point about 16 miles N. 70°
W. It has a projecting southern point, and is at its widest part, from south to north,
about 5 miles across. Between it and the main lies the islet Catalinita, bearing from
the rocky north-eastern point of Saona N. 50° W., distant 53 miles. A large horse-
shoe reef extends from Catalinita towards Saona, affording, however, between the
north coast of the latter and the south-eastern extent of the reef, a fine channel with
6 fathoms water. When the reef has been cleared, the vessel ought to keep north-
westerly, to avoid a shallow that runs out from Saona, and anchor in 5 futhoms
water, Catalinita bearing N. by E.

Small vessels may pass through the channel between Saona and the main coast of
Santo Domingo; at its eastern outlet, however, are mud banks, with only 7 feet water
over them.

When keeping for the anchorage of Catalinita, you may make bold with the
northern shore of Saona until the horse-shoe is cleared. ‘The anchorage is well
protected, and the bottom clear and sandy. The currents sweep with great force
towards the N.W. The brig Ravenswood, of Glasgow, was wrecked and totally lost
during the night of the 19th October, 1852, at the east end of Catalinita, believing
herself, at the time the disaster occurred, opposite the west end of Saona, and many
miles to the south of it.

The north-eastern point of Saona is bold, consisting of high cliffs; but its south-
eastern point is low, and there stretches a reef to the south-castward, which breaks
near the shore, and extends under the water for nearly three miles, with only 4 and 5
fathoms over it. The reef keeps this depth until within a mile of the low south-
eastern point of Saona. Large vessels coming from the east ought not to approach
the shore to within 4 miles, until the extreme southern point is cleared.*

The reef is about 5 miles south of Cabello Bay, Saona Island. At low water it is

Other rocks, about 9 or 10 miles distant from the south-west part of the island of

BOCA DE QUIABON. 21

There is a good anchorage about 8 miles to the west of the south-eastern point, in
front of a sandy beach called Bahia Cabello; but at about 12 to 2 miles to the south
of the bay, where the sandy beach ends and the shore becomes rocky, lies a dangerous
shoal, on which several vessels have struck ; and in August, 1850, the British barque
Alert, of Halifax, N.S. The shallowest part has only 6 feet water breaking upon it
during a heavy sea.* A quarter of a mile to the N.N.W. of it is another dangerous
shoal, with from 9 to 3 fathoms water. There is a good pass between it} and the
eastern shoal. Vessels frequent occasionally Bahia Cabello for the sake of firewood
and fresh water.

The opening or western entrance to the channel of Catalinita, between Saona and
the main coast, is called Boca del Catujano. As already observed, it has only 7 feet
water at its shallowest part, being narrowed in by mud banks and coral rocks.

It ought likewise to be noticed, that a reef stretches from the western point of
Saona towards the main shore, which must be guarded against, should a yessel on
beating up keep the shore.+

Boca de Quiabon (vulgarly called Chabon).—This is an open roadstead, with
good anchoring-ground. Large vessels anchor in from 8 to 9 fathoms water. The
mark for the anchorage is, to keep the Point Las Minas in one with Point Aguila,
that forms the eastern point of La Romano, and to bring the two cocoa-nut trees on
the shore, in front of the largest house, in the small village, to bear north. The
bottom shallows very gradually, and at the distance of 3 cables’ length from the
shore there is still a depth of 3 fathoms. The ground to windward of the mark just
given is rocky, and there is likewise said to be a shoal with only 13 feet water on it.

The mouth of the river Quiabon is impeded by a bar, which affords only from 22
to 3 feet water ; and that small depth is sometimes reduced to half a foot during dry
weather, while freshes, on the other hand, deepen and widen the entrance ; some-
times the mouth of the river is entirely blocked up by sand-banks. Formerly vessels
drawing 12 feet could go up the river as far as the Malena, but the river is now much
impeded; boats, nevertheless, manage to ascend the Quiabon to the small village
Gato, which may be called the port of the town of Higuey. This village is on the
left bank, and is, following the course of the river, 5 miles from the mouth.

The village of Quiabon consists merely of a number of buhios, or small huts, built
of wood and covered with palm-leaves. It suffers from want of fresh water, though
this might easily he remedied by Artesian wells. In June, 1852, fresh water was
found at a distance of little more than two miles from the mouth. The tides rise
seldom more than 22 inches or 2 feet, hence the sea does not extend far up the river.
According to Sir Robert’s determination, the weather point, or Punta Barlovento, is
in lat. 18° 24’ 20’, and long. 68° 54’ 23”.

Two miles and a half E.S.E. of Punta Barlovento is Bayahibe, where vessels have
recently commenced to load wood. It is considered to afford a better anchorage than
Quiabon. The sea is smoother, as Saona and the projecting point of Las Palmillas
protect the anchorage. The vessels lie in from 6 to 7 fathoms, distant about a mile
from the shore, on a sandy bottom.

Guaraguao and Las Palmillas.—S.H. $ E., nearly 8 miles from Punta Barlo-
vento, lies the anchoring-piace of Guaraguao; and some miles further to the east is

3 miles. We have already alluded to the reefs that extend from the north-western

as Minas and Burgado.—About 4 a mile to the west of the anchorage at
Quiabon is the loading-place of Las Minas, and, somewhat downward, El Burgado.
Las Minas is a sheltered place for small vessels; but those of large burden must lie
in 20 fathoms. Masters of vessels frequently prefer to remain with their vessels at
the anchorage of Quiabon, and to send the launch for the wood to Las Minas and
Burgado.

Caleton.—This loading-place, to the east of Punta Aguila, offers scarcely a good
‘anchorage. The tides sweep with great strength, and render it laborious, when wind
and tide are contrary, to reach the ship at anchor.

Boca de la Romano.—The river Romano affords, within a short distance from its
mouth, one of the best-sheltered ports on the south coast of the island. The entrance
is narrow, it being not quite a cable’s length from point to point; and 34 fathoms
from the lee point there is a small shoal, with only 33 to 4 feet water on its shallowest
part.

On entering the river, which must be with a leading breeze, and having reduced
your soundings to 9 or 10 fathoms, keep the two inner points of the river (the first
or western of which is then about 600 fathoms, the second or eastern 800 fathoms
distant, bearing N. 173° W.) about 13 degree open of each other; the two inner
points being in one is a mark for the shoal. Continue that course until you are
abreast of the weather point, remembering that there is a reef a little to the east of
that point. Having entered the river, you will observe two rocks, from 6 to 10 feet
above water, on your starboard. Keep the lee bank a little closer than the weather
bank, and proceed up the river until you are near the inner lee point. Keeping now
the northern rock you noticed on entering the river on your starboard, (looking over
your stern,) in one with the weather point at the mouth, come to anchor in 5 fathoms.
You will then notice two rocks a little south of the inner lee point, around one of
which you may make fast,* and if you do not wish the vessel to swing to the tides,
do the same round a rock on the eastern bank. Small vessels anchor round the inner
lee point, in 10 or 11 feet water. A short distance to the north of this anchorage is
a shallow with only 6 feet.

I need scarcely observe, the river being so narrow, and not permitting any room
for working a ship, the vessel ought to take her departure only with a land-breeze
sufficiently strong to give her headway. The two dangers against which she has to
guard, are the sunken rock off the lee point and the weather reef. The river Romano
has broken through the hills of coralline limestone which frequently approach the
shore in perpendicular walls. Small sailing-vessels may ascend for nearly 2 miles
from the mouth, but they require a pilot. Boats frequently get as high up as the
Derumbaderos, and even to the rapid for fresh water. There are no difficulties for
boats until coming to the little island, where a shelf of rocks shallows the river to 24
feet during its mean stand, and to only one foot on approaching the rapid. The
river falls here over a shelf of rocks, so that the boat may almost lie under it, and
permit the water to run into the casks.

The small village La Romano lies on the hills above the river on its right or
western bank; the ascent is steep and very incommodious. The Commandant has
his residence on the left bank, opposite the village. The position of this place was,
according to my observation, in lat. 18° 27’ 32’, and long. 68° 58’ 37",+ from which

Santa Catalina.—The island of Santa Catalina, or merely Catalina, lies about 2
miles off the southern coast, between the mouths of the rivers Cumayasa and La
Romano. The channel between the main of the principal island and the islet extends
east and west, and affords a passage for the largest vessel by keeping the mainland
close on board, ‘There is good anchorage in 35 fathoms on the north-western part of
Catalina, near a bay, where the vessel is protected by the two jutting points of the
island. The north-western point has a reef, on which the water breaks to warn
against the danger.

Boca de Cumayasa.—I have not examined the mouth of this river, which it is
well known affords as good an anchorage as La Romano, with the preference that the
entrance is not endangered by a shoal. Mr. Lundstrom, master of the Swedish barque
Jenny Lind, has communicated to me the sketch of the entrance, with the following
particulars :—‘“ The anchorage for vessels that require more than 18 feet is about 14
cable’s length from the entrance, on the river’s eastern bank. ‘There is a rock above
water, near which the vessel may anchor. ‘The bank of the river forms, on the left
or eastern side, two small coves, and has much more the appearance of an inlet of the
sea than the mouth of the river.* Large vessels may anchor in 4 fathoms, a little
south of the small cove.

“ On ascending the river, a large mud flat extends from the first point on its left
or eastern bank. ‘There is a channel close on the right bank, with only from 6 to 8
feet water. Small craft that draw no more than 6 feet pass over it, and may ascend
to the rock of San Pedro, about 1$ mile from the entrance. Higher up there are
three islands, beyond which the river gets quite narrow, and is only passable for
boats up to the Derumbadero of San Juan, 34 miles from the entrance.”

Fresh water is somewhat higher up than San Juan, where the river forms a basin,
called Agua Dulce, but the boats cannot approach within a couple of hundred of
yards.

The River Soco, although one of the largest that flows from the mountains in
the eastern part towards the sea, is unfortunately impeded by a bar, and narrowed in
by sand-banks covered with drift-wood, so that only boats can enter to the fine basin
that extends beyond the bar. Vessels of 300 tons have to anchor in 5 fathoms,
distant about 3 miles from the shore, the mouth of the river bearing N. by E. or
N.N.E.; smaller ones may lie in 3 or 4 fathoms. The anchorage is naturally open
to the winds, and receives scarcely any protection from Point Mortero, which bears
from the mouth of the river 8. by E.

The embarcadero, or loading-place, is about a cable’s length from the mouth, on
the river’s right or western bank, and has deep water close in. According to my
observations, the house of Dona Felipe Morales is in lat. 18° 27’ 45’, and long.
69° 12'44". The mouth of the river bears from hence §. by E., distant about 2
cables’ length.

The Port of Macoris.—On coming in sight of the bay, which the river Macoris
forms at its mouth, one is struck with that fine expanse of water, which it seems
nature intended fora harbour. A nearer glance, and the lead proves that such a
supposition is delusive; the bay, with the exception of the channel, which the river
has pathed itself, is a mud flat. An islet, with a reef extending north-eastward,
protects the anchorage. ‘The channel affords here only 18 feet water, and shoals
to 16 and 14 feet as soon as the south point is abreast. Between this point and the

north passage point lies, about 4 a cable’s length from the former, a dangerous shoal,
with only from 6 to 7 feet water on it. The British barque Edward struck here in
May, 1851, and received so much injury that she was condemned on her arrival at
the port of Santo Domingo. The mark for this shoal is, the north passage point on
with the second cocoanut-tree, near the Commandant’s house.

If the draught of your vessel permits it, and you have cleared the-outer reef on
entering the harbour, keep your course for Mr. Peck’s house, at the north-western
bight of the bay, until you have fairly opened the small sandy beach, Playa Peter.
The soundings give you then 12 feet. Steer for the Playa until you are abreast of
the north-passage point, keeping the shore on board, and let go in 11} feet water.
This anchorage can only convene small vessels, as at a short distance to the north-
west from the north passage point, the water shoals to 74 and 6 fect. The rise of
the tide is scarcely 2 feet. Schooners and sloops requiring no more than 10 feet
water may anchor in front of the village and ascend the river for some distance.
The anchorage can only be left with a good land-breeze, and it ought to be noted
that the current sets towards the shoal. The south passage point and Playa Muerto,
being in one, is a mark, on leaving the bay, that you are free of the ‘“ Edward’s”
shoal, and may now take a south-eastern course until the reef of the Isleta is astern.

There are two small villages on the shores of the bay. The larger lies on the left
or eastern shore, and bears, in common parlance, the name of Mosquito y Sol; the
first, from the large number of mosquitoes, which, in consequence of the adjacent
mangrove or manglebush, frequent the place—the latter, from its exposed situation to
a tropical sun. ‘The village belongs to the district of Seybo, and surpasses, in the
number of houses and inhabitants, La Punta, the rival village, on the projecting right
or western point of the river, which belongs to the jurisdiction of Los Llanos. The
situation of the latter is much healthier and the prospect more open, but it has the
drawback, that even small sloops cannot come close to it in consequence of the mud
flat. My observations give me for the projecting point of La Punta lat. 18° 27’ 0’,
long. 69° 19 17’, according to which, Punta Macoris would be in lat. 18° 25’ 50”, and
long. 69° 19 25’. There is no fresh water in either village that can be recommended,
except it be procured by ascending the river for about 2 miles,

Guayacanes.—About 8 or 9 miles to the west of Macoris is the anchorage of
Guayacanes; it is an open roadstead, with a reef inside of it. The anchorage is
from 1 mile to 1} mile off the land, in 8 to 9 fathoms, entirely exposed; but the
bottom is sandy and holds well. The boats, in order to take off the cargo, have to
pass the reef. There are a few inhabitants settled at the beach.

Juan d’Olio is equally exposed as the former, and the anchorage is about the
same distance from the land. There are likewise some houses on the shore.

Magdalena forms the easternmost, and Cancedo the westernmost point of the Bay
of Andres. It is an open and bad anchorage, and vessels prefer to lie in Agua del
Rey, 4 miles further inside the bay, sending their boats to Magdalena for the wood
they have to take off there.

Agua del Rey, on the castern shore of the Bay of Andres, affords the best
anchorage within that expanse of water. Vessels of 300 tons may lie in 5 fathoms,
being protected against the east and south-east by Magdalena Point. The beach is
good for loading ; it must, however, be noted that the swell sets in with great force,
in consequence of the bay being so large and open to the sea.

Playa de Andres.—The anchorage is from 2 to 3 miles from the land; there is a
large reef, with breakers inside, which affords a passage 9 feet in depth. The Playa
de Andres is famed for the prodigious and almost incredible number of pigeons that,
between the months of May and October, come to roost there ; their numbers are so
large that they may be knocked down with sticks.

Punta Cancedo.—There is a Derumbadero near Punta Cancedo, only approach-
able for boats ; large vessels must lie off and on to take in cargo from here,

SANTO DOMINGO. 25

La Caleta, to the north-west of Punta Cancedo, although small, is a very good
port, where the vessel at anchor is protected against south-easterly winds. There are
no dangers, and the vessel may select her anchorage from 3 to 7 fathoms. The
expanse of the bay is small, and affords only place to a few ships; the landing is
good.

SANTO DOMINGO.—This city, which is the metropolis of the eastern division
of the island, is situate on the western bank of the river Ozama, the entrance of
which may be known by the city and fort built on that side of the river. An exten-
sive savannah lies to the westward of it, enclosed by an amphitheatre of hills. The
city is surrounded by a wall, and defended by the fort at the entrance of the river
and several other outworks. The population in 1864 was estimated at about 15,000,
when the Captain-General and principal Spanish authorities resided here. The city
is built on a rocky point; the cathedral is spacious and magnificent, and the streets
are at right angles with each other, and have footways of brick. It has a market
that is sometimes sparely provided; but the fresh meat is excellent and cheap. Salt
provisions, flour, and rice are imported from the United States.

Light.—A fixed Light, visible 9 miles, has been established on the bastion of San
José, on the western side of the river; the lantern is 113 feet above the sea, and its
range extends nearly in a half-circle from south to east and westward.

Vessels coming from the east and running for St. Domingo Roads ought to keep in
mind, that having doubled Punta Cancedo, the Light will show over the land, some-
what to the north of Punta Torricilla; and that from this poiut, from whence the
Light bears N. 58° W., distant 1,423 yards, a short reef extends south-westward,
which breaks when the sea is agitated. When bearing up for this anchorage, this
reef should be guarded against.

The entrance to the harbour was surveyed by the officers of H.M.S. Hound in
1849, at which time there was a depth of 2 fathoms immediately before the town,
aud 6 to 14 fathoms half a mile off, thence suddenly deepening to 20 and 30 fathoms.
The best anchorage appears to be off the town in 5 to 10 fathoms water. The stream
out of the river Ozama runs with great velocity. The rise and fall of the tide is
seldom more than 20 inches, and the time of high water is uncertain.

Directions FOR THE Port oF ST. Dominco. By Sir R. H. Schomburgh.

The port is formed by the river Ozama, where it enters the sea. Unfortunately
there is a bar at its mouth, with only 13 feet water. After passing the same, there
are from 16 to 19 feet water for more than 3 miles up the river. Large vessels are
therefore prevented from entering this port, otherwise so commodious and secure ; for
a vessel can lie so close to the shore, that she discharges her cargo by means of
planks. With such steep banks, it would be easy to construct the necessary works
for careening and repairing vessels within the river.

The bar extends from east to west; it is larger on the left than on the right bank,
and ends in a narrow strip close to the rocky point, on the right or western bank,
somewhat south of the signal-tower.

The tide rises seldom more than 20 inches, and the current sweeps with great
strength through the mouth. It prevents the vessel from obeying the helm when
not favoured by a fair land-breeze, and has in several instances caused the ship to
touch when leaving the harbour. The same danger threatens vessels on entering the
river. It should not be attempted, under any circumstances, to enter the port without
a pilot on board, or a good breeze to fill the sails.

Large vessels anchor in the roads, in from § to 12 fathoms water, distant about
a mile from the shore. They are here exposed to the south wind, and the heavy swell
of the sea. The anchorage consists of good holding-ground; but it must be con-

[W. Inpizs, Parr II.] E

26 SANTO DOMINGO.

sidered, that should a misfortune befall a vessel, she would be sure to be smashed to
pieces against the steep rocks that form the shore at this part of the coast. If the
weather has a threatening appearance, chiefly during the hurricane months, all pre-
paration should be made to be able to slip and stand out to sea.

Through the kindness of Mr. Joseph Walker, Master of H.M.S. Tricomalee, which
vessel was in 1849 at anchor in this roadstead, I have received the following “ Sailing
Directions” :—

“The bank of auchoring-ground off St. Domingo is very steep, and for the first few
casts irregular—40, 15, 10, 8. After that, the soundings decrease gradually towards
the shore. In coming in, give the east point a berth of 2 cables’ length, to avoid a
rocky reef with 24 fathoms on it, which stretches off to that distance. This danger
will show itself by the breakers when there is any swell.

“Tf bound inside, keep a square white house on the east bank of the river twice its
breadth open of the west point, on which stands the signal-tower. Keep this mark
on till you are within 2 cables’ length of the west point, you will then discern a low
sandy spit running off from the eastern side ; steer directly for it, and pass it close ;
there is no danger, as there are 16 feet at a distance of 10 feet from it; but on the
other side is a sunken rock, with only 2 feet on it. With the remarks given above,
you will carry 13 feet over the bar; and, after passing the sandy spit, you will have
from 16 to 19 feet, three miles up the river.*

“If intending to anchor outside, do not shut in the houses on the east side of the
river at all, but anchor with them rather open; the last point bearing N.E, by E., in
8 fathoms sand and mud. With the houses open, the bank extends off, rather more
than one nautical mile from the shore, narrowing considerably to the westward. The
bottom also becomes rocky and uneven, when the houses on the eastern bank become
shut in by the west point. The best anchorage is decidedly when they are well
open.”

Port Regulations.

_ Art. 1, Every master of a vessel entering from abroad, shall remit to the pilot
who comes on board all the letters and newspapers intended for this port, excepting
the consignees’ letters. It remains at the option of the master to take the pilot or
not, in order to anchor his vessel in the roadstead, or to bring her into the port.

“Art. 2. When the health officer visits the vessel, the master will deliver the
requisite bill of health, and will muster the whole of the crew and passengers.

“ Art. 3. After the vessel has anchored, the officers of the custom-house will come
on board, to whom the master shall give up the register of the vessel, and the
manifest of his whole cargo; he shall afford them every facility to affix the seals, and

shall allow one of their number to remain on board until the vessel has finished
discharging.

“Art. 4. The pilot will bring the vessel, whether with cargo or in ballast, to

anchor in the proper place for its discharge; and in no instance can the vessel change
place without previous authorization of the commandant of the port.

“ Art. 5, Throwing overboard of ballast is prohibited to all masters of vessels, as
well in the port as in the roadstead; they have to address themselves to the captain

of the port in case of such a necessity, who will assign to them the proper place for
its discharge.

“ Art. 6. In order to obtain a coast pilot and the necessary labourers for a vessel
which is to load on the coast, the master, accompanied by his consignee, will address
