TuE Coast CONTINUED :—

Boca de Zaina.—The anchorage is entirely exposed and foul; the vessels are
obliged to lie off at a great distance, the swell being at all times very heavy ; calms
and northerly winds afford the only period when loads can be taken off. It ought
not to be included into charter-parties. It is worthy of remark, that Vice-Admiral
Penn landed here the troops under Venables, in 1655; the men-of-war disembarking
the army while under sail.

Boca Nigua.—Although vessels frequently take a part of their cargo at this place,
it is considered to be one of the most difficult loading-places on the south coast of St.
Domingo. ‘The anchorage seems to be merely on a bank, with a difference in
soundings of 12 or 13 fathoms, by the vessel swinging to the tides or currents. A
strong breeze and current forces the sea with such violence into the anchorage, that it
rises from 12 to 15 fect. It is only safe to load here when the wind is from the
north. The banks on the shore are so steep, that such wood as lignum vite can be
taken at once in the boat from the rocks above. A gale from any other point than
north would inevitably cause the loss of the vessel lying at anchor at Boca Nigua.
The miasma of the river is considered very unhealthy ; indeed, it is only with
reluctance resorted to asa loading-place. There isa small village a short distance
from the mouth, and fresh water may be procured { of a mile up the river; the
water is not considered healthy.

Boca de Najallo.—The bight which the river forms at its mouth is somewhat
more than a mile in extent, but the anchorage is as objectionable as that of Boca
Nigua, with the difference, that the landing is better than at the former. The vessels
lie about 2 of a mile from the land.

Palenque.,—This is the next port to the west. It would be a most desirable
anchorage did the port afford more space ; the vessels lie in 4 fathoms water, gravelly
bottom, and well sheltered; the water is so deep, that close to the beach are 3
fathoms. A south wind would prevent a vessel fiom leaving port, but she can get
out with the usual trade winds. A reef, which stretches from the windward point
§.E. and N.W., ought to be guarded against.

Boca de Nizao.—To the west of Punta Nizao is an open roadstead, where vessels
very frequently take wood on board. The ground shallows gradually, and vessels of
from 250 to 300 tons have to lie in from 7 to 9 fathoms water, at a distance of 13 or
2 miles from the mouth of the river. Smaller vessels may anchor in 4 fathoms, but
it must be recollected that the sea breaks often a great distance from the shore.

This anchorage is no more dangerous than other open roadsteads along the coast ;
indeed, more vessels load here than at Bani, and the other southern anchoring-
places.

The tide runs frequently with a strength of from 4 to 5 knots, and renders the
loading of the vessels somewhat tedious. It is next to an impossibility for a boat to
enter the river; the current sweeps out with very great force. On proceeding,
therefore, from on board to the place where the rafts of wood are to be made up, it is
better to land the people at Palenque, and to let them walk overland to Nizao. With
regard to these local arrangements, however, and the manner in which the raft of

28 SAVANA,

wood is to be got on board, it is best to trust to the orders of the pilot, and to the
labourers acquainted with the management.

The water of the river is good, and may be procured fresh + of a mile from the

mouth. There is at a short distance from the shore a small village.

Puerto Viejo.—About 4 miles west from the mouth of Nizao is a better landing-
place. Like the former it is only an open roadstead; the anchorage is in 7 fathoms,
distant about 13 mile from the shore.

Punta Catalina is not much frequented as a loading-place. There is no anchorage
on the east part; but on the western small vessels may anchor in 33 fathoms. ‘To
the south of Punta Catalina, distant one mile, is a shoal, with only 12 feet water
over it, which ought to be guarded against when beating up the coast. Punta
Palenque forms the eastern point, and Punta Catalina the western of a large bight,
which contains Boca Nizao and Puerto Viejo as loading-places in that extent of the
coast.

Savana.—About 3 to 4 miles west of Punta Catalina is Savana, where large
vessels may anchor with safety in from 5 to 6 fathoms ; the anchorage is good, but to
the windward only protected by Point Catalina, which bears about E.S.E.

Paya is an open roadstead, shallowing very gradually, so that a vessel of 200 to
300 tons has to lie at a distance of from 23 to3 miles. It is much frequented as a
loading-place,

Aqua de la Estancia is the anchoring-place of the village Bani, and is, like the
former, an open roadstead. Vessels have to lie at anchor at the same distance, but it
is good holding-ground, consisting of mud and weeds, with sand.

Estancia Calorada.—Somewhat further to the westward is La Estancia Calorada,
to which the same remarks refer that have been made With regard to the previous
place.

Za Salina.—The soundings are from 15 to 18 fathoms, at a distance of a cable’s
length from the shore. Two mountain cabbage-trees, kept in a line with a large sea-
side grape-tree, bearing then between E. and E. by N., are a mark for a good
anchorage. Small vessels anchor in 5 fathoms, with a hawser ashore, for fear the
anchors might not hold. The depth increases so suddenly, that with 5 fathoms for-
ward, the vessel will probably have from 18 to 20 fathoms over the stern.

La Caldera.—This is one of the finest ports on the south coast; a vessel may
anchor here in from 14 to 8 fathoms of water, as may best suit her.

Playa Vieja.—Outside of La Caldera, about N. by E. from La Salina, is Playa
Vieja, affording a good anchorage under the hills of Ocoa. The bottom is so clear
that it may be seen in 6 fathoms of water. Three or four hedges of mango-trees,
visible at a great distance, are a good mark for this anchorage.

Ocoa.—This beautiful bay affords an excellent and well-protected port, near the
mouth of the river of that name. You may anchor close in on either side of the
river, but the northern is more preferable. ‘It received in ancient times the name of
Puerto Hermoso, from the Spaniards ; and Columbus found shelter here with a small
squadron during the hurricane on the Ist of July, 1502, when Ovando refused him to
enter the port of St. Domingo. A whole fleet may anchor here in safety, and during
the war at the commencement of the century, it was much resorted to by ships.

Caracoles, at the bight of the bay of Ocoa 3 you have to anchor at the distance of
13 mile from the shore, in 5 or 6 fathoms of water. The landing is good, but the
large bay is sometimes subjected to a heavy swell when the breeze is southerly.

Azua, ox Tortuguero.—The sea sets into this anchorage with great force. When
the breeze arises the vessels labour much, and the boats seldom can go off with wood
to the ships after 11 o’clock in the morning. There is no room for working a vessel
in the bay. On the western point is a reef, and near the east point is broken ground.

BARAONA, OR BARAHONA. 29°

Vessels leave the bay with the land-breeze. Tortuguero is the port of Azua, and is
considered to be a tolerably good anchoring-place.

Puerto Viejo de Azua.—This is an excellent port for small vessels, where they
lie quite land-locked. Unfortunately it has only from 12 to 15 feet water at the
entrance ; but for such vessels as require no greater depth, it is one of the safest ports
in the Republic. The entrance is very narrow, and there is a reef on the north
point. Large vessels lie before the entrance, in from 9 to 8 fathoms, as circumstances
may require.

The Bay of Neyba, or Juliana, extends from Punta Martin Garcia to Punta
Truxillo, 94 miles, and has a depth of 83 miles; the largest vessels of war may
anchor in the bay along its eastern coast. It contains the anchorages of Rancho del
Cura and Bahia Alejandro on the eastern, and the port of Baraona on the western
coast. The river Neyba, or Yaque, enters the bay N. 844° W., 10 miles from Punta
Martin Garcia. The ground shallows to 11 feet, and has a bar with less water, which
prevents small sailing-vessels entering the river. Its course has been very changeable,
and formerly it entered the bay further southward in several arms.

Rancho del Cura.—aAt the distance of a mile from Punta Martin Garcia in the
fine bay of Neyba, and a little to the north of some red cliffs is a very good anchorage
under the above name. You lie two cables’ length from the shore in d fathoms,
protected by Punta Martin Garcia from the east winds. To the north of the

anchorage are some white cliffs, almost equidistant from the anchorage and the red
cliffs.

Bahia Alejandro.—The anchorage is very exposed, and there is a reef inside. I
_ have not visited it personally, but I learn that it is no desirable place for loading a
| Vessel.

Baraona, or Barahona.—This harbour offers a very good anchorage, but vessels
ought to wait for a pilot to lead them through the passage between the reefs. On
entering the bay of Neyba, and being abreast of the red cliffs, hold a W.S.W. course
for the entrance; the water is bold, close into the reef. At 4 cables’ length from the
reef you have no bottom with 120 fathoms, and it suddenly shallows to 5 fathoms
and 10 feet. When you are within 2 miles of the reef, you will discern the village
very plainly, and you will note above it two ridges of hills, one overtopping the
other ; each ridge has a saddle or hummock, in a direction of nearly W.S.W. with
the village: keep these two saddles in one. Coming close to the entrance, your
soundings being probably:10 fathoms, you will note on the square of the little village
a house, larger and more prominent than the others, with a palm-tree_before it,
standing likewise on the square. Bring that palm-tree in one line with the northern
gable end of the house, or with the gate that leads to the yard, bearing then south
693° west, and let go your anchor. After having cleared the weather reef in 5 or 4
fathoms, there is a good anchorage in 7 or 8 fathoms, the little islet bearing west, and
sometimes vessels anchor much closer in shore, in 22 feet; but some sunken rocks,
called the fishing rocks, may prove of danger in getting the vessel under weigh.
The reefs possess several passages for schooners and smaller vessels. According to
my determination, the village of Baraona is in latitude 18° 12’ 2 N., and longitude
71° 5’ 45” W.

Barburuco.—This place ought to be avoided, although vessels have loaded there
at various times. The British brig, Honor, of London, was entirely lost here in
March, 1852. Atanaval court held in the city of St. Domingo, to examine into
the causes that led to this loss, it was clearly ascertained that Barburuco was not
a proper shipping-place for large vessels, and that masters should be careful in
accepting any charter in which that place is included. here is scarcely sufficient
room for a vessel to lie at anchor, and with the wind blowing on shore, there is not
sufficient opening to tack out; moreover, a very heavy sea sets into the anchorage.
The vessels are anchored in from 12 to 17 fathoms, at a distance of 14 mile from the
shore, with a reef towards the south of the anchorage, and one to the north. The
shore is uninhabited.

0 MALA PASA.

Wiala Pasa.—About 3 miles S.W. of Barburuco is Mala Pasa. It may be easily
recognized by its steep white cliffs. It is less qualified for an anchorage than Bar-
buruco ; the same refers to Paradise and Petit Banane.

Riocito is about 5 miles from Mala Pasa. The water is so deep that the vessel is
obliged to anchor close in, which renders her situation dangerous ; the anchorage is,
moreover, exposed to every wind and all the sweeping of the sea. Vessels have
loaded here, to my knowledge, during fair weather, but it cannot be recommended as
a loading-place. After Riocito follows Punta de Carlos, and—

Petit Trou, or Ajugero Chico.—A long reef, about 3 miles in extent, encom-
passes this anchorage. This barrier has two passages; the windward passage is
about 2 cables’ length in width, with several sunken rocks, one of which has only
102 feet water ; but there is deeper water on both sides ; this entrance is called Reef
Passage. The lower entrance, or sea passage, has 18 to 20 feet, but the room within,
when having once cleared the passage, is so narrow and impeded by sunken rocks,
that no vessel could beat up to the proper anchorage; it is, therefore, only of use for
vessels that stand out to sea. A vessel bound for Petit Trou ought not to draw more
than 102 feet. In approaching the reef, some of the sails should be taken in, to
prevent the vessel going too quick through the water. ‘The time for passing through
the passage ought to be between 11 o’clock in the morning and 1 o’clock in the after-
noon, when the sun is high and shows the rocks under water more clearly. ‘The
pilot stands on the bowsprit, and gives directions how to steer the vessel through the
rocks (some of which are only covered 6 or 7 feet water), to the anchorage. It is,
therefore, requisite to have a clever and quick person at the helm.*

The ground for anchoring is not very good. Captain Sleeboom told me that the
anchor could only hold when lying against a rock, while others have assured me that
they prefer to let the anchor drop in white water—a sign of sandy bottom. There is
scarcely a berth to be found where a vessel with 70 fathoms chain can swing round
without striking a rock; it is, therefore, advisable to moor the craft. The bottom
shallows gradually, and at a distance of 13 mile from the land there are only 3
fathoms water. The breeze blows fresh from the N.E., and the weather is uncertain and
squally. Captain Sleeboom, of the Hamburg brig Withelmine, who was lying there
for some time, informed me that the north-easterly breeze sets in about 2 o’clock in
the morning, and continues to blow from that quarter until half-past 7 or 8 o'clock
P.M., when it veers more to the eastward, and blows from E. by 8. until midnight.
During increasing moon the current sets regularly for 12 hours, with the ebb to the
east, with a velocity of from 2 to 1 knot per hour. The flood rises at Petit Trou
about 8 feet. Mr. Sleeboom observed, that during a decreasing moon the flood sets
uninterruptedly towards the west, and that there is no ebb at all. It runs then with
a velocity of from 1 to 14 knot.

In spite of these drawbacks, vessels load frequently at Petit Trou; and a person
acquainted with the dangers he has to meet will accordingly take the requisite pre-
cautions, if that place should be included in his charter-party. A careful master
will lay-to when he has the slightest mistrust in his pilot, and sound the passage ;
placing, moreover, a buoy on the 103-feet rock, which presents the greatest danger to
a vessel on ‘entering. Ihave already observed, that the sea pessage affords more
water and less danger. It is, nevertheless, necessary to be cautious when standing
out to sea, as there are sunken rocks in the course before the reef is cleared.

Petit Trou is the most western loading-place on the south coast of the Republic
that is at present resorted to.

while entering the passage, and was entirely lost. At the examination of the pilot, it
became evident that either the grossest ignorance or his dishonesty had caused the loss of
that vessel.

OCOA BAY. 31

Directions.—F Rom THE DERROTERO.— Point Nisao, the western point of the
great bay of St. Domingo, bears from the entrance of the harbour nearly $.W. 2 §.,
9 leagues; to clear it in going out from that anchorage, you must steer S. by W. or
§.8.W., and having run on either of these courses a distance of 20 miles, you will be
to the southward of it; or run 6 miles on the first course, and then steer on the second,
From Nisao Point, the coast trends about 8. W. and W.S.W. to Salinas, and is so clear
that you may run along it at less than two miles’ distance. From the Point of Salinas
it bends to the northward, and forms the bay of Ocoa (or Neiva), in which there are
various harbours and anchorages.

OCOA BAY.—“ From Salinas Point (which is the east point of Ocoa Bay),
the coast extends to the N.E. a mile anda half, to Caldera Point, at which a large
bight begins to form, running in two miles to the east ; here every class of vessel
may anchor in the greatest security, sheltered from both sea and wind. The mouth
of this harbour—that is, the space between Caldera Point and the nearest land—is half
a mile wide; but the good and deep channel is reduced to a cable’s length, for a
rocky shoal, at the edge of which are 43 fathoms water, runs out about 3 cables’
length from the coast; and another of the same kind, and with the same depth of
water at its edge, runs out half a cable from Caldera Point. The depth of water in
the channel is from 7 to 8 fathoms, on oazy sand. Although this harbour of Caldera
is large, the ledge of rocks which borders all the coast of the interior of it, reduces it
much; it is also farther reduced by various rocky shoals in the very anchorage ; but
they have good and deep channels between them. As these shoals obstruct it so
much, it is extremely difficult, even with a good knowledge of it, to enter under
sail, and impossible if not acquainted with it. In addition to this, on account of the
narrowness of the channel, you cannot work in; and therefore it is not advisable to
enter into this bight otherwise than by warping or towing, having previously anchored
to the north of Caldera Point, at about a cable’s length from it. To do this, you
must pass within 2 cables’ length from Salinas Point, and run along at that distance
until you are past a small point, formed by the coast between Salinas and Caldera
Point, which is foul, and sends off a rocky shoal with not more than 2 or 3 fathoms
water on it. Having passed that point, which is called Ranceros, you may run along
at less than a cable’s length from the coast, if you intend to anchor in the vicinity of
Caldera Point. If once anchored outside, you must carry out a warp with your
boats, which must also examine and ascertain the proper channel; and, having
warped 2 or 3 cables’ length farther in, you will be in an anchorage very secure and
well sheltered.

“From Caldera Point the coast bends to the N.W. to the Point and River of
Ocoa, whence it returns towards the N.E., and forms a very extensive roadstead,
sheltered from the breezes; but the bank of sand is so steep, that the anchors are
apt to drag and the cables sometimes fail, being damaged by the loose stones at the
bottom. On these accounts, vessels anchor very near the shore, and make fast a
cable to some of the palm-trees that are on the bank, having also a cable laid out for
the changes of wind from the W. and W.N.W., which take place in the night; and
which obliges those who take this anchorage to wait until the breeze comes in,
which is at 10 in the morning. With the breeze it is necessary to leave Ocoa Point,
well prepared to receive the gusts of wind which come off the coast, for they are
very heavy.

“From the Road of Ocoa the coast follows fo the north for the space of 4 miles
and then to the west 8 more, where it begins to bend to the south, to form the west
coast of the great bay. Near where the coast begins to turn to the south, there is a
harbour, named Escondido, or Hidden Harbour, the mouth cf which is more than
half a mile wide. To enter it you must pass near its south point, which is clean, and
the water so deep, that at halfa cable’s length from it there are 54 and 6 fathoms.
The north point sends outa reef about a cable’s length. Half a mile within the
harbour, and in the direction of the middle of its mouth, there is a rocky shoal of 2

32 ALTA VELA.

cables’ length in extent from north to south, and one from east to west, and upon
which a vessel would run, if keeping in the middle of the harbour, and steering N.W.
To avoid it, you must keep within 2 cables’ length of the south shore, and anchor
about half a mile within the harbour, but not farther in with large vessels: for the
depth diminishes that at 2 cables’ length farther in, there are only 15 feet water.
You may also anchor to the north of the shoal, in 5 fathoms, but not farther in than
8 or 4 cables’ length from the mouth. This is an excellent harbour for vessels not
drawing more than 13 feet, which may enter, and be sheltered from all winds.
Frigates and ships of the line remain always exposed to some swell from the §.E.,
and in this case had better be nearer to the south than the north part.

“ This Port Escondido lies about N.W. from Salinas Point.”

In navigating along this coast, allowance should always be made for the currents,
which generally set to the westward. At the entrance of Ocoa Bay they set very
commonly, but feebly, to the northward ; but sometimes a strong indraught sets into
that bay.*

ALTA VELA, or the Little Mount, which is a high rocky islet, lies at the distance
of 2 leagues, S.W. 4 S. from Beata, or Little Mongon Point, the southernmost
extremity of Haiti; it is in latitude 17° 28’ 50”, and longitude 71° 39’ 44”. Alta, Vela
is peaked, but its summit has a rotundity resembling the upper part of a bell. It is
generally seen before any other land in its vicinity, particularly from the southward,
and appears like a dome emerging above a mist or fog; at ashort distance N.W.
from it is a small rock, and a mile and a half farther a shoal of sandy ground
stretches out, on which is a depth of 16 fathoms.

Nearly 2 leagues N.E. 5 N. from Alta Vela lies the south end of Beata Island;
between is a good and very deep channel. The island of Beata is nearly 5 miles in
length from north to south, and about 2 miles broad; it is low, and covered with
bushes. A reef or breaker extends from the N. by E. side of it, towards Cape
Mongon, at the extremity of which is a white shoal, which very much narrows the
passage between Beata and the shore; this reef is called the Bridge. The passage has
only 3 fathoms water in it.

There is anchorage to the westward of Beata, in from 7 to 12 fathoms water, sandy
bottom, with the N.W. end of the island about N.N.E. or N. by E., one mile. To
the eastward of the island the water is deep; there is, however, a shoal stretching off
from its 8.W. point, to which a berth must be given, as there are only 4 fathoms
water at 3 cables to the westward of that point.

Los Frailes or Friars Rocks.—From Beata Point to False Cape, the bearing and
distance are W.N.W. 5 W., 6 leagues, At the distance of 83 miles, 8. + E., from the
latter, and 9} miles, N. by W. 2 W. from Alta Vela, is the centre of a number of rocks
called the Frayles, or Friars; they are above water, and so steep-to that vessels may
sail within a quarter of a mile of them all around.

You may generally see the bottom near all these islands; but the water is very
deep near the coast of Haiti. The coast hereabout is a flat of white and hard rocks,
about 40 feet high, in which appear large holes and breakings, with some prickly
shrubs.

The “Derrotero” says,—“ From Punta Avarena the coast trends about S.W.
10 leagues to Beata Point, or Little Point Mongon, the southernmost point of the
Island of Haiti. To the southward of this point, about 13 league, is the island
Beata, about a league in extent from north to south, and half a league from east to

west. The channel, which is formed by Beata Point and the island, is obstructed a
a white shoal and reef that projects from Beata, and narrows the passage, in whic
is 3 fathoms water.

Two and a half leagues to the southwest of Beata is the islet called Alta Vela,
very clear, and having between a good and deep channel. There cannot, however, be
any motive for preferring a passage between these islands to passing southward of
Alta Vela; and, therefore, vessels bound to the westward from QOcoa Bay, should
steer South or §. 30° W. true. Having run on the first course 225 leagues, they may
steer West, and pass about 24 leagues to the southward of Alta Vela; or steer on the
second course 242 leagues, and then steer West; they will then pass at nearly the
same distance to the southward of it. The first course is, however, to be preferred,
in order to avoid danger in the event of the wind becoming scant, with a westerly
current, which often prevails here with considerable strength.

Cape Lopez ox False Cape, bears north, 5 miles from Point Agujas. The coast
between forms the Bay of Agujas, in which there is good anchorage ; and N. by W.7W.,
8 miles from Point Agujas, is Cape Roxo, having between them the Ensenada Sin
Fondo, or Bottomless Bay; N.W. 4 N., 14 miles from Cape Roxo, is the river Peder-
nales, which constituted the old limit between Hispaniola and Haiti. At this place
there is good anchorage on a bank which extends along shore ; and as there is no risk
in nearing the coast, it is easy to take. At 2 miles from the shore the water is deep.
W.N.W. 2 W., 53 leagues from the entrance of this river, is the promontory, called
Morne Rouge, or Red Hill, which bears also from Point Agujas N.W., distant 13
leagues. From the river Pedernales to Morne Rouge, the coast bends somewhat to
the northward; and at nearly a league to the north-westward of the former is the
Ances 4 Pitres, or Pitre Coves, where there is good anchorage; to the westward of
this 11 miles, and about 3 miles before you come to Morne Rouge, is Sale Trou, or
Foul Hole, where there is good anchorage for vessels drawing less than 16 feet;
larger ships must anchor farther out, where the ground is not so good.

All this part of the coast appears white, being chalky ; and being also clear, it may
be approached with great safety. You may anchor before the plains of Ances a
Pitres, or southward of a small cape, before the mouth of the river Pedernales, which
is easily distinguished. The water is smooth, and you will lie well sheltered in 6 or
8 fathoms, good ground, or nearer the shore in 4 fathoms.

From Morne Rouge the coast first trends to the northward a short distance, then
to the west, W.S.W., and S.W., to Cape Jacquemel, which bears from the former
W.S.W. i W., distant 28 miles. In the intervening space are Ance a Gravois, Fesle,
Les Cayes, and Jacquemel, called also Jacmel. In approaching Morne Rouge from
the westward, it may be known by its white hummocks.

JACQUEMEL, or JACMEL.—N. by E. from Cape Jacquemel, nearly 3 miles,
is Cape Maréchaud; between these lies the bay of Jacquemel, in the upper part of
which there is anchorage for shipping of every description. The locality of J acmel
may be distinguished, at a distance, by the sudden cut off or drop of a hill, seen over
another long hill at the upper part of the harbour. Running in towards that drop
will lead directly to the entrance of the harbour.

The town of Jacquemel stands at the head of the bay, to the eastward of the river
Guache, which disembogues at several mouths in the beach, near which is an old
battery. From Cape Jacquemel the coast lies about N.W. up the bay, as far as the
Redoubt Point, in all which extent no bottom is to be found. When arrived between
the two capes, and nearly in the middle of the bay, you will at the bottom of it
descry a reef of rocks nearly half a mile long, and extending 3 cables’ length from
the shore ; this must be left to starboard in proceeding towards the anchorage, which
is on a bank that borders the coast, and extends about 3 cables’ length from shore,
having from 8 fathoms near the shore to 20 and 30 on its outer edge; therefore it is
necessary to anchor near the shore, otherwise you will find too great a depth of
water. Large ships anchor eastward of a white hummock in the bottom of the bay,
and west of the great reef.

In the other places small vessels may anchor, but in none of them will they be
sheltered.

Light.—A fixed red Light has been established at Jacquemel Bay, which is visible
about 12 miles. The Light-house is placed on the summit of the white cliff in the
bay, in lat. 18° 12’, and long. 72° 34’. The Light is intended to indicate the position
of the bay at night.

Bayenette.—From Cape Jacquemel to Cape Bayenette the bearing and distance
are, W. ; S., 5 leagues; the latter may be known by the white hummocks and cliffs
on its extremity. To the northward of the cape is a bay of the same name, which
is open to the 8.E.; it has a great depth of water, and is entirely clear of shoals.
The anchorage is on the north side, near the shore, but it is not sheltered.

ISLE VACHE.—Variation about 4° easterly. From Cape Bayenette, 14 leagues
W.S.W. 4 W., is the east end of Isle Vache, which thence extends westward
35 leagues, and is nearly 4 miles wide. This island is hilly, and at the distance
of 5 or 6 leagues appears like an assemblage of small islands. ‘The south side
is bold, and along the whole length a reef extends to the distance of a cable’s
length. From the east point a white shoal extends northerly to an islet, called La

Folle, or the Fool’s Rock.

From the Fool’s Rock the shoal extends still farther to the northward, and_ bends
westward at the distance of 4 miles from the island; at the northern part of this reef
are two cays, called Water Cays, having to the southward of them’several rocks and
cays, extending almost to the western point of the island. There is’gaid to be good
anchorage between the Water Cays in 4 or 5 fathoms water, and also to the west-
ward of them in 16 or 17 fathoms. : : F

The western end of the Isle Vache forms the east side of the entrance of the
great bay, called the Bay of Cayes; and from its S.W. point, called Point Diamond.
Point Abacoa bears W.S.W. 3 W., about 43 miles.* In mid-channel there is a depth
of 25 fathoms, thence decreasing towards the island to 10 fathoms, near the edge of
the White Bank, which extends from the west side thereof about a mile, with ‘but
little water on it at that distance.

Light.—Isle Vache.—A fixed red Light has been established. on. the eastern
extremity of Vache Island, which is visible about 12 miles. The Light-is placed at
the south entrance of the bay in lat. 18° 4’ 30", and long. 73° 34’ 30’, and is intended
to indicate the position of the bay at night.

The BAY of AUX CAYES, &c.—Point Abacou is composed of two points or
reefs, which extend two-thirds of a mile to seaward; but you may pass without
danger at the distance of a mile and a half, where the depth is more than 40 fathoms.
The town of Cayes lies 11 miles N. 3 E. from Abacou Point. In sailing towards it
as you approach Point Diamond you will not find the White Ground more than |
three-quarters of a mile from it; and the ground is good in the depth of 6 or 7
fathoms. With Point Diamond bearing E. by N., there are soundings all across the
entrance. A ship may anchor to the west and north-westward of Diamond Point in
6 or 7 fathoms, on mud and sand.

To sail into Cayes, you should run along the west side of Isle Vache, in 6
fathoms, steering about N. by E. so as to have the white hummocks of Cavaillon half
a point or more on your starhoard bow ; you will then pass, on your port side, a large
reef, surrounded by a white shoal, which occupies nearly all the middle of the bay.
So soon as you have brought the town to bear N.W. 2 W., you may anchor if you do
not intend to go into the road.

The road of Cayes lies directly to the southward of the town; to go into it you
must shorten sail at a mile from shore, and wait for a pilot. The channel is not more
than two-thirds of a cable’s length across, and ships drawing more than 13 feet
cannot goin. Those drawing from 18 to 17 feet always anchor at Chateaudun.

Chateaudun Road is to the westward of Cayes Road. In proceeding for it
from the anchorage to the westward of Diamond Point, Isle Vache, you should steer
direct for Torbec, a small town, readily distinguishable in the bottom of the bay,
and when within two miles of the shore, you will discover a little white flag, which is
on a shoal (it is probable that a beacon has been substituted for this flag) ; haul
round at about 4 a cable’s length to the westward of it, leaving it on your starboard.
hand; and when you have brought it to bear 8. 3 E., steer along the coast for the
road, and anchor in 6 or 7 fathoms, muddy bottom. In all this passage, if the
proper channel be kept, there will be found not less than 7 fathoms, and sometimes
from 10 to 16, muddy bottom.

From Cayes the coast trends towards E.N.E. for about a league to the Tapion,
or Hummock of Cavaillon, at the entrance of the bay of that name. About half way
between is the Company’s Island, where you may anchor if you please. As you
advance towards the Tapion of Cavaillon, you must not approach near its 8.E. side,
as a shoal of only 6 feet water, called Le Mouton, lies S.E. $ E. at the distance of
half a mile from the eastern point; there are 8 fathoms water between it and the
coast.

Cavaillon Bay.—This bay is spacious, but its anchorage is of small extent, and
is on the eastern side, opposite a coast covered with mangroves, which may be
approached without fear, as the bottom is clean, with 5 fathoms close to the shore.
The coast on the western side is very steep, and the bottom full of rocks, which must
be carefully avoided. “The anchoring-ground is sheltered from the sea breezes by the
eastern point of an island, between which and the main is a passage into Flamingo
Bay, next described.

36 FLAMINGO BAY.—BAY OF sf. LOUIS.

Flamingo Bay, by some called Flamand Bay, lies nearly a mile to the eastward of
Cavaillon Bay, and extends inwards towards the N.E., having both its entrance and
shores clear and bold. This is the place where ships lie up during the hurricane
months. There is anchorage in every part, and a good careening place.

From Flamingo Bay the coast runs about E. 3 N., 2 miles to the Grande Baie du
Meste, throughout the whole of which the anchorage is good ; but the entrance of the
Baie is so broad, and being open to the southward, that it affords no shelter from
southerly winds. From hence the coast continues its direction to Point Pascal; and
about half way is the Petite Baie du Meste, in which a vessel may anchor, but with-
out shelter, even from the sea breeze. Off the Grand Baie du Meste is a shoal, lying
across the bay like a bar, which extends to opposite the point which is to the west-
ward of the Petit Baie du Meste. On this bank, at some places, there are not more
than from 15 to 18 feet water; but it is very narrow, and between it and the coast

»there is a passage of three-quarters of a mile wide. To the southward it extends
about half a league from the shore. ‘To sail into the Graud Baie, if your ship draws
more than 15 feet, you must keep close to the shore on the western side, and pass in
by Point Paulin, which forms that side of the entrance.

Bay of St. Louis.—The great entrance of this bay.lies between Point Pascal,
which is steep and white, and a little isle called Orange Cay, bearing from the former
E. 3 N., about a mile and one-third. This isle may be seen from the entrance of the
Cayes, 13 miles distant, whence it appears nearly in a line with the southern extre-
mities of the intermediate coast. N:E. 4 N., about two-thirds of a mile from*Pascal
Point, is the Vigie or Old Look Out Point; between which is a cove called the Bay
of Paradise. Being*offthe' Vigie Point, the whole of the Bay of St. Louis will be
in sight. ‘The bay %8’shut*in, on the eastern side, by Cape Bonite, which lies one

In proceeding to the Bay of St. Louis, run along past Points Pascal and Vigie, and
thence along the’western edastcof the bay, in 8 or 10 fathoms water. The anchorage
is to the westward-of the Old Fort, at about a quarter of a mile from the western

the shore at the'Gottom of the bay. The Old Fort stands on an island of rocks.near

Cay, clear.of shoals, unless-very close to it; sg that :you, may.pass either within or

or/Pigeon Cay,'which lies 2 miles E. 3 N. from Moustique Cay, and is known by:a
“white hummock, rather steep, and seen at some distance. Between Pigecn and
Moustique. Cays is a deep passage, through which ships pass into the bay of
Aquin.

A shoal, with only 3 fathoms on-it, extends a mile and a half south from Pigeon
Cay. E.%4N.from the same cay is a small isle, called L’Anguille, or the Eel; and

veach. side. beingja milesand,ac:half in length. Two miles and a quarter N.E. by E.

It extends E. by N., and its south side is bold-to; but the white shoals of L’Anguille
extend to its western point, so as to prevent a passage between it and Pigeon Cay,
for ships drawing more than 12 or 13 feet.

To sail in through the passage between Pigeon Cay and Moustique Cay, steer
about E.N.E., or so as to get in the mid-channel between the shore and the island.
Having doubled Pigeon Cay, you will see La Regala, which is a very low isle of
sand; this you leave on your starboard side, keeping in mid-channel between it and
the shore; then haul up for Aquin Cay, as close as the wind will permit, and anchor

extensive, and runs a considerable way inland, but the water is shallow, and there
are only 3 fathoms at some distance from the shore. The best anchorage is to the

About two-thirds of a mile to the eastward of the Great Cay of Aquin is a white
insulated rock, called Le Diamant, or the Diamond; and at 2 cables’ length to the
eastward of this is the western extremity of Morne Rouge, or Red Hummock; so
that the eastern end of Aquin Cay, the Diamond Rock, and the Point of Morne
Rouge, form two passages into the bay. In the Morne Rouge Passage are 5 and 6
fathoms water ; and in that between the Diamond and Aquin Cay there are 6, 7, and
8 fathoms; the Diamond and both shores are bold-to. :

The Point of Morne Rouge is easily known at a distance by three very high white

hummocks, called the Tapions of Aquin, and, together, form a great promontory,

, under which is anchorage in 10 or 12 fathoms, at a moderate distance from land ; and

this bottom continues as far as Flamand Bay, which is about 4 miles to the eastward
of the point of Morne Rouge.

38 TIBURON BAY.—LEIGHTON ROCK.

Cape Tiburon is a great and very high mountain, which declines gradually to the
sea; it has three points, which at a great distance appear as one. The northernmost
is named Carcase Point, the middle Locos, or Fool’s Point, and the third is the true
Point of Tiburon ; this last is that which, with Burgos Point, forms Tiburon Bay.
From Carcase Point to Tiburon no bottom can be found at 50 fathoms, at 2 cables’
length from the shore; but at that distance from the latter, bottom may be found
with 24 and 30 fathoms.”

TIBURON BAY, as before said, lies between Point Burgos and Cape Tiburon,
and in most parts of it the ground is clear and good, excepting near Point Burgos,
where the bottom is rocky. The anchorage is to the northward of this point, at
three-quarters of a mile from the town, in 7 or 8 fathoms, muddy bottom. Here ships
may lie sheltered from the east, and partly from the southerly winds by Point Burgos,
from which a reef extends to the distance of a cable’s length or more; and small
vessels may anchor so near to the east shore, in 8 or 4 fathoms, as to be sheltered
from these winds by that point. With all other winds the water is smooth, the
landing easy, and excellent water may be readily obtained. You may either land
your casks, and roll them over a narrow neck of land into the river, or fill them in
your boats with buckets.

Leighton Rock (awash) lies in latitude 17° 37’ 40’, and longitude 73° 21’ 31’,
and is 29 miles S.S.E. 3 KE. from the east end of the island Vaches. The position
of this rock was determined by Captain Leighton, of the Samuel, in 1847.

The Loos Shoal, said to have 3 feet upon, has been laid down 10 miles N.W. of the
position of the Leighton Rock ; these may probably be one and the same danger.

Nautical Magazine, June, 1838.

“ A vessel having made Alta Vela, if bound to Jacquemel, should pass on its outside ;
for by going inside you will be likely to meet with calms, particularly during the
summer season. Nevertheless the passage between Alta Vela and Beata, and also
between the Frayles and the mainland is good, there being no dangers about the
Frayles, except those which may be seen; and although the water appears white off
the south end of Beata Island, a vessel may run down within 2 miles of it, or nearer
if necessary.

“The course from Alta Vela to Jacquemel is N.W. 4 W., and the distance 67 miles.
Jacquemel is easily distinguished from seaward, as there is no seaport or town all the
way down from the Alta Vela, and the land has no appearance of cultivation ; the
numerous cliffs near the sea are all of a chalky nature. The port is situate within
Cape Jacquemel, which constitutes the west and S.W. sides of the bay; but it
affords no protection from southerly winds. The town bears from the cape N. by W.,
and is distant about 3 miles. When a vessel is running down and the cape bears
north, then the town will be quite shut in.

“The best mark for distinguishing the port is the termination of a range of moun-
tains which commence inland of Cape Beata, and, rising up gradually to a great
height, extend nearly to Jacquemel. The base of these mountains forms the coast at
least 30 miles to windward of the port; the highest mountain, in particular, termi-
nates abruptly inland, a little to the eastward of the port.

“ Having advanced so far as Cape Jacquemel, you may run in to the middle of the
bay, leaving the cape to the port; but, as a reef, commencing at the eastern shore,
about a mile from the town, extends partly across the bay, full half a mile ina
W.S.W. direction, it will be advisable to pass round its western end, and anchor
inside and abreast of the town. Good anchorage will be found by bringing’ a large

RUNNING DOWN THE SOUTH COAST OF HAITI. 39

house close to the wharf, from N.E. to N.N.E., distant half a mile. Vessels obtain a
pilot after entering the bay, but have to run well in before they wiil come off to you.

“The next bay to Jacquemel is Bayenette, about 15 miles to the westward. This
is sometimes mistaken for Jacquemel; but few vessels visit this port,- excepting
coasters.

“The course from Cape Jacquemel to the Isle Vache is W. by 8. 25%., distant 58
miles. When you are abreast of the east end, you may run down the south side of
the island, giving the S.W. point a berth of 2 of a mile; the ground will be visible,
but there is plenty of water over it.

“ After you have rounded the 8.W. point, haul up to the N.W. point; between
these two points, on the west side of the island, anchorage may be found nearly
everywhere in from 7 to 23 fathoms, not more than a mile from the-shore; but you
should anchor only on the white bottom, for the dark groufd is generally rocky.
However, vessels seldom stop here, unless too late to reach Aux Cayes ‘with daylight.

“ After, passing within a mile and a half of the N.W. point.of Vache, you should
haul up N.:by E., or keep the remarkable white cliffs on Cavaillon about a point on
the starboard bow, standing on until’the town of Aux Cayes bears west. The town
will be‘visible on leaving Vache Island; it lies low, and so does ali the land round
the bay, but the interior is elevated all the way from Point Abacou to the eastward,
as far'as théseye can distinguish, and rather lessening to the E.N. eastward of Aux
Cayes. . The reason for hauling up N. by E. for the white cliffs, is to avoid an exten-
sive shoal that lies in a S:H-direction from Aux Cayes; this is always visible, there
being: two of its patches above water. When the town bears due west, that course
may be run on under easy sail until you get a pilot on board, these will not come far
out to meet you, but will take the vessel to anchorage within the harbour reefs.

“The harbour of Aux Cayes is also exposed to 8. and S.E. gales; and when
caught here during a hurricane you have little chance of escape from being wrecked.
In running across’ from’ La’ Vache to the white cliffs, you will have from 4 to 6
fathoms, with the bottom visible, until you get half way across; the colour then
changes to a light green, you lose sight of the ground, and increase your depth from
7 to 16 fathoms. :

“The anchorage to the eastward of the town is a mixture of clay, sand, and
shells; with the white cliffs north, and the town W. by S., is the best riding for a
vessel not bound in, and is also the best berth for leaving the bay and clearing the
reef already spoken of, lying about 3 miles S.E. of the town.

“ When going out to sea, the pilot will take you clear of the reefs that form the
harbour, after which, you must work to windward and make short tacks, unless you
have the advantage of the land breeze, to sail to the berth above stated. In hauling
over, for the Isle. Vache, care:must be taken that the white cliffs are not brought to
thé eastward‘of N. by E., or the island to the east of S. by E.; and so soon as the
town, comes N.W., you will be clear of the reefs, and may make the best of your way
round ‘Point Abacou, off which point a reef extends about a mile; but this danger is
clearly visible. ,

“The best passage into Aux Cayes is to run along shore after passing Cape Bay-
enette, and whén’the Isle-Vache and thé cays to.the northward become visible, they
are to.be left on the: port side, keeping within a mile of the starboard shore, which,
at this part,-is formed of several, high islands. The.cays to the northward of La
Vache are low and small, with bushes upon them; when abreast of Pascal Point, a
vessel will have Water Cay, which is the northernmost cay on the reef to the north-
ward of La Vache, on her port bow, and, Aux.Cayes nearly west, which may be
steered for until you arrive at the part. already.described. . There is good anchorage
all the way down from Pascal Point-to Aux Cayes, and a vessel may choose her depth
of water by hauling in or off the shore.”

LOOS SHOAL and LEIGHTON ROCK.—These dangers, reported
as lying to the southeast of Cayes Bay, the Loos Shoal in lat. 17° 45’
N., long. 74° 30’ W.; the Leighton Rock in lat. 17° 37’ N., long. 73° 21’
W., have lately been searched for by H. M. 8. Philomel and Plover,
under the orders of Commander Douglas Walker, R. N. (April, 1872).

These vessels spent respectively eighteen and fourteen days sounding
on and near the assigned position of these reported dangers; no bottom
was found near the above position of the Loos Shoal with 450 fathoms
of line, or near the position of the Leighton Rock with 690 fathoms.

Commander Walker reports that both the Loos Shoal and Leighton
Rock are imaginary dangers; and they have, consequently, been removed
from the charts.
