side is iron bound and steep-to. To the southward of the west point is a sandy bay,
where there is good anchorage; but the south side is almost everywhere bordered
with shoals, surrounded by reefs. There is an anchorage opposite to some barracks,
at about one-third from the west end of the island, called La Valleé. The only good
anchorage, which must be for ships not drawing more than 14 or 16 feet water, is
that of Basse Terre, within the reef, about 14 league from the east point. The
passage is narrow, but of easy access. You must keep the weather reefs on board,
leaving them on your starboard side, and steer N.N.W. and north, to double the reefs
that you leave on the port side; do not be afraid of going near to the land, and
anchor so soon as you have brought the lee reef to bear S.W. Large ships may
anchor outside the reef, upon white ground, at about a mile to leeward of Basse
Terre.

To the eastward of Basse Terre, towards Portugal Point, there are several bays or
coves, in which boats or schooners may anchor, but nothing of a larger size.

CHANNEL of TORTUGA.—The channel of Tortuga begins at Point Icague,
and terminates to the westward, nearly abreast of Moustique Bay, being narrowest
at the Careenage Point, where it is not quite 2 leagues wide; farther to the westward
it widens to 23 and 3 leagues. It is very safe, and ships may work up through it,
for the current running up (which it generally does, to the eastward), is of
great advantage to those bound to windward of the island. Stand as close as possible
to both shores, as the wind and current are most favourable near the shore. You may
safely stand within a mile, as all the dangers are visible. There are several bays on
each side, which cause the current to set in various directions ; and sometimes in the
middle of the channel, the stream runs directly contrary to that in-shore. When
there is a lee or westerly current, (which only occurs in summer, during the Souths,)
its strength is so great, that it would be useless to attempt the passage; in that case
vessels should stand 6 or 7 leagues to the northward of Tortuga, and work up very
easily.

From Port Paix the course is nearly straight to Moustique Bay, which is nearly
4 leagues W. by S., the whole space being an iron-bound shore, and very safe.

Moustique Bay, though very small, may shelter a ship in distress. It has a
battery on the eastern side ; so soon as you have passed it, anchor in 12 or 15 fathoms,
a cable and a half from shore. The ground is uneven and rocky in some parts of the
bay, but in other parts it is good. Be careful not to let go your anchor before you
have sounded, as at the entrance of the bay there is no ground at 40 fathoms; you
Toust at least bring the battery to bear N.N.E. A shoal runs into the bay a cable’s
length from the west point.

Port-a-l’Ecu is nearly 5 miles to the westward of Moustique, and the shore
between is rocky, with deep water close to it. The anchorage is better here, but not
so easy of access for large ships as Moustique Bay, on account of a reef and a
shoal, with only 3 fathoms water, which extend two cables’ length off the east point,
and which rounds the point to the inside of the bay. To sail in here, give the shoal
off the east point a small berth on your port hand; then haul your wind, ranging
along the eastern reef, and anchor nearly in the middle of the bay, in from 8 to 10
fathoms, oazy bottom, with a house at the bottom of the bay, bearing S. by W. 4 W.
You may advance towards the house to the depth of 4 fathoms. The south-west
fuk is steep-to and safe, so that you may stand close into the white ground near the
shore.

Jean Rabel.—From the Port-d-l’Ecu the coast trends west, about 6 miles to
the anchorage of Jean Rabel. It is good, safe, and of easy access, Large ships
anchor at about 2 cables’ length from the eastern breakers, in a depth of 16 fathoms,
taking care not to shut in the two points on the east coast. You. may go‘so'far in
as the depth of 8 fathoms; but is is not safe, because the water shoalens suddenly,
and the ground is not so clean, The ground holds well, and the only winds to
fear are from North to N.W.

Should you be to the north-westward of Jean Rabel, at a short league’s distance

from the land, and have half the Island of Tortuga open of the point, you will find
60 fathoms water, oazy ground; and a little farther out 80 fathoms.

From Jean Rabel, the coast forms a bight or bay as far as the peninsula of St.
Nicholas, the western point of which, called the Mole Point, lies S.W. by W. 3 W.,
13 miles from it. All the shore between is rocky, and does not afford any shelter.
At all times the currents here are very perceptible near the shore, and generally set
on it; at 2 leagues off they are less so, and generally set north-eastward. On ap-
proaching the peninsula, they become much stronger, and commonly set northward.

ST. NICHOLAS MOLE or HARBOUR.—This is a spacious harbour, being
nearly a mile in breadth at its entrance, whence it extends eastward 13 mile to the
town, and thence one mile northward; it becomes narrower as you approach the
town, where it is about three-eighths of a mile in width. The west part of the
peninsula forms the north point of the entrance, and as soon as you have doubled
this cape you will perceive the town. You may stand quite close to cither shore ; but
it is advisable to allow on the south side more room for tacking than on the
north side, because there is no anchoring ground, which you have on the north side,
though very near the shore. The anchorage is before the town, and under the
barracks, in 15 or 16 fathoms, sandy bottom. In going in you must be prepared
against the puffs of baffling squalls, which come down from the land, sometimes with
such violence as to endanger the masts.

Ships may lie in the Inner Mole or north part of the harbour, sheltered from every
wind. There isa river which runs through the town, where you get water, and
places where a ship may be careened by the shore. When it blows hard, working up
to the anchorage is attended with some difficulty, and if you are not quick at anchor-
ing, you will soon drive off from 6 to 30 or 35 fathoms.

The sea breeze is from N.E. by N.; it comes on at 8 in the morning, and blows
very strong until 10 or 11 at night. The land breeze comes on moderately at 8.E.,
continues till 6 in the morning, then dies away, and it remains calm till 8. Ships
bound to the northward, generally get under weigh at 8 or 10 at night, when the sea
breeze begins to slacken, but early enough to run out with before it ceases. Lat. of
Fort St. George 19° 49’ 30’, and long. 73° 22’ 34”,

DrIREcTIONS FOR SHIPS BOUND TO CAPE HAITIEN FROM THE WESTWARD.—
It has been before remarked that the current sets northward round Cape St.
Nicholas, and afterwards, at the distance of 2 leagues from the coast, changes to a
north-easterly direction. Ships working to windward from Cape St. Nicholas ought
not to approach nearer the shore than 2 leagues, until having passed Little Jean
Rabel Point; then, if intending working through Tortuga Channel, may stand
into a discretionary distance, and attend to the directions already given for that
channel; but, if they have to work outside to the northward of Tortuga, they should
give the N.E. part of that island a good berth; and after getting to windward of
the east end of the island, if the weather be clear, will descry Cape Haitien.

The land to the westward of Port Paix juts to the northward in a low point, and
rises gradually towards the south to a high mountain, with a sugar-loaf top, and
then it falls lower on the same side toa large valley, whence it rises quickly to a
considerable high mountain, which is smooth at the top, and is the highest land in
this part of Haiti; it bears about S.E. 3 S. from the east end of Tortuga. The next
high land to the southward of this is of a sugar-loaf form, with a smaller one to the
south of it, which are about 10 or 12 miles up the country. The next high land or
point, which is seen by the water side, is Cape Haitien, making at first like a saddle,
but on a nearer approach, a low point will appear, which shuts from the eastward
the eastern part of the saddle land; this low land is Point Picolet, or the extremity
of the cape land, already described. -

THE WESTERN COAST OF HAITI, OR ST. DOMINGO.

FROM CAPE ST. NICHOLAS TO CAPE TIBURON.

Leaving the harbour of St. Nicholas Mole, you will see to the southward the Cape
St. Nicholas, which forms its entrance; and farther to the southward Point du Cap 4
Foux, or Fool’s Cape; this lies at the western extremity of a large point, at the
distance of 44 miles from Cape St. Nicholas. The coast then trends 8.S. eastward,
about 24 leagues more, to the Point a la Perle, or Pearl Point.

Fool’s Cape is easily known by a small rock which lies close to its foot; the shore
is steep, without any shelter. A calm generally prevails here. The currents in-shore
set to the northward, and at 2 leagues off they set to the West and W.S.W.

PLATFORM.—From Pearl Point the coast rounds to the S.E. and E.S. east-
ward, to the Point of the Platform, which is distant from it about 3 leagues. This
point is easily distinguished, as well by its flat form as by its being the southernmost
point of this part of the island. The anchorage is before a small sandy cove, at the
bottom of which are some houses. You anchor near the shore in 8, 9, or 10 fathoms,
on weedy bottom, with the southernmost point bearing about E. by S., the western-
most point in sight W.N.W., and the watering place N.N.E. The bank is very
steep, and in a greater depth than 9 fathoms, the bottom is rocky ; but the nearer the
shore the clearer the bottom. Fresh water may be obtained after rains, but there is
nove to be had at other times.

From the Platform Point to Point la Pierre, on the north side of the entrance
of Gonaives Bay, the bearing and distance are, about E.S.E. 2 E., 12 leagues.
The point is rather high and steep, and the coast between trenches in some-
what to the northward, and goes rounding to Port 4 Piment, or Pimento Harbour,
whence it trends gradually more to the southward as far as Point la Pierre. All this
coast is safe and bold, and may be approached very near; there is anchorage, even for
large ships at Henne Bay, and at Port Piment, but it ought to be used only in case
of necessity. During the hurricane months there are gales of wind almost every
night, coming from the §.E., some of which are violent ; and unless you have business
on this part of the coast, it is best to stand off 2 or 3 leagues, so that you may, with
any wind, keep to the westward.

The BAY of GONAIVES.—The Bay of Gonaives is very large and fine, the
anchorage excellent, and the entrance very easy. You range along by the north
shore at the distance of 13 or 2 miles, steering about East, and when in, anchor
in from 6 to 10 fathoms water. You will find, from the entrance under Gonaives
Point, which is low, and one mile to the eastward of Point la Pierre, 15 and 12
fathoms; and a decreasing depth as you advance into the bay. After you have
doubled Gonaives Point, leaving it on the port hand, you will see Fort Castries on
the top of a little hill, which do not approach too near, as there is a cay lying
about a mile south of the point; there is also a reef extending north eastward
from the south point of the bay, a quarter of a mile, with 6 fathoms of water close to
He s The best anchorage is with Fort Castries, bearing from N. to N.N.W. in 6 or 6
athoms.

From Point la Pierre to Cape St. Mark the distance is about 8 leagues, in a direc-
tion south a little westerly, which is also the direction of the coast. About 13 league
to the southward of Gonaives is Artibonite Point, and 14 league farther south,
Artibonite River. In sailing from Gonaives along shore, keep your lead going,
and as you approach near to Artibonite River, you will find the water shoalen to
about 4 fathoms, and then deepen again to 7 or 8 fathoms. The land on the coast

is low, all the way from Gonaives to about a mile to the southward of Artibonite
River, but there is very high land within it; at the south end of the low land, it
rises to a hummock, and the coast projects a little to the westward, forming a point,
which is the north extremity of St, Mark’s Bay, and is called Point du Morne au
Diable, or Devil’s Hummock Point. This is a good mark by which to know Artibo-
nite River.

ST. MARK BAY.

There is anchorage all along this coast for small vessels; but to anchor off Arti-
bonite River, bring 5 or 6 small houses, which will be seen by the waterside to the
northward of its entrance, to bear E.S.E., distant 2 miles, and the mouth of the river
S.E.; with these bearings you will be on a bank, and may anchor in from 7
to 20 fathoms water. Within this bank the water is very deep, and there are from
50 to 80 or 90 fathoms at less than halfa mile from shore; from that depth you
suddenly fall into 6 or 5 fathoms. Artibonite River ebbs almost dry at low water,
and, therefore, is not a place of great note; it has no town, but there are some
plantations 5 or 6 miles up from the entrance. Water may be procured here, but no
wood.

ST. MARK BAY.—The opening of the bay of St. Mark is to the southward of the
Devil’s Hummock Point, between it and Cape St. Mark ; it extends a league within,
and the water is of great depth. Ships anchor in the bottom of the bay under the
town, in from 15 to 18 fathoms water; small vessels may anchor in a less depth,
but they will be close inshore. Cape St. Mark is high, and of a round form ; the
mount which forms it is a mile back from the sea side, and may be seen at a great
distance.

Platform Point to the north, the coast from Gonaives to Cape St. Mark to the
east, and the north coast of Gonaive Island to the south, form the Gulf of Gonaives.
Cape St. Mark on the north, and the N.E. point of Gonaive Island on the south side,
form the entrance of St. Mark’s Channel; they lie nearly north and south, distant
4% leagues.

From the Point of St. Mark, the Coast of Haiti runs about S.E. % 8. for the
space of 63 leagues to the Punta de Vasos, and from thence S.E. by E. 4 E.
another 5 leagues, and then another 8 to the southward to Port au Prince. The
coast from St. Mark to Port au Prince is generally clean and bold, and may be
run along at the distance of a mile, in 10, 16, and 20 fathoms water; in doing which,
you will first see the Magazine of Montrovi, and afterwards the villages Arcahais and
Boucassin, and finally the city of Port au Prince. About half way between St.
Mark’s Point and Port au Prince, and a little less than a league W.S.W. from a low
point on the coast, are three small islets, named the Arcadins, separated by channels
about half a mile in breadth. They are not much to be feared, as there are 6 and 5
fathoms water near them on every side; and in the channel between them and the
coast there are not more tham 20 fathoms, nor less than 7.

The Arcadins are three small bushy islets, and cover a space of about a mile, in a
north and south direction, and the nearest being about 33 miles from the shore.
They may be safely approached by the lead on all sides, and are on the east side
bold and steep-to, with from 20 to 6 fathoms water between them and the main, but
the soundings are variable; adjacent to them, the bottom is hard, but becomes soft
and muddy as the shore is approached. A coral bank extends N.N.W. about a cable
from the smallest islet. ‘There is a shallow bank of 3 fathoms, at the distance of 3
miles cast alittle southerly from the southern islet, and about 2 miles from the
coast. Between it and the islets there are from 6 to 18 fathoms, and between it and
the shore 7 and 14 fathoms.

The best anchorage will be found in 11 or 12 fathoms water, with the smallest
islets bearing S.W. by W., distant about a mile. Vessels bound to Port au Prince
would find this a good place to anchor for the night, if in the neighbourhood, with
sunset coming on and a land breeze.

To the E.S.E. from the village of Boucassin, and very near the coast, is an islet

im

PORT AU PRINCE. 63

named Carnero or Sheep Cay, the passage between which and the coast should never
be attempted; but close to it on the outside, the coast is clear, and the water deep.
About 2 leagues to the southward of this island is the roadstead of Foso; this to the
N.E. and Lamentin Point to the S. W. form the entrance of the bay of Port au Prince.
To the westward of this roadstead, as far as the meridian of Lamentin Point, is a
cluster of islets, of which the easternmost is distant about 2 miles from Foso Road-
stead, and the southernmost three miles from Lamentin Point. Besides these, there
are two others, which lie nearly in the direction of the two points of the bay, distant
4 miles from Foso Roadstead, and 2 miles from Lamentin Point.

PORT au PRINCE.—In the bottom of the bay of Port au Prince the coast is
very foul, and has a group of islets, within which is the inner anchorage, and to take
this a pilot is indispensable; but without these, is the anchorage called the Great
Road, which may be entered without a pilot.

Light.—A fixed light is exhibited from a tower on Lamentin Point, at 80 feet
above the sea, and visible 9 miles. There is a fixed light on a mast of a pontoon
close to the islet, and may be mistaken for the light on the point.

Those bound to Port au Prince from the N.W., after having seen St. Mark’s Point,
may shape their course either to pass between the Arcadins and the coast, or between
them and the Island Gonaive. The first route seems preferable; not only because
you will avoid the foul grounds on the S.E. side of Gonaive ; but it is also to be
observed, that the wind in the channel is generally from the N.E., therefore the
nearer you pass to the shore of Haiti, the more free you will run to the anchorage
of the port. Moreover, almost every afternoon in the rainy season, there are torna-
does in the channel, which compel vessels to lie to, and to shift on different tacks,
that they may not fall upon the reefs of Gonaive. If you can foresee the approach
of the gale, it will be best to seek an anchorage near Arcahais Point, and there ride
it out.

When past the Arcadins, you must steer §.8.E., somewhat easterly, to get near
Lamentin Point; and if caught by night to the eastward of this point, you may
anchor. From Point Lamentin to the anchorage of Port au Prince, it is 4 miles; and
to take it you must steer towards the city, and anchor about half a mile outside the
islets in 10 to 15 fathoms.

From Pearl Point to the entrance of St. Mark’s Channel, midway between Cape
St. Mark and the Island of Gonaive, the course and distance are 8.E. + S., 16 leagues.
This will bring you to the westward of Cape St. Mark, for which you may steer, or
continue the same course .7 leagues farther, which will lead clear, but abreast of
the islets or cays, called the Arcadins. But if it should be night, after having run
4 or 5 leagues, steer S.8.E. 3 E., in order to pass in mid-channel between the
Arcadins and the east point of Gonaive Island; and when you have run 8 or 4 leagues
on this course, steer S.E. by E. § E., 4 or 5 leagues, to make Cape Lamentin, which
is on the south side. You must range this coast within a short distance, which you
may do without fear, to avoid the shoals of the sandy cay, which lie a short league
northward of the point. Should you pass this point in the night, you would do right
after you have run a mile, or a mile and a half, to anchor; this you may do in from
12 to 18 fathoms water, good ground, and the water always smooth.

Should you, on account of adverse winds, be obliged to turn in the channel of St.
Mark, you must not stand so near to the Gonaive as to the Haitien side; the latter
being safe, may be approached anywhere to the distance of half a league.

The Arcadins are not much to be feared; a shoal stretches out from them a mile, or
a mile and a half at most, with 5 or 6 fathoms on it; on the edge of the west and
8.W. sides, you will have from 12 to 15 fathoms, corally ground.

During the hurricane months, in this part, there are almost every night violent
storms. Should you be caught in a gale, the best method will be to lie to, sometimes
on one tack, and then on the other, as well to avoid the force of the wind, as the
shoals of the Little Gonaive. If you can foresee the gale, it will be better to get
an anchorage on the Haitien side, near Arcapie Point, or on the north of Leogane, to

the S.E. of the Little Goinave, as there are soundings from the white shoals of Little
Gonaive across to Leogane.

There is a channel between the Arcadins and Haiti 2 miles in breadth, having in
the middle of it not less than 7 fathoms:; but the depth decreases as you approach the
Arcadins, on the coast side. Towards the Arcadins you will have 6 or 8 fathoms
water, corally ground; at the same distance from the Haitien shore there is a like
depth, but with a muddy bottom.

Port au Prince was surveyed by Commander (now Captain) R. Owen, in H.M.S.
Blossom, in which survey the leading mark up to the town is shown to be the Fort
Alexander, situate on the hill to the east of the town, open to the southward of
Fort Isle, on the bearing of EK. by 8.48. The anchorage in the outer road to be a
little more than 3 mile from Fort Isle, or more over toward the southern shore,
according to the depth of water.

DIRECTIONS FOR Port AU PRINCE, BY Mr. GEORGE PEACOCK, of H.M.S. Hyacinth.
“ Vessels bound to Port au Prince, should endeavour to get hold of the northern
shore of the bay; for with the land and sea breezes they will be enabled to get up
to Port St. Mark, and from thence to Petit Lamentin, much more readily than by
beating up along the south side of Gonaive. In the latter channel a strong lee
current runs.

Having advanced to Cape St. Mark (to the northward of the Arcadins, a point
resembling a small low island), a S.E. course seven leagues will carry them to the
Arcadins, which are low cays, having good anchorage inside; pass about two miles
from them, or with the land wind they may pass inside, and steer 8.E. 4 E., 6 leagues
for Point Lamentin, which may be easily known, from its having a fine green patch
of land immediately over it. Having proceeded 12 or 14 miles, four cays will be
seen on the port hand; give them a birth of at least four miles, for a coral reef
extends from them to the southward upwards of three miles, nearly level with the
water, and steep-to. H.M.S. Hyacinth grounded on its outer extremity on the
evening of the 25th of August, 1831, having shoaled suddenly from 15 to 9 and 5
fathoms, and the helm being put a-port, before her head altered two points, she
struck with 9 feet under her bows; by keeping Lamentin Point to the eastward of
§.E. you will be sure to avoid it. You may anchor off this point in 13 fathoms,
bringing it to bear S.W., or W.S.W.; half a mile off from hence, or an E. by S.
course 44 miles, will take you to the outer anchorage, where the bottom is excellent
in 10 fathoms.

Outer Fort, or Fort Isle bearing east, Point Lamentin west, and Outer Cay N.W.
by N., the town of Port au Prince will be open between the cays. In turning up to
the anchorage, there are two dangerous reefs to be avoided on the port hand; but as
they always show themselves by the colour of the water, and are steep-to, you
may oe Sl them without fear. Latitude of the anchorage 18° 33’ 30’, longi-
tude 72° 17’ 17” ;

GONAIVE ISLAND lies E.S.E. and W.N.W., is 104 leagues in length; its
breadth, which is very regular, is nearly 24 leagues. The N.E. point, called Galet
Point, is low, and bordered with a reef, which runs out half a league eastward from
it, and extends along shore to the southward, at the same distance from the land,
to opposite the place called Trou a l’Eau, or Water Hole; having within it a white
ground, with a depth of 4 to 6 fathoms water.

Vessels of 9 and 10 feet draught, may sail within this reef; to do which, in coming
from the eastward, they must take a channel which is opposite a fisherman’s hut ;
there are also several other channels, which are easily known by the non-appearance
of white ground. At about 90 fathoms within the reef, you may range along the
coast as far as Anse 4 Galet, or Galet Cove; if the wind should fail, you may anchor
anywhere, but the best places are Piron Cove, Constantion’s Hole, and Galet Cove,
particularly the latter, which is very convenient, the ground being good, and being
sheltered by the reefs from the swell of the sea,

MIRAGOANE. 65

The Eastern Point of Gonaive is high and steep, and Little Gonaive lies off this
point; the former has no white shoals off it, but the white grounds off the latter
are very dangerous. These shoals extend from the S.E. point of Gonaive along
by, and within a quarter of a league of Little Gonaive, but not much to the northward
of the east point of it; they project a league or more to the eastward. South-east of
Little Gonaive is another white shoal, separate from the former about half a
mile ; its outward extremity is 2 leagues from the island, but it is not dangerous, for
although the bottom appears white, there are on it from 7 to 12 fathoms. A large
ship ought not to go within 4 miles of Little Gonaive ; but small vessels, drawing 8
or 9 feet, may find good anchorage on the west side of it, which may be best entered
from the southward.

The currents about here run very strong and irregular; but generally to the
N.N.E. and between the two Gonaives.

The western part of the island is an iron-bound coast, and may be approached to a
moderate distance; but from the S.W. point to Point a Retoures, are several small
detached reefs, almost even with the water. There is anchorage for small vessels in
that part, on a spot called Les Baleines, or the Whales ; but should not be used unless
well acquainted with. ‘he only place where a large ship can anchor, is to the N.W.
of Point Fantasque, the south point of the island, in a bay called Baie du Pare, or
Park Bay ; but several detached reefs lying about here, render its entrance dangerous.

Schooners and other small craft may anchor at the following places on the north
coast of the island, namely L’ Islet a Mare, Grand Lagoon, and Bahama Channel,
where they are equally well sheltered. The other parts of it are bordered with reefg
also, but they are very near the shore.

THE COAST.—Port av PRINCE To THE WESTWARD.—On leaving Port au
Prince, and bound to Little Goave, you may run along the coast at the distance
of one or two miles, as far as Point Leogane, all the shore being bold and safe.
From Point Lamentine to Leogane Point there is no anchorage ; but you will find
good ground for anchoring between the latter point and the anchorage off the town
of Leogane.

Having passed Leogane, you must steer for the Tapion, or hummock of Little
Goave, and run in the bay, leaving on your port hand a little island that lies off
the coast to the northward of the town, and to the W.S.W. of which you may
anchor. As some charts exhibit a shoal in the middle of the entrance, and some rocks
off Point Antoine, on the west side, it is necessary to give attention to them, when
sailing in or out.

Petit Goave is 9} leagues from Port au Prince, but as you are obliged to double
Point Leogane, the run is longer.

MIRAGOANE.—From the hummock of Little Goave to the Tapion du Trou
Chouchoux, or hummock of Miragoane, the coast runs W. 2 N., 83 miles, and W.S.W.
3 W., 7 miles to the Careening Island of Miragoane Bay. To anchor at Miragoane,
go within a mile of the Careening Island, when you will perceive a small town at
the foot of a mountain, and some mangrove islands to the westward. Keep in mid-
channel between the first island and the shore where the town is situate; leave
the island on the starboard side, and anchor within, in from 8 to 18 fathoms water,
on sandy bottom. This anchorage ought not to be taken without a pilot ; the channel
being not more than a cable’s length wide; and you must anchor as soon as you are
within.

From Miragoane Careening Island the coast bends in, and forms the bay of that
name. It is shut in on the north by Frigate Island, off which stretches a large white
shoal half a league to the eastward, and nearly north to the anchorage of Miragoane ;
which obliges you, when going in or out, to keep the island shore close aboard, and
makes it dangerous to those who are not acquainted. From this place the coast
runs west as far as the village of Rochelois, which is situate at the foot of a large
hummock.

66 BARADAIRES BAY.

ROCHELOIS REEF.—N. 3 E., 34 leagues from the village, lies the centre of
the reef of Rochelois, part of which is above water. This reef lies in the channel
which separates the south coast of Gonaive from that of Haiti, and has been fatal
to many ships; its true situation having never been well ascertained until it was
surveyed by M. De Lieude de Sepmanville in 1788. He anchored within a cable’s
length of the rocks, which are above water, and landed on the rocks, where he took
four observations of latitude, as well as the bearing of all the objects in sight; and,
having measured the whole extent of the shoal, he found it to be 3,155 toises (not
quite 4 English statute miles) in length from east to west, and 2,000 toises (nearly
21 English statute miles) in breadth from north to south,

These dry rocks are called Pirogues, and lie near the middle of the reef; their
extent is 125 toises; they are quite uncovered at low water, but three heads only are
seen at high water ; their latitude, deduced from the four observations, is 18° 37’ 20”.
He also found two other shoals of very small extent, which are very dangerous, since
they have only 2 fathoms water on them. They lie to the N.W. of the dry rocks ;
one at 300 toises distance, aud the other at 800. There is also a shallow spot, said to
lie off the south side, at about three-quarters of a mile to the S.W. of the dry rocks ;
and it is supposed that there are other dangers near it; but, as he was only four days
on the survey, he had not time to make himself sure of it. Prudence requires that
large ships should avoid this shoal entirely ; there is more room for tacking on the
north side of it than there is on the south side. You must not approach Gonaive
nearer than a mile, if you pass to the northward of it; whereas, in passing to the
southward, you may range along the Haitien coast, which is clear and safe. About
a league to the eastward of the Rochelois breakers, the bottom is rocky, but hardly
visible, having from 6 to 8 fathoms water, and therefore not dangerous.

BARADAIRES BAY.—From the village of Rochelois to the entrance of the
bay of Baradaires the coast lies W. 7 N., 5 leagues. This bay is formed towards the
S.E. by Roitelets, Point, and to the N.W. by the eastern extremity of the Bec du
Marsoin, or the Porpoise Snout; these points bear from each other nearly N.W. and
S.E., about 42 miles. Contiguous to the east coast of the bay there is an island with
several islets, from which extend a reef and shallow that almost join the western
coast, leaving a pass or channel of only 5 or 6 cables’ length in breadth.

To sail into this bay, keep one-third nearer to the Porpoise Snout than to the other
side, and run along by the peninsula of the Snout until you get in from 10 to 8
fathoms, where you may anchor. There isa good depth of water in the middle of
the bay, which is of great extent; but there are several weedy shoals, which are
dangerous.

The CAYMITES.—The north extremity of the Porpoise Snout, and the north
port of Grand Caymite Island, bearing nearly W.N.W. and E.S.E., are distant 4
leagues.

The coast west of the peninsula of the Snout bends in to the southward, and forms
a bight of 5 miles; then rounding out a little, it rans W.N.W. 3 W.., 9 leagues, as far
as Jeremie. This bight and Grand Caymite Island form a large bay, called Caymite
Bay, which affords very good anchorage for all sorts of vessels. You may sail in
without a pilot, and anchor under the island in what depth you choose. You may
also anchor in Flamand’s Bay, near the peninsula, ranging along the peninsula side;
and when you get opposite a sandy beach, anchor in any depth that suits you.

The Bay of Caymites presents several fine anchorages, very easy of access, with the
assistance of the lead alone; but observe that there is not a good passage between the
Great Caymite and the shore; and you will not find more than 13 feet water upon
the white shoals of the Little Caymite, or off Foucard Islet ; there are besides several
coral rocks within 2 or 8 feet of the surface of the water, so that no vessels but very
small ones ever attempt it without a pilot. These white shoals extend 3 leagues
W.S.W. from the Great Caymite.

Salee (Salt River Point), which is a league and a half W.N.W. of Point Jeremie,
the bearing and distance are west, 94 leagues; this Salt River Point is the northern-
most point westward from Port au Prince. Under Point Jeremie is the village of
that name; the anchorage is very small, and not proper for large ships; schooners
and small vessels may anchor within the reef, but no ship whose draught exceeds 12
or 18 feet should ever anchor here, except in case of necessity, as for such there is no
shelter. In short, it is a bad anchorage, which must be avoided during the Norths.

From Salt River Point, or Cape Rosa, to Cape Dame Maria, or Donna Maria, the
coast runs W.S.W., 13 miles.

All this shore is safe and bold-to within a quarter of a league; but it presents no
shelter, though, in case of necessity, you may anchor in Clare Bay, which is a league
and a quarter from Salt River. ‘This bay, or rather cove, is so very small, that two
ships of 100 feet long could not swing clear of each other; it can only serve as a
shelter for very small vessels, and is easily discovered by keeping along shore.

CAPE DAME MARIA, or DONNA MARIA.—So soon as you discover Cape
Donna Maria by the false cape of that name, and are half a league distant from it,
you will get ground in from 18 to 15 fathoms water, and may run along by it at the
distance of a quarter of a league, in from 12 to 8 fathoms, weedy bottom.

To enter the Bay of Donna Maria, keep about half a mile off, but not less, in order
to avoid a reef, which spits off a cable and a half from the point westward. Preserve
the same distance of haif a mile from the coast, until past the cape to the southward
of Cape Donna Maria, named the False Cape, which is also foul. Then you may
haul to the wind, and steer S.E., keeping the lead going, and anchor W.N.W. of a
large white tapion, or hummock, on which stands a battery, and within a musket-shot
of which you will find 5 fathoms. There.is anchorage all over this bay; at a mile
from the shore there are from 4 to 6 fathoms, and at 2 miles from 6 to 10 fathoms.
Here you are sheltered from the winds between the north and south, passing by the
east; notwithstanding which, ships that lie in 8 or 10 fathoms jwill feel the swell
when there is a fresh breeze without.

From Cape Donna Maria the coast runs S. by W., 16 miles, to Point des Trois, or
Irish Point, and forms in that distance several bays and coves, where vessels may
anchor. In general, along this coast, a frigate may run in by her lead, and anchor
in any part, there being no shoals nor any danger under water, the depth gradually
decreasing towards the shore.

To the S. by W. of Cape Donna Maria, 8 miles distant, and at about half a league
off Point Ministre, or Minister Point, are some rocks, called Les Baleines, or the
Whales; these rocks are above water, and surrounded with a white shoal, which
extends about half a cable’s length from them, having 4 fathoms water on it. A
ship may sail between them and the shore, and carry 6 fathoms in mid-channel; you
may go as close as you please to them on the outside ; the sea always breaks on them.

One league anda half farther to the southward lies the Isle of Pierre Joseph,
where a convoy might anchor. The anchorage is very good and easy; large ships
anchor to the 8. W. of the isle.

All along this west part of the coast you will find ground at 2 leagues from shore,
the depth gradually increasing with the distance from land; so that, in general, 4 or
5 fathoms will be found at one mile distance, 10 or 12 at 2 miles, and regularly from
15 to 17 at 3 miles; after getting 30 fathoms, you will suddenly lose soundings.

Point des Irois, or Irish Point, is the westernmost point of Haiti; it is not very
high, though remarkable for a small hummock on its extremity, which appears
detached from the coast and makes like an island. This point forms the north part
of the Bay des Irois, or Irish Bay. You may pass very close to the land on the north
side of the bay, there being from 18 to 9 fathoms close to the shore. The anchorage
is to the N.W. of a black rock, which is seen a little way to the south-westward of
the town, in from 9 to 10 fathoms water, shelly ground.. You may anchor likewise

68 CAPE TIBURON.

to the southward of the rocky islet N.N.W. of a small hummock, towards the middle
of the bay, in 8 or 9 fathoms, sand and mud.

This bay is exposed to southerly winds, which always send in a great sea; and the
debarcadier, or landing-place, is consequently a bad one. It is situate in the eddy of
the currents, which set to the northward on the west side, and to the S.H. on the east
coast. Besides, the sea in the offing is alternately agitated with violence by the N.E.
and east breezes which prevail on the west coast, and by the 8.E. winds which blow _
on the south coast. Irish Bay is terminated to the south by Cape Carcasse, which,
with False or Fool’s Cape, forms a large roundish point, which ends at Cape Tiburon.

CAPE TIBURON.—The above three capes, seen at a distance, form but one,
which is called Cape Tiburon, and is very easily known by its form and great height ;
its top is rounded like the back of a basket, called a Dosser, and declines gradually
down towards the sea.

Cape Tiburon, properly speaking, is 7 miles 8.E. by S. from Point Des Irois, and
forms the entrance of Tiburon Bay, which is to the eastward of it. You will get no
ground with 50 fathoms of line at 2 cables’ length from the coast, between Cape
Carcasse and to very near Cape Tiburon ; but off the latter, at that distance, you will
have from 24 to 80 fathoms, and at a little farther out, quickly lose soundings.

Tiburon Bay has already been described. See page 38.

DIRECTIONS FOR MAKING THE ISLAND OF HAITI, AND FOR
NAVIGATING ON ITS COASTS.

From the Derrotero.— Ships from Europe, bound to the Island of Haiti, must be
guided in their course according to circumstances. If a vessel is bound to a port
on the north coast, she may, as before directed (page 50), get into the latitude of
Cape Cabron, without making any land to windward, and thus ensure a landfall to
windward of her port of destination. Having made Cape Cabron, vo more is
necessary than to follow the coast, at a proper distance from the most projecting
capes, and without going into the bays until approaching your destined port, when
you may keep so near to the coast (to windward of it) as to make sure not to pass it.

If bound to the south coast, it is advisable to make the Island of St. Bartholomew,
or St. Martin; and passing between, or to the southward of them, run down by the
south of Porto Rico, to make the Island of Saona, if you are bound to the Harbour
of St. Domingo or to Ocoa Bay ; but if not, you may follow a course to make Beata
and Alta Vela; and passing to the south of them, so direct your course as to approach
the coast to windward of your destined port sufficiently far as to be certain of not
overrunning it.

Those bound direct for harbours on the west end of the island ought to make the
north side in the rainy season, and the south side in the dry season ; thus they free
themselves from the dangers and anxieties which the Souths cause in the first
instance, and which the Norths cause in the second ; for it is well known to every
seaman, that an off-shore wind is not dangerous; and it permits a continuation of
your voyage; for though it may blow very hard, it can raise no sea, and you can
carry sail accordingly.

In navigating from leeward to windward, this island affords the great advantage
of land breezes. It is well known that the nearer you are to the land, the fresher
the land breezes are, and, therefore, the farther you can run with them; thus, in this
case, you should keep as near along shore as you can, which is very easy ; and keep-
ing in mind the particular description of the coast, you need not fear danger.

If it be a matter of indifference to you whether you beat up on the south or the
north side, you ought to choose the first in the season of the Norths, and the second

DIRECTIONS FOR SAILING TO THE ISLAND OF JAMAICA
FROM THE EASTWARD.

Ships bound to Jamaica from the eastward, having come in to the southward of
the Islands Antigua and Montserrat, should steer thence west, or west a little
northerly, until they get into the latitude of 17° 20’, and continue on this parallel by
making good a true west course, until they make Alta Vela, or the Little Mount,
which lies 5 leagues S. 3 W. from the southernmost extremity of Haiti, described in
page 32. By keeping in the above latitude, they will avoid the dangerous shoals in

the vicinity of the Bay of Nieva, towards which the currents frequently set, as before
noticed.

But should hazy weather or night prevent them from seeing Alta Vela, when
passing it, it is recommended to steer W. by N. or more northerly, to make the land
to the westward of it. By so doing, you will probably make the Harbour of Jacque-
mel, or, if not, the next promontory of Haiti, of which Point Abacou and Point a
Gravois are the southern extremities. Jacquemel may, as already explained, be easily
distinguished by the sudden cut-off, or drop of a hill, scen over another long hill at
the upper part of the harbour ; which mark leads directly to the harbour’s mouth.

From Alta Vela to the east end of Isle Vache, the bearing and distance are, W. by
N. northerly, 38 leagues; and from the former to Point 4 Gravois, W. 2 N., 45
leagues. When off at sea, abreast of Isle Vache, the middle of the Saddle Hill over
Port St. Louis bears N. by E.; the island will be between you and the hill; and
from its being so low, and lying so under the land of the main, it is not distinguish-
able from the mainland at any considerable distance. This island is low, though
hilly, and its west end is the highest, the east end being low and woody ; and at the
distance of 5 or 6 leagues off it appears, as already said, like an assemblage of small
islands, of about 33 leagues in length.

The Saddle Hills over Port St. Louis, named the Grand Ance Mountains, are the
second high lands from the west end of Haiti; the westernmost is the highest, and
may be seen in clear weather 30 or 40 leagues off on both sides of the island. It
must, however, be observed that, after noon, the exhalation of vapour is sometimes so
great as to render them invisible. Be cautious, therefore, at such times of making
the land hereabout, lest you get amongst the dangers near Isle Vache.

From Point 4 Gravois to Cape Tiburon the bearing and distance are N.W. by
W. 3 W., 13 leagues. The land about. Cape Tiburon is high, and has often been seen
at more than 20 leagues distance. From Cape Tiburon to the little island of Navassa
the bearing and distance are W. 3 N., 12 leagues.

The charts of the West Indies will give the best idea of this passage, wherein will
be seen the Island Navassa, the Formigas or Ants, and farther to the S.W. the
Morant Cays and the surrounding bank. The distance between Cape St. Nicholas
and Cape Maysi, in Cuba, is 45 miles, and the bearing W.N.W., and between Cape
Tiburon and Morant Point, Jamaica, the bearing and distance are W.S.W. 4 W., 100
miles. The direct course through this passage to the northward, from a little to the
eastward of the Morant Cays, will be N.N.E. 7 E., which will lead to the westward
of the Isle Navassa.

NAVASSA is about 2 miles in length, E.S.E. and W.N.W., and about 14 mile
broad at its widest part. It was surveyed in 1803 by Mr. Francis Owen, Master,
R.N., who says,—‘ This island is a flat level rock, apparently of volcanic origin, is
above 300 feet in height, and covered with small shrubs. . It may be seen, on a clear
day, from the deck of a line-of-battle ship, about 7 leagues. very part thereof
shows a rocky perpendicular cliff, except a small space on the northern side, which is
but little above the surface of the sea. From the western extremity of the island a
coral reef stretches to the westward about 100 fathoms, on which is only 27 feet,
with 15 fathoms all round it; in every other part there are 12 fathoms water close to
the shore.

On the western and southern sides, soundings from 16 to 40 fathoms, sand, extend
to the distance of ¢ of a mile, on which you may anchor and lie smooth in a strong
sea breeze. On the north side the bottom is rocky, and‘ the bank does not extend.
beyond half a mile. In passing this island, on its eastern side, at the distance of
about one-third of a mile, you will have 34, 25, and 18 fathoms; and at half a mile
88, and soon after no ground with 75 fathoms. At the distance of 13 mile from the
east end no bottom will be found with 230 fathoms. With the N.W. end bearing
North or N. by E., and the S.E. point E.S.E., or a little more southerly, you may
anchor in 16 fathoms, fine sand, about half a mile from the shore. Great quantities
of sea-fowl are found on the island; and round the rocks, cod and red snappers in
abundance.”

Between Navassa and Cape Tiburon there is a small bank of fine white sand, with
plenty of fish thereon ; the depth is from 14 to 16 fathoms, with the following bear-
ings ;—Navassa W. 3 §., Cape Tiburon E.S.E. 3 E., and Cape Dame Maria N.E. 3 E.

From Navassa to Cape Dame Maria the bearing and distance are N.E. by E. 3 E.,
36 miles; and to Morant Point S.W. by W.4 W., 71 miles

The FORMIGAS, or ANTS, are some dangerous coral spots, upon a sand-bank
about 103 miles long, N.E. by B. and §.W. by W., and 74 miles wide. The north-
eastern part of this bank bears W. 2N., 73 miles from Navassa ; and N.E. by N., 45
miles from Morant Point; its south-western extremity bears N.E. by N. ; N., 40
miles from Morant Point. From the N.E. end of Jamaica the body of the shoal
bears N.E. by E., 40 miles. The eastern part is the shoalest, having in some places
no more than 14 feet water. The edge here is nearly steep-to, and there is generally
a great swell upon it. A mile to the westward, from the eastern edge, there are from
41 to 5 fathoms, increasing in depth, thence westward to 63 fathoms, where vessels
may anchor on sandy ground; the depth thence suddenly increases to 10, 13, 1, and
90 fathoms. On the eastern edge the bottom is dark, and not easily seen in hazy
weather, but to the westward the water appears lighter.

THE ISLAND OF JAMAICA. a

The MORANT CAYS consist of four low islets, or cays, situate in form of a
crescent, and are surrounded by a dangerous reef. They lie S.S.E. 1 E. from Morant
Point, distant 35 miles. Vessels may approach within 22 miles of any part of them;
they are distinguished by N.E. Cay, Sand Cay, Savanna or Bird Cay, and S.W. Cay.
To the N.W. of them there is good anchorage in 5 or 6 fathoms, white sand and
shells. To sail to this anchorage, give the N.E. Cay a berth of 1§ or 2- miles; and
when the 8.W. Cay bears 8. by E.., steer directly for it, and you will pass close to
the westward of a rocky spit, which extends westward from the N.E. Cay more than
2 miles, and on which there is but little more than 3 fathoms water. When the
N.E. Cay bears E. by N. or E.N.E., you may haul more to the eastward, and anchor
with the S.W. Cay bearing South or S. by W., and Savanna Cay S.E., in from 6 to 6
fathoms, sandy bottom. As there are some spots of coral, it is necessary to ascertain
that the bottom is clear.

These cays are only 8 or 9 feet above the water, and have bushes on them; on
Savanna Cay there were formerly some cocoa-nut trees. The cays and surrounding
reefs occupy a space of 6 miles N.N.E., and contrary. The body of the cays bear
from Yallah’s Hill, Jamaica, §.E. 4 E., distant from Yallah’s Point 40 miles ; and
from Cape Tiburon S.W. 2 W., distant 103 miles. With the N.E. Cay bearing 8.W.,
about 3 miles, there are 17 fathoms water, stony ground, mixed with red speckled
gravel; and when it bears 8.8. W., about 2 miles, there are 14 fathoms water.

Ships cruising, or beating to windward, near these cays, should observe that
Morant Point and the N.E. end of Jamaica bear from each other N.W. 3 N. and
S.E. 3 8. nearly ; so that when the N.E. end, which is high and bluff, is seen on that
bearing, you will be to the north-eastward of the Morant Cays; and also, if when
coming in from the southward for Jamaica, they keep Yallah’s Hill to the northward
of N.W. 3 N., they will pass clear to the westward of them; but great caution is
necessary by night or in hazy weather, lest they be driven on them by the current.

There is good turning room between the Morant Cays and the east end of Jamaica,
the channel being 28 miles wide; and if the island is seen before night, its bearings
may direct in standing towards it; and afterwards it will not be necessary to stand so
far off as the cays.

THE ISLAND OF JAMAICA,

Variation 4° 30’ Easterly.

JAMAICA’ is about 128 miles in length from east to west, and 40 miles in breadth
at the broadest part. An irregular ridge of high mountains extends nearly east and
west along the whole length of the island, which, in some parts, appears as an assem-
blage of steep rocks tumbled stupendously upon each other, and interspersed with a
variety of trees flourishing in perpetual verdure. From the fissures issue a great
number of small rivers of pure water, which falls in cataracts, and descends to the sea.
The elevated land may be seen from a great distance, particularly the eastern part
named the Blue Mountains.

The island is divided into three counties :—Surrey in the east, Middlesex in the
centre, and Cornwall in the west. In the county of Middlesex is St. JAGo DE LA
VAGO, commonly called SpANIsH Town. Kingston and Port Royal are situate in
the county of Surrey ; the latter on the west end of the sandy peninsula that forms
Port Royal Harbour. The towns of the county of Cornwall, in the west, are Savanna
la Mar, the town of Montego Bay, ard Falmouth; the latter two are on the north
coast ; all of which, with the other places worthy of notice, are hereafter described
in the sailing directions. f

In the eastern part of the island the grand ridge of Blue Mountains, which is
called the Cold Ridge, has three very remarkable peaks, the summits of which are
respectively 8,184, 7,656, and 7,576 feet above the level of the sea ; and there are some
other hills in this ridge which exceed a mile in height. Catherine Hill, which is
about 74 miles to. the north-eastward of Kingston, is 5,075 feet high; and Hardwar
Hill, which is to the westward of it, is nearly of equal height; these form the
summits of another grand ridge, which crosses the island diagonally, and has a
gradual descent to both coasts. Of the mountains to the westward, in the counties
of Middlesex and Cornwall, there are none that reach to the height of a mile, and
but few to that of half a mile. Lunan’s Mountain, in the county of Middlesex, at
about 6 miles to the northward of Spanish Town, is 2,282 feet high; and the Bull’s
Head, in Clarendon, near the centre of the island, on the meridian of Carlisle Bay,
is 3,140 feet high. In the west the Dolphin Head, south of Lucea, is 3,450 feet high.
On the S.E. coast, Yallah’s Hill, which is within the point of the same name, is only
2,706 feet high; but not being enveloped in clouds, as the Blue Mountains generally
are, it is a more certain guide to mariners.

SEA AND LAND BREEZES.—The air of Jamaica is in most places excessively
hot and unfavourable to European constitutions ; but the cold sea breezes, which set
in every morning, render the air more tolerable ; that upon the high land is temperate
and pure. Lightning oecurs almost every night, but without much thunder; never-
theless, when the latter happens, it is very heavy.

On the southern side of the island, the sea breeze from the south-eastward comes
on at nine or ten in the morning, and gradually increases till noon, when it is
strongest ; at two or three in the afternoon its force diminishes, and in general it
entirely ceases by five o’clock. About eight in the evening the land breeze begins;
this breeze extends to the distance of four leagues to the southward of the island.
It increases until midnight, and ceases about four in the morning.

The sea and land breezes are pretty regular from the latter end of January until
May. In the middle of May the sea breeze generally prevails for several days and
nights, especially about the time of full and change of the moon; and thus they con-
tinue throughout June and part of July ; from that time the sea breeze diminishes,
and veers round to 8. by W. or §.8.W., with frequent calms. August, September,
and October are the hurricane months, in which there are generally strong gales of
wind, with much rain.

In December, January, and February, when the north winds predominate, their
force checks the sea breeze. The southern coast is that, which, of course, is least
exposed to these winds, being sheltered in a great measure by the mountains. When,
combined with the land breeze, they render the air very cold and unhealthy.

On the northern side of the island, during the greatest part of July and the whole
of August, the sea breeze generally blows hard, with frequent squalls; therefore, at
this season, vessels bound hence to Europe would have the most advantageous passage
through the Strait or Stream of Florida; but in October northerly winds prevail,
and frequently extend over all the Bahamas and Cuba; and for some time on the
north side of Jamaica, where the current of air is forced upwards by the mountains,
and its strength spent in the heights ; but it sometimes reaches the southern coast,
particularly in the neighbourhood of Kingston, and has been known to continue for
some days.

During the winter season the land breeze is more general off the shores than in
summer; and it sometimes continues through the day as well as night. Westerly
winds prevail also over the whole space between Jamaica and Cuba, and even so far
as the Island of Haiti.

On the south side of the island, during the month of November, southerly winds
generally prevail, and have been known to extend from the Mosquito shore. ‘These
winds are generally faint; nor do they reach tho land until it be heated by the sun,
and soon.after mid-day are often expelled by a fresh land breeze, which also abates
in a few hours.

I have never seen the barometer for the last two years, during my residence here,
below 29° 98’, which was with a continuance of light southerly weather; nor above
30° 30’, which was with light northerly winds with clear weather (sent with what is
termed northers, as they are always accompanied by dense white clouds when the
glass falls) until the Sth of October, on which day a hurricanc took place at
Havannah; and a heavy swell set into Montego Bay, one of the ports on the north
side of this island; and although they had not much wind, yet the swell set in with
such violence, that every vessel in the bay became a total wreck, even the Mole was
torn to pieces, and several houses near the beach washed down. The strength of it
at Morant Bay was at 10 a.m., nearly the same time as we had the heavy squall.
Several of the roads in the island were impassable for the torrents of rain; but there
was not much damage in any of the ports, except Montego Bay. The weather con-
tinued more or less squally, with occasional rain, until the 10th, when it settled down
with light southerly winds, which continued throughout the month, with the excep-
tion of a violent squall from the westward, with rain, thunder, and lightning, for
several hours on the 27th.

DIRECTIONS FOR THE COAST OF JAMAICA.

MORANT POINT to KINGSTON.—The southernmost high land of Jamaica,
to the eastward of Port Royal, is Yallah’s Hill, which is very remarkable, and has
been already described. Should you make this hill bearing W. by S. at the distance
of 12 or 13 leagues, you should haul up S.W. by 8. to clear Morant Point, the east
end of the island, which is low, and cannot be seen ata greater distance than 4

76

leagues; and observe also, that a current frequently sets to the north-westward.

around this end of the island. When the fall of Yallah’s Hill bears W. 3 N., steer-
ing W. by S. will carry a vessel a league or more to the southward of Morant Point.

Moxant Point Lighthouse is in latitude 17° 55’ 45”, and longitude 76° 11” 10’.
The easternmost point of the island bears from the lighthouse S. 31° 55’ E., distant
about 500 yards; the N.B. point bears N. 33° 6’ W., and the elbow of the point to
the southward bears S. 4° 5’ W. (true bearings).

The light, which is very brilliant, revolves every minute, with a continued dim
light between the intervals of the strong flashes, and can be seen distinctly at an
elevation of 12 feet above the horizon, 19 miles in the circle described from the N.E.
end of the island to the direction of 8. W. by W. (magnetic), consequently, vessels
working to the eastward should never lose sight of the light until it bears N.W., or
N.W. by W., which would avoid any chance of their falling in with the dangerous
Morant Cays; and when bound to the westward, after passing Point Morant, by
keeping the light in sight, they will avoid any chance of coming near the shoals on
the southern shore, as the light is lost sight of when bearing to the eastward of N.E.
by E. The tower is painted white, and is 103 feet above the horizon ; the centre of
the light is 96 feet.

From off Morant Point, vessels bound'to Port Royal should keep at the distance
of 3 or 4 miles from shore until they are past Morant Bay, to avoid a reef that
extends from the east end to Rocky Point, 2 miles from shore, over part of which the
sea generally breaks. The coast thence to the entrance of Port Morant (hereafter
described) is rocky for about a mile from shore, and from Port Morant to Morant
Bay itis the same. From Morant Bay to near the white cliffs, called the Upper
White Horses, the coast is clear ; but from those cliffs some rocks extend néarly half
a mile from shore. From the Upper White Horses to Yallah’s Point the distance is
3 miles. In running along shore, when the former bears north and Yallah’s Point
west, the ground may frequently be seen in 73 to 10 fathoms; as you approach
Yallah’s Point the water will be found to deepen. Lamotte’s Bank, on which there
are only 3 fathoms, lies E.S.E. from Yallah’s Point, and extends about 14 mile from
shore; it should be avoided.

PORT ROYAL AND KINGSTON.

Yallah’s Point, after passing Lamotte’s Bank, may be approached to the distance of
one-third of a mile, if necessary ; from this point to Cow Bay Point the cost is clear.
The latter point is low and bold-to, as well as all the coast to the westward, as far
as:Great Plum Point. The course and distance from Cow Bay Point to Great Plum
Point are W. by N., 10 miles.

PORT ROYAL and KINGSTON.—The Palisadoes is a narrow tongue of low
sandy land, projecting to the westward from the head of Bull Bay 83 miles, termi-
nating in Port Royal Point. This strip of land is more or less overrun with mangrove
bushes, and forms as well as protects the harbours of Port Royal and Kingston.
Near its extremity is Fort Charles, and within, on its western face, is the town of
Port Royal and arsenal.

Plom Point is the §.E. point of the Palisadoes, from which a reef extends to
nearly a quarter of @ mile; and between it and the Eastern Middle Ground, which
lies 1 mile $.8.W. from it, is the entrance of the Eastern Channel.

Lights aT THE ENTRANCE oF Port Royat.—The approach to Port Royal has
of late years been much facilitated by the establishment of lighthouses upon Plum
Point and Fort Augusta, which, together with the beacons and buoys, render the
navigation more easy, than formerly.

Prum Point.—The lighthouse on Plum Point, which is painted white, stands
about 66 yards to the northward of the southern extremity of the point, in lat.
17° 55’ 45", and long. 76° 47’, and shows a fixed light at 68 feet above the level of the
sea, visible at the distance of 12 miles. When the light is seen between the
bearings of N.W. by W. ? W. and N. 3 E. it will appear as a red light; but between
those of N. 3 E. to 8.E., bright.

THE NARROWS.—tThe northern side of the narrow channel near
Fort Augusta separating Port Royal’ and Kingston harbors is marked
by black piles, and the southern side by white piles; it has however
been remarked that the pelicans frequenting the neighborhood seon
color the piles alike.

Directions from PORT ROYAL to KINGSTON.—In proceeding
from Port Royal to Kingston the mark to run into the channel is
Helshire Point just open of Small Point bearing S. S.W. 4 W., or
Fort Augusta beacon bearing N. } E., until the center of Lindo’s
House—standing in the interior on the northern shore—comes im one
with the center of the lower red-topped house, called Old Greenwich
Hospital, bearing N.E. 2 E., which mark will lead into The Narrows.
Upon nearing the elbow, or No. 13 pile, the upper house must be opened
entirely to the left of the lower one; or to appear exactly half way
between the lower one and another white house left of it; this leads past
the elbow in not less than 42 feet; then the two houses may be brought
again in line, and when Gallows Point comes on with the coal stores at
Port Royal Yard, haul round toward Kingston.

Vessels turning through The Narrows and nearing the elbow, or No.
13 pile, should be careful not to open the center of Lindo’s House to
the eastward of the center of the red-topped house at Greenwich, and
should not stand into less than 27 feet on either side.

The center of the two houses in line leads very near the edge of the
bank at the elbow in not less than 23 feet, but the least deviation beyond

get on shore with the two houses still in line, or at least not open.

A guide for running up to Kingston is the fall of Yallahs Hills(towards

running down, and after having passed the pile off Creek Pond, a bushy
cay (just north of Fort Augusta) to be brought in line with a large
straggling cotton tree on the low-land toward Spanish Town. These
are the marks used by the black pilots, but are hardly necessary.

KINGSTON.—The English Church at Kingston may be known by
a brick tower and small wooden spire. The new market place is built
of iron, and its wharf, situated in the middle of the town, forms the best

78 PORT ROYAL——EASTERN CHANNEL.

The Maiden Rock Beacon, biack, with a vane at its summit, 30 feet above the
horizon, placed on the northern part of the rock, which is about 50 fathoms in an
east and west direction, about 25 fathoms in a north and south direction, above
water, and the shoal extends to the N.E, in the Eastern Channel about 100 fathoms;
but in the direction of Lime Cay it extends nearly 2 of the distance, with rocks
occasionally above water, with a small channel about 300 yards broad (of 10 to 15
fathoms water) between it and the reef extending S.E. of Lime Cay.

The Rackum Cay Buoy, black, on the north extreme of the reef extending from
the cay, in 21 feet water, with 5 fathoms close to the north of it.

A Black-and-White Buoy is placed in 20 feet water on the knoll off Port Royal
Point ; it lies 70 fathoms from the point. Vessels may pass 40 yards on either side
of the buoy in from 7 to 9 fathoms.

SHOALS AND Cays IN THE EASTERN CHANNEL.—The first to be noticed in this
channel are the East Middle Shoals, lying S.S.W. from Plum Point, about 14 mile ;
they are divided into two shoals, with a small channel between them of 14 fathoms
water, with 11 feet on the easternmost, and 18 feet on the westernmost, both coral
reefs, and very steep-to, with the sea frequently breaking over them when the sea
breeze sets in; a black buoy is placed to the N.E. of the shoals, before described.

The first cay to be passed is the Maiden Cay Rock (barren), which is readily dis-
tinguished by the black beacon on it, as before described.

The next cay, at the distance of 2 of a mile, is Lime Cay, the principal part of
which is covered with trees; its northern side is rocky, and the southern sandy, sur-
rounded by a reef, and extending in a N.W. direction near 150 fathoms.

To the westward of Lime Cay, } of a mile distant, is Lime Cay rocky shoal, with

6 feet water in some parts, and a passage of 10 to 16 fathoms between it and Lime

" Cay, where a good anchorage of sand and mud may be had, if necessary, for a

quarantine ground; with the north part of Lime Cay E. by §., and the Maiden

(sandy) Cay 8.E., quite protected from the sea breezes by Lime Cay and the shoals

adjacent to Maiden Cay, and from S.W. winds by Lime Cay Shoal, which extends

in a N.W. and S.E. direction nearly 4 a mile, and then you are prepared to run into
Port Royal, through the Eastern Channel, in the event of bad weather.

Rackum Cay is very low, with a ridge of rocks extending from it to the northward,

and a contiguous reef, on the northern extremity of which the black buoy is placed,
as before described.

Gun Cay is low, with a quantity of bushes upon it, surrounded by areef. The
mark for going clear to the northward of the reef is the flagstaff of the Apostle’s
Battery, on with, or open a little to the northward of the flagstaff of Fort Charles ;
and for going clear to the southward, the flagstaff of Port Henderson in line with
rae guy Point, which is the leading mark, through which passage you haye 10 to

6 fathoms.

The Knoll off Port Royal Point is about 70 fathoms from the shore, with 20 feet
water; a black-and-white buoy is placed upon it, before- described; outside of it is a
coral bank of 14 feet, with a white pile mounted with a red triangle, 110 fathoms
from the shore, as before described.

Note.—In the Eastern Channel the bottom is generally formed of mud and sand,
except just to the eastward of Gun Cay, where it is more of mud than sand. Inside
Port Royal Harbour it is mud with a little sand all over, except where you get near
the shoals, when you have portions of broken coral and sand.

Port Royal, through the South Channel, should be under weigh as soon as the day
breaks, if there is a land wind (or if the wind will allow them to lie §. by E., they
may get out); the current is generally setting to the southward as far as Drunken-
man’s Cay, when it takes a more westerly direction. The leading mark through the
channel for vessels not drawing oyer 17 feet is the black-and-white floating beacon

Turning out of the South Channel.Few vessels should attempt it, unless they
work well. The mark cannot be described better than by Mr. Dunsterville, Master,

Buoys AND BEACONS ON THE WESTERN SIDE OF THE SouTH CHANNEL. — The
Helshire White Beacon iserected close to the beach in Helshire Bay. The outer
3-fathom-bank Buoy, white, with a staff and vane 15 feet above the horizon, lies

ton Church Steeple in line with Rackum Cay, N.E. § N.; the notch in the mountain,

Buoys and Beacons on the Eastern Side of the South Channel.—The Portuguese
Buoy, red, with staff and vane 15 feet above the horizon, lies on the western edge of

The West Middle Buoy, red, with a staff and vane 10 feet above the horizon, lies

In the South Channel.—A floating beacon, 30 feet above the horizon, with a vane
of rails 4 feet square, painted white on its upper part, with the lower part black, is
moored on the shoal of 22 feet, which lies about 440 yards, in a N.N.W. % W.
direction, from the West Middle Buoy, and is the leading mark into the South
Channel, when in a line with the black beacon on the east part of Fort Augusta.

SHOALS AND CAyYs IN THE SouTH CHANNEL.—The West Middle Ground is a coral
reef, some part of which has only 2 feet water; it is steep-to, particularly on the
S.W. side. There is a red buoy on its N.W. part, before described.

The Turtle Heads are dangerous reefs of coral; the eastern shoal has 8 feet over

and sand, occasionally clay; but near the reefs it is sand, with portions of broken

Port RoyaL To PortLanp.— About half-way between Port Royal and Old
Harbour, and at the distance of more than a mile from shore, lies Wreck Reef, which
is a large shoal, composed of dry rocks and breakers, This danger, which appears
in the day, consists of two principal parts, having between them a channel of 4
fathoms water. Ships passing this way in the night, unless absolutely certain of
their position, should approach no nearer than into the depth of 12 fathoms, or come

anchorage in 4 and 5 fathoms, sandy bottom, with shells and some mud, where
vessels may occasionally ride during the prevalence of a breeze, &c.

The distance from Port Royal to Portland, on a circuitous route, is 8 leagues. In

this course, being clear of the South Channel, give Wreck Reef a berth of 2 miles.
The distance from off Portland Point to Carlisle or Withy-yood Bay is 9 miles,

OLD HARBOUR. 81

OLD HARBOUR, LONG’S WHARF, &c.—From Helshire Point to Portland
Point the bearing and distance are S.W. 2? W., 15 miles; the land between forming
an extensive bay, in which there are several anchorages sheltered by islands, reefs,
&c. Between these points, and somewhat without their line of direction, are also
several banks or reefs with cays on them, which form various channels or entrances
to the interior of the bay. Within, the anchorages are Walker’s Bay, Galleon Har-
bour, Old Harbour, Long’s Wharf, Salt River, Peake Bay, and West Harbour. To
take either of these, it is necessary first to enter between the exterior banks, which
consist of three large and some smaller ones.

The first is Pelican Bank; this is rather more than 3 miles in length EH. by N. and
W. by S., and 1 mile in breadth. Near its middle rise the two rocks or islets named.
Pelican Cays; to the southward and eastward of them are breakers. At the west
end is a part named the Dry Shoal, consisting of rocks at the water’s edge, by which
it is easily discovered. Between this hank and Cabrietta Point to the northward, the
channel is two miles wide; but it has only 3 and 34 fathoms water, and is therefore
but seldom used, excepting by small vessels. Walker’s Bay is to the eastward of
Cabrietta Point.

The second is Bare Bush Bank, which lies S.E. and N.W., about 2 miles, and is one
mile wide at its broadest part. Oa this bank, at nearly half a mile from its N.E. end,
an islet or rock, called Bare Bush Cay, rises above the water ; and there are breakers
over the whole extent of the S.E. side.. The channel between this and the Pelican
Bank is 12 mile in width, and has a depth of 7 to 9 fathoms ; this is the channel that
is generally used to enter the bay.

The third bank, which also lies about N.E. and §.W., is 3} miles in length, and
nearly 2 in breadth at the widest part. On this bank, near its N.E. part, rise two
islets, named Half-moon Cays, and on its northern part are several breakers. On the
S.W. part are three islets or rocks, named Portland Cays, and South and §.8.E. from
these, about 2 miles, is a shoal, with 34 and 4 fathoms on it. The channel formed by
this bank and the Bare Bush Cay Bank is about a mile wide, with 5 to 12 fathoms
in it; and that which is formed between this bank and Portland Point is three-
quarters of a mile in breadth, but having only 2 to 4 fathoms water in it, is only fit
for vessels of little draught of water.

Between the Half-mso0n Cay Bank and that of Bare Bush Cay is another small
one about one-third of a mile from east to west, and a quarter of a mile from north
to south; this is named Morris Shoal. The extremity of this is three-quarters of a
mile distant from the nearest part of Bare Bush Cay Bank, and one mile from the
northern part of Half-moon Cay Bank; in both the channels is a depth of from 9 to
13 fathoms.

W.S.W. 3 W., 13 mile from the western part of Pelican Bank, is an islet named
Pigeon Island, which is low and bushy; from its east end a reef of rocks projects
about a cable’s length northward, and from its west end another reef projects a
similar distance N.W. ‘These reefs form a bay, with anchorage in from 4 to 6
fathoms. Three-quarters of a mile northward from this island is a small white shoal
of 18 fect water, which it is necessary to avoid in a ship of great draught of water.

To Sain Into OLD Harpour, Lone’s Warr, &c.—The most frequented and
best channel for entering into this great bay is that before mentioned, between
Pelican Cay and Bare Bush Cay Banks; and to take it, vessels from Cow Point
should steer W.S.W. 2 W., until the fall of the south side of Brazaletta Hill bears
about W. by N. This hill cannot be mistaken, it being the northernmost of two seen
in the west, and the southernmost is of a round figure. It is the valley or notch
formed between these hills thatis used asa leading mark, bearing W. by N. Steering
in this direction, will lead you to the southward of the foul ground of the Pelican
Oays, and as you approach them you will discover Pigeon Island, in a direction
with the fall of Brazaletta Hill; keep it so, and pass the Pelican Cays in 73, 7, and
65 fathoms.

82 SALT RIVER ANCHORAGE.

As you advance to the westward, you will see to the northward a large island,
named Goat Island, which has two hills, one at the east, the other to the west end ;
and to the northward of it, inland, a remarkable hummock on the mountain, called
Cudjoe Hill. When this hummock comes on the west extremity of the slant fall of
the eastern hill of Goat Island, bearing about N. 3 W., you may haul up N.N.W. 3 W.
for Old Harbour. This last mark leads clear to the westward of Dry Shoal, part of
which, as before said, is even with the surface of the water, and you will see it. In
passing Dry Shoal you will have from 63 to 6 and 53 fathoms; continue steering
N.N.W. 4 W., and you will deepen the water to 8 fathoms; and as you approach
Careening Islet or Cay (which lies off the west erd of Goat Island), it will shoalen
to 7 or 6 fathoms. You must give Careening Cay a berth of nearly half a mile to
avoid a reef which surrounds it; and steer direct for the wharf at Old Harbour, and
anchor in 43 or 4 fathoms at about two-thirds of a mile southward of the village,
taking care to avoid the reef on the §.W. side of the anchorage, which generally
shows itself.

Lone’s WHARF.—If you are bound to Long’s Wharf, you may pass about 2 cables’
length to the northward of Pigeon Island, in about 7 fathoms water, and when the
west end of the island bears south, steer about N.W. by N., and bring the top house
at Long’s Wharf about one-third from the north side of the large opening or gap in
the mountains, bearing N.W.; and this mark will lead between the reefs to the
anchorage at Long’s Wharf, in 4 or 33 fathoms, at about half or three-quarters of a
mile from shore. This entrance is only 2 cables’ length wide, has 4 fathoms in it,
and is rather more than a mile from the coast.

Satt River ANCHORAGE.—If you are bound to Salt River, steer as before, and
pass about 2 cables’ length to the northward of Pigeon Island; then keep the south
part of Brazaletta Hill open a little on your port bow, and it will lead close to
Salt Island; you may either go to the northward or southward of it, but the north
side is the best. You may approach the north and west parts of Salt Island within
a cable and a half; but on the south side is a reef, which shows itself, and is steep
close-to. There is a reef extending eastward from the Salt River shore to within 3
cables’ length from Salt Island, which sometimes breaks, and also a reef extending
along the east side of Long Island, which you will see; it extends to within two-
thirds of a mile from Salt Island. To sail in, pass about 2 or 24 cables’ length to the
northward of Salt Island, and then steer towards the entrance of Salt River, until
you bring the south end of Pigeon Island almost in a line with the south end of Salt
Island; keep them in that direction, and when you get in 43, 4, or 33 fathoms,
anchor, according to the size of your ship. If you are ina low vessel, it will be
necessary to go a little up the shrouds to see Pigeon Island over Salt Island. The
south end of Pigeon Island, a little open to the southward of Salt Island, leads on
the edge of the Salt River Reef. There is good anchorage under the west part of
Salt Island, about 2 or 3 cables’ length off, in 65 fathoms water, good holding ground.

PEAKE Bay.—To sail into this bay, it is necessary to give the reef that runs
Rocky Point (the north. point of the bay) a Bett of 4 cable’s length or nee
and steer towards the north part of the sandy beach. The anchorage is in 43, 4 or
33 fathoms, at about 3 cables’ length from the north shore; the ground holds well
but with strong sea breezes there is a great sea in this bay. The reef off Rocky
Point and the reef on the south side of the bay are nearly even with the surface of
the water, so that you generally see them.

West Harsour.—the entrance into this harbour is between two Coral Reefs, that
are nearly even with the surface of the water; and the heads of coral frequently ake
above water. The channel between the reefs is about half a mile wide, with 6 and 64
fathoms water in it. There is very good anchorage just to the westward of the North
Reef, in 53, 5, or 43 fathoms, on good holding ground, and always smooth water
The land to the westward does not show any mark to guide you to this anchorage but
it is not difficult, as the dangers can be seen. To sail to this anchorage it is not
necessary to pass to the northward of Pigeon Island; on the contrary, pass about 2
