eables’ length to the southward of it, and then steer about W. by S., until you discover
the North Reef, which you must pass to the southward of, at the distance of 1 or 2
cables’ length, until you gain the anchorage on its west side, before mentioned. To
the westward of this anchorage the water shoalens to 9 or 8 feet; it is also shoal on
the south side towards the mangroves, with smooth water.

GOING TO SEA from either of the before-mentioned plaeces.—Ships generally get
under weigh with the land wind, so as to get clear of the reefs near the anchorage
before the sea breeze comes on. Being clear of the reefs, you may turn out with the
sea breeze, and go on either side of Pigeon Island. The channel between Pigeon
Island and the reef of the Half-moon Cays is 2 miles wide, with 12 or 13 fathoms
water; but the smoothest water is to the northward of Pigeon Island. You may
stand towards Goat Island and Cabrietta Point by your lead, the soundings being
gradual, and tack in 6 or 43 fathoms. If the sea breeze should be very strong, you
may anchor under the Dry Shoal, and wait for the land wind to sail out between the
Pelican and Bare Bush Banks, with the same marks used for sailing in. But with
moderate sea breezes, any ship may turn out between the cays and reefs.

Being so far to the eastward as Dry Shoal, and in standing to the southward, the
leading mark for the channel between Bare Bush Cay and Morris Shoal is Cudjoe
Hill, on the west extremity of the slant fall of the eastern hill of Goat Island, bearing
about N. 4 W., the same as for Dry Shoal; keep it so until the Half-moon Cays come
in one, about 8.W. + W., then you will be to the eastward of Morris Shoal, and may
edge away alittle, bringing Cudjoe Hill about a large sail’s breadth on the lower part
from the aforesaid slant of Goat Island, which mark wil] lead you along the white
water on Bare Bush side to sea. But, if in standing to the southward from Dry
Shoal, the wind should be so far to the south-eastward as to prevent you from weather-
ing Morris Shoal, which you will know by the fall of Cudjoe Hiil, not being within
a sail’s breadth of the fall of Goat Island, before mentioned; in this case you must
tack when Bare Bush Cay bears E.S.E., or when a Saddle Hill to the north-west of
Pigeon Island is just coming to the north end of that island ; and in standing to the
northward, tack when the fall of Brazaletta Hill comes on the centre, or near the
north end of Pigeon Island. You may approach the white water on the side of Bare
Bush to 5 fathoms.

The channel between Morris Shoal and the Half-moon Cays is very good ; but it is
dangerous to approach the Half-moon Cay Bank on the §.E. side, for you will have
from 6 or 7 fathoms to 2, in one or two casts of the lead. After you have passed
those cays and banks, in sailing to the westward, go no nearer to Portland than 2 or
21 miles, or into 8 or 7 fathoms, because the reef off Rocky Point, which is the west
part of Portland, extends nearly 2 miles to the southward.

PEDRO BANK.—S.S.W. from Portland Point, at the distance of 13 leagues,
and in latitude 17° 8’, lies the Portland Rock, which is a little higher than Drunken-
man’s Cay, off Port Royal, and has 7 fathoms near it. This rock is on the east part
of the Pedro Bank.* ‘This bank extends 31 leagues westward from Portland Rock,
the western part turning somewhat to the N.W., being at its extremity 15 leagues
wide, and extending from 16° 52’ to 17° 36’ north latitude. Over all this part, and
in the space of 11 leagues from the west end, the soundings appear regular, from 20
to 15 and 11 fathoms, on sand of various descriptions, coral, and stones, excepting
one part of about 4 leagues in length and 4 miles in breadth, which is rocky, with
from 7 to 12 fathoms on it. This is about 5 leagues from the S.W. extremity.

* Remarks on Portland Rock.—The position of this rock appears to have been finally

77° 95/19", The rock is quite barren ; its greatest extent under 2 cables’ length. It is

East, 2 of a mile in 8 or 10 fathoms, fine sand.—JVautical Magazine, Vol. 4 p. 138,

84 CARLISLE, OR WITHY-WOOD BAY.

.. PepRro Cays.—On the south-eastern part there are several cays and breakers; of
these, the first is the North-east Cay, about a mile long; this lies W.S.W. % W., 19
miles from Portland Rock, and south 16 leagues from Pedro Bluff, in Jamaica.
S.S.W. 2 W., 9 miles from North-east Cay, lies the South Cay; and between these
are the Middle and South-west Cays, all of which are surrounded with reefs; and
between them and Portland Rock are some shoal patches and breakers. §.W. by
W. 3 W., 22 miles from South Cay, is a rock 5 feet above water, surrounded by a
reef or bed of dangerous rocks; these are in latitude 16° 48’, and longitude 78° 10’ 32”;
and on the edge of the bank, close to the southward of them, there is no bottom at
140 fathoms; here the bank is 28 miles wide. Between these rocks and the South
Cay are 3 or 4 patches of rocks and breakers, all of which are dangerous to ships
from the southward in the night, because they lie near the edge of the bank, which
appears to be steep-to all along this side. On the north side the soundings will be a
sufficient warning, which will be best understood by inspecting the chart.*

CARLISLE, on WITHY-WOOD BAY, on the west side of Portland, is open to
all winds, from West to S.E. The Rocky Point of Portland is the S.E. extremity of
the bay, from which a spit extends about 3 a mile to the S.W., with 12 to 16 feet
water on it. In an angle from the point from West to N.W., to the distance of a
mile, there is also a shoal, called Robertson’s Shoal, with 5 feet on its shoalest
parts, which are to the N.H., at 6, of a mile from the point; the other parts have
2 to 3 fathoms;

To sail into this bay, you must keep so far westward as to bring a little round hill
in the bay to bear N. $ W. or North, in order to avoid the shoals off Rocky Point,
and keep the same bearing as you run in for it, and you will have 10, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4,
and 383 fathoms; then you will be within a mile anda half of the shore. As you
proceed toward the hill on the above bearing, you will perceive the Old Fort between
you and the hill, With the hill bearing N. 2 E. there is a spot of 34 fathoms, at
about 2 miles from the beach. The best berth to anchor is with Rocky Point in
a line with the southernmost point of Portland, bearing E. 28., and the Old Fort
north, in 4 fathoms; because your boats can sail both on shore and on board with sea
winds. Here is no tide, but a strong westerly current generally runs in the offing.

Along the coast to the westward, to the distance of nearly 20 miles from Carlisle
Bay, at a mile and a half from shore, there is a regular depth of 4 to 44 fathoms
of water.

ALLIGATOR CAY anp Rezr.—This is a dry cay, 2 or 3 miles in length, with a
reef all around it. It lies at the distance of about 3 miles from shore, and 64 leagues
W.3N. from Rocky Point. There is good anchorage for small yessels, between it
and the main, in 6 or 7 fathoms. ;

BRUNE BANK.—Six miles 8.E. of Alligator Reef there is a small bank, having
on it but little more than 4 fathoms water, with 12 or 13 fathoms close to it, with
Portland E. by N., the fall of the high land to the westward of Milk River, N.N.E.
4 E., and Pedro Bluff W.N.W. Its distance from shore is about 7 miles. The shoal
is about 1? mile in extent from east to west, and 13 mile in breadth, and there are
from 4 to 6 fathoms water on it.

PEDRO BAY, &c.—Pedro Bluff is a very remarkable piece of land, and is easily
known from any other land on the coast. There is a remarkable spot in the cliff,
called the White Horses, about 4 or 5 miles to the eastward of the bluff, which,
when first seen from the eastward, appears like a schooner under sail, close to the
land.

* Remarks in H.M.S. Winchester—The §. W. breakers are dangerous, and require a
strict look out. The sea breaks over two small rocks not more than 3 feet above the level
of the sea, constantly, but so irregular, that from the deck of a vessel, and in a moderate
breeze, a high breaker might not be distinguished oftener than once in 5 minutes, and the

SAVANNA LA MER. 85

In Pedro Bay, to the westward of Pedro Bluff, there is good anchorage for any
vessels, but it is open to southerly winds. The coast hence to the westward, nearly
to Parattee Point, is bold-to. Off Parattee Point is a reef, which extends west-
ward nearly a mile; and to the N.W. of this point is Black River, which is fronted
by extensive reefs. To sail clear of these reefs, keep Pedro Bluff open of Parattee

oint.

BLACK RIVER.—The anchorage is situate between Parattee Point and Luana
Point, the latter bearing from the former N.W. 5 W. distant 7 miles. Off Parattee
Point as observed a reef extends westward, and this continues along shore northward
a little over 2 miles; and then takes a sweep ina W. by N. direction for 4 miles,
forming several detached reefs, designated the Long Reefs, the Barrack and Outer
Barrack Reefs, and the Ravient Reefs. These reefs have in several places as little as
3 feet water over them, ranging from that depth to 12 and 15 feet; they are divided
by channels of deeper water, but of irregular soundings, and not available for shipping.
The northern edge of the reefs is about 1} mile from the shore of the island, and
protect the inner anchorage of the town, which is erected on the western side of the
Black River. The shore to the westward of the town has several rocky heads stretch-
ing nearly 4 a mile off, and similar patches off Longacre and Luana Points.

In approaching Black River from the eastward bring Luana Point to bear N.N.E.,
and steer towards it until the church is brought a little to the left of the North
shoulder of Santa Cruz Mountains, E. by N. 4. N. Steer towards it on that bearing
until Malcolm Point bears north, when the course to the anchorage is H.$ 8. A
vessel over 16 feet must not go farther in than to bring Moco Point north, when she
will have 4 fathoms water. Smaller vessels may stand on until the Court House
bears N.N.E. and anchor in 3 fathoms. The holding ground is very good, and the
anchorage, one of the best in Jamaica. Large vessels should anchor farther out in 8
or 9 fathoms, with Pedro Bluff shut in about a cable of Parattee Point 8.E. ¢ 8. and
the town N.E. by N. Itis to be observed that Parratee Point should not be ap-
proached nearer than a mile.

From Luana Point the coast is clear 3 or 4 miles, or until you are within 1
or 2 miles of Crab Pond Point, where it again becomes encumbered with reefs, and so
continues to Blewfield’s Bay, &c. The bearing and distance from Luana Point to
St. John’s Point are, N.W. by W. 2 W., 10 miles. About 9 or 10 miles S.W. by W.
3 W. from Luana Point lies the inner edge of a Rocky Bank, discovered in 1821, and
called De Mayne’s Bank. It is 3 or 4 miles in breadth north, and south, and has from
12 to 20 fathoms water on it; its length has not been explored.

BLEWFIELD’S BAY.—This part of the coast is environed by reefs, and the an-
chorage here for large ships is without a rocky ledge, which extends from Crab Pond
Point to the west of Blewfield’s, and joins the reef of Savanna la Mer. Vessels,
coming from the eastward to anchor in this bay, must keep down by the outside of
the reef, or keep the land to the eastward open of the point, until the leading mark is

rought on, which is the Overseer’s House, which stands a little to the southward of
the large house on the estate above, just open to the southward of the Tavern at the
entrance of the river, N.E. 2 E. Ships drawing no more than 16 or 17 feet water
may sail over the rocky ledge in 32 or 4 fathoms, until finding a sandy bottom, and
a depth of 5% or 6 fathoms; they may then anchor with the Fort bearing about
E.S.E. 4 8., and the Tavern E.N.E.3N. The watering place is to the northward
of the Bluff Point, on the lee side of the bay; water may also be obtained ata
stream of Blewfield’s River, near the Tavern. Large ships anchor outside the reef
in from 8 to 5 fathoms, with Crab Pond Point about §.E. by S., and the Tavern
E.N.E., or E. by N. In running in here, keep the lead going, and be ready to anchor

as the water shoalens rather suddenly.

SAVANNA LA MER lies about 24 leagues W.N.W. from Blewfield’s. The
coast between is rocky in some places to nearly 2 miles from shore. The entrance
to Savanna la Mer is very narrow, between a small rock called the Middle Ground,
0 n which is a depth of only 4 feet on the east side, and a reef of 7 or 8 feet on the

on the high land, called the Dolphin Head, in a line with a remarkable large tree on
the low land, to the eastward of the town, bearing N. by W. This leads close to the
Middle Ground, which will be seen; and after passing it, haul to the westward, and
anchor in from 15 to 17 feet water. Strangers should never attempt this channel
without a pilot.

About a mile and a half to the westward of this is the Great Channel of Savanna
la Mer, which is nearly a mile in breadth, with a depth of from 24 to 20, and 13 feet
towards the shore. The fort bearing N.N.E. leads directly through it.

The Derrotero says,—“In this vicinity it is necessary to be very particular in the
use of the lead; for the reef which extends along in front of Blewfield’s, and thence
to opposite Savanna la Mer, and 3 or 4 miles to the westward, is rocky, and has on
its edge from 20 to 24 feet water. On it, as on the White Banks, there are various
shoals with little water, some of which uncover, and have many breakers. Outside,
but very near to the edge of the reef, are 5 fathoms water, which augments to 13
fathoms, at three-quarters of a mile off; the depth, therefore, is the best guide, for
when you get from 8 to 10 fathoms you will be from one-third to half a mile from
the edge of the reef; and when you get 13 fathoms, you will be three-quarters of a
mile from it; therefore do not go into the depth of 10 to 8 fathoms, but keep in 13 to
15, for you should have the former depth only near to the anchorage sought.

WESTERN END OF JAMAICA.

The anchorage of Savanna Ja Mer is of the same nature as that of Blewfield’s.
Large ships must anchor outside the reef, in which position they will not be sheltered
from the wind and sea, from east by the south, to west. It is probable that such very
seldom come to this place, as they run much risk of losing their anchors; for the
instant there is the least appearance of the wind freshening, they must stand out to
sea. Such vessels as do not draw more than 12 or 13 feet water, may anchor upon
the bank under the lee of the reefs, in 15 or 16 feet water, about two-thirds of a
mile §.S.E. 4 E. from the town.”

On the southern extremity of this bank, which extends from the shore, between
Savanna la Mer and St. John’s Point, His Majesty’s ship Monarch struck in 1782,
upon a bottom of coral. From this spot St. John’s Point bears N.W. by W. Ships
may pass to the southward of it, by keeping one-half of the high land of South Negril
open to the southward of St. John’s Point.

WESTERN END OF JAMAICA.—From St. John’s Point to South Negril the
coast is bold-to. Between South Negril and North Negril, is the long bight or
indent, called Negril Bay, which affords tolerable anchorage. Close to the south side
of North Negril is Negril Harbour; it is small, but has good anchorage for small
vessels; and on the north side are Orange Bay, and Half-Moon Bay, fit only for
very small vessels. Six miles to the N.E. from North Negril is Green Island
Harbour, and about 24 miles from the latter is Davis's Cove. These places are
seldom resorted to, but by those who go thither on purpose to load, and have pilots
on board.

South Negril, about $ a mile, with irregular appearances of rdcky patches; but in
the bay formed between North and South Negril, there is good anchorage, in 5 to 7
fathoms, sandy bottom, with North Negril N.E.; South Negril S.S.W.; and the

From Negril to North Pedro the coast is bold, excepting at Green Island, which is
low, and to the northward of which a reef stretches out. From Pedro Point to the
Harbour of Lucea, vessels may stand within a mile of the shore.

LUCEA.—This harbour is one of the best on the north side of the island; its
entrance is easily known by a remarkable notch in the mountain, called the Dolphin
Head ; at a little distance to the westward of the entrance there is also a remarkable
white spot in the land, which may be seen 3 leagues off. Vessels having opened the
harbour, may steer directly in, giving the Fort Point, on the western side, a berth, on
account of a small reef which runs off it, nearly a cable’s length. The harbour
is otherwise very safe, with little danger in sailing in or out. To sail in, bring the
remarkable mountain, called the Dolphin Head, open to the westward of Barbara
Hill, which has a house on the top of it, and is on the east side of the harbour, bear-
ing 8. by E. Continue on in this direction, until the Fort bears West, when you will
be within the Fort Reef, which has generally a buoy on its extreme edge. Hence
proceed towards the town, and anchor in 6 or 6 fathoms, muddy bottom, with the Fort
bearing from N. by W. to N.N.W., and Lucea Point at the east side of the entrance,
from N. by E. to N.N.E. 3 E.

Vessels from the eastward must observe to keep at least 3 miles from shore, until
past Buckner’s Reef, which lies off Musquito Cove, and sometimes breaks. It is also
to be observed, that round Lucea Point to the northward, there is a rocky flat,
extending more than a mile from shore, having on it from 4 to 7 fathoms; and within
Lucea Point the reef extends to the distance of a cable’s length or more from shore ;
but it is nearly steep-to, and the heads of coral sometimes appear above water. The
leading mark to clear the eastern bank is Malcom House, which stands on a small
hill or rising at the east end of Lucea Town, on with the east end of the Fort, bearing
8.S.W. 3 W.; keep it so, until you bring the Dolphin Head to the westward of Bar-
bara Hill, as already mentioned. This mark leads through 8, 7, and 6 fathoms, then
deepening to 12 or 13, and shoaling again into the harbour.

FurtHer Drrecrions ror Lucza Harsour.—*The best guide for knowing
Lucea Harbour, from the offing, is the Dolphin Head; a remarkable mountain,
situate nearly in the middle line of the island, between Lucca and the north shore,
and Bluefield’s on the south ; it is so named from its resemblance to the vertical fall
of the head of the Dolphin.

“Excepting Port Royal, Lucea is the largest and most commodious harbour in the
Island of Jamaica. A reef extends some distance on each side of the entrance to the
port. To sail in, bring the middle of the entrance to bear S. by E., or S.S.E., and
steer in on that course until past the fort, when anchorage may be taken where most
convenient, from 7 to 4 fathoms. Throughout the harbour the bottom is formed of
soft clay, and there are 4 fathoms water within 2 cables’ length of the shore, next the
town ; under Barbara Hill the water is deep, and on the east side it is steep to the
cliffs.

“In working out, do not stand too close to the shore, from the fort towards the
church; a frigate once grounded in doing so, and had some trouble in getting off.
There are no hidden dangers; and the channel of entrance is so wide and deep, that
the eye alone is sufficient to lead in; and a vessel may either go out with the land
wind, or work out with the sea breeze, with equal safety.”—Nautical Magazine,
March, 1835.

MOSQUITO COVE lies 3 miles to the eastward of the entrance of Lucea Harbour.
This is an excellent harbour, secure from all winds, where a hundred sail of merchant
ships might lie in safety. The channel, at the entrance, is little more than half a
cable’s length in breadth, but widens inward, to where the harbour has from 42 to 7
fathoms, The bottom in general is muddy. To sail in, pass to the eastward of

88 FALMOUTH HARBOUR.

Buckner’s Reef, or you may pass over its eastern end in 6 or 53 fathoms. The course
in is about S.E. by S., but the entrance is too narrow to be attempted by a stranger,
as there is a reef which stretches off the east point.

MONTEGO BAY, the northern point of which is in latitude 18° 31’ 30’, is a good
bay, sheltered from all winds from N.N.E. round to the eastward and southward, but
it is open to those from north to west, and there are several instances of the northerly
winds in December and January having driven vessels on shore.

To sail into this bay from the eastward, give the point, on coming down, a good
berth of 2 or 3 miles, in order to avcid a reef which runs off it, until you open
the Town, and bring the Gun Tavern to bear S.E. by E.; then stand in for it, which
will carry you clear to the westward of the reef, and thus run until you shut in the
point to the northward of the fort; you will then have come upon the soundings in
the bay. To anchor, bring the Old Fort Point to bear from North to N. by W., and
the Church from East to E.N.E., you will then have 9, 10, and 11 fathoms water ;

but with small vessels you may go farther up the bay, and anchor in 7, 6, 5, or 4
fathoms.

With the sea breeze, which is from N.E. to E.N.E., you should endeavour to keep .
well to windward, and for this purpose you may, as soon as you have opened the
town, approach the reef off the Old Fort, which is tolerably steep, to the depth of 10,
9, or 8 fathoms, and see the bottom.

In sailing along by the reef, you will have 10, 12, 14, 16, 20, and so on, to 30
fathoms water, in the bay, it being a shelving bank; therefore you must not venture
to anchor until you have shut in the Sandy Point without the bay, on the north, with
Old Fort Point as above. For if you anchor in 20 or 30 fathoms it will not hold, and
with the sea breeze, you will be in danger of driving off the bank, and grounding on
the lee reefs. On entering the bay from the westward, with a fair wind, the Church
bearing East, will lead you directly to the anchorage.

From Lucea Harbour to Montego Bay, the bearing and distance are, E.N.E. ¢ E.,
14 miles. About 4 miles to the westward of Montego Bay is a smali creek, without
which is a bay, called Great Roads, where merchant vessels lie to load; there being
a shoal extending nearly the whole of the way across, affords good shelter for ships
lying here during the north winds.

Ships bound from Montego Bay to the eastward, should leave the bay in the
evening, so soon as the land wind comes off, with which they can run clear of the bay,
and generally obtain a good offing for the sea breeze; but if bound to Falmouth
Harbour, endeavour to keep the shore close on board, and the land wind will lead
them to the eastward in the night.

In working hence to windward, in clear weather, when Cuba is visible, a remark-
able hill will be seen. This is the Pico de Tarquino, the highest land on this side of
Cuba: it bears from Montego Point N.E. by N., distant 39 leagues; from St. Anne’s
Bay, N. by E., distant 31 leagues; and from the east end of Jamaica, N.N.W. + W.,
distant 40 leagues, by which you may judge how far you are to the windward at any
other bearings.

FALMOUTH HARBOUR, or MARTHA BRAE, which lies about 16 miles to
the eastward of Montego Bay, is a bar harbour. Its channel, which is very narrow,
and not more than 16 or 17 feet deep, is too intricate to be attempted by a stranger
without a pilot. The town of Falmouth is situate on the west side of the harbour ;
throughout the great part of which there isa regular depth of from 5 to 10, and 11
feet water.

Marabona Bay is about 2% leagues to the eastward of Falmouth, and is very remark-
able by having a low pleasant plantation close to it, and on the hill over it, a large
house or castle.

RIO BUENO and DRY HARBOUR.—Rio Bueno lies 34 leagues to the eastward
of Falmouth, and about 13 mile from Marabona Bay. It is an open bay, exposed to

ST. ANN’S BAY.—-PORT MARIA. 89

all winds from north to W.N.W.; and has but indifferent anchorage, the bank being
steep. It is seldom used by any but merchant ships, which go there to load. The
harbour is formed by two reefs, and from the entrance to the anchorage the distance
is about 2 miles. A ship may lie here, with the point bearing N.N.W., in 8 or 9
fathoms, but it is considered particularly dangerous with north winds. Dry Harbour,
which lies 3 miles more to the eastward, is, however, a good harbour for small vessels.
The channel is narrow, and has but 16 feet of water.

ST. ANNE’S BAY.—The entrance of this bay is narrow, and lies between two
reefs, which have on their edges 3 and 3} fathoms, deepening suddenly in the channel
to 10 or 11 fathoms, which is less than half a cable’s length in breadth; the mark for
it is the barracks on the rise of the hill, bearing about S.4 E. The usual method of
going in, as the water is clear, is to sail close by the westernmost reef, leaving it on the
starboard side; but it is not to be attempted by a stranger; pilots are always ready.
The anchorage is in 6 to 9 fathoms. With a northerly wind, a stream of considerable
strength sets directly out of the channel, which is caused by the great quantity of
water thrown over the reefs by the swell. This bay may be known by it having a
regular row of cocoa-nut trees, close to the sea, and by the town, which stands on the
8.E. side of the bay, on the side of a hill.

OCHO RIOS lies 5 miles to the eastward of St. Anne, and is an anchorage open
to north and N.W. winds. You sail in by the reef which spits off from the east side
of the bay ; then haul up and bring the westernmost part of it to bear N.N.W., or
N.W., and anchor in about 7 fathoms. There is another reef to the northward, but
as the water is very clear your eye may be your guide. This place is frequented by
merchant vessels only, which go there to load.

ORA CABECA lies 9 miles to the eastward of Ocho Rios, and is an anchorage
exposed in like manner to north and N.W. winds. To sail in here from the eastward,
first make Galina Point ; and in order to fall in with that point, if off at sea, bring
the westernmost high land of the Blue Mountains S.S.E., which thus kept on will
lead to the point. To anchor in the roadstead of Ora Cabega, give the small reef on
the east side a berth, and bring the easternmost part to bear N.E. by N., distant
about a quarter of a mile, and a house upon the hill on the port side, 8.K. by S.; the
guard-house on the west side of the river S.W. by S., distant half a mile, and the
westernmost bluff point W. by N., and you will then have 55 fathoms sandy ground.
You may also anchor farther in, under the Red Cliff, bearing W.S.W., in deeper
water.

GALINA POINT lies 33 miles to the westward of Ora Cabega: it is a low point,
rising gradually to a high hill within, which is very remarkable, when seen from the
westward.

PORT MARIA lies to the south-eastward of Galina Point, and is opon to N.N.E,
north, and N.W. winds. ‘To sail in from the eastward, the high island named Cabrita,
which you will see, must be kept a little on the port bow, so as to give the north
part of it a berth of two cables’ length in passing; you may then luff, and run right
in. Anchor under the island, at the distance of a cable or a little more from it, with
its N.W. point bearing about east, in 7 fathoms, and at about a cable and a half from
the main. Small vessels, drawing no more than 6 feet water, may anchor between
the island and the main. The bottom in the outer part of the bay is foul, and many
ships have hove their ballast there, so that there is not room or more than 8 or 10
vessels to ride on clear ground.

Port Maria is a safe roadstead with very good holding ground. Northers send in
a heavy sea, but a strong undertow or outset prevents any strain on thecables. There
is temporary fair weather anchorage § a mile outside the reefs in from 7 to 11 fathoms,
with the church bearing 8. by W. $ W.; Hast extreme of town S.S.H.. Salt Marsh
Hill 8. W. by S.

From Port Maria the coasts trends E.S.E., 6 miles to Blowing Point, and thence
S.S.E. 3 E., 5 miles to Anatto Bay.

(W. InpieEs, Part IT.] N

90 PORT ANTONIO.—PORT MORANT.

ANNATTO BAY has an anchorage exposed to north and N.W. winds. To sail
in, give the reef on its eastern side, which is called the Schoolmaster, a sufficient
berth; then steer down until you bring the Tavern to bear S. by W., or South. When
you are within the Schoolmaster, which is the only shoal in the bay, haul a little to
the eastward, and have your anchor clear, the bank being steep and narrow. Your
first soundings will be 10 or 9 fathoms; so soon as you get 7 fathoms let go your
anchor, and you will have good holding ground, at about a quarter of a mile from
shore. Avoid anchoring on the western edge of the bank, as it will not hold, and
you may be in danger of getting on shore to the westward.

PORT ANTONIO lies about 18 miles to the eastward of Annatto Bay, and about
6 miles to the westward of the N.E. end of Jamaica. Its situation may be known at
a distance, before the lower objects rise to the view, by two remarkable peaks of Blue
Mountains which lie aback of it. It was formerly a \\ing’s port, and there are still
to be seen the remains of the careening wharf, &c. It is formed by nature into two
harbours, divided by a peninsula, on which stands the town of Titchfield, to the
northward of which is the island called Navy Island, about half a mile in length from
east to west.

To sail into the Eastern Harbour, first bring the eastern part of the Blue Mountains
to bear 8.S.W. and steer in that direction until you approach near to Folly Point,
which is the eastern point of the Eastern Harbour. Then bring the church (which
is a large square buiiding on the eastern side of a hill in the S.W. part of the bay),
open a little to the westward of the eastern wharf, bearing 8S.S.W. ; W., and you
will thus go safely into the harbour. But observe, that in appreaching the fort,
which stands on the west side, upon the point of Litchfield Peninsula, to open the
church to the eastward of the wharf: when the fort bears N.W., anchor in 9, 10, or
11 fathoms, good holding ground, ‘The ground is indeed so stiff, that it is somewhat
difficult to get up the anchors.

Itis necessary to pay particular attention to the preceding directions, in order to
avoid a reef which stretches from the east end of Navy Island, as well as from the
point of the peninsula. ‘The eastern side of the harbour is also shoal, and there is a
reef nearly in the middle, with only 10 feet water on it.

The East Harbour is not so secure as the West, because it is exposed to the north
winds, which send in a great swell; but its channel being broader, it is not so difficult
to take. ‘The channel of the West Harbour is not more than 70 fathoms wide, and
must not be attempted without a leading wind.

To sail into the Western Harbour, after having brought the Church well open to
the eastward of the Fort, run under easy sail into the entrance of the channel
between Navy Island and Titchfield Peninsula, bringing a long building, (which is a
storehouse, standing ona hill to the westward,) open southward point of Navy Island,
about W. by 8S. 48. - Keep this mark until the church appears open to the westward
of the Peninsula, then haul round to the 8.W., and anchor in from 7 to 5 fathoms,
wherever you find convenient, on good ground.

There is achannel called the Hog Channel, which leads directly from sea into the
Western Harbour, from the west point of an extensive reef that stretches off
Navy Island; but it is crooked and narrow, and has only 13 or 14 feet water in some
parts of it; it is therefore difficult, and only used by small vessels.

The tides here are not regular, but influenced by the winds.

PORT MORANT is on the S.E. part of the island, at about 10 miles south-
westward from Morant Point. This is a good harbour, but the reefs extend to the
distance of half a mile from shore, on each side of the entrance, and the breadth of
the channel between is only a cable’s length and a half. The leading mark isa
remarkable building which stands upon the top of a hill in a line with the east end
of the easternmost red cliff, bearing N. 4 W. ‘Yo sail in, a ship must lie north, or
N. by E. until the leading mark is on, which can only be done with a sea breeze, or
between the hours of ten and two in the day. Be careful and keep the leading mark

THE CAYMAN ISLANDS. 91
on, exactly as described, and you will have 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, and 4 fathoms water; but if
the mark should be either way open, you would be too near the reefs. You may
anchor with the leading mark on in 63 or 7 fathoms, and Pero Battery, which is on
the eastern side, bearing E.S8.E.

MORANT BAY is 4 miles to the westward of Port Morant: it is exposed to
southerly and westerly winds, but sheltered from all others. To sail in, bring the
church to bear N.W. by N., and run in that direction, passing to the westward of the
breakers which shelter the anchorage. As soon as you have passed them, or are in
the depth of 6 fathoms, ‘haul up north-eastward, and anchor in 6 or 43 fathoms
water, about a quarter of a mile to the southward of the wharf.

About 3 miles to the eastward of this anchorage, is a snug little cove in the reef,
named Fisherman’s Bay; there are 10 fathoms in the entrance, which is only 40
fathoms wide, and about a quarter of a mile to the westward of the point of land.
The course in is N. by W., and when within, there is a space of a quarter of a mile
over, with depth of 4 to 2 fathoms.

THE CAYMAN ISLANDS.

THE CAYMANS are three islands, lying to the north-westward of Jamaica, and
in the track of ships sailing from that island to Cape San Antonio, in the Island of
Cuba; they are between the meridians of 79° 38’, and 81° 30’, and parallels of
19° 14’. and 19° 46’. The westernmost is named the Grand Cayman, from its being
the largest ; the second, the Little Cayman ; and the easternmost the Cayman Brack.

The GRAND CAYMAN is 8 leagues long, and generally about 2% leagues broad ;
the N.E. point is in latitude 19° 22’, the S.E. point 19° 177, and the S.W. point in
latitude 19° 14’. The longitude of the S.W. point is 81° 24’, and that of the east end
81° 7’. Boatswains’ Point, the northernmost point of the island, is on the west side
of the entrance of a large bay called North Sound; the east point cf the entrance,
called Rum Point, lies nearly 23 leagues to the eastward of the former, and 10 miles
W.1N. form the N.E. point. With the exception of the west end, this island is
entirely surrounded by a reef, which at the east end extends a mile and a half from
shore, and on the north side runs directly across the entrance of North Sound, making
it very shallow.

About 23 miles to the northward of the S.W. point, is a place called the Hogsties,
where there is a village named George Town, and a watering place. You may anchor
abreast of the village, in 15 fathoms water, at a cable’s length from shore; but great
caution is necessary in anchoring, lest you drop your anchor on the rocks. The best
place to anchor is about half a mile from shore in from 7 to 12 fathoms, with the
southernmost house in the village bearing E. 3 S.,or E. by S. Even here the bottom
is rocky, but you may see the ground, as the water is very clear ; it will, however, be
advisable to steady the ship with a small anchor. Refreshments may be obtained
here; as fowl, turtle, yams, plantains, &c., but neither beef nor mutton. Water may
be procured from a well about 20 yards from the beach, the well bearing N. by E.,
or N.N.E, from the anchorage.

It is necessary to observe, that in hauling round the 8.W. point, a sufficient berth
must be given to the small cay that lies off it: there is nothing else to fear in
sailing to the anchorage, but do not stretch far beyond the village, as there is a shoal.
In the day time, as the water is clear, every danger may be seen. It is useless to
heave the lead before you can see the bottom ; you will find 16 or 17 fathoms at ebout

three-quarters of a mile cff shore, whence it shallows gradually till you get into 8
fathoms, where you may come-to in one of the white patches.

THE LITTLE CAYMAN.

The land is very low, and many ships have passed the island in clear moonlight
nights without seeing it; hence, a near approach to the eastern part, during the night,
would be attended with great danger. Indeed, every degree of caution should be
taken, as it is very common for ships to be out of their reckoning, particularly with
light winds and variable currents, which frequently prevail hereabout.

Bank or SOUNDINGS OFF THE WEsT END oF THE GRAND CaYMAN.—Lieutenant
B. Bagot, commanding H.M.S. Pickle, whilst cruising off the Grand Cayman in Feb-
ruary, 1833, struck soundings in 17 fathoms, on a bank off the west end of the island,
that did not appear then to be laid down in the charts. The Pickle was anchored on
the bank with the following bearings :—The N.W. point of the Grand Cayman N.E.
by E. 2 E.; the S.W. Point E.2S. Latitude 19°17’, longitude 81° 56’.

From the §.W. end of the Grand Cayman to Cape Corrientes the true bearing and
Se ag are, N.W. 3 W., 74 leagues; and to Cape San Antonio N.W. 2 W., 84
eagues.

Tur LITTLE CAYMAN.—From the N.E. point of the Grand Cayman to the
west end of the Little Cayman the bearing and distance are said to be E.N.E. 4 E.,
21 leagues, and that it thence extends 7 miles E.N.E.; and nearly 2 leagues on the
same bearing is the west end of Cayman Brack, which extends also E.N.E. about 3
leagues, and has a reef projecting to a considerable distance from the east end, having
between the two a good channel with 20 fathoms water; but a reef runs off the
east end of the Little Cayman. The Cayman Brack is the boldest of the two, but
they are both very low, and can be seen only at a very short distance. Of these we
possess no further description, as they are seldom visited by any but turtlers. Py
the late Spanish chart of Captain Don José del Rio, the east end of Cayman Brack is
placed in latitude 19°44’, at the distance of 38 leagues S. 87° W. true, from Cape
de Cruz in Cuba.

PICKLE BANK.—Licutenant Holland, R.N., commanding the Pickle schooner,
reports having struck soundings at 7h. P.M. on the evening of the 19th of August,
1840, on his passage from Port Royal, Jamaica, to Havana. He had 16 fathoms,
hard sand, and continued sounding in 15, 14, and 17 fathoms, for an extent of 2.miies,
steering a W. by N. 34 N. course. Lost soundings at 7h. 40 P.M., and observed lati-
tude by Polaris to be 20° 17’ 20/, latitude by D. R. 20° 20’, longitude computed by.
D, R. from good forenoon’s sights, 80° 23’ 0’. On looking at the charts, late
English and Spanish, he found a small patch laid down in latitude, English, 20° 10’,
Spanish, 20° 11’, and longitude English, 80° 2’, Spanish, 80° 38’, as having been seen
in 1800, and concludes that this must be the same over which he passed, but which
was always considered as doubtful.

THE ISLAND OF CUBA.

CUBA is the largest Island in the West Indies, and is situate at the western
extremity of the multitude of islands, cays, and banks, which separate the Carribean
Sea from the Atlantic Ocean. Its length from Cape Maysi on the east to Cape St.
Antonio on the west, is about 220 leagues, its breadth is very unequal, being from 15
to 86 leagues. It is intersected nearly throughout its whole length, by a range of
irregularly high mountains, decreasing towards the west, from the basis of which the
country opens into extensive meadows, or beautiful plains and savannas, in which are
many plantations ; but on account of the indolence and bad policy of its possessors,
uot a tenth part of the island is yet cleared.. Forests of mahogany, ebony, and cedar
(of the latter, some of the largest trees in the West Indies), are plentiful; the plains

FHE ISLAND OF CUBA. 93

are watered with a great number of rivers and rivulets, which produce coolness,
verdure, and fruitfulness ; so that the fields are covered with flowers and odoriferous
plants throughout the year. The climate is hot and dry during the greater part of
the year; rain often descends in torrents, from July to September, and occasional
showers fall fora month or two before and after that period. In December and
January, the air is much cooled by the north winds.

The capital, HAVANA, is situate on the north coast, and has an excellent harbour.
St. JAGO DE CuBA, on the south coast, was formerly the capital; it has now fallen
into decay, but still has a considerable trade.

The winding and indented shores of Cuba form a number of excellent harbours, but
the coasts are extremely foul, excepting the following parts :—On the south side from
Punta de Maysi, or Cape Maize, to Cabo de Cruz; the N.E. part from Cape Maize to
Point Maternillo; and the north coast, from the Port of Mariel to Mantanzas. Almost
all the other parts have, to a considerable distance, shallows, cays, and reefs, so
thickly scattered and numerous, that in several places they form barriers, which
prevent access to the shores of the island; this will be best understood by reference
to the chart.

We shall first commence with a description of the south coast, from Punta de Maysi,
westward, to Cape San Antonio, including the Isle of Pines, with the cays and reefs;
then of the N.W. and North coasts, from Cape San Antonio, eastward, to Havana
and Mantanzas ; and, finally, with the N.E. coast, from Punta de Maysi, westward,
to. Mantanzas and Havana.

The following is chiefly from the Derrotero de las Antillas :-—

PUNTA DE MAYSI, or CAPE MAIZE, is the most easterly point of the east
front of Cuba. The point itself is a low beach, and cannot be clearly seen until you
are yery near to it, A reef extends from it nearly a mile to the eastward; and
advancing towards it in the night was formerly very unsafe, unless you had previously

noticed the high lands, which rise in the interior of the country ; but the light will
now warn the mariner of his approach.

Light.—A lighthouse is erected on the east point of Cape Maysi, showing a fixed
light, elevated 128 feet above the sea, and may be seen 17 miles off. The tower is
circular, on an octagonal base.

A little to the southward of Cape Maize, at about half a mile from it, the coast
begins to be high and clean, and it trends about S.W. 4 W., 62 miles, forming a
small bay with a sandy beach, named Cala de Overado, From this bay the shore
trends. about 8. by W. $ W., 4 miles to Punta Negra, whence it turns to S.W. by
W. 3% W., about 4 miles more, to Punta Celeta; from which, W. 3 8., 25 miles, lies
Point Savanna la Mer; and 4, miles W. $8, from it is the Port of Baitiqueri.

From. Cape Maize to Punta Negra, the shore should not be approached nearer than
2 leagues, as the coast lies completely open to the breezes, and along which there is
no.anchorage. From Punta Negra to Baitiqueri there is no risk in running along
shore at the distance of a mile; and along this part, and to leeward of the various
points thereon, you may anchor in any depth of water that suits you, from 35 to 7
fathoms; but the best ground is in 16 fathoms, where you will be at a good distance
from the shore. In this part seyeral rivers disembogue, from which you may obtain
excellent water, and plenty of fire-wood may be procured.

Cape Guanos, or Ocoa Point, lies to the eastward of the Punta Caleta of the Spanish,
and, as well as Ocoa Bay, is not noticed in the Derrotero ; yet it has been said by a
British navigator,—That within this cape is the Bay of Ocoa, in which there is good
anchorage. ‘The anchoring mark is the easternmost point, distant about a mile and a
half, in a line with the Table Land of St. Nicholas Mole, bearing E.S.E. The depths
are from 35 to 7 fathoms, but 16 or 17 fathoms are the best, and plenty of fish may
be caught with hook and line. ‘Two rivulets of fresh water run into the bay, the one
named Rio. do Mel, or Honey River, lying 2 or 3.miles to the westward of the anchor-
age; the other, which: lies nearer, is: to the eastward, at the bottom of the eastern-

94 THE HARBOUR OF BAITIQUERI.

most gully; but it is generally dry from the infrequency of rain. There are at most
times, on the coast, Spanish hunters and shepherds, of whom you may purchase fresh
provisions.

THe HARBOUR oF BAITIQUERI is very small, with a very narrow entrance ;
the depths are 15 and 20 feet, and therefore can receive none but small vessels; it is
well sheltered from all winds, and at the farther end has a rivulet of the same name,
from whence water may be obtained. There is somewhat more than a cable’s length
between the two outer points of the entrance, but from the windward point a rocky
reef runs off, with from 10 to 17 feet on the edge of it; and the leeward point also
sends off a reef about a quarter of a cable. Between these two reefs lies the entrance
channel, which is only 50 yards wide. Having passed this narrow part, which is
about a cable’s length, it widens as you approach the two interior points; and the
depth of water admits of approaching the shore.

Mr. W. C. Middlemist, late Master of H.M.S. Isis, says,—*The Harbour of
Baitiqueri is very difficult to distinguish at any distance from shure, along which you
may coast with great safety at half a mile; at that distance you may get soundings
of from 19 to 11 fathoms; the bottom may be seen very plainly, consisting of large
spread-leaf coral and sand, with some patches of weed. There is no conspicuous
object as a mark directly over the harbour, but a little to the eastward is a remark-
able round lump, apparently rising from the beach, which is here of white sand.

The entrance is from N.N.W. to N.W. by N., situate between two reefs, the
easternmost of which is the largest; this breaks, having in many places rocks just
above water, on which large trees and pieces of timber have fastened, and appears,
even when close to it, to forma bar right across. This reef stretches off Point
Barlovento a short half cable, and has from 3 to 14 fathom close to it. The leeward
or westernmost reef is about a quarter of a cable off shore, and has from 2 to 13
fathom close to it. Between these reefs is the channel, which is not more than 30 or
25 fathoms wide, and about two-thirds of a cable in length. The eye must be your
guide, for the channel is so narrow and short that your vessel would be on shore
without this precaution. I found no more than 3} fathoms in the channel. In going
in, the first cast we got was 10, then 9, 7, 54, and 4, which is close to the entrance;
after you are through, and have opened the west end of the harbour, you will have
37, 3, and 2¢ in the middle. It did not appear to me that any part of this harbour
opened to the eastward of north, but rounded to the S.W. and N.W.

In the S.W. part there is a small river, which only affords water after heavy rains.
To the N.W. there is a landing place, but completely hidden by bushes. Schooners
of a light draught may go in.”

From the Harbour of Baitiqueri the coast trends about S.W. by W. 2 W., a
distance of 5 miles, to Punta de la Tortuguilla, from which it follows W. 5 8., &
distance of 3 miles, to the river Yateras. From this it runs about S.W. 2 S., 4 miles
to Punta de Malano; and at 3 miles W.45S. from it lies the entrance of Puerto
Escondido, or Hidden Port. All the coast between Baitiqueri and Port Escondido is
clean, and may be passed at the distance of a mile.

PORT ESCONDIDO is an anchorage sheltered from all winds, forming in the
interior various bays fit for all classes of vessels. The entrance is very narrow, for
between the outer points it is only one cable’s length, and as each of the points sends
out a reef, of which the windward one runs off one-third of a cable, the channel is
only 90 yards wide, but luckily it presents no windings ; and the whole length of the
narrow strait is not more than a cable and a half. To enter it you must steer
N. 43° W., which may always be dcne with the wind free, although the breeze should
even be at N.E. To enter this harbour, it is better to order a boat to be placed on
the outer point of the windward reef, which is about mid-length of the channel, and
it will serve as a mark to sailin by. You have then only to bring the vessel’s head
N. 43° W., and run in that direction, passing close to the boat, until you have passed
the inner point to leeward, where you may anchor in 6 or 63 fathoms, on clay.

GUANTANAMO. 95

As there are no leading marks in this harbour, it is necessary to keep in the mid-
channel. The entrance is very narrow, and sufficient sea room should be taken to alter
the vessel’s course from West to N. 43° W., in order to enter the channel. For this
purpose we advise, although the coast to windward of the entrance may be passed at
half a cable’s length, that it should not be passed at less than 3 or 4; then, although
in luffing, the vessel may pass to leeward of N. 43° W., yet there will be room
sufficient to rectify this, by getting to windward, so as to gain the proper bearing,
before you are between the points, which is requisite, as the channel cannot otherwise
be passed without danger. Any one desirous of proceeding farther into the interior
of the harbour, instead of bringing up in the anchorage just described, may readily
do so by the eye, by towing, or even under sail, there being no difficulty ; but it is
necessary to consult a plan of the harbour for further guidance.

As there is no trade or commerce here, it is seldom that vessels are bound into it ;
and if in the event of bad weather are obliged to seck anchorage, we would advise
every exertion to be made to reach Guantanamo; for, if it be difficult at any time to
enter this port, it must be much more so in storms and obscure weather ; and it would
not be strange if, without a pilot, or even with one, a vessel might be driven on one
of the reefs at the entrance; or, what is worse, might get embayed, and on the rocks
at some point of the coast, which might be mistaken for the entrance of this harbour.

GUANTANAMO, or CUMBERLAND HARBOUR.—From Port Escondido to
Guantanamo, the coast trends west, inclined to the south, for the space of 12 miles;
it is very clear, and forms some small sandy coves. The Port of Guantanamo, called
by the English, Cumberland Bay, is excellent, having within it an archipelago, in the
harbours of which a number of squadrons may anchor, entirely separate from each
other. The mouth or entrance is spacious, inasmuch as between the two exterior
points, it is almost two miles in extent. The east point is very clean, and may be
approached without fear, as there is no danger but what is visible. From this point
the coast turns N. 3 W., about 14 mile, whence it changes to the eastward to form
the harbour. On the windward side of the entrance, at about half a mile within the
outer point, a rocky shoal stretches from shore, on the edge of which are from 4 to 6
fathoms water. ‘This shoal extends to the west somewhat more than half a mile ; the
most projecting part lying EB. } N. from the mouth of the River Guantanamo, which
is on the leeward side, about half a mile within the outer point. On this side there
is also a reef of rocks, which extends from without the point to within, and to the
distance of 2 cables’ length from it.

As you approach the entrance from the southward, you will perceive in the middle
a remarkable light-coloured cliff on the side of a hill, at some distance inland, which
from the westward resembles a kite. To sailin, bring this cliff to bear N. by W., or
N. by W. 4 W., and run in with that bearing, until you open Fisherman’s Point,
which is sandy, has two huts on it, and cannot be mistaken, for there is no other
sandy point on that side. Having opened Fisherman’s Point, you may steer N. by
E. 4 E., or N.N.&., until the huts bear E. by S., then haul up N.E., or N.E. by E.
for the anchorage, where you may lie in 6 or 7 fathoms, on mud, with Fisherman’s
Point bearing S. by E., or S.S.E., the west head of the harbour about S.W. 3 W., and
the light-coloured cliff from West to W. by S.

A reef lies off the point a short distance to the S.W. of Fisherman’s Point,
which must be avoided; it is about 13 or 2 cables in length, N. by W., and
S. by E., and 20 to 30 fathoms in breadth ; has 16 or 17 feet on the shoalest part,
34 fathoms within it, and 5 fathoms close to its outer edge, which is about 22 or 3
cables’ length from shore. The marks for its south end are the two huts on Fisher-
man’s Point in a line, bearing N.E. by E., and the point within the east head 8. by
E.; the marks for the north end are—the N.E. hut about its breadth open to the
northward of the other hut, bearing N.E. by E. 2 E., and the point within the east
head 8. § E.

Ships from the eastward may pass so near to the east head as convenient, there
being 9 and 10 fathoms close to it, but must run to the westward, and bring on the

i

96

before-mentioned bearing of the cliff before they run in, in order to avoid the reef
just described.

Ships from the westward may approach the west head to two cables’ length, but
when they are within it, must haul more to the eastward, in order to avoid a flat that
extends from Augusta or Guantanamo River, nearly in a direction towards the light-
coloured cliff, and to nearly one-third across the harbour, towards Fisherman’s Point.
It may be approached by the lead, as the soundings towards it are regular, but do not
approach the eastern shore nearer than three cables’ length. There is no bottom
at a short distance, without the points of the entrance; between them are 20 or 18
fathoms, decreasing regularly to 8 or 7 fathoms.

‘Water only can be obtained, and that by going 10 or 12 miles up on the eastern
side of the harbour to a small river, named Water River.

The following remarks on Guantanamo are by a correspondent of the Nautical
Magazine, 1844, p. 611 :—

“This harbour is one of the most extraordinary inlets in the island of Cuba, or
perhaps anywhere, having many hiding recessés within its entrance. That so
perfect and uncommonly fine sheet of water, or rather series of deep-water lagoons,
as this inlet presents, and which the celebrated Admiral Vernon was pleased to re-
name in honour of the royal soldier (Cumberland), should be left by the Spaniards in
the same state it and the surrounding country were found at the time of the discovery,
would seem remarkable if we were unacquainted with the fact that scarcely an island
in any part of the world has on its shores so many land-locked harbours, or sea-lakes,
as, I believe, the seaman’s old friend, Dampier, termed this class of enclosed waters.

By the early English adventurers it was called Walthenham Harbour, and it has
always been considered as the ‘refuge’ haven (by way of eminence) of the station for
vessels during the season of hurricanes; and, unquestionably, as a place of retreat, it
affords good shelter, especially from East round to N.W., as I have experiericed during
one of those awful storms, but it is inferior to St. Jago in this respect.

On the starboard hand in the channel of entrance, the land at the base of the little
hills forms a shelf, the margin of which is cliffy throughout; on this side, more than
half-way in, there is a sunken rock to be avoided, otherwise the passage is clear. At
a distance of a few miles the position of the harbour may be readily known by
several remarkable mounds of reddish-brown colour intermixed with green. The
port side of the channel is low and wooded. Augusta River (the Rio Aqua Anima of
the Spaniards) debouches near to the entrance.”

From Guantanamo the coast runs W. 3 S., is clear, and may be passed at the dis-
tance of a mile, to Punta de Berracos, which is distant 26 miles from it. This point
may be known by a morro or hill which rises on it. From Punta de Berracos the
coast bends to the northward, and forms the Bay of Cabo Baxo, or Low Cape, wherice
it trends westward to the River Juragua. ‘he intermediate coast between Cabo
Baxo and Juragua is named Los Altares, or the Altars, because it forms three separate
beachy bays, separated from each other by high scarped mounts. The River Juragua
is 10 miles distant from Point Berracos. From the River Juragua, the coast continues
west for the distance of 12 miles, to the entrance of the Port of St. Jago de Cuba:
it is all clean, and may be passed at a mile distant; the Rivers de Sardinero and de
Aguadares disembogue in this space, and near the latter may be seen some small
houses, inhabited by water-carriers.

The HARBOUR cf St. JAGO DE CUBA is very good, but the entrance
being very narrow and crooked, is difficult to take. On the east point stands the
Morro Castle, and somewhat farther in that of the Estrella, or Star Castle, which is
separated from the first by a bay, at the end of which is another small fort or battery.

THE HARBOUR OF ST. JAGO DE CUBA.

- The coast to windward sends off a rocky shoal, which extends from the Morro Point

about 25 cables, and the coast to leeward sends off another, which stretches from the
point to the south about one cable. Between these two shoals lies the channel. At
its entrance it is a cable’s length in width, and farther in is reduced by about one-

CAPE DE CRUZ. 97

third of a cable; so that when abreast of the bay, between the Morro and Estrella
Castles, which is the narrowest part, it is only two-thirds of a cable in width; and
from this it continues of the same breadth, until past Cape Smith, when the harbour
begins to open.

Light.—A Lighthouse, exhibiting a revolving light, has been established about
800 feet eastward of the Morro Castle, on the east side of the entrance of the Harbour
of St. Jago de Cuba. The light is elevated 226 feet above the level of the sea, revolves
in two minutes, and may be seen in clear weather 5 leagues. The building is of iron,
painted white, being 20 feet in height from base to vane.

Directions.—To make this harbour, sail at half a league or two miles off the shore,
until the Estrella Castle bears N.E. § N., and steering that course, you will enter the
channel formed by the reefs ; but so soon as abreast of the Morro Point—which pass at
a quarter of a cable’s length—begin to keep away; so that when up, abreast of the
battery, which is at the end of the bay, the vessel’s head shall be N. 4 W., which
course it is necessary to continue, until you are past Cape Smith, when you may
anchor.

The necessity (from the crookedness of the channel) of keeping away four points,
renders it needful, especially for a large vessel, that she may have sufficient space to
make the turn in; for this purpose we advise, that so soon as abreast of the Morro
Point, to keep away ; neglecting this, you run the risk of getting ashore at Estrella
Castle, It is necessary to remark, that the vessel’s head should not be kept away to
the N.  W.at once, though it may sometimes be done under favourable circumstances ;
as you might be on shore on the steep edge of the Leeward Reef; the distance from
the Morro Point to abreast of the battery, at the bottom of the bay, on the east, being
but one cable.

At the bottom of this harbour is the city of Sr. Jaco DE CuBA, which is the most
ancient city the Spaniards had in the island.

The assigned position of the Morro Castle is latitude 19° 57’ 42”, longitude
75° 54’ 20",

From St. Jago de Cuba, the coast continues to the west, forming various bays, but
their anchorages are of little consideration, the knowledge of which is alone useful to
ccasters. Upon this coast are the high copper mountains, Montanus del Cobre,
which are about 11 miles distant from St. Jago; these mountains, in clear weather,
have been seen from various points of the north coast of Jamaica; and thus it is
known that they can be seen more than 33 leagues off. Forty miles west from
St. Jago de Cuba rises another high land, named Tarquino, which is an excellent
landmark,

CAPE DE CRUZ.—The point Cape de Cruz is the last place on this part of
the island, where the coast is clean; it is 33 leagues distant from St. Jago; and
you may run along the whole intermediate coast at the distance of a league, or even
less; but, as there is no motive to induce one to go so near, it seems more advisable
for those bound to the westward, to run along at a proportionate distance of 2 or 3
leagues.

Light.—A lighthouse is erecting upon Cape de Cruz intended to show a fixed
light, to be visible at the distance of about 15 miles. At present a provisional fixed
light is shown at 46 feet above the level of the sea, and visible 6 miles.

A Rock orF CAPE DE CRUZ, in latitude 19° 25’, and longitude 78° 9’, was seen on
the 20th of March, 1850, by Mons. P. Jarrot, master of the French barque La Jeune
Estella, who reports that he suddenly came upon a large rock, which at first he
mistook for a sail close upon him ; by a hasty manceuvre he escaped collision, but in
the hurry he had not time to ascertain the soundings in its immediate vicinity. He

[W. Inpigs, Parr II. ] 10)

98 CAPE DE CRUZ.

affirms that none of the charts contain any information of this dangerous tenant of
the ocean.

From Cape de Cruz the coast turns to the N.E., and forms a great bay, in the
bottom of which the river Cauto disembogues; it afterwards trends to the West,
North, and West, to Trinidad; from whence it again first bends to the northward,
and afterward to the southward of West; continuing westward to Cape St. Antonio,
which is the westernmost point of the island.

At Cape de Cruz a white bank commences, which terminates at Trinidad. Upon
this bank rise cays and reefs without number, which form channels of more or less
width. he principal cays on the edge of the bank are those called the Cayos de las
docé Leguas, or the Twelve League Cays, which occupy an extent of 20 leagues, in
nearly a W.N.W. direction.

To COAST ALONG THE CAYOS DE LAS DOCE T.EGUAS.—Directions.—Being three
miles to the southward of Cape de Cruz, steer W.N.W. 2 W., which course will take
you along the edge of the bank ; and having run 125 miles in this direction, alter your
course to N.W. 2 N., with which you will enter upon the bank in 40 fathoms, on sand
and rocks; continue on this course 23 miles, when, with the edge in sight, you will
leave it in 50 fathoms nearly. Still keep on the same course for 17 miles more, and

ou will again find 40 fathoms, or less; and shortly afterwards see Levesa Cay to the
N.N.B., and ahead will be seen the Eastern Head of the Cayos de las docé Leguas.

Having recognized these two points, you must run along on the bank, but without
getting into less than 4 fathoms, until you are 3 miles to the south of the Kastern
Head, and in 7 fathoms water, over a bottom of sand; you must then run W. ‘by N.
With this course you will shortly run off the bank, and may keep along the Cayos de
las docé Leguas, at the distance of a league, without fear, and having run 213 miles,
steer W.N.W., 184 miles, and you will then have the Boca de Caballones open ;
it may easily be known by being broader than any other to the eastward, and because
the south and east point of its entrance are very low, with edges of Soboruco rock.*

Having ascertained your situation, from seeing this boca or channel, you may
continue coasting along by the cays, at the distance of 3 miles, continuing on the
preceding course, and having run 21 miles, you will perceive to the northward a great
opening formed by the cays, which is the Boca Grande: passing it, pursue the same
course, keeping the Cinco Balas, or Five Balls’ Cays, in sight, at the distance of 2
leagues, and observing that a reef extends 4 miles to the 8.W. from Cayo Breton:
this is the westernmost of the Cayos de las docé Leguas. Nearly in a line between
Cayo Breton and Puerto Casilda, on the main of Cuba, lies the Placer de la Paz, a
sand-bank, having on its eastern part good anchorage, and not less than 14 fathoms,
on sand and shells.

Should night come on when you are in the vicinity of Cape de Cruz, or to the south
of it, as before assumed, you must steer W, 3 S., 14 miles, and thence N.W. 2 W., in
order to keep completely clear of the Cayos de las docé Leguas. Continue this
course till daylight, then change it so as to make and recognize these cays, and thus
get into the route already recommended. Should night overtake you between Cape
de Cruz and the Eastern Head, when it might be desirable to anchor on the bank,
you may do so on any part of it, observing only that the edges of the bank are rocky,
and that to get clean ground, you should run upon it, into between 20 and 10
fathoms, on sand.

If night comes on, when you are coasting by the Cayos de las docé Leguas,
steer W. + S., until you are from 3 to 3} leagues from them, and even then con-
tinue the same course, considering that hereabout the current sets N.E. and 8.W.,
and if the tide happens to set in, it is very possible to get aground on the reef.

* Soboruco is a hard rock, resembling sponge or honeycomb, formed into sharp cutting
points.
