THE CITY OF TRINIDAD. 99

When in sight of the Caballones Channel, and you wish to anchor in its mouth,
from case of emergency, you can do so without getting into less than 3 fathoms, on
sand.

The CITY of TRINIDAD is situate on high ground, about 33 miles from the
sea. At little more than half a mile to the north of it, the River Guaurabo, or of
Trinidad passes, and disembogues into the sea, ‘Trinidad has open communication
into the sea by this river, the mouth of which is scarcely 8 miles distant; by Puerta
Casilda, from which it is distant 24 miles, and by Puerta de Masio, the distance
from which is 44 miles. The mouth of the river Guaurabo is to the north of the
point of Maria Aguilar, at which terminate the White Grounds extending from Cape
de Cruz. The harbours of Casilda and Masio are to the eastward of this point, and
to arrive at them, it is necessary to enter upon the White Grounds.

Directions.—To avoid the White Grounds, a ship, at about 3 leagues south from
Cape de Cruz, and intending to proceed to Trinidad, ought to steer W.25., 24 miles,
when having run thus far, should luff up, or alter to N.W. 3 W. With this course, and
a distance of 31 leagues, she will be 10 or 12 miles from Cayo Grande; ard although,
with these courses, she may pass the edge of the White Grounds at the distance of
10 or 12 miles, she ought, nevertheless, to navigate with a good look out and the
deep sea-lead going, especially by night, lest she should be driven on it by the
current.

Having recognized Cayo Grande, continue the N.W. course until you are S.W.
from Cayo Breton, which is the westernmost of the group of cays, and lies N.W.
from Cayo Grande, and is separated by an opening or break in the reef, called Boca
Grande. When Cayo Grande bears N.E., at the distance of 9 miles, a N.N.W. 3 W.
course, 38 miles, will bring you to a spot, from which the Pan de Azucar, or
Sugar-loaf Hill of Sancti Espiritus, will appear in one with the hills of Bonao,
which are some high ridges immediately to the westward of it. In this navigation
the Cayo Zarza and Cayo Machos will be seen from without ; and when the leading
mark just mentioned is on, you will still be in sight of the Machos, and another very
small cay, named Puga; this latter is very remarkable by the breaking of the sea upon
it, and it will bear about N. 3 W.,a mile distant. From the samé spot, the Cayo
Blanco will be seen, bearing about N.N.W. 4 W. This cay is remarkable, both
as being the westernmost cay of them all, and because it is bordered with white
rocks.

The best place to enter upon the White Grounds is between Cayo Puga and Cayo
Blanco; steer so as to pass about half a mile, or rather less, from the reef of Puga,
which is always seen; and in the passage you will always have 6 fathoms water.
Having passed Puga, you must steer N. 3 W., in order to anchor in 4 fathoms, sand
and weed, with the south part of Cayo Blanco W. 3 8., that is, if the approach of
night, or waiting for a pilot.

In the route between Cayo Grande and Cayo Blanco, there is little difficulty for any
one who wishes to enter upon the bank by the Boca Grande, provided his vessel does
not draw more than 14 or 15 feet water ; and it may sometimes be convenient to run
in here to anchor, under the shelter of Cayo Grande, or that of Cinco Balas, in case
of an appearance of bad weather coming on, which will frequently happen, and which
is much to be feared in the months of August, September, and October ; or, if he does
not choose to anchor under the shelter of these cays, he may run on until he recog-
nizes Cayo Rabihorcado, which he will pass on his port hand, and will presently see
Cayo Burgao, which he will pass to the eastward of, and may then run N.N.W. 3 W.,
without fear, being guided in running by the vessel’s draught of water ; and entering
by the Machos Channel, he may run for Masio, or Puerta Casilda, just as he thinks
proper. The bank has very excellent and well-sheltered anchorages between the
Maganos de Minati and Zarza de Afuera.

Between Cayo Blanco de Zarza and the coast there is anchorage, as also in various
other places hereabout, which will be found more or less commodious, according to the

100 THE CITY OF TRINIDAD.

winds and draught of the vessel. The cays in general have but little elevation
above the surface of the water, and their low edges present no extent of beach;
but rocky banks stretch out a short distance from their points, excepting those which
form the Machos Channel, which, within the narrow strait, are very clean.

The coast from Point Jatibonico, westward to that of Pasabanao, forms an exten-
sive bay with a depth of 24 and 3 fathoms. The shore is overflowed and covered
with mangroves. At Point Jatibonico, the river of the same name disembogues ;
and to obtain water, it is necessary to go a league up the river. To the west of
Pasabanao is the Estera de las Caovas or Mahogany Creek, in which small vessels,
not drawing more than 6 feet, may find shelter from the 8.E. winds. After Estero
de las Caovas follows Point Manati, on which are some wells of tolerably sweet
water ; Point Monati with Point Tolete, which lies to the westward of it, forms a
little bay, about the middle of which is the mouth of Estero Neuvo, or New Creek.
The Point Tolete and that of Zarza (to the westward) form another bay, in which is
the Estero de San Marcos, with very little water at its entrance. On the eastern
part of Point Zarza the river Zarza disembogues ; by this river much traffic is carried
on with the town of Sancti Espiritus, which is distant from the entrance 13 leagues.
The water of this river is not sweet within 8 leagues of the sea. To the westward of
the point Zarza is the creek of the same name, with a depth of 7 feet, where small
vessels may find shelter from the S.E., as they may also to the westward of the same
point, under the lee of a reef, which runs out to the W.S.W. from it, to the distance
of a mile, and which forms a bay, with a depth of 3 and 33 fathoms on clay.

To the westward of Point Zarza is Point Caney, with which it forms a little bay,
with 3 and 5 fathoms, on clay and grass. To the west of Point Caney is the Estero
or Creek of the same name, with 7 feet water: south of this point is Cayo Blanco de
Zarza; and between the reef which runs out from it and the point, there is a good
channel, navigable for all classes of vessels, which, as before said, may find good shelter
to the west of the cay. To the westward of Point Caney is that of Ciego, which
forms with it a bay, with from 3 to 5 fathoms water: in the middle of it is the river
Tallabacoa, which has very little water in the dry season; and that of a brook, ata
very short distance to the westward of Point Ciego, is always preferable.

Next to Point Ciego follows that of Iguanojo, at which the river of the same name
disembogues, the water of which is excellent; but to obtain it, it is necessary to
ascend the river a league. Westward from the Point Iguanojo is the Point Agabama,
to the eastward of which runs out the Cayos de Tierra, or Cays of the Land, which
with Point Iguanojo form a bay, called San Pedro, with a depth of 3% to 6 fathoms,
on clay. In this bay are the landing places of Tolloso, Golonduro, Seyba, and Brujas,
which serve for the traffic carried on here in wood, tobacco, and salt. The Cayos de
Tierra with Point Agabama, form another small bay with a depth of 7, 6, and 4
fathoms, on clay and sand. At Point Agabama is the river of the same name, the
water of which is not sweet within 6 leagues from its mouth.

The shores from Agabama to Point Casilda are overflowed and covered with man-
groves; and from Point Casilda to Guaurabo, they are of sand and scarped rock.
Poterillo, which is the highest point of the mountains above Trinidad, may be seen
in clear days, at the distance of 21 leagues, and together with that the Pan de Azucar
or Sugar Loaf, are excellent marks for ascertaining your position.

From Boea Grande the reef admits of no entrance on the shoal ground, as far as
the Outer Zarza; but between it and the Outer Machos, there is a spacious entrance,
and depth sufficient for every class of vessel. Nevertheless, if when in sight of Cayo
Breton, and to leeward of Boca Grande, you wish to anchor on the bank for the
purpose of regulating the time for making Puga and Cayo Blanco, or for any other
cause, it may be done by steering east, towards Cayo Breton, until the N.W. part of
that cay bear E. 5 N.; but in steering thus, take care and sound frequently, until
you have from 4 to 3 fathoms, sand; then you may anchor. If the wind will not
allow you to steer directly east for the anchorage, and you are obliged to work to

PORT MASIO—PORT CASILDA. 101

windward, observe not to prolong the tacks to the northward longer than until the
N.W. part of the cay bears E.S.E., nor to the southward farther than until the same
point of the cay bears N.E. 3 E.; between these bearings you may work, tack and
tack, until you reach the anchorage, in which there is shelter from the winds, from
north round by east, to §.W., by the reefs and cays, which lie in these directions.
All these reefs are seen above water, and the outer part of them is nearly 3 miles
§.W. from the westernmost part of Cayo Breton.

Any large vessel seeking shelter from the weather, or any other cause, upon the
bank, may enter between the Outer Zarza and Outer Machos, and may run over the
whole of the interior of the bank, there being sufficient depth for every class of vessel.

TrpEs.—We shall now observe that the tides produce currents more or less rapid,
and in various directions, according to the channels which are formed by the reefs ;
but they are always ‘of little importance, as the greatest rise of the water, which
is at the time of the new moon, is not more than a foot and a half, except with 8.E.
winds, when it rises 3 fect.

PORT MASIO.—Directions.—To enter Port Masio, being within the bank, steer
N. 4 W., until the south part of Cayo Blanco is at W.7S., and the top of Puga
§.E. 4S., in which situation you will find 4 fathoms, on clay and weeds. ‘Thence steer
N. 49° W., and run for the middle of the channel of Masio, which is formed
by a ridge of rocks extending N.W. ? W. from Cayo Blanco, and a shoal with
some heads nearly even with the water, on the land side; and you ought to continue
thus until Point Jobabo bears N.$ W., which point may readily be known by a
sandy beach. From this situation you must luff up, towards the west point of the
entrance to the port; and steering N. by W.? W., take care to keep very little
away, until you have passed the Point of the Guard-house, that you may avoid the
reef which stretches off it. Having passed this, keep the ship’s head as before
directed, toward the west point, until near the entrance, when you may run up the
middle of it by the eye, Having run up the middle of the entrance, luff up N. by
E., until having passed the points, and being in 4 or 33 fathoms, you may anchor
where it suits you, being cautious only of a clay bank, which runs off the landing
place on the west shore, the extremity of which is in one with the west point of the
port, bearing North and South.

Passing in for Masio, you leave the Bay of Caballones on the starboard; and if you
wish to anchor in it for shelter from the North and 8.E. winds, you have only to keep
in the middle between the points which form it, and steering N.E. by E. 4 E., anchor
immediately you are in 33 fathoms, on clay.

PORT CASILDA.—To enter Port Casilda, observe the same route as that given
for Port Masio, until the south part of Cayo de Guayos comes on with the south part
of the mainland of Casilda, in which direction is the break or mouth of Jababo, by
which you may enter; run in in the middle of the mouth by the eye and the lead.
The entrance is 110 yards wide, with a depth of 4 fathoms. Being at the west part
of this opening, at one cable’s distance, steer W.S.W., sailing in 6, 7, and 8 fathoms,
clay, until you bring Point Casilda on with the north point of Cayo Ratones; then
steer for the westernmost part of the City of Trinidad, avoiding the rocky reef which
runs out §.S.W. from Cayo Guayos, which will be passed when the south part of this
cay is on with the south part of Tobaco ; and then make towards the easternmost part
of the city, until the south part of Cayo Ratones comes on with the westernmost
part of the high mountains of Rio Honda, when you must steer towards these
objects to pass clear of the shoal Emmedio; and following the same mark, with the
precaution of keeping a little to starboard, you will go clear of Point Casilda, which
is somewhat foul; and proceeding on for the interior, go to the southward of Cayo
Ratones, allowing a berth to its south point, after passing which, you may steer
N.W. 4 W., and soon afterwards anchor in 3 or 33 fathoms on clay.

102 GUAUROBO.

Tf well acquainted, and circumstances require it, you may anchor in any part of
these channels, on a bottom of clay. You may also take Port Casilda, entering by the
channel of Agabama, by the north of Cayo Guayos, or from the west of Cayo Blanco,
and by the breaks or mouths of this part of the reef, as by Boca Grande, the
ene and Mulatas; but the entrances are dangerous, and there are no leading
marks.

GUAUROBO, or TRINIDAD RIVER.—To take the mouth of the Guaurobo, or
Trinidad River, steer along outside the bank, and run in without fear to within a
musket-shot of the shore, which in this part is very clean; and running along at the
same distance you will see the bay of the entrance, formed by the Punta de los
Ciriales to the south, and that of the River Canas to the north ; and when you have
got it well open, steer, with little sail set, so as to pass nearer to Point Canas than to
Point Ciriales, because it is much cleaner, with the precaution to sound frequently ;
and, ifin a large vessel, anchor immediately upon getting bottom, because the anchorage
is of very small extent. If the vessel is small, you may run in, steering towards the
south shore of the bay, keeping the ship’s head between two sandy beaches, which
are the only ones on it, until you are in 8 or 6 fathoms water on sand, when you may
anchor. :

After having described this part of the bank, and the anchorages in the neighbour-
hood of Trinidad, it only now remains to add, that Masio is preferable to Casilda, not
only on account of its deeper water, and that you can sail out of it with the trade
wind, but that it is more easy to take; while, on the contrary, at Port Casilda,
the anchorage is not more than 4 cables in extent, is very difficult to get out of with
the trade wind ; and finally, in order to obtain water, it is necessary to send boats
to the River Guaurab. Port Masio is, therefore, the only one which vessels, intending
to load or discharge, or remain any time at Trinidad, ought to take.

REMARKS on toe SOUTH COAST or CUBA, From THE OJO DE TORO
(ABOUT 15 MILES TO THE WESTWARD OF CAPE DE Cruz) To TRINIDAD.
From the Journals of Mr. H. Davy, late Master of H.M.8. Victor, 1829 § 1830.

‘The Ojo de Toro is a small break in the land, with a white spot, and somewhat
resembles the name given it. The land from Ojo de Toro to the westward descends
gradually to Cape Cruz, which is low, and may be known by the white notched rocks
which form it. The land eastward of Ojo Toro is high and ridgy. The Peak of
Tarquino is high, of a conic form, and may be seen in clear weather 20 or 30 leagues,
and is a good landmark. Eastward of this the land continues high and peaked, and
just to the westward of St. Jago de Cuba are the Sierras del Cobre. The shores of
this range are quite clean, and vessels may run along the land at the distance of 3
miles with great safety.

At Cape Cruz there are some dangerous reefs, which stretch to the southward
about 2 miles; immediately to the westward of these dangers, which are all visible,
you may enter on the bank in 6 fathoms, sand and weeds. This is the commencement
of that extensive bank which, beginning at Cape Cruz, runs in various directions to
the northward and westward, and at last terminates at Trinidad, being a distance of
more than 60 leagues. On this bank are numerous shoals and cays, with some good
passages between them. ‘The interior navigation of this bank is represented as being
very safe, and to afford good shelter from bad weather. ‘The depth of water varies
from 12 to 3 fathoms, but there are many shoals and dangers which require ex-
perienced pilots to avoid.

SOUTH COAST OF CUBA. 103

To navigate from without, and having entered on the bank, as above noticed, you
will continue sounding in from 8 to 40 fathoms, according to the course steered ; the
chart and time will best point out the direction. Nineteen leagues N.W. from Cape
Cruz is a small cay, called the Kastern Head of the Docé Leguas; this is the first of
a range of cays called after the same name, or the Twelve-league Cays; they are on
the outer edge of the bank, and run in a W.N.W. direction. The cays resemble each
other very much, being low and woody, with here and there a few sandy beaches ;
sometimes rocks or low mangrove points running into the water. The channels in
this range are the Boca de Caballones and Boca Grande; the latter is the best, with a
depth of 3 to 5 fathoms; the water has a silvery appearance. Vessels may run along
these cays at a distance of 4 to 5 miles with great safety until near Cayo Breton, the
westernmost of the Docé Leguas. Some dangerous reefs stretch out from this cay,
and you ought not to approach it nearer than 8 miles.

In navigating near these cays it is necessary to be very guarded against the
currents, which frequently set right on the bank. About 7 leagues N.N.W. from
Cayo Breton is thé cay called Zarza Fuera, or Cayo Zarza, the intermediate space
being studded with rocks and shoals. When in the vicinity of this cay, and night
coming on, it is advisable to run on the bank, between Zarza Fuera and the cays
Zarza and Machos, situate to the N.W., and anchor in 4 to 6 fathoms, coarse sand.

While at anchor in December, 1829, we found the current settting N.K., 14 mile per
hour.

In sailing from this, which ought to be at daylight, do not approach Zarza and
Machos nearer than 5 miles; they are joined by a ridge of rocks, and a dangerous
reef stretches out to the southward 4 miles, having on its outer part 2% fathoms;
thence gradually deepening. When Machos bears N.N.W., steer W.N.W. for Cayo
Blanco; and when the Pan de Azucar, or Sugar Loaf, is just on with the eastern part
of the high lands of Bonoa, which are just to the westward of it, Puga Reef will bear
N. by W., 13 mile distant, and Cayo Blanco will be right ahead. Cayo Blanco is a
small, low bushy island, surrounded by white rocks. Reefs extend off this island,
and it ought not to be approached nearer than half a mile.

Puga is a reef of rocks, encompassed by shoals running out half a mile, and the

~ whole forms a square. We anchored between Puga and Blanco, in 4 fathoms, sand ;

centre of Puga Reef §.E. 3 E.; shipping at Casilda N.W. 4 W.; and south point of
Cayo Blanco West; Machos and Zarza K. by 8.7 S%., to H.S.E.; and the centre of
Trinidad N.W.2W. ‘The navigation from this place to Casilda is too intricate to
venture without a pilot} some of the passes are very narrow, and vessels must be
worked quickly. There are no beacons or buoys, and the pilots place sticks and
branches of trees as they come out. With southerly winds, instead of anchorage at
Puga, pass to the westward of Cayo Blanco, keeping the discoloured water in sight ;
and when the Point of Cayo Guayo and the Point of Tobaco Cay appear open, haul
in; you will soon have 10, 8, 7, and 6 fathoms; anchor in 4 fathoms, and make
signals for a pilot. From this anchorage the harbour is more easy of access.

On Punta Casilda is a wooden fort, and a reef stretches off the point. The
anchorage is inside Cayo Ratones, which is in the centre of the harbour. The depth
of water is 13 to 15 feet, and capable of holding a number of vessels under 300 tons.
The sides of the harbour and coast are low swampy mangrove lands. Casilda is a
small scattered village on the north side of the river, and stands abreast of the
anchorage in a little bight of the harbour. The city of Trinidad is an irregularly
built place, 24 miles from Casilda ; it is situate on a plain, at the foot of a lofty range
of hills, and the road is broad and better than usually met with.”

TRINIDAD TO XAGUA, OR JAGUA.—From the River Guaurabo, westward, the coast
is very clean, and may be sailed along at the distance of a league. It first runs
W. 2N., a little more than 8 miles to the west point of the River Honda; from
this it trends N.W. by W. 2 W., 9 miles to the Point of St. Juan, which is easily

known, as the coast from it turns to N. by W. 4 W., rather more than a mile,
to the River Guaigimico,

104 THE HARBOUR OF XAGUA, OR JAGUA.

Between the River Guaurabo and the Point of San Juan, the Rivers Guanayara,
Cabagon, Honda, Yaguanabo, and San Juan, disembogue; in all these, coasting
vessels, which do not draw more than 6 feet, sometimes anchor. To obtain fresh
water from either of them, it is necessary to proceed a league up from their mouths.
All along this part of the coast the water is deep, and the bottom clean, excepting a
little reef, which juts out nearly half a mile, between the rivers Yaguanabo and San
Juan. The shore is scarped, and composed of Soboruco Rock. The land is moun-
tainous or hilly, to a short distance westward from Point San Juan, and at it com-
mences the mountain of San Juan or of Trinidad.

From the River Guaigimico the coast trends N.W. by W., 14 miles to the Punta
de los Colorados, or Colorados Point, and is so clean that it may be run along at less
than half a cable’s length; the land is level, without mountains, and init are the
rivers Gavilan, Gavalancito, and Arimao, but they are of little importance.

The BAY or HARBOUR of XAGUA, or JAGUA, is very spacious, secure
at all times, and has deep water; but its mouth is very narrow and crooked. The
east point, named Colorados, and the west, named Sabanilla or de la Vigia, are the
exterior points of this port, and the distance between them is rather more than a
mile. The shore to windward, from Point Colorados trends N.W. 3.N., a distance
of 2 miles to Point Pasa Caballo, whence it turns to the N. by E. 3 E., about two-
thirds of a mile, to Point Milpa, which is the interior eastern point of the strait.
The shore to leeward follows nearly the same direction, and narrows the channel so
much, that opposite Point Pasa Caballo it is only 14 cable in width, and continues
so to Point Milpa.

Light.—A fixed light is exhibited on Point Colorados, the eastern point of the
entrance, in latitude 22° 1’; the light is elevated 81 feet, and is visible 14 miles.
“VILLA NuEva” is painted upon the lighthouse. Pilots are always stationed at the
entrance to conduct vessels into the harbour, which should not be attempted without
their assistance.

Buoys.—The following are the positions of four buoys, laid down in February,
1858, from the entrance of Port Xagua to Milpa Point :—White buoy, in 18 fathoms
water, stony bottom, marks the channel at 4 cables’ length from the western, and 1
eable’s length from the eastern shore, Diablo Point bearing S.E. 2 E.; Vigia Point
S.W., and the Fort N.W.4N.; white buoy, in 23 fathoms, stony bottom, 1 cable’s
length from either shore, and 4 a mile from the first buoy, Diablo Point bearing S.E.;
Vigia Point S.S.E., and the fort N.W.; red buoy, in 18 fathoms, stony bottom, 1
cable’s length from the shore, and 3 cables’ length from the second buoy, Pasa Caballo
Point bearing E.N.E., Milpa Point N.N.E., and the Fort N.E.; and a red buoy, in 25
fathoms, muddy bottom, 1 mile from the shore, and 2 miles from the third buoy, Cay
Carenas bearing North, Milpa Point N.N.E., and Caleton de las Damas Point east.

Vessels can tack between the buoys, as there is plenty of water, and no danger.

A pilot is in attendance at all times near the outer buoy, at the entrance of the
port.

It is high water, full and change, in Port Xagua at 4h. 57m., and the rise and fall
is 2 feet. The streams run at the rate of 3 knots. Water is plentiful, and easily
obtained.

Directions.—To enter this port, steer so as to pass Colorados Point at one-fourth of
a cable’s length ; but you must avoid the exterior coast to windward, as it sends off a
reef, and ought not to be approached nearer than a mile. Run on, inwards, preserving
the same distance of a quarter of a cable, until you arrive at Point Pasa Caballo,
whence you must luff, in order to keep mid-channel, or rather somewhat nearer to the
leeward side; and when abreast of the interior points, run towards the S.E. part of
Cayo de Carenas, to avoid a bank which lies to the northward of Point Milpa, and of
which you will be clear when the northern point of Cayo Alcatraz bears east.
Having passed the interior points, you may anchor according to circumstances,

COCHINOS BAY. 105

The coast from Xagua trends W. 3 S., a distance of 213 miles, to the Point of
Caleta Bueno, or Good Cove; it is all of Soboruco Rock, without bank or shoal; it
thence trends W.N.W.i W., nearly 7 miles, to Oriental Point, the east point of
Cochinos, or Swine’s Bay.

COCHINOS BAY.—This bay is formed by the point above mentioned, and another
named Punta del Padre, or Father’s Point, which lies W.S.W., 7 miles from it;
the bay extends 13 miles to the N.N.W. Its eastern coast is of Soboruco Rock, without
a bank, until at about half a mile from the shore, where bottom is found of sand and
rock, in 15 fathoms, diminishing rapidly towards the coast. The western coast is a
sandy beach, which sends out a rocky bank to a short distance. In the northern part
of the bay is a landing place, which leads to the Haciendas de Ganado, or stock farms,
but it is little frequented on account of its having so little bank, and the little that is,
being generally composed of sharp rocks.

Point Padre, on the mainland, is very low, with a sandy beach; at the distance of
nearly 7 miles 8.E. } E. from it lies Piedras Cay, low, and of small extent. A little to
the east of the point, the bank which borders the west coast of the bay continues
towards the south, having along its edge a reef, which almost joins the north part of
Piedras Cay. The east side of this reef is very steep-to, and has some breaks or
openings of 3 or 4 fathoms, which allow a passage on to the bank. The one most
frequented is that formed by the southern extremity of the reef and Piedras Cay,
because the cay serves as a mark for it, and also because it has a greater depth of
water than either of the others. The break which terminates this reef ends to the
westward at the Levandera Rocks, which lie about 4 leagues W. 3 N. from Piedras
Cay.

Light.—On the north part of Piedras Cay, on the western side of the entrance to
Cochinos Bay, light is exhibited from a mast which rises from the Keeper’s dwelling,
which is a square brown building, showing a fixed light at 80 feet above the sea,
visible 7 miles.

From Point Padre to that of Don Christoval, all the coast is broken with lagoons,
forming many cays, but having no navigable channel. In this space is comprised
Cayo Blanco, or White Cay, the south side of which isa sandy beach; and at its
eastern part there is fresh water, in holes.. On that side, at the distance of 1} mile
from the shore, is the Levandera Reef, extending 2 miles east and west. ‘The west
point of Cayo Blanco lies W. 4 N., 15 miles from Point Padre; and with another
cay, which is to the N.W., forms the Boqueron, or Little Mouth of Calvario, which
has little depth.

The Boqueron of Calvario, with the southern extremity of Diego Perez Cay, which
lies at the distance of 6 miles S.W. by W. from it, forms the Bay of Cazones, which
runs inland about 7 miles N.W. by W., having at its bottom Masio Cay. There are
various small channels formed by Masio Cay, at the bottom of the bay, which are
connected with lagoons, lying along the sides, and at the north end of the bay. To
the south of this cay is a bank of sand and rock, having 8 and 25 fathoms on it.
At a distance of more than 15 mile eastward from the south point of Diego
Perez Cay, a reef begins, which, stretching out with a turn to the 8.H., unites with
the eastern part of the Jardinillos, and is steep-to. Between the same point of the
Diego Perez and the beginning of the reef, is a passage on to the western bank,
beginning with 6 fathoms, but in a short distance decreases to 14 feet. Four miles
to the S.E. of the same point there is another channel, having at first 3 fathoms,
and very soon after only 2 fathoms; there is no good mark for it, and the former is
most frequented.

Nearly 2 miles W. by S. 3S. from the point of Diego Perez, is the southernmost
part of Flamenco Cay; after which follow to the N.W. by W. % W.,a chain of
cays, named Sal and Fabrica, and which, connecting with the mainland of Cuba at
Don Christoval’s Point, form innumerable passages, but with very little water. The
southernmost cays of this chain, named Bointo, Cacao, and Palanca, are the guides
for vessels sailing along the bank, which, in many places, has not more than 11 feet

[W. Inpizs, Parr II.] P

106 BATABANO.

water; and the bottom, of fine white sand, is studded with rocks, with only 6 feet
over them; but their colour is a sufficient guide to avoid them. ‘This passage is
bounded by the cays above mentioned on the north, and by another cay, Rabihorcada,
and the edge of the Jardines Bank, on the south. From Palanca Cay, which is dis-
tant 12 miles W.N.W. 4 W. from Flamenco Cay, the western Fabrica Cays take a
bend to N.N.E. 4 E., towards the main land, and form a passage or channel with
another chain of cays, to the west of them, named Don Christoval’s Cays.

Don Christoval’s Point lies N. by W. 3 W., 5 miles from Palanca Cay; and from it the
coast, which is low, trends W.N.W., 19 miles to a little cay, at the entrance ofa
small bay, named Mata-hambre. ‘The interior along this part of the coast is firm
land, and is called the Savannas of Juan Luis; and to the southward of it extends a
chain of cays, which are called Juan Luis Cays. Between the cays and the coast
there is a passage, as there is also between the east part of them and the west part of
Don Christoyal’s Cays; but either passage is fit only for vessels which draw no more
than 10 feet.

Three miles and a half N.W. from the Little Cay, in the mouth of Mata-hambre,
js Punta Gorda, where the swampy land ceases. From this point the coast turns
to N.N.E. and-N.E. for a short distance ; it then trends to the eastward, and forms
the Ensenada, or Bay of Broa, which extends in that direction about 6 leagues. On
the north it is bounded by the Point of Mayabequeé, which lies N. 2 W., 153 miles
distant from the Punta Gorda. ‘The shores of this bay are all of mangrove and
swampy land; and on its north side are the branches of the- Cienega, or Shallow
Lake, which the natives have named the River Guines, Guanamon, Mora, Nueva, and
Belen, as far as Mayabequé Point. In this bay, and also in the whole space of sea
comprised between the coast of Batabano and the cays in front of it, as far as the
Cayamas Channel, the general depth is from 3 to 4 fathoms, on clay ground.

BATABANO.—About a mile to the N.W. from the Point of Mayabequeé is the
river of that name, in which vessels trading to Batabano can easily procure water.
Thence to the anchorage of Batabano the coast trends W. i S8., 83 miles. From
Batabano the coast continues about W.4S., 15 miles, to Punta Cayamas, having in
the intermediate space, the Point of Cagio, and the river of that name, in which the
Batabano vessels sometimes procure water.

Light.—At Batabano a small fixed light is shown all night, from a lantern ona
mast, 31 feet in height, and visible 3 miles.

The River Cagio, formed by the branches of the Cienega before mentioned, runs
into the anchorage of that name, in which, at a moderate distance from the coast, are
24 and 3 fathoms water, sheltered from all winds by the chain of cays which are in
front of it. The bight of the Cienega, comprised between its mouth and the main-
land, is more extensive than that of Batabano or Mayabequé.

Cayamas Point, with the chain of cays to the southward of it, form the channel of
that name, in which there are 7 feet of water. This chain extends, bending to S.E.
by S., about 11 miles, where it forms the channel of La Hacha, which divides it from
another chain of cays, extending from this place as far as Cayo de Cruz, lying 8. by
E.3E., 14 miles from Batabano. There are 11 feet of water in the Canal de la
Hacha, and it is much frequented by vessels trading to Batabano, when they either
enter or sail out to the westward of the Isles of Pines and the Cayos de San Felipe.

Atashort distance westward from Cayo de Cruz, lies another, named Redondo,
under which the vessels belonging to Batabano secure themselves in the season when
the fresh south-east winds blow; that is, in the months from July to October (the
hurritane months), which are much to be feared on all this coast. ‘lo the southward
of Cayo de Cruz, at the distance of 5 miles, lies Cayo de la Monté Rey ; and between
it is a channel of 23 fathoms on clay. This channel is the largest of those which lead
to Batabano, although care must be taken to keep clear of a spit, which runs off about
8 miles to the $.W. from the former cay ; andalso of the heads, which lie to the south-
ward of these cays, forming the north side of the channel,

a

BAY OF CORTEZ. 107

From Cayamas Point, the coast trends W. 2 N., forming a regular bay, named
Ensenada de Majana, and terminating to the south at Punta Salinas, which lies 13
miles to the W.S.W. from the former. In the intermediate space, and near to
Cayamas Point, is the mouth of the river Guanima, at which the Cienega terminates.
8.W. by W., 113 miles from Punta Salinas, a little point stretches outward ; and at
a short distance to the northward of it is the Estero, or creek of Savanna la Mar,
much frequented by trading vessels. From the same little point, the coast continues,
forming a bay with Mediacasa or Carraguao Point, which lies 15 miles to the 8. W. of it.
Between this coast and the Bank, or Middle Ground, on which are the Cayos, to the
northward of the Isle of Pines, the depth of water is from 3 to 4 fathoms, on a bottom
of clay ; excepting a spit with 14 and 2 fathoms, which runs out about two leagues to
the S.W. by W., from the Guanima Cays; the extremity of this spit lies S.S.E., 6
miles from Punta Salinas. The Guanima Cays are included in the group which form
the west side of the Channel of La Hacha, and are situate to the southward of the
river Guanima and Point Cayamas.

S. by E., 163 miles from Mediacasa Point lies Dios Cay : between which is the pas-
sage for vessels trading from this quarter to Batabano. Dios Cay is low, of small
extent, and detached ; the bank on which it rises turns to the eastward, and unites
with that which surrounds the cays to the north and east of the Isle of Pines. It
also, with the Cayos de San Felipe and the Cayos de los Indios, forms a channe! with
from 12 to 4 fathoms water.

From Mediacasa Point the coast bends W. 3 S. for about 2 leagues, after which,
following to the S. Westward, it terminates at Punta de la Fisga, forming the
Ensenada, or Bay of Dayaniguas: this point lies S.W. 4 W., 164 miles from the
former. In the bay is the Point of Canaguao, the river S. Diego, the Point of Gato,
and the Convent Creek: but there is not more than 1 fathom ot water in it.

About S.E. 3 E., 13 miles from Fisga Point, lies the easternmost of the Cayos de
San Felipe, from which this chain of cays extends in a westerly direction as far as
the meridian of Calonna Point, a distance of 13 miles: between these cays and the
Cayos de los Indios, there is a passage with 12 fathoms water. The sea between
the coast and the north part of the Cayos de San Felipe, is generally from 4 to 4%
fathoms in depth, on clay and weeds.

From Calonna Point the coast follows to the westward, for about 4 miles to
St. Domingo Point and Greek of Guamo, where the ‘Bay of Cortez commences. From
this place the coast runs nearly west for about 23 leagues to the bottom of the said
bay ; where the small rivers of San Juan and Galafié disembogue. About W.S.W.,
32 leagues from the Point of Guamo, the river Cuyaguatege disembogues; and
south from it, at the distance of about a mile, begin three little cays, which, bend-
ing a little to the east, extend to the southward about a league, and form, with the
mainland of Cuba, the Lagoon of Cortez, having in it about 24 fathoms water; but
the little channels formed by the cays have not more than 7 feet. The southern ex-
tremity of this lagoon, which is nearly on the parallel with the Cayos de San Felipe, and
about 6 leagues distant from them, is the termination of the Bay of Cortez, in which
there are 3 or 4 fathoms water, on a grassy bottom. About 2 miles to the eastward
of the south end of the said lagoon, commences the deep water, with a very steep
edge: it begins with 7 or 8 fathoms on rocky bottom, and continues so as to join the
coast, close to the northward of Punta Piedras: which point lies about S. by W., 7
miles from the bight of the Bay of Cortez; the coast is low, but of firm land and
rocky, with some spaces of sandy beach, running nearly in the same direction.

From Punta Piedras, the coast bends S. by W. 4 W. to Cape Frances, distant about
8 miles, and then S.W. by W. + W., 4 miles to Mangle Point or Punta de la Llana.
This is a low point, and has no other marks to distinguish it, than the different direc-
tions of the coast, and a hut near it; and having to the westward of it a small sandy
beach. To the 8.E. a reef runs off about 2 cables’ length, which is very steep-to.
From Punta de la Llana the coast trends W. by S., 5 leagues, and then S.W. by
W. 3 W. to Cape Corrientes. All this part of the coast is of high Soboruco rock, and
free from danger at the distance of a stone’s throw.

108 CAPE SAN ANTONIO.

CAPE CORRIENTES ends in a low point with a sandy beach, and the S.W.
of it, to the distance of about a mile, a narrow bank runs off, having on its edge 15
fathoms, and close to the shore some rocks, on which the sea breaks.

From the cape, the coast, without any bank, turns about N. } W., for about a league
to Cape Cayman, or Punta de la Maria Gorda, and from it to the bottom of the bay
N. i W., about 7 miles. The place named Maria Gorda is remarkable, being of
Soboruco rock, scarped, and higher than any other part of the bay. Here a bank
again begins to run off a short distance, with bad holding ground, the bottom being
rocky; although farther to the north, from the inflexion which the coast makes, the
bottom is sand, and an anchor may be let go in 5 fathoms, very near the beach, with
the precaution of having a cable on shore, as the edge of the bank is very steep. This
is the only anchorage in this bay, and affords shelter from the strong trade winds,
and §.E. Winds; no other part of the bay has any bank.

From the bottom of Corrientes Bay, the coast trends W.S.W. to the Balcones, which
is a short piece of coast, of high scarped Soboruco rock : and from this place it turns
to S.W.15S., so far as Punta del Holandes, or Holandes Point. This point which
bears W. 1 N., distant 54 leagues from Cape Corrientes, terminates to the westward
of the bay of that name. Near to and on the east of it begins a reef, which extends
in that direction about half a mile, but has no danger, as it lies very close along the
coast, and is very steep-to. Point Holandes presents an agreeable appearance, having
a resemblance to the curtains of a wall, and extending with this figure about two
miles; beyond which it descends in somewhat like falls or steps, and the shore con-
tinues woody after passing it. ;

From Punta del Holandes the eoast trends W.iN., 9 miles, to the Point of
Cayuelos, which is the southernmost point of the front of Cape St. Antonio, and
is distant from the westernmost point of the same cape, 14 mile, 8. by KE. The
westernmost point of the cape is named De Pocillos, and from this point the coast
trends nearly north, about ,%; of a mile to Sorda Point, whence it bends more to the
north-eastward..

To the eastward of and near the Point of Cayuelos, the bank begins, which thence
surrounds the cape, half a mile from shore, and continues on to the northward, where
it forms the Colorados Bank. It begins with a depth of 20 to 25 fathoms, on a rocky
bottom, and diminishes regularly towards the coast, with some spots of sandy bottom.

CAPE SAN ANTONTIO.—The front of Cape San Antonio is of low land, very
rocky, and appears with mixed streaks of Soboruco rock and sandy beach. In its
wells, named Cueva de la Sorda and Pocillos (Deaf Woman’s Cave and the Little
Wells), water is abundant and of good quality.

Light.—On Cape San Antonio a lighthouse is erected, 115 feet in height from base
to vane, and the lantern 107 feet above H.W. It exhibits a light, varied by flashes
every half-minute, visible 20 miles in clear weather. The word “ Roncali” is painted
on the building.

Cape Corrientes appears much like Cape St. Antonio; and, in order to distinguish
it, observe that it is rather level land, and of moderate height, with some trees ; and
being off it, in clear weather, some hills, which rise on the north part of the island,
named the Sierras del Rosavi, may be seen over it, bearing nearly true North; they
are the only hills that can be seen from a similar situation, and present to the view
two summits only.

THE ISLE OF PINES, JARDINES, JARDINILLOS, ETC.

The principal reef which surrounds the shoals and cays named the Jardines, and
Jardinillos, commences near Diego Perez Cay, and the edge of the bank extends
thence to the S.E., forming a bight at the Medano, or Islet of Viscayno, whence it

ROSARIO CAY. 109

continues to the easternmost cay of the Jardines. This cay lies about 7 leagues,
§. 4 E., from Cayo de Piedras, and forms with it the entrance of the Gulf of Cazones.
From the north end of this easternmost cay a reef spits off to the eastward about
a mile, and the bank extends E.S.E., about 4 leagues, and nearly 2 north and
south, with a depth of 15 fathoms at the edges, and 7 or 8 on the whole of it,
excepting near the cay, where there are 4 fathoms on sand and rocks. This cay, as
well as all the following ones to the westward, under the name of Jardinillos, and
which extend as far as Cayo Largo, are regularly high, and scarped at their edges.
From the easternmost cay the shoal water follows about 2 leagues to the 8,W.,
whence it takes a westerly direction about 4 leagues, and is studded with reefs, as far
as a cay, which lies a league to the west of Trabuco. For about 53 miles the same
edge forms a bight as it approximates the east end of Cayo Largo.

Cayo Largo extends N.E. by E., and S.W. by W., 12 miles. It is the east-
ernmost of the Jardines, under which denomination are comprehended. all those
that follow it to the westward as far as the Isle of Pines. The south side of Cayo
Largo is a sandy beach, bordered with a reef, which extends more than a mile from
the east end, and approaches nearer as it advances westward, so as almost to join the
west end of the cay, whence it continues without any break W.S.W. % W., and W.zN.,
to the Canal del Rosario, or Rosario Channel, which is 6 leagues distant from Cayo
Largo.*

Qn the same reef, and near to the west part of Cayo Largo, lie two rocky cays,
named the Ballenates, distant a league from each other, and of moderate height. In
all the space comprehended between the eastern head of the Jardinillos and the
Rosario Channel, the bank, which extends along by the south side of the cays, does
not extend farther out than one or two miles; on its edge the depth begins with lo
to 18 fathoms water, on a rocky bottom, and diminishes rapidly to the reef itself.

ROSARIO CAY.—The west end of this cay bears N. 2 W. from the channel to”
which it gives name, and forms, with another cay to the westward of it, named
Cantiles, a channel of 3 and 4 fathoms water; but its outlet on the interior bank to
the westward of the Passage Cays, has not more than 10 feet water. The opening,
or channel, through the reef is one-third of a mile in width, with a depth of 3
fathoms in the middle, and steep at the sides; at half a mile from its north part lies
a rock, which shows above water.

From the Rosario Channel the reef trends $.W. + W., to the distance of about 19
miles, to the Calapatech Mehegan Reef, and then W.N.W. { W., 19 miles, to join the
east point of the Isle of Pines, in which space are included the cays Cantiles, Duck
Cays, Calapatch, Abalo, Campas, Malias, and several others which have no names.
The outer edge of the bank is parallel to the reef, and generally extends out about
2 miles, excepting to the south of Abalo Cay, where it runs out almost 3 miles, and
is about 7 miles distant from the cay. ‘The least water on all this bank is 5 fathoms,
on rocky bottom, with some spots of sand.

heavily.

110 THE ISLE OF PINES.

The ISLE OF PINES, when first seen, appears mountainous or hilly; it is of a
moderate height, and the tops of the mountains are very definite, or sharp. From its
East Point the south coast trends S.W. 3 W., a distance of 6 miles, with sandy
beach, to a point which may be easily known, being of high Soboruco rock, and
having a farallon, or detached rock, very near it. From this point the coast continues
S.W. by W. 4 W., a distance of 19 miles, to another little point, which, with the East
oa are the boundaries of that part of the coast named Playa Larga, or Long

each.

From the western point of Playa Larga the coast continues W. 4 N., 10 miles to
Cape Pepe, which is the S.W. point of the island; and from it, 83 miles to the N.W.,
is Crocodile Cove. In this cove fishing-vessels sometimes take shelter.

Light proposed—On Cape Pepe (the Crocodile Point of the Spanish charts) a
lighthouse is proposed to be built, which, when complete, is to be 111 feet above the
sea, and to show a revolving light, visible 16 miles.

The coast continues N.W., a distance of 82 miles, to Point Pedernales. The space
which is comprehended between this point and the extreme west part of Playa Larga
is low and rocky, with shore of Soboruco, and may be coasted along at less than half
a mile distant.

PUERTO FRANCES.—From Point Pedernales the coast, forming a bay, bends
N.W, by N., a distance of 33 miles to Punta Frances, which is the westernmost part
of the island. Near to the point are the anchorage and watering-place of Puerto
Frances. This little roadstead, the bank of which extends-about half a mile from
the sandy beach, with a depth of 5 fathoms on sand, is much frequented by vessels
going there for timber, and affords shelter from winds of the N.E. and 8.E. quarters.

Commander Grant, R.N., says “ Puerto Frances is very convenient for vessels sta-
tioned on the south coast of Cuba, affording good shelter in the strong trade winds.
The anchorage all over the bay is good, by picking out the white spots. The most
convenient for weighing under sail is with the following marks :—Pedernales Point,
S. 28° E.; N.W. extreme of Bush Cay, N. 37° W.; Small Cay, S. 75° E.

A sand bank, bordered on the west edge by a coral reef, and very shallow, extends
for some distance round Bush Cay. Spring lobsters abound, and rays and alligators
frequent the boat channel.”

Punta Frances forms the south point of the Bay of Siguanea; the coast from that
point trends to the §.E. to the distance of 5 leagues, all covered with water, and
broken, or formed into cays; it thence turns to the N.E., 6 miles, to the Lageon of
Siguanea, which lies at the foot of the hills of the same name, and has from 4 to 6
fathoms water in it, but at its entrance, not more than 9 feet; from it, branches run
off in nearly an east and west direction, which divide the island into two parts. At
the foot of the hills of Siguanea there are two filters of excellent water, which spring
out of the land, at a short distance from the beach.

From the Lagoon of Siguanea, the coast trends N.N.W., a distance of 12 miles, to
Punta de los Indios, which is the northernmost point of Siguanea Bay, and is distant
14 miles N.E. by N. from Punta Frances. Siguanea Bay extends 174 miles, N.W.
and §.E., and has from 24 to 5% fathoms, on a grassy bottom ; but the passage between
Punta Frances, and the southernmost of the Cayos de los Indios, has not above 34
fathoms, on sandy and grassy bottom.

The Cayos de los Indios, or Indian Cays, are separated by small channels, and
extend to the N.N.W. 2 W., and W.N.W. + N. from the southernmost of them, which
is distant 8 miles from the northernmost. The southern extremity lies N. by E. % E.
from Punta Frances, distant 93 miles, and $.W. by W. 2% W., 52 miles from Punta
de los Indios; in the channel, between them and the latter, there are 4 to 5 fathoms
water, on clayey and grassy bottom.

From Punta de los Indios the coast inclines to the eastward as far as the Cala
or Cove of Barcos, and the point of that name, which terminates it to the north, and
lies at the distance of 3 leagues N.N.E. from the former. From the last point the

THE WEST END OF CUBA. 111

coast trends E.2N., 16 miles to Monte Diablo, thence S.E. another 16 miles to
Corral Point, and S. 4 W. to Piedras Point, the S.E. point of the island of Pines.

CAYOS DE LOS INDIOS, &c.—From the Punta Frances, the edge of deep water
follows about north, a distance of 15 miles, and then turns to the N.W. and West
until it joins the main land of Cuba, about Punta Frances. Generally, from Punta
Frances to the parallel of the southernmost of the Cayos de los Indios, there are from
13 to 25 fathoms on the edge of the bank; and from thence to the meridian of the
easternmost of the Cayos de San Felipe, from 39 to 50 fathoms. To the southward
of these cays, as far as the westernmost, 9 to 10 fathoms; and between it and the
main land of Cuba, about 26 fathoms, except in the proximity of the latter, where
there are only 7 or 8 fathoms. The bottom of the whole is rocky; and at a short
distance within the edge of the bank, the depth diminishes to 5, 4, and 3 fathoms,
onsand. All these cays have sandy beaches toward the south ; and on them, as well
as on the Jardines, there are huts belonging to the hawk’s-bill turtle fishermen.

This Great Bank, which we have just described, from the Bay of Cazones to Punta
Frances, is studded with cays, which, with the coast, form the outer channels of
Diego Perez, of the Rosario, of Siguanea, and of Cortez ; which admit of passages to
Batabano, by the inner narrows of Don Christoval, Las Gordas, Monte Rey, and of
La Hacha, all with a depth of 11 feet, except that of Monte Rey or Cayo Redondo,
which has 23 fathoms, on clay.

REMARKS ON THE WEST END OF CUBA.

By Mr. William Campbell Middlemist, while Master of H.M.S. Isis.

Cape San Antonio, the west end of Cuba, is low, and covered with wood; it is
bold-to, and while it bears anything to the westward of north, may be approached
as near as you please. The coast continues bold to the eastward as far as Point
Holandes, off which, at a short distance, are some sunken rocks; this is also called
Rocky Point, and Cape False, and is 16 miles of longitude eastward of Cape San
Antonio.

At Point Holandes, the coast begins to bend in to the north-eastward, forming a
deep bay, which is clear and bold to the shore, but there are no soundings on it. The
shore, after trending north-eastward, about 20 miles, bends out again 8.S.E., South,
and §.8.W., toa bluff headland,* which is to the northward of Cape Corrientes ;
here was observed white water and foul ground.

Cape Corrientes resembles Cape San Antonio, and has often been mistaken for it
by strangers, when coming along shore from the eastward. But to prevent the
danger that might happen to those who mistake the land here, observe, that at about
3 miles round Cape Corrientes, there is the remarkable bluff headland, before men-
. tioned, of a rugged and black appearance, which you will always see as soon as you
have doubled the cape; this object will enable you to decide whether you have run
the length of Cape San Antonio, to which your course will now be about W.3N.,
31 miles. The bay above mentioned (Corrientes) is much deeper than was laid down
in the charts; and unless the weather be clear, you cannot see the land to the west-
ward when you are abreast of Cape Corrientes. And this is the reason why some
navigators have been induced to haul round it, thinking they had got the length of
Cape San Antonio, particularly if it should happen at the close of day, when land
cannot be seen to the windward. ‘There is a reef extending in a westerly direction
from Cape Corrientes, and white water a little beyond it, but I believe no danger is
to be apprehended from it, as no breakers were seen, except on the reef.

* Cape Cayman, or the Point of Maria Gorda of the Spaniards,

112 THE NORTH-WEST COAST OF CUBA.

Cape Corrientes is remarkable from the eastward, being a low point, on which
are several clusters of trees, resembling buildings, one, in particular, being like a
lighthouse or tower, and when it bears W. by N., appears to stand on the extreme
point. Although these parts of the coast appear so much alike at a distance, yet, on a
near approach to the shore, the land will be found remarkable-in many places; there
is Point Leones, to the eastward of Cape Corrientes, which, when bearing from Hast
to N.E., shows an abrupt headland, perpendicular from the sea.

Latitude of Cape San Antonio extreme 21° 51’ 30’, and longitude 84° 58’ 4’.
Another British navigator has said, that—

“The best place to anchor under Cape San Antonio is in 9 or 8 fathoms, with the
cape bearing N. by E. 5 &., or N.N.E., and the extremity of the land S.E. by E., or
S.H. by E.3 E. Here you will be about half a mile, ora little more, from shore,
and have clean white sandy ground. From this situation the cape shows like two
points, the northernmost of which islow and sandy. You cannot sail to this anchorage
from the northward, because of rocks and shallow water; but, in sailing to it from
south-eastward, you will first have 14, and a gradual decrease to-7 fathoms, on white
sand. Here is plenty of fish and turtle, with good firewood, and the anchorage is
safer and better than that near Cape Corrientes.”

THE NORTH-WEST COAST OF CUBA,

FROM CAPE SAN ANTONIO, TO HAVANNA AND YCACOS POINT.

The high land of the Islands of Cuba, are in many places particularly marked.
The principal lands which are thus remarkable, in regular suecession, from west to
east, are the High Lands of Buenavista, the Cock’s-comb, the Saddle Hill, to the
westward of Bahia Honda, and the Dolphin’s Head, or Pan de Cabanas, to the east-
ward of it; the Table of Mariel, the Maiden’s Paps, to the southward of Havana; the
Iron Hills to the eastward, and the Pan of Matanzas to the southwest of Port
Matanzas.

CAPE SAN ANTONIO may be doubled within two miles with safety. The bank,
which appears of a whitish colour, with only 10 or 12 feet water, with coral rocks, to
the N.W. of the cape, trends thence about N.N.E., as far as 22° 8’ N. latitude, with
very uneven soundings, from 3 to 6 fathoms, rocks and sand on the edge of it; and a
gradually decreasing depth south-eastward to the shore, all fine sandy ground. Ata
short distance without the edge no soundings are to be found. It is high water, full
and change, at the cape, at 9h. 30m., and the vertical rise is about 18 inches; the
flood runs to the southward, and bends with the southerly current to the eastward,
within the Isle of Pines, &c.; the ebb sets to the northward, at the rate of about
three-quarters of a mile an hour.

SHOALS oFF CAPE SAN ANTONIO.—About 43 leagues N. by W. $ W. from Cape
San Antonio, lies a rock or shoal, that was seen by the Spanish officers in 1797. It
seems that Captain Bishop was once near this spot, in 1758 or 1759. He says, “ that
having worked from Cape San Antonio to the N.N.W., distant 5 leagues, he had 15
fathoms water. He thea from the main-top-gallant mast-head of the Sphynx, a 20-
gun ship, saw the tops of three small hills to the eastward, and Cape San Antonio,
bearing 8.S.E., distant 6 leagues.” In the day-time you may safely take the passage
between this shoal and the edge of the bank; but in the night, or in obscure weather,
it is better to make sure of passing to the westward of it.

Ship Kingston, Benjamin Baynton, Commander, and ship David Lyon, Captain
Selby, being in company on the 27th May, 183d, at 9h. 40m., A.m., Cape Antonio

COLORADOS REEFS, 113

bearing S.E. by S., 7 or 8 miles, saw the bottom, and sounded in 10 fathoms;
kept away to N.W., and ran off the bank, the extent of which could not be ascertained.
The arming of the lead brought up coarse sand. At noon, Cape San Antonio bore
S.E. 3 S., latitude by observation, 22° 4’; both ships agreeing in latitude, supposing
ourselves about 5 leagues off the cape, which could be just seen off the deck (height
of the eye, about thirteen feet),

We were at least a quarter of an hour on the shoal, and there might be much less
water on some parts of it; supposed latitude 22° 0’, supposed longitude 85° 0’. No
discoloured water could be seen to the eastward from the mast-head, either at noon, or
when on the bank. Captain Owen Jones found a coral bank in this situation, with
10 to 15 fathoms on it; it extends full 15 miles, in a N.E. and S.W. direction, and
about half of that extentin breadth. There are 165 and 130 fathoms close to it,

There is also another bank, named Sancho Pardo, which lies about 6 leagues W.N.W.
2 W. from Cape San Antonio, and has 2 fathoms on it. In 1827, the ships Clara,
Captain Thompson, and S¢. Vincent, Captain Green, both of Bristol, ran over a shoal,
the bottom was plainly seen ; Captain Green sounded in 6 or 6 fathoms, sandy bottom,
with Cape San Antonio bearing S.S.E., distant 15 or 16 miles. The ships were two
hours running over it. In 1828, the ship William Miles, Captain Escott, passed over
it in 5 fathoms.*

Another shoal of 10 to 15 fathoms, is marked on Commander Owen, and Barnett’s
charts, at about 7 miles N.W. 2 W. from Point Cajou, the northern point of Cape
Antonio, The bottom is of coral, and close to there ave 117 to 165 fathoms, and then
no bottom.

COLORADOS REEFS, &c.—To the northward of the bank, which extends
northward from the cape, lies the S.W. extremity of the Colorados Reefs and Cays,
which are, in general, steep-to. But it appears from a suryey lately published, that
the Colorados Reefs are not so dangerous, and do not extend so far to the N.W. as
has been formerly represented; the S.W. extremity of the Reefs, or Drowned Cays,
lies about latitude 22° 8’. and longitude 84° 48’, and from thence extend nearly N.E.
for about 35 miles. Of the principal rocks or cays, the westernmost, or Black Cay,
shows above water, like the hull of a ship, and may he seen 4 or 6 miles off; the other
Colorados, or Red Cays, are not visible, except when the weather is quite clear and
calm ; they have not more than 2 feet water over them; and at the distance of less
than a mile to the westward there are 100 fathoms, and shortly no bottom.+

Light proposed.—On Cay Jutias, a fixed light, varied by flashes, to be 129 feet above
the sea, and visible 16 miles.

BANKS OF ISABELLA.—These banks, three in number, lie to the north-east-
ward of the Colorados Reefs, being separated therefrom by a narrow channel of about
a mile in width: they extend E.N.E. 4 E., 14 leagues: and their eastern end is about
23 leagues from the nearest shore. Within these banks is the Channel of Rosario,
which joins that of Guaniguanico, inside the Colorados. To the southward of the
east end of the Banks of Isabella lies a cay, and to the eastward of it two others,
the easternmost of which, called Cayo Blanco, is nearly 13 miles W.S.W.2% W.
from Bahia Honda, and bears about N. 3 W. from the Pan de Guaijabon, or
Saddle Hill. A reef also extends from within a mile of the east end of those banks

to the west point of Bahia Honda, having two breaks through it, one of which bears
north from Cayo Blanco, called Blanco Break, the other 4 or 6 miles to the eastward

BAHIA HONDA, or Deep Bay, is situate at the eastern end of the cays and
reefs just described, and at the distance of about 40 leagues north-eastward from
Cape San Antonio. The Saddle Hill, or Pan de Guaijabon, bearing S.W. 4 W., will
lead directly to it, and when off it, the entrance will bear about S. 3 E.; but you
cannot get in until the sea breeze comes on, at about 10 o’clock in the morning.

BAHIA HONDA.

Light proposed.—On Gobernadora Point a revolving light to be 111 feet above
the sea, and visible 15 miles.

Bahia Honda is an excellent, spacious, and well-sheltered harbour, but the points
which form its eutrance, as well as the interior coast, are bordered with a reef, on
the edge of which there is but little water. The exterior point on the east or wind-
ward side, named El Morrillo, or Little Morro, from its having a rising ground on
it, sends off a reef or shoal two-thirds of a mile to the N.W., having at its extremity
a depth of 5 fathoms. The exterior point to leeward is Punta de Pescadores, or
Fisherman’s Point; this sends a reef to the north-eastward about one-third of a
mile. These two points, which lie nearly east and west (true), are distant from each
other about three-quarters of a mile; but the channel formed by the edges of the
shoals is only a cable and a half wide.

Within these points (about one-third of a mile) are two others, which also lie
nearly east and west from each other: that on the east side isnamed Punta del Real,
that on the west, Punta del Cayman ; and between these, the breadth of the charnel
does not exceed two cable’s length. The edge of the bank extends from Punta del
Real two-thirds of a cable; but from Punta del Cayman, not more than one-third
ofa cable’s length. Lastly (at nearly two-thirds of a mile), within these points are
two others, which terminate the entrance of the port; from these it begins to open
and form the bay ; that to windward is named Punta del Carenero, and the other to
leeward, Punta del Placer; somewhat to the south from Punta del Carenero is an
island, named Cayo Largo or Long Cay (Wood Island), the west point of which,
Punta de Difuntos, lies more to the west than that of Carenero, so that it can be
seen from the sea.

Directions.—To enter this port, it is necessary to pass at some distance from the
coast, and outside the edges of the reefs, till about N. 2 W. from the entrance, when
steer for it. Having approached it to about the distance of a mile, you may perceive
Punta de Difuntos, and steer S. 3 E.; with this course proceed in mid-channel,
and in sufficient depth of water, from 6 to 18 fathoms, and when abreast of
Punta del Carenero, you will see Punta del Mangles, or Mangrove Point, on the
starboard side; steer then about S.W., taking care to keep that point in sight to star-
board, and having arrived on a line between it and Punta de Difuntos, anchor in 7
fathoms, upon clay.

The following directions for this port have been given by Mr. C. P. Bellamy,
Master of H.M. sloop Espeigle, from observations made by him in 1826:

Bahia Honda is an excellent harbour, perfectly sheltered from all winds, and is
capable of containing upwards of 100 sail of shipping ; but as the breadth between
the reefs is not more than 23 cables’ length, it is difficult for a stranger to enter, and
should never. be attempted, except with a leading wind. On the east side of the
entrance is a watch-house and battery of four guns, standing on a hill, which com-
mands the harbour, and by which it may be easily known.

The best leading mark for the channel is the east end of a remarkable square
hill, at the back of the sugar estates, on with the west point of Fisherman's Island :*

* Wood Island of the old English, and Cayo Largo, or Long Kay, of the new Spanish charts

with this mark you will carry not less than 5 fathoms in the narrowest part of the
channel. Great care should be taken not to get on the edge of the leeward reef, as
it stretches off some distance beyond where it is laid down in the chart.

When within the reefs, which may be known by the colour of the water, you may
anchor. The most convenient anchorage is off, or below Fisherman’s Island.
Wood is plentiful, and water may be obtained in small quantities around the har-
bour, but not without some difficulty.’’*

PUERTO DE CABANOS, or Porto de Cavanas, lies about 43 leagues to the
eastward of Bahia Honda. This is a very fine deep bay, having at its entrance,
between two extensive reefs, 44 or 5 fathoms water, and 8 or 10 within, but to enter
it, you should have the assistance of a pilot.

The coast between Bahia Honda and Cabanas, may be run along at the distance
of 2 miles. Port Cabanas is a good anchorage, sheltered from all winds, and of
sufficient depth for every class of vessel. It may be known by a round hill which
forms a break or gap, and upon the summit of which there is a grove of trees; and
by another hill, named the Pan de Cabanas.t The round hill descends gradually
towards the east, until it ends in low, equal, or level land, which continues in that
manner for a long league, until it meets with the Table-hill of Mariel. Besides
these marks, you may see upon the coast two rows of hillocks, which resemble shep-
herds’ huts (Cabanas de pastores), and from which the place has derived its name.
These hillocks run to the eastward of Bahia Honda, and the Pan de Cabanas appears
as if in the middle of them. , "

Directions.—To enter this port, keep well out, until its entrance, and the extreme
east end of an island, which is within the harbour on the west side, bears 8. 5 E.{
Then steer in that direction until past the reef of Punta Larga, when luff up, and
anchor in from 7 to 9 fathoms. It is necessary to take care of the reefs which run off
both sides of the channel, or entrance; that to windward extends out more than half
a mile, and that to leeward about 2 cables’ length. ‘The reef extends out from Punta
Larga, about two-thirds of a cable; another reef extends almost to the same distance
from the east point of Isla Larga.

PUERTO DE MARIEL, or Port Mariel, lies about 43 leagues to the eastward of
Puerto de Uabanas. The Derrotero says:'“ This port is large, well sheltered, and
fit for every class of vessel. You may know when to the north of it by the
Tables of Mariel, which are moderately high, and form very broad table-lands; and
as you approach them, some white patches will be perceived on the north part. The
coast hence trends eastward, and is very low to Havana; in which direction are
distinguished the Tetas, or Paps of Managua (named Maiden’s Paps by the English),
which are two round hillocks, lying near to each other, and on the meridian of the
Port of Havana. The coast to the westward of Mariel is also low, for the space of
9 or 10 miles, where it rises and forms the Hill of Cabanas; and farther to the west
may be distinguished, as if surrounded with water, other high lands, in the vicinity
of Bahia Honda, d

Directions.—To enter Port Mariel, steer towards the western extremity of the
Tables; and having recognized it, run along by the coast to windward, at about a
cable’s length (at which distance you will go clear of the reef, which extends off the
coast, and on which the sea breaks), until the mouth of the harbour is well open.
Now run towards a little rocky cay, which lies off the leeward point; and when
within two-thirds of a cable, steer S. $ E.; or, what is the same, steer in that direc-
tion, when the leeward interior point of the entrance has the same bearing ; continue
on this course until past the Round Tower, on the windward shore, and then luff to
port, so as to keep at a cable’s length distance from the eastern shore, and there anchor
in 8 or 10 fathoms water; or run into the interior of the harbour, by consulting the
plan of the harbour. As the narrowest part at the entrance of the channel is only
50 yards wide, it is necessary to be very cautious with a large-vessel.

Mr. Bellamy says :—“ As the entrance of Mariel Harbour is only a quarter of a
cable in width, and rather winding, great caution is necessary in entering it. The
greatest depth in the narrowest part of the channel is 44 fathoms. To sail in, steer
for a small rocky cay, at the west side of the entrance, until within one-third of the
distance between this cay and the windward shore; then steer about 8. by E., until
past the Martello Tower on the windward point, when you may haul up for the
weather shore, and berth your ship in any part of the harbour in 6, 7, or 8 fathoms,
good holding ground.

“This harbour is defended by a battery of 5 guns on Point Gorda, and a Martello
Tower of 1 gun on the east point of the entrance. Water and other refreshments
are scarce, but wood is plentiful.”

HAVAWNA,—Eleven leagues E.N.E. 4 E. from Port Cabanas is Havana, which,
in point of importance, is the principal harbour of Cuba, being sufficiently capacious
to accommodate some hundreds of ships of war in perfect security. The entrance
is by a channel rather more than half a mile long, and about 1} cable’s length wide,
and fortified throughout the whole distance. The mouth of this channel is defended
by two strong castles; that on the east point, on the morro or hill, and hence called
the Morro Castle, is built in the form of a triangle; that on the west side is also a
strong fort, and called the Castle of La Punta, to the south-east of which is the city,
also well fortified.

Light.—The lighthouse erected upon the Morro Castle, on the east side of entrance,
is a stone building, 79 feet in height, with “ O*Donnel” painted thereon. It shows
a fixed light, varied by flashes every half minute, at 144 feet above the sea, and
visible 21 miles. The light is extinguished for 10 minutes after midnight to clean
and trim the lamps.

The Morro Castle has lately been assigned as in latitude 23° 9’ 20’, and longitude
82° 22’ 4”.
Buoys.—1. All the mooring buoys are square, and coloured red.
All the warping buoys are conical, and coloured red.
All the mark buoys are coloured black.
