‘Birections.—The Derrotero says :—“ The harbour of Havana may be distinguished

at a distance by the Tetas or Paps of Managua, or the Maiden’s Paps, which, as
before said, lie on the meridian of the harbour’s mouth; the coast, both to the east

HAVANA. 117

and west of it, is low and equal, with the exception of one little hill, or morro,
which is surmounted by fortifications. At 6 leagues to the eastward, the Sierras de
Jaruco, or Iron Hills, may be discovered, of moderate height, and insulated; and
. 6 leagues to the westward, the Tables of Mariel, and sometimes the Hill of
-Cabanas.*

The entrance lies nearly 8.E. by E. 4 E., and N.W. by W.§ W.; and as you must
steer S.E. by E. 4 E. to take it, it is difficult when the breeze is not to the northward
of N.E. by E. ‘The breeze enters or begins at about 10 o’clock A.m., and blows till
sunset; and therefore it is only between these hours that you can enter the port under
sail. It is very difficult, or impossible, to sail in when the breeze is from E.N.E, to 8.E.,
which is very frequently in the rainy season, and sometimes even in the dry season.
Under such circumstance, there is no other resource than anchoring on the Morro
Shoal, or Bank, and enter by towing or warping, when the breeze falls to a calm,
which, as before stated, is at night.

Leaving the harbour is sometimes attended with difficulty ; for when the breeze
comes from the N.E., which it often does in the dry season, or that of the Norths,
it is not only inconvenient, from the winds being scant, but also from the swell
which sets into the mouth of the harbour. Generally speaking, it is best to enter
about mid-day, and to go out about the dawn of day.

The Morro Bank affords a secure anchorage in the time of the ordinary breezes
and land winds, but is much exposed in the season of the Norths, and of the hurri-
canes; therefore it is necessary to anchor so as to have thé mouth of the harbour
open, and to be extremely vigilant, that you may not be surprised. To enter this
harbour, there is no necessity for other guide than the mariner’s eye, inasmuch as in
the channel there is no other obstacle than the shallows which stretch off both
sides. That on the Morro side is named the Cabrestante Bank,t and extends only
one-third of a cable from the shore; therefore, by keeping half a cable’s length
off you will go clear of danger; and to prevent getting on the edge of the
shoal to leeward, it is necessary not to go farther from the Morro shore than a
cable’s length; working your vessel so as to run along between half a cable and a
cable’s length from that shore, the mid-channel being about three-quarters of a cable ;
and an experienced eye cannot mistake half a cable when the whole distance is only
one. When so far advanced as the middle of the fort La Cabana, which will be when
abreast of the N.E. front of the city, keep away, and anchor opposite the eastern
front of the city af any distance you choose, as-the largest ships may lie near
enough to lay a plank on the shore.

At a short distance to the south and west of the Morro Point, isa very small
shoal, with 5 fathoms water on it; this bank is to be feared only when there is
much swell of the sea, as at other times the largest ships may pass over it without
risk of touching. Even when the water has fallen or decreased in depth, there is
nothing to fear, inasmuch at half a cable’s length from the Morro you will be per-
fectly clear of it. Finally, if you wish to pass through the entrance, without risk
of a mistake in estimating the distance at which you ought to pass the Morro, look
out for the outer buoys near the Morro Point, and passing them to the westward,
keep midway between the buoys on either side of entrance, six buoys to the east-
ward and three to the westward.”

* A shoal has been reported lying N.N.E., distant a mile from Morro Castle, and up-
wards of a mile from the shore, and on which the ship Mariner, of Port Glasgow, grounded
in 1815; the ship drew 17 feet water. When approaching the harbour from the east-
ward, care should be taken to avoid this shoal.

+ The Cabrestante, or Capstan, is the projecting edge of the shelf within the Morro, at
about a cable’s length from the Light Tower ; and about a cable’s length farther in, on
the same side, is a similar projection, named the Pastora, or Shepherdess Shoal. That on
the opposite, or leeward side, is named the St. Telmo Shoal.

118 HAVANA.

We here subjoin a description of the shoals in the entrance, and directions for
taking this harbour, by Mr. C. P. Bellamy :—

“The entrance of Havana Harbour lies about S.E.$E., and N.W. £ W., and
is so narrow, that with a scant wind two vessels should never attempt to enter it
abreast ; and, as the wind from the high land inside the Morro is generally baffling
and squally, vessels should always be prepared to shorten sail, and anchor imme-
diately after rounding the Morro Point, in case they should not be able to weather
the shoal of St. Telmo, which stretches about half the distance across towards
the weather shore. On the outer edge of this shoal is a buoy, in 22 fathoms
water; and a boat’s length on the outside of it, is a depth of 5 fathoms. ‘lhe Morro
Castle is steep-to, having 5 fathoms under that part which overhangs; but at a short
distance within the Morro the Capstan Shoal commences, and extends off to about a
frigate’s length to the first battery within the Morro, in the depth of 3 fathoms: it
then suddenly deepens to 6 and 7 fathoms. The’ west, or extreme part of the
Shepherdess, lies about the same distance from a point on which are several huts, and
ends in the depth of 25 fathoms; in which depth is a buoy: at about 30 feet on
the outside of this buoy is the depth of 6 and 7 fathoms. A bank also stretches off
the first angle of the fortifications, below the custom house, and extends to the great.
drain of the city; on the outer edge of which, at about a ship's length from the battery,
is the depth of 3 fathoms.

“To enter this harbour, the eye must be your guide: if the wind is scant, pass
within a ship’s length of the Morro Lighthouse, luffing up as you round it; and if the
wind baffles, take advantage of every favourable flaw, passing about 30 fathoms from
the weather shore (after rounding the Morro), and between the buoys of the
Shepherdess and the shoals of St. Telmo. The most favourable time for entering this
harbour is generally about noon, as the wind at that time of the day draws more to
the northward ; and at night you always have the land wind, except when blowing
hard, or in the season of the Norths, therefore the most favourable time for sailing in
is always in the day. Ifthe wind is to the northward of N.E. in the offing about
noon, you will be able to fetch into the interior of the harbour; but if it is at E.N.E.
you will be compelled to anchor in the entrance, and warp in; the best time for doing
which is in the evening or morning, as there may be little wind.

‘ Men-of-war generally anchor in the broadest part of the harbour, between Regla
and the Gate of La Lux. Merchant ships lie moored head and stern in tiers, between
the outer port of Cabanas and Casa Blanca, or at the custom-house quay. Ships of
war always obtain water by application to the senior naval officer’s ship for the use
of a tank at the dock-yard. Pilots always go out, in fine weather, on the customary
signal being made, but they never go far from the Morro.”

The following extract by a Liverpool trader* :—

“This is one of the finest harbours throughout the West Indies ; it is capable of
containing several hundred sail, completely protected from all winds, and is very
seldom visited by the destructive hurricanes so frequent in Jamaica, and other neigh-
bouring islands.

The entrance to Havana Harbour lies N.W. and S.E. nearly, and is about half a
mile wide, from the Morro Castle to what is called the Punta, or opposite shore
(which bears from the Morro S.8.W.), and it continues the same breadth, or a little
wider, all the way up the Public Wharf, where it is the narrowest. It is there less
than a quarter of a mile, and the wharf, which is on the starboard hand going in, is
about a mile and a quarter from the Morro.

Above the wharf the harbour opens out into a large basin, where a vessel may
choose her anchorage ; but as merchant vessels have no choice, if with a cargo, they
anchor abreast of the wharf ; and if in ballast, on the opposite, or Casa Blanca side.
The Public Wharf, as before stated, is on the starboard hand going in, and there is

* Nautical Magazine, June, 1833.

HAVANA. 119

sufficient depth to haul the largest merchant vessel bows on to discharge or load, and
there is room for mooring upwards of 100 sail, large and small, in the same manner,

A square-rigged vessel bound to Havana, after having made the Morro (which is
easily known from sea, by the Maiden’s Paps in the interior, bearing a little east of
south from the Morro), must wait the sea breeze, which commonly sets in about 11
A.M., and takes off about 4 P.M., and most commonly from the N.E.

It is best to haul close round the Morro, and keep on the Morro side all the way
up to the guard-ship, if the wind permits, there being no danger, as there are 4 to 5
fathoms alongside the rocks. A vessel coming in after passing the Morro, if she be
taken aback, it is better to run out and come in the same way again, as by that
time the wind may so far favour her, ‘as to allow her to lay all the way up, and she
must then keep all sail on so as to be under command, with her anchor ready, and a
good range of cable. But should the wind be favourable for running in, it is only
necessary to keep about mid-channel, and before coming abreast of the wharf the
harbour-master will go on board, and give directions where to anchor.

Tn other circumstances, there is good anchorage all the way up, and a vessel obliged
to come-to, must wait until the evening, and warp up.

The guard-ship lies about two-thirds up the harbour from the Morro to the wharf,
and about a cable’s length from the north shore. Between her and about four berths
above the wharf, all vessels moor head and stern with bower or stream anchor, and
not more than three abreast from Casa Blanca side, but higher up the harbour, the
vessels lie at single anchor.

The depth of water from the Morro up to the harbour is from 16 to 10 and 6
fathoms; in the harbour from 10 to 6 and 56 fathoms, all tough clay, mixed with
shells.*

No directions are requisite for going out, as it is either done in the morning or
evening, when the wind is fair out; and a vessel is clear off as soon as it is past the
Morro.”

H. M. Ship Cornwallis, from Havana to Bermuda. Nautical Magazine, September,
1839.—* March 20th 1839, at daylight made sail and stood out of the harbour; came
out with a fine breeze at S.E., which we found outside to be E.S.E.; stood to the N.E.
going 6 knots, at noon tacked ship.

It is advisable to sail from Havana early in the morning; and stand off on the
starboard tack till noon, when it generally happens that the wind draws to the east or
E.N.E., allowing a good lay along the land: in this way a ship will have worked up
to the Matanzas by sunset, and be in the most favourable position for going off all
night on the starboard tack. If the wind will allow, keep a good full at N.E., which
will reach into mid-channel of the Florida stream. No fear need be entertained about
Cay Sal, as the current sets about N.E., 2 or 3 knots per hour. Of course during the
Norths, the current will have a more easterly direction, and incline towards the Cay
Sal, and Bahama Banks, at which time it will be necessary to borrow more on the
Florida Shore.

Having left Matanzas at 6h. 45m. P.M. we continued on the starboard tack, and at
noon next day, were 55 miles from Gun Cay, having had the current N. 40° E.,
2 miles per hour; Gun Cay Lighthouse, which is white, was, when first seen from
the mast head, reported to be a sail. At 6h. 30m. P.M, the light bore E. by 8. 28.,
and being just visible from the sixth ratline of the mizen rigging, which is 40 feet
above the level of the sea, must have been 15 miles distant. Working up the reckon~-
ing, from the noon to this time, viz., 65 hours, gives the current, N. 11° E., 22 miles.

* Tt has been stated that the entrance to the Harbour of Havana is rapidly filling up.
The channel by which three-deckers formerly entered, will now barely permit 44 gun
frigates to enter; but this evil will, no doubt, be greatly diminished by the frequent use of
the dredging machines, .

We now steered N. 4 W., which cleared the strait, and at noon of the 22nd, the
Matanilla Reef bore S.S.E., 42 miles, the stream having set in, during the remaining
173 hours, N. 7° W., 48 miles.

We were now fairly in the Atlantic, and the wind drawing round from east to
§.E. and south, a N.K. by E. course was shaped for Bermuda; which, though not
direct, is yet to be preferred, as in eight cases out of ten, the wind will be at S.W.
west, and N.W. to north. A gale, or very strong breeze, may be expected from the
N.W. quarter; when, having obtained a good weather position, it will be easy on the
port tack to make the islands. This was the case with the Cornwallis ; and we got a
pilot on the seventh day from the Havana, which is considered a most excellent
passage.”

From the Havana to Point Yeacos, the bearing and distance are nearly H. 3 N.,
24 leagues. At 124 leagues eastward from the Morro, and 11; leagues W. by S. from
Point Ycacos, is Point de Guanos, the west point of the entrance to the Bay of
Matanzas; and to the south-westward of it, about 7 miles, is the remarkable hill,
called the Pan of Matanzas, hereafter described. This hill may be seen from Point
Yeacos, bearing S.W. by W. 2 W., at the distance of about 7 leagues, and constitutes
the grand point of departure for ships bound northward through the Gulf or Strait
of Florida.

Light.—At Port Santa Crvz, about 24 miles to the eastward of Havana, in lat.
23° 9’ 0, and long. 82° 1’ 15’, a fixed light is exhibited, visible 7 or 8 miles. 4

Light (proposed).—On Point Guanos, 18 miles to the eastward of Santa Cruz, a
light of the 8rd order is proposed. ‘The tower is to be 92 feet in height, and to show
a revolving light every minute (1668).

To the north-eastward of Point Ycacos, at about a mile, within the edge of soundings,
are the three islets, called by the Spaniards Cayo de Piedras, Mono, and Monillo.
Of these the southernmost and smallest is Monillo, lying 3 miles N.N.E. $ E. from
the point; the next is Piedras, a rocky cay, lying about half a mile N.E. from the
former ; and, lastly, Mono, lying about 2 miles in the same direction from Piedras.
At 11 mile N.E. 2 E. from Mono lies a dangerous reef. To the south-eastward of
Piedras and Mono there is a good and convenient anchorage in 5 or 6 fathoms, on
clean sandy ground, sheltered from northerly winds, which may be taken by sailing
in through the middle of either passage. As this anchorage, together with the coast
from Ycacos Point westward and the Bay of Mantanzas, are included in the north-
east and north coast of Cuba, from Cape Maize to the Havana, immediately follow-
ing, we forbear giving a farther description in this place.

Light.—On Prepras Oay, at the entrance of Cardenas Bay, in latitude 23° 14’ 24’,
and longitude 81° 7’ 28’, a fixed light is established, showing a red flash every half
minute. The tower is white, and erected upon the house, 75 feet in height, and 68
feet above the sea, visible about 15 miles,

Light.—On Cay p’ANA, within the Bay Cardenas, is a fixed light, eleyated on a
a at and visible 7 miles. Small vessels lie well sheltered to the westward of
this light.

CURRENTS ON THE NORTH-WEST COAST OF CUBA.—The great body of
water, which sets to the south-eastward from the Gulf of Mexico, diverges to the
eastward and westward on approaching the N.W. coast of Cuba; from Bahia Honda
westward it runs to leeward; but from thence, eastward, it runs to the eastward.
This has been experienced by several navigators. Mr. Romans, in treating of it,
says, ‘I have always observed that a lee current does not extend eastward of Bahia
Honda; at least, I have found it so during five or six times that I have met the
current setting westward; but at those times, and in eight or ten other passages
along this coast, I have always found a strong windward current east of that place ;
so that, if I once weathered it, I was seldom more than twelve hours in getting up to
Point de Guanos, being the west point of the Bay of Mantanzas.”

BARACOA. 121

About the Banks of Isabella and the Colorados Reefs the current generally runs to
the west and south-westward. Mr. Bishop says, “ Were I to come round Cape St.
Antonio, I should not choose to come near the Colorados, because I look upon the
current as a tide’s way, or as one of the points of the River Thames. If you presume
to go close by the point, it isa hundred to one if you are not caught in the eddy.
Trying it at 2 or 3 miles off the Colorados, it sets S.S.W. at the rate of a mile anda
half in an hour.” Hence it appears, that a vortex of current prevails somewhere
about these reefs. We now proceed to describe

THE NORTH-EAST AND NORTH COASTS OF CUBA.
FROM CAPE MAIZE TO HAVANA.

From PUNTA DE MAYSI, on CAPE MAIZE, the easternmost point of Cuba
(already described, page 93), the coast trends to the N.N.W., and forms the east
front of the island, as far as River Maysi, at 15 mile from the cape. From this
river, as far as the Point Azules, which is another mile on the N.E. coast, the
coast is bounded by a reef, which extends out a cable’s length, and forms a break at
the mouth of the River Maysi. From Point Azules the land begins to rise, and the
coast is clean, trending about W.N.W. 3 W., the space of 5 miles to the Punta del
Frayle, or Friar’s Point, and from thence it trends W. 3 8., a distance of 7 miles
to the River Yumari, and continues about 3 miles more in the same direction
to the Port of Mata. All this coast is very clean, and may be passed at less than
half a mile.

The Port of Mata is very small, and haying but little depth, can admit none but
small vessels. ‘Io enter it, keep in mid-channel, and anchor in from 14 to 15 feet
water, almost in the middle of the bay. All the shores have projecting banks, with
shallow water, which terminate in a space of only 2 cables’ length in diameter, in
which there is sufficient depth for anchoring. The course in is §.8.W. x W.; the
breadth of the channel less than a cable,

From Port Mata the coast trends about N.W. by W. 4 W., to the Punta Majana,
and at 2 short miles from the port is the mouth of the River Bono. This part of the
coast, as well as the preceding, is very clean.

BARACOA.—The Point of Majana and the Point of Baracoa, which lie nearly
east and west, 2 miles distant from each other, form a bay, in the east part of which
is the anchorage of Playa de Miel, or Honey Beach; and in the west, the mouth of
the Harbour of Baracoa: in the middle, between these two anchorages is the town
of Baracoa, standing on the south point of the harbour of the same name. In this
town reside the pilots for the Bahama, or Old Channel; and, therefore, vessels which
have not taken one at Aguadilla, in Porto Rico, come here for one.

The anchorage of Playa de Miel is quite exposed to the Norths; to take it steer
round Point Majana, and anchor something to the south of it, in from 10 to 13
fathoms water, on a sandy bottom, taking care not to get to the east of that point,
because you would immediately be in 4, or less than 4, fathoms water. As the
general object for going to Baracoa is only to obtain a pilot, there is no necessity to
anchor; but approaching Point Majana, within 2 cables’ length, if you please, dis-
charge a cannon or gun, and a pilot will come off. As the Playa de Miel is entirely
open to tne Norths, in the season of those winds, it is much exposed ; and, therefore,
any vessel under the necessity of anchoring, should proceed at once for Baracoa, to
the entrance of which there is no obstacle, as it is entirely clean, having no danger
but what may be seen.

BARACOA HARBOUR, which is very secure and well sheltered, has the great
inconvenience of having its mouth open to the prevailing winds, which throw in a
heavy sea. It isseldom visited except by coasters, and these anchor close up under the

town; and not being able to get out of it with the land breeze, vessels are often
detained much time during the Norths, when the land breezes are very scanty; but
in the rainy season you may be assured of having it every night. El Yunque, or the
Anvil of Baracoa, which is a little mountain about 5 miles to the west of the harbour,
is an excellent point to recognise it by, as in clear days it may be seen at more than
12 leagues’ distance.

As the entrance is approached, a small fort will be observed, and soon after the
town, which stands a little below it, on the eastern side of the port; a small fort
will also be seen at the entrance. The port or bay is about $a mile wide from
N.W. to S.E., but scarcely + of a mile deep. It has, however, sufficient water in
it for vessels of the largest draught.

From the Harbour of Baracoa the coast trends N.N.W. 4 W., a distance of
22 miles to the Punta de Canas, and although it is a clean strand, it ought not to be
approached, because, being entirely open to the breeze, there is always a heavy sweil
of the sea setting on it. From Punta de Canas to the Harbour of Maravi is 23 miles;
the coast trends W. by N., and is very clean.

The HARBOUR or MARAVI, is merely a small inlet, 2 cables deep and 1 cable
wide, with a depth of 8 fathoms in the centre, and no danger whatever at the
entrance. It is, however, exposed to the N.E., and consequently not a safe anchorage,
except under favourable circumstances.

From the Port of Maravi the coast trends about N.N.W. 2 W., making a bay or
bend as far as Punta de Vaez, and from thence it bends about N.W. 2N., forming
another bay or bend as far as Puerta de Navas, which is an opening, in form of a
herse-shoe, of about 2 cables’ length in extent, in all directions, with its mouth to the
north, but sheltered as far as N.E. It is about 3 cables deep and a cable wide, with
a depth of 9 and 10 fathoms, and of easy access. :

From Port Navas to that of Cayaguaneque is scarcely 2 miles. The Port of
Cayaguaneque is fit for very small vessels only; its entrance is very narrow, the
channel being no more than 40 yards wide, and open to the N.E.

PUERTO DE TACO, situate 3$ miles to the westward of Cayaguaneque, is a
small deep basin, but its channel is so exceedingly intricate that it is only fit for
handy coasters drawing not more than 10 feet water.

PUERTO DE JARAGUA.—From the Harbour of Taco to the Point of Jaragua, is 3
miles; and the coast is a sandy beach, and clean. At the Point of Jaragua it ceases
to be so, but all between it and Punta de Maysi, may be run along at a mile distant.
The Point of Jaragua sends out a reef, which stretches to the N.W. of it: this point
is the easternmost of the anchorage of the same name, which is no other than an
opening or break in the reef, by which a vessel may enter upon the bank or shoal,
and have shelter from the sea, behind the said reef. The break or mouth is only
two-thirds of a cable wide; and from it to some islets, which are 8.W. of it, the
distance is 2 cables. The islets are three in number; the northernmost is the least;
the middle are somewhat larger; and the southernmost the largest. The anchorage
for large vessels extends only till you are EK.  N., and W. 3 S., with the south part
of the middle islet ; and from that, farther in, there is only from 12 to 18 feet water.
To take this anchorage it is necessary to sail outside the reef, which projects from
Peint Jaragua, until the east part of the great islet bears 5.W.; and steer directly
for it; and if the vessel be large, anchor K. 4 N., from the south end of the middle
islet, in 6 fathoms, on sandy bottom; but if the vessel draw not more than 14 feet,
run farther in, passing within a quarter of a cable of the great islet, and about a
cable’s length south from the middle of it, and anchor in 19 feet, on clay. You may
also enter the mouth, without attending to the given mark, because the reef itself
shows the opening. This harbour should never be taken, unless forced by great
necessity, as there can be no other motive for vessels going to it.

From the Point of Jaragua, the coast trends first to the W.N.W., and afterwards
to N. 3 W., forming a great bay to Punta Guarico, or Mangle Point, which is 7 miles

CABONICO AND LIVISA. 123

distant from the former. The reef, which extends from Point Jaragua, rounds the
whole of it, and stretches out from Mangle Point, about 2 miles. Be careful not to
mistake this cape for Cape Maysi; it being dangerous at night and in obscure
weather, when you cannot recognise and use as marks the eastern lands of the island,
and particularly when you are uncertain of your latitude.

Puerto pr Cayo Moa.—From Mangle Point the coast trends about W.N.W. 4 Wy
a distance of 8 miles to the River Moa; all this is bordered by a reef, which extends
2 and 23 miles into the sea. Almost N. 3 W., from the mouth of that river, and
between the reef and the shore, is an islet, named Cayo Moa, which offers excellent
anchorage, sheltered from all sea; it is entered by an opening in the reef, almost north
from the entrance of the river. This opening is about 2 cables’ length wide, and
continues westward, forming the channel and anchorage, so far as north and south,
with the east end of Cayo Moa. To take it, run along the east side of the reef,
until you are at the opening, which will be when the east point of the River Moa
bears south; then steer §.W. 4S, until the south part of Cayo Moa bears W.N.W.
= W.; then alter course to W. $ S., and continue steering so until you anchor
S. 3 E., from the eastern part of Cayo Moa, distant about 2 cables’ length, in 63 or
7 fathoms, upon clay. The mark for recognizing or finding this anchorage is a moun-
tain about 4 leagues inland, named the Sierra de Moa.

From the anchorage of Moa, the coast trends about W. by S., all bounded by a reef,
which extends about 2 or 3 miles off, as far as Puerto de Yaguaneque, distant from
the former 11 miles. On this part of the coast, and between it and the reefs, there
are two cays, the eastern one named Burro, and the western Arena, or Sands; these
cays may serve as marks for knowing this part of the coast. The harbour of
Yaguaneque is fit for small vessels only, because its bottom is shallow and uneven,
and its entrance narrow, and very difficult to take, for its mouth is formed by a break
or opening in the reef. To take this port, it is necessary to follow by the edge of the
reef to windward, to the opening, which lies N.W., two-thirds of a cable from Arena
Cay: then steer 8. 3 E., keeping along by the edge of the weather reef, as near as
you-may, in the supposition that the reef to leeward, which commences about west
from Arena Cay, narrows the entrance so much, that the channel is scarcely a cable’s
length wide. ‘This harbour is fit for small craft only.

CANANOVA.—A mile and a half from Yaguaneque is the Port of Cananova,
which is properly no more than an opening of the coast, which must be entered by
another opening formed by the reef. This port, also, is fit for very small vessels
only. Three miles to the westward of this port, is that of Cebollas, which is difficult
to enter, or to get out of; and therefore unfit for large vessels.

TANAMO.—Eleven miles west from Cebollas is the Port Tanamo, and the inter-
mediate coast is foul, with a reef which extends off about 2 miles. ‘This port is of
considerable extent, and studded with small islets, between which are channels deep
enough for the largest vessels. The cut through the reef and the channel into the
port are, however, both very narrow, but the dangers are easily seen, and the eye
will be the best guide.

CABONICO AND LIVISA.—From Tanamo the coast trends W. i S., 10 miles,
to the entrance of the Ports of Cabonico and Livisa: this piece of coast also sends
out a reef about 2 miles from it. ‘These two harbours are entered by one mouth or
opening, which, within, divides into two branches; one to the eastward, leading to
Cabonico, and the other to the westward, leading to Livisa. Both are very tortuous
and intricate, but have sufficient water for vessels of the largest draught. Most of
the dangers are seen, and the eye will guide in mic-channel.

NIPE.—From the entrance of the above ports, the coast continues foul, with a
reef, about W.N.W., a distance of 6 miles, to the Hargour or Bay of Nipe. This
bay, from its magnitude and depth, is capable of holding all the fleets of Europe, has
a spacious entrance, to take which, a plan will be sufficient guide. The entrance is
always attainable, for, with either the breezes or the Norths, you will run into the
harbour with a free wind; but coming out is quite the reverse, for it is necessary to

124 POINT LUCBECIA.

have the land breeze, which, as we have before said, is often very rare in the season
of the norths.

To distinguish all this part of the coast, the mountains of Christal may serve as a
mark ; these are a continuation of the Cordillera, or range, which comes from Baracoa,
and extends on the south of Port Livisa, about 13 miles inland. The Pan of Sama is
also another excellent mark; its figure being such as cannot be mistaken, because
the summit of it forms a table: it rises on the land to the north of Nipe and Banes,
and is nearly north and south with the Port of Sama. As the mountains of Christal
rise 13 miles inland to a great height, and the Pan of Sama, (which begins to rise“
gradually, almost from Point Mulas,) form an opening or break in the chain, or con-
finuation of the mountains, it is almost impossible for any one to mistake this coast.
The Pan of Sama may be seen 20 miles off.

BANES.—From the Bay of Nipe the coast rounds to the N.W., a distance of 12
miles to the Port of Banes; it is all clean, and may be passed at half a mile distance.
The entrance of the port is in the middle of a bay formed by the coast, which has
between its exterior points an opening of 24 miles, whence it narrows to 13 cable
in width, so that it resembles a funnel. The shores of the bay, and also of the
channel, are uncommonly clean and deep, and there is nothing to fear but what is
visible. This harbour forms an excellent anchorage for all classes of vessels. It is
extremely difficult, however, to get out of, because its mouth is open to the sea breeze,
and it is necessary to take advantage of the land breeze to get out clear, at least as
far as the middle of the bay, to have room to tack and weather the outer points, and
the coast, which there trends about N. $ E., a distance of 10 miles to Punta de Mulas.
This latter point is foul with a reef extending more than a mile eastward, and which
borders the coast from the northern point of the Bay of Banes. The mountains of
Christal, and Pan of Sama form a good mark for this point.

POINT LUCRECIA.—From the north point of Puerto de Banas the shore runs
in a N.N.E. direction 6 miles to Mulas Point, and is foul all the way to within the
distance of a mile. From Mulas Point it trends N.N.W., 3 miles to Manglito Point,
and then N.W. to Lucrecia Point where a lighthouse is in course of erection, and a
temporary light at present exhibited (1868).

Light.—On Lucrecia Point, in latitude 21° 5’ 0" and longitude 75° 87’ 30’, a light-
house is building. The tower is to be 112 feet above the sea, and will exhibit a
revolving light, visible 15 miles (not lighted in March, 1866). A temporary light
is exhibited 52 feet above high water.

From Luerecia Point the land trends N.W. 4 W., 64 miles, and then W. by N.,
2 miles to Sama Point (formerly called Lucrecia), a headland which is 200 feet high,
amile inland. All this part of the shore is clean and steep-to, and about midway is
the small river Seco, at the bottom of a sandy bay.

From Lucrecia Point the coast takes a somewhat sudden turn, and trends to the
W.S.W. for 33 miles to Port Sama. Temporary anchorage may be found off Port
Sama.

PUERTO DE SAMA is a small inlet about 13 mile long N. and 8. from 1 to 2
cables’ wide, and only fit for vessels drawing not more than 12 feet water. The
entrance may readily be found by the Pan de Sama, which rises south of it. To the
westward of the port there is also a flat-topped ridge of mountains running N.W.
and §.E. and terminating at its west end in a bold scarped rock of a whitish
appearance.

PUERTO DE NARANJO. Between Sama and Port Naranjo, 5 miles to the
westward, the shore is composed of sand, and named Guardo-laboca. To the south-
ward of it there is a detached sugar-loaf hill, and to the S.W., the Maseta de Naranjo,
a small wooded mountain with a flat summit. Naranjo lies between these two
objects, and about 3 miles to the windward of it there is a remarkable red cliff, and
on the east side of the entrance there is also another of the same appearance, high
and scarped. ‘The shore between it and Sama is foul to the distance of about 3 mile.
The entrance to the port is only a cable wide, but it opens out into an irregular

PUERTO DE GIBARA. 125

shaped basin, containing several inlets deep enough for vessels of all classes, sheltered
from all winds, and they can sail in and out of it with the usual sea breeze.

There is good wooding and watering in Puerto Naranjo. The latter is at a stream
on the southern shores at the head of the Carenage, abreast a small mound named
the l'able of Naranjo, but there will be some difficulty in finding the opening in the
bushes leading to it.

Directions.—In running down for Port Naranjo it is necessary to keep a good
offing until the entrance bears S. by E. when a vessel may haul in. Give the
weather point a berth of a cables’ length, and after clearing the ledge which runs
a tle eee length to the northward off the lee point, the eye will guide in mid-
channel.

If intending to make only a short stay, it will be more convenient to anchor close
off the first sandy beach on the eastern shore, in 10 or 11 fathoms, with the weather
point bearing N.N.W.; otherwise proceed further up into what fishermen call the
Carenage or Western Bight. The best berth here will be in about 10 fathoms, with
the centre of the Table Naranjo, W.S.W., and the north point of the Carenage in
one with the red cliff at the entrance north. The table from this quarter has a
conical appearance.

The rise and fall at Port Naranjo is about 4 feet, but nothing is known of the
period of high water.

PUERTO DE VITA. From Naranjo the shore trends W.N.W., 23 miles to
Pisquero Nuero Point, and then S.W. by W., 3 miles Port Vita. This part of the
coast is low and sandy ; the first portion is foul to a short distance, the latter is clean
and steep to. Vita is a small, narrow, irregular shaped inlet which may be used and
easily navigated by vessels not drawing more than 18 feet.

At 3 miles to the westward of Vita is Port Bariay, and a mile further to leeward
Port Jururu.

PUERTO DE BARIAY is open to the northward, and therefore not safe in the
winter months, but there is good temporary anchorage close under the weather shore
off the second sandy beach from the entrance.

PUERTO DE JURURU is more extensive than that of Bariay, and the interior
completely sheltered, with a depth in it of 4 fathoms, but the entrance is so
narrow and tortuous that it is only fit for small fore and aft rigged vessels of light
draught.

PUERTO DE GIBARA lies 5 miles to the westward of Jururu, and is merely
a small bay, about a mile in extent, with a depth just within the entrance of 20 feet.
It is quite open to the northward, and only fit for small coasters, which find shelter
close under the weather shore, as far round as N. by W. ‘The town stands on the
western shore, and may be seen 9 miles off. To the southward of it are three
remarkable hills; the easternmost, from the shape of its summit, is cal led the Saddle
of Gibara; the middle one somewhat resembles a sugar-boiler ; and to the westward
of the other are some hills of regular height.

Although the bay is only adapted for small vessels, it is the port of Holguin or
Holgeia, a large town about 15 miles in the interior, in a cultivated part of the
country. The river Gibara flows into the bay, and is navigable for boats some
distance up.

From the west point of the bay the coast runs N.W. by N. for 2 miles to Brava
Point, and is bold and rocky. It then bends to the N.W. for 7 miles to Gorda Point,
and N.W. by W., 6 miles to Mangle Point, so that Gibara lies at.the bottom of a
deep bight. For 10 miles from Brava Point the shore is rocky, sloping and clean
to Mangle Point, but it then becomes sandy and steep-to as far as Heradura Bay,
a distance of 7 miles ina W. by N.3N. direction, hence it takes a more westerly
direction 8 miles to Port Padre. ‘his part is low, and foul to some distance, and the
shore is skirted by remarkable palm-trees.

126 PUERTO DE MANATIL

PUERTO DEL PADRE is a secure basin, carrying a depth over the greater
part of it of 4 fathoms; the channel into it however, is very narrow and somewhat
tortuous, but the dangers are all visible. Close to the westward of the port are two
small hummocks, which are good guides for it. The entrance lies at the bottom of
a bay or funnel, which is about a mile deep, and at the outer part, between Jarro
Point on the east, and Guinchos Point on the west, is 2 miles wide. Close off the latter
there is a small cay, and this side is steep-to. All, therefore, that is required in
entering is to give the reef which skirts the coast a berth until Jarro Point bears
S.E., when haul in, keeping the western shore aboard. The interior of the port is
almost separated into two parts; the easternmost will be found the most convenient

for leaving, and the channel into it is between the cays at the inner end of the
entrance channel.

PUERTO DE MALAGUETA. The shore from Point Padre continues its

westerly direction for 5 miles, and is skirted by a reef to some distance. There.

is here a small opening leading into the bay or port of Malagueta, an extensive
navigable lagoon. The land around is low and swampy. Thence the coast takes

a N.W. direction, 3 miles to Cobarrubiag Point, and then W.N.W., 6 miles to
Port Manati.

PUERTO DE MANATI carries a depth of 44 to 53 fathoms, but it is merely a
narrow creek leading into a shallow lagoon, and only fit for coasters. On its western
side there is a remarkable sugar-loaf mount called,El Manueco, and a little beyond
it another, not quite as lofty, named Tardo or Table of Manati, which may be seen
15 or 20 miles, and are good guides for the offing. It» must be borne in mind,
however, that when nearly in a‘line they somewhat resemble the Saddle of Gibara,
and care should be taken not to mistake them,

PUERTO DE NEURAS GRANDES. From Manati Point the coast trends
N.W. by N., 3 miles to Braba Point, and then N.W. by W. 2 W., 33 miles to the
entrance of Nuevas Grandes 6 del Bayamo, a small tortuous creek, in some parts
only 3 a cable wide, and only navigable for droghers of 12 feet draught. All this
part of the shore is foul and the reef extends off 2 of a mile from the entrance of the
creek. Thence the coast runs N.W., 54 miles to Ganado Point, and N.W. by W., 74
miles to Puerto de las Nuevitas del Principe, and is skirted by a reef all the way, and
should not be approached within 2 miles.

ight.—On BARLoveEnto or Pinors’ Porn7, the east point of entrance to Nuevitas,
a small fixed light is shown 49 feet above high water, and visible 9 miles. The light
is hoisted on a white mast from the centre of the keeper’s dwelling, which is a quad-
rangular building coloured yellow.

PUERTO DE LAS NUEVITAS DEL PRINCIPE.—This is the sea-port. of
Principe, a large commercial town about 25 miles in the interior, and which com-
municates with it by a single line of railway. The harbour is completely sheltered,
and capable of admitting vessels of the largest draught, but the channel into the
interior is so narrow, and its turning so sharp, that a pilot is absolutely necessary ;
in his absence it must be navigated by the eye. ‘The entrance points are low and
about 3a mile apart. On the eastern point the lighthouse is erected, and there are
some huts, the residence of the pilots, and near them a flagstaff.

Near the south shore of the harbour are three small hills, and in the middle of the
harbour 3 small islets, somewhat higher than the surrounding lands, and good guides
from the offing. Should a vessel merely wish to communicate with the town, it will
be found more convenient to anchor off the fort, which is about 1; mile within the
entrance. In this case, all that is to be done is to steer in mid-channel, taking care,
as the entrance is approached, to avoid a dry shoal near the west end of the eastern
reef bearing N.E. by E. one mile from the flagstaff on the point. The tide runs
strong at the entrance, but they are scarcely sensible in the harbour.

There is a small stream of good water near the town of Nuevitas, on the western
shore of the harbour, but it is difficult to get at, as the mouth is nearly dry.

CAY VERDE. 127

Light.—This part of the coast is pointed out by the lighthouse on Maternillo
Point, which bears N.N.W., 4 miles from the entrance of Port Nuevitas. The coast
between is very low, but free from danger. The lighthouse is in latitude 21° 40° 10",
and longitude 77° 9’ 7’, and is 170 feet in height, and 174 feet above the level of the
sea, exhibiting a revolving light every minute, visible 20 miles. The building is white,
with the word “ CoLon ” painted thereon.

LA SABINAL.—From Maternillo Point the coast trends N.W. by W. } W., 20
miles to the Boca de Caravelas. ‘This part of the coast is called La Sabinal, and is

" very low, with a sandy shore, backed by numerous lagoons and swamps, and skirted

by a broken reef to the distance of a mile to a mile and a half, with soundings about
one third of a mile outside it. On the shore there are four fishing stations, named
Cruces, Las Palmas, Punta Piedra, and Eusefada-Honda, before which small vessels,
drawing 7 or 8 feet, find anchoring ground under shelter of the reefs. The only
remarkable object on the coast is a large clump of Mangrove trees about 10 miles
from Maternillo Point, called the Alto de Juan Danue.

BOCA DE CARAVELA has 6 feet water over its bar, and the same depth may
be carried through an intricate channel between the mangrove cays, to the fishing
village of Guanaja, about 22 miles to the westward. At the entrance of the opening
the tide runs 3 knots.

GUAJABA ISLAND.—From the entrance of the Caravela the N.E, side of the
island of Guajaba trends N.W. 3 W.,10 miles. For the first 4 miles it is a low
mangrove shore skirted by small cays; the remainder is a sandy beach. On this
island are two small hills; the S.E. hill is about a mile in extent N.W. to S.E., and
90 feet high; the other is a smaller round lump, anda little less elevated. When
first seen from the eastward they have the appearance of four small hummocks, and
serve as guides to this part of the coast.

BOCA DE GUAJABA, which separates the island of that name from Cay Romano,
has a depth of 5 feet at its entrance at low water, and there is a boat-channel of 3
feet up to Guajaba. About 7 miles to the N.N.W. of the opening there is a remark-
able hill on the eastern end of Cay Romano, 230 feet high, which cannot be mistaken.
Under it will be seen two fishing stations near the beach.

CAY VERDE.—About 5 miles to the northward of the above hill is a small, low
islet, of a circular form, and a cable in diameter, covered with bushes to the height
of 10 feet above high water, called Cay Verde. From the Caravelas opening to this
islet the broken reef still skirts the shore to about the same distance, inside which
boats or vessels not drawing more than 7 feet find good shelter. N. by E. from the
River Guajaba there is an opening through which 10 feet water may be carried,
and +a mile S.W. of Cay Verde there is shelter for vessels of this draught against
Northers. The best channel to take is that round the north end of the reef, about
13 mile from the cay, but it requires good local knowledge of the place to enable a

~ vessel to thread her way safely through the shoals.

CAY CONFITES.—This low cay is half a mile in length N. and S., a cable wide,
and lies close on the edge of soundings at 4 miles N. by W. of Cay Verde; 45 miles
EK. by N. from the §.E. end of Cay Cruz; 12 miles S. by W.% W. from Cay Lobos, and
19 miles west of the Diamond Point, at the entrance of the Old Bahama Channel.
On its south end there isa pile of stones, and near the north end a solitary tree,
which is the first object seen when coming from the S.E. Off the north end a
dry reef extends to the distance of a mile, leaving a small channel of 12 feet
water between it and the end of the cay. A dry reef extends also a mile from
the south end.

Between this latter dry reef and the reef running off to the northward of Cay
Verde there is a clear channel carrying a depth of 5 fathoms, and leading into
anchorage under Cay Confites in 2 to 3 fathoms, on white sand. The best sheltered
berth will be with the cay bearing N.E. about a mile off, or nearer, according to the
yessel’s draught. Observe, however, that with the wind to the southward of east,

128 CAY PAREDON GRANDE.

a heavy roll sets in round the south end of the cay. This is the only anchorage on
this side of the Bahama Channel between Nuevitas and Paredon Grande, where a
vessel drawing more than 12 feet can ride out a Norther in safety.

CAY CRUZ is 11 miles long, in a N.W. 4 N. and S.E § S. direction, very low and
flat, with a sandy shore, and at its N.E. point there is a remarkable clump of trees,
30 feet high. ‘The cay is divided in the centre by a small cut, and abreast it on
Cay Romano there is a remarkable hummock, 100 feet high, called the Alte de Asi.
Between these two cays there is only a foot of water at low tides, and the bottom is
like pipe clay. Within Romano, it is olive mud covered with weeds.

TRIBUTARIOS DE MENERVA isa small dry reef lying } of a mile from the
edge of soundings, north, 2 miles from the north end of Cay Cruz, and east 33 miles
from the N. end of Cay Cayman. The edge of the bank between Cay Confites and
this reef runs N.W. 4 W. inastraight line for 143 miles, and may be seen from aloft,
the white sandy bottom showing itself distinetly just within the line of soundings,
which is very steep-to. This part is extremely dangerous and should be approached
very cautiously, as there is no safe anchorage whatever.

CAY PAREDON GRANDE, Light.—On the north part of this cay, an iron
lighthouse is erected, coloured brown, with base of stone. It is 128 feet in height,
and 159 fect above the level of the sea, exhibiting a fixed light, varied by a flash
every minute, visible 14 and 20 miles, latitude 22° 29” 3”, longitude 77° 10’ 6”.

From the Tributarios the edge of the bank takes a W.N.W. 5 N. direction Altes
miles, when it eomes within 2 miles of the north end of Cay Paredon Grande, which
is rocky and woody and about 40 feet high. ‘The shore between Cayman and
Paredon cays is filled with numerous small low isiets, sandbanks and reefs, and is
very dangerous.

PAREDON MEDIO is a small rocky islet, 25 feet high, lying 24 miles to the
westward of the north point of Paredon Grande. Guinchos (or Ginger Cay) on the
edge of the Bahama Bank, bears from the latter point N. 4 E., 16 miles.

Between Paredon Medio and Cay Confites there is no anchorage for vessels, it
being throughout full of shoals, not sufficiently large to afford shelter under them.
The kank should not be entered without some urgent necessity. There is no good
water to be obtained on any of these cays. In some places, by digging in the sand
it may be found, but generally brackish.

The streams of tide set right on and off the bank at the rate of about 3 knot an
hour, but in the openings between the cays they run from 2 to 3 knots.

It is high water, full and change at 7h. 30m., and the rise at springs is 3 feet, at
neaps 2 feet. Between the cays and the main, the rise and fall is not more than
a foot, and the stream is scarcely perceptible.

From the noth point of Paredon Grande the edge of the bank takes about a
W. by N. direction for 48 miles, and reaches the meridian of 79° within a short
distance of the west end of the Cay Santa Maria. The whole of this part is very
imperfectly represented on the present charts, but it is equally dangerous, and
affords no anchorage whatever to any but small coasters that are well acquainted
with it. Thence it trends to the W.S.W. for 17 miles, when it comes within 4 miles
of Cay Francés.

CAY FRANCES.—The port of San Juan de los Remedios is at Point Caybarien,.
Nine feet only can be carried at the point, which is connected by railway with San
Juan. Vessels drawing over 9 feet anchor under the lee of Cay Francés, which affords
good shelter and excellent holding ground.

Cape Francés may be known by the flagstaff and a few houses on the N.W. point;
there are also scattered trees of large size on the point, which make an excellent
landmark.

Tn running in bring the flagstaff to bear from S. to $.E.; give the point a berth of

SAGUA DE LA GRANDE. 129

1 mile, gradually hauling up around the bank; anchor with the white cliff bearing
east in 24 to 4 fathoms. ‘The soundings are very irregular. é

The channel to Point Caybarien is staked out.

Ten miles N.W. by W. 4 W. from Cay Francés there is a dangerous shoal called
Bajos Almedinas, on which the sea breaks in moderate weather.

‘Water.—There are some good wells at the south end of Cay Lobos, and water
will be found on the north side of Cay Coco, about 20 miles to the westward of Paredon
Grande.

From abreast of Cay Francés the edge of the bank takes about a N.W. by W.
direction for 40 miles, when it comes within 3 or 4 miles of Julias Cay.

ALMEDINAS REEF, which always breaks N.W., 10 miles from the west
end of Cay Francés, and close to the edge of soundings, about 3 miles from Cay
Fragoso, and north of Mount Guajabana on the main shore. From the Julias Cays,
the edge trends more westerly, and 10 miles from thence is the Boca de Marillanes,
the eastern channel to the river Sagua de la Grande.

SAGUA DE LA GRANDE.—Between Cayo de la Cruz and Cayo Mariposa, in
latitude 22° 59’ 40’; and longitude 79° 58’ 27", is Boca de Marillanes, the best entrance
into the harbour of Sagua de la Grande.

In making this port there is a remarkable range of lofty hills lying to the 8.W. of
the cay, known as the Loma of Sagua. With these hills bearing to the eastward of
south, they appear as separate mountains, but when to the northward of south, they
present the appearance of one range. Cristo Cay also affords a good landmark, it
having a white beach; there are also 4 or 5 pilots’ huts and a flagstaff on its N.E.
point, on the top of which there is a barrel, with the staves painted black and white,
and a blue flag with a white P in the centre.

Buoys.—There are 2 buoys on the banks, outside the harbour, both of which are
to be left on the port hand going in. Fifteen feet only can be carried into the
anchorage. Run for the N.E. point of Cayo del Cristo, which may be known by its
white beach and large pilot, and fisherman’s house on the point, until it bears west,
distant 13 mile, and the S.E end of Cayo de la Cruz S. by W. 7 W.; then steer S.E.
until the S.E. point of Cayo de la Cruz is on with the large white store house at the
mouth of the Sagua River, and bearing S.W. by S., when stand in. This range
clears the shoal ground called Cabezo de Marillanes, and crosses the bar in the best
water, say from 19 to 24 feet.

When abreast of the pilot house on the S.E. point of Cayo de la Cruz, steer S.W.
by S. 2S., watching carefully the shoal ripples on either hand. When abreast of

two small islands ealled Cayo Palemitas, luff up from them to the eastward, and anchor

in 17 to 18 feet water, good holding ground.

Cabezo de Marillanes has but 7 feet upon it, and bears E. by S. 3 S. from the huts
in Cayo del Cristo, distant 23 miles.

Cabaza de Canete has but 4 feet upon it, and bears S.E. by E. 3 E. from the huts on
Cayo del Cristo, and N.E. by N. from the pilot-house on Cayo de la Cruz.

ALCATRAZES SHOALS lie 2 miles to the westward of the Nicolao Reef, and seldom
break. This part of the bank is extremely dangerous, and not well known. From
Médano, Cay Sal bears N. by W., 28 miles.

REMARKABLE MOUNTAINS.—About 21 miles to the southward of Médano
is the Sierra Morena, a remarkable mountain with several pointed peaks; the two
nearest the N.W. extreme of the ridge, r south from St. Nicolao Reef. A short
distance to the w f Morena, there is another remarkable range of lofty hills
forming three | entre one being the highest, called Tetas de la Bella, or
La Bella Paps, s south of Cadiz Cay, and is a good guide for it. Still
further to the westward is the Sierras del Limonar, which may also be seen from
without the shoals ; and between it and the peaks of Camarioca is the hill of Santa
Clara equally conspicuous.

BABIA DE CADIZ CAY lies about 9 miles to the westward of Médano Island,
and on its N.E. part there is a fishing establishment and flagstaff.

Light.—On the above cay a lighthouse of iron is erected in latitude 23° 12’ 24’,
and longitude 80° 29’ 18”. It is 159 feet in height and 175 feet above the sea,
slightly conical, and painted white. It stands on the N.E. end of the cay, with the
keeper’s dwelling and storehouse on either side. The light is fixed, varied by a
bright flash every minute, and should be seen in clear weather at the distance of 24
miles.

Anchorage.—This cay affords good anchorage. To run for it bring the flagstaff
to bear 8.8.E. to 8.E., and run in and anchor about 1 mile from the cay, with its
point bearing east, in 4 fathoms. It will be observed that there is deep water
nearly to the anchorage ; with the north point of the cay bearing east, distant one
mile, the soundings are 75 fathoms, after which the water shoals rapidly to 5 and 8
fathoms, latitude 23° 13’, and longitude 80° 31”.

There is good fishing and wooding at Cay Cadiz, but no water. High water, full
and change, 6h. 20m. Rise and fall, 3 feet.

Cabezas Cay, lying W. by N., 6 miles to the westward of Cadiz Cay, has a dangerous
ledge running off it to the westward, and as it lies on the edge of the soundings it
should be approached with great caution. From this cay the edge of the bank takes
a W. 3 N. direction for 17 miles to the north end of Cayo Cruz del Padre, which is
the northernmost cay of the whole range. Thence the bank sweeps round to the
S.W. to Mona Cay, W. by S. 2 8., 9 miles distant.

CAYO CRUZ DEL PADRE.—This cay lies W. by N., 23 miles from Bahia
de Cadiz Cay, and E.N.E., 13 miles from the next light to the westward, on Cay
Piedras, which, together with an inner light to be noticed hereafter, are established
for the safer navigation of Cardenas Bay, and the increasing trade thereof.

MONO, PIEDRAS AND MONILLO CAYS, are the westernmost of the cays
situate on the reef off the northern coast of Cuba, and which in progressing from
the eastward may be said to terminate at Point Ycacos. The three cays above

mentioned lie about a mile within the edge of the bank. The latter lies N. by E.+E.,
3 miles from the huts on Ycacos Point, and is merely a very small black rock,
scarcely above the sea. Cay Piedras, lying about a mile N.E. of it, is about 100
yards in extent, composed of rock and sand, and partially covered with low bushes.
Close off the north side are two small dry rocks; the N.W. side is steep-to, the
S.W. and south sides are foul to the distance of 3 of a mile, and a ledge runs off a
cable’s length from the S.E. end. A lighthouse is erected on this cay, to be noticed
presently.

The channel between Piedras and Monillo is said to be free from danger. The
soundings decrease as it is approached, and in the middle the depth is 5 fathoms,
and 3 of a mile E.N.E. of Monillo, 3 fathoms. About a mile to the S.E. of it there
is a shoal with only 23 fathoms on it, with 4$ and 5 fathoms around. To sail through
this channel a vessel should be able to lay up E.S.E.

Cay Mono, which lies N.E. $ E., 13 mile from Piedras, is a rocky islet, and not so
large as Piedras. In the channel about midway between these two, there is a small
coral shoal of 3 fathoms, which should be carefully approached, as the water over it
is not discoloured, and it breaks in heavy weather. ‘There is deep water on either
side of it to within 1} cable’s length of the cays. Between the shoal and Piedras
the depth gradually increases to 9 fathoms about midway, and midway between
it and Mono the depth is 54 fathoms; when on the shallowest part, the Pan of
Matanzas will be seen between the two dry rocks off the north side of Piedras
W.S.W., and Mono will bear N.E. by N. From Mono a shallow ledge runs off to
the N.E. full { of a mile, and a mile from the cay in the same direction there is a
dangerous small shoal of 2 fathoms. :

There is excellent anchorage within the cays, in 6 fathoms sandy bottom, with
Cay Piedras west, and Cay Mono from N. by E. to N.N.W.; or, in 4 fathoms with
Piedras N.W. by W. to N.W. by N., a mile distant.

It is high water, full and change, at Cay Piedras at 8h., and the rise and fall is
23 feet.

Lights.—Cay Piedras (Los Pinzones) lighthouse exhibits a fixed light, varied by
a red flash every half minute, placed at an elevation of 68 feet above mean level of
the sea, and should be seen in clear weather at the distance of 15 miles. The tower
is 75 feet in height, and coloured white, and springs from the keeper’s house; latitude
23° 14’ 24”, longitude 81° 7’ 28".

Diana on AnA Cay.—On this cay, which is situate S.E. by S. 4 S., 2 miles from,
and within the outer extreme of Point Ycacos, a small fixed light is exhibited,
visible in clear weather 7 miles. The light is 43 feet above the level of the sea, and
is shown from a mast at the top of a dwelling house, which is painted white.

CARDENAS BAY.—This bay, which of late is coming into considerable note,
is 9 miles long from N.E. to 8. W., and from 6 to 10 miles wide. ‘he north side is
bounded by a very narrow strip of low, sandy wooded land, which terminates to the
eastward of Point Ycacos. ‘he entrance to this bay is so blocked up by small cays
and shoals, that it is only navigable for vessels throuvhout, of not more than 10 feet
draught. Some good authorities, however, say 14 feet. Small steamers and droghers
navigate within the cays as far eastward as the River Sagua la Grande.

Directions.—In approaching Cardenas the easiest way is by the passage between
Mona and Piedras. Vessels of more than 16 feet draught must beware of a small
shoal spot lying nearly midway between the two cays, but by keeping Mono on
beard, it is safely p: When past Mono, steer 8. by E. for a sma]l cay named
Chalapa. When the west end of Cay Mangla bears S.W. by W., and is on with the
westernmost peak of Camarisca, steer 8. $ W. heading midway between Calapa and
Cay d’Ana, until the south shore of Cay Mangla is on with the peak, when steer
for Cay d’Ana. When the peak is fairly open half way between Magla and Cay
d’Ana, steer 8.W. by W. 3 W., when the cut between Cay Mangla and the point

north of it is just open, edge off gradually to §.S.W. for the town, carrying not less
than 13 feet water.

The pilots board when about 2 to 3 miles inside Mono. Should no pilot come out,
or if too hazy to see the peak of Camarisca, it is advisable to anchor in 3 fathoms
with soft bottom, Chalapa bearing S.E. by 8. There is also good anchorage in
4 fathoms, hard bottom.

Piedras light is good, visible 15 miles. The light on the Cay d’Ana is lighted
only steamer nights.

Vessels bound to the ports on the north side of Cuba, to the eastward of Cardenas
Bay, should approach them from the eastward, passing through one of the N.E.
Bahama channels or to the eastward of them, and along the north side of Haiti.

From Punta de Yeacos, or Ycacos Point, where the White Grounds, which
began at Maternillos, terminate, a different kind of coast presents itself, running
W.S.W., 26 miles to Punta de Maya, the eastern point of the great Bay of Mantanzas,
This coast may be sailed by, at the distance of 3 miles; and the bay may be known
by the Pan of Mantanzas, which is an insulated mountain, round on the surface,
without peaks, water-courses, precipices, or other inequalities than a small fissure,
near the 8.E. part of the summit, which can scarcely be noted at a distance, being of
so little depth. The land from Vamaricoa is even, and not very low, and continues
thus without any notable prominence to the proximity of Matanzas, whence it begins
to form a gradual slope, and rises in such a manner, that to the westward. the coast
is high enough to be seen at the distance of 8 leagues; but it is alike equal or level,
without any remarkable height, other than the Pan of Matanzas.

PORT MATANZAS.—The entrance to this port or inlet, which is 4 miles deep
and open to the E.N.E., lies between Sabanilla and Maya points, which bear E. by
N. and W. by S. from each other, distant 2 miles apart. From Maya Point, which
is very low, and has some huts on its extremity, a rocky ledge runs off a mile to the
northward, and there is a narrow bank of soundings under its west side on which
temporary anchorage will be found. Southward of the point, in the S.E. corner of
the port, is the little river Canima.

The western shore of the port is bold and steep-tc, and a vessel will have no
soundings until she is close up to the shoals which shelter the anchorage. La Laja,
the outermost of these, lies south, 14 mile from Sabanilla Point, and on the north
end of it there is a pole-beacon, with a small white flag, not easily seen, in 12 feet
water, with 9 fathoms a ship’s length outside it. Thence the shoal extends across
nearly to the south shore, leaving only a narrow channel for coasters between it and
the fort on the beach. Baja Nuevo Shoal lies N.W. nearly a 3 of a mile from
La Laja, and on its shallowest part there is a similar pole-beacon and flag. Between
this bank and the northern shore, the channel is 2 cables wide, and the soundings,
which are from 6 to 8 fathoms in the middle of it, gradually decrease on either side.
There is also a small black buoy on a bank lying W. by 8., about $ a mile from the
Baja Nuevo.

The town is on the western. shore on a tongue of land, which separates the
rivers Yumuris and San Juan or Matanzas, and communicates by stone bridges with
extensive suburbs on the opposite banks. A shallow flat runs off in front of it, which
prevents vessels from coming within 3 a mile of the wharfs.

The best water for use will be found about 3 miles up the River Matanzas.

Dirvections.—Vessels bound to Port Matanzas will find the Pan of Matanzas, which
overlooks it from the west, an excellent guide. In entering it will be better to keep
the western shore aboard within about $ a mile, and when the castle of San Severino,
a conspicuous object on the northern shore of the port, opens out, the beacons wil! be
seen. Steer midway between the beacons, and anchor as most convenient within
them. The best berth for a temporary anchorage will be in 6 or 6 fathoms, about }
of a mile off shore, with the above castle N.W. $ N.; the pole of the. Bajo Nuevo

farther to the westward, according to her draught.

It frequently happens, however, that the flags blow off, or the beacons break adrift.
In this event, after sighting the castle as before, bring the large church in the north
part of the town in line with the summit of the Pan of Matanzas W. by S. ;5.,
which will lead about $a cable’s length from the north end of La Laja. At the
same time will be seen on the side of the rising ground, north of the town, two houses
about + of a mile from each other, with white fronts and roofs, and these in line, and
in one with the highest part of the rising ground W. ¢§., will lead about 80 yards
to the southward of the Bajo Nuevo, in 43 or 5 fathoms.

Another mark is the south side or notch in the Pan, in one with a large white
house, the westernmost in sight, on a hill at the back of the town W. by 8.3 58.;
this will lead between the above shoals, and when the castle bears from N.W. 3 W.
to N.W. 2 N, anchor as before directed.

The port being exposed to the E.N.E., a heavy roll is sent in with strong winds.

The land wind in Northers is frequently interrupted, and a vessel may be detained
for a few days, as it is difficult and hazardous to beat out against the stream

It is high water in Port Matanzas, full and change at about 8h. A.M. and dh. P.M.,
and the rise and fall 24 feet. The stream runs in with the sea breeze, and out with
the land wind.

From the port of Matanzas the coast trends N.W. by W. 2 W., to Punta Guanos,
which is the most projecting point to the northward, and is distant from the mouth
of the bay about 8 miles,

Light (proposed).—A light-house to be erected on Guanos Point, to exhibit a
revolving light every minute.

From Point Guanos the coast runs W. 4 §., 15 miles to Santa Cruz.

Light.—At Port Santa Cruz, in latitude 23° 9’ 0", and longitude 82° 1’ 15’, is a
small fixed light, visible 7 or 8 miles.

From Santa Cruz the coast continues in the same direction 21 miles to the Morro
of Havana; it is all clean and bold-to, and may be run along at the distance of 3
miles, or less if required, to the eastward of Santa Cruz; inasmuch as there is no
other risk than a rocky shoal with little water on it, which stretches off the coast
between the Rincon or Corner, and the Punta de Tarara or Cobre. All along this
coast are soundings on sand, which extend more or less from shore, and of which the
edges are steep and clear, so that you suddenly get from 100 to 20 fathoms. With
the lead going, there is no risk in running along, as the soundings will give warning
of the limits into which you may stand without danger; and in fair weather a night
may be passed by dropping a kedge upon these soundings, which may sometimes be
convenient, either to avoid missing your port, if the wind blows fresh at night, or to
hold your ownif the land breeze is light, or calm, as the current constantly runs
eastward, at the mean rate of 1 mile per hour. The hills or mountains of Jaruco,
which rise nearly in the middle of this part of the coast, serve to recognize it by,
and ascertain your position.

The Cay of St. Domingo is arid; it is a cable’s length long, and half of one broad,
and its middle forms a small hill 15 feet high, covered with the Indian fig-bush,
which appears like a vessel upset, and may be seen at the distance of 3 leagues,
From its §.S.W. side, a breaker extends to the distance of a cable; and W. by S.,
from its middle, at the distance of 2 or 3 cables, there is a bank of 6 or 7 fathoms
water, very clear, where shelter from the breezes may be found. E.N.E., at 23 miles
distant, is a spot of only 9 feet, which generally breaks ; and as far as 6 miles to the
northward of the cay are some dangerous ledges and Rocky Heads, with 1 and 2
fathoms upon them.

From this cay, the bank continues to the westward, with inflexions to the north
and south, some parts very foul, and others tolerably clean, all of which may be seen
on the chart. The only spots above water are the cays of Lobos and Guinchos, or
Wolf, and Ginger Cays, both of which have foul ground about them, from north,
round by east to south; so that they must not be approached in these directions,
nearer than a mile: both may be seen at the distance of 7 or 8 miles. ‘The chart
contains a correct delineation of this bank; but it is necessary to notice, that the
shoal grounds, named Las Mucaras, which are about 20 miles to the south-eastward
of Lobos Cay, have weeds or grass at the bottom, and that the colour of the water on
them is as dark as that in mid-channel; for which reason, and also because there are
no soundings without them, it is necessary to navigate here with great caution, as
without this a vessel may easily be lost, even in the day. On the very edge of the
bank, between Lobos and Guinchos, there are some other shoal spots, and therefore
vessels of great draught should not venture upon the bank: and though the bank to
the westward of Guinchos is not so foul as that to the eastward of it, there are also
on it some rocky spots with little water.

Light.—On Lobos Cay, in latitude 22° 22’ 30’, and longitude 70° 35’ 5”, a light-
house is erected, exhibiting a fixed light, visible 16 or 17 miles, all round the horizon.
The building is of iron, circular, 150 feet in height, and 146 feet above the sea, and
painted with 7 broad red bands, and 6 white bands, with the lantern white.

Tides.—The tides on the west part of the bank, being much influenced by the Gulf
Stream, run in various directions. The flood sets strong through all the openings, or .
between the rocks, towards the centre of the bank, and the ebb contrary; it is high
water, on full and change days, at Anguila Island at three-quarters after 8, and at
Water Island at 9 o'clock. Spring tides generally rise 8 feet 4 inches, neaps 2 feet
3 inches ; but much depends on the wind.

The Derrotero says;—“ Cay Sal may be discovered at the distance of 10 miles, and
fresh water may be procured oniit with facility, although there is not any on Anguila
or the other cays in its vicinity. This bank has three rocky shoals upon it; but
vessels may navigate upon it without danger, in 74, 8, and 9 fathoms water, in all the
months from October to May. Whenever the appearance of the sky indicates a hard
Norther, it is advisable to enter on the bank, and anchor under shelter of the cays;
or lie-to there, being careful only to make use of the lead, until the wind changes,
so as to enable you to proceed.”

Light.—At the north-western extremity of the Cay Salt Bank, on the elbow, or

DIRECTIONS FOR APPROACHING AND NAVIGATING
THE COASTS OF CUBA.

It has been before said that in the rainy season, or that of the Souths, vessels
ought to pass to the northward of Porto Rico and St. Domingo or Haiti, and in the
season of the Norths to the southward of these islands, unless their port of destination
requires a deviation ; we now repeat it, with other reasons for observing this rule in
navigating on the coasts of Cuba.

If bound to Santiago de Cuba, it is necessary in the season of the Norths, to lay
a course from Cape Tiburon, and stand towards some point on the south coast of
Cuba, to windward of the intended port, or even to windward of Guantanamo ; and
in the season of the Souths, to direct your course from Cape St. Nicholas, almost west
for the port, first observing well the various points on the coast of Cuba (heretofore
described, page 92, e¢ seq). But if bound to Havana, attend to the season; that is, if
in the time of the Norths, the course should be to the south of Cuba, although you
will have to return the distance between Cape San Antonio and Havana; for this

BAHAMA CHANNEL. 137

inconvenience is not comparable to that which might be oecasioned on the north
coast, by a hard Norther, which would not only expose your vessel to great risks,
but might also retard her progress much longer than the time required ‘to navigate
from Cape San Antonio to Havana, because ‘this distance, as you work up, will be
shortened by the current, always running to the E.N.E.

Those who navigate on the south side of Cuba, and have no occasion to touch at
Trinidad, or at any other port on that part of the coast, should proceed to the west-
ward from Cape de Cruz, observing that at the distance of 108 miles, 8. 87° W.
(true) from that cape, is the easternmost of the two islands, called Cayman Brack,
and Little Cayman (heretofore described, page 91). These are dangerous to approach
in the night, because they are but of little height, and can be descried only at a very
short distance, and also on account of the reefs in their environs, and the variable
currents which generally prevail there: between these and Cuba, the current is said
to run westward, at the rate of 20 miles in a day.* The most convenient course is to
the northward of the Caymans; but here you must be careful of a shoal bank of 13
fathoms, which was discovered by a Spanish packet, bound to Trinidad, in 1800; and
which, there is reason to suspect, has some spots with very little water on them.
This shoal, according to the Spanish chart of 1821, is in latitude 20° 12’, and longitude
80° 38’; to the N.N.E. of it, the same chart exhibits another shoal of 8 fathoms, in
eee 20° 30°, and longitude 80° 27’ (see page 92). A course should be shaped
from abreast of Cape de Cruz, to avoid these shoals, in proceeding toward Cape San
Antonio. A description of the coast in these parts has already been given; and
directions for navigating round Cape San Antonio, and_thence to Havana, will be
found in our subsequent pages.

NAVIGATION OF THE OLD CHANNEL OF BAHAMA.

For this navigation it is customary to take a pilot who has a particular knowledge
of the coast of Cuba; this may be done either at Aguadilla in Porto Rico, or ‘at
Baracoa, near the east end of Cuba. In order to proceed to Baracoa for this purpose,
it will be necessary to approach the land, and determine the ship’s place in the
vicinity of Cape Maize, lest you should happen to fall in to leeward of that place;
and even without the necessity of taking a pilot, it will be proper to make the coast
in the neighbourhood of Cape Maize, for the purpose of taking a departure, and
noting the remarkable points, &c., by which the coast may be known, and the true
situation of the ship determined, so to proceed westward without risk of dan-
ger, which could not be done from a doubtful situation of the ship, arising either
from an error in estimation, or the influence of the currents. ‘These reasons should
determine the navigator to maintain his course at a convenient distance from the
coast; but not so near as to run a risk of falling on any of its various projecting reefs,
nor so far off as to lose the knowledge of the: various points, heretofore described,
page 121, e¢ seg., and which are sufficiently remarkable.

It is to be noted, that in this channel, there is on the coast and on the edge of the
bank a regular tide. The current itself, being very irregular, is embarrassing : at
one time it runs to the W.N. W.., at another to ‘the E.8.E. , or H.N.E. Sometimes its
velocity is one mile an hour, at another, only half a mile, and at another time it is

will show the effect of the current experienced, and which you may apply in the
calculation for the night, and thereby obtain the ship’s place within 6 or 8 miles.
Although you may, at times, be assured of your situation within the said distance,
nevertheless a vessel ought not to cross the meridian of Point Maternillos, without
having seen and remarked it well, so as to keep clear of the Mucuras Shoal, which
shows no appearance of its existence, until a vessel is aground upon it. Therefore,
during the night, stand off and on, taking care not to prolong the board farther off,
than will completely and certainly clear the Mucaras. Having passed over the night
in this manner, so soon as it is clear day, steer so as to make the coast, and recognize
it well; and if too far off to see it, steer to the southward, until you make it.

Having once well recognized Maternillos Point, and its lighthouse, direct your
course so as to pass about 6 miles to the southward of Cayo de Guinchos, or Ginger
Cay, if by night, or to see it, if by day ; thence toward the edges of the Great Bank,
and Anguila Bank, in preference to the céys on the Coast of Cuba, many of which
are not well situate to be seen, and they offer but few marks that can be depended
on; therefore it is dangerous to navigate in their vicinity. Having passed al] these
chains of cays, and come abreast of Point Ycacos, proceed along by the coast, about
a mile distant, as before directed. ;

From what has been observed on the navigation of this channel, it is preferable
to sail along the Cvast of Cuba, from the vicinity of Cape Maize, as far as Point
Maternillos; and from that point, on the contrary, along the edges of the Great
Bahama and Anguila, or Salt Cay Banks, until on the meridian: of the west part

Cay, that of Cruz del Padre, and also of the light on Piedras Cay; then steer
W.S.W., if by day ; but W. by S., if by night, to draw near the coast. To be secure
in your dead reckoning in the night, apply to it a correction for the currents experi-

As we have now reached the Coast of the United States, the following preliminary
instruction will be found useful:—Ships approaching or passing light-vessels of the
United States, in thick or foggy weather, are warned of their proximity by the
alternate ringing of a bell and sounding of a fog-horn on board of the light-vessel,
at intervals not exceeding five minutes. The Commercial Code of Signals for the
Use of all Nations, and Rogers’s American Edition and Flags, with the British
Vocabulary, have been placed on board light-vessels occupying seaward stations, and
at the sea-coast lighthouses along the Florida Reefs, from Loggerhead Cay, Tortugas,
to Jupiter Inlet, inclusive. Masters of ships desiring to communicate with any of
the light-vessels or light-houses by signal may do so, provided they have a set of these
signal-books and flags on-board.

CAPE CANAVERAL.—Light.—On the N.E. pitch of the cape a light-house
is erected, in latitude 28° 27’, and longitude 80° 33’, coloured white, 55 feet in height,
and 65 feet above the sea, exhibiting a revolving light, visible 14 miles. A new
structure is in course of erection at this station, to carry a 1st order lens.

DanGERouS SHOALS OFF THE CaApE.—From the cape itself a dangerous reef of
sand extends to the S.E. some 6% miles, and breaks at that distance, being a consider-

house ; the Ohio Shoal, N.E. § N., 11} miles ; the Bull Shoal, N.E. by E. 4 E., 6%

Tue BANK or SounpINGs off Cape Canaveral is very steep; you will haye 30

From off Cape Canaveral, with the lighthouse bearing W.8.W. or west, distant

Within the inlets the tides run strong. The River St. Sebastian, and other rivers,

From the northern side of the entrance to Indian River Inlet, a reef of rocks runs

The shores of this coast are lined with a bank of regular soundings, which run off
