FLORIDA REEF.

The Florida Reef is an extensive and dangerous collection of sand, rocks, and low
islands, running along the western side of the Strait of Florida, from Cape Florida
to beyond the 83° of longitude, and sweeps round to the westward in a semicircular
direction, having numerous passages between the rocks and islands.

The islands upon this reef are called the Martyrs, and may be divided into two
classes :—the High Islands and the Low and Drowned Islands. The High Islands
are grounded upon rocks, some grey, some white, and some black, as hard as flint ;
and the Low (that is, the Mangrove Islands), are founded on coral rocks, all covered
with rich but wet soil. The High Islands are covered in places with sand, on which
little or nothing grows; and in other places they have a stratum of blueish marl.
Great quantities of fish, as well as turtle, are caught amongst these islands.

CAY WEST in the longitude of 81° 47’, is the principal place on these islands, and

formed a Maritime Prize Court during the civil war. It is well lighted and buoyed,
and forms a secure harbour when snugly moored therein.

There are several openings or inlets and outlets over the reef, most of which are
safe communications between the Hawke Channel and Florida Stream.

CARYSFORT TO TORTUGAS.—From Carysfort Light, the course to run
parallel to the reef is S.S.W. (magnetic) 22 miles; this will bring you abreast of the
Pickles Reef (marked with beacon F), and nearly up with Conch Reef (E); thence
steer §.W. by W., 32 miles past Viper Cay, to longitude 80° 50’; then W.S.W., 45
miles to beacon A on Cay Sambo (on this course after running 15 miles you will be
abreast of Cay Sombrero and light-house); from beacon A steer W. by S. for 50
miles, when shape your course to, pass between the Tortugas and the reef, or around
the Torgugas. Twelve miles on this latter course will be abreast of Sand Cay light
at the entrance to Cay West harbour. The passage between the Tortugas and the
reef is safe, as there is only the Rebecca Shoal of 14 feet, which bears east, 20 miles
from Loggerhead Cay. Between the shoal and the Tortugas Bank (Kast Cay), there is
a channel, 12 miles in width. During the United States Coast Survey a shoal of
18 feet was discovered 24 miles to the north of Rebecca Shoal, which there is little
doubt is a continuation of that shoal. On the Rebecca Shoal a buoy was placed, but -
doubtful if there now.

During the United States Coast Survey of these reefs, signals were placed on the
reefs ; since when, regular day-marks have been erected to occupy the positions.
They are each composed of an iron shaft, 36 feet in height, erected upon iron screw
foundations, distinguished by a vane, upon which one of the letters of the alphabet is
painted, and above it a lattice-work, hoop-iron cylinder or barrel.

Three colours (white, black, and red), are used in painting each signal, to render
them as striking to the eye as possible, and are so arranged that no two adjacent
day-marks have the same colours upon like parts.

The day-marks are placed upon the most projecting and dangerous points of the
Florida Reef, and are in general from 4 to 6 miles from the outside (seaward) shores
of the Florida Cays, and within 4 a mile, in every case, of the edge of the Gulf

Stream.

The water where these signals stand does not exceed 4 feet at low tide, in any
case, and just outside them to the eastward, in the Gulf Stream, it falls into deep
water ; so that they may be said to to be erected on the very edge of the wall of this
reef.

You may approach any of these day-marks from seaward within a few hundred
yards, but it will always be prudent to give them a good berth, particularly in light
winds, or in bad weather. In steering the courses along the edge of the reef be
cautious, in moderate weather, and especially after easterly gales, that the force and

THE TORTUGAS BANKS.

The Tortugas consist of 11 small islands or cays, as exhibited on the chart, and
are situate on the southern edge of soundings which extend off the western coast of
Florida, They are very low, and some of them being covered with Mangrove Bushes,
may be seen 4 leagues. They lie about 10 leagues from the westernmost of the
Florida Cays, 30 leagues from Havana, and the same distance from the nearest part
of the Coast of Florida. These cays are the westernmost land, and in coming down.
the Gulf of Mexico, give warning of approach to Florida Reefs in general.

The Tortugas (often called the Dry Tortugas), are generally looked upon to be very
dangerous, and to a person unacquainted with them, they undoubtedly are so, espe-
cially in the night time; yet when they are known, on many occasions, they may be
found both useful and convenient. They extend east and west, 9 miles, and north and
south, 6 miles. You should not come nearer than 6 miles, as they have some rocky spits
which extend that distance from them. To the west there is a large bank of coral
rocks, intermixed with white patches of sand, on which the soundings are irregular;
but as the bottom shows itself there is no danger. This bank is of an oblong form,
and between it and the Tortugas Islands there is a clear channel of 3 miles wide, with
soundings from 13 to 17 fathoms water.

LoGGERHEAD Cay, on which the principal light-house is situate, is according to
the U.S. authorities in latitude 24° 37’ 20’, and longitude 82° 55’ 10’, and is the south
westernmost cay of the group, which in sailing from Pensacola or the Mississippi, is
the corner to be turned, and in stretching north-eastward from Cape Antonio, is the
point to be avoided. A reef of coral rocks stretches about ; of a mile 8.W. from the
cay, the water on which is discoloured; and, in general, whenever there is danger, it
may easily be seen in the day time from the mast-head.

The light-houses on Loggerhead and Garden Cay have both been noticed previously.

If bound to the eastward, and meeting with a strong easterly gale, which is

There is a channel 17 miles in width between the eastern cay and the west end of

THE GULE STREAM.

Of the cause of this most remarkable current we are by no means well informed.
In the opinion of some, it is occasioned by the influx of waters from the Caribbean
‘Seas ; and of others, that it originates with the flooding of the Mississippi and other
great rivers, which discharge themselves into the Gulf of Mexico,

This great body of water collected within the gulf acquires an elevation, and
therefore naturally seeks its level with the surrounding waters through those open-
ings which are most convenient and present the least impediments; accordingly,
taking a south-easterly direction from the coasts of Louisiana and Florida, it sets
directly over the Tortugas and Florida Reefs, and being stopped in its progress to the
southward by the Island of Cuba, turns northward through the Gulf into the Atlantic
Ocean, thence pressing on in a most powerful, connected, and extensive stream along
the eastern coast of America, reaching almost as far as the Banks of Newfoundland,
from whence it crosses the Atlantic Ocean in an easterly direction, inclining to the
southward, continuing and spreading almost to the shores of Europe.

No change of winds or seasons have power to prevent its progress, or, generally
speaking, retard its velocity, though that velocity, which is first occasioned’ by its
being confined between the narrow channel of the gulf, where it sets out with great
rapidity, decreases as it advances into the Atlantic; thus, in the meridian of Bahia
Honda, its direction is E.N.E., at the rate of 1 or 2 miles an hour; advancing to
Cape Florida, it accelerates its force to 3 miles, and farther: north its velocity is still
greater; but, having passed Cape Canaveral, it begins to lessen its rapidity, running
from the latitude of 26° to 28°, a little easterly, at 24 miles an hour; from 28° to 31°
it inclines to the westward; then, about Cape Hatteras, it takes a N.E. by E. direc-
tion, to the northward of which it runs &.N.E. to the longitude of 70°, and then
E. by N., east, and H.S.E., with diminished strength, till, lost in the wide Atlantic,
it becomes scarcely perceptible. North, N.E., and east winds are said to have a
partial effect upon it, by driving it nearer the land, contracting its breadth and in-
creasing its rapidity, while contrary winds have an opposite tendency, forcing it
farther from the land, extending its body, and diminishing its velocity ; but, however
its boundaries may vary, it must still continue of unvarying importance to naviga-
tion, and can always be known by the remarkable peculiarities which attend it.

Beginning to notice this stream as it appears on entering the Gulf of Florida,
a remarkable line will be perceived, as smooth as glass, of various divisions ‘and
different colours: but in the deep channel it takes the appearance of boiling water, of
a blue colour—in some places bursting into foam, even in the greatest calm; and
where the bottom is fathomless. 3

As you approach towards the Martyrs, there is an eddy; the water at its edge
remains blue, but soon changes to a green, and still nearer the cays and reefs it
becomes milk-white; this is attributed to the ground over which thé water flows;
thus, under the blue water is a bottom of fine white marl; under the green, sponges,
feathers, grass, and rocks; and under the milk-white water are rocks, white marl,

a)

THE ‘GULF STREAM. 149

and' white sand. ‘This’ eddy, the direction ‘of which runs in the opposite to that of
the Gulf Stream, as we have already noticed, is of the utmost importance to mariners,
enabling them to pass to the westward with much facility. It will readily be seen,
by referring to the chart, how far the extent of the eddy reaches, and also the sound-
ings upon it. :

It is of no Small consequence to notice the change of water before mentioned, and,
if ‘bound to'the northward, thus avoid the eddy. When you find ground, stand
immediately off again, for many vessels, not knowing soundings could be had under

‘the blue water, have imagined themselves safe and within the stream, while they

were insénsibly swept to the westward by it, and by supposing themselves clear of
Cape Florida, have steered to the northward, and been lost on the reefs.

The'stream is in this part much influenced by the winds; the moon also at full and
change will oftentimes have considerable effect, and, if ‘both are united, the water
becomes elevated, and its rapidity increases.

In the month of September the east, north-east, and north winds generally set in,
continuing until March, when, should the moon’s full and change fall in with the
season, they generally end with a violent gale or hurricane. Should then a vessel
be within the Gulf, between Havana and Cape Florida, she should make imme-
diately for the Bahama Islands, and proceed if possible, under their lee side: if to
the northward of them, keep on the eastern side of the stream, or she will not be
able to clear the gulf, nor get along the Coast of Florida. During the storms, when
a northerly wind opposes the stream, the Martyr Islands and Reefs have been com-
pletely overflowed.

It is now generally believed the northern edge of the Gulf Stream reaches as far
as the latitude of 41° 30’.

We have already noticed the effect of the winds in somewhat altering its course
and checking its velocity: thus, by those heavy gales proceeding from the north and
west, which frequently happen between the latitudes of Cape Hatteras and St.
George’s Bank, in the months of December to March, together with the waters
from the great rivers in that vicinity, the stream will be so driven to the eastward,
that it becomes scarcely possible for a vessel to make the coast while the gale con-
tinues; and it has been known, during south and easterly winds, that the stream has
been driven into the westward, so’as to encroach even upon soundings; this having
been observed along the coasts of Georgia, Carolina, and as far as Nantucket Shoals.

It will therefore be obvious, that the edges of the stream must vary according to
circumstances, and that no fixed or decisive boundary can be given to it; but the
mariner cannot well fail discovering its limits, for on approaching it from the east-
ward, its edge in lower latitudes will be marked by a rippling, which constantly
attends it, and the quantity of seaweed just outside of it. Within the stream the
clusters are few, the water flowing with a clear, smooth, blue surface; but the best
and infallible guide will always be the temperature of the water, for on the outside
of the stream the sea and air are nearly of the same degree of heat, but having
entered the stream, the water becomes warmer than the air; passing through to the
westward, and between the stream and the land, it again becomes colder, so that the
mariner may always discover his approach to, his situation within, and his egress out
of the stream, by his thermometer. Thus, in quitting the stream and approaching
the coast, it has been known to fall in summer from 77° to 61°, and in winter from
70° to 47°; if, therefore, the mariner will use his thermometer, and make proper
comparison frequently between the heat of the air and water, he may always know
when:he enters, is within, or quits the stream.

There are considerable eddies on the inner and outer edge of the stream, but those
on the inner are inconsiderable, while those on the outer side are strong and extensive.
Counter currents are observed on both sides; that between the stream and coast runs
in 4 south-westerly direction, and is of the utmost importance to navigation, for, by
means of this current, vessels are enabled to perform their voyages to the southward

150 THE GULF OF FLORIDA.

with more celerity; and, by taking advantage of the Gulf Stream, vessels from the
southward may also expedite their respective passages with facility and safety.

To take advantage of this counter current, care must be taken not to run too far
from land, but to keep within soundings; for should you stretch out as far as the
Gulf Stream, you will inevitably be drifted to the northward, and out of your course ;
for which reason, mariners entering the stream from the eastward should always run
down to a latitude more southerly than the place they are bound to. It is a generally
received opinion, that the weather is considerably influenced by the stream ; but this
appears very doubtful. It certainly may communicate to the surrounding air an
nadine warmth, but its further effect on the atmosphere must be left to future
observers,

We shall conclude these remarks with observing, that the use of thermometers on
this coast appears capable of contributing greatly to the mariner’s safety, for by these
he may always be warned of his approach to the stream, to dangers, or the land; and
when it is considered how low the shores from the Delaware to Florida in general
are, surrounded in many places with dangerous and extensive shoals, which run into
the sea beyond the sight of land, we cannot too highly recommend their use. In
northern latitudes, and on the Newfoundland Banks, they will indicate your approach
to islands of ice, which so often at night or in foggy weather have proved fatal to
many ; and by leading to a certain and unerring knowledge of the course and situa-
tion of the Gulf Stream, and your consequent proximity to land, will become one of
the chief and most essential means of securing your safety on this hitherto considered
dangerous coast.

Upon coming into soundings, the water changes from blue to green, and from
green toa dirty mud colour. The counter-current in general runs parallel to the
coast, except at the mouths of the great bays of Delaware and the Chesapeake, where
the floods sometimes influence its direction.

SAILING THROUGH THE GULF OF FLORIDA.

If the weather be thick when about to take your departure from Cuba, and there
is no object in view, it would be far more prudent to lie off that island for a day or
two than to run the risk of shipwreck.

You may round Cape St. Antonio either to the eastward or westward of the Sancho
Pardo Shoal; but you must be cautious not to go nearer than 2 or 3 leagues of the
land with the deep-sea lead going.

If the deep-sea lead was frequently used, there is reason to believe it would prevent
many disasters ; for though the ground be not yet known with that degree of accuracy
as to point out off what part of the Martyr Islands a vessel must be, yet the
soundings everywhere give warning of the vessel’s approach to the reefs. ‘Those on
the Bahama side are not so regular. Near the bank of double-headed Shot Cays and
to that of Great Bahama, a vessel must be pretty close before she will find bottom.

The following remarks are by Mr. Middlemist :—

“Tt is of the greatest consequence to know which shore you are nearest to ; indeed,
it seems to be the only thing to be depended upon for making a safe passage through.

It is recommended by some persons to keep a certain parallel of latitude, and to
beat up in the strength of the stream; but however this practice may be sometimes
preferred, I should never be induced to follow it, as you cannot sce either side of the
Gulf of Florida; nor would I advise other persons to do so, for it is attended with
great risk.

CAPE DAME MARIE. 151

You ought to see the land at least once in 24 hours while to the southward of Cape
Florida. This is easily done by working on the Florida side. Be inshore in the
evening, and stand off 8 or 10 leagues during the night, in again next morning, and
0 on; by which means you will always know how to shape a course, should the wind
come fair in the night, because you are certain which side you are nearest to.

Supposing, in the other case, the land had not been seen for 3 or 4 days, you would
possibly be much perplexed how to steer a safe course on a sudden change of wind in
your favour ; and, even if you considered your reckoning right, and were to shape a
course which was also considered right, to take you clear of all dangers, I am of
opinion you would not know how to act did you fall in with breakers right ahead, by
being uncertain what side you were upon, and that in so dreadful a situation you
would be liable to put your helm the wrong way, and it would be impossible to act
with that promptness you would do if you knew which side you were upon. There-
fore be guarded against a disaster which is likely to happen to those best acquainted,
and always see the land as often as possible, or at least once in 24 hours.

The deep-sea lead should be hove frequently in the night, because there are sound-
ings on the Floridas, and also on the Bahamas, which you will obtain before coming
to the shoals; and this precaution may sometimes save your ship from being lost.

It is needless to say, there ought to be anchor clear, cable range, &e., as every
prudent navigator will see done while he continues in the Gulf of Florida.”

WINDWARD CHANNEL.

DESCRIPTION OF AND DIRECTIONS FOR NAVIGATING IN THE WINDWARD CHANNEL,

FRoM JAMAICA To CAPE MAIZE AND Carr St. NICHOLAS.

From Morant Point, or the east end of Jamaica to Navaza, the bearing and distance
are N.E. by E. 3 E., 73 miles; to Cape Tiburon, E.N.E. i E., 102 miles; to Cape St.
Nicholas Mole, N.E.+ E., 197 miles; and to Cape Guanos, Cuba, N.E. 2 N., 168
miles; thence to Cape St. Nicholas Mole, E. by S., 49 miles.

On approaching Cape Tiburon, its top will appear with many white places, like
ways on roads, and is the highest land of the western coast of Haiti: it has been
described in page 68, and it forms the north side of Tiburon Bay. When running in
with the sea breeze, give the south point a berth of one-third of a mile, and run in
directly for the houses. It shoalens gradually from 16 to 7,6, and 5 fathoms, and in
any of the latter depths you may anchor on good ground, with Point Burgos bearing
S. by E.3 E., or S. by E., and Cape Tiburon W.N.W. Here a fresh land breeze
blows all night at N..; and all day fresh sea breezes blow at 8.E. by E. There is
generally a great swell in the bay, with a great surf on the beach, unless in very
moderate winds.

CAPE DAME MARIE, or Donna Maria, is about the height of Beachy head in
the English Channel, bluff and steep to the water side, and of reddish colour. The
bay to the southward of the cape, which is called by its name, ‘shoalens gradually,
and affords good anchorage, as before described, page 67. This is a good place for
wood, water, and fish.

From Cape Dame Maria to Salt River Point the coast runs E.N.E. 3 E., 14 miles;
the land all along is high and uneven, and there is some foul ground near the cape.
Between Salt River Point and the Caymites, to the E.S. Eastward, the land toward
Pctit Goave appears very high. There is some foul ground about the Caymites,
before described, to which a good berth must be given, as well as to the Rochelois

152 WINDWARD CHANNEL:

Reef (described page 60). Although it has been said that, there is more room for
working on the north than on the south side of Rochelois Reef, it is, nevertheless, by.
many persons, considered safest to work up between it and the main, because the
main is bold, and continues so all the way-up to the Road of Leogane ; but in stand-
ing over towards the island, you will meet with overfalls of 13, 10, 8, and 7 fathoms
water. You may run aleng the south coast at two miles from shore, without danger :
the ground may be seen under the ship a long way, but there is a sufficient depth of
water.

‘To anchor in Leogane Road, give the Fort Point a berth of about a mile, and anchor
with the Fort bearing about N.E.4 N. at that distance, in 18 fathoms water, muddy
ground; it is very rocky about the point, and the white water may be readily seen.

The coast between Leogane and Cape St. Nicholas have been described in proceed-
ing from the northward. See page 61, &c.

THE SOUTH SIDE OF CUBA.—The high peak of the Copper Hills, or Peak of
Tarquino, which we have already mentioned, is the highest land on the southern part
of the Island of Cuba, and bears from Morant Point, in Jamaica, N.N.W. northerly,
distant 123 miles. It stands but a little inland, and may be descried from most parts
of the north side of Jamaica.

The bearing and distance from the east end of Jamaica, to St. Jago de Cuba, are
N, 4 E., 123 miles; to Guantanamo, or Cumberland Harbour, N. by E. 2 E., 132
miles. But the course to either of these places must be directed by judgment, accord-
ing to circumstances, so as to avoid the Formigas, already described.

The entrance of the Harbour of St. Jago lies about 52 miles to the eastward of the
Peak of Tarquino. The harbour is distinguished by the Morro Castle, which stands
on the eastern side. For a description of, and direction for this harbour, see page 96.

GUATANAMO, or Cumberland Harbour, is 38 miles to the eastward of that of St.
Jago. Directions for taking this harbour will be found in page 95.

Twelve miles to the eastward of Cumberland Harbour is the mouth of Puerto
Escondido, or the Hidden Port, described in page 94.

From Port Escondido to Cape Guanos, the bearing and distance are E. by N. ¢ N.,
45 miles, and from Cape Guanos to the extreme point of Cape Maize, the bearing and
distance are N.E. 2 N., 12 miles. The point of Cape Maize is low and sandy, and is
bordered with a reef. About 22 miles to the westward of the cape, on the north side
of Cuba, is Baracoa, a very good harbour, but narrow at the entrance. Its situation
may be known by a remarkable round table hill, called El Yunque, or the Anvil,
which stands 5 miles to the westward of the entrance. Directions for this harbour
will be found in the description of the North Coast of Cuba, page 121.

SHIPS BOUND FROM JAMAICA TO EUROPE, or anywhere to the north-
eastward, should if possible, take the Crooked Island Passage in preference to any
other. It is to be observed, however, that with strong N.N.E. winds, itis very difficult
to work round Cape Maize, owing to a strong lee current which generally prevails
with those winds, particularly in January, February, March, and April, during which
months the strong northerly winds prevail. This current runs strongest between
Cape Maize and Cape Dame Marie, and occupies a space in breadth equal to the
distance between the contracting points: its velocity is about 2 knots, and with
strong N.E. winds sets to the S.W., between the east end of Jamaica and the Morant
Cays.

This current has been experienced in the whole extent of sea between Jamaica and
Cuba, by several commanders, who, after having cleared the east end of Jamaica,
have stood over to the Cuba shore, in order to beat up to, and round Cape Maize.
They have there found a strong lee current during those months, and little or no land
wind to assist them in working up along shore, so that they have at last been obliged
to bear up for the Gulf Passage. Nevertheless, it is to be understood, that, in the
fine season, there are variable winds, and sometimes a favourable current.

WINDWARD PASSAGES. 153

The Montagnes de la Hotte, or Grand Ance Mountains, the westernmost high land
of Haiti, are often seen by, and are of great use to, ships sailing between Cape Maize
and Cape St. Nicholas; they may be descried at the distance of 90 or 120 miles, and
by their situation and bearing, become a good guide in working up through the
Windward Channel.

Should a strong lee current prevail, when working from Jamaica to windward,
stand well out, and work in the stream of the Morant Cays, endeavouring to get to
the eastward of them, as soon as possible. They are not dangerous, as they can, at
all times of the day, be seen at a distance sufficient to avoid the danger with which
they are surrounded, and there is anchorage under their N.W. side, if cireumstances
should render it necessary.—See page 71.

Having passed the Morant Cays, stretch well to the eastward, and work nearly in
a direct line from the high land over Point Boucan, which is 84 miles to the eastward
of Cape Tiburon, taking care, when standing north-westward, not to bring Cape
Tiburon to the eastward of N.E.; you will then avoid the stream of the lee cur-
rent, and may gain ground very fast. When you have advanced so far to the north-
ward as 17° 40’, you will at times meet with a counter current, and during the night
with frequent squalls from the southward, which are occasioned by the high lands of
Haiti. When this happens, stand to the eastward, and endeavour to get well in under
Cape Tiburon; then work along that shore, to Cape Dame Maria, which is bold, and
may be approached to the distance of 4 a mile, except off Ministre Point, where the
Baleines lie about 14 mile from shore. See page 67. By keeping within 7 or 8
miles of the shore, you will avoid the strength of the lee current, and find very little
against you.

As the current sets with great strength in the channel between Cape St. Nicholas
and Cape Maize, particularly on the Cuba side, it is necessary to work well up toward
Cape St. Nicholas before attempting to stretch across toward Cape Maize. This
will easily be done by keeping within the line of Cape Dame Maria and Cape St.
Nicholas; and when Cape Maize it brought to bear to the westward of N. by W.,
you may venture to stand across the channel to the northward, and will, generally,
as you proceed in that direction, find the wind more easterly.

THE WINDWARD PASSAGES IN GENERAL.

DEscRIPTION of, and Directions for, the WINDWARD PassaGEs, by M. CHASTENET
DE PuyseGuR, with Emendations and Additions.

The four principal channels, called the Windward Passages, are the Crooked
Islands, or Leewardmost Passage; the Caicos Passage, which is to leeward of the
Caicos Islands ; the Turk’s Island Passage, which is to windward of Caicos, and to
leeward of the Turk’s Islands; the Silver Cay Passage, which is between the Silver
Cays and Mouchoir Bank. :

CROOKED IsLAND PASSAGE.

This passage is the longest, but it is far the most convenient for ships coming out
of the Gulf of Gonaives, or from the southern part of Haiti, and for those bound to
the United States.

From Cape Maize to the S.W. point of Great Inagua the bearing and distance are
N.N.E, ? E., 48 miles; and if Cape Maize be brought to bear N.N.W., 5 leagues
distant (from the parallel of 20°), the course to the S.W. point of the same island
will be N. by E. 2 E., and the distance 60 miles; but it is generally necessary to
steer half a point to the eastward of this course, because a strong lee current fre-
quently sets towards the Bahama Channel.

INAGUA.—Great Inagua, like all the islands which bound the windward passages,
is very low, with small hummocks, which at a distance appear like detached islets ;
it cannot be seen at a considerable distance, in consequence of the haze which almost

[W. Inpiks, Parr II.] x

154 INAGUA.

constantly prevails in these latitudes; but in clear weather it may be seen at the
distance of 5 or 6 leagues. In making the west end there is no danger whatever.
Two sandy bays at that end afford good anchorage; but, from the trade winds blow-
ing over the island, the northernmost bay is the best.

This island is 45 miles in length, and from 7 to 17 miles in breadth: its middle is
said to be swampy. ‘There are several inlets on the south side, which abound with
fish and turtle. Fresh water may be procured in the northernmost bay, on the west
side, at a short distance from the beach. ‘here are several rocks about the S.W.
point, with a reef, which stretches out to nearly the extent of a mile. The bay
between this and the west or middle point is called Shallow Bay; it is surrounded by
a reef, which, however, shows itself, although there are 2 or 3 fathoms on it: without
the reef is a white sand, to the distance of 3 cables’ length, and on this sand is the
anchorage in 7 or 8 fathoms water. Farther out there are 15 fathoms, rocky ground.
This bay is not so deep as the next, or Man of War Bay, but the bank is less steep,
and ships are not so liable to drive here; neither is the landing so easy; but there
are some clear places in the reef. Water can be obtained in the rainy season only,
and then it is not very good, as it lies among the mangrove bushes.

Man of War Bay. is 6 miles wide, and 23 deep, and has allalong the shore a border
of sand 4 cables’ length wide, on which there are, at a pistol-shot from shore, 5
fathoms, increasing onits outer edge to 15; and at $ a cable’s length from that, to 45
fathoms water. Stand in, and you will perceive the line of soundings by the colour
of the water, extending, as before said, about 3 a mile from the beach. When you
are in soundings, let go your anchor in 7 or 6 fathoms, on white bottom, choosing
the ground by the eye, as in many parts of such bottom there are stones, which
sometimes rise to a considerable height above the level of the sand, This bay is
sheltered from the north by the N.W. Point, and from the south by the West or
Middle Point: it is easy landing in every part of it. At a short half mile up is a
Savanna, 6 miles in length; there is also a-salt-pond, which produces good salt, and
some wells, with soft stony bottoms, from which, in the rainy seasons, fresh water may
be procured. Wood-pigeons and doves resort therein abundance: and there is plenty
of good fish, which may be taken either with hook and line, or a seine, as dorades,
pikes, sargues, &c., and several sorts of shell fish ; but the crabs have a poisonous
quality from the Manchin eels.

Having passed the N.W. Point, you will see a little islet to the E.N.E., and a ledge
of rocks extending more than a league along the shore, and upwards of a mile from it.
You may know this coast by the hummock, called Le Mornet or James’ Hill, 90 feet
in height, the only one on the north side, which is covered with bushes, and lower
than the south side. At the eastern part of the-north side of the island there is a
bay 21 miles wide, and 25 deep, called the Ocean Bight, where there is anchorage ;
but it is sheltered from southerly winds only, and but very little known. All
the east side of the island is skirted with reefs, and about 5 miles off the S.E.
Point isa little islet, around which the bottom appears white: upon this you may
anchor if necessary, about a musket-shot from the islet. About 5 miles S.E. from
this islet is the Statira Shoal, extending 3 miles N.E. and S.W., with 3 fathoms on
it. The white bottom extends along the south part of Inagua, interspersed with some
reefs and breakers.*

There is also said to be a dangerous reef bearing E.S.E. from the reef at the N.E. Point

CROOKED ISLANDS. 155

At Alfred Sound, to the eastward of the N.W. Point it is high water, full and
change at 8h. Springs rise 3} feet, neaps 25.

Light (Building).—On the S.W. point of Great Inagua, a lighthouse is in course of
erection.

THE HOGSTIES are three small sandy islets, or cays, very low, having on their
east side a white shoal, which is surrounded by a reef, extending 4 or 5 miles.
They lie at the distance of 11 leagues N. by W. 3 W. from the N.W. point of Inagua.
About them are many rocks and broken ground, and in blowing weather the sea
breaks over them all. The southernmost is the smallest, and requires a good berth, it
being shoal all around; it bears from the middle cay about 8.8.E. This is the largest,
and is clean on the west side, where you may anchor in from 7 to 5 fathoms, to the
W.N.W. of it, with the north cay bearing from N. by K. to N.N.E. About a mile
to the westward of the cays is a depth of 20 fathoms. Ships having occasion to pass
them in the night, should always keep their deep-sea lead going.

Beacon.—At both ends of the Hogsties, there is a small, low, sandy cay, nearly
devoid of vegetation. A stone beacon 62 feet high, 8 feet in diameter at base, and
3 feet at top, stands on the N.W. cay ; there is also a tank for rain-water.

THE MIRA-POR-VOS is an assemblage of barren rocks, with one low sandy
islet, lying on a shoal similar to that of the Hogsties, of nearly 7 miles extent from
north to south, and about half that in breadth. On the west side is an indifferent
anchorage : the east side is bold, and on the south-east side, at a mile distance, there
are from 20 to 25 fathoms water, coral and rocky ground. As this shoal is: to lee-
ward, it is not often seen by vessels ranging along Castle Island; however, if adverse
winds should render it necessary to turn, you may approach the bank to the distance
of 14 mile. All the dangerous parts break, and the white ground will give you timely
notice. You may, if necessary, go to leeward of them, but be cautious not to
approach too near, because a reef extends westward about 23 miles from the
south-westernmost cay, having on its extremity 9 or 10 fathoms: it thence extends
to the §.S.E. a considerable distance. The middle of the group bears W. by S., about
12 miles from Castle Island. In approaching them from the southward, and getting
the depth of 12 or 11 fathoms, you should then bear up, if it be your, intention to pass
to leeward of them; but the customary channel is between them and Castle Island.

The Mira-por-vos group range nearly N.E. and 8.W.: several of them are above
water, and, as before stated, are all barren rocks, excepting the south-westernmost,
which is a low sandy island, about 4 a mile in length, and covered with brushwood.

At the southern part of the Mira-por-vos it is high water, full and ‘change, at
9h. 80m.; springs rise 3 feet, neaps 25 feet.

HOBART’S SHOAL lies to the south-eastward of the Mira-por-vos, and was first
discovered by William James, commander of the packet Lord Hobart, who gives the
following account of it. Thursday, Sept. 13, 1821. At th. 30m. P.M., saw Castle
Tsland bearing N. by W., 14 or 15 miles; at 3h. 30m. saw heavy breakers ahead; at
4 tacked to the eastward, the Mira-por-vos bearing N.W.; Castle Island N.E., and
the breakers N.W. by N., distance about half a mile. :

“ The above shoal I saw on a former voyage, on March 25, 1818, when working up
the passage from Jamaica: the weather was firé, water quite smooth: it did not
break, and was not seen until the vessel was on the outer part of the bank, in 5
fathoms water: the shcalest water we had, in crossing the outer edge, was 4 fathoms,
sandy bottom, which was plain to be seen.”*

CROOKED ISLANDS.—These consist of Acklin, or the South Crooked Island,
Fortune Island, or Long Cay, and the northernmost or Crooked Island, connected
together by a white ground, which surrounds them entirely.

_* There is said to be a shoal of 2 or 3 feet water on its shoalest part, lying 8.E. by 8.
distant 31 miles from Cape Verde, called Brown’s Shoal. 2 : .

156 FORTUNE ISLAND.

CASTLE IsLAND is an islet lying off the south point of Acklin, having several white
rocks between. It is very remarkable, appearing, when first seen, like a white fort
or castle, whence it takes its name, it bears from the N.W. point of Great Inagua
Dae by N., distant 70 miles, and from the beacon on the Hogsties N.W. } W., 37
miles.

Light.—(Building.)—On Castle Island a lighthouse is in course of erection, intended
to exhibit a fixed light; is expected to be lighted in 1868.

From Castle Island to the south point of Fortune Island, the bearing and distance
are N. 2 W., 26 miles, and from the south point of Fortune Island to the Bird Rock,
off the west point of Crooked Island, the bearing is north, 18 miles. Between is a
large space, named:the Great Bay, navigable for small vessels only ; at the entrance
of which lie the Fish Cays, which must be approached with caution, as they are sur-
rounded by a flat. About 23 miles north-eastward from Castle Island, and on the
west side of Acklin, is Salina Point; between these is a fine sandy bay, called Jamaica
Bay, wherein ships may anchor in 9 fathoms water, well sheltered. To the N.E. of
this bay are two wells, named Jamaica Wells, with excellent water, and wood may
also be obtained.

Fortune IsiANnD is 10 miles in length, about N.N.E., and §.S.W., and about 13
mile in breadth. It is distinguished by a hill about two miles from its south end; to
the northward of which is a long salt-pond, and some wharfs, where vessels load salt..
The south end of this island is very bold. Off the north end are two islets, and a
little to the northward of these is a sandy point, which is the south point of Crooked
Island, known by the name of the French Wells. From this a small settlement
will be seen on the high land to the northward. A vessel may anchor with the
French Wells bearing about E. 3 N., at the distance of 1$ or 2 miles. It is best to
anchor so soon as you get on the bank, but it is necessary to look out for a clear
spot. There is good anchorage at 13 mile W. 3S. of the two islets. At this place
good water may be procured at the wells, which give name to the point; stock and
wood may be procured also.

Crooked IsLanp.—This is the principal island, and has a town at its west point,
called Pitt’s Town, which is the port of entry. About two miles to the eastward of
the south point is the mouth of a salt-water lake, which extends two-thirds of the
way to Pitt’s Town.

Tuer Birp Rock, or Passage Islet, is a low islet lying off the west point of Crooked
Island, to the southward of which is a sandy bay, called Portland Harbour. Near
the middle of this bay, close to the beach, is a well of spring water. In this place
the best anchorage is off the first rocky point to the southward of the sandy bay, at
about 8 cables’ length from shore, in from 6 to 8 fathoms; at about a cable’s length
farther in there are only 3 fathoms. Anchor so soon as you get on the bank,
with the Bird Rock bearing about N.N.W., or N.N.W.32 W. Be careful to avoid
a rocky: head, which lies off the middle of the bay, at about three-fourths of the
distance from the beach to the edge of soundings; it has only 16 feet of water on it.
Wood, water, and stock, may be obtained from Pitt’s Town.

A very dangerous reef extends about two miles in a N.N.W. direction from Bird
Rock; it thence trends in a circular direction to the E.S.E., or towards the shore.
This reef forms the Bird Rock’s anchorage, which is very indifferent, the ground
being foul in many places. At about 15 miles to the eastward of the Bird Rock is
a cove, named Major’s Bay, where small vessels may lie.

Light (proposed) on Bird Island.

AcKLIN IsLAND lies to the south-eastward of Crooked Island, from which it is
separated by a narrow channel. From the north part of this island to its S.E. point
is 12 miles S. + E., and thence to the south point nearly 34 miles 8.W. 7 S.
Between the north point of Acklin and the island next to the eastward of it, is a
small anchorage, named Atwood’s Harbour ; its entrance is between the reefs.

RUM CAY. 157

These islands are bold on the eastern side, but they are bordered with reefs. The
east point of Crooked Island has a reef which runs off 13 mlle, and extends along
the north side of Acklin. The land is low, with some hillocks, and a few shrubs ;
there are also some plantations.

On the north side of Crooked Island it is high water, full and change, at 8h.,
springs rise 23 feet.

Winps.—The N.E. trade generally prevails here, excepting in the winter months,
that is, from October to April. During these months there are sometimes strong

gales from the N.W., and very variable weather, particularly about the full and
change of the moon, which ought to be guarded against. ;

DIANA BANK bears S. by E., 18 miles from the south end of Long Island, and
W. 2 S., 20 miles from the south end of Fortune Island. This bank is composed of
sand and coral, 4 miles in extent east and west, and 3 miles north and south, having
from 9 to 15 fathoms water on it, and 20 fathoms on its edges, and may be of service
to vessels beating through the Crooked Island Passage in the night-time, by getting
a cast of the lead upon it.

From the Bird Rock off the west end of Crooked Island, to the 8.E, end of Yuma,
or Long Island, the bearing and distance are W. ; S., 27 miles.

RUM. CAY.—The S.E. end of Rum Cay lies N.N.W. 3 W., about 52 miles from
the Bird Rock. This cay, or more correctly speaking, island, is nearly as large as
Watling’s Island, next to be described, and appears at first sight very hilly, ranging
nearly east and west, about 9 miles in length, and is 5 miles broad. Ona nearer
approach two white cliffs may be seen, which form the 8.K. end of the island; these
cliffs are very remarkable, and may be seen 6 leagues off. The south side of this
island is bold-to, and may be approached with safety. The anchorage, which is on
the 8.E. side of the island, at about half a mile from the beach, is good for vessels of
any size, and affords shelter from S.E., E.N.E., and round to N.W., no accident
having ever happened to vessels loading here at all seasons.

On making this island from the eastward, several houses on its highest summits
will be seen near its S.E. part, where there is a village. There are settlements all
round the island, and it has two good salt-ponds; pilots will go out on vessels making
the usual signal. There is always a considerable quantity of large grained salt for
sale, and every despatch is given while loading. ‘The new pond is at the west end
of the island; and vessels can anchor off it, within 500 fathoms of the shore abreast
of a signal flagstaff, which is not far from the beach.

In 1861, H.M.S. Conqueror was wrecked on the reefs at the south-east part of this
island, and the flood stream was found setting along the shore to the westward ; and

the current frequently sets strong to the N.W. between Rum Cay and Conception, as
it does also in the vicinity of Conception.

WATLING’S ISLAND.—From the Bird Rock to the 8.W. point of Watling’s
Island the bearing and distance are N. by W., 67 miles. This island is nearly 5
leagues in length, N.N.E. and 8.8.W., and 4 miles wide, and is of moderate height,
rather low than otherwise. On approaching the south side, several houses may be
seen on the summit ofa hill. Two remarkable rocks, called the Pigeons, lie off the
§.E. point, and on the east side of the island are several rocky spots. The White
Rocks lie on the north side, and are very dangerous: and a reef extends 4 or 5 miles
to the N.W., which requires great caution in rounding: there is also a small reef
projecting from the 8.W. point. Every other part of the island may be approached
without danger.

CONCEPTION ISLAND.—From the west end of Rum Cay to the S.W. end of
Conception Island, the bearing and distance are N.W., nearly 13 miles; it thence
extends about three miles to the north, and is about 2 miles broad. It is mostly
surrounded by a shoal, and from the N.E. end a reef runs off 7 miles N.N.E. easterly,
extending to latitude 23° 55’ 30’, called Southampton Reef. Its N.E. extremity

158 ATWOOD’S GAY.

bears from the east end of Rum Cay, N:W. 4 W., 19 miles, and from the S.W. point
of Watling’s Island W. 2 S., 27 miles.

ATWOOD'S CAY, or the Isle of Samana, the west end of which lies N.E. by E.
3 E., 35 miles from the Bird Rock, is about 8 miles in length from west to east, and
about 2 miles in width. It is entirely surrounded with a white shoal, bordered by a
reef. Off the west end the reef runs out 3 miles; and under this point, in the
extent of a similar distance along the shore, on the south side, there is no reef; and
here vessels may anchor on the white ground, in 7 or 8 fathoms, but very close to the
shore. Off the edge of the white ground no soundings are to be found. To the
eastward of the island are two islets, 41 miles from the shore, surrounded also by
reefs and white shoals. he island is generally low, but the centre hill rises to about
100 feet, and presents the same appearance as the others in this passage. See another
description of this island hereafter given,

DIRECTIONS FOR THE CROOKED ISLAND PASSAGE.

Ships from the Gulf of Gonaives, or southern part of Haiti, generally take their
departure from Cape St. Nicholas; and being 6 miles from the cape in the offing,
should steer N. by W., 63 miles, in order to make the §.W. point of Great Inagua;
this course will generally lead to about 2 leagues to the westward of that point.

It is necessary to mention here, that in proceeding for the Crooked Island Passage,
either from Cape St. Nicholas or Cape Maize, it is best to make the Island of Inagua
if possible, because short departures are best in navigating amongst these islands,
where the currents set in various directions; and, in proceeding from*Great Inagua
to Castle Island, endeavour to leave Inagua so as to allow sufficient time for entering
the Crooked Island Passage before dark, or leave in the evening so as to arrive
by daylight in the morning, according to the strength of wind and rate of sailing;
the latter is generally preferred. The new lights at Inagua, Castle Island, and Bird
Island, when established, will greatly facilitate the run between these islands.

Being opposite the west end of Great Inagua, about 6 miles distant, steer N.N.W.
4 W., about 75 miles, to the eastward of the position of Hobart’s Shoal and the
Mira-por-vos, when, if it be daylight and clear weather, you will make Castle
Island, which may he approached within 2 miles or nearer, without fear.

When abreast of, and on the west side of Castle Island, steer N. by W., 25 miles,
to make the west end of Fortune Island. This course and distance will lead within
3 miles of it, and directly opposite. Continue in the same direction, or N. 4 W., to
make the western extremity of Crooked Island, off which lies the Bird Rock.
Having thus run 18 miles, you will be about 4 or 5 miles to the westward of this
islet, so that the distance from Castle Island to the Bird Rock is 43 miles.

When arrived off the Bird Rock you may consider yourself out of the passage ;
nevertheless, should the wind happen to be N.E. or E.N.E., you have to fear Wat-
ling’s Island, the S.E. point of which bears from Bird Rock N. by W., and is
distant 67 miles; be careful, therefore, in leaving the passage, to keep as much to the
eastward as the wind will permit ; but, should the wind be at S.E., which sometimes
happens, a N.E. course will endanger running on Atwoed’s Cay; so that observe not
to steer more easterly than N.E. 2 N., not more to leeward than N. by E.

CURRENTS.—There is no occasion to fear the currents in this passage, which, in
afresh breeze, are scarcely perceptible; but in calms, or light winds, they may set
to the westward, but so feebly, that in a passage so short you need not mind
them, especially“as-it is generally made with a free wind. Nevertheless, in the
months of June, July, and August, when calms or light westerly winds are common,

THE CAICOS PASSAGE. 159

a current setting to the westward may be met with strong enough to affect your
course, which effect can only happen in this passage. This is occasioned by the
proximity of the extensive shoals forming the channel of Bahama, and those of
Providence Island. Therefore, in this season, it would be proper, if going at the rate
of 2 knots, or less, to allow a quarter of a mile an hour for a current setting westward ;
but if going at the rate of 3 knots, this allowance will be unnecessary.

THE CAICOS PASSAGE.

The Caicos are an assemblage of several islands and islets, inclosing a white shoal,
some parts of which are very shallow, and others tolerably deep. There are four
principal islands, viz..—the Great Caicos, the North Caicos, the N.W. or Providence
Caicos, and the Little Caicos; they form together a semicircle, from the east to the
west, rounding to the northward, and terminating on the south part by a great bank,
on which there are from 3 to 15 feet water.

The northern part of these islands is bordered with a white shoal, on which is a
reef extending 1} mile from shore. At the north-east part the white shoal runs
out in a point full 3 miles, having on its extremity a reef, called Basse St. Philippe,
or St. Philip’s Shoal, on which the sea breaks with great violence. At a cable’s
length to the north and the east of the shoal there are not less than 7 fathoms water ;
the white bottom extends to the southward of it, and approaches insensibly towards
the shore. Between this shoal and the shore there is a channel of 4 to 6 fathoms
water, which, in case of necessity, may be safely used.

The east coast of the Great Caicos, and the west coast of the Little or West Caicos,
are safe and bold-to, within 13 mile of the shore. From the south point of the
Little Caicos a chain of breakers extends to the E.S.-eastward, 16 miles, decreasing
thence to the southward, where they join a sandy islet, called French Cay. This cay
is low, with some bushes on it, and bears from the south point of the Little Caicos
E.S.E., nearly 18 miles. From the French Cay the reef stretches eastward and
southward to join another sandy islet, distant from the former 8 miles, 8.S.E. 3 E.
This islet is not more than 20 paces in extent, and is entirely drowned at high water.
All this part of the reef is bold, and as the water breaks strongly upon it, it is easily
perceived ; but to the southward of the islet there are no breakers, and the edge of
the bank is defined only by the whiteness of the water.

From this sandy islet the bank trends about 5 miles to the eastward, whence it
stretches irregularly 22 miles 8.K.3$8. toits S.W. point, on which is the South
Shoal, and then about N.E. by E., 9 miles, and H.S.E. 4 E., 9 miles nearly, to the
Elbow, or S.E. point, on which is the Swimmer Shoal. About 6 or 7 miles within
the southern edge of the bank, in latitude 21° 10’, lie a range of islets nearly 15 miles
in extent from west to east, called the Southern or Seal Cays.

From the sandy islets, above mentioned, to the part opposite the Southern Cays,
the bank is very dangerous; no land can be seen, and you come suddenly from a sea
without bottom into 3 or 2 fathoms. The colour of the water is the only indication
of danger; and this is by no means certain, for navigators accustomed to see on the
surface of the water the shadow of clouds, which sometimes has the appearance of
shoals, are often lulled into a fatal security. Therefore it would be imprudent to
approach this part of the bank.

If, after turning to windward some days in this neighbourhood, and not seen the
land, the safest way is never to cross the latitude of 21° in the night, but to wait
for daylight; then, should you perceive any change in the water, which indicates
white grounds, without seeing either land or breakers, be sure you are on the western

160 THE CAICOS PASSAGE.

side, and steer N.W. 3 W., along by the edge of the bank to fetch the Little or West
Caicos, in order to go through the passage to leeward of these islands.

Should you see the Southern or Seal Cays, bearing about north or N .W., stand on
upon the white water in from 12 to 7 fathoms; make a tack or two, get to windward,
and go through the Turk’s Island Passage, which is to windward of the Caicos, and
hereafter described.

From the Elbow, or S.E. point, the bank trends N. 2 W., about 24 miles to the
southernmost of the Eastern Caicos, called Long Cay. The Great and Little Am-
bergris Cays lie on this part of the bank; the Great Ambergris, which has an
eminence of 100 feet, being about 15 miles from the 8.E. point, the Little Ambergris
being low, and situate to the westward.

There is anchorage on the White Shoal, near the south point of Great Caicos,
which will serve for vessels that do not draw more than 15 or 16 feet water. West-
ward of this point there is a lagoon of fresh water.

The best anchorage for small vessels is to the westward of the North Caicos, near
the little Island of Pines, in the inlet which that island makes with Providence
Island. Within the reefs that border that part of the coast, lies L’Ance a L’RKan
(Watering Bay), where you may anchor in 3 fathoms, upon a white bottom ; there is
very good water, and it is the watering-place of the Providenciers. The entrance of
the bay will-be discovered by coasting along the reef, from the rounding in of the
coast, after passing the west point of the Three Maries, or Booby Rocks. When you
perceive a great extent of white water within the reef, send a boat to find the channel,
and moor her in it, making use of the lead; and, as you go in, be not afraid of
getting near the reef. When within the reef, drop your anchor in 3 fathoms; and,
if necessary, go farther in, by towing or turning with caution. The entrance is not
more than 1} or 2 miles from shore.

From the east part of the Isle of Pines you may descry several of the islands and
cays, which are scattered within the Caicos, from north to S.E.

W.S.W., 193 miles from the Booby Rocks, is the N.W. point of Providence Caicos,
which is of a white colour and middling height, upon which there is a pile of stones,
erected as a beacon, and off which a reef is reported to extend between 2 and 3 miles
N.W. by N. (1862). You may range along by the west side of this point within a
quarter of a league. Ships may anchor off this coast, in 8 or 10 fathoms; but they
must range along the shore pretty close to be on the White Ground, bringing a steep
hummock, seen a little inland, to bear S.W.; then you will see the shoals recede a
little from the shore, and afford a large space for turning the ship.

From the N.W. point of Providence Caicos to the N.W. point of the Little Ciacos,
is nearly 12 miles 8.W. by S., and thence about 6 miles south to its south point.

Three or four miles to the southward of the N.W., point of Providence Caicos a
reef commences from the shore, running off S.W., westerly, 3 or 4 miles; this reef is
terminated by asmall sandy islet, almost under water, lying nearly 6 miles S.W. by
§. from the said N.W. point. From this sandy islet the reef runs in to the eastward,
and afterwards trenches out to join the north part of the Little Caicos, which is sur-
rounded with white shoals.

On the west side of Providence Caicos, is Malcolm Road, in which there is sufficient
water for all sorts of ships, sheltered from the Norths, which in this passage should
always be guarded against. The largest ships may anchor on a sandy bottom, in 6
or 7 fathoms, being careful to avoid the rocky patches. Here they lie within the west
point, which should be brought to bear north, taking care to avoid the reef, that
runs round this point a quarter of a league, and there ends: it begins again nearly 2
miles farther to leeward, and bears about S. by W. from the anchorage.

In this road ships are sheltered from the north, round by east, to S.E. by S. It
lies N.N.E., about 104 miles from the N.W. part of the Little Caicos; but a more

LITTLE INAGUA. 161

westerly course must be made in order to avoid the sandy islet and veef, already
spoken of.

You may range along the N.W. part of the Little Caicos, close to the edge of the
White Grounds; the west side is very bold to the south point, where anchorage may
be had in from 5 to 7 fathoms on the white bottom ; but the best place to anchor,
being more known, is under the N.W. point, rather within it, in 7 or 8 fathoms, on
sandy bottom, sheltered from the easterly winds. It is advisable, however, to have
another anchor to the southward in 14 or 15 fathoms, to secure you against a sudden
westerly wind.

EAST or COCKBURN HARBOUR.—From Cape Comete, which is the north-
eastern point of the East Caicos, the eastern shore of the cays on the east side of
Caicos Bank takes a southerly direction 13 miles, and bends suddenly to the west-
ward 2 miles, and forms thesouth end of South Caicos. Long Cay lies to the south-
westward of this point, leaving an opening § a mile wide, called East or Cockburn
Harbour, which is W. 4 S., 22 miles from the lighthouse oa Grand Turk.

This anchorage is of small extent, with a depth of 35 fathoms, decreasing gradually ;
a pilot, however, is necessary to take this harbour, or to navigate upon the reef, and
these may be had at the Grand Turk.

LITTLE INAGUA.—To leeward of the Little Ciacos is the Little Inagua, whieh
is seldom seen by navigators, whose endeavour, in generai, is to cross this archipelago
as quickly as possible ; nevertheless, as it is possible to meet with a N.E. wind in the
mid-channel, between Haiti and the Caicos, it is necessary to know the east side
of Great aud Little Inagua.

The east point of Little Inagua, bears from the south point of the Little Caicos,
W.S.W., 24 miles ; this island is very low, and uneven, with the exception of a little
hummock, which appears to be situate near the middle of theisland, and is very much
like the islands above described: from this east point, the N.E. point of Great Inagua
bears 8.S.W., 9 or 10 miles. Between the Great and Little Inagua, there is a channel
4 miles in width, steep-to on both sides, at a cable’s length from shore. You may
approach within a mile of any part of Little Inagua; there is a reef which runs off
a little less than a mile from the 8.EK. part, and on the south side, there is a white
bottom bordered with a reef, at the foot of which there are 406 fathoms.

The east coast of Great Inagua is very little frequented, and is skirted by’a reef
the whole way, from a cable to half a mile from the beach, with soundings outside it
to the distance of about half a mile. Towards the N.E. point there are some sand
hills, somewhat higher than the rest of the coast, where the reef extends off nearly a
mile, and curves round to the N.E. point.

Ciupapo RErF is about 3 miles in length, north and south ; it bears from the east
point of Little Inagua N. 3 E., nearly 24 miles; from the south point of Little Caicos
N.W. 2 W., 30 miles, and from the S.W. Point of Mariguana §.8.E. 3 E., 27 miles.
It is a very dangerous reef of sunken rocks; was seen by Mr. De Mayne, in the
Landrail, surveying cutter, 1816, and requires particular notice, as lying in a direct
line between the Little Inagua, and the eastern part of Mariguana, and only a few
miles to the 8.W. of a line between the West or Little Caicos and the 8.W. point of
Mariguana, being nearly in mid-channel between each.

MARIGUANA ISLAND is about § leagues in length, east and west, and from
3 to 6 miles in breadth. It is surrounded by a reef, which extends 4 or 5 miles to
the eastward of the east point, having on its eastern part several cays, and 5 or 6
large rocks above water. Near the northernmost point of it is an islet, three quarters
of a mile long, with a small cay to the S.W. of it; the rest of the reef is bordered
with rocks under water, on which the sea breaks. On the south side is a passage for
small vessels to go through, and be sheltered by Mariguana on one side, and the reef
on the other.

From the §.W. to the N.W. point of the island, the coast is clear, and forms two

bays, the bottom of which are of white sand, where there is anchorage at about
2 cables’ length from the land. The two points lie about N. by E. and 8. by W. from
each other, distance 7 or 8 miles. It is necessary to be acquainted with these anchor-
ing places, as you might be caught here with a norther; it would then be better to
anchor under the N.W. point, sheltered from the N.N.W., N.E., E., and S.E. winds,
and as far as the south, and that by the islands and the reefs, which run a long
league to the N.W., and on which the sea breaks with great violence. From the N.W.
point, to the northward of which lies a remarkable large rock, the coast inclines to
E. by S., forming a kind of bay, bordered with reefs 3 miles from the land, having
some passages for very small vessels. At the east point of this bay, a little inland,
are two hillocks, whence the coast continues to run E. by S., and E.S.E., full 18 miles
to the east point, which has already been described.

Mariguana is of moderate height: and like the other islands, is covered with
bushes and thickets, among which are some trees larger than the rest, but none of
them fit for ship building.

The PLANAS are very low, and have been said to be threein number; but what
probably give rise to that, is arock, which appears above water as high as a boat, at
about 2 a mile to the N.E. of the westernmost island, among the reefs and banks
which extend from one to the other. A little hill, about 70 feet high, on the western-
most island, bears W.N.W. from the S.W. point of Mariguana; the east point of the
easternmost island bears N.W. by W. from the same point; and from the east end of
Samana, or Atwood’s Cay, the eastern point of the Planas bears 8.S.K., about 31 miles.
You may go tolerably close to the north, east, and south sides, the white bottom which
surrounds them being pretty steep.

The westernmost, which is also the largest, is about 3 miles in length north and
south, and half that in breadth; the east and north sides are bordered with reefs
which break. There is anchorage on its west side on the White Ground, at about
2 cables’ length from shore, and 3 of a mile from the south point, near which
is a landing place, and by digging 3 or 4 feet in the sand, good fresh water may
be obtained. There is'also a small lagoon of water supplied entirely by the rain,
but it is sometimes very brackish. The other island lies east and west, about 2 miles
to the eastward of this, but the passage between them, made very narrow by the reefs
on both sides, is not a mile wide, and fit only for small craft. These islands consist of
nothing but sand and rock, with some bushes upon them, fit only for firing.

DIRECTIONS FOR SAILING THROUGH THE CAICOS
PASSAGE,

This is the best passage for ships bound from Cape Haiti Harbour, or Guarico,
formerly Cape Francais, when the winds. are not steady from the E.S.E. You will
always sail with a large wind, which is of great advantage, and avoid all the
White Grounds to the 8.E. of the Caicos, which it has been customary to make, and
which are very dangerous ; whereas, there is no risk in making the land some leagues
to leeward, between the Sandy Islet, or French Cay, and the Little Caicos.

Directions for working up from Cape St. Nicholas to Cape Haitien have been given,
page 60.

On leaving the harbour of Cape Haitien, and having the cape bearing south about
3 miles, steer a N. by W. course, and after having run 105 miles, will carry to about
4 to 6 miles to the S.W, of the Little Ciacos; then haul your wind, first as high as
north only, on account of the sandy islet and reef which lie to the northward, of the
Little Caicos; after which, that is, when the N.W. point of Providence Caicos bears

TURK’S ISLAND PASSAGE. 163

N.E., steer N. by E., 12 miles, then haul up N.E. if necessary, or continue to steer
N. by E. or north, without any fear. Having run 30 or 40 miles on either of these
courses, you will be clear of the passage.

When about 6 miles §.W. of the Little Caicos, and the winds do not permit, you to
steer N. by E., or to make good a north course, after having run about 40 miles
without getting sight of Mariguana Island, the best way, if night comes on, is to
tack and stand to the S.E. until near midnight: then tack and stand to the north-
ward, so as to have daylight to approach the breakers off the east end of Mariguana,
if you should not be sufficiently to windward to clear them; but it is very probable
that you will clear them by 10 or 12 miles.

Again, when 8.W. of Little Caicos, and the wind will not admit of lying north,
you should not attempt to go to windward of Mariguana, but steer for the channel
between it and the Planas or French Cays. First steer N.W. 2 N., 30 miles, then
N.W. 2 W., 30 miles; having run these courses and distances, you will have passed
on the N.E. of the Ciudado Reef,* at the distance of 5 or 6 miles, and be about 5 or 6
miles from the §. W. point of Mariguana, which ought to bear about north. This point
may be approached with safety; a small white shoal runs off it, with 3 fathoms
water almost close to the shore.

Having doubled the S.W. point of Mariguana, so as to bring it to bear east, steer
north, if the wind will permit. In that case you will pass about 10 miles to the east-
ward of the Planas, and 15 to 20 miles to the eastward of Atwood’s Cay and reefs; but,
if your course is not better than N. by W. made good, after having run 30 to 35 miles,
and the night comes on before you see that island, tack and stand south-east ward
15 to 20 miles; then, if you can make good a N. by W. course on the other tack, you
will weather the eastern breakers of Atwood’s Cay, at about 10 or 12 miles. Should

ou be 6 miles from the S.W. point of Mariguana, and the wind will permit only a
NNW. course, after having run thus 18 miles, the Planas, or Flat Islands, will bear
about west 5 or 6 miles. (These-islands may be passed on either side according to
circumstances). Continue on the same course until they bear S.W. by W. about
6 or 7 miles distant; then N.W. by W., or N.W. = W., 38 or 40 miles, will be abreast
and clear of the reef off the west end of Atwood’s Cay, when you will be clear of the
passage, and may haul close to the wind. Do not go in the least to the northward
of this course, as the breakers off the west end of Atwood’s Cay bear nearly N.W.
by N. from the middle of the Planas.

On leaving Cape Haitien you will generally find the wind at 8.E. or E.S.E.,
and near the shore the current runs to windward; these two circumstances will
induce you to steer N.E. or N.E. by N. for the Turk’s Islands Passage; but, at about
10 or 11 o’clock, the wind generally chops round to the northward of east, and some-
times so faras N.E. Being then 15 or 18 miles from the coast, and the current no
longer felt, you would necessarily fall in with the white grounds to the southward
of the Caicos, already described. This circumstance has caused many shipwrecks,
merely from the eagerness of gaining 60 miles to windward in a voyage of perhaps
1500 leagues. Under these circumstances it is most advisable for mariners to steer
from the Cape Haitien direct for Little Caicos.

TURK’S ISLANDS PASSAGE.

The TURKS are three principal islands, viz., La Grande Saline, or Grand Turk
La Petit Saline, or Salt Cay; and Sand Cay.

164 THE GRAND TURK.

The western side of these islands is bold, and may be approached very near; but

. there is a white shoal, with rocky spots, which extends three-quarters of a mile from
the shore.

SAND KAY, the southernmost of these islands, is about a mile in length, and
may be seen 9 miles off: from. the southward it appears like two islands, the middle
part being very low land. Off its south point, at about 2 cables’ length, are three
rocks, close to each other, by which it may be known; but they are not discernible
far off, neither can they be seen, if the south point of the island bears to the east-
ward of N.E. This cay is low and barren, producing only a few bushes, being con-
a beaten by the winds and the sea, and the sand upon it appears quite white
in the sun.

Sand Cay is surrounded by a white bank, which extends to the 8.W. On this
bank is a reef running off N. by W. and N.N.W. from the N.W. point of the cay,
which breaks every where, having 8 fathoms within pistol-shot of it. You may
anchor on the west side, on the white grounds, in from 6 to 4 fathoms, within swivel-
shot of the shore; but ships which draw much water must anchor about 4 a mile
off, with the south point bearing about S.E., and the middle of it east, or E. by N.:
here is shelter by the reef, as far to the northward as N.N.E.; and you may easily
get under weigh with any wind, as the Norths, which are the most dangerous, blow
only along the coast; so that this may be reckoned a tolerably good roadstead.
You must not approach so near to the other parts of the island, for there are some
ee with only 2 fathoms or less on them. ‘The east side has high breakers quite
to the shore.

To the south-westward of Sand Cay lies the Endymion Reef or Shoal, of small
extent; lying S.W. 3 S., 5§ miles from the south end of Sand Cay, and a cable
within the western edge of the bank. The rock has only 4 feet water on it, breaks
in heavy weather, and is surrounded by a small cluster of rocky heads within the
compass of ; ofa mile. When the water is smooth, and the rock is not distinguish-
able by the breakers, it becomes dangerous. The soundings between it and the cay
are from 7 to 9 fathoms, quite clear. The Swimmer Rock which lies on the S.E.
point of the Caicos Bank, bears from the Endymion W. by. S., 12 miles.

SALT CAY, or La Petit Saline, lies about 5 miles N. by E. from Sand Cay; is of
a triangular form, being nearly 33 miles in length N. by E. on its west side. It is
higher than Sand Cay, and has some hillocks, and a great number of bushes and
small trees, fit only for firewood. The soil is nothing but sand at a great depth, and
there are but few spots fit for cultivation.

The white bank with which all these islands or cays are surrounded, after passing
the reef off the N.W. end of Sand Cay, falls in to the eastward between it and Salt
Cay ; so that in sailing from one to the other you would lose soundings.

From the reef off the N.W. end of Sand Cay to the N.W. point of Salt Cay is 6
miles, near which you may anchor, but the bank is very steep; for, with your anchor
in 5 fathoms, within musket-shot of the shore, you will have 20 fathoms under the
ship, and a little farther off no ground. Here you have the N.W. point bearing from
N.N.E. to N.E. by N., and the south point from 8S, by W. toS.8S.W. Here is no
other fresh water but the rain water found in the hollows of the rocks.

The GRAND TURK, or Grande Saline.—From the N.W. point of Salt Cay, the
south end of the Grand Turk may be seen, bearing N.N.E., at the distance of 6 miles.
This cay has the best ground of the three, being covered with grass fit for cattle,
and in several places might be cultivated; but the trees, though higher than those
of Salt Cay, are, like them, fit only for firewood. There are two salt-ponds, but one
only furnishes salt: this produces three times as much as the pond of Salt Cay. The
town, which is the seat of government, stands on the western shore, and in front of
an extensive cultivated salt-pond.

Light.—On the N.E. extremity of the Grand Turk Island an iron light-house has

THE GRAND TURK. 165

been erected in latitude 21° 31’, and longitude 71° 7' 40’. The tower is painted white,
and the light is elevated 108 feet.

The light revolves every half-minute, and at each revolution flares up into a
brilliant flash, and may be seen from the deck of a moderate sized vessel, in clear
weather, 15 miles. The mariner should however be aware, that when approaching
this light from the southward, it will be eclipsed by the southern part of the island,
on which it stands, between the bearings of N. 4 W. and N.25.; by Salt Cay,
between N. by EH. and N. by E. 2 E., and by the eastern group of cays between
N. by W. 2 W. and N. by W. 2 W.

With the light bearing south, it may be approached within 2 miles; but vessels
running for the Turk’s Islands Passage should make the light ona bearing to the
westward of south, and it should not be forgotten that from the limited distance at
which it can be seen, it will not protect them from Philip’s Reef, and the dangers off
East Caicos. They must also remember that the reef projects 3 miles from the north
point of Turk’s Island, and continues along its whole eastern side.

Dixections.—In proceeding from Salt Cay to the Grand Turk, so soon as you are
clear of the reefs, which stretch off 2 cables’ length from the former, you may steer
N.N.E. for the south point of the latter. The edge of the bank runs nearly ina
N. by E. direction, until nearly in the latitude of the south point of the Grand Turk,
when it turns in abruptly towards it. You may run along on the edge of the bank
in 4 or 5 fathoms, or anchor upon it, well-sheltered from the trade-winds by the
bank, and cays upon it. A reef stretches W. by N. from Cotton Cay, almost as far
as the south point of the Grand Turk, but which seldom shows itself in moderate
weather,

There is anchorage at two places off the Grand Turk, one towards the middle of the
island, opposite the huts, the other to the southward of English Point, off the south
end of the island. The former is most convenient for ships to load salt at, it being
nearest to the salt-pond. Let go the anchor so soon as you are on the white ground,
but take care to pick out a clear bottom, as in some places the rocks rise within 8 or
10 feet of the surface of the water. Having anchored and veered to half a cable,
you may possibly, by a cast of the lead under the stern, get no bottom.

To sail to the other anchorage, it is advisable to keep along on the bank, but
do not go within the white water until English Point bears E. by N.; for off that
point there are breakers, and shoal water close to the shore. Being to the southward
of that point, haul in and anchor in 4 or 6d fathoms, about half a cable’s length
from shore; .and having veered half a cable, the ship will be in 12 or 14
fathoms, and a little farther out you will get no bottom. Be careful, and find a clear
place to drop anchor in. Here English Point will bear north; a little hillock
E. by 8.; and the south point S.E. This is far superior to the former anchorage ;
but these, as well as that at Salt Cay, are fit only when the trade wind is settled, for
it is very dangerous to be caught with any other. It is high water at half-past one
o’clock on full and change days; spring tides rise 3 or 4 feet.

On the east side of these islands are several islets and rocks, which are connected
by white shoals, with very little water on them. Several of these rocks have beacons
erected upon them, as guides for the anchorage, but they are of very little use to
strangers, without the assistance of a pilot, and vessels drawing over 17 fect should
not attempt the Hawk’s Nest anchorage. ‘They are bold, and surrounded with a
white ground, which extends to the southward and §.W., and joins that southward
of Sand Cay.

The North Point of the Grand Turk lies in latitude 21° 31’; and it appears that
the bank with which these islands are surrounded extends about 2 miles to the north-
ward of that point.

The Turk’s Islands Channel is upwards of 15 miles across in the narrowest part.
From the elbow, or §.E. point of the Caicos Bank to the Endymion Shoal, is 11 or
12 miles E.N.E.
