DIRECTIONS FOR SAILING THROUGH THE TURK’S
ISLANDS PASSAGE.

This passage is very short, and tolerably fair, but cannot always be made from
Cape Haitien. The proper course to steer will be N.E. by N., but the wind often
will not admit to steer so much to the eastward; it is therefore recommended, in
leaving Cape Haitien to keep as close as you can with the land or early breeze, and
tack so as to gain sight of the Grange before night. You will generally bring it to
bear from 8.E. to E.S.E., distant about 9 or 10 miles. (If your ship sails well, or
has been favoured by the breeze, you may bring it to bear south).* From the Grange,
bearing S.K. by S.,a N. by E. $ E. course made good, 60 or 65 miles, will bring you
in sight of Sand Cay, the southernmost of the Turk’s Islands ; but great care is requi-
site to avoid the Endymion Shoal. If your last course should not have better than
N. by E., or North, take particular care not to pass the latitude of 21°. In the
night, when near that parallel, be sure to sound, and the moment you find bottom,
about ship, and stand the other way till morning, when you may tack again, and
perhaps fetch to windward of the white shoals of the Caicos.

The white bottom here is very easily seen; you may run on the edge of the bank
to the southward of the Southern Cays for 4 or 6 miles, in from 14 to 7 fathoms
water ; but farther on there are rocks with 3 fathoms or less on them. In the day
time you may stand on to the northward (supposing you have not seen the land),
and you will see the Seal or Southern Cays of the Caicos, or if you are farther to
windward, perhaps Sand Cay. Be careful not to go to leeward of the white shoals
which extend south of the small sandy islet, which is entirely drowned at high
water ; this islet, as before said, is very difficult to be seen, and your iead even cannot
give warning, as you fall suddenly into the depth of 3 fathoms.

To the south-westward of Sand Cay is a white shoal, extending about 3% miles
from shore, with from 9 to 7 fathoms. When you have Sand Cay bearing east, at
the distance of 6, 9, or 12 miles, steering N. by E. 3 E., or N.N.E., 35 to 40 miles will
entirely clear the passage. In going through, always keep the Turk’s Islands side
on board, in order to avoid the Reefs of St. Philip, which extend from the N.E. point
of the Great Caicos, heretofore described.

THE SILVER CAY PASSAGE.

THE SQUARE HANDKERCHIEF, or Mouchoir Quarre, is a very dangerous
and extensive shoal; its S.W. point bears §.E., 21 miles distant from Sand Cay, of
Turk’s Islands, whence it extends 30 miles north-eastward. On the N.W. edge
there is a bank of rocky heads, some of which are just awash. From this shoal the
bottom runs east about 8 miles to a similar patch of rocks just awash, and to the N.E.
about 3 miles, and in latitude 21° 6’ is the northernmost rocky head, which breaks at
times with great violence. From this N.E. breaker the cast side of the bank runs
south for 20 miles, and then about W. by N., 30 miles to the west end. It is natural
to suppose that all the interval is full of sunken cays, which render its approach very
dangerous. On the south and south-west parts the bottom shows and gives warning,
and you will find from 10 to 15 fathoms ; however, the best way is to bear up, and
pass to leeward, unless you are sure of being on the east end of the white grounds,
and can weather them the next tack.

* On approaching the Grange, be careful of the reefs that lie off it, heretofore described
in page 53.

THE SILVER CAY BANK. 167

THE SILVER CAY BANK.—These shoals have more extent than the Square
Handkerchief; the southern point is in latitude 20° 17’, and the northernmost part
in 20° 55’. It is very white in many places, particularly on the north part, and very
brown on the south and south-east parts.

The eastern side of the bank is 27 miles long ina N.E. by N. and §.W. by S.
direction, but bends near the middle ; and at the bottom of the bight, near the edge,
there is a dangerous shoal. Its S.E. and N.E. points appear to have no danger, but
regular soundings from 12 to 15 fathoms.

The north side of the bank runs nearly straight N.W. by W. % W. for 38 miles;
but at about 8 miles from the N.E. point it becomes exceedingly dangerous all the
way to the N.W. point; and near the middle of this side, rocky heads, which are
awash, extend 5 miles inward from the edge. The west side also runs nearly straight
north and south 37 miles, on the meridian of 70° W.; and 7 miles from the S.W.
point there is a foul patch close to the edge of soundings; but to the northward of
this, to within 7 miles of the N.W., the bank appears to be free of danger for some
distance from the edges.

From the 8.W. point the south side trends E. by §., 24 miles, and for about the
first 8 miles of this distance the edge is very dangerous; but to the eastward of
this it appears to be clear; it will be better, however, not to venture on any part of
the bank, for it has not been closely examined. As the water on the bank is not
discoloured, except over the shoals, where it has a white appearance, the lead must
be well attended when approaching it from any quarter.

DIRECTIONS FOR SAILING THROUGH THE SILVER
CAY PASSAGE.

Tf, by any circumstances, a vessel is forced to proceed from Cape Haitien through the —
passage between the Mouchoir Bank and the Silver Cay Bank, which is perfectly safe,

-and 28 miles wide, you should at departure steer N.E. by N., 48 miles, then E.N.E., 90

or 100 miles will lead through and over the S.E. tail of the Mouchoir Bank, in 12 to
15 fathoms, about longitude 70° 30’. If the wind will admit of steering these
courses, you will pass in mid-channel; but if you are obliged to work to windward,
and should not get sight of the Haiti shore, after you have got so far to the eastward
as 70° 20’ longitude, ‘you must not pass the latitude of 20° 15’ without frequently
heaving the lead. If you get into 20° 25’ without finding bottom, you have nothing
to fear from the Silver Cays, but must then look out for the Mouchoir Bank, which
is not dangerous on the south side, as the bottom will give notice in 10 and 15
fathoms. Continue to get on to the eastward; and when in the latitude of 21° 20’
you will be entirely out of the passage.

Weak currents generally set along the edges of these banks. On the Mouchoir
Bank they are scarcely felt; on the south-east part of the Silver Cays you may find
them setting to the west and N.W.; at a league from the bank they are not per-
ceptible. In general, they need not be regarded in the reckoning.

GENERAL REMARKS ON THE TURK’S ISLANDS
PASSAGE, FROM THE NORTHWARD.

Although Turk’s Islands Passage may be considered tedious and hazardous for ships
from the south-westward, yet for those from the north-ecastward it appears preferable
to the passage by the Caicos.

As the north point of the Grand Turk lies in latitude 21° 31’, ships coming
from sea should run down in the parallel of 21° 40’, and when night comes on, if
nothing is seen, stand to the northward under easy sail, and endeavour to be as near
the same place at daylight as they were the preceding evening, or not farther to the
westward than could be seen the night before, and then keep running down in the
above latitude. There may be occasion to do the same thing the second night, but
that will depend on the correctness of the reckoning.* It will be almost impossible
to pass the Turk’s Islands without seeing them, from the latitude above recom-
mended, and the revolving light on the N.K. part of the Grand Turk, which is visible
15 miles, will be of great service in making this Island; but if they should, they
would make the N.E. part of the Great Caicos, which lies to the N.W. of the Grand
Turk. The Reef of St. Philip, described in page 159, lies to N.E. of the former, and
the reef, which runs off to the northward of the latter, will be discernible by the
breakers. The course through is S. by W., 40 miles; they then will be in an open
channel, between the islands and the north side of Haiti, and may shape what course
they please. 3

The channel between the Caicos and Mariguana is certainly wide; but when the
difficulties which arise from blowing, hazy weather, and night coming on, are taken
into consideration, from being more in the stream of currents between the east reef of
Mariguana and the back of the Caicos, and from the possibility of driving or passing
between without seeing them, it will appear that Turk’s Islands Passage should have
the preference. Besides, in steering for the Caicos Passage, from the northward, it
would be as dangerous to run for it in the night, as it would be for the other; and in
case of a continuation of blowing, hazy weather, the mariner might be puzzled and at
a loss what to do, if he should be surprised with the breach of Ciudada Reef, or of the
Hogsties; whereas, by endeavouring to make the Turk’s Islands, though he should
pass them, he would be certain of making the Great Caicos; and then, if too far to
leeward to go through Turk’s Islands Passage, he could run down on the north side
of the Caicos, and choose his time and channel, either to windward or leeward of
Inagua, having a good departure to run from.

DESCRIPTION OF THE BAHAMA BANKS AND ISLANDS.

These consist of the Great and Little Banks, on both of which are a great number
of islands, cays, islets, and rocks. The banks are generally composed of sand, with

THE ISLAND OF NEW PROVIDENCE. 169

coral. The islands are low, flat, and interspersed with broken porous rocks ; the soil
is generally light and sandy, producing an abundance of small trees, among which
will be found mahogany, brasiletto, lignum vite, wild cinnamon, pimento, satinwood,
cedars, &c.; there are, however, many patches of good soil, which is used for the cul-
tivation of cotton and the rearing of cattle. Fresh water is scanty, and is to be
obtained only from pools formed during the rains, or from wells dug in the sand.

The climate is rather temperate than otherwise, the northern isles being refreshed
in the winter months by the cool north-westerly winds, and the southern isles, with
little interruption, almost constantly by the general trade wind of the ocean,

THE GREAT BAHAMA BANK.

The ISLAND of NEW PROVIDENCE, situate on the Great Bahama Bank,
is the chief of the Bahama Islands. It is 16 miles in length from east to west,
and its greatest breadth, in the middle, is 7 miles. On the north side of the
island is the Harbour of Nassau, fit for vessels drawing 12 or 13 feet water; those
vessels drawing 15 feet should wait till nearly high water. The harbour is sheltered
on the north by Hog Island. Nassau Town is situate in latitude 25° 5’, and
longitude 77° 21’, and is built near the western part of the harbour. It is the seat
of government of the Bahama Islands,* and is one of the best constructed towns in
the West Indies, the streets being wide and airy, and the houses well built. It haga
considerable trade; the principal exports are cotton, pimento, pine apples, and salt,
for which it receives lumber from New Brunswick, and British manufactures from
England.

Lights.—The entrance to the harbour of Nassau is at the western end of Hog
Island, which is distinguished by the lighthouse. It is a conical stone tower, coloured
white, 58 feet in height; the light is fixed, elevated 68 feet, and visible 10 miles
from the deck of a small vessel, between the bearings of N.E. and N.W.

At Athol Island, on cupola of Quarantine Officers’ dwellings, a lantern showing a
fixed light, 50 feet above the sea, visible between the bearings of N.N.W. 2 W. and
W.iN.

ANDROS ISLAND.—This island lies 21 miles to the westward of New Provi-
dence, and is the largest of the Bahamas: it is 95 miles in length, in a N.N.W. and
S.S.E. direction, and 35 miles broad in its widest part, which is about one-third from
its northern end. The whole island is low and swampy; but it is well wooded, with
pines, cedar, satinwood, and mangroves. ‘The whole of the eastern shore is bounded
by a reef, within which there is a passage for small vessels and boats; in this reef are
several inlets between the cays, through which vessels may pass, from the Tongue of
the Ocean to different anchorages within the reef, which is very steep the whole
length of the east side of the island. The western shores of this.island are so
shallow, that they are difficult to approach, even in a boat. Previous to the late
surveys of Commanders Owen and Barnett, this island and the cays surrounding it
were little known.

To the southward of Andros Island, about 10 miles, lies the Jonas Cay, in latitude
28° 34’ 30’, and longitude 77° 47’ 40’; there is no safe passage between. Near the
western side of the island lie William and Billys Islands, in latitude 24° 40’, and
longitude 78° 31’. To the northward of Andros Island lie the extensive J oulter Cays,
running in a N.W. by N. direction, 14 miles, to latitude 25° 22. There is no passage

The Berry Islands + occupy a space of 28 miles from north to south; and at the

Vessels crossing the bank through the N.W. ent, between Berry Isles and Joulter

GINGERBREAD Grounp.—The east end of this ground lies 34 miles west of Little

THE LITTLE ISAACS are three small rocks, and named the Little, Middle, and
East Isaac. The western, or Little Isaac is 8 feet high; the Middle Isaac is 12 feet;
and East Isaac is 11 feet in height, and in latitude 25° 57’ 30’, and longitude 70° 51’ 30",
and bears E.S.E., 3 miles from the western rock, and 2.of a mile from the middle
rock. There isa rock, which is just awash at high water, 13 mile E. ¢ 8. from the
East Isaac. You may anchor on the bank, to the southward of the Isaacs, in 44 to 4
fathoms, by taking daylight, and having a good chart.

THE BROTHERS are two small rocks appearing above water, having shoal water
around them, and named the East and West Brothers: the former is 7, and the latter
is 6 feet high: they lie N. 63° W., distant 7 miles from the west Little Isaac, and 4
miles within the edge of the bank. This isa good passage on to the bank between
the Brothers and the Little Isaac. The deepest water is near the former.

THE GREAT ISAAC lies 4 miles from the West Brothers, and is in latiude 26° 2’,
and longitude 79° 6’ 30"; it is 40 feet high.. The N.E. rock, which is 12 feet high,
lies 13 mile to the north-eastward of the Great Isaac. There are 3 fathoms at some
distance south-westward of the Great Isaac, and is good anchorage in 43 or 5
fathoms, southward of the east end of the island; for here, should the wind shift to
the northward, you will have plenty of room to get under weigh ; it is a better berth
than on the north side of the island. The Hen and Chickens are a cluster of little
cays and rocks, lying 3 miles S.W. by S. from the Great Isaac ; the Hen, which is the
northernmost, is 14 feet high; they are about a mile in extent from the N.E. to 8.W.
To the southward of the Chickens the bank is all clear until you approach the north
end of the North Bemini, off which lies the Mosella Bank, which has only from 3 to6
feet upon it, and lies 23 miles N.N.W. from the north point of North Bremini. It is
nearly a mile in extent from N.N.E. to 8.S.W., and about 3 of a mile broad. The
tides rise here between 3 and 4 feet; the flood setting N.E., 1, and the ebb 8.W.,
3 miles an hour, forms a rippling on the bank.

Light.—A lighthouse is erected on the Great Isaac, in latitude 26° 2’ 0’, and longi-
tude 79° 6’ 30’, exhibiting a revolving light every minute, visible 16 miles. The
tower, 145 feet in height, and 158 feet above the sea, is built of iron, with broad
red bands, 8 in number, and 7 white bands, horizontally, lantern white. Shows a
fixed light for a distance of 6 miles between the flashes.

The BEMINI ISLANDS are the north-westernmost islands in the Great Bank;
they lie nearly 6 leagues $.S,W. from the Great Isaac. The ground about them is

generally rocky and shoal; but there is good anchorage on the S.W., in 5, 6, 7, and
8 fathoms. On each of them is a well of fresh water.

These islands extend §.S.W. and N.N.E., 7 miles, and have an extensive flat running
off them south-eastward, nearly 10 miles, with only 3 or 4 feet water on it. The
south part of the Bemini Islands is in latitude 25° 41’, and longitude 79° 20’. The
bank of soundings extends about a mile to the westward of them. The bar at the
mouth, is liable to shift generally ; the best entrance is near the small rocky point 2 of
a mile to the southward of it, conspicuous, having a white sandy beach between them.
Here 6 or 6 feet water may be found. The well is on the beach, 4 of a mile to the
southward of the harbour, about 60 yards from the sea; the water is sometimes
brackish after heavy westerly gales. ‘The highest trees are from 40 to 50 feet high,
growing on swamps. The island in uninhabited, but it abounds with flamingo and
curlew ; wild hogs are also found here. On the high sandy beaches, on the western
shore, large quantities of turtle are procured during the season.

The Turtle Rocks form a chain of low cays and rocks, which extend from the South
Bemini 2 or 3 miles, and are 18 feet high; a chain of rocks, black and barren, extend
to the southward as far as the Gun Cay ; the principal of these are the Picket Rocks,
12 feet high ; southward of this is the Holm Cay, 10 feet high, lying off the north
end of Gun Cay. Barnett’s Harbour is so badly sheltered with westerly or easterly
winds, that it is seldom used.

The Derrotero does not mention Barnett’s Harbour, but of the Cat Cays, it says,
“The northern one is named Dog Cay (which is Gun Cay of Mr. De Mayne’s chart),
the second Wolf Cay, and the southern one Cat Cay. The northern point of Dog Cay
has a mangrove thicket, and to the west of its south point there is a good anchorage
in 8% fathoms. Wolf Cay has on its southern part two palm-trees, of equal size,
which serve as a mark to know it by.”

These cays are from 2 of a mile to 2 miles within the edge of the bank, and the
depths decrease as you approach them. To the S.W. of Cat Cay, more than a mile,
are some islets, named, 8. W. Rocks.

Light.—The British government has caused a lighthouse to be erected on Gun Cay,
at 250 yards from the southern extreme. This lighthouse stands in latitude 25° 34’ 30’,
and longitude 79° 18’ 50”. Its base is 25 feet above high water, and the height of the
tower is 55 feet. The light revolves onceevery minute and a half, and may be seen
in all directions, except between the bearings of 8. by W. 1 W., and S. 2 E. where,
at the distance of about 8 miles, it will be intercepted by the Bemini Islands. It is
considered to be rather an indifferent light.

When within 5 miles distance, vessels should not bring the light to the southward
of 8.E., as the chain of cays and reefs project in a curve to the westward, and as they
lie within a mile of the outer edge of the bank, there might be scarcely time to obtain
soundings. The flood-tide also sets strongly to the eastward through the intervals of
the cays, where it is high water at full and change at 7h. 30m., and the tide rises
3 feet.

The light being 80 feet above the level of the sea, it will be visible in clear weather
at the distance of 12 miles to an eye elevated 10 feet.

It has been observed that the Gun Cay Light is of more importance than the whole
on the Florida shore together ; and ought at all times to be made (as the bank extends
sufficiently for striking it) by running obliquely on the edge (say about N.N.E.), and
attending carefully to the lead, to prevent accidents, even should the weather be
thick, and the light not seen. There is an intricate channel round the south end of
this cay, with 12 feet over the bars; all, however, is a sheet of breakers. Small -
vessels may cross the flat to the eastward of Gun Cay ; by bringing the lighthouse to
bear W.N.W. it will lead across in 7 feet.

THe Cat Cays.—The North and South Cat Cays, which are nearly joined, run in a
S.E. by 8. direction, 4 miles from Gun Cay Light. The western edge of these cays is

foul and rocky. The Round Rocks lie off the middle of the cays a mile within the —
edge of the bank, where there are 6, 7, and 8 fathoms.

The Rabbit Rock is awash, and lies S.S.E., a mile from the Round Rocks, and
N.N.W. westerly, a mile from the Wedge Rock, which is 14 feet high. The Rabbit
has 43 fathoms close to its western edge, and 2 fathoms between it and the south end
of the Cat Cay. The mark to clear the Rabbit Rock is Gun Cay Lighthouse, kept
open to the westward of the Round Rocks.

North Cat Cay is the largest, and has the best land; it is surrounded by a belt of
sand, 30 feet high. Inside are some good trees, notwithstanding the quantity cut
yearly. Near the S.E. end are several casks sunk, which yield an abundant supply
of excellent fresh water for the small wrecking vessels, which resort to this place in
numbers.

DOLLAR HARBOUR is on the south side of Little or South Cat Cay. It is
the only place worthy the name of a harbour in this neighbourhood, in latitude
25° 31’ 30", and longitude 79° 16’ 40’. Vessels of 12 feet may find shelter by giving
the point of Cat Cay a berth of acable’s length, and avoiding the shifting sand-
bores by the eye; this harbour is sheltered by the S.W. Cat Rocks, and round the
eastward by dry sand-bores. There is a little swell at high water; but nothing
in strong easterly winds to prevent.a vessel riding here. On the bank, 10 miles
eastward of Dollar Harbour, the tide flows, full and change, at 8h. 40m., and rises
3 feet.

The edge of the bank, from abreast of Dollar Harbour, to the South Riding Rocks,
runs in a 8.S.E. 3 E. direction, 18 miles. The Factory Cays lie 14 mile to the south-
ward of Dollar Harbour, and are 12 feet high. At 5 miles 8.E. by 8. from the
Factory Cays lie the Sandy Cays, 12 feet high. The bay between the latter cays is
clean sand, with gradual soundings, decreasing towards the sand-bores. Here a
vessel may stand well on the bank, taking care not to get within the line of the
cays. Sandy Cay is covered with grass and shrubs; a cask is sunk near the centre,
which will produce several hogsheads of excellent water; and it is much more con-
venient for small vessels than Cat Cay, as they can anchor on either side, sheltered
from all but westerly winds.

BROWN’S CAY lies 8.S.E., 13 mile from Sandy Cay, and is about 13 feet high.
Here is a channel at the south end of Brown’s Cay, which leads on to the bank, and
is called Brown’s Nine Feet Channel. The tides are very regular here through the
whole flood, which runs about east, and the ebb west. This channel is in latitude
25° 23’ 20".

BEAK’S CAY, which is about three-quarters of a mile long, and 13 feet high, lies
about a mile 8.8.E. of Brown’s, and forms the south side of the channel, before men-
tioned. From Beak’s Cay a chain of low barren rocks, connected by sunken ones,
runs in a 8.8.H. direction 6} miles, to the Riding Rocks. The edge of the bank is a
little more than a mile from this chain of rocks, having from 20 to 4 fathoms on it.
Good clear anchorage may be found in 5 to 12 fathoms, with easterly winds on the
bank; and with S.E. winds it would be advisable to anchor wherever you fetch
between the Great Isaacs and the Orange Cays, for the Gulf Stream sweeps close to
the edge, and would prevent the fastest vessels from beating against it.

THE RIDING ROCKS are the southernmost of the range extending from Gun
Cay; they are small narrow strips of rocks, the northernmost only having verdure
and bushes about 14 feet high, and is in latitude 25° 16’, and longitude 79° 10’ ; the
smaller rocks are quite barren. The channels between them are shallow, and the
bars of sand and coral are numerous, and continually shifting, so that none but small
vessels, and those well acquainted, should attempt them.

The bank to the southward and westward of the South Riding Rock is clean, and
has well sheltered anchorage, in 4 to 7 fathoms, from northerly winds; it is 18 feet
high, and has a beacon of stones upon it, which will assist to point out this anchorage,

174 THE ORANGE GAYS.

which is in latitude 25° 13’ 30’; you will have 4 fathoms to the eastward of the
south end of these rocks.

The Castle Rock, which is 12 feet high, lies near the east side of the South Riding
Rock, and northward of the anchorage; eastward of which is a ridge, of 25 and 2
fathoms ; to cross this ridge, in passing to or from the Great Bank, you must keep
the South Riding Rock just opening south of the Castle Rock, and it will lead you
over in 15 feet water: from hence to the Orange Cays there are several places where
you may cross the reef; but it is not recommenced, as there are several shoal spots
within 2 miles of the outer edge of the bank.

THE ORANGE CAYS are a cluster of shoals and cays, lying near the western
edge of the bank, about 15 miles to the southward of the Riding Rocks. They extend
from latitude 24° 54’ to.24° 58’, and are in longitude 79° 9’ 15”; they are a narrow
ridge, and there are only 12 feet for upwards of a mile to the south of them. The
largest rock is about three-quarters of a mile long, and 120 yards broad at its widest
part, and 13 feet high. It is a barren rock, straight on its eastern side, and lying
nearly N.N.E.and8.8.W. About three-quarters of a mile from the main cay are two
rocks, about 6 feet above water; and half a mile southward of the latter, are two
smaller rocks. It is dangerous to pass between any of these rocks. You may safely
enter the bank 3 or 4 miles to the southward of the latter rocks. In about 24° 50’,
numbers of vessels of alight draught of water cross the bank from here to the westward
of the Stirrip Cays. The Orange Cays are solid rocks and steep-to, having 12 to 15
feet close to their western side, which is 2 miles within the edge of the bank. The
tide on the great hank, 15 miles eastward of the Orange Cays, has been found to flow,
full and change, at 10h.'15m., and rises 3 feet. The flood sets South to S.W.; the
ebb sets North to N.E., nearly 2 knots.

The Roquillas are described as 4 little rocks, lying about 2 miles to the southward
of the Orange Cays; they are connected by a reef. There is good anchorage to the
N.W. of them, and west of the Orange Cays; there is also good anchorage to the N.E.
and east of the same, in 3 and 33 fathoms, to the distance of 3 to 18 miles.

Between the Rocky Cays and the Orange Cays, the edge of soundings is very clear,
and you may enter without any other pecaution than the lead. From the Orange
Cays the edge trends about south, and is clear, with various depths, as shown by the
charts, to the parallel of 24° 31’; from thence to 24° 10’ there are numerous white and
black spots of shoal water; and a ridge of 12 to 24 feet continues along the edge of
the bank to latitude 23° 52’.

For the shoal spots and depths of water on the Great Bahama Bank, we refer our
readers to our Chart of the Gulf and Bahama Islands. We shall, therefore, only
remark, that many persons have mistaken the Orange Cays for the Riding Rocks, on
the north of which there is no passage for vessels, but to the northward of the Orange
Cays there is. It is not, however, recommended to strangers, because there are some
dangerous shoal spots; indeed, the western edge of the bank, hereabouts, seems con-
nected by one chain of cays and rocks.

From the latitude of 24° 10’ the edge of the bank seems to trend about S. by E.
i E., to latitude 23° 40’, then S.E. by 5., 50 miles, to the S.W. corner: it then turns
to E.8.E., 24 miles to Cayo de Guinchos, or Ginger Cay, under which there is
anchorage on its S.W. side. From Ginger Cay to Wolf Cay is 34 miles S.E. ? H.
The edge of the bank continues 21 miles farther, in the same direction, to Diamond
Point, forming the north side of the narrowest part of the Old Bahama Channel.

From Diamond Point to St. Domingo Cay, is 87 miles, E. by S.; the bank between
forming a bay with various windings: and from St. Domingo Cay to Cay Verde, the
bearing and distance are N.E. by E., 36 miles; the latter cay is near the S.H. ex-
tremity of the Great Bank.

Hurricane Fuars.—These are flats extending from the southern part of Andros
Island to the westward, two-thirds across the Great Bank, having from 1 to 23
fathoms on them, shoaling gradually from the westward towards Andros; but, from

‘oleae

ELEUTHERA—CAT ISLAND. 175

the south end of the island, in a southerly direction for nearly 40 miles, or to latitude
23° north, it is all foul ground, full of rocky and dry sand ridges. Near to the
southern edges of this foul ground lie three patches of rocks, called the Lark’s Nest,
Copper Rocks, and Wolf Rocks ; they lie between the latitude 23° 5’ and 23° 10’, and
longitude 77° 27’, and 77° 35’. When crossing the south end of the bank, you should
not go to the northward of latitude 23°, when between the meridians of 77° and 77° 45’.

The hurricanes which so frequently visit the windward islands, and are the scourge
of the West Indies, sometimes extend across the Great Bahama Banks and the Florida
Stream.

ELEUTHERA is one of the largest islands, and is of very irregular shape. Its
west end bears N.E. 3 N., distant about 42 miles from the east end of New Provi-
dence; it thence extends south-eastward, about 42 miles to Palmetto Point; and,
lastly, about S. 4 E., 33 miles to its south end, denominated Powel’s Point, being of
irregular breadth from 2 to 4 miles. The east and N.E. shores are washed by the
Atlantic Ocean; while on the west is the shallow and smooth water of the bank, On
the west side are the settlements of Rock Sound.

CAT ISLAND.—The N.W. end of this island lies about 19 miles E.N.E. $ E.
from Powel’s Point, in Eleuthera; it thence extends south-eastward 42 miles, having
a breadth of 3 to 7 miles. Its eastern side is lined by a reef, on which the sea con-
tinually breaks, and renders it inaccessible: on the §.W. side is good anchorage.
Between its N.W. end and Powel’s Point, at the distance of 13 miles, 8.E. from the
latter, is the N.W. end of Little Cat Island, joined to Cat Island by a bank which
surrounds both of them.

Between the south end of Eleuthera and Little Cat Island is a channel 6 miles
wide, with from 9 to 13 fathoms in it.

ConcEPTION IsLAND.—Eighteen miles south-eastward from Cat Island is Concep-
tion Island, about 8 miles in length, north and south, and 23 miles in breadth; a
reef runs off it about 7 miles north-eastward, as far as the latitude of 23° 55’ 30’,
called Southampton Reef. It is very dangerous on the N.W. side, not having bottom
at 40 fathoms, within a cable’s length to the westward of it. Here the sea breaks,
which renders it less dangerous to approach than the north and east sides, which is
composed of sunken rocks, of a dark colour, and appear very much like the deep
ocean water. The Booby Cays lie about a mile to the eastward of the island; the
largest is 100 feet high, and higher than any part of the island. Off the south point
is a cluster of rocks, nearly 13 mile from the island; here the reef is nearly dry and
steep-to. From the §.W. end of this island the west end of Rum Cay bears 8.E.,
distant 12 miles.

LONG ISLAND, so called from being peculiarly narrow in proportion to its
length, is nearly 57 miles in length from 8.E. to N.W. The north-west end lies 27
miles south from Cat Island, and its south-east end bears from the Bird Rock, at the
west end of Crooked Island, W.;8., 27 miles. There is an anchorage on its east
side, called Great Harbour, from whence salt is exported.

S. by W. 4 W., 52 miles from the south point of Long Island, is Cayo Verde, or
Green Cay. It lies about 5.E. and N.W., and has an islet about a cable’s length
from its S.E. part; it is of moderate height, and is in latitude 22° 1’, and longitude
75° 10’.

From Cayo Verde the edge of the bank forms a great and deep bay to the N.W.;
in the S.W. part of which is Great Ragged Island, at the distance of 30 miles from
the former. To the northward of the latter is a chain of cays, called Los Jumentos,
which rise within the bank, and are followed by another chain of a similar descrip-
tion, which terminate near Long Island.

EXUMA, &c.—The islands called Great and Little Exuma, lie to the westward of

Long Island, and to the southward of Cat Island. Their chief produce is salt, and
the Great Isle has a port of entry.

176 DOUGLAS PASSAGE.

North-westward of Exuma, to the distance of 66 miles, on the eastern edge of the
Great Bank, are a number of little islands, distinguished by the name of Exuma
Cays; to these succeed several others in a more northerly direction, to a distance of
21 miles, the northernmost of which, called Ship Channel Cay, lies E.8.E., 27 miles,
from the east end of New Providence.

Between the bank which surrounds the Cat Islands and the east edge of the Great
Bahama Bank is a channel 21 miles wide, called Exuma Sound, on the western side
of which is a cay, called Leeward Stocking Island. Tarpum Bay is on the west side
of Eleuthera Island; here is anchorage in 4 to 6 fathoms and no tide; to the south-
ward of this is Rock Sound, with 12 feet water in it.

HARBOUR ISLAND lies near the N.E. part of Eleuthera Island, and is about 4
miles long and one in breadth. A reef extends nearly 5 miles to the northward of
it, to which a berth must be given, on account of several rocks lying near the outer
edge, very little under the surface of the water. However, as the water is perfectly
clear, they may be seen from the fore-yard or bowsprit end in time to be easily
avoided. ‘Two remarkable rocks, called the Cow and Bull, are to be seen to the
southward of Harbour Island, appearing like two large trees; a little to the west-
ward of which is a gap, or separation of the land, very conspicuous. §.W. by W. 2 W.,
9 miles from the north point of Eleuthera, lies Egg Island, having between them
Russel Island and Royal Island, with several reefs lying off to the distance of 2 or 3
miles, amongst which is the Lorton Rock, to which a good berth must be given.

EGG ISLAND is asmall island covered with brushwood, with a rise of land in
the middle of it, in latitude 25° 31’: a reef runs off it N.N.W. i W., above
3 miles. From Egg Island to Booby Rock is 21 miles 8.S.W., there being several
cays between, near the edge of the bank, which is steep-to. Three miles and a
quarter 8.S.W. 4 W. from Booby Rock is the N.E. end of Rose Island, which
extends thence W.S.W., and W. 3 N., 9 miles; its S.W. end being nearly 3 miles to
the northward of the N.K. side of New Providence. Between Booby Rocks and the
east end of Rose Island, nearly midway, is the west end of Booby Island, which
thence extends N.E. by E. 5 E., 13 mile, forming between it and the Booby Rocks,
on its N.W. side, a good anchorage with N.E. winds for small vessels in 2 to 24
fathoms.

DOUGLAS PASSAGE.—S.W. ;5., 3 of a mile from the west end of Booby
Island, and N.N.E. + E.,a large mile from the east end of Rose Island, lie the
Douglas Rocks, on which are erected 2 beacons, bearing from-each other S.E. 2 E.,
and contrary. The Douglas Rocks are surrounded with a reef, and on the N.E.
extremity of the reef is placed a black buoy, bearing N. by E. 3 E.,-179 fathoms
from the highest or south-easternmost beacon on the rocks; the buoy lies in 9 feet
water, but at a boat’s length from it there are 4 fathoms. Opposite to it is the end
of a reef which extends from Booby Island one-third of a mile, leaving a passage of
160 fathoms in breadth, which has a depth of 44 fathoms at very low tides ; this is
called Douglas Passage, and is that which is used by ships of war to and from the
New or Cochrane’s anchorage. .

To the southward of Douglas Rocks is another of nearly the same breadth, called
the South Passage; it has only 25 fathoms in the shoalest part, and lies between a
dangerous sunken rock, at the distance of a large quarter of a mile, S. by W. 3 W.
from the high beacon and the Douglas Reef. Some islets and a reef extend from the
N.E. end of Rose Island to within a cable’s length of the above-mentioned dangerous
rock, in which space is a depth of 2 fathoms; but the tides run through with great
velocity, and render it very hazardous to attempt. Immediately within these passages
the water deepens to 43 fathoms, and at the distance of half a mile 8.8.E. from the
Douglas Beacons is a depth of 5 and 55 fathoms, where the small class of 74-gun
ships may lie well sheltered, observing not to bring the beacons to the northward of

N. by W. 3 W.

177

THE LITTLE BAHAMA BANK.

This bank and its islands have been very erroneously represented, both in shape
and position, until lately. The following description is from the survey of Mr. A.
De Mayne :—

“ From the remarkable perforated rock at the S.E. point of Abaco, called the Hole
in the Rock, the bank extends 141 miles to the N.W. extremity of the Matanilla
Reef, and is from 30 to 50 miles in breadth. The largest and easternmost island,
called Great Abaco, is 70 miles in length, nearly N.N.W. and 8.S.E., and about
12 miles in breadth; and contiguous to its western end is Little Abaco, stretching
about 24 miles W.N.W. The Great Bahama Island lies on the 8.W. part of the
bank, is 64 miles in length, and 6 or 7 miles in breadth; to the northward and east-
ward of these islands are a number of islets and cays, and they are all, in general,
environed by a reef.

GREAT ABAGO.—The Hole in the Rock is in latitude 25° 51’, and longitude
77° 103’;* and from this point the land on the east side of the island runs nearly
N. § W., 16 miles, and there forms a point from which a reef extends nearly a league,
called the Cross Rocks; the land between these points bends a little to the west, and
is called High Bank Bay. Hight miles N.E. by N. from the above-mentioned point
is another, called Rocky Point, and nearly 7 miles farther, about N.N.E. 3 E., is the
N.E. point of the island, in latitude 26’ 20’, and longitude about 76° 58’. The land
between the Cross Rocks and Rocky Point forms a bay, called Cheerie Sound, and
between the latter and the N.E. point, the little bay called Hurricane Bay ; it is all
bordered by the general reef which lines this part of the shore of Abaco.

About 2 miles to the northward of N.E. Point is an islet, called Little Harbour
Cay, about 2 miles in length; then follow the Falcon Cays, Linyard’s, or Abaco
Cay, and Little Guana Cay; the north end of the latter being in latitude 26° 34’. In
the space between these cays and Great Abaco isa fine sandy bottom, and good
anchorage; but the entrance is narrow and fit only for small vessels.

MAN-or-WaAr Cay ANcHORAGE.—The north point of Man-of-War Cay is in latitude
26° 42’, longitude 77° 1’; here is good anchorage to the westward of the cay, in 23
and 3 fathoms, but in some spots it is rocky. The entrance is between Man-of-War
Rocks and Man-of-War Cay; there is a rocky reef on each side, but these show
themselves at low spring tides, and with N.E. winds commonly break very high.
Elbow Reef is very dangerous, and lies to the southward of the above, between Man-
of-War Cay and Little Guana Cay ; its extreme point is in latitude 26° 37’, longitude
76° 56’. The current sets from the eastward right upon it, and many vessels have
been wrecked here, which might have been saved had they known of Man-of-War
Anchorage. There is also. anchorage for small vessels at Marsh Harbour, situate
at the northern part of Great Abaco Island. High water, full and change, 8h. 10m.
Spring tides rise 4 feet.

Whale Cay and Green Turtle Cay anchorages were surveyed by Mr. De Mayne,
who says the N.W. channel may easily be known by the high sandy cliffs of Great
Guana Cay and the White Cay, both being very conspicuous, as there is no other
land of a similar appearance on this part of the coast. In running for this harbour,
with strong north-easterly gales, the breakers on the reefs will, in great measure,

be a guide, by steering through the rocks which form the channel. Fresh water and
wood may be obtained here.

The S.E. point of Green Turtle Cay is in latitude 26° 49’, longitude 77° 12’. High
water half an hour after 7. Spring tides rise 4 feet.

The extensive chain of cays which borders the northern side of the bank, extends
from Turtle Cays 51 miles in a W.N.W. direction, and then 24 miles W. by N.
The westernmost of these, named Walker’s Cay, is in latitude 27°16’. All these
cays are bordered with a reef, both on the north and south sides, that on the north
extending from 2 to 5 miles off. From Walker’s Cay the bank takes a direction
about W.N.W. 3 W., 39 miles to the N.W. extremity of Matanilla Reef, which,
according to Mr. De Mayne, terminates in latitude 27° 34’, and longitude 79° 8’.
All the reefs on the north side of the cays are steep-to, and very dangerous to those
who are unacquainted with them.

THE MATANILLA, or MATERNILLA SHOAL, lies near the N.W. point of
the bank; it is small, and has only 12 feet on it; but to the southward of it is an
extensive shallow, running to the southward 12 miles, with 9 to 18 feet upon it ;
about 12 miles to the eastward of this shallow the extensive Maternilla Reef com-
mences, and stretches along the north edge of the bank to nearly opposite Walker’s
Cay. Its north side forms a very dangerous coast, steep-to, with sharp coral rocks,
and high breakers ; nevertheless, some passages have been found over it. To the
southward of its western part there is clear ground, with regular soundings of 33 to
5 fathoms on the bank, as will be seen by the chart.

Tue Hote IN THE Rock AND PRovVIDENCE N.W. CHANNEL.

The south end of Abaco, called the S.W. point, lies about a league or more south-
westward from the Hole in the Rock. A bank extends round this point, and con-
tinues 6 miles E.S.E. from the Hole in the Rock, having on it from 10 to 17 fathoms
water; this part is from 23 to 3 miles in breadth, and is steep-to; you may readily
discover when you are on it, as the water suddenly changes from a dark sea-blue to
a vivid green, and is more agitated, like a ground swell, which resumes its original
colour and state, the moment you are off again. To the N.W. of the S.W. point,
vessels may anchor on it, in from 6 to 12 fathoms, on good ground.

Light.—About } of a mile from the Hole in the Wall, a lighthouse has been
erected, in latitude 25° 49’ 17’, and longitude 77° 11’ 11”. Its base is 80 feet above high
water, and the tower is 80 feet high. The light revolves once in every minute, and
may be seen in all directions, except where the high parts of the island intervene,
between the bearings of S.W. to E.8.E., by the east; and being 160 feet above the
level of the sea, it will be visible in clear weather at the distance of 16 miles.

There is good anchorage (during ordinary winds) in 10 and 11 fathoms, with the
lighthouse, bearing E. by N., about 3 a mile from the shore. The time of high
water, at full and change, is at 8h. Om., and the tide rises 3 feet. 3

The coast hereabout is covered with fragments of vessels, &c., and the western side
has a complete barrier of stones. The land is low, and covered with brushwood.
Vessels, even of moderate size, ought not to approach nearer to the land than 2 cables’
length, where they may lie in about 4 fathoms water; farther in, the depth suddenly
decreases to 2 fathoms and less. Off the 8.W. point there are only 2 fathoms, at a
+ of a mile from it; the bottom is level and sandy. ;

From the S.W. point to Rock Point, the bearing and distance are N.W. 2 W., 14
miles; and from the latter to Cay Gorda, is N.W. by W. 2 W., 9 miles; on this cay
fresh water may be had. From Cay Gorda to Burrows Cays the bearing and dis-
tance are N.W. 4 N., 21 miles. Between, along the edge of the bank to the distance
of 18 miles from the former, is a continued chain of cays and reefs, and within these
and a league within the bank, is Mosse Island. ;

GREAT BAHAMA ISLAND.—Irom Burrows Cays, about 12 miles N. by W.
2W., is the south part of the east head of Great Bahama Island; off this head are

a

GREAT BAHAMA ISLAND. 179

a cluster of islets extending 6 miles to the southward. From the East Head to the
S.E. point of the island is 43 miles, W. by S.; the whole of the S.E. coast is
bordered with a reef, and forms a bight which is very dangerous, with strong S.W.
winds. The S.E. point is in latitude 26° 28’; it lies 90 miles W.N.W. a little west-
erly from the S.W. point of Great Abaco. Within the point there is fresh water,
and before it is a spot of anchoring ground, with 10 and 11 fathoms on it. From
this point to the West Head of the island, the bearing and distance are N.W. by W.
2 W., 22 miles. West Head is also called Settlement Point, and has trees upon it
40 feet high. Towards the south coast there is generally a current setting from the
Florida Stream, which, however, varies according to the wind; but at all times it is
necessary to give the west end of Great Bahama a good berth, both on account of
its shoals, and to avoid getting embayed, if the wind should be in the south-west
quarter.

On the western edge of the Little Bahama Bank, are several cays and dangerous
reefs. Off the N.W. point of Great Bahama Island, which is in latitude 26° 43’, and
about longitude 7° 0’ 30’, lie the Indian and Wood Cays; the latter is about 3 miles
N.W. by N. from the point, and nearly a league N.N.E. from it is Sandy Cay, about
2 miles in length, north and south, About 6 miles N. by W. from Sandy Cay, is
Memory Rock, in latitude 26° 57’, longitude 79° 7, very remarkable, standing alone,
about 14 mile within the edge of the bank. It is about 14 feet in height, and
ragged at the top. Between them, and also to the westward of Sandy Cay, are reefs
on the edge of the bank.

From Memory Rock the bank trends to the N.N.W., and at the distance of 4 miles
from the rock is the §.E. end of another reef, which is even with the water’s edge,
and extends thence about 7 miles northward, having several shallow patches of 3 to
6 feet, on which the sea breaks ; northward of this, a shoal of from 9 to 15 feet runs
to the northward full 10 miles, and is about 2 miles broad; it lies close to the edge
of soundings. All the western edge of the Little Bahama Bank, from Settlement
Point, or West Head, to near Matanilla Shoal, is extremely dangerous to approach.
The current from the Florida Stream sets in upon the bank from W.S.W.; and when
near the Matanilla Reef, it sets in towards the centre of the bank.

It appears by recent surveys of Captain Barnett, R.N., that the Matanilla Reefs
have always been considered to lie much farther north than they really are. It is
now ascertained that the N.W. part of the Little Bahama Bank extends no farther
northward than 27° 25’, and is in longitude 79° 8’. About 4 miles within the edge
of the bank, in latitude 27° 22’, and longitude 79° 4’, lies the north-westernmost, or
Matanilla Shoal, of 12 feet; 4 miles farther eastward is another shoal of 12 feet in
the same latitude, having 8 or 6 fathoms between them ; this is called the Middle
Shoal; both these shoals are of small extent. The western end of the Matanilla
Reef commences 7 miles eastward of the Middle Shoal, in longitude 78° 50’, extending
from thence to the eastward 15 miles; the northern edge of the reef is bordered with
rocks, on which the sea always breaks. From the east end of the reef to Walker’s
Cay, which is 55 feet high, the distance is 7 miles, having 3 to 4 fathoms between.

Between the Great and Little Bahama Bank, the channel is from 19 to 27 miles
across. This is called Providence North-West Channel; that between New Provi-
dence and the Berry Islands, is called Providence North-East Channel.

DIRECTIONS FOR SAILING FROM THE CROOKED
ISLANDS, AND FROM EUROPE TO NEW PROVIDENCE.

From the Bird Rock, near the N.W. end of Crooked Island, steer N. by W. for
the S.W. point of Watling’s Island; the distance is 66 miles. In this track you
will pass 9 or 12 miles to the eastward of Rum Cay. Having made Watling’s
Island, you should proceed along by the west side of it, between it and Conception
Island: but you must be very careful not to approach the latter, on account of the
reef which extends N:N.E., about 4 miles from it, and which has been already
described; for on this reef are several dangerous rocky heads, which cannot be
perceived, by the colour of the water, before you are close to them. This is the most
dangerous reef among the Bahama Islands.

On leaving Watling’s Island, particularly if it be late in the evening, you should
make a N. by W., or even a north course good, until you get into 24° 55’, or 25° of
latitude, before you steer to the westward, on account of a very strong indraught
which sets to the westward, through the Ship Channel, between Cat Island and
Eleuthera.

Having arrived in 24° 58’, or 25° latitude, you may edge away more to the west-
ward, round Palmetto Point, and endeavour to make the land to the westward of
Harbour Island, which is very remarkable, particularly the Cow and Bull, heretofore
described. This is the best route, if the wind is from the eastward, and fine weather ;
but if blowing strong from the northward, endeavour to make the Hole in the Wall,
at the S.E. end of Great Abaco.

Vessels from Europe had best run for Eleuthera, in a tract between the parallels of
25° 20’ and 25° 30’, not exceeding the latter, that being nearly the parallel of Har-
bour Island.

Having made the land about Harbour Island, or the Cow and Bull, care must be taken
when rounding the reefs northward of Harbour Island. From Harbour Island to
Egg Island the shore, as before said, is very rocky, and must not be approached
during the night; in the day you can always perceive the dangers. In running
along shore you will pass some remarkable rocks, called the Pierre Rocks; but the
islands are too closely connected to be distinguished. Egg Island may be known by
the hillock on it. Being off this island, keep well out, to avoid the reef, and you
will open a small rocky island situate to the southward of Egg Island, called Little
Egg Island; and when the centre of Egg Island bears §.S8.E. % E., you will be
abreast of the pitch of the reef; and the course to the lighthouse on Hog Island will
be S.W. by 8., 36 miles; and to Douglas Passage, S. by W. 2 W., 27 miles.

Bo

The direct course from abreast of Abaco Lighthouse to Nassau Bar is 8. by W.,
45 miles; to the pitch of Egg Island Reef it is S.E. 4 S., 21 miles.

Eoe Istaxp.—From off the western point of Egg Island a rocky reef runs out
to the north-westward, full 3 miles, upon which the sea breaks high, and many of
the coral reefs are even with the water’s edge. When Great Egg Island bears
8.S.E., and Little Egg Island is well open of the southern point of Great Egg Island,
you will be abreast of the pitch of the reef. There is a small knowl of 8 feet a mile
to the eastward of the pitch of the reef. There is good anchorage for small vessels
on the south side of Royal Island, in a snug little harbour, with 9 feet water; but the
passage in is narrow. Also to the eastward of Egg Island and south of Royal
Island in 23 ana 3 fathoms with N.W. winds. Your channel in is between Great
and Little Egg Islands in 12 feet, and to the southward of Little Egg Island in 23
and 3 fathoms. High water at 7£h.; tide rises 34 feet.

The cays between Egg Island and Nassau Bar form a deep bay, bordered with

ed

DOUGLAS PASSAGE. 181

reefs; it is particularly necessary, in the winter, or during the prevalence of northerly
winds, to avoid getting embayed there, without you are acquainted with Douglas
Passage, the channel to the New or Cochrane’s Anchorage. But, as in summer,
northerly winds are seldom found here, and the trade wind generally blows, the
shore may be kept well on board; because, should the current carry you to leeward
of Nassau Harbour, it would be regained with difficulty.

The town of Nassau is on the north side of the island, and may be readily known
by a large white house upon the top of a hill, seen over Hog Island. This is the
Government-house. Bring it to bear 8.S.W. or 8.S.W. 3 W., and keep it so until
you are within 2 or 3 miles of Hog Island, where a pilot may be obtained.

The entrance to the harbour is at the west end of Hog Island; it has 18 feet of
water, with sandy ground. The bottom is not good for holding ; and there is, in the
middle of the entrance, a bank of 3 or 4 feet water, extending over a considerable
space, but there is a channel on each side of it. The marks for the bank are, Fort
Fincastle in one with Vandue House, bearing S.E. 2 E., and Toney’s Rock on with
the west end of Fort Charlotte Barracks, bearing S. 4 W.; the latter leads on the
eastern edge of the bank. A spar buoy, with a circular basket on its summit, has
been placed on the north end of Toney Rock, in 123 feet at low water ; and vessels
entering without a pilot should, after crossing the bar, pass to the eastward of this
buoy. ‘The beacon on Toney Rock and the obelisk on Nassau Fort, S. by W., leads
in past Hog Island until you get the jail and look-out house in one, S.E. by E.; this
mark leads up the harbour.

In the event of making the Hole in the Rock or Egg Island in the afternoon, with
a strong wind at N.E., you should haul close round Egg Island Reef, and steer
S. by W., 24 miles, for the beacons on Douglas Rocks. Having made the beacons,
bring them in one, bearing S.E. ¢ E., and steer for them, Keep your lead going, for
the soundings are gradual ; and when you have got the depth of 9 fathoms, you may
anchor with the marks in one, on fine sandy bottom, well sheltered from north-
easterly winds by the Booby Rocks.

FLEEMING, or SIX SHILLINGS CHANNEL.—There is also a passage about 9 miles to
the N.E. of Booby Island, running in between the Samphire Reef and the Six Shil-
lings Cays, in which are 6, 5, and 4 fathoms water; this is called the Six Shillings
Channel, and is about one mile broad, running in §.E., and then turning south-
westerly, leading to the southward of the Samphire Cays, and Booby Island and
Rocks. The passage is safe, and only requires a good look-out. The entrance to this
channel may be distinguished by a very conspicuous beacon, standing on the 8.W.
cay, of a triangular shape; it appears like a steeple 7 or 8 miles off, and is about 50
feet high. Observe, when entering, to give the S.W. rocks, off the Six Shillings
Cays, a berth of about half a mile.

DOUGLAS PASSAGE.—It has been before observed, that two beacons on the
Douglas Rocks, and a black buoy at the extremity of the reef, on the west side, point
out the entrance. To sail into this passage, you must bring the two beacons ina
line bearing S.E.2 E., and steer directly towards them, until you bring Booby
Island end on; then haul up for the buoy, and pass about 30 fathoms to the east-
ward of it; you will then perceive every other danger, as you proceed to the south-
ward; and may anchor in 43 fathoms, with the two beacons in one, bearing N.W. ¢ W.,
distant 1 mile, Here is good holding-ground, and good shelter from the N.W. winds.

A frigate, drawing 18 or 20 feet water, may proceed between the Turtle Head and
the Hook of the Horse Shoe Sand, with the lowest Douglas Beacon open ta the west-
ward of the highest, and thence into the New, or Cochrane’s Anchorage, and proceed
along by the 8.E. side of Rose Island, to the distance of 6 miles from the town of
Nassau, and there anchor in 4% fathoms, with the Block House on Potter’s Ca:
(Nassau Harbour), just open to the southward of Montague Fort, bearing nearly W.
by N., well sheltered from N.W. winds by Rose Island, and from the 8.E. by the
Great Bahama Bank.

182 WATLING’S ISLAND.

Persons not acquainted with Douglas Passage and the New Anchorage should not
attempt to pass the Hole in the Rock with a N.N.W. or N.W. wind blowing strong,
for there is no other safe anchorage, except at the Stirrip Cays, Berry Islands.

DIRECTIONS FOR SAILING OVER NASSAU BAR IN STORMY WEATHER,
WHEN A PILOT-BOAT CANNOT GO OUT.

A white flag will, as heretofore, be hoisted upon the flagstaff on the west point of
Hog Island, near the lighthouse, when the bar is passable for a vessel; but if the
pilot-boat cannot come out, she will be in attendance inside, with the pilot’s dis-
tinguishing flag (half white, half red horizontal), flying. The vessel about to enter
must in that case steer in, giving the west point of Hog Island, (upon which the
lighthouse stands) a berth of about eighty fathoms, and keeping Toney Rock, upon
which there is a white beacon, and the beacon upon the hill to the eastward of the
west fort in one, until the white flag upon the lighthouse point bears east, and then
haul up for the pilot-boat, when a pilot will be put on board to conduct the vessel to
her anchorage. A red flag will be hoisted upon the flagstaff near the lighthouse,
when the pilot considers it would be very hazardous, and would by no means recom-
mend a vessel to attempt to cross the bar. Lest, however, any case of extreme
necessity should induce a vessel to make the attempt, the pilot-boat (with the white
and red flag flying) will be in attendance within the bar. Should such necessity not
exist, it would be advisable for the vessel to haul off (should the wind be in the north-
east quarter) to the westward, and keeping about 3 or 4 miles from the land, run for
the west end, and rounding the cay near the point, she will have excellent anchorage
in the south-west bay, by bringing Gaulding Cay (the cay near the west end) to bear
N.W. 3 W., and Wylly Cliff (a remarkable cliff forming the bay) N.W. by N., in
from 4 to 8 fathoms water, about 14 cable within soundings, in clear sandy bottom
and good holding ground,—the only danger to be avoided is a rocky shoal, with only
12 feet water upon it, bearing S. by E. 2 E., distant about 3 miles from Wylly Cliff,
and which can always be seen during daylight.

Should the wind be from the north-west quarter, it would then be advisable for the
vessel to haul off to the northward and eastward, and steering about E.N.E., for 18
or 14 miles, she will then be abreast of the Booby Rocks, or off the entrance to
Douglas Passage.

TIDES AND CURRENTS BETWEEN WATLING’S ISLAND
AND NEW PROVIDENCE.

The tides, or currents, between Watling’s Island and the Hole in the Rock, are
generally found to set to the S.W.; about Egg Island Reef, it sets in various direc-
tions. Off Douglas Rocks, New Providence, the tide runs very regular: and at the
entrance of the New Anchorage, it flows, on full and change days, until half-past
eight. The flood sets to the N.E., and very strong between the rocks. Spring-tides
rise 4 feet. Between Egg Island and Nassau, the stream has been found to run at
the rate of 4 knots ; the flood stream setting east very strongly over the reefs. The
stream sets very strongly over the Egg Island Reef, when the wind is at N.W., and
as the currents are very irregular near that place, great caution is necessary when
passing it.

In the North West Channel of Providence, the current generally sets to the east-
ward at the rate of from % to 1 knot.

DIRECTIONS FOR SAILING FROM CROOKED ISLANDS,
THROUGH EXUMA SOUND, TO NEW PROVIDENCE.

From the Bird Rock steer about N.W. 3 N., 63 miles, to make Rum Cay; from thence
the west end of Long Island will bear W. 4 N., about 11 miles ; a W.N.W. course for
18 miles, will clear it, and S.W. by W., for about 24 miles, will bring you to the cays
before the Salt Pond of Exuma. In sailing from Exuma to New Providence, you
must either sail through Exuma Sound and the channel between Little Cat Island,
and the south end of Hleuthera, and thence along the eastern side of Eleuthera; or
proceed from Exuma along the east side of Leeward Stocking Island on a N.W. 2 N.
course, about 93 miles, through Exuma Sound and Ship Channel, which is about 27
miles to the eastward of New Providence Island. From hence you may pass over the
bank in 13 or 25 fathoms at low water. You must keep a good look out for sunken
rocks, which in some places lie very thick; the water being very clear, they are
easily seen before you come to them, and therefore can be avoided. If you have
occasion to anchor at night, choose a clear sandy berth for that purpose. In Exuma
Sound it is high water at 9h., and the tide runs strong through all the openings
between the cays on the west side.

CLARENCE, on GREAT HARBOUR.—This harbour is situate in latitude 23° 6’,
at about 17 miles from the S.E. end of Long Island, and on its N.E. side. It lies
W.N.W. from the Bird Rock, Crooked Islands, and south from Rum Cay.

Clarence Harbour is found between the shore and some low islets, which extend
off about 13 mile tothe N.W. It is capable of admitting a few vessels of 13 feet
draught, but will require the assistance of a pilot, and being open to the northward,
it is much exposed, and frequently very difficult to get out of.

Wood and water may be obtained in Clarence Harbour, also a small supply of beef
and vegetables.

Directions.—Should a vessel be forced to run into Clarence Harbour without a
pilot, the following may be useful. ‘The south shore of the harbour is skirted at the
back by a ridge of low hills, and on the western fall of the highest part there is the
ruin of a large building, and about a mile to the N.W. of it, at the end of the ridge,
a house, and near it a flagstaff. Run in with the staff in one with Harbour Point
bearing S. by W. until the ruin bears S.S.E., when haul up directly for it, and anchor
in this line in 18 feet water, just within the W. end of Strachan Cay, the northern-
most of the larger islets. A beacon 40 feet high, the base and upper part red, and the
middle part white, is erected on Lark Point, the S.W. extreme of this cay, to point
out the position of the harbour. The channel within is littie more than a cable wide,
and the outer part generally shows itself on either side by the breakers, which extend
out nearly 2 cables’ length from the Booby Rocks off the north end of Strachan Cay.
Being open to the N.N.W. it is by no means a desirable place in the winter months
for large vessels that cannot get under shelter of the cay. The cultivated salt ponds -
are situate close to the shore, and are very productive, and the salt is readily shipped.
High water, full and change at 8h. 30m., springs rise 4 feet, neaps 22 feet.

DIRECTIONS FOR VESSELS BOUND FROM THE EAST-
WARD OVER THE GREAT BAHAMA BANK.
First, make the Hole in the Rock at the S§.E. end of Great Abaco, and from

abreast of it, steer W.7S%., or about 39 miles, for Stirrip Cay, the northernmost of
the Berry Islands, rounding this cay on its west side. In crossing these banks, it is

184

not presumed the same depth of water can always be carried, even in the same track,
as a strong easterly wind will drive the water off the bank, as well as strong northerly
winds increase its quantity. In all parts of the channel the bottom is of a sticky
quality, but to windward the bottom is hard, and spots thicken as you shoal your
water. Almost every regular trader has a different course to run across the bank;
but the principal object is to clear the Sheep Cays, and other extensive shoals stretch-
ing off the N.W. point of Andros Island. It is necessary to have a leadsman con-
stantly in the chains, and a good look out, to avoid the shoal patches, with every
attention being paid to the steering, log, &c.

Mackie Bank.—Buoys.—A black buoy and black basket ball, in 2 fathoms, low
water, on the N.E. part of the Mackie Bank, in latitude 25° 39’ 57’, longitude
78° 40' 31”. Also a chequered buoy (black and white) staff, and two basket balls,
on the 8.E. edge of the Mackie Bank, in 2 fathoms, in latitude 35° 28’, longitude
78° 45’ 25”. These buoys bear from each other N. 17° E. and S. 17° W., 122 miles.
They are intended to guard vessels from falling too far to the westward, when
crossing the Bahama Bank from Stirrup to Orange Cays, as also to correct their
positions for the latter part of the run; they are good sound buoys, and can be seen
5 or 6 miles off.

THE GREAT BAHAMA BANK.

You ought not to see any land after you leave the Berry Islands, until you make
the Orange Cays: these cays are two in number, besides four small rocks, called
Roquillas, without bush or shrub on them. From Orange Cay to the westernmost of
the Double-headed Shot Cays, on Salt Cay Bank, the bearing and distance are S.W.,
93 miles.

DIRECTIONS FOR CROSSING THE GREAT BAHAMA BANK.
From the American Coast Pilot.

In taking your departure from the Hole in the Wall for the Great Bahama Bank,
steer west, 36 miles, and if the land be not in sight, haul W.S.W., or S.W. by W.,
and make the Berry Islands ; keep down past, these islands, and keep a good look out
for the Western Cay, called Stirrip Cay, which lies in latitude 25° 49’ 40’, and longi-
tude 77° 53’ 55’. The moment you get on soundings, in approaching the Berry
Islands, the water changes colour.

The best courses for crossing the bank, are the following, viz. :—When Stirrip Cay
bears south, 8 miles distant (at which time it can be just seen from the deck) steer
W.S.W., 18 miles; then haul to S.W. by S., 80 miles; thence S.S.W., or between
that and S.W. by S., to latitude 24° 55’, when you may keep away west and make
the Orange Cays, or continue on your course to 24° 45’, when you may keep down
west and leave the bank without danger. In case you should prefer hauling-to sooner
than directed, in crossing the bank, and find your water shoaling, you may, by keep-
ing off west, 9 miles or more, find the deep water of the channel, which is 15 miles in
breadth; bear up as soon as you get but 24 fathoms; as it shoals suddenly and
irregularly from that depth.

You may even run 21 miles on your W.S.W. course, after leaving Stirrip Cay,
without danger; be careful to allow for the tide. On the north side the flood sets
S8.S.E. and ebb N.W., and as you draw on the bank the force of the tide decreases ;
for when you have got 12 or 15 miles on the bank, the tide has but a slight set; or when
Stirrip Cay bears south, 5 miles distance, you may steer S.W. by W., 44 miles, and
then 8.8.W. till off the bank. The water in the regular channel is milky-white; to
the eastward you have it clear, with black spots on the bottom, and to the westward,
clear with hard white bottom.

By crossing the bank as before directed, you will see few or no spots of sponge,
and the bottom is with difficulty discerned, and may be sure of 3 fathoms all the way.

NASSAU——HAVANA. 185

Be careful of the Orange Cays in the night-time, as they are very low, and cannot
be seen until close on board of them, and the soundings are deepened regularly, until
very near them on the east side.

S.W. from Orange Cays, 24 or 3 miles distance, is good anchorage, in 20 fathoms
‘water. When up with these cays, a passage is secured through the gulf, for then you
may make sail either in the morning or at midnight. Steering S.W., 30, or 33 miles,
will enable you to fall in with Salt Cay Bank, which for 30 miles on the north side
stretches E.N.E. and W.S.W. Here the current sets stronger as you come to the
westward. In coming over, you have soundings all along by it. There is anchorage
by spots all the way in; but the soundings are narrow at the Double-headed Shot,
the N.W. point of which lies in latitude 23° 56’ 30’. This route, however, demands
the most zealous care, in order to avoid any shoal that may exist, although unknown.

In starlight nights the Bahama Bank reflects a bright light into the air, which
may be seen at 4 or 5 leagues. You may observe this reflection all over both the
Bahama Banks, but not on the Salt Cay Bank; neither can you see it while on the
bank; but when in the gulf, you can plainly distinguish the Providence Channel,
having none of this reflection between the two reflections of the Great and Little
Bahama Banks.

DIRECTIONS FOR SAILING FROM THE EASTWARD,
THROUGH THE CHANNEL OF PROVIDENCE,

TO NASSAU, AND ALSO TOWARDS HAVANA;
From the Derrotero, §c.

Those from the eastward, who are bound to Providence, should enter by the N.E,
Channel. Proceed for the middle of the entrance, in latitude 25° 42’, until you see
either Harbour Island or the Hole in the Rock; for with the wind at 8.E. the
southern horizon is clear; and with the wind from east to N.E., the northern is the
same. ‘This method of entering is most convenient in the summer season, or from
May to October, but in the other months it may be varied, keeping a little to the
north of the point of the Hole in the Rock, in order to be more to windward, to
take the anchorage to the N.W. if necessary. When the land is seen and known,
and you are bound to Nassau, close in to a proper distance with Egg Island, from
which shape your course for that place, taking care to stand in shore by day, with
precaution.

Those who are bound to Havana, or the Gulf of Mexico, without passing through
the Bahama Old Channel, ought to use this channel; but in this case they should
close in, and make the land about the Hole in the Rock; on the soundings of
which they may anchor, to wait the proper time of departure, according to the sailing
of the vessel, state of the wind, &c.; in order to make the Berry Islands early in the
morning. But if the making this traverse by night is unavoidable, the most certain
way will be, not to cross the meridian of the Berry Island, but to keep lying-to to the
N.E. of them, sounding frequently, and having the anchors ready to let go the
moment the lead gets 20 or 25 fathoms. When the Berrys are recognised, coast
them at a convenient distance, until you have passed the Stirrip Cays, which are the
most westerly of them ; from which, to the west, you may enter upon the Great Bank,
and navigate it, steering 8.W. 3 8., and 8.8.W. 3 W., so as to go over its western
edge, to the southward of the Roquillas ; from which, direct your course across the
Santaren Channel, for the south-eastern part of the Anguila Cay, on the Salt Cay
Bank; and thence to catch the coast of (the Havana) Cuba, in the manner before
directed for navigating the Bahama Old Channel.

186 NASSAU-——-HAVANA.

The navigation over the Great Bank is only to be done by vessels drawing not
more than 11 feet water. On the bank the bottom is stony, with banks of sand,
haying little water over them, which extend westward from the western part of St.
Andros, 16 miles. At clearing the bank, in latitude 24° 38’, you will perceive some
weeds and rocks at the bottom, but there are 10 fathoms water; this navigation
requires the greatest care, to avoid any shallows that may have escaped observation.

As large vessels cannot cross the Great Bank from the Berry Islands to the Roquillas,
as above described, it is necessary that they should run along the edge of it from the
Berry Islands, until they reach Isaac Cays ; when, having doubled these, sail south-
ward to the Roquillas. ‘To navigate from the Berry Islands until you double the
Great Isaac, it is advisable to keep on the edge of the green water, taking care to
keep in 12 to 16 fathoms; in which depth you ought to pass north of the Great Isaac,
at 5 miles distant, and then to steer S. by W. 3 W.; and 8. 3 E., using the utmost
care not to go from the edge of soundings, because, from the instant you go from
it, and enter into the green water, you will be in the general current, or Gulf
Stream, which runs with great strength northward; for which reason, if the wind
does not permit steering along the edge of the bank, you ought to anchor on it, and
wait till the wind be favourable. Those who have not had practice in this place,
should not leave the bank at the Great Isaac by night, but should anchor on it to the
N.E. of the centre of the island, in from 7 to 10 fathoms, on sand, to wait for
daylight.

Buoys —MosEtLE Suoats.—North end, a black buoy, with staff and black
basket ball, in latitude 25° 49’ 45", and longitude 79° 17’ 15”. The following marks
indicate its position. ‘The north rock of Bemini in line with the left extreme N.E.
point of the North Bemini, with an angle of 33° to its right extreme.

To sail along the edge of these banks, you have only to attend to the lead; with
which guide, and the notice we have given in the description, you will have sufficient
information to enable you to avoid all danger. From the Roquillas you may enter

into the water of the gulf, without any fear of the current; and may take the route

by the Santaren Channel, as we have before said for vessels of light draught. On
the edge of soundings, although they do not feel the general current, yet there is a
little, produced by the tides, which might drive a vessel from the margin, or upon the
rocks; but this does not frequently happen; for if the lead, which ought to be kept
going, be attended to, it will warn you, whether to keep a little to port or starboard,
in order to preserve a suitable depth.

The navigation which we have just described, will not generally be practised by
vessels from Europe, bound to Havana, or the Gulf of Mexico; for it offers no
advantage over the other, by the Bahama Old Channel, or by the south of Cuba; but
it may be very good for vessels sailing from the United States, or for those who have
been involuntarily carried out of the (Bahama Channel) Strait of Florida, by calms,
or other accidents, and which seek to avoid the long circuit that would be made, in
working up so far east as would be necessary to reach Cape Maize, in order to return
to Havana, by the Old Channel; this is more direct and natural.

For the better understanding this navigation of which we have been treating,
observe, that when you anchor on any part of the edge of the bank, in order to pass
the night, or to wait for a favourable time, you should have everything ready to
make sail the moment it may be necessary; and, also, if the sky looks threatening,
to have the topsails reefed. From either of these anchorages you may make sail with
any wind; and, generally speaking, every one who in these parts requires to anchor,
may find a proper place to do so, sheltered from adverse winds.

From the Orange Cays you may leave the bank and enter the gulf, without dread
of the current, steering towards the north part of the bank of the Roques, or Double-
headed Shot Cays; and having doubled the west corner, may shape a course for the
coast of Cuba, navigating along its edges. ‘To do this, it is necessary to steer
S. by W. 3 W., and to have the breeze sufficiently strang in your favour as to run by
the log more than 4 miles an hour, without which yeu may possibly be carried out
of the strait, and for which reason, on all occasions, we recommend, in preference, the
route by the Santaren Channel.
