BRITISH GUAYANA.

DESCRIPTION.—We have already stated that British Guayana properly extends
from the River Corentyn to the Essequibo and Mazaroni, although it appears some
late settlements have been formed to the northward of the banks of the Pomeroon;
whence some writers have considered that river to constitutelits present boundary,
while others place its northern frontier at Cape Barima; but the limits have never yet
been completely settled.

Within the territory now belonging to the British, are the rivers Berbice, Demerara,
and Essequibo, ‘These colonies were ceded to Great Britain, by the Sovereign of the
Netherlands, in 1814, on condition that the Dutch proprietors of lands, or effects,
should be at liberty, under certain regulations, to carry on trade between the said
settlements and the territories in Europe of the said Sovereign Prince.

The RIVER BERBICE.—This river has its source in the mountains, about 100
miles inland, and flows in a serpentine direction to the north-eastward, until it reaches
the Atlantic Ocean, in latitude 6°20’ north. Its entrance, a little to the northward of
Fort St. Andrew, is a league wide; the land on both sides is low, and covered with
trees. Directly in the middle of the channel lies a smail island, commonly called
Crab Island, having a spit of sand running out both to the northward and southward.
This island divides the course of the river into two passages, both of which are
navigable; but, about 8 miles to the northward of this island, there is a bar of sand,
over which are only 7 feet at low water; this very materially lessens the importance
of the harbour, and confines its utility to vessels of small draught of water only ; on
which account few vessels rendezvous here, but make the Port of Demerara their
anchorage, whence the supplies from the mother-country are transported, and the
produce of the colony drafted; for the River Berbice, though broad, is in some places
very shallow. The channel on the east side of Crab Island has from 17 to 20 feet, while
that to the westward is less deep, having from 8 to 13 feet only. :

Small vessels can go up the river so far as Fort Nassau, which is at the distance of
45 miles from the entrance; the banks of the river are generally low, and covered
with mangroves; the plantations are numerous, extending full 40 leagues up, and
produce sugar, cotton, coffee, cocoa, and tobacco. The territory of Berbice, under
the British Government, extends from the River Corentyn to Abary Creek, having a
sea coast of nearly 60 miles; this has been surveyed, and laid out in different
allotments, which are now cultivated by the additional settlers. Carriage roads have
been made, which run to the west bank of the Corentyn, and are extended to the
Demerara.

Thus, by British capital and industry, has a tract of ground, 150 miles in lengths
which heretofore was useless and unproductive—presen ting the aspect of an impene-
trable forest, on the shores of which was a border of low ground, covered, between
high and low water marks, with mangroves, having’ several feet of water over it when
the tide flowed, and when it ebbed, forming an extensive mud-bank—now become dry -
and productive.

New Amsterdam stands at the confluence of the two rivers, Berbice and Canje, about
2 miles above Crab Island, on the eastern bank of the river; it is intersected by canals,
which have all the advantages of the tides. There are two batteries to protect the
entrance of the river; one of these is on the eastern side, and the other, York
redoubt, on the western side, opposite to Crab Island. The other town of this colony
is Fort Nassau, which, in a straight line, is above 37 miles up the River Berbice; but,
by the windings of the river, its distance becomes considerably more. The Berbice
and Canje are the only two rivers that water the district; the former is considered
navigable for vessels drawing 14 feet water, about 200 miles up, but the Canje only
30 miles, being there stopped by tremendous cataracts. : rae

BRITISH GUAYANA. 7

The RIVER DEMERARA lies to the westward of the bar of Berbice, distant
19 leagues, and to the south-eastward of the Essequibo, being about 16 miles to the
eastward of the Leguan Island. This river, at its entrance, is not quite 2 miles
broad, and becomes narrower as you advance within it. Georgetown is situated on
its eastern bank, about} a mile from the fortress, and between which the lighthouse
is situated ; the river is navigable for ships of burthen for 100 miles up, and so far as
the cataracts; affording an excellent harbour, capable of holding the whole navy of
Great Britain ; but, unfortunately, the bar will not allow vessels that draw more than
18 feet to go over it at high water.

Under the Dutch government, this district comprehended an extent of sea coast of
nearly 80 miles, running west and N.W., and east and §.E., from the banks of the
Essequibo to the River Berbice. For 20 miles inland, along the banks of the
Demerara, the country consists of extensive meadows, level, and without any
inequalities to diversify the surface; several sand hills then appear; and as you get
further up the river, the Jand becomes more broken and mountainous. Plantations
of sugar, coffee, plantains, with others of cocoa and rice, appear regularly arranged.
Houses close to the water’s edge, and scattered about in different directions, together
with wind, water, and cattle mills, form a pleasing variety, and indicate considerable
traffic. Rice also appears well calculated to thrive in this soil, into which it has
been lately introducd. Large herds of cattle are reared on the savannahs in the
interior. The crops of sugar are most abundant, and their rum is in general request
in the American markets, on account of its superior flavour. :

The RIVER ESSEQUIBO is to the north-westward of the River Demerara, as
will be best seen by inspecting the charts; its entrance from one side of the mainland
to the other is full 1 miles wide; but there are so many islands and shoals which
obstruct the current, and divide it into separate channels, that to enter by any one of
them becomes a task of difficulty and danger; for these islands are generally low and
bushy, with sandy spits extending from their northern parts a considerable way into
the sea. The easternmost of these is called the Leguan Island, between which and the
eastern side of the river is the Ship Channel; this passage is wide, but much encum-
bered with shoals. To the westward is a long and narrow island, called Wakenham,
its length being about 3 leagues, and its breadth 3 miles. To the north-westward of
Wakenham is Tiger Island, which is small, and lies near the western shore.

Other islands lie further up the river, on one of which a fort is erected. There are
channels between all these; and vessels can anchor in front of the fort in a good
depth of water. From the Fort Island the course of the river runs nearly south for
about 10 leagues, where it is joined by the River Cuyuni, and further on by the
Mazarony, the former river running to the south-westward, and afterwards north-
westward, through the province of Colombian Guayana, where it is supposed to
join some of the interior branches of the Orinoco.

The settlements of Essequibo, when in the hands of the Dutch, were principally
confined to the plantations established along the banks of the river, where coffee,
cotton, cocoa, and sugar were cultivated ; it was then considered to be swampy and
unproductive, and therefore made only on the higher grounds, 100 miles up the river;
but the present planters have found the lower grounds to be equally fertile, and now
cultivate them with considerable success. The rise of the tides is felt more than
30 leagues up the river, and so far as the lower cataracts; but there is no town
or city on its banks.

N.W. by W., distant 51 leagues from the Essequibo, is the Great Mouth, or
entrance to the Orinoco; which, from what has already been stated, may be properly
considered to be—

‘8

COLOMBIAN GUAYANA.

From the Essequibo to the River Orinoco the whole of the intermediaté coast is
low, covered with trees, and intersected with the rivers Pomeroon, Maruceo, and
Wayena; the most considerable of these is the Pomeroon, situated about 15 or 16
leagues to the north-westward of the Essequibo; here the channel in is a mile wide,
running between low bushy lands. Its eastern point is called, in the charts, Cape
Nassau. ‘There are now several settlements of the British on the banks of this river,
and about 15 leagues up it is the town or village of Middleburg, now in ruins. Cocoa
Point is to the westward of Pomeroon, forming a kind of bay to the southward, and
having, a little to the westward of it, some tall cocoa-nut trees, which are the only
ones on the coast, and therefore constitute an object rather remarkable; all others
are only mangroves. The whole shore is lined with a bank of sand, which flattens a
considerable way out, so that vessels should not approach nearer than to have a depth
of 5 or 6 fathoms water. :

The RIVER ORINOCO.—This noble and magnificent river forms the most
remarkable feature on this part of the coast of Colombia, pouring its vast volume of
waters through numerous channels, which extend from Cape Barima to the Gulf of
Paria; the land therefore is low, broken, and composed of a multitude of swampy
islands; these are mostly overflowed in the rainy season, and then present to the
spectator a boundless expense of water; the Delta of the Orinoco commencing nearly
100 miles inland. It is generally asserted, there are ‘not less,than fifty outlets or
channels, which communicate with the great branch of the river; of these, seven are
said to be navigable by small vessels, and but only one by ships of large dimensions,

The navigation of these lesser channels is attended with great danger, and requires
considerable skill, as well as knowledge of their course; it is not an uncommon
occurrence for the native tribes to lose themselves among the various currents, being
compelled to return again to the sea.

The Great Mouth, or Ship Channel of the Orinoco, is situated between Cape
Sabaneta and Barima on one side, and several of the low islands to the northward,
the outermost of which is commonly called Congrejos, or Crab Island. The entrance
is nearly 12 miles wide; but there is a shoal of hurd sand, resembling ground coffee,
which runs out from Crab Island to the east and north-eastward, full 6 miles; and a
spit also extends from Sabaneta to the northward, which narrows the channel, and
renders it somewhat dangerous. Also between these sands is a bar or flat, stretching
right across the mouth of the river, over which at lew water there is only a depth of
15 feet. The course of this great branch of the Orinoco runs to the westward, full
60 miles, on to Angostura, the capital of the province.

ANGOSTURA is situated at the foot of a hill. The banks of the Orinoco are
richly clothed with verdure, and stately trees, which for beauty and grandeur surpass
description ; and its situation possesses superior advantages to all others in its vicinity,
as it affords a more ready and prompt communication with Europe. The voyage from
Cadiz to Point Barima has been frequently performed in 18 and 20 days; and the
return again to Europe in from 30 to 35 days ; for being to windward of the Caribbean
Islands, vessels from Angostura can maintain ‘a more expeditious commerce with those
islands than either La Guayra or Porto Cabello.

The flux and reflux of the tides are felt, in the month of April, when the tide is
lowest, beyond Angostura, and so far as 85 leagues inland. At the confluence of the
Caroni, which is about 40 leagues from the coast, the waters rise only a foot and 3
inches; but this suspension of the river’s course must not be confounded with the tide
as it flows up.

It was formerly supposed that the prodigious body of water which constantly issues
from this gigantic river, commonly caused a change in the colour and current of the
sea, to the distance of two and even three degrees off, giving a freshness to the waters

COLOMBIAN GUAYANA. )

of the Gulf of Paria; but this is now known to be erroneous, for the common course
of the current along the whole coast is to the northward, and the transparency and
reflected colour of the sea vety seldom extends beyond 3 or 4 leagues E.N.E, from
Crab Island; while the waters in the Gulf of Paria are always salt, although in a
somewhat less proportion than those of the open sea; this perhaps may be attributed
to the mass of water descending from the River Guarapiche, and from the various
small streams to the northward of the great branch of the Orinoco.

The navigation of the river, whether entered by the lesser channels, or by the
Great Ship Passage, will require various precautions, according as the bed may be fall,
or the waters very low. Immediately after the vernal equinox, or about the 25th of
March, the commencement of its rising becomes perceptible ; at first it advances only
an inch in 24 hours; sometimes in April, it will sink again, but it arrives at its
greatest height in July; it remains full and level from the end of July to the 25th of
August, and then decreases, but more slowly than it increased; its least depth is
during January and February.

At Angostura, the mean rise of the water was found to be about 24 or 25 feet.
Captain Ambrose states that the common rise of the bar at the Orinoco is about
12 feet; but in the rainy season upwards of 40 feet; at such times to sail up this
river becomes impracticable. The prodigious length of the Orinoco is estimated at
1380 miles; at 200 leagues distance from the sea, it is from 2500 to 3000 fathoms
broad, without the interruption of a single island. Abreast of Angostura, its breadth
is 3850 fathoms, and its depth there at low water was found to be 65 feet. It
abounds with fish of various descriptions ; amphibious animals are found on its shores
in great numbers; among these are the lapa, or rivcr-dog; the manati, or sea-cow;
and the chiquiri, or river-sheep; caymans and alligators are numerous and formidable;
while the adjacent forests are inhabited by monkeys, and birds of the most brilliant
and beautiful descriptions. Both sides of the river are well covered with trees. The
northern banks of the river are in the province of Cumana, now called the district of
Orinoco,

Having described the great branch of the Orinoco, we proceed to notice the lesser
channels to the north-westward, which are said to be navigable for small vessels.
‘The first of these is about 8 leagues to the north-westward of Crab Island, and called
the Mariusas Channel; but between the great entrance and this channel there are
several smaller passages, named by the Spaniards Bocas de los Canos. The second is
the Boca de Vega, or River Chaguanes, and is situated to the north-westward of the
Mariusas. The third is the Macurio River, or Branch, and runs in about 15 leagues
from the Mariusas; this is said to be navigable for small craft. Nearly 6 leagues
further’is the fourth, or channel of Capure, or Capura, fit for boats only. Beyond
this is the Canal de Pedernales, about 12 miles to the southward of the Soldier’s
Island, and 6 leagues to the westward of the Capure; this also is only navigable
by boats. There is yet another branch to the westward, called the Grand Manamo,
and situated within the Gulf of Paria, and to the westward of the Soldada, or
Soldier’s Island.

The various islands composing the Delta of the Orinoco, are inhabited by two
independent Indian tribes, cailed the Guaraunus, and the Mariusas; the former oc-
cupying the northernmost islands, and during the rainy season erecting their dwellings
upon the palm trees with which the ground is covered.

The annual rising of the waters of the Orinoco commences in April, and ends in
. August ; all September it remains nearly stationary, with all the vast bedy of water
it has acquired during the five preceding months; but in the early part of October
it begins to fall, and continues almost imperceptibly to leave the plains till the latter
end of February, at which time it is at its lowest ebb, and continucs so until the
beginning of April. The common rise of the tides,as already noticed, is about 12 feet;
but in the rainy seasons, it will often rise 40 feet and upwards.

fhe GULF of PARIA, or TRINIDAD, is bounded on the westward by
the land of Cumana and Paria, and to the eastward by the Island of Trinidad. Its
breadth from east to west is 26 leagues, and from north to south i3 leagues; in it is

[GUAYANA. ] : C

10 ON MAKING THE COAST

good anchorage for vessels of all descriptions, with few dangers, and in whatever depth
of water is best suitable. There are two entrances into it; that from the south-
ward is between the broken islands of the Orinoco and the southern shores of the
island of Trinidad; that to the northward is from the Atlantic Ocean, between the
said island and the promontory or isthmus of Paria: here several islands are situ-
ated, having channels between each; these will be described hereafter. “ Nothing,”
says the Derrotero de las Antillas, “ would be more easy than to enter the Gulf of
Paria, either from the north or south, and to navigate it, were it not for the currents
* which are experienced in it; these emanate not only from the general current, which
runs to the north-westward, along all the coast of Guayana, but also from another,
produced by the tides, which offer some obstacles that should be provided against,
by a knowledge of the effects which the currents cause in the different parts of the
gulf.”

The coast of Colombia, within the gulf, is low, swampy, and divided by a number
of rivers, which discharge their waters into it. Of these, the largest and most fre-
quented is the Guarapiche, which is fit for large schooners, and by this the chief
commerce of this part of Cumana is carried on. All the eastern coast of the gulf is
low land also,—the mountain of Naparima, on the island of Trinidad, excepted; and
this appears high and round, visible on clear days at the distance of 10 leagues, and
serves as a good mark to know this part of the gulf by ; but this will be more parti-
cularly described hereafter.

DIRECTIONS FOR THE COAST OF GUAYANA.

General Observations on making and naviyating the Coast of Guayana.

Extract from a letter of Captain Andrew Davidson, of the brig Lady Sale, dated
Paramaribo, Nov. 3rd, 1856.—* My passage out here was 14 days longer than it
really should have been. All strangers bound to Surinam should be warned of it;
there is no mention made in any of the charts or direction books of what I am
going to state. In latitude 7° 0’ N. longitude 45° 0’ a strong current begins to set
east, at the rate of 3 to 4 miles an hour. For 14 days I had mostly fresh breezes
from E. to E. by S. and E. by N. with all possible sail set, and steering W. by S._ I
had Massey’s patent log towing constantly, showing some days 110 miles in 24 hours,
I at first supposed the watches were wrong; I could not suppose that a current of
such velocity could have existed in that quarter. At last I got an observation which
convinced me it was a current that was retarding our progress. I then steered to
the §.W., and in 24 hours was out of it, and found another setting W.N.W., which
speedily took us in with the land. This should be reported, as it is easy so get out
of it, which must be done by steering S.W. or N.W. according to circumstances.
The breadth of this gulf-stream is about 120 miles. It is no doubt caused by
the Amazon River. It runs strongest in latitude 6° north.’— Shipping Gazette,
7th January, 1857.

It is aremarkable feature throughout. the coast of Guayana, that the whole face
of the country, from the Maranon to the Orinoco, is low and mostly bordered with a
sandy flat, which extends far out to seaward, and renders the approach shallow ; for
the various large rivers with which it is intersected continually bring down and
deposit vast quantities of alluvial matter, which constantly is accumulating on the
shores, and forms a margin of low ground: this, between high and low water mark,
is generally covered with mangroves, which, when the tide is out appear like an
inaccessible barrier ; but as the water rises, these become inundated and hid. Abou

SEASONS, WINDS, ETC. 11

500 paces within these mangroves commences low, level, and swampy savannahs,
extending irregularly, according to the elevation or declivities of the adjacent inland
mountains. The water on all the coast is bad, and of a brackish quality.

In the course of the year there are two rainy and two dry seasons; the first wet
season isin December, January, and February; the second is in June, July, and August.
During these periods land winds commonly prevail, rendering the air very unhealthy;
but in the dry season of March, April, and May, and again in September, October,
and November, the climate is wholesome, as the land is then constantly refreshed by
diurnal sea breezes.

It does not appear that all the various points of this extensive land have been
accurately and indisputably settled ; and on a coast where few or no ‘objects exist to
ascertain the different places, except their latitude, it will be very likely for you to get
to leeward of the port where you are bound to. For this reason it will always be
advisable to run down the coast, from windward to leeward, taking care to examine
and distinctly make out the various places and mouths of the respective rivers; for
during the period of the rains, the latitude cannot often be observed. In doing so,
the mariner will recollect that all these rivers have bars, with shallow water over
them; and the best way for those who have not a practical knowledge of these rivers,
will be to obtain such information by means of their boats, or else to get a pilot, and
never to enter a river without one.

The winds that commonly prevail on this coast are from E.N.E. to N.E. or E.S.E.
and §.E., and the current, which always runs W.N.W., makes the lesser latitude to
windward. Hence, on all the coast, it will be very easy to increase your north
latitude, but very difficult to decrease it. The current, which is here alluded to, is the
general tendency of the sea, and not that produced by the flux of the rivers; for these
latter will always be found to prevail near the land, and their influence reaches about
12 miles from the shore, or to about 9 fathoms water, which may be considered their
outer limits; beyond, and to the eastward of that, the general current only prevails ;
and within that, or between it and the land, no other current than that produced by
the tides will be felt ; here the fiood sets towards the coast, and the ebb away from
it. ‘The tides flow, on full and change days, as follow: at Cape North, at 7 o'clock;
about the coast of Mayez, at 6 o’clock; at Cayenne, at 5 o'clock; off Surinam, at 6
o’clock; at the mouth of the Essequibo, at 3-after 6 o’clock; at the great mouth of
the Orinoco, at 6 o’clock ; and in the Gulf of Paria, at }-after 4 o’clock.

From what has been stated, it will clearly appear advantageous for ships bound
from Europe to Guayana, to make the land to the southward of the port they are
destined, somewhere about the environs of Mayez; but not to get too near the
Maranon, because of the vast agitation that river produces, and which, as already
noticed, extends far out to seaward, and might endanger your vessel.

But having made the coast, and well understanding your situation, you may run
along it, taking advantage of the general current, in 7, 8, and 9 fathoms water,
keeping your lead going constantly, and taking care not to lessen your water, lest you
should strike on some of these shoals which environ the coast. In this depth, you will
not, in some places, be able to see the land, yet that can produce no inconvenience ;
for when you get near the latitude of the port you are bound to, or are desirous of
examining the coast, it will be an easy thing to put your vessel about on the port tack,
and run in sight of the shore. If night is approaching, and you are nearly abreast of
the place of your destination, you should always anchor; or if in a calm, and within
the boundary of the tides, you should always anchor, for otherwise the flood-tide will
inevitably drift you towards the coast, and into danger.

Should you run aground upon this coast, you, generally, will not sustain much
damage, for the bottom is mostly clayey and soft; but it always should, if possible,
be avoided, because it will occasion much loss of time, and great trouble to get your
vessel off again. And of such a consistency is the sea in some places hereabout, and
so impregnated with earthyp articles, that when sailing along in the proper track, and
in 9 fathoms water, the ship will apparently raise up the mud, as though she was

12 DEAD RECKONING.

ploughing it with her keel; yet keep but a sufficient depth of water, and there will
be no danger. A

The only part of this coast which can occasion the loss of a vessel is abeut the
environs of Cayenne; for off here lie several rocky islets, the Constables, Remire,
Islands, and the Devil's or Health Islands; but if the mariner will pay but a proper
attention to the currents, and not attempt to pass between the Constabies, unless with
a fair wind, anchoring at the distance of 3 leagues off, if necessary, giving them always
a wide berth, and going on their outside, he will encounter no danger whatever.

The harbours on this coast are only at the mouths of the rivers, there are none
other; and these require a pilot, or some person of practical knowledge, to conduct a
vessel into them with safety, for bars and shoals encumber them all; but as storms
are occurrences unknown, there is no risk in waiting outside, and anchoring there until
you obtain the assistance required.

Should you be desirous of beating up to windward, or going from the Orinoco to
Surinam or Cayenne, it will be advisable to work along the coast with the ebb-tide,
in from 33 to 4 fathoms water, and out to 7, 8, and 9 fathoms, for although you may
be driven away to the north-eastward by the tide-current, you may gain on the 8.5.
or E.S.§. tack; but with the flood, you should anchor; for then, both wind and tide
being against you, you will rua great hazard in being driven upon the shore.

. Vessels coming from the Caribbean Islands, ought to keep their port tacks on board,
until they get into a convenient latitude to make the land; which, as before observed,
should always be to the southward of the place they are bound to; this will be best
regulated by the practice and knowledge of the navigator; but upon all the coast,
from Cayenne to Orinoco, even the most experienced are frequently unable to
ascertain their exact situations; and, without having observations for their latitude,
occasion them to run into very serious mistakes.

For this reason, it has been recommended to make the land about Mount Mayez;
but now the newly-established lights at British Guayana, may much facilitate the
mariner’s knowledge of that part of the coast; and the environs of Demerara having
the trees burnt and cleared away, forming gaps and openings where houses are
visible, will greatly add to assure him of the respective position he is in; but should
he find himself bewildered, and at a loss to determine his situation, let him anchor
until his doubts are removed; and although some time will be lost by thus anchoring,
yet he will thereby keep to windward, which, if lost, it would be difficult to recover.

Dead reckoning in shoal water.—As great uncertainty will arise in the dead
reckoning, caused by currents, it is advisable to take off the log-chip from the log-line,
and to substitute a leaden weight of 4, 5, or 6 pounds; this taking the bottom, when
the log is hove with it, instead of the log-chip, will not so easily follow the vessel or
be influenced by the currents. By this method, the log will show the whole distance
the ship runs, whether caused by winds or currents. Then, having made fast the log-
line before you haul it in, mark the bearing of it, and the opposite point or direction
will be the course which the vessel makes good. hus the course and distance ought
to be as exactly found as if no current existed. If you heave the log with a chip, in
the usual manner, as well as a log with a lead attached to it, and compare the distance
by it, and the course which the ship makes by the compass, with the distance and
course found by this proposed method, you will be able to ascertain the direction and
velocity of the current. It is suggested that a few fathoms of extra stray line should
be used, and if great accuracy be required, as in making the comparison between this
mode and the common log, to ascertain the strength of the current, an allowance
should be made for the angle the line makes with the surface of the sea, in order to
equalise it with the log-line as usually hove.

It has been already stated, that the whole coast of Guayana, from Cape North to the
Orinoco, is very low, and soundings run off it all the way to a great distance, which
is a circumstance that can never fail to indicate the mariner’s approach towards the
land, if he only will carefully, after getting soundings, keep the lead going; and this
becomes the more necessary, since any other method of recognising the coast is so very

CAPE NORTH AND ORANGE. 13

difficult; for, in the clearest-day, the land will not be discernible at the distance of
5 leagues off; and the general shoalness of the water all along it, and the nwmerous
banks of sand, clay, and mud, with which it is everywhere lined, will always prevent
your vessel coming nearer to it than the distance of 2 leagues.

CAPE NORTE, which lies in latitude, about 1° 44’ north, is the north-eastern
point of the Island Carpori, and forms the most easterly projecting land of Guayana;
that and the land adjacent is frequently overflowed, and the southern and western
parts of Carpori are bounded by the River Arawary, or Aruari. There is a large
island, called Maraca, to the northward of Carpori, from which it is divided by a strait
or opening, forming a branch of the Arawary. These islands are fronted by sand
banks, formed of the alluvial ground, which the rivers here continually disembogue,
and which contributes to shallow the water for a considerable distance, and extends the
soundings far to the north-eastward.

From Cape North to Cape Cassipour, the land continues low, and covered thickly
with trees; there are some rivulets descending to the sea within this space, but none
of any importance. The chief and only object by which this part of the coast may
be recognised is the little hill of Mayez, which makes it a kind of platform shape, and
is commonly visible 5 or 6 leagues off. his hill, by the best authorities, is situated
in 2° 60’ north latitude, and is generally the object vessels bound from Europe to
Guayana are recommended to get sight of. Cape Cassipour lies in latitude 3° 46’ 30’
north, being distant from Mount Mayez about 19 leagues, and is the eastern point of
a river of the same name. ‘The land about its entrance is low, and a great bank of
clay stretches out from it full 5 leagues to seaward, having 8, 4, and 5 fathoms over
it; but as possibly there may be spots of less water upon it, mariners, in approaching
or passing this Cape, will always do well by giving it a berth of 5 or 6 leagues; and
having so done, they will have no difficulty in recognising Cape Orange. But should
that not be within sight, yet your proximity to it may be ascertained beyond any
doubt; for, by steering north, your soundings will deepen from 5 and 6, to 9, 10, and
11 fathoms, in only running a short mile out; and when that is found to be the case,
you should, steer W.N.W., or even more westerly, in order that you may be able to
recover your former depth. When a ship is off Cape Cassipour, in 5 fathoms water,
it will be advisable to continue on to the north-westward in a similar depth; and if
you should, by steering north, or N. by E., deepen your soundings to 7, 8, and 9
fathoms, then the land will no longer be visible; but by not getting into more than 7
fathoms, and steering N.N.W., or N.W., you will certainly get abreast of Cape Orange,
and will then, when only 2 or 3 leagues off the land, have 8 or 9 fathoms.

CAPE ORANGE is a remarkable point of land, stretching out to the north-east-
ward, and forming the south-eastern point of what is called Oyapok Bay; it may be
known by a cut point, Punto Cortada, appearing from seaward, as though the side
next the ocean, the highest land, sonth-eastward of the Cape, had been shortened and
cut off. You will also discover when you are in the vicinity of the Cape, by the
various little hills, which appear over the point which forms the entrance to the
River Oyapok.

THE RIVER OYAPOK is full 2 leagues wide at its entrance. On its western
shores, and situated near the point of land which divides the River Ounari from the
Oyapok, stands Mount Lucas, a small but tolerably elevated hill; the mariner, in
ascending the river, will endeavour to bring this hill to bear west, keeping from it
about ? of a league; and when he has advanced a league up the river, he will perceive
the low island of Venados, which, at very high tides, is frequently under water; the
best channel is to the westward of it, where he will have 4 fathoms close to the shore.
Having passed the Venados, he will see several other islets, but these do not embarrass
the navigation of the river; and when he gets 5 or 6 leagues within the river, a fine
bay opens, which serves for a harbour, where vessels may find anchorage in 4, 5, or 6
fathoms water, lying as close to the land as may be convenient. Here is situated Fort
St. Louis, of Oyapok, and further up is another fortress, called St. Paul. ‘The river
rises far in the interior of the country, and, being joined by several lesser streams,
conveys a strong body of water into the sea; so that to get in here, you should always
take advantage of the making of the flood.

14 ISLANDS OF REMIRE.

THE RIVER APROUAK.—About 8 leagues to the north-westward of Cape
Orange is Garimore Point, which is the eastern point of the River Aprouak, or
Aprouague River, called also the Approbaque ; this, from the size, is of some import-
ance, although very little is known of the nature of its navigation. Its entrance
is full 2 leagues wide, and has 3 or 4 fathoms water in it; the banks are low, marshy,
and covered with mangrove trees. About 2 leagues up the river, and nearly in mid-
channel, is an island, low and narrow, and generally named the Fisherman’s Island.
To the northward of this a bank of sand stretches out about 12 mile; therefore, those
who navigate this river should always take care to give it a good berth; there is said
to be a passage on either side, but that to the westward has only 2 fathoms water ;
the eastern channel is somewhat deeper, having 3 fathoms and more within it. The
river winds inland far to the westward, and is reported to join the Maroni.

To the southward of Point Garimore are some hills, called Argent, or the Silver
Mountains; these, being surrounded entirely by low land, form a remarkable object;
because rising in a swampy country, and gradually descending to the sea, they form
various peaks, appearing insulated and detached from each other, and are the first
high land you will meet with in coming from the northward, and consequently form
a mark for this part of the coast. From the Aprouak River the coast takes a north-
westerly direction to the River Maroni, a distance of 47 leagues. his is the province
of Cayenne ; and at the northern extremity of an island, distant 11 leagues from the
entrance of Aprouak is the town of Cayenne, which gives its name to the district.
Off this part, and between it and the River Sinnamari, are several rocky islets, which,
as before observed, are the only objects on all the coast of Guayana where shipwreck
is to be apprehended. The first, or most southerly of these, are the Constables, or
Gunners, two bare rocks, very conspicuous, and generally white with the dung of
birds ; the outermost of these is called the Great Constable, or Gunner; it is some-
what high, in shape like half an orange, and visible 8 or 10 leagues to seaward; the
Little Constable lies within it, and nearer to the shore, being distant from the Great
Constable a full mile, and appearing nearly level with the water’s edge. They lie
nearly N.N.W., distant 15 or 16 leagues from Cape Orange; and by keeping in 8 or
9 fathoms water, you may go between them. The Great Constable has 3 fathoms all
round it, and the ground quite clear of danger; they lie E.N.E., and W.S.W., of each
other; and in passing between them you will always find 8 and 9 fathoms water,
keeping the great island about two muskets’ shot distance, and leaving the little one
to the port. This passage is commonly taken to avoid a rocky shoal, which has been
stated to lie 3 or 4 miles N.N.W. from the Great Constable, and appears principally
to rest on the information of Za Gironde, a French man-of-war, which vessel, bound
to Cayenne in 1738, after passing the Constables, and leaving the great one to the
starboard, steered N.W. by W. towards the Remire Islands, or Mother and Daughters,
and discovered breakers, which appeared to be rocks, bearing N. by W., about a
league distant; the Great Constable then bore E. by S., and the little one S. by E.
From this account it should appear to be N. 39° W. (true), from the Great Constable,
distant 4 miles. Its extent is supposed to be about 4 cables’ length, and to lie N.W.
and S.E.

‘The ISLANDS of REMIRE are five in number, the Mother and Two Daughters,
the Father and Malingre, or the Son. The latter of these lies a league to the north-
eastward of the Island of Cayenne, N.N.E. from the Romontabo Mountain, and N.W.
by W., distant 4 miles from the Father; it is but small, and wears a sterile appear-
ance. The Father is the largest of these islets, and bears from Mount Joli,
E.N.E. | E. distant about 4 miles; it is $a mile long, and lies E.S.E. and W.N.W.
The Mother is of a similar description and appearance, but not sc large as the Father;
the Two Daughters are merely little rocks lying close to one another; but distant
from the Mother nearly a mile, from which they bear E.S.E. At the Mother, pilots
may now be obtained.

If the mariner should be desirous of taking this passage, he should steer from the
Constables N.W. by W., which will carry him outside of the Remire Islands. The
distance from the Constables to the Mother and Daughters is about 5 leagues. In
pursuing the above course, your depth of water will lessen, and you will not find

CAYENNE. 15

near the Malingre, or Son, more than 6 fathoms; near the E.N.E. part of which you
may anchor, if necessary, in 3 fathoms at low water. But the vessel may pass outside
of all these islands, keeping them at the distance of 3 miles, or even less, with a
certainty of having not less than 5 and 6 fathoms water. Should you attempt going
within them, and between them and the main land of Cayenne, you will get only 14,
15, and 16 feet water in your passage; and this is not safe, on account of a rocky
shoal, which extends between the Father and the Mother, lying N. by W. from
Mount Joli, and nearly east from Romontabo. The Malingre Islet shallows all round,
and a reef stretches out from its western point nearly N.N.W.

Besides these islands, which lie off the entrance to Cayenne, there is another, called
the Forlorn Hope: this lies N.W. by W., distant full 3 leagues from the Malingre,
and nearly upon the meridian of Cayenne, from which it is distant 8 miles. Off the
south-eastern part of this island is a rock under water.

To make the land and sail into Cayenne Harbour.—lIt is generally advisable to make
the land somewhere to the northward of Cape North, and about the vicinity of Mount
Mayez; but by no means to go further to the southward of the Cape, on account of
the vast body of water which continually issues from the Maranon, and is felt, parti-
cularly in the rainy seasons, far out to seaward. Having made the land about Mount
Mayez you may sail along it to the north-westward, keeping your lead constantly
going, so as to run along, as already directed, in 7, 8, and 9 fathoms; you will then
be 8 or 9 miles distant from the land.

The soundings hereabont extend to a great distance from the land, so that at 10
leagues off, you will find from 15 to 20 fathoms water; while from 15 to 20 leagues
off, there will be 25, 30, 40, and 50 fathoms; the ground being a soft clay, or fine sand
of various colours. When you are in 8 or 9 fathoms, and distant 10 or 12 leagues from
the shore, the current always sets to the N.N.W., but when you get within this, and
are nearer to the land, it will vary with the tide, being influenced to that extent by
the waters that issue from the several rivers adjacent; remember that the flood sets
always towards the coast, and the ebb the contrary; the flood, therefore, will run
about W.N.W., and the ebb N.E., at a general ratio of 3 miles an hour; but the com-
mon velocity of the general or outside current will be 2 miles an hour; on which
account, as before observed, it will be always advantageous to make the land to the
southward of the port of your destination. Therefore, those desirous of going to
Cayenne, should make their first soundings, as here directed, where, at the distance
of 60 or 70 miles from land, there will be 40 and 50 fathoms; then steering W. and
N.W., they will inevitably make the land about Mount Mayez, or the Silver Moun-
tains, and can then shape their course accordingly.

To sail into Cayenne Harbour, it will first be absolutely proper you should come
to an anchor between Malingre and the Forlorn Hope, both for the purpose of waiting
for the tide, and for getting a pilot to enable you to cross and avoid the shallows at
the entrance to the harbour ; but should you anchor between Malingre and the Father,
you will be much inconvenienced by north-easterly winds, which always occasion a
heavy sea, and catching vessels on the beam, and making them roll; your anchor too,
will be apt to drag, and therefore it will be requisite you should be possessed of
another, ready to let go, and many times you will have to wait several days before
you can communicate with the land. In this anchorage there will be from 20 to 25
feet at low water, the bottom a clayey ground.

Vessels in general anchor to the E.N.E., or N.E., or north of Malingre, at the
distance of 2 miles; others anchor to the E.N.E., or N.E. of the Forlorn Hope, at the
distance of 2 miles, or even nearer. To the southward of the Forlorn Hope the ground
shallows to 8 and 10 feet, but deepens again to 12 and 13 feet as you advance towards
the river; but you must take great care not to go too near the land, for there is a flat,
over which is only 1} foot at low water.

The tides here rise 7 and 8 feet. and it is high water, full and change, at 5 o'clock.

At Cayenne a fixed white light is shown from a wooden structure, 39 feet high,
erected on the glacis of Fort Cépéron; elevation 130 feet above the sea, visible
10 miles.

16 RIVER MAROWINE.

A fixed green light is shown from the north-west angle of the infantry barracks,
at an elevation of 60 feet above the sea, and visible 8 miles. It stands N.W. of the
fort, and N.W. by N. from Cépéron lighthouse. The two lights in line, bearing S.E.
by E., lead over the Amiable Rock. A vessel entering the River of Cayenne should
therefore keep the white light a little open westward of the green light.

A fixed red light is shown from the jetty head, to assist in entering the river
at night.

Having advanced abreast of the opening of the River Cayenne, and being 2 miles
to the eastward of the Forlorn Hope, a S. by W. course will carry you into the river;
but you must be careful to guard against the current, particularly in dark and rainy
seasons, or from January to June, for, if accompanied by an easterly wind, it will be
sure to drift you among the rocks. There are 12, 14, and 16 feet at the entrance of
the River Cayenne, but so many sunken rocks lie about it, that it should neyer be
entered without a pilot.

N.W. by N. from the Forlorn Hope, distant 8 or 9 leagues, lie three small islands,
forming a triangle, and making an excellent harbour, well sheltered; they were
formerly called the Devil's Islets, but now are named Isles du Salut, the Islands of
Heulth ; the best anchorage will be to the E.S.E. of the southernmost islet: here you
will have 6 and 6 fathoms water, hard clayey ground, at the distance of a musket
shot from the islet. On this islet is a reservoir of fresh water, but you must get the
water with kegs, which are to be carried, as the roughness and steepness of the ground
render it impossible to obtain it with large casks. Between the Forlorn Hope and
the Islands of Health, are 5, 6, and 7 fathoms water, at the distance of 4 or 3 leagues
from the land; near the Islands of Health are 9 fathoms; and to the north-east-
ward are 20, 30, and 40 fathoms, increasing your depth as you increase your distance
from them.

About 6 leagues to the north-westward of Cayenne, is Macouri, a small village.
There is also a small islet, called Green Island, lying near the land, and not far distant
from the entratice to the Sinnamari River; this is the northernmost of these rocky
islands which distinguish this part of the coast from any other in the vicinity: having
therefore passed these, you will perceive the land turn more westerly, towards the
River Maroni, which forms the northern limit of French Guayana.

Tur RIVER MAROWINE, or MARONI.—The entrance of this river bears from
Cayenne N.W. by W., distant 37 leagues; there is no remarkable object to the east-
ward which may indicate the mariner’s approach, except those which we have already
enumerated. To sail into this river is both difficult and dangerous, on account of
the shoals of sand and clay with which it is encumbered, consequently it is but little
frequented; there are several channels or passages into it, but these occasionally vary,
the banks being chiefly formed of alluvial matter, which the river from time to time
discharges; the entrances, therefore, are in many places shallow, and the passages
intricate.’ When you get within these, the river becomes a league wide, and the
stream is navigable to a great distance from the sea, but not for vessels ot large
dimensions, ;

On the western point of the Maroni is a Dutch post, and from off this point a
sand bank stretches out north-eastward 4 or 5 miles. A similar spit runs from the
eastern point of the river to nearly the same distance, and upon this point is a French
post. Vessels that have occasion to anchor, may do so, at the entrance of the river,
between the two posts just mentioned.

Before the river, at the distance of about 8 miles, the Marowine Banks begin,
having at this part 2 fathoms over them; beyond which, to the north-eastward, the
depth gradually increases to 4, 6, 8, 10, and 12 fathoms, the latter depth being nearly
30 miles off the land: the current there runs to the N.W., from 2 to 8 miles an hour.
Should a vessel from the northward be desirous of making the land hereabouts, she
should run down in the longitude of about 53° 30’, and when in latitude 6° 30’, she will
have soundings of from 30 to 40 fathoms, being 16 leagues off the land, and somewhat
to the eastward of the Maroni Liver.

SURINAM. 17
’ Besides the above directions, the mariner must observe, that he will be rear, and to
the windward of the Maroni, when his soundings are coarse ground, so that by
hauling to the northward the bottom will become of a finer quality, and the water
Lai at and when he gets to leeward of the shoals, he will have sand and oaze. It
will always be proper to keep on the edge of the bank, in from 23 to 3 and 4 fathoms,
and in the rainy season to come to an anchor soon, or if he should be in the least
doubtful, or even should sail but a few yards to leeward, he will have much difficulty
in getting back again, even with a fast-sailing ship; but by observing the foregoing
precautions, he will rarely fail to make the land properly.

To make the land, and sail into Surinam.—The western bank of the Maroni
belongs to the Dutch, their territory continuing westerly to the River Courantin.
From the entrance of the. Maroni to Surinam, the land runs W. 3 N., the distance
being 28 leagues. The coast which separates them is all so much alike, and so low,
that it is almost impossible to distinguish one part from another. Should the mariner
approach from the northward, and make the land hereabout, he must not expect to be
able, by the appearance of the shore, to rectify the position of his vessel, but will find
it absolutely necessary to steer out so as to fall in with the Maroni, or thereabout,
in order to make good his passage to Surinam.

The coast all the way from the Maroni to the Surinam has banks of clayey ground,
with sandy and muddy flats extending from it, full 2 and 3 leagues out, thus rendering
it necessary to keep at a still greater distance than that from the land in sailing along
it; the entrance to the river, when coming from the eastward, may be known by its

oint, in form like a crow’s bill, and can be discerned at the distance of 4 and 5
leagues off; but, as yet, the western point will be hidden from your sight, until you
get within the entrance of the river.

Ships bound to Surinam from Europe, ought to get into the latitude of 6° or 6° 55°
by the time they reckon themselves in the longitude of 50° or 51°, (especially in the
months of June, July, and August, when the sunis often obscured for days,) unless
they are well assured of their true position; for during the rainy season, you cannot
depend upon getting a meridianal observation ; and the current, constantly setting to
the north-westward, will require you to remember carefully to try the soundings in
time, for you will have from 60 to 40 fathoms, when you are full 20 leagues to the
eastward of the Maroni, on a bottom of sand, and still further off to the northward,
‘are soundings with deeper water and finer sand. The colour of the water changes as
you approach the shore, and before you get sight of the land, you frequently meet
with fragments of trees and bushes, floating on the surface of the sea.

Should the weather be hazy, keep the lead constantly going, but do not come into
less than 10 or 9 fathoms; the ground becoming coarse as you approach the
Maroni Shoals: to the northward, the depth is greater, and the sand finer. The
mariner may always know whether he is to the east or the west of these shoals;
for from about 6 leagues to the westward all the way to Bram’s Point, the
bottom is soft mud, while to the eastward the ground is coarse; therefore, when
the ground becomes coarse, and the depth 10 fathoms, if in the night, heave-to, with
your head to the northward, and you will drive clear to the N.W. of these shoals, so
as to be able, with daylight, to make the land, between the Maroni River and Post
Orange. This part is remarkable, being the only high land, and that appears a great
way inland.

About 5 miles west of Post Orange, is Mot Creek, where the Dutch flag is hoisted,
as a mark for vessels; there are also a few houses among the trees. The land from
the Maroni to Surinam remains in an uncultivated state, excepting a plantation,
‘called Cameron’s Castle, which is the next mark, from Mot Creek, towards Bram’s
Point; this consists of several buildings, painted white, with a larger one in the
middle which has a steeple, and forms the best mark on this part of the coast.

Tue River SuRINAM.—Bram’s Point is the eastern point of the entrance to Surinam ;
Post Orange is about 13 leagues to the eastward of that point, and has been formerly
often mistaken for the latter; this error has proved fatal to many. ‘To prevent sucha
mistake, in future, you will observe at Post Orange a few houses of a brownish aspect

among the trees; and a flagstaff with the Dutch flag serves to distinguish the Post.
On Bram’s Point is a beacon, surmounted by a ball.

' Surinam LiGHT-VESSEL.—A light-vessel is moored in 21 fathoms, at the entrance
of the River Surinam, N.W. of Bram’s Point, at the distance of 32 miles, the beacon
at Bram’s Point bearing S.E. 3 E. The light is fixed, and at an elevation of 30 English
feet above the water, visible in clear weather at a distance of 7 miles; by day she
carries a red ball at her mast-head, with “ Surinam” painted on each side.*

Approaching from the eastward, in 4 fathoms, along the coast, the light may be
seen; but in coming from the northward, soundings of 4 fathoms may be obtained
for some time before sighting it in dark weather.

' Buoys.—The channel into the river Surinam is also marked by the following buoys,
coloured black, which must be left on the port-hand by vessels entering.

The 3rd or outer buoy lies in 12 feet at low water, with the light-vessel bearing
south ; the eastern extreme of land E. 3 S., and Bram’s Point beacon S.E. 2S

No. 2 buoy, the largest in size, is moored in 14 feet, with the light-vessel
N. by W. 2 W.; outer buoy N. by W.; eastern extreme of land E. by N. 2N.; and
Bram’s Point beacon S.E. by E. $ E.

No. 1 buoy lies in 16 feet, with the light-vessel bearing N.N.W.; No. 2 buoy,
N.W. by W.; and Bram’s Point beacon 8.E. by E. 2 E.

In steering for the entrance you may approach as near the mud bank as your
draught of water will allow, into 3 or 24 fathoms; if you touch the edge of the bank
it will not injure you, being everywhere soft mud; and, hauling to the northward,
A as readily deepen your water; when in 32 and 4 fathoms. you will be off
the bank. ‘

' Sailing in for the river, you should look out for a break in the land, having been
cleared for a plantation, and the trees on each side appear burnt down: and if ebb
tide, or towards the evening, haul to the northward, and anchor in 4 fathoms water,
lest the current should drift you toward Coppename River ; in which case you may be
weeks in recovering your lost station, or perhaps obliged to bear up for Berbice, it
being next to impossible to stem both wind and current. But having a flood-tide,
bring Bram’s Point to bear §.8.E., or half a point more easterly ; by keeping it open on
the port bow, and steering on, you will clear the shoal that stretches out to the
northward, pick up the outer buoy, and being in the channel-way, anchoring, if
necessary, in 4 fathoms water. From the outer buoy the course is 8. } E., past the
light-vessel, 3 of a mile, then S.S.E. for 12 mile past the second buoy; from hence,
‘a S.E. by E. course, 73 miles, will bring you to Fort Amsterdam.

When you have passed Bram’s Point, keep the eastern shore on board, then you
will always have the deepest water, but there isa kind of bar 3 miles within the
‘point, over which in some places are less than two fathoms at low water; this is called
the Resolutie Shallows, and extends to within about 2 miles of the entrance to the
Commewyne River; having reached which, be careful to guard against the flood-tide,
setting strongly into the Commewyne, or you will get drifted on a spit of sand which
stretches from Fort Amsterdam almost across the Commewyne. On the other hand,
be equally cautious to avoid the bank on the western shore.

Having passed Fort Amsterdam, you will be in 18 feet water; and from thence to
the bar is considered the deepest part of the river, Vessels, therefore, which draw
too much water to go over the inner bar, anchor, and take their cargoes in here. At
Lion’s Hole there are 6 fathoms, abreast of a place called Voorburg, from whence
you will have a leading wind up the river, keeping three quarters over toward the
eastern shore, in from 11 feet at low to 18 feet at high water, and anchor abreast of
Paramaribo in 4 fathoms, in the deepest water, which is close to the town.

High water, full and change, at 6h. 0m. Spring tides rise 53 feet, and during
heavy rains, about 8 feet.

“THE RIVER COPPENAME lies about 8 leagues to the westward of Surinam,
and is the estuary through which the Rivers Saramacca, Coesoewine, and other
smaller rivulets discharge their waters into the sea; they are at present of little im-
portance, their banks are uninhabited, and at the general entrance there are but 2
fathoms water, while a bank of mud and sand lines the shore all the way from the
Surinam to the Coppename.

THE RIVER CORENTYN, or COURANTIN, lies still further to the westward ;
the coast here begins to take a little inclination to the northward. Corentyn, which
is the boundary between the Dutch and English territories, is 19 leagues distant
from the Coppename, and 27 leagues from the entrance of Surinam; the shore ail the
way is shallow, and the soundings, as you approach it gradually lessen their depth ;
at the distance of 30 miles off land, you will only have 12 fathoms. The entrance to
this river is about a league wide; butits access is rendered dangerous by several sand-
banks, which extend nearly 3 leagues into the sea. ‘The river itself is shallow, and
obstructed by many small islands and quicksands ; nevertheless, there are three
islands within it, where the ground is clear and free from danger; between these, it
is said, good anchorage may be found, with a depth of 5 fathoms; the anchorage and
entrance are both on the western side; the islands wear a fertile appearance, and are
covered with trees. There are now several plantations on the western banks of the
river, which, under the British jurisdiction, are in an improving state. There isa
little river on its eastern side, called Nickerrie,—which winds through the Dutch
territories, and joins the Coppename,—-the banks of which are cultivated.

Sailing Directions for the Entrance of the River Corentyn, by Mr. Schomburgh.*

The whole of the coast about the entrance of the river is low and wooded, with
occasionally a sandy beach. On the western side, 3 miles to the northward of the
plantation, Mary’s Hope, or, in latitude 6° 5’ north, a soft mud flat, commonly called
the Bar of the River, extends in a true S.E. by E. direction, to the distance of 75 miles,
with a depth over it, in every direction traversed by Mr: Schomburgk, of 73 feet at
low water. Continuing in this south-easterly direction across the entrance of the
river, a channel of 2 miles wide, with 83 feet water, occurs; then a sandy patch of
5 feet (its centre exactly in latitude 6° north), of about a mile long from north to
south, by 4a mile in breadth, and again a channel 2 miles wide, with 8} feet water,
between the sand and the Dutch coast; either of these channels may be used by small
craft bound to the Dutch port of Nickerrie, taking care to avoid this patch of sand, of
which the Jead, if attended to, will give due warning.

In the centre of the eastern channel, which should be preferred by vessels bound to
the Dutch coast, a depth gradually decreasing from seaward, of 11, 10, and 9 feet, at
the distance of 13 mile off shore, may be carried to the bar of the River Nickerrie,
which has a depth over it of 8 feet; but as the entrance is only 200 yards wide, vessels
that wish to run up the river, 4a mile, to the settlement, should cross the bar only
with the Battery Point bearing between E. by S. and E.S.E., which will lead up to
the anchorage off the fort in 10 feet water, soft mud.

To return to the Westward.—From the south-eastern extremity of the before-
mentioned mud flat, which stretches from the western shore half across the river, a
bank of sand, with only 5 feet water, 73 miles long, by nearly 2 in width, extends to
the southward directly in the centre of the river, leaving a channel 2 miles wide on
either side, with 9 and 10 feet at low water. The bank lies between 6° 2’ and 5° 543’
north latitude; at the southern extremity it dries at half-tide. Supposing, therefore,
a vessel not drawing more than 9 feet water, bound to Skeldon, or any plantation
higher up the river, and desirous of entering on the western or British side, she may
approach boldly in any direction at half-flood, the proper time for entering, till the
houses at Mary’s Hope bear due west, at which time she must not be more than 8
miles off shore; and she should keep on the parallel till a remarkable lofty umbrella-

As the wind is constantly from the eastward, there can be no difficulty in entering
or leaving the river; and by using the western entrance, the great central sand-bank,
which is the chief danger, is left to windward. The current is strong in the wet
season, from 3 to 33 knots an hour; but as it sets N.N.E. and S.S.W., or nearly in
the direction of the river, it is not of so much importance, yet should not be neg-
lected; above all, pay strict attention to the lead.

In approaching from the Eastward, keep within a mile of the Surinam shore,
gradually closing to 4 a mile, as you approach Bluff Point; when shape a mid-channel
course between Parrot Island and the western shore.

Four estates on the British side of the Corentyn produce 2000 hogsheads of sugar
annually; all of which, with the other productions, timber, &c., the planters
send to Berbice to be shipped, and for which purpose they are obliged to keep
up schooners or droghers at a very great extra expense; whereas by the eastern
channel, any vessel, drawing only 10 feet water, might safely sail 40 miles up this
river, and ship the produce at once from the various estates on which it is grown.

BERBICE.—7o make the land and sail into Berbice—The entrance to the River
Berbice is situated about 10 leagues to the westward of Corentyn, and 18 leagues to
windward of Demerara; there are several small creeks on the coust, but none navi-
gable, except for boats; a shallow flat covers the shore all the way, so that you
cannot approach within a league of the land, unless with vessels of small draught of
water; the soundings on all this part extend many leagues into the sea, and there-
fore, in making the land, you may approach with safety, trusting for your distance
to the lead. In making Berbice, the land appears like a number of islands, having
several tall trees scattered about, their appearance is very bare, and somewhat resem-
bles the masts of ships; but the coast here is much cleared of brushwood, and a
number of white houses, with red tops, become visible as you advance. Vessels
standing in for the river, may gradually decrease their depth to 4 and 33 fathoms;
they will then be able to see the houses on the western shore, and should haul their
wind until they open the eastern channel into the river; which, haying done, they
may enter in S. § W.

From the eastern point of the river a large shelly bank stretches out, over which
the sea frequently breaks very high; but be not alarmed, for there is deep water close
to it. The western side is also encumbered with a bank of mud, upon the edge of
which are no more than 23 fathoms at high water; during the spring-tides it dries
nearly 6 miles from the shore.

The bar is 2 leagues distant from the mouth of the river, having at low water 74
feet upon it, and is remarkable for the soundings varying from sand to mud; suffi-
cient water to pass it is absolutely necessary to be obtained, and therefore the lead
must not be neglected. Crab Island makes two channels in the mouth of the river ;
the lee one has generally been thought adapted only for small craft, but lately vessels
of 13 feet draught have passed; however, it is advisable for all ships to use the eastern
one, because it is deeper, and anchorage can be easier chosen. In sailing in, keep
(Crab Island just open with the point of Canje River; by this you will avoid the
middle ground or bank which runs out from Crab Island.

Neap-tides rise from 8 to 9 feet, and springs 11. In the month of September, just
before the equinox, they rise 14 and 15. The flood sets strongly to the west, and the
ebb to the east. On the eastern shore, opposite Crab Island, is Fort St. Andrew,
between which and the southern end of Crab Island are 20 feet water ; and beyond
the entrance of Canje River is the town of New Amsterdam, before which vessels

ebb at springs 15 or 20 miles off the land attaining a velocity of from
24 to 3 knots, the flood tide from 2 to 24 knots. Off the east coast of
Demerara the tides are felt only a few miles from the land. In 6° 50’ N.
and 57° 50’ W., with the land 10 miles distant, no tide or current was
felt, the vessel at anchor on every occasion was alone influenced by the
wind.

Winds.—The most unsettled and stormy months are December and
January; sometimes it blows strong from the northeast, accompanied
with hard squalls and rain. During March, April, May, and June, the
winds still hold to the northeast, but become gradually lighter; in the
latter month and in July the land wind beats back the trade wind, and
is accompanied by heavy rain. In August and September the wind veers
round to the southeast, heavy rains are less frequent, and calins of several
hours duration often prevail. During these months of light wind it was
found that in general the wind veered round to the northeast during the
night, backing towards the southeast in the forenoon.

Weather.—The seasons in Demerara are variable; there would appear
at the present time to be no fixed period when the long and short rainy
seasons commence; formerly they were looked for with certainty, as they
came every year within a few days of the same date. During the last
two years, December and January have been especially wet months; in
1870, the rainfall in December was 35 inches; in January, 19 inches;
during the whole year it amounted to 129 inches.

DEMERARA.—To make the land and navigate the Rivers Demeraraand Essequibo.
The entrance to the River Demerara is about 18 leagues to the north-westward of
Berbice, and 55 leagues from Surinam. In advancing towards this river, vessels
coming from Europe, or North America, should run within 1} or 2 degrees of Bar-
badoes, for by doing so they will have the advantage of a steady wind, and keep out
of the way of the currents: but should you get down so far as the third or fourth
degree of latitude, you will experience strong currents and light winds, which will
inevitably retard your voyage.

Vessels coming from the Caribbee Islands should keep well to the eastward, and by
no means give up their éasting till they get well to the southward; for the strong
current that runs through the Gulf of Paria is apt to set them to leeward, particularly
when they are to the southward of Tobago, and more so during the rainy season,
when the freshes set strong out of the large rivers. This precaution is also necessary
during the hurricane months, when the winds are commonly light. About latitude
7° 40°, and on the meridian of Demerara, the water begins to colour; a vessel may
then steer in, south, nearly to latitude 7°, and have 5 fathoms by the lead; she will
then be certain of being abrest of Leguan Island; haul in upon this for the eastern
coast, sounding constantly, in order to avoid the Hssequibo Banks ; after getting well
in, keep the coast aboard with 3} or 35 fathoms. Hence you will observe the lighthouse
built on Corrobana Point, at the east side of the entrance.

LIGHTHOUSE.—This is an octagonal building, exhibiting a fixed light, at 100
feet high. In clear weather it may be seen from the mast-head, about 7 leagues off.
Upon it is a signal-staff, to communicate on the appearance of vessels in the offing ;
this lighthouse is painted white-and-red, in alternate stripes, vertically.

LIGHT-VESSEL.—This vessel is moored off the bar, in 4 fathoms, at low water,
spring-tides, and exhibits a fixed ruby-coloured light. It is notified that the light

lamps. This will occupy not more than 15 minutes, during which time a common
lantern will be hoisted at the mast-head.

..The entrance of the Demerara River is encumbered, on the. western side, with a
long flat, composed of mud, and called the Sugar Bank, running 3 leagues into the
sea, the greatest depth upon it being 9 to 10 feet at low spring-ebbs, decreasing to 5,
4, and 3 feet towards the coast. The channel or passage into the river is to the east-
ward of the Sugar Bank, and the ground is all soft and oazy. Be careful not to stand
too near the western side; for, should the wind be adverse, the flood-tide may set you
upon some spots of hard sand ; but the eastern side is all soft and muddy, so that your
vessel may touch the ground without injury.

The best mark for entering the river, after having passed the light-vessel, will be
to steer direct towards the lighthouse on a S.W. by S. bearing, or do not bring it to
the southward of §.S.W. 4 W., by which means you will avoid the eastern part of the
Sugar Bank, one part of which, having but 5 fect, has a beacon erected on it, and
bears N. by W. 3 W., nearly 8 miles from the lighthouse. The channel is in general
a mile wide, and when you have advanced sufficiently on either of the above
bearings, and have brought the cabbage-trees, already noticed, to bear S.W. 3 W.,
you will have arrived at its narrowest part, which here takes a turn to the westward
towards the mouth of the river, and is about 4 mile wide. Steer towards the
cabbage-tree on that bearing, till you get the mouth of the river open, bearing
S. ¢ W., when you may round up towards the eastern side, passing the white buoy
to the port, and also the tub-beacon, a short distance from the eastern point. But
you must be careful not to bring the cabbage-tree to the southward of S.W. 5 W.,
for to the N.E. by N., 14 mile from the white buoy, the bank is very steep: so much
80, that the lead will be no guide, as you may be aground before you can get a
second cast.

The entrance of the river is nearly 2 miles wide, and is navigable for vessels
drawing 12 feet water for nearly a league. But this port should never be attempted
by a person unacquainted with the navigation, therefore all vessels should obtain a
pilot; indeed all merchant-vessels are compelled to take one, should they offer outside
the bar. This is in accordance with the harbour regulations. The pilot vessels are very
conspicuous, sloop-rigged, and carrying a large white flag; they are very assiduous,
frequently meeting vessels at a considerable distance to windward of the bar. The
pilotage is heavy.

The best anchorage, as stated before, is on the eastern side, in 4 fathoms, the
western side being shoal, and it will be found necessary to weigh the anchors every
8 or 10 days; they will otherwise sink astonishingly deep in the mud.

Remarks on making Demerara.—Vessels frequently fall in with the coast to the
leeward of Demerara, which occasions much anxiety and loss of time in gaining their
port, particularly as the sands at the mouth of the Essequibo run out so far from
the land, and are therefore dangerous. To know when the mariner is to windward
or to leeward of Demerara, he should observe when to the northward of the latitude
of 7° 12’ north; if he should make the land to the westward, he may be assured of
being to the leeward, and must haul on a bow-line directly to the southward and
eastward ; but if the land be not seen in the parallel of 7° 12’, then he must be to the
windward. If he should be to leeward of Demerara, he must endeavour to ascertain
which way the current is running, for if it is flood, the Essequibo stream will drift
him further to leeward ; let him, in that case, anchor immediately, and wait for the
ebb, which, after heavy rains, will run long and strongly towards the north. Then,
by weighing at the first of the ebb, and taking, by turning to windward in the
stream, the advantage of a whole tide, a vessel may always gain sufficient offing to
fetch Demerara on the port tack; then make a long stretch to the eastward, with
the first of the following ebb. By pursuing this plan, there will be as little difficulty
ia going from the Pomeroon to the Demerara, as from the Demerara to the

omeroon.

It is generally high water at Demerara, at the full and change, at 4h. and 45m.,
P.M. At the entrance of the river an E.N.E. and W.S.W. moon makes a full sea,
and the spring-tides rise 9 feet; neaps 3 feet. The tide continues to flow on the

Remarks on the Coast and Harbour of Demerara, by H. MaPLeton, Master
of H.M.S. Arachne.*

In sailing for the coast of Demerara from the northward, you must keep well to
windward, as the general set of the current along the coast to west, or W.N.W.,
is about 2 miles an hour.

At the distance of 20 miles off shore the currents vary according to the wind, and
it may be observed as a general rule, that where there is any westing in the wind, a
strong easterly set will be found along the whole coast; and that when the wind
inclines to the eastward, the set then will be westerly.

The trade wind blowing between N.N.E. and S.E., causes the westerly set usually
found; but as the wind occasionally veers to the northward, and even so far as
N.N.W., particularly in the winter months, the easterly current, above alluded to,
sometimes exists.

The flood-tide sets along the coast 8.W., and the ebb N.E.; their influence is not
felt beyond 8 miles off shore.

As the passage from Demerara to Berbice, or other parts to windward, exposes you
to the general westerly current, it is well to keep close in-shore, and take advantage
of the in-shore tide ; and, should the winds be light, it will be necessary to anchor
with the flood.

Cruising to windward in the Arachne, we found the trade winds incline so much to
the northward as to enable us to lay up east and E. by N., when we found the
easterly set, as before mentioned, running at least 23 knots an hour. This, however,
is not common, and ought not to be calculated upon in making a passage to wind-
ward, unless the wind, as previously noticed, enables you to lay EK. by N., or east.

The colour of the water along the coast, to 19 miles off shore, is thick and muddy,
and on many parts of it there are very dark patches, apparently shoals, but the
soundings on them are the same as the surrounding water.

Off the mouths or entrances of the different rivers, the bottom is hard, but in
general, along the coast, it is mud.

In working to windward, stand no nearer to the shore than 4 fathoms, nor off
beyond 9. You will then be enabled to take advantage of the regular ebb and
flood in-shore.

About 9 miles to the eastward of Corrobana Point are five or six single cocoa-nut
trees; 10 miles further to the eastward are two rows of the same trees, appearing
like white cliffs.

At-26 miles to the eastward of the river there is a hillock, formed by a large
eotton-tree. ‘This towers above the low land, and forms like a sugar-loaf; it is called
General Murray’s tree.

_ About 46 miles to the eastward of the river are two hillocks close together ;
they also form like sugar-loaves, and show themselves above the low land,

Vessels on the coast of British Guayana, and bound to Demerara, will clearly make
these objects, as they alone alter the appearance of the low land.

Crab Island, at the entrance of the river Berbice, will point this part of the coast
out, there being no other island between Demerara and Surinam. :

At 14 miles to the eastward of Berbice, there is a building close down to the water;
its sides and top are white, and a little to the westward of it isa deep gap in
the land.

The pilotage going in and out of Demerara being so heavy, it is advisable to anchor

HaRBour oF DEMERARA.—This harbour is formed at the entrance of the river
of the same name; Point Corrobana, which has a lighthouse on it, being the eastern
point of the harbour.

Directions to sail for the River—Being to windward, and running for the river,
keep at the distance of 4 or 5 miles off shore, in 43 and 5 fathoms. At 16 miles to the
eastward of the river are two very remarkable rows of cabbage-trees ; 3 miles to the
a of them are seven single ones. These trees have the appearance of white
cliffs.

Having passed them, stand on with the same soundings until you see Corrobana
Point, which is low, and the northernmost point of land, and has a lighthouse on it.
Steer about west, until the lighthouse bears 8.8. W., then steer S.W., until the light-
house bears south; then steer S.W. by S., until it bears 8. by E. You will then
have the river and ships open; steer for the lighthouse, and you will have a white
buoy on your left, and a black one on your right. Your anchorage is abreast of the
lighthouse; it will bear E.38.; at low water you have 17 feet. The flood runs
21 knots, and the ebb 3 knots an hour. The holding-ground is good, being mud and
clay.

In working out, you must not bring the lighthouse to the westward of 5.W. by W.,
or to the southward of S. by W.

The water that is generally used is rain water. In the dry seasons it would be
necessary for a ship in want of water to go 15 or 20 miles up the river, where it is
quite fresh and good.

The pilots for this harbour are very good, and keep a sharp look-out for vessels
coming down, picking up vessels 16 and 20 miles to windward of the river.

The RIVER ESSEQUIBO.—The entrance to the Essequibo is full 165 miles
wide; but there are so many islands and shoals which obstruct the passage, and divide
it into separate channels, that to enter by any of them becomes difficult ; these
islands are low and bushy, having sandy spits running out from them a considerable
way to the northward; the westernmost is called Tiger Island, which is a narrow
island 8 or 4 miles in length, and divided from the main by a small channel, having
from 13 to 26 feet water; but a spit of dry sand runs out from its northern end full
4 miles, and there are several small shoals at its entrance, which render it unfit for
ships of much burden. To the eastward of Tiger is Wakenaam Island; this is 11
miles in length, running S.S.W., and about 2 in breadth; from its northern part
stretches a large shoal, to the E.N.E., called the Kiwakewaraba; this is hard ground,
and dries at low water ; the passage between Tiger and Wakenaam Islands is encum-
bered with shoals of 8 feet and less water; but having passed these dangers, the
channel becomes wider and the water deeper. Leguan Island lies to the south-
eastward of Wakenaam, and is 3 leagues long, and 3 miles broad at its eastern part;
it then gradually becomes narrower, and ends in a point to the south-westward.
From its north-eastern part a sand extends, W. by_N., full 3 leagues; this also dries
at low water, and has a small island, called Little Leguan, sitated near the eastern
