The north-easternmost part of the coast of Paria forms a high scarped islet,
named the Morro, whence the coast trends to (W. by S.) W. by S. 1S. with some
inflections, for the space of 18 miles, to the cove of Mexillones; whence it bends a
little towards the north (W. 3 N.) westward as far as Cabo de Tres Puntas, or Cape
Three Points, which is distant from the Morro Islet about 50 miles. All this land is
very high and hilly, and the coast chiefly clean; you may run along by it at halfa
mile distance ; and so deep, that at a mile from the shore, you will meet from 20 to
30 fathoms water, with muddy sand.

CAPE THREE POINTS is the most northerly part of this coast; and from it,
the bottom which is equally clean and deep as the former, continues so for the space
of two miles to the Cove of Unare.

THE ENSENADA, or COVE OF UNARE.—This cove affords good anchor-
age and shelter from the sea breezes; and to enter it, it is necessary to keep a mile
from its N.H. point, around which a rocky shoal extends off half a mile; then direct
your course for the interior of the cove, and so soon as you have rounded the point,

THE TESTIGOS.

you may anchor in 5 fathoms on a sandy bottom. In this cove a rivulet empties
itself; and to the eastward of it, upon a small hill, is an Indian village, named San
Juan de Unare. The S.W. point of this cove has also a reef stretching off half a mile,
which has some islets on it. By passing outside of these, at about two cables’ length
from the northernmost, you will go safe from all danger.

From this cove the coast trends (W.S.W. 3 W.) W.S.W. 3 W.., about four leagues,
and afterwards turns gently towards the north for a space of seven miles to Cape
Mala Pascua. All the intermediate coast between Cape Three Points and Cape
Mala Pascua is clean, and may be run along by the distance of a mile, when you will
have 8 fathoms water, on a bottom of sand.

The 'TESTIGOS.—Almost (north) N. 4 W. from Cape Mala Pascua, at the
distance of 40 miles, are the islets called Testigos; they consist of seven principal
islets, and some other farallones, or detached rocks. The passes or channels between
these islets are free and clear, and may be taken without any risk; but not so with
those which are formed by the farallones, because they are very narrow. All the
islets may be approached within two cables’ length, or even less, if necessary,
excepting the northernmost one, which is environed by a reef, extending off about
half a mile. Between these islets the bottom is of sand, on which you may anchor,
in case of necessity. The principal islet is called Testigo Grande; this extends
N.W. and 8.E., and in this direction is about 2} miles in extent.. On its S.W. part it
has a good anchorage, sheltered from the sea breezes, with a depth of from 9 to 17
fathoms, on coarse sand. You may sail to this anchorage either by the N.W. or 8.E.
point of the islet. If you seek it by the first, it is necessary to pass outside the rocks
which lie out from that part ; and if you go on by the second, you may pass between
the Great Islet and another, to the S.W. of it, which forms a channel sufficiently
spacious ; the narrowest part is formed by a rock, which lies to the eastward of the
little islet, and another which runs off about a cable’s length from the S.W. side of
the Great Islet. The channel is halfa mile in width, from 9 to 10 fathoms of water,
on red gravel.

Between the Testigos and the main land there are soundings; and to the 8. by E.
of them about 5 miles is a large sand-bank, with 4% to 6 fathoms water over it,
which large ships ought to avoid.

From Cape Mala Pascua the coast follows about (west) W. 3 S., a distance of 7 or
8 miles to the Morro, or Hill of Puerto Santo; this Morro is united to the coast by
a low sandy tongue. West ofthe Morro, and very near to it, is theislet of Puerto
Santo; and about the tongue just mentioned, there is anchorage, sheltered from the
sea breezes, in 5 and 6 fathoms of water, on sand and mud. The north part of this
Morro and Islet may be approached within 3 cables’ length, if requisite ; and to
take the anchorage, steer (south or S. by W.) 8. E., or S. 2 W.; and when you
have passed the islet, and are sufficiently sheltered from the breezes, you may anchor
in 5 or 6 fathoms water. Take care not to get to the eastward of the western
meridian of the islet, because there is a shoal of 3 fathoms water. To the south of
the Morro, at about 2 leagues inland, you will see a mountain, called Monte de
Puerto Santo.

From this bay or anchorage of Puerto Santo, the coast trends about (W.S.W.)
S.W. by W. 2 W., 3 miles; and a shoal with little water on it, stretches along about
half a mile from the shore, as far as the point of Hernan Vasques, which point forms
another little bay, with anchorage in 6 or 7 fathoms water, sheltered from the
breezes. A river from which water may be procured, empties itself into this bay ;
and in the bight of the west point, in which there is a small islet, is the village of
Carupano ; to the westward of which, at 2 miles’ distance, is the point aud morro
of Salinas, or del Jarro, which has also an islet close to it. This bay of Hernan
Vasques has two shoals, somewhat to the northward of the parallel of the point of
that name, and to the westward of the meridian of the village of Carupano; there is
also a place of little depth, which extends about two-thirds of a mile off from the
west part of that village.

BAY OF ESMERALDA. 5

From the point and morro of Salinas the coast is clear; but there are some
patches of rocks almost joining the shore, as far as Morro Blanco, which is distant 3
miles from it. About 3 leagues inland, to the south of Morro Blanco, the mountain
of San Josef may be seen.

From Morro Blanco, er White Hill, a shoal stretches off to the westward, with so
little water on it, that it is unsafe to approach the coast hereabout nearer than 2 miles.
Here you may see, Ist, the Point and Morro of Padilla, which is known by an_tslet
and cluster of rocks, which lie off at a very short distance from it: 2nd, the Point
and Morro of Tarquien, which lies a little more to the north than the former, and
which also has some islets close to it: 3rd, the Morro of Lebranche, which is united
to the main land by a low and wet tongue of land and sand: and 4th, the Morro of
Esmeralda, which is an islet, separated from the coast by a little channel of about
half a cable’s length in width.

Between Lebranche and Morro Esmeralda, at a considerable distance off the
coast, are some islets named Garrapatas, between which you cannot pass, on account
of rocky shoals, and although between the southernmost and the coast, there is a
good passage, yet it is advisible always to go outside of them, especially with a large
ship. From Morro Blanco to Esmeralda the distance is 11 miles: and to the south-
ward of the last, about 4 leagues inland, there is a mountain called Monte Redondo,
or the Round Hill.

To the westward of Morro Esmeralda is formed a great ensenada, or bay of the
same name: this is obstructed by a shoal of very unequal depth, which projecting
from the middle of the Morro, and lying nearly north and south, extends along the
coast at the distance of about one-third of a mile. In this bay, and upon this shoal
there are three islets, which lie nearly east and west, and are called the Cascable, or
Rattlesnake Islets. To anchor in this bay you may steer as close as you please to
the north and west parts of the Morro, and drop your anchor under shelter of it, at
about 2 cables’ length distant from it, in 6 or 7 fathoms water, on mud mixed with
sand.

From the Ensenada, or Bay of Esmeralda, the coast runs to the westward, about
5 miles to the Point and Morro of Manzanilla; and the shoal which projects from
Esmeralda extends along it at the distance of one-third of a mile from shore. Point
Manzanilla forms a bay, but it is entirely obstructed by the shoal of which we have
spoken, and which ends at the first scarped point to leeward of this, and at the
distance of about two-thirds of a mile. This shoal is so situated, that it not only
prevents entering into the bay, but it also hinders from going anything to the
southward, until to the westward of this scarped point. To the westward of it, the
coast is very clean for the distance of 8 miles, to Point Guarapoturo, at which begins
a shoal, which projects out from the coast about two-thirds of a mile.

To the N.E. of the said Point Guarapoturo, and at about a mile distance, there is
a sunken rock, to which it is necessary to give a wide berth. Somewhat to the east-
ward of this point, and about a league inland, there rises a peaked mountain, called
Pico del Este, or Peak of the East.

Three miles westward from Point Guarapoturo is the Point del Escudo Blanco, or
White Shield, and the coast between is high and cliffy, but thence the shore runs
about N.W., very low and swampy, a distance of 23 miles to the Morro of
Chacopata, which forms a point projecting into the sea almost 2 miles. From this
point, the coast runs to the southward, forming a great bay, in which, at about 13 mile
to the westward of the middle of the Morro, there is an islet, called Caribes; and
west from this islet, about a mile, there is a smaller islet, called Lobos, or Wolves
Islet, which has a rock close to its eastern side. The shoal which we have already
mentioned, as projecting out from Point Guarapoturo, borders all this coast, and
stretching out from the Morro Point about one-third of a mile, it continues thence
to Caribes Isle, from which it inclines to the south, and nears the coast so much,
that, at the Point and Morro de Cayman, which is the south and west point of the
bay, it extends out only half a mile.

6 ISLAND OF MARGARITA.

On the meridian of the Morro of Chacopata lies the east point of the Island:
Margarita, which forms with the coast a channel of 11 miles wide: in the middle:
of this channel are the Islands Coche, and Cuagua or Cubagua; and to navigate:
therein, it is neccessary to describe all the coasts which form it; we shall follow
without interruption, the description of the coast so far as Araya, and then return to
Margarita and the adjacent islands.

From the Point and Morro de Cayman, the coast runs nearly west, moderately
level, and without any other projecting point than that of Tuna, which is distant
1§ mile from the former, and the Point and Morro del Castillo, which is 2 miles.
westward from Tuna Point. From Punta Castillo, or Castle Point, the coast bends
somewhat towards the north, as far as the Point and Morro de la Pena, which is.
distant from the former 4 miles; and from thence it inclines somewhat towards the
south, to Punta Gorda, whence it forms a bay, the shores of which are beachy and
very low, to Point Guachin, or Guaranache ; this point is formed by a piece of land,
cliffy and high, which rises above this low land, and is insulated by it. In the
bottom and middle of the bay, there is a small scarped point of very little extent,
ealled Punta de las Minas. From Punta Gorda to that of Guachin it is 63 miles.

From Punta Guachin the shore continues low and flat to Punta del Escarceo, or
Eddy Point, where it rises a little: the distance from one to the other is 34 miles.
Point Escarceo forms a front, extending half a mile about it, the western point of
which is called Point Cardon, from whence the coast, which is a low sandy beach,
trends 8.W. about 2 miles to Punta de Araya, upon which there are a few small:
houses inhabited by persons employed in the salt works. The whole of the coast
from Point Cayman to Point Escarceo, has a reef extending along it, about half a-
mile broad, but it extends 4 miles westward from the latter, and forms what is called
the Shoal of Araya, the south edge of which lies about half a mile from the Point of
Araya and will be cleared by bringing the most southerly of the houses on it to
bear (East) E.;.N. If necessary, you may run along the shore to the southward, at
2 cables’ length ; for although the sandy shore is flat, at that distance there are 6:
fathoms water. This beachy shore continues for 2 miles about 8.S.E., to Punta de
Piedras, or Rock Point, which is formed by the western extremity of the ridge of,
Guaranache.

Point Piedras shows a front of about half a mile, and then unites itself to the high
land of the ridge: on the south point of it there is a sanctuary or chapel, dedicated:
to the Virgin of Agua Santa. The coast continues in the same direction of 8.S.E. to
Point Barrigon, which at first is low and sandy, and afterwards scarped or cliffy, but
all of it so clean, that you may safely run by it, at a cable’s length distance. This
coast forms the little Bay of Araya, on the south point of which, where the high
land of Point Barrigon begins, there is a fort. From Point Barrigon the coast
continues scarped and very clean about S.E., 2 miles to Point Caney; it then turns
to the E.S8.E. for a long mile to Punta de Arenas, or Sandy Point, which is the most
southerly point of this coast, and the northern point of the Gulf of Cariaco. From
Point Caney a bank extends along the coast as far as half a mile south of Sandy
Point. ’ Here we suspend our description of the coast and return to the island of
Margarita.

THE ISLAND of MARGARITA.—The greatest length of this island is, from
east to west, about 37 miles: it is mountainous, and when seen from a distance on the
north, it appears like two islets, from a space of low swampy land in the middle of
it. On the eastern part there are several heights, which in clear weather, may be
seen from Cape Three Points, and on the western part a ridge of heights, called
Macanao. The east point is named Ballena Point, and lies nearly on the meridian of
the Morro of Chacopata; the coast runs thence about N.N.W. 3 W. to Cape de la
Isla, a distance of 13 miles, forming the N.E. front of the island, the whole of which
is clean, only sending off a bank about 3 cables in breadth. From Cape de la Isla
the coast trends nearly §.W. by W. to Punta de Galera, a space of 7 miles, all clean :
from Point Galera to that of Maria Libre is about S.W.S., 31 miles, Between.

LOS FRAYLES. ih

‘these points there is a large bay, with-a bank projecting from the shores of it, which
‘In the centre, runs out nearly a mile; on the shore, opposite the widest part of the
‘bank, stands an Indian village.

From Point Maria Libre to Point de la Tuna it is 11} miles (W. £N.) W.2N.;
in the intermediate space there is a very large bay running in about 5 miles, the
coast of which is very clean, and presents no other danger than the bank which
borders it, and which, at the broadest part, extends only about half a mile from the
land: the shore at the extremity of the bay isa low swampy beach. From Point
de la Tuna the coast runs (W. by 8.) W.S.W. 2 W., 8 miles to Punta del Tigre, the
whole sufficiently clear to be coasted within half a mile. From the latter point, the
coast bends more to the southward for 24 miles, to the Morro of Robledar, and thence
(S. by W. 3 W.) 8S. by W. 4 W., 45 miles to Point Arenas, or Sandy Point, which is
the western extremity of the island. The bank which surrounds the coast, extends
about 1} mile from this western side of the island between the Morro of Robledar and
Point Arenas. To the N.W. of this front, about 5$ miles, lies the eastern edge of a
rocky shoal that has 45 fathoms on its shallowest part; the direction of this shoal is
N.W. and S8.E., extending about 3-miles. The channel between this shoal and the
island is wide and free, and the least depth of water in it is 5} fathoms, sandy
bottom.

At 3% miles (S.W.) 8.W.48. from Point Ballena are the Point and Morro of
Moreno; ‘the coast between forms a spacious bay, on the north side of which stands
the town of Pamtapar. Nearly in a line between the two points, and about midway,
lies an islet, called Blanco, which is very clean, and the passage between it and the
land very safe. In all this bay, the depths are from 6 to 9 fathoms, sand, at the
distance of two-thirds of a mile from the beach: with the breeze blowing fresh, it is
rather exposed, as there is no shelter; and, although such a wind does not send in
much sea, it will be advisable to anchor in such a position, that in case of need there
may be room to run freely for the Morro Moreno, which, if necessary, may be passed
cat the distance of a cable’s length on the east part.

From the Morro Moreno the direction of the coast is (S.W.3 W.) S.W.2W., 6 miles
to Punta de Mosquitos; on the north side of the bay between these points stands the
Town of la Mar, so called, but more correctly a cluster of straw huts. The coast from
Moreno to Mosquito Point is so foul, that it would be dangerous to go within 2 miles
of it,—the same character may be given to that further westward. From Mosquito
Point to Punta de Mangles, or Mangrove Point, the distance is 104 miles; the coast
lies about W.28. and E.2N. (true), but it is very foul, from a rocky shoal that runs
off about a mile. From Mangrove Point, the coast trends to the north-westward,
forming a bay between it and the Punta de Piedras, or Rock Point, a distance of
3% miles: from the latter point it trends more to the northward, forming another
bay with Point Pozo, which is distant from Piedra 62 miles; and from Point Pozo the
coast trends about W. by N., a distance of 10% miles, to Point Arenas, which, as before
said, is the west point of the island. All the coast from Mangrove Point to Arenas is
foul, like the anterior, and not to be approached with safety within 2 miles.

LOS FRAYLES.—About 9 miles to the eastward and northward of Margarita
lies a group of islets, called Los Frayles (the Friars), of which the most southerly
one is the largest; they are all very clean, except the most northerly one, which is
surrounded by a reef, extending about 2 cables’ length from it.

SOLA ISLAND.—About 12 miles (N.E.}E.) N.E. from the largest of the Frayles,
and 20 miles (N. 63° E.) N.E. by E. 3 E. from Cape de la Isla lies the little Island of
Sola, very clean. From Sola to the Testigos the distance is 27 miles (N. 83° E.)
E.by N. The passages between the Testigos and Sola, Sola and the Frayles, the
Frayles and Margarita, are also clean, and ships of all sizes may navigate them in
any kind of weather.

COCHE ISLAND.—In the channel formed by Margarita and the coast of the
main land are two large islands: the most easterly is named El Coche (the Coach),

CUBAGUA ISLAND.

and that on the west Cuagua or Cubagua. Coach Island is low, lying N.W. and S.E.,
surrounded by a rocky shoal and a reef, which extends from the N.W. and 8.E. points
about 14 mile, so as to form two channels; that on the north with the island Mar-
garita, which in its narrowest part is 2 miles in width, and that on the south with the
main land, of nearly similar breadth in its most confined part. In either of them the
passage is perfectly clear; the bottom is good, and a ship may ride at anchor in them
as securely as in port.

CUBAGUA ISLAND is less than Coach Island, and lies nearly east and west:
from the eastern point there is a shoal and a reef running out abouta mile. The
north and south sides are very clean. On the west side a rocky shoal extends about
one third of a mile from the shore; this, like Coach Island, forms two channels, one
to the northward with the Island Margarita, and one to the southward with the main
land: both are very free. In the narrowest part of the northern channel, which
is between the shoal and reef, stretching off from the eastern point of Cubagua, and
the shoal which stretches off from the Punta de Mangles of Margarita, the breadth
is 3 miles.

To navigate in the channel to the northward of these islands, it is only necessary
to give a berth to the shoals which extend from the shore of Margarita, that which
projects from the N.W. point of the Island Coche, and that which stretches off from
the east point of the Island Cubagua; but, for greater certainty, you may bring the
little and most northerly point of Cubagua to bear (West) W.+5S., and run with it
in that direction until you are well past the Punta de Mangles, when you may edge
a little to the northward; it being well understood, at the same time, that the north
point of Cubagua may be passed at the distance of a cable’s length, without any risk.

To sail through the South Channel, you have to keep close to the Islas de Caribes,
and de Lobos, which will clear the bank that stretches off from the 8.E. end of Coach
Island; and then shape a westerly course, without any fear for the three islets that
lie to the northward of Punta de la Tuna, and which are called Islotes de la Tuna:
these are very clean, and you may pass between them, if necessary. From these islets
westward, the channel widens considerably, and consequently requires less caution.

His Majesty’s sloop, “ Sapphire,” A. Montgomerie, Esq., commander, when beating
to windward in the South Passage, on the 29th April, 1821, struck on a shoal of
15 feet water; the Morro of Chacopata bearing about K.S.E. $ E., distant 23 miles,
and the west end of the Caribes Island about 8. ¢ E., 2 miles.

In all these channels it is advisable to anchor at night, in whatever part of them
you may happen to be, whether your object is to go to Araya or to Cumana; as the
current would perhaps carry you to leeward; and, besides, it is not proper to run for
these ports without daylight, when you can see to give a berth to the shoal of Point
Araya, and also to that which extends from Cumana.

To anchor at Araya, the only thing to guard against is the shoal off Point Araya,
which, as before observed, stretches 24 miles to the N.W. from it. This may be done
by standing on rather more than 3 miles to the westward of the point before you
alter your course to the southward; or, what is the same, not to steer at all to the
southward until you have lost soundings. Butif it should be thought preferable to
be guided by landmarks, endeavour not to cross the parallel of Punta Escarceo, until
the most westerly peak of four,—formed by the Mountain of Macanao—on the Island
of Margarita, bears to the eastward of north; with the understanding that, when that
peak bears (N. 5° E.) N.1E., the edge of the shoal will be cleared about half a mile.
The Island of Cubagua will also afford a mark; for, by bringing the west point of it
to bear (N.E.) N.E. 1N., you will pass 2 miles to to the westward of the shoal.*

is an extract from the Log Book.

According to what has been stated, a ship bound to Araya, coasting along the main
land, and between it and the Coach and Cubagua Islands, should pass about a mile
north of Punta del Kscarceo, and steer west, until the west point of Cubagua bears

getting so far to leeward, it may be done by steering west, until the most westerly
peak of Macanao bears (N. 5° KE.) N.3E., or rather more easterly; then bring her
head to the south, and she will pass within one mile of it. The southerly course must
be kept to get abreast of the southernmost of the houses on Point Araya, then haul to
the wind to fetch into the little bay of Araya, which will be known by the fort on the
south side, and the sanctuary or chapel of Nuestra Senora de Agua Santa on the north
side and on the south slope of Guaranache. Either in the bay, or on any part of this
coast, as far as Point Arenas, a ship may anchor in any convenient depth, and, if you
choose, within a cable’s length of the shore.

In the same manner, all those who have to double Point Araya from the north, that
is, from Cubagua, or from Margarita, ought not to cross the parallel of Escarceo,
without attending to the preceding directions; and if, by accident, those bearings
should be brought on before getting into that parallel, steer immediately in the opposite
direction, until you have Punta Escarceo bearing due (east) E.1N. of you, and then
to the south, so as to be able to haul to the wind on getting abreast of the last house
to the southward, on Point Araya. The soundings may also guide those who come
from the northward, by keeping without them altogether, or by going into no less
than 36 fathoms, until they have crossed the parallel before mentioned.

There is a shallow bank and a reef stretching out about half a mile to the south
from Point Arenas, which has been already spoken of, as the north point of the
GULF of CARIACO. This gulf which runs in to the eastward about 35 miles, and
is in general about 8 miles wide, may be considered as a spacious and well sheltered
harbour, for you may anchor in any part of it, the deepest water being 40 fathoms.
‘The shores of it are very clean, and may be approached to about half a mile, except
in the vicinity of Cumana, where a shallow bank extends about two-thirds of a mile
from the river. On the north coast there are two harbours, calied Laguna Chica and
Laguna Grande, or Obispo (Bishop’s Lagoon). ‘The first is very small, but the latter
is spacious, and besides having from 9 to 20 fathoms water, is so clean, that to
navigate it, you have only to keep clear of what is seen.

Within the gulf there is no town of consequence, or any inducement for ships
from Europe to visit it, as the point to which all of them direct their course is
Cumana, situated on the south point of the mouth of the gulf; this point is low and
sandy, with a bank running from it to the west and south, so steep, that from 11
fathoms there is immediately 5, and from 5 a vessel may immediately be aground.
The edge of the bank, that is, the shallow water running eastward, keeps almost east
and west with the point, and extends along about four miles to Point Delgada, whence
it turns to 8.E. with the coast, narrowing towards the vicinity of Monte Blanco;
where it terminates on a clean shore.

The edge of the bank that runs to the southward from the point is very close to

the shore, and forms with it the mouth of the River Manzanares, whence it increases
in breadth to the S.W.; so that N.W. of the Morro Colorado, or Red Morro, a little

wind; at 4h. 25m., the ship, under a press of sail, running at the rate of 10 knots, 8.8. W., being
about 6 miles from Point Araya, and (by the leadsmen in both chains) in 9 fathoms water,
suddenly shoaled, and immediately struck the ground; shortened and furled sails; hoisted out
the boats, and sounded in every direction round the ship; laid the stream anchor out N.W. in
3 fathoms; at 6h., parted the stream cable, of which 90 fathoms were lost,—Point Araya then

CUMANA.—The town and fort of Cumana stand on the high land of the point,
on the banks of the Manzanares: on the low land, and nearer to the beach, is an
Indian town, separated from Cumana by the river. The anchorage is nearly in front
of and to the west of the river’s mouth. To fetch it, steer from Punta del Caney for
the Red Morro, but not more to windward until the bank of Punta de Arenas is
cleared; when this is done, keep to the wind and steer a direct course for the mouth
of the river, on the south point of which stands a fort. Keep the lead going, and on
getting a depth of water suitable for the size of the vessel, let go an anchor, with
- which, and a small one carried on shore, the ship will be moored. But, if the wind
be scant, or the current sets the vessel to leeward, so as to be obliged to beat up
to the anchorage, it is necessary, in order to keep clear of the outer point of the
shoal, not to stand to the southward, further than to bring the Castle of San Antonio
to bear east ; the castle is situated on the most elevated part of the town of Cumana.
To the northward there is no danger, and the tack may be prolonged as far as is
thought to be advantageous.

To the southward of the Red Morro, and somewhat to the eastward of Point
Piedras, the River Bordones falls into the sea. From Point Piedras the coast runs
about (West) W. ;S.; in some places scarped, and in others a sandy beach, for
82 miles to Puerto Escondido, or Hidden Port, which is a bay formed by the coast,
running in about half a mile, and three cables wide at the entrance; in the middle of
it there are 44 fathoms sand; but nearer to the shore, only 3 and 2; off the west
point there are some rocks, which may be avoided by keeping at little more than
a cable’s length from the point.

From the west point of Puerto Escondido, the shore runs about (West) W. z&.,
11 mile to Point Campanarito, which is searped and clean, except one sunken rock,
about half a cable’s length from the shore, and two or three cables’ lengths to the
westward of the west point of Puerto Escondido.

From Point Campanarito to the Morro and signal-tower of Mochima, the distance
is only three quarters of a mile; between the two points there is a very fine bay,
varying in depth of water from 16 to 44 fathoms, which is to be found within a
cable’s length of the shore. This bay is remarkably clean, except that N.W. from
Point Campanarito, there are a few rocks, extending rather less than half a cable’s
length from it; but it is advisable not to pass at less than one cable’s length of it.

MOCHIMA HARBOUR.—About W.S.W. from the signal-tower of Mochima,
there is a little tongue of land forming the east point of the Harbour of Mochima,
which is capacious, handsome, and well-sheltered ; the shore is indented with several
little bays, or coves, which form natural docks. The depth of water is very regular,
nowhere exceeding 14 fathoms, or being less than 43 fathoms; the latter from 1 to
14 cable’s length from the shore, which is generally very clean. Take care to pass a
cable and a half’s length from every visible obstruction, and all danger will be
avoided. ‘To these advantages may be added that of free ingress and egress with the
trade wind, altogether making it the best harbour in all this part of America, and
indeed one of the best in the world.

PUERTO DE MANARE.—About a mile to the westward of Mochima is the
Harbour of Manare, which is also an excellent one; the depth of water is from
14 to 43 fathoms, the latter at half a cable’s length from its shores, and these are very
clean. As the entrance is ‘wide, a vessel may sail in with the trade wind at any
time, and quit it with equal facility. The west point of this harbour is called
Cape Manare.

From Cape Manare the coast trends about W.S.W. nearly 13 mile to Punta de
Tigrillo, which has a reef around it, stretching off to about a cable’s length from
the shore; the coast hence inclines to the south and eastward for 23 miles, when
it turns to W. by S., 5 miles, to Punta Gorda, the western extremity of the Bay

PUERTO DE MANARE.

GULF OF SANTA FE. let

of Tigrillo; at the eastern extremity of the bay there is a canal communicating with
the harbour of Mochima. In this bay there are three islands; the first, or the
easternmost, is called Venados; the second, or middle one, Caraca del Este; and the
third, Caraca del Oeste; all the shores of the bay, as well as of these islands, are
very clean; only at the north point of the island Venados, which is called Punta
Campanaria, there is a rock about a cable’s length off, and a small shallow bank,
running off about the same distance from the 8.W. end of the island. All the
passages or straits between these islands, and that between them and the main land,
are safe and navigable for ships of any class; and although some of them are
narrow, yet the soundings in all of them are such, that anchor may be let go in
case of necessity.

The only danger to be guarded against is a rocky shoal, called the Caracas, lying
to the north-westward of the Eastern Caraca, at the distance of rather more than a
mile; this shoal is about half a mile in length from east to west, and presents no
danger ; for in passing between it and the Caraca Isles, it will be avoided by keeping
near to the latter; and, in going outside of it, keeping to the northward of Point
Manare, will clear it in that direction.

GULF OF SANTA FE.—To the southward of Punta Gorda, about 3 miles, lies
Punta del Escarpado Roxo, or Red Cliff Point; these form the entrance of the Gulf
of Santa Fé, which extends about 6 miles inland towards the east. The shores of it
throughout are very clean, but at the entrance only, about one third of a mile from
the north coast, lies a fowl rock, which should not be approached within 13 or 2 cables’
length: the depth of water in the gulf is from 30 to 20 fathoms, muddy bottom.

From the point of Escarpado Roxo the coast inclines to the southward and then
to the westward for 23 miles, to Point de la Cruz, forming a bay that is very clean,
and affords an excellent anchorage, called the Bay of Santa Cruz. About 1 mile
W.N.W. from the latter point lies the easternmost of the little islands called the
Arapos, which are about halfa mile in extent in that direction: they are very clean,
except in the strait between them, whichis impassable, on account of a bank and
reef that joins them together. The passage between the eastern isle and the coast is
free from danger: there are two small rocks at the west part of the western isle, but
they are also very clean.

From Point de Cruz the coast continues westward, inclining a little to the south,
for nearly 4 miles, to Punta Comona, the whole of which is clean, and navigable within
2 cables’ length of the land without any risk. To the westward of Point Comona, at
the distance of 2 short miles, is Punta Pertigalete, the land between forming a beau-
tiful bay, in which there are 12 fathoms water, at a cable’s length from the shore.
The bottom of this bay is a sandy beach, and two little rivulets run into it; it is all
very clean except on the eastern side, which sends off a reef about a cable’s length
from the shore. In front of this bay, and about 3 cables’ length north from Punta
Pertigalete, lies the south coast of the Isla de Monos, or Guaracaro, the shores of which
are steep and clean; but at about 2 cables’ length from the north part of it there is a
rock, which is foul, with a reef, which must not be approached nearer than half a
cable’s length. The strait between this rock and Isla de Monos is very clean, with 26
fathoms water in it: to pass through it you ought to keep nearest to the island. The
passage between the island and the main is also very clean, and has 45 to 50 fathoms
in its middle, and nearly the same depth close to the island, which it is best to keep
near to unless you wish to pass in the middle of the strait.

At 14 mile west from Punta Pertigalete is Punta de Guanta, and between them is
the Cove of Pertigalete, in which are several islets, and a rivulet runs into it. If any
one wishes to anchor in this cove, it is necessary to avoid the western part of Point
Pertigalete, passing it at a cable’s length at least, to clear a reef which stretches from
that part. It is also necessary to beware of a reef and shoal that project out in the
centre of the bay, but they will be cleared by not getting anything to the westward
of the eastern part of the first islet to the northward. Attending to this a vessel may

12 BARCELONA.

anchor north from the mouth of the riyulet in 43 fathoms of water, about 15 cable’s
length from the eastern beach.

Westward from Punta de Guanta, and at the distance of 3 miles, is the Punta de
Bergantin: between the two, and about a mile from the first, is the little Bay of
Guanta, in the mouth of which are several islets and rocks, forming very narrow
passes, although with deep water, and very clear. Within the bay there are from lo
to 9 fathoms water, which is found at half a cable’s length from the shore. On the
western front of the bay there is a reef, extending off about 2 cables’ length; this will
be avoided by running along by the eastern shore, which is very clean.

The Punta de Bergantin is foul, with a reef, which stretches out about a cable’s
length, and extends to the southward nearly a mile: on the S.W. side of the point
there is an islet, so very foul all round as not to leave a clear passage between it and
the point. From the latter the coast continues trending westward, forming the Bay
of Bergantin, the south coast of which is very foul, with a reef and shoal that continue
to border the coast to the westward as far as the Morro of Barcelona.

BARCELONA.—The Morro of Barcelona is high land, lying north and south,
about a mile in extent, and joined to the coast by a narrow isthmus or tongue of sand,
rather more than a mile in length. ‘The distance between Punta de Bergantin and
the Morro of Barcelona is about 43 miles: and the coast which turns to the south-
ward, forms a great bay called Pozuelos. Along all this tract of coast, which is a
sandy beach, and very low land, the shoa/ extends about a mile from the shore: and,
therefore, in navigating it ships should steer direct from Punta de Bergantin to the
north part of the Morro, which is clean and steep-to, and may be passed within a
cable’s length; or should it be thought advisable to enter the bay, the lead must be
kept going, and care taken not to go into less than 8 fathoms water on sandy bottom.
The western coast of the Morro of Barcelona is foul, and should not be passed nearer
than 2 cables’ length. From the north point of this Morro to Punta Maurica to the
southward of it, the distance is about 4 miles ; and the coast, which is a low sandy
beach, turns to the eastward, and in it the river of Barcelona disembogues, forming
a large bank of sandy mud. About 14 mile inland, and on the west bank of the river,
stands the City of Barcelona. To anchor in this bay, the lead will be the best guide ;
for being very shoal, every ship may anchor in a berth suitable to its draught of
water.

CHIMANA AND OTHER ISLES.—Of this coast, between Cape Manare and
the Morro of Barcelona, besides the islands already mentioned, there are several
others called the Piendas, the Chimanas, and the Borrachas. The Great Picuda lies
to the westward of the west Caraca, with which it forms a channel rather more than
a mile wide, and so clean that you have only to beware of a sunken rock that lies
about 2 cables’ length east from the east point of Picuda. This island lies 8. W. and
N.E., a little more than a mile in length: its shores are very clean, but to the north-
ward of its extreme east point there are two rocks, the first about 1 cable’s length,
and the other 3 cables’ length off.

About S.W. by W., 33 miles from the Great Picuda, lies the second Picuda; an
islet of a circular figure, about 3 cables’ length in extent, and very clean. About
3.S.E. from the last, at the distance of one mile, is the East Chimana, another islet
less than it, and equally clean. ‘Two miles further west is the east point of the
Second Chimana, which lies east and west, and is about 13 mile in extent: this also
is very clean. Off its east end are two small islets, the nearest being about 1 cable’s
length off, and the other 5 cables: on the west side is another small islet, at a cable’s
length distance,

At 2 cables’ length south-westward from the west point of the Second Chimana,
lies the eastern point of the Great Chimana, which island is of a very irregular figure,
and its greatest extent, nearly east and west, is 33 miles. To the westward of it,
about one-third of a mile, lies the West Chimana, joined to the great one by a shoal

BLANQUILLA. 1

of rocks and sand, extending a full half mile to the northward from the north part of
the Great Chimana. Upon this shoal, and midway between the two islands there is
a small islet; and also another at a very short distance from the west part of
the West Chimana. Finally, to the southward of the eastern end of the Great
Chimana, lies the South Chimana, which in its greatest extent from N.E. to 8.W.
measures 2 miles. his island forms two channels; one on the north with the Great
Chimana, about a cable anda half in width, and perfectly clean, with a depth of
20 fathoms, muddy bottom ; and the other to the south, between the island and Punta
del Bergantin, of half a mile in width, also very clean, for in passing through it
you have only to avoid the reef that runs off from Punta del Bergantin about a
cable’s tength. Between the Great and the South Chimana there are various small
islets, but all very clean.

From what has been said of these islands and islets, it will be seen that they are
clean and navigable, the only dangers being the rock on the east of the Great Picuda,
and the shoal in the channel between the Great and the West Chimana ; consequently
all the passages between the islands and islets are navigable, although some of them,
from being very narrow, are not so eligible for large ships; this circumstance, how-
ever, is a matter of choice for the navigator; in other respects he has no hidden peril
to guard against.

The ISLAND BORRACHA lies about 3 miles to the westward of the West
Chimana. It is about 2 miles in extent, nearly north and south, and 13 at its
greatest breadth. All the east and north sides of it are very clean; but on the N.W.
there is a very foul rocky bank, with very little water over it, and on which are several
little islets: all these should be passed on the outside, at 2 cables’ length distance from
the westernmost. About south from the south extremity of thisisland there isa large
sand-bank, on which there is an islet, called Borracho, and two little islets, called
los Borrachitos: the latter are distant from the Borracho 2 large miles; they should
always be passed on the south side, at not less than 3 cables’ length distance, for
between them and the Borracha, as well as between it and the principal island, the
water is very shallow.

From the anchorage of Barcelona, the direction of the coast is west, inclining a
little to the south, a distance of 32 miles, to the Morro of Unare; whence it trends
to the northward of west, a distance of 57 miles, to Cape Codera. The whole of this
coast is low land, and upon it are seen the Morros of Piritu, and of Unare, 8 miles
distant from each other. All along it the water is shallow, but cleau, so that in
running along by it, no other guide than the lead is necessary for navigating it. ‘There
are only two islands lying off it, called Piritu, which are 12 miles to the westward
of the anchorage of Barcelona, and rather more than 3 miles out from the shore.
These isles lie nearly east and west, are low, like the coast, and. have a reef, extend-
ing nearly 13 cable’s length from them. ‘There is a passage between them, but it is
hazardous, on account of the reefs which stretch out from both islands, and which
leave a clear channel of only 2 cables’ length wide, with a depth of 55 fathoms. The
passage between them and the coast is fit for ships of any size, and in going through
it no other guide than the lead is necessary.

BLANQUILLA, &c.—Nearly (North) N. + W., 40 miles from the N.W. point
of Margarita, lies the southernmost of seven islands, called los Hermanos or the
Brothers; they are all clean, and so steep that there are no soundings in the straits
between them, and they extend about 7 miles from south to north.

Seven miles to the westward of the northernmost Hermanos is the Island Blan-
quilla, in extent about 6 miles from north to south, and 3 from east to west; it is very
flat, and entirely desert ; but its shores are very clean, with the exception of the S.W.
side, which has several reefs and rocks, extending off about 3 cables’ length from the
shore, and some points on the west side; and off the north point also there are some
single rocks, about 2 cables’ length from the shore. On the N.W. side there is
anchorage in from 18 fathoms, at a mile from the shore, to 6 or 7, at 3 cables’

14 TORTUGA.

length from it. All the bottom of the anchorage is sand. At about the middle of
the western coast, at alittle cove in the beach, there is a cazimba, spring or rill,
whence fresh water may be obtained.

TORTUGA.—Forty-six miles to the westward of Margarita is the Isla Tortuga
(Turtle Island) which is about 12 miles long from east to west, and 5} wide at its
greatest breadth ; all the Hast and N.E. sides are clean, except at Point Delgada, the
N.E. extremity, where a reef extends off about 2 cables’ length. The south side is
also very clean, but at the eastern point there are several islets: the west point of the
island is named Punta de Arenas; from which to the north point, called Punta Norte,
the water is very shallow, so that it will be necessary to keep the lead going in passing
that space. On this side there is, first, Cayo Anguila, which is half a mile distant from
the coast, and the channel between is very foul; second, Cayo Herradura (Horse
Shoe Cay), forming with the coast a channel a mile in width, but which ought not
to be attempted with a large vessel: from the N.E. point of this cay a rocky reef
projects out about 23 cables’ length eastward; third, Cayos del Fondeadero, or
‘Tortuaguillos, two in number, entirely surrounded by a bank, with little water on it.
The anchorage of Tortguga is between the Tortuaguillos, and the coast of the prin-
cipal island ; it may be entered from the S.W., or on the north, through the channel
formed by the Tortuaguillos, and the Herradura. In all this anchorage, and in the
channels leading to it, there are no more than 6 to 7 fathoms, on sandy bottom in the
middle of it ; to direct yourself into it, the only care required is not to have less than
6 fathoms water.

FRONTIER ISLANDS, FROM CAPE CODERA
TO CAPE ROMAN.

CAPE CODERA, a part well known on this coast, is a very round Morro, or hill,
on the north of which, to the distance of a mile, a tongue of low land extends, so
clean that at half a cable’s length from it there are 9 fathoms water, on sandy
bottom. This tongue forms a very fine anchorage to the westward, called Puerto
Corsarios, or Privateer’s Harbour; to enter it you have only to double the west point
of the tongue of land, which has a rock above water very close to it, and anchor, so
soon as you find yourself sheltered from the wind, in any depth that suits you, with
the understanding, that at 2 cables’ length from the shore, tnere are 7 fathoms,
on sandy bottom. At the south extremity of the bay, for the space of about 3 cables’
length, the coast is a low, swampy beach; whence to the westward it is foul, sending
off a reef half a cable’s length from the shore. The west point of the bay, called
Caracoles, has on the north side a rock close to it, from which a reef extends about a
cable’s length.

From Cape Codera the high mountains of Caracas are visible, extending to the
westward, many leagues. (N. 8° W.) N. by W., 14 miles from the Cape lies an zs/et,
which has the appearance of a ship under sail; it is very clean, except about a musket-
shot to the north, where there are two sunken rocks, having between them and the
islet, a channel of great depth; this rock is called the Sentinel.

From Caracoles Point the direction of the coast is (W.N.W.) W.N.W. + W. for the
distance of 94 miles to Point Maspa whence it turns to (W. by 8.) W.S.W. 3 W.,
2* miles to Point Chuspa, which is the eastern extremity of an anchorage of the same
name. The whole of this space sends off a reef, which at Point Maspa extends a mile
from shore, and terminates at Point Chuspa. Ships should not run along shore at a
less distance than 2 miles.

THE PORT OF LA GUAYRA. 15

CHUSPA BAY.—The anchorage in this bay is excellent: from Chuspa Point,
which is the N.E. point of the bay, the shore runs about 8.W. for the space of
12 mile, to the mouth of the river of the same name, on the east bank of which stands
the Town of Chuspa, about 2 cables’ length from the beach. From the mouth of the
river the coast rounds to the westward for the distance of 13 mile to Point Curuau,
to the southward of which, at about one-third of a mile inland, stands the Town of
Curuau. From Point Chuspa to that of Curuau all the shore is very clean, and the
only guide necessary for entering the anchorage is the lead; but from Point Curuau
the coast is very foul with a reef running 2 cables’ length off, and continuing so far
as Punta del Frayle, or Friar’s Point, which has a rock of the same name, about a
cable's length from it. This point lies nearly 4 miles to the westward of Point
Curuau, and between them there is a projection of cliff to the northward, called de
Sabana, and to the north of it lies a bank, the south edge of which is little more than a
mile from the shore ; its greatest extent is a mile from S.E. to N.W., on a bottom of
rock ; and although in general it has from 9 to 45 fathoms water on it, yet there are
some spots with not more than 4 and 2§ fathoms, for which reason it should be
carefully avoided. It lies 3 miles from the anchorage of Chuspa; and to enter that
anchorage, it is necessary to pass close to the Point of ‘Chuspa; you will thereby
avoid the shoal; and also if you take care to be to the northward of the parallel of
Point Chuspa, before you cross the meridian of Curuau.

From Punta del Frayle the coast trends to westward, inclining somewhat to the
south for the distance of 29 miles to the anchorage of La Guayra; and along the
whole space a ship may be anchored at half a mile from the shore, or even at the
distance of a musket-shot.

WACUTA.—About three miles to the eastward of La Guayra is the little village
of Macuta, situated in a small bay of that name, and is an excellent place for
watering. The water is procured from three iron pipes or spouts, distant about
84 feet from the beach. There is good anchorage all over the bay, and the soundings
are very regular in approaching the watering place. On going in towards the
village, keep the watering place ina line with the N.W. corner of the Chapel, and
the highest cocoa-nut tree over the east angle of the fort west of the village. There
is a depth of 20 fathonis at about three-quarters of a mile from the shore, with the
street of the village close to the watering place open or end on, and the eastern-
most point about a sail’s breadth open of the point to the westward of it.—(Capt. J.
Wilson, R.N., 1819.)

THE PORT of LA GUAYRA, on account of its commerce, is the principal
port on this coast; it cannot properly be called either a harbour or a roadstead, but a
bend in the open coast, between Point Carabullera on the east, and Cape Blanco on
the west; consequently it has no shelter from the N.E. and N.W. quarters, and the
east wind, which is constant, sends in a heavy swell. Hence, vessels moor with an
anchor and hawser out astern to the westward, to prevent them from lying athwart
the sea, when the wind moderates or falls calm. The bottom is good holding ground,
and at a cable’s length from the shore there are nearly 3 fathoms water. At this
anchorage it is seldom that any other wind than the regular breeze is experienced ;
but sometimes it changes to the westward, in which case the hawser must be shifted
forward: the land wind seldom blows here, but there are frequent squalls from the
§.E. during the rainy season. In 1821, nineteen vessels were totally wrecked here by
a northerly swell, although there was but little wind.

Captain F. Chamier says, “La Guayra cannot be called anything else thana
dangerous roadstead, but as the trade wind blows right along shore, by being
prepared, a ship may always, clear the land. The town and fortifications, which
may be distinguished at a long distance, mark the anchorage; the former bearing
S. by E., in a depth of 10 fathoms, at 13 mile from shore, is as secure as any other.
The rollers are very heavy, and oftentimes it is dangerous to attempt landing. The
ground is very bad for holding, and in a good strong sea breeze you may’expect to
bring your anchors home.”

16 OCUMARE COVE.

Captain G. G. Lennock, in his remarks on this place, observes, “that although,
during the hurricane of 1815, at the Leeward Islands, they did not experience any
wind here, yet there was a very heavy swell at the anchorage, which drove the vessels
from their anchor on shore and dashed them to pieces against the rocks.”

In proceeding towards the anchorage from sea, the mariner will have a good mark
in a very high and sharp peak, called the Peak of Cares, situated inland, about
20 miles to the eastward; and to the westward of it is another, called the Peak of
Niquatar, and thence a range of mountains running towards La Guayra, among
which the Silla de Caraccas (Saddle of Caraccas) and Mount Avila may be distin-
guished, the latter being nearly S.S.E. from the anchorage. But it is most advisable
to make the land well to windward, when there will be no risk in running down to
the anchorage.

From the anchorage of La Guayra the coast trends nearly W. by S., and is suffi-
ciently clean to run down at the distance of half a mile so far as the little harbour
of La Cruz, about 26 miles. The port of La Cruz isa little bay of about 13 cable
wide at the mouth, and 2 cables’ length in depth; it is very clean, having at half a
ship’s length from the shore, on all sides of it, 43 fathoms water. In the south part
of the interior of this harbour a river discharges; and at the east point, which is
called Point la Cruz, there is a rock close to it. This anchorage would be excellent
if it were larger; but as it is, small vessels only can use it.

From this port the coast continues about (W. by S.) W.S.W. 2 W., for the distance
of 23 miles, to the Bay or Cove of Cata; it is also very clean, and may be safely
approached within a mile, if you choose, Two leagues to the eastward of Cata Bay,
and 5 miles inland is a mountain called La Meseta (the Little Table); and about the
same distance inland on the meridian of Cata is another, named Mount Ocumare,
which will serve as landmarks, either for the Cove of Cata, or that of Ocumare
further to the west.

The Cove of Cata is half a mile wide at its entrance, and about the same in depth ;
at the east point there is an islet almost close to it, whence the coast trends to the
south to the bottom of the cove, where a river disembogues, forming a bank with
little water on it, which extends nearly a cable’s length from the shore. Every other
part of the cove is clean, and the depth of water from 25 to 44 fathoms; the latter
depth being found at 13 cable’s length from the beach.

OCUMARE COVE.—Two-thirds of a mile westward from the west point of Cata
is the eastern point of the Cove of Ocumare, which has also very good anchorage.
N.W. of the east point there is an islet, between which and the point there is a strait
of half a cable’s length in width, quite clear, and the least water in it is 63 fathoms.
In taking this anchorage pass close by the islet, and then to the southward, until you
are sheltered, when you may anchor in 63 fathoms, on sandy bottom, at about a
cable’s length to the southward of the islet. This cove is shallow, and the lead is a
good guide to it; care must however be taken, for as the anchorage is of little extent
from north to south, a large vessel may possibly touch the ground, unless attention
be paid to luff up, and deaden the headway in sufficient time. A river falls into
the bottom of the cove a little to the southward of the islet, and on its banks there
are some fishermen’s huts.

At 25 miles from the islet of Ocumare is the east point of the Cove, named the
Cienega of Ocumare which is nothing more than a swampy opening of the land,
having between two shallow parts of the reef a channel of a cable or 13 cable’s length
in breadth, with a depth of 12 to 44 fathoms in it. The western point of this cove is
formed by an insulated Morro, which rises on the low land. This anchorage is very
bad, and fit only for small coasting vessels.

PORTO TURIAMO.—At 1} mile to the westward of the Morro of Cienega, is
the harbour of Turiamo, which is excellent, and capable of receiving every class of
ships. At the exterior points it is about a mile wide, but decreases inwards to ? of a

PORTO CABELLO. 17

mile. It is 2 miles deep, from north to south, and in every part of it there are from
26 to 18 fathoms water, on mud and sand. All the shore of it is lined by a reef,
extending outward about one-third of a cable’s length; and if you take care to
approach no nearer than half a cable’s length, you will avoid all danger. At the
further extremity of the harbour the river Turiamo discharges itself on a sandy beach ;
and at a cable’s length off the N.W. part of the eastern point of the entrance there is
an islet of the same name.

PORTO CABELLO.—From the Port of Turiamo, westward, at the distance
of 9 miles, is Porto Cabello; this part of the coast is all clean, and may be run along
at amile distance. ‘There are several detached islets lying off it, to the eastward of
Porto Cabello; to sail among which, sufficient information will be obtained by con-
sulting the particular chart of this port, in which these islets are represented.

Porto Cabello is a harbour, formed by several islets and tongues of low land,
covered with mangroves. Ships must be warped into it, and those of the largest size
may be made fast to the mole, not requiring even the use of a plank or board to land
from them. The mouth of this channel opens into a spacious bay, with excellent
anchorage in from 11 to 5 fathoms, sandy mud, and well sheltered from the breeze.
Being in 5 fathoms, you will be near enough to the beach, which is rather foul with
rocks ; the best berth is about due west from the entrance of the port, at about 3 or
4 cables’ distance. In this harbour all the Spanish merchant-ships that heretofore
traded to La Guayra were careened and wintered; each ship, so soon as it had de-
livered its cargo at La Guayra, proceeded to Porto Cabello for greater sccurity, to
receive such repairs as were required, and took in part of the homeward-bound cargo;
she then returned to La Guayra to complete her lading. Porto Caballo had, therefore,
always a body of good shipwrights, &c., though not very numerous.

Light.— At Brava Point, Porto Cabello, a quadrangular lighthouse is erected
79 feet above the level of the sea; which exhibits a revolving light every 40 seconds,
consisting of alternate red and white flashes, which are visible about 14 miles.

Ships of war should only enter the harbour when it may be necessary to careen
them; for other purposes it is not only useless, but it is prejudicial; they should,
therefore, always remain in the bay, for the excessive heat in the harbour, the
mangroves with which it is surrounded, and the difficulty of keeping the crews from
intemperance, occasion almost immediate attacks of putrid fevers and the black vomit,
both of which make dreadful ravages among Europeans.

Captain James Murray, of H.M.S. “Valorous,” remarks, that “ there is a very good
and spacious anchorage between Isle Largo, or Long Island, and the main, about
33 miles to windward of Porto Cabello: there is plenty of room for a large fleet, in
10 or 12 fathoms water. You may sail into or out of this anchorage, between any
of the islands, but the best passage is considered to be round the east end of Long
Island, between it and the main, in order to take a berth well to windward. ‘The
‘Valorous’ anchored here on February 27th, 1823, in 11 fathoms, with the S.W.
end of Long Island bearing N.N.W., distant 2 cables’ length; the east end of
the island, East; and the Fort on the Hill above Porto Cabello, W.S.W., distant
3 or 4 miles. This is a very good place to get wood; and fresh water may be
procured from the river on the main, a little to leeward. It is necessary to be
cautious of a shoal that lies about a cable’s length to the southward of the west end of
Long Island.”

The coast to leeward or westward of Porto Cabello, forms an extensive bay, called
Tucacas, or Gulf of Triste, in which there are several islets, or small islands. With
the regular breeze it is a lee-shore; ships from Europe, not having occasion to call
here, should keep clear of it.

The north point of this bay, named Point Tucacas, bears (N. 28° W.) N.W. by N.

; N. from the entrance of Porto Cabello, and is 25 miles distant from it. Vessels
bound westward from Porto Cabello should steer about (N. hy W.)N. by W.2 W..

until they are abreast of Point Tucacas; or N.N.W., if they intend to keep close in
by the point, and take the anchorage near it, called Chichirivichi.

The BAY of TUCACAS, or GULF oF TRISTE, was surveyed by the officers of
H.M.S. “ Larne,” and from their notes we extract the following directions :—

“From Puerto Cabello to Point Tucacas, the course is N.W. by N., distant 25
miles; within this space is the Gulf of Triste, the shores of which are low, and
generally formed by a sandy beach, covered with mangroves ; the interior country is
formed of ranges of mountains thickly wooded, following the direction of the coast
round the gulf,

“The Spaniards in their survey of the coast, appear to have neglected this gulf,
as no directions are given for its navigation, and ships are cautioned that it should be
altogether avoided. The country, in its immediate vicinity, to the westward of
Puerto Cabello, was, at the time of the Spanish survey, inhabited only by a few
Indians; and it did not then, perhaps, appear probable that it would ever become a
place of commerce ; but the subsequent discovery, and working of the Bolivar Copper
Mines, to which it is the nearest part of the coast, has occasioned it being frequented
by many British ships; and the increasing value of the mines renders a correct
knowledge of its hydrography an object of great importance.

“The Bolivar Mines are about 60 miles from the coast: the copper is brought
down part of the way by mules, and the remainder by the River Aroa, the depth of
water in which, varying with the seasons, regulates the length of the land-carriage.
From Aroa it is conveyed to Isla Brava, near Tucacas (a distance of 6 miles), in a
small sloop, and there placed in a building called the Ore House, until it is shipped
for England. The ore thus embarked, in the year 1835, amounted to nearly five
thousand tons, furnishing cargoes for thirty-three vessels.

“There are three cays in the Gulf of Triste, named the North, Middle, and South
Cays. The North Cay, which lies N.E, and 8.W., is rather less than half a mile in
length, and is steep-to on all sides except the north, whence a reef runs out N.E.,
three-quarters of a mile, and in some parts of which are only 2 fathoms. It bears
N.W. by N., 20 miles from Puerto Cabello, and S. 3 E., distant 6 miles from Point
Tucacas. About 2 miles to the northward of this cay, we discovered a bank suddenly
shoaling from 24 to 17, 9, and 6 fathoms, coral bottom ; it appeared to be of con-
siderable extent, running N.W. by N., towards Point Tucacas; but we had not time
to investigate it sufficiently to determine its shoalest part.

“The Middle Cay lies N.E. and §.W., rather more than one-third of a mile in
length, and is steep-to on all sides except the north, whence a reef extends N.E., a
quarter of a mile, and which is the only danger to be avoided between it and the
North Cay, from which it bears S.W. ?S., distant 25 miles. In the mid-channel,
between the Middle and North Cays, there is a depth of 51 fathoms, shoaling
gradually to 15 fathoms, within a quarter of a mile of the North Cay, and to 12 and
14 within the same distance of the reef of the Middle Cay.

“The South Cay is about one-fifth of a mile in length, but has some rocks above
water, lying offits north and south points. Those off the south point are steep-to,
having 7 fathoms within half a cable’s length of them, and 12 or 14 fathoms within
a quarter of a mile. Its north ends bears 8.W. 2 S., distant nearly three-quarters of
a mile from the Middle Cay, towards which, from this point, a reef extends one-fifth
of a mile, having on its outer part 22 fathoms. About a quarter of a mile N.E. from
this reef there is another, 2 cables’ length in extent, and having only 3 fathoms onits
shoalest part, though between it and South Cay Reef there are 12 and 13: there is
also a channel between it and the Middle Cay, about 13 cable in breadth, having 12
and 10 fathoms inits centre. There are 7 fathoms within a ship’s length of the south
part of the Middle Cay. The latitude of the south point of the South Cay, as
determined from observations, is 10° 42’ 56” north.

“Isla Brava, off which the ships lie, and embark the copper ore, is the southern-

BAY OF TUCACAS. 19

most of a series of low swampy cays, which, covered with mangroves and rocky
points, and coral reefs towards the sea, form the north-west coast of the Gulf of
Triste. They are separated from the main land by extensive lagoons, which are
navigable only by boats. Behind these is a range of mountains of moderate height,
which, attaining their greatest elevation near the parallel of Isla Brava, slope gra-
dually down towards Point Tucacas: a deep notch in this range, bearing N.W. 4 W.
from Puerto Cabello, W.N.W. from the North Cay, and N.W. 1 N. from the South
Cay, forms an excellent mark for the anchorage, whence it bears N.W. 4 W.; and
some white cliffs, a little to the southward of this notch, in the same range of moun-
tains, when bearing N.W. by W. 3 W., are right over the Village of Tucacas.

“Punta Brava is the south-east point of Isla Brava, and has a reef, above water,
extending from it to the eastward about a quarter of a mile, which is steep-to upon
its south side, having 4 fathoms elose to the rocks; but on its eastern side it should
not be approached within a quarter of a mile, as a bank runs out from it, 2 cables’
length in that direction.

“ The Ore House is a white building, on the south side of Isla Brava, bearing west,
5? miles from the North Cay, N.W. by N., 4} miles from the Middle Cay, and
N.W. 3 W., 43 miles from the South Cay ; near this house is a wharf, which, having
16 feet water at its outer end, admits of a vessel lying along side and loading.

“The harbour is formed by an elbow-shaped reef, which, extending from Punta
Brava in a westerly direction, encloses sufficient space for one ship to moor alongside
the wharf in safety. On the elbow of the reef is a staff and vane buoy in 53 fathoms;
and on the west end, a black buoy, in 33 fathoms. From the latter buoy, the Ore
House wharf bears north, distant 60 fathoms, the depths between them being 20, 22,
24, and 18 feet. From the west side of the wharf, a reef extends along the south
side of Isla Brava, having 6 feet on its outer edge, about halfa cable’s length from
the shore. There is also a rocky coral shoal, of 9 feet, with the Ore House bearing
N.E. by E., distant a quarter of a mile; the staff and vane buoy E. by N., one-third
ofamile. There are 5 fathoms within half a cable’s length to the southward of
the reef.

“In proceeding towards the anchorage of Isla Brava from the eastward, pass
between the North and Middle Cays, and a W. by N. course will lead towards the
staff aud vane buoy, which steer for, as soon as seen, passing close to the southward
of it, and then steer so as to pass close to the southward of the black buoy. If no
other ship is alongside the wharf, you may let go the anchor when about 20 fathoms
to the westward of it, and warpin. ‘The best anchorage in the roads, is with the Ore
House bearing north, in 7 fathoms.

“From Boca Aroa to Tucacas, the soundings decrease regularly towards the shore,
having 3 fathoms about three-quarters of a mile from the beach. But to the north-
ward of Punta Brava the soundings are very irregular, there being in many places
12 fathoms close to the reefs, and again, spots of 5 and 6 fathoms at upwards of a
mile from the shore. When a ship is coming in, a flag is hoisted on the Ore House
by day, and a light by night.

“The village of Tucacas is 1} mile fromthe Ore House. It is built on a sandy
plain, which was formerly covered with mangroves, and is nearly surrounded by
swamps and lagoons. ‘The inhabitants obtain their supplies from Boca Aroa. The
village consists chiefly of Indian huts, but there are a few wooden houses belonging
to the officers of the Mining Association. Vessels of 8 feet water can go close up
to the wharf; but even these require a pilot, as the channel is impeded by several
shoals.

“ Boca Aroa, off which place ships formerly anchored and took in their cargoes,

was found to be very inconvenient on account of the heavy swell that frequently
prevails there. There is a bar across the mouth of the river, on which there is a

considerable surf. The ore is embarked in iron flat-bottomed boats, drawing only 14
inches water when loaded, put into a sloop, and taken to Isla Brava.

“Tn the Gulf of Triste, there is no fresh water to be obtained to the northward of
the river Aroa; Tucacas is supplied from it, and the river Piclass of the charts is
merely an opening into a salt-water lagoon.

“The winds that prevail in the Gulf are alternate land and sea breezes, the sea
breeze being the trade wind, prevailing from N. to S.E., which, when it dies away,
is, after a short interval of calm, succeeded by the land wind from south to W.S.W.
But the times when this change takes place vary daily, and cannot be depended on;
the general rule is, that the sea breeze commences at 10 in the forenoon, and lasts
till sunset, and the land wind from 10 P.m., till 8 in the morning; but it frequently
happens that the sea breeze blows all night, and in that case, there will be calm and
light (land) winds till the afternoon of the next day.

“The current, when setting to the westward in the offing, is, by the natural
formation of the Gulf, forced out to the northward, between the cays and the main :
therefore, if from the strength of the sea breeze, or from any other reason, it is
suspected that the current is settting in that direction, it would be advisable for a ship
bound to Porto Cabello to work up the south point of the North Cay before
stretching across.

“The Ore-house on Isla Brava is in latitude 10°46’ 15’ N., and longitude 68° 22’
west, its meridian distance from Porto Cabello, being Oh. 1m. 8s.; rise of the tide 3
feet.”— Nautical Magazine, August, 1836.

Point Tucacas is formed by a low swampy land covered with mangroves, extending
about a mile from the high land: on the east side of it, there isa cay of about a
mile in length from S.E. to N.W., named Sombrero, having between it and the coast
a channel nearly half a mile wide ; which, although there is a depth of 11 fathoms in
it, is obstructed by shoals and reefs extending from the shores. A cay on the N.E,
side, is also surrounded by a reef of 2 cables’ length broad; it is not advisable to
approach it nearer than a mile. From Point Tucacas, which is to the westward of
the most northerly part of Sombrero Cay, the coast trends about N.W., low and foul,
with a reef half a mile broad, extending as far as the mouth of the Harbour of
Chichirivichi, distant 3 miles from the point.

The HARBOUR of CHICHIRIVICHI is formed by low lands covered with
mangroves, and although well sheltered from all winds, with 63 fathoms good holding
ground, the entrance to it is rather difficult on account of shoals and reefs. The east
point, named Chichirivichi, is nearly a mile in length, and a reef extends from it
about 3 cables’ length, upon which are some islets; these must all be passed on the
outside. ‘To the northward of these lies a cay, named Peraza, with a foul reef all
round it, half a cable broad. This cay and the islets off the point, form a channel
2 cables’ length wide, with about 8 fathoms of water in it. Westward of Peraza Cay
lies another, named Chichirivichi, rather larger, but also surrounded by a reef half a
cable’s length broad: between these two there is a channel of more than 2 cables’
length wide, with 63 and 7 fathoms water. The west point of the harbour lies to
the westward of Chichirivichi Cay, and there is a channel between them of 2 cables’
length broad, with 53, 6, and 7 fathoms water: there are, however, two shoals in it,
with only 2 fathoms over them. MHalfamile north of Chichirivichi Vay, there is a
larger one, named Salt Cay, from the salterns on it; this is also surrounded by a reef,
a cable’s length wide, except at the S.W. part. Finally, about 13 mile N. by E. from
Salt Cay, lies Borracho Cay, which is very foul, with a reef extending half a mile
from the N.E. and south points of it. All this part of the sea which we have just
described is so shoal, and of so regular a bottom, that at little more than half a mile
from the coast, there are 63 fathoms, and the water deepens so gradually, that at 2
miles north of Borracho Cay, there are 14 fathoms, sandy mud.

HARBOUR OF CHICHIRIVICHI.

To enter the port, after you are abreast of the northernmost part of Sombrero Cay,
which must always be passed on the outside, lay the ship’s head towards Peyaza Cay,
