in order to pass about midway between it and the islets off the point; and then steer
to the westward, until Peraza Cay bears (N.E. by E.) N.E. 2 E., when you must
steer (S.W. by W.) S.W. 3 W., edging to south, so soon as the largest islet off Point
Chichirivichi bears (East) E. + N., thence run under shelter of the point, changing the
course as convenient to §.8.E., and anchor in 63 fathoms, mud.

From the Harbour of Chichirivichi, the coast trends about (N.N.W.) N.N.W. 2 W.,
a distance of 18 miles to Point St. Juan ; the ground is so flat and regular in all that
space, that at the distance of 4 miles from the shore, there are only 14 fathoms. ‘The
only obstruction is a small shoal, lying off a little point named Manatie, about 4 miles
to the eastward of Point St. Juan; it does not, however, extend more than a mile
from the shore.

Point St. Juan forms, on its west side, a large bay, but so shallow, that at a mile
from the beach, there are no more than 8 fathoms water. To the north-westward of
the point there are two cays; the first at half a mile distant, called St. Juan’s Cay
and the second, 2 miles further, named the N.W. Cay. On the N.W. side of
the point there isa reef about 2 cables’ length broad, and St. Juan’s Cay is sur-
rounded by another, about half that breadth: the other cay is also surrounded by a
reef, which extends off from its S.E. point about half a mile, having on it several
cays and islets, The anchorage is to the 8.W. of St. Juan’s Cay, to enter it, it will
be necessary to pass to the N.W. of that cay, and anchor in any depth of water
suitable to the ship’s draught. It is directed to go outside St. Juan’s Cay, because
the channel between it and the point is eligible for small vessels only; not alone from
its narrowness and the foulness of the reef, but because the greatest depth of water
therein is only 3% fathoms.

From Point St. Juan the coast trends (N. 60° W.) N.W. by W. 4 W., a distance of
19 miles, to Punta del Ubero, and is all shallow and clean. To the west of Point Ubero
it forms a short bay, which on account of the little depth in it, will not admit large
vessels far enough in to receive shelter from the breeze. About N.N.W. from the
point, distant 13 mile, there is a shoal, the least water on which is 43 fathoms: it has
some loose stones on it.

From Ubero Point to Zamuro Point the distance is 12 miles, the coast running in
the same direction as the former. From Zamuro Point, the coast continues to the
distance of 40 miles, forming various sinuosities or bends, to the Bay of Vela de
Coro ; it is all shallow and clean, and may be coasted at the distance of half a league
by keeping the lead going. On this coast rise various mountains, which are plainly
seen from the sea.

VELA DE CORO.—In the bay of Vela de Coro there is anchorage, to take which,
no other direction is necessary than the lead; for the bottom is very shallow and
clean. On the east side of this bay is the town named la Vela de Coro; and about
2 miles inland, and to the eastward of it, an Indian village, named Carrizal. The
river Coro falls into the sea, 14 mile to the westward of la Vela de Coro. From this
river the coast runs abruptly to the north, forming a chain of sand-banks or hills,
about 19 miles in length, uniting the peninsula of Paraguana with the coast. The
eastern point of this peninsula runs (North) N. 4 W. for 15 miles, to Point Aricula,
which point bears (N. 24° W.) N.N.W. $ W. from the Bay of Coro, at the distance of
31 miles; off all this coast the soundings are very regular, and at 10 miles from the
shore the depth is only 18 fathoms.

From Aricula Point the coast runs about N.N.W. the distance of 17 miles to the
Point of Tumatey ; from which to Cape St. Roman, the northernmost point of the
peninsula, it is 4 miles, and the coast trends about W.N.W. The mountain of Santa
Anna is situated near the S.E. part of this peninsula, and may be seen many leagues
out at sea.

The ISLAND ORCHILLA.—Due (North) N. { W. from Cape Codera, at the
distance of 23% leagues, lies the Island of Orchilla, the greatest extent of which is
from east to west. It is rather low, but on its north coast there are some peaks, the

ae THE ROQUES.

highest of which is near the western extremity of the island. From the extreme east
point, a cay extends to the north about 33 miles; and to the west of it, a great reef
extends in that direction to near the middle of the island, having upon it several cays.
All the rest of the coast is clean, and may be run along by, at the distance of a cable’s
length. On the S.W. part, and near the western extremity, there is a clear sandy
beach, in front of which there is good anchorage in 6 or 7 fathoms water, on sand,
at the distance of a cable and a half from the beach, well sheltered from the trade
breezes. Off the west extremity of the island, at the distance of half a mile W.N.W.,
there is a farallon or rock, very clean and steep-to; the channel between is eligible
for ships of any class.

The ROQUES.—To the westward of Orchilla, at the distance of 22 miles, lie the
Roques, which are a cluster of low cays, raised on a very dangerous reef. This group
has an extension of 12 miles from north to south, and 23 from east to west. You may
pass all the exterior cays on the edge of the reef, at a mile distance, except on the
eastern part, where the reef extends upwards of 3 miles beyond them. You ought not
to venture between the cays, because most of them are barred by the reef; and only
by the western part of El Roque Cay you may enter into a large and very fine bay,
formed by the cays and reef, in which there are from 15 to 20 fathoms water. ‘The
anchorage is at the west part of the said cay, in 17 or 18 fathoms water, on sand
and mud, at about 3 cables’ length from the beach. El Roque Cay, which is one of
the most northerly isles, may be readily known, because there are severai hillocks
or peaks on it, which may be seen at a good distance. The best way is, never to
approach this group but to pass at a good distance from it, as it offers no advantages,
and is very dangerous, especially in the night.

PORT EL ROQUE.—In October, 1827, while H.M.S. “ Arachne,” Captain W.R.
A. Pettman, lay at the above anchorage, a very fine harbour was discovered to the
eastward of El Roque, and surveyed by Lieutenant E. O. Johnes. It is sheltered
on the north by the French Cays; from the east by the N.E. Cay and the reef; and
on the south by Pirate and Naman’s Cays and their reefs. From a plan, published
at the Hydrographical Office, it will be seen that there is a space of about 2 miles in
length, half a mile wide at the narrowest part, between the reefs, where ships may
anchor in 12 to 14 fathoms, and five entrances or outlets, quite clean.

The Instruction says, “ Port El Roque presents considerable advantages, as a safe
and convenient anchorage, over that which seems to have been heretofore made use
of by ships of war and in which H.M.S. ‘Arachne,’ came to anchor; as it will be
evident by a reference to the plan, that from whetever quarter of the compass the
wind might blow, a vessel could scarcely find a difficulty in getting to sea; nor, from
the manner in which it is locked in by the cays and reef (a circumstance of course
productive of a constant smoothness of water), is it probable she could receive any
injury, should her commander deem it necessary to ride out a gale at her anchors.

“ Beside which, a ship will find another important advantage over the old anchor-
ages,—that of having, almost invariably, a clear unobstructed trade breeze across the
reef, which can bring with it no decaying vegetables, or other impure effluvia, to
render the place unwholesome; a circumstance not unlikely to occur, to the detriment
of a ship’s company’s health, in the road where the ‘ Arachne’ lay, from its leeward
proximity to a mangrove marsh.

“The channels are clean, and, without an exception, steep to the reefs on either
side, which are of coral, and have scarcely sufficient water on their edges for a four-
oared gig; thus displaying, by the contrast between the shades of deep and shallow
soundings, a secure guide to a stranger on entering. The bottom is mostly of a hard
sandy nature, though there was found a patch of stiff clay off the N.E. point of Pirate
Cay, in 13 fathoms.

“ The islands, with the exception of El Roque, appear to be of a coral formation,
with a light sandy soil, thickly covered with the samphire plant, most having salt
marshes either in their interior, or just within the reefs which are skirted with

BUEN AYRE. Zo

mangrove and other timber trees, affording shelter to innumerable families of boobies
and other aquatic birds; as the marshes likewise abound in several delicious kinds of
snipe genus, that are by no means difficult to be got at.

“Fish of excellent quality may be caught in plenty, either with a seine (the
method we adopted), or by anchoring in a boat near the reefs, and employing hook
and line for. that purpose. ‘lhe only quadruped that came under observation, was a
small description of rat, several of which were met with in visiting the Peaks of El
Roque. These heights are of limestone, which is removed by slaves and burnt in a
kiln at their foot (the property of a Dutchman), and then conveyed to the island of
Curazoa, to be made use of in the erection of forts, and for other government
purposes,

“Turtle are met with, but are not numerous.

“ Ships requiring small plank, fine wood, boats’ knees, and breast hooks, can be
well supplied, for the labour of cutting them; through it is recommended, should time
admit of it, to have it always barked, split, or sawed up before embarkation; as,
should the sap lodge upon decks or any thing else, the stains will be found difficult
to eradicate. There is a well of water upon the S.W. end of El Roque; the supply is
uncertain, never however exceeding 80 gallons a day. The lime-burners obtain
that which they make use of by digging wells in the sand; and although it was
of indifferent quality, it is not improbable, that by a deeper excavation, better may
be procured.

“ A stranger, in running for the harbour, is recommended to pass to the westward
of the peaks, and then stretch across towards Blackman’s Cay (which may be easily
known, as appearing — without the use of a glass —like a single large rock, though
actually a low islet with bushes upon it), until he can fetch through the South Channel,
which will open clearly to sea at the bearing of N. 16° E., when he can pass with
safety between Pirate Cay on the port, and a small dry sand-bank on the starboard
side, both of which are bold within the channel; but a reef extends 338 fathoms off
the 8.8.W. end of the former, which, like all others, is easily traced from a vessel’s
deck by the eye.

“On the full and change of the moon, it is high water at 4h. 30m., p.m. Spring-
tides rise 3 feet perpendicular.”

ISLAS DE AVES (Bird Islands) lie 30 miles to the westward of the Roques.
They are two groups of cays, rising on two distinct reefs, and which form between
them a channel 9 miles in breadth. These cays are very low; and as the east group
has a reef extending 4 miles to the north, and the western another extending 6 miles
in the same direction, therefore an approach to them, especially from the north, is
extremely dangerous, and it is best to give them a wide berth.

BUEN AYRE is 33 miles to the westward of Aves. The land is sufficiently
high, and there are several mounts and hillocks upon it, the highest of which is very
near to the western point. The south point of the island is very low, and is named
Punta del Lacre; in the middle of it, and upon the western side, there is a village
with a fort; there also is the anchorage, which, at 14 cable’s length from the shore,
has 17 fathoms water ; and the depth afterwards increases so rapidly, that at a cable’s
length further out there are 60 fathoms water: for this reason it is necessary to have
a cable on shore, and to have it ready in your boat, that you may not drag; for should
this happen, you will be driven from the anchorage, and have to regain it.

From the west part of the anchorage, at the distance of one mile, there is an islet
named Little Buen Ayre; and although the passage formed by it on the N.E. is fit
for any class of vessels, yet it is better either to enter or sail out by the S.W. of it,
as there is a greater space free. A reef runs along the east part of the island, from
whence it extends in some places more than half a mile off; and off the south end of
Buen Ayre, which is low, a dangerous reef of sand and coral extends a considerable
distance ; but the N.E. point is clean.

CURAZOA.

Light.—A lighthouse is erected on Point Lacre, the southern point of Buen Ayre,
which shows a fixed light at 85 feet above the level of the sea; the tower is painted
white, with vertical red stripes. In clear weather it may be seen at the distance of 12
nautical miles, from an elevatiion of 14 feet, on a circle described from N. by E. sea-
ward, to W. by N., the remaining part of the circle, being the shore side, is not lighted.
By this light vessels are warned off the dangerous point Lacre, and those bound to
Curazoa may clear it by Little Curazoa, which is almost level with the sea.

CURAZOA is 27 miles to the westward of Buen Ayre, lying nearly N.W. and
S.E., in which direction it is 35 miles in extent, but the greatest breadth does not
exceed 6 miles. It is moderately high, with some mountains that may be seen from
a considerable distance at sea. All the coasts are very clean, and there is no danger
in any part of it at a cable’s length distance.

LITTLE CURAZOA.—S.E. from the S.E. point of Curazao, named Cannon, and
at the distance of 4 miles from it, there is a very low and sandy islet, named Little
Curazoa, which, although very clean, is, from its lowness, dangerous at night or
in thick weather.

Light.—Little Curazoa Lighthouse is erected on the south side; it shows a red
fixed light, visible 10 miles. _ From this light the low eastern extremity of Curazoa
Island, called Cannon Point, bears W.N.W., 43 miles, and the light on the southern
point of Buen Ayre east, 20 miles.

The Island of Curazoa has many bays and harbours, the principal of which, where
all the commerce of the island is carried on, is that of Santa Anna, or St. Ann,
situated on the west coast, 14 miles from Point Cannon; before reaching it you will
meet another bay, named St. Barbara. Those bound to the Bay or Harbour of
St. Ann, ought to make Point Cannon, so as to run down the coast from one to two
miles distant, taking care not to get to leeward of the harbour’s mouth, as the
current sets strongly to the westward. The entrance of the harbour is very narrow,
and is formed by very low tongues of sand, which, in the interior part, form some
lagoons. On the eastern part is the fort, named Fort Amsterdam, and the principal
town in the island, inhabited by Protestants and Jews. On an islet immediately off
the west point is a battery, which, with Fort Amsterdam, defends the mouth of the
harbour; and on the western side is the town in which the Catholics reside. The
channel which conducts to the bay extends about N.N.E., is about three-quarters of a
mile long, and a cable’s length wide; and between the forts at the entrance, it is
searcely half a cable’s length wide. The towns, wharf and warehouses, are on the
banks of the channel, where the vessels anchor and careen.

Light.—At St. Ann’s Harbour is a fixed light, shown all night.

To enter this harbour it is necessary to close in with the coast to windward, and
run down, but not nearer than 1 cable’s length from the shore, as there are rocks
and a reef, which extend off about a cable’s length ; and so soon as you are abreast of
the batteries on the point at Fort Amsterdam, luff up towards the battery on the islet,
at the west point; and keeping in mid-channel, run in. The Dutch have a launch
ready for towing vessels into the harbour.

sea. ‘I'he Table Mount, situated near the S.E. end, Rounde Klige (round rock)
towards the N.E., and Table Mount, St. Hieronymus, with St. Christopher’s Moun-

The soil, formed of a calcareous rocky substance, and but thinly covered with
strata of fertile earth, is rendered still more barren by long series of dry weather, and
a total want of running water; so that at present it only produces maize, some sort of
pot-herbs, earth-roots, and a tolerable quantity of fruits, renowned for their excellence.
A few species of wood, like campeche, mahogany, yellow, and mansanilla trees grow
here and there, though in small quantities; besides an abundance of cactus, aloa, and
other shrubs. ‘The only productions still exported are salt and lime, which, with the
occupation of breeding large herds of cattle, and raising vegetables, form the pursuits
of the country people. The population in 1833, according to a published statement,
was 15,027, of whom 2,602 were white, 6,531 coloured, and 5,894 black people. The
climate is healthy, and even favourable for the cure of some diseases. The wind, nearly
always from the E.N.E. to E.S.E., blowing with a fresh breeze, very seldom increases
toastorm, The periods at which it has its greatest force are when the sun has
greatest north and south declination} increasing with the rising, and diminishing with
the setting of the sun. The whole atmosphere is thickened by the mist which
it brings from the sea; but during night, when there is only a gentle breeze, the
air is pure and fresh, and the sky with its glittering stars, extremely beautiful.
Hurricanes do not reach so far as Curazoa in general, although they now and then
have crossed this way. Earthquakes are unknown here. Although destitute of
rivers, there is plenty of good well-water; and rain-water, collected in cisterns, is also
to be obtained.

“The Coast of Curazoa may be considered clean, though you are obliged to keep
at least half a mile from shore, along the south side, on account of a bank of sand
and coral, extending about a cable’s length off. To the north the coast is every-
where bluff and clean, and its rocky shores almost overhang the sea. On the
southern side there are several harbours, the principal of which is that called St.
Ann, situated 14 miles from the east point (Point Cannon), and indisputably one
of the finest in the West Indies. Its entrance, formed by two very low tongues
of land, strongly fortified, is narrowed inward like the neck of a goglet, and be-
tween the batteries, not more than 110 yards wide. On the eastern side stands
Fort Amsterdam, and the principal town, named Williamstadt, containing 1900
inhabitants.

“On the west side stands Rif Fort, and a part of the town formerly occupied only
by Spaniards, and distinguished by the name of Otrabanda (other side). Having
passed the narrow entrance, you are in that part of the bay called the Haven; on the
quays of which are warehouses and stores, and excellent shelter, where ships of every
size may careen and refit. From the Haven extends the inner part of the bay, called
Schottegat, where a hundred ships may ride in safety.

“Ships bound to the Harbour of St. Ann, should make Point Cannon, and run
down the coast at 1 or 2 miles’ distance, so as to avoid getting to leeward of the
entrance of the harbour, as the current sets strongly to the westward. Ata mile to
windward, the pilot, or master-attendant, will be found generally in his gig. He
directs every necessary precaution, the most common of which is to have a hawser
ready to carry on shore, and an anchor to let goin case the hawser should not reach
it in due time, a boat to be lowered, and your sails to be clewed up in a moment,
especially when blowing hard from the N.E. With the breeze large, or from the 8.E.
quarter, entering the harbour is much facilitated, because, by standing off a little you
may luff up gradually ; but on the other hand, with northerly winds you are obliged
to keep close along the reef, which stretches a cable’s length off the east point of
the harbour. The best mark in coming down is to keep the westernmost point of
the Rif Fort directly under the sharp point of Priest Mount, and the moment you see
from the forecastle the crane or crab situated on an elevated spot, coming forth from
behind Fort Amsterdam, you must luff up boldly, and stand in, keeping a little to the
windward side of the channel. Be careful that your yards be braced up sharp, pre-
vious to coming in, and to be ready to clue up your square-sails in a moment, as soon

“This island was delivered over to Captain Frederick Watkins, by a treaty dated
the 13th of September, 1800, to protect it (although in open war with the Batavian
Government), against a number of French banditti, who, under one Bresseau, were
plundering and ravaging the country ; and it was restored in 1803. Such events of

of unrestrained generosity to protect the feeble, although an enemy, against an op-

ORUBA is 48 miles to the westward of the northernmost part of Curazoa ; it extends
from S.E. to N.W.,17 miles. Although this island is low, it has some hills which
may be seen at a moderate distance, particularly one, which is named Pan de Azucar
(Sugar Loaf), The whole of the east coast is clean, though there are some islets
lying close to it: on the southern coast there is a chain of cays, which extend along
to the west point, and which may be coasted on the outside at 2 cables’ length. his
island which lies to the north of Cape Roman, forms with it a channel of 13 miles in
width, which is perfectly clean.

OxvBA IsLAND was visited by Lieut. D. F. Campbell, commanding His Majesty’s
schooner “ Monkey,” in September, 1826, who remarks that “ The island is moderately
high; the east part even, and gradually lowering toa point. The west end at a
distance appears like broken hummocks; the Sugar Loaf Hill, which is about 7 miles
from the N.W. Point is the highest part of the island, and may be seen at the dis-
tance of 18 or 20 miles. A chain of low bushy cays stretches along the south shore,
bold-to, having at a cable’s length off no soundings with the hand lead: these cays ter-
minate in a rocky islet, considerably higher than the rest, about 3 miles tothe westward
of the east point, and 2 cables’ length off shore. About 3 miles to the westward of
the Sugar Loaf there is a projecting point, having au opening between the cays to
leeward of it. To take the shelter afforded by this point, it is necessary to get close
in with the land so far to windward as the Sugar Loaf, and running along shore till
the Port bears N.N.W., when the flagstaff will come on with asmall red house stand-
ing by itself on a hill behind. These marks kept ina line will lead clear of a rocky ledge
at the extremity of the point: to leeward it is ull clear. When far enough in to be
sheltered from the breeze, you may anchor in 4 or 5 fathoms on sandy bottom; there
are, however, some rocky patches to be carefully avoided. It is particularly necessary
for a stranger to get close in with the cays well to windward, otherwise the current
will sweep him so far past the opening as will require half a day to beat up again.
There is also good anchorage in from 6 to 12 fathoms under the west end of the
island ; but as procuring provisions or temporary refit can be the only inducement for
visiting Oruba, it is advisable to go into the harbour, which is distinguished by the
town along the beach, close to leeward of the sandy point, and named Port Caballas.
The pilots are skilful and attentive ; and the anchorage within the reefs and close to
the town, in 3 fathoms water, sandy bottom, is very good. Fresh water is scarce,
there being no spring: it is collected in tanks in the months of September and
October, but is good and wholesome.

GULF OF VENEZUELA OR MARACAYBO.

From Cape St. Roman the coast runs nearly 8.W., a distance of 12 miles, to the
Punta de la Macolla; it is shallow and clean, and may be safely coasted by the lead.
This Point Macolla, and that named Punta de Espada or Sword Point, which lie
nearly true east and west of each other, distant 50 miles, form the entrance to the
Gulf of Venezuela or Maracaybo. In the south extremity of this gulf, the Great
Lagoon of Maracaybo disembogues through a Delta, which has only one mouth
navigable; and that only for vessels of 10 feet draught, because there is a bar, on
which there are no more than 11 feet. Although no chart of the coasts of this gulf
has been constructed from actual survey, nor the position of the bar accurately de-
termined ; yet from practice, the course to it is tolerably well known, both from Point
Macolla and from Point Espada. The Hydrographic Commission, under the command
of Don Joaquin Francisco Fidalgo, surveyed the eastern coast from Point Macolla to
Point Arenas, which is somewhat to the eastward of the bar; and the inspection of
the chart will be sufficient to shape a course by; and as the water is shallow, but
without shoals or detached islands, the lead is recommended as the best guide. The
same may be said of the west coast, which, although not surveyed, has been explored,
and is well known, and you may with safety approach every part of it to the depth
of 6 or 5 fathoms.

Being 4 leagues to the westward of Cape St. Roman, and steering S.W. by S. true
course, you will proceed so as to get sight of the Mesas de Borojo, which are some
level hillocks of sand, situated to the eastward of the bar; from this situation the
course to the bar will be about west, keeping at the distance of 2 leagues from the
coast, and in a depth of from 5 to 6 fathoms, until you get sight of the Castles of Zapara
and San Carlos, which defend the entrance of the lagoon, and are placed the first on
the eastern point, and the second on the western point. You will not be then on the
bar, but to the northward of it; for it is formed by the shoals, which extend out 23
or 3 miles to the W.N.W. of the Bajo Seco, or Dry Shoal. The sea breaks on all
these shoals, and the deeper water is easily distinguished by its having no breakers ;
and to find this you have only to pass at 13 cable’s length from the outermost
breakers, which extend from Bajo Seco. This bank is an islet of sand, which ex-~
tends about 13 cable in every direction, and lies about 13 mile N.N.E. from the
Castle of San Carlos: and about east from it you will see the other called Zapara.
The islet of this name has some very high mangroves, and without it, in 6 or 7
fathoms depth, the ground is hard mud, mixed with sand, and this is the spot where
you ought to anchor in case of necessity, observing to have good ground tackle, as
the breeze blows very fresh here.

If being off Espada Point at the distance of 2 leagues, steer S.S.W. 5° W. true with
which you make the land to the N.E. of the islet called Bajo Seco.

On this course, as well as on the former, the depth decreases to the southward ; and it
is advisable not to approach the coast or the bar at night, but to stand off and make
short boards, at about 4 leagues off, until daylight. The breezes in this gulf are fresh,
and from N.N.E., which send in a heavy sea upon the bar, and all on the south
shore, so that there is risk of getting aground.

It is high water on this bar on the days of full and change at a quarter past 5
o'clock, P.M.; and spring-tides rise about 2 or 23 feet: the least water on the bar at
high water, in the time of breezes, is 10 feet, and 12 feet in the rainy season, which,
isin the months of August, September, October, and November.

28 GULF OF VENEZUELA.

You cannot enter on this bar without a pilot ; and therefore, so soon as your vessel
is on the meridian of the Castle of San Carlos, or nearly so, and in 51 fathoms water,
you should alter your course to the westward, until you get into 41 fathoms from
which depth you will see the sea breaking on the shoals in a line about W.N.W. In
the said depth of 4% fathoms, continue steering to the westward luffing or keeping
away, as may be necessary, so as to keep the same depth until you get abreast of the
last breakers, which will be near the mouth; and heaving to on the starboard tack,
or, what is better, maintaining yourself in your situation by short boards until you
get a pilot.

On steering a course for the bar, the first thing you will discover, because it is the
highest thereabout, will be the Island of Todos, which lies about south from the
Castle of San Carlos; and you should steer towards it, until you discover the Castles
and the Bajo Seco, when you must steer as before directed.

It is very necessary to know that the situation of the mouth of the bar is to the
westward of the meridian of the Castle of San Carlos; for, without knowing it, any
one would believe it was between Bajo Seco and the coast to the eastward, where the
Castle of Zapara stands: and under this mistake, might be cast away on the shoals ;
or lost, if attempting to enter, as has been the case in several instances.

Vessels drawing from 9 to 10 feet water, should calculate to enter at or near high
water, to avoid danger of even touching; for, should a vessel lose her rudder, the
channel is so narrow, that shipwreck would be inevitable.

In sailing out over the bar, you ought to take a pilot, until you are without the
shoals; afterwards, particular instructions for quitting the gulf ‘are unnecessary ; for
though it must be done by making various tacks, yet every navigator knows how to
regulate them, so that {hey may be more or less favourable: and here he may pro-
long either tack without any other guide than the lead. It may, however, prove
useful to remark, that, in the gulf, the wind generally shifts to the north, or nearly
so, at 4 or 5 o'clock P.m.; therefore you should endeavour to get near the western
coast about that time, in order to take advantage of it, for along stretch to the
H.N.E.; and to go on the other tack again, so soon as the wind rounds back to the
eastward ; not only to gain northing by it, but also to get again over to the west
coast, in order to make the best use of the next shift of wind to the north.*

DIRECTIONS FOR NAVIGATING FROM SANTA MARTA TO THE
BAY OF MARACAYBO,
By Captain Frederick Chamier, R.N., 1826.

“In sailing from Santa Marta to Maracaybo, I rounded Cape Aguja quite close ;
and by keeping within 5 miles of the foot of the Snow Mountains carried the easterly
set of the Magdalena up to Cape la Vela, and had likewise light winds from the
westward.

“On nearing Rio dela Hacha, you must: keep the lead going, as you will be in 5
and 7 fathoms water the whole night. After passing Cape la Vela the best plan is
to make one good stretch to sea, and the next morning, you will in all probability,
weather Cape Chichibacoa; in which case you will weather Punta Espada, and be
able to stand for the Bar of Maracaybo. You will run the greater distance from
Punta Espada in 9 and 10 fathoms, and the shoaling of the water will be a guide to
shorten sail for daylight.

“The best anchorage is with the Castle of the Bajo Seco in a line with that of St.
Carlos, and distant from the latter about 7 miles, in about 6 fathoms water.

“The entrance of the bar is in latitude 11° 2’; longitude by chronometer, 71° 43’
west.

«© The Bar of Maracaybo is a shifting bar ; formerly the entrance was by the Island
of Zapara, on the west end of which stands the Old Fort. It then formed its channel
to the southward of Bajo Seco, (which at that time was not ahove water, although
now an Island of some magnitude, and the principal defence of the entrance) ; but
now it seems to have settled into a permanent Channel of 13 feet depth, to the N.W.
of Bajo Seco. The whole bar is a quicksand, and when the ‘ Britomart’ grounded in
passing, although the stream anchor was towed in the cutter a cable’s length astern,
and dropped instantly, yet we hove it up again without starting the vessel in the
slightest degree. Having ultimately been obliged to heave the guns overboard, the
sand covered them so deeply, that the buoy rope, which was the same as is allowed
for an anchor of 16 cwt., snapped before we could raise the gun sufficiently to sweep
it, and that only the next day.

“To pass the bar, a pilot should always be taken: the difficulty is to get one, an

old Spanish ordinance being stillin force, that no foreign man-of-war is to be taken
across.

“ The town of Maracaybo stands 21 miles up the lake, and you have to pass over
the Tablazos ; a shoal of soft mud, with about 10 feet in some places, which you may
drag through with ease.

“T came out over the bar against a head sea, drawing 11 feet fore and aft, and
never touched. Water can be procured, if you are outside the bar, from the main
land, exactly opposite the fort of Bajo Seco; and if inside, the lake is fresh water ; 10
miles above the bar, the Seine may be drawn any where in the sandy bays, but the
alligators are very plentiful.

* Although the ‘Derrotero de las Antillas’ and others mention the depthof water on
the bar in the rainy season, from August to November, to be 163 feet, yet no more

LOS MONGES.

DESCRIPTION OF THE COAST FROM POINT
ESPADA TO CARTHAGENA.

We have before said that Point Espada is the west point of the entrance to the
Gulf of Venezuela or of Maracaybo; from it the coast trends about (N.W. by N.)
N.W. 2N., a distance of 13 miles to Cape Chichibacoa; the whole space being clean
and shallow, so that to run along by it, the lead is the best guide; and although the
coast is low, there are several peaks and mountains which rise inland, the most
elevated of which are named Sierras de Aciete.

LOS MONGES, or THE MONKS.—At the distance of 19 miles (N. 75° E.)
E.N.E 3 E., from Cape Chichibacoa, are the Monges del Sur, or Southern Monks,
which are two very small and perfectly clean islets, that may be passed at half a cable’s
length. About E.N.E. from them, at the distance of 3 miles, there is another, called
Monge del Este, or Eastern Monk, which is also very clean; and about (North)
N. 3 W. from the first, at the distance of 8 miles, is another group of seven, called
Monges del Norte, or Northern Monks, which are foul with a reef, and should not be
approached nearer than a mile. The passages which are formed by the Northern
Monks, with the Eastern and Southern Monks, as well as with the’mainland, are
very open and clean, so that there is no risk in navigating through them.

From Cape Chichibacoa the coast lies nearly W.N.W., 25 miles to Point Gallinas,
which is the northernmost part of the whole of it.* From Point Gallinas the coast
bends to (W.S.W.) S.W. by W. # W. for the distance of 5 miles to Point Aguja, off
which there is shallow water a mile out. At Point Aguja the coast falls to the
southward, and forms a bay of small extent, named Bahia Honda Chica, or Little
Bay Honda, which has very shallow water, and affords no shelter: next to this is
the harbour of Bahia Honda, the eastern point of which is 4 miles from Point Aguja.

BAHIA HONDA is of great extent, and its mouth is 3 miles wide. In entering
this bay you must avoid a shoal which lies in the mouth of it, and in a line with the
two points of the entrance; and which is distant from the west point a mile, and from
the east point a mile and two-thirds. This bank, the greatest extent of which is
about one-third of a mile, or perhaps a little more, nearly east and west, has on its
shoalest part, which is at the eastern end, only one foot of water; and with very
little wind, the sea breaks over it. In other respects the bay is so shaliow and clean,
that no other guide than the lead is neccessary for choosing an anchoring place in it.
The coast from Cape Chichibacoa to this bay is low and level, but clean and shallow,
so that it may be coasted safely with no other guide than the lead.

BAHIA HONDA TO CAPE LA VELA.—From the west point of Bahia Honda,
the coast trends about (S.W.) S.W.35S., a distance of 11 miles, to a bay named El
Portete, the entrance to which is very narrow, and the depth of water in the interior
will admit small vessels only. From El Portete, the coast lies about (West) W. 3S.
for a distance of 14 miles, to Cape la Vela: this coast is clean, and from Bahia

CAPE LA VELA. ay)

Honda the land begins to rise higher. One league before you come to Cape la Vela,
there is a little hill in form of a Sugar T.oaf, against which the sea breaks, and which
projects about half a mile to the northward of the rest of the shore. From this hill
the land continues of a good height, and rounds southward to the: west point, which
is that properly named Cape la Vela. At the distance of 24 cables’ length to the
westward of this cape, there is an tslet or rock, very clean and steep-to, which may
be passed within a ship’s length if necessary: the channel between it and the cape
is quite clear, and may be run through without risk of danger, there being 54
fathoms in the middle of it: but it is better to pass nearer the islet than the cape,
because there are 5} fathoms close to the former, and only 4, or even less than 3
fathoms, near the latter. The land about Cape la Vela is very sterile; and 8.K. from
it, about 7 miles inland, rises a mountain, named Sierra del Carpintero, or the
Carpenter’s Mountain.

From the Cape the coast turns to the southward, forming a large bay, where there
is shelter from the breezes; to enter it, you need no other guide than the lead, for
all the bottom is clean, and so shallow, that at 2 miles from the coast, there are only
os fathoms of water; and from that, the depth diminishes gradually towards the
shore.

From CAPE LA VELA to RIO DE HACHA, &c.—From Cape la Vela the
coast trends about south, with some inclination to the west, for a distance of 23 miles
to Castillettes Point, on which there isa grove or group of mangroves, and from
which the cape bears (N. 21° E.) N. by E.3E. From this point it bends to (S. 74° W.)
W.S.W. i W., a distance of 14 miles, to Menare Point; and between the two, bends
a little to the southward, with some projecting points.

(S. 72° W.) W.S.W. 4 W.., at the distance of 13 miles from Menare Point is Point
de la Cruz, the intermediate coast being nearly straight, although the points of
Almidones, Pajaro, and the Fronton de Jerote, project a little. Between the two
latter, at 13 mile to seaward, lies the Pajaro, or Bird’s Shoal, with 2 fathoms water on
it, on sandy bottom.

At (8. 54° W.) S.W. § W. from Point de la Cruz, at the distance of 4 miles, is
Vela Point: and at 7 miles from it, (S. 42° W.) 8.W. 48. are the City and River of
La Hacha. The coast thence trends (S. 64° W.) S.W. by W. % W., and (S. 53° W.)
8.W. 3 W. to Punta Dibulle which is 314 miles distant from the City of La Hacha.
From Point Dibulle, the coast runs (W. and N. 75° W.) W. i S., and W. by N. to
Cape San Juan de Guia, which is distant 383 miles from Dibulle Point. The whole
of this coast, from Cape la Vela to 12 miles east of San Juan de Guia, sends out a
bank of soundings, more or less projecting into the sea, as may be seen in the charts ;
but it is dangerous on account of several shoals lying on it, which extend a consi-
derable distance off to sea. Of these, the first has been already noticed, named
Pajaro; and the second, named Navio Quebrado, or Wrecked Ship is situated at
2% miles from the coast, between the Leguna Grande, and the Leguna Navio
Quebrado, in latitude 11° 26’ 15” N., and longitude 73° 14’ 30” W.; for this reason, it
is dangerous to approach the coast to a less distance than 4 leagues, and care should
be taken, not to get into less than 20 fathoms water. This coast is generally low:
but somewhat to the westward of the city of La Hacha, there rise in the interior
the celebrated mountains, named Sierras Nevadas, or Snowy Mountains, well known,
not only from their great elevation, but because the summit terminates in two peaks,
like sugar loaves, which are always covered with snow. These mountains extend to
the west, and terminate in the meridian of Cape Aguja.

Although we have said it is not advisable to approach this coast, but to steer a
direct course from Cape la Vela to Cape Aguja, and to take care and get into no less
than 20 fathoms water ; nevertheless, as vessels bound to La Hacha must, of necessity,
stand in towards the shore, it becomes requisite to give some directions whereby it
may be done with safety. ‘To take the anchorage of the City of La Hacha, and being

32 LA HACHA.

near the farallon or rock off Cape la Vela, it will be necessary to steer (8. 53° or 55°
W.) about S.W. 4 W., with which course you will run in sight of the coast; and
having run 51 miles, you will be on the meridian of the City of La Hacha, in 52 to
64 fathoms water, or sandy bottom; and may direct yourself to the anchorage, without
more attention than by the chart appears necessary ; only observing that large vessels
ought to anchor N.N.W. of the City, in 5 or 6 fathoms; and when they sail from it,
they ought to steer this course until they are 3 leagues out.

In taking this anchorage, as well as all others which have no certain distin-
guishing marks, it requires some vigilance; and, as a case may happen in which
a vessel may pass it, the bank of 43 and 4 fathoms, on gravel, sand, and rock, which
lies 153 miles to the westward of the City of La Hacha, may serve as a mark for
ascertaining her situation, The Snowy Mountains of Santa Marta may also serve
for the same purpose.

Light.—On the Church at Rio de la Hacha is a fied light, 69 feet above the sea,
visible 6 miles.

REMARKS ON RIO DE LA HACHA,
by Captain C. Osterloh, commanding the Bremen Brig “ Margaret.”

BREMEN, November 30th, 1851.—‘ Captain Osterloh, arrived at this port from St.
Thomas, reports as follows, in order to meet incorrect statements: Rio de la Hacha,
(or La-Hacha, as it is called commonly) belonging to the republic of New Granada,
has no harbour or bay, but is situated on the open coast, in latitude 11° 33’ N., and
longitude 72°52’ 80” W. of Greenwich. This was ascertained by a chronometer that
had been examined four days before arrival in La Hacha, at St. Thomas, and at La
Hacha itself, and by means of which, it was determined that St. Thomas (Fort
Christian), was situated 4h. 19m. 40s. west of Greenwich. Vessels destined for this
place, and coming from the eastward, do best if they run for Cape la Vela, about 13
German miles (52 English) east of La Hacha. The country at the Cape is tolerably
high, hilly, and towards the interior, mountainous and uncultivated. It is to be
known particularly by a small rocky island close to the Cape. From this Cape take
your course; but do not come closer to the land than 18 fathoms, because there are
banks between La Vela and La Hacha, which extend certainly much further from
the shore than noted in the direction books. Vessels bound to Santa Marta have
been lost on these banks, although it is to be supposed that they have kept from the
land at least 13 English mile.

“The coast to the westward of La Vela is very low and dangerous, on account of
the malevolent Indians, who inhabit the whole extent as far as close to La Hacha.
When you have made good the distance until about the meridian of La Hacha, steer
towards the land, and you will perceive some woodland east of the town, which

‘appears much higher and darker than the other parts of the country. This woodland

borders immediately on the eastern part of the town of La Hacha, from which it is
separated only by a small river (where the territory of the Indians commences); it is
the only mark on this coast, as the town, on account of its low situation, is not to be
seen so soon. When you are so close to the shore as to see the town—which you can
know by a high church, with a square, obtuse steeple, in the middle—make use of the
lead continually, and do not fear because the water begins to become shallow, until
you meet with adepth suitable for your vessel; you will find the best anchorage
ground N.N.W. of the church, on a sandy bottom. Pilots are not to be had here.
If you do not make use of the lead, but think yourself sufficiently distant from the
shore, you will run the risk of getting aground, because about 2 English miles from
the shore there are only 18 feet water.

SANTA MARTA. 33

“Should you have to pass Rio Hacha, you will have a good mark in the Snowy
Mountains east of Santa Marta, which rise their summits through the clouds. It
will, however, be very difficult to beat up, as there is commonly a strong breeze in the
day-time. During my sojourn, from the Ist to the 23rd of April, we had a very
strong sea breeze from N.E. to north, which mostly commenced at 9 o’clock in the
morning, and lasted until 8 o’clock in the evening, being particularly severe from 2
till 4 in the afternoon. At night there is mostly a calm and very little land
breeze.

“The principal articles of export are dividivi, redwood, and fustic, particularly
the two former articles, which are brought to market by the Indians in large
quantities.”

From Cape San Juan de Guia, the coast runs (W.N.W., West, and W.S.W.)
W.N.W.2 W., W.25S., and S.W. by W. 2 W., 125 miles, to the north point of the
Islet off Cape Aguja, which forms a prominent front of high hills, scarped, and with
deep water close-to, with several coves or bights, and good anchorages. ‘The islet of
Cape Aguja forms, with the cape, a channel of three-tenths of a mile in breadth ; but
the passage is very narrow, on account of the reefs which extend out both from the
cape, and the south part of the islet, so that, although there is water enough for any
vessel, yet none should attempt it, as by so doing they would run the risk of being
wrecked.

To the N.W. of the Islet of Cape Aguja thre are three rocks very near each other;
the one which extends farthest out, which is also the largest, lies at the distance
of 3 cables’ length. There is another to the westward of the west point, which is
higher than the two former; this is at a short distance: they are all clean and
steep-to. From Cape Aguja, the coast runs (S. 31° W.) 8.S.W. 3 W. for the distance
of 34 miles to Betin Point, which is the north point of the Bay of Santa Marta, and
the south point of the Ancon or open Bay of Taganga: the coast is high and precipi-
tous, with some beaches and indents.

SANTA MARTA.—The Harbour of Santa Marta may be considered as one of
the best on this coast. Westward, at the distance of half a cable ftom its northern
point there is a farallon, or rock, which is very clean, so that you may pass it at the
distance of half a ship’s length, if necessary ; between it and the point there are from
5 to 8 fathoms water, but we advise that no person should attempt this passage,
which is very narrow, as there is nothing to be gained by it. At about 4 cables’
length to the westward of the same point there is an islet called the Morro, also very
clean, so that you may pass on either side of it, at the distance of halfa cable’s length.
Upon this islet there is a fortification, which with other batteries on the shore, defends
the harbour and city. The channel between the Morro and the rock off the point is
very open and clean, with a depth of from 13 to 27 fathoms. The bay is also very
clean, and the bottom good; there is nothing in it to avoid but a bank before the city,
which stretches out about half a mile from the beach; but as the depth diminishes
gradually from the edge, there is no danger in approaching it by the lead. The best
anchorage is to the northward of the city, as much as possible within the cove or
basin. To enter it you should endeavour to pass at about half a cable’s length outside
of the rock off the point, steering thence so as to pass at the same distance from some
rocks which extend southward from the point ;* and so soon as you have passed them,

* Probably there are sunken rocks lying at a greater distance from Point Betin, for Captain
§. Chambers, of H.M.S. “ Druid,” says, that ‘having been driven out from the anchorage by
heavy squalls twice, on the morning of the 27th February, 1828, in again taking the harbour,
the ship grounded on a rock not laid down on the chart, and which he had passed inside of on
the previous morning. It bore from the east end of El Morro-chica S. 45° E., from the 8.E.
Point of Betin 8. 46° W!, and from the west point 8. 10° W., all true bearings. On its inside
it is quite perpendicular, with 5 fathoms, decreasing gradually to the shore; its outside is a
quick descent to 9, 12, and 15 fathoms, and on the top of it are exactly 12 feet.”

[CoLoMBIA. ] F

34 MAGDALENA RIVER.

luff as much as you can, and anchor where most convenient, being on your guard
against the edges which extend from the coast and the points shown in the particular
plan of the harbour. On entering into this anchorage be particularly attentive to the
sails, &c., for the gusts of wind come off the land very heavy. The River Manzanares
disembogues a little to the southward of the city, which, although not large, has very
good water.

Comus SHOAL.—H.M.S. “Comus,” when on her passage from St. Marta to Cartha-
gena, on the 14th of August, 1840, discovered a shoul of 3 miles distant from the land,
on which was found from 10 to 3 fathoms. Cape Aguja bearing N.E. 3 N., extreme
of land, W.S.W.—WNautical Magazine, December, 1842.

MAGDALENA RIVER.—From Gaira Point, the south point of Santa Marta,
the coast trends south 133 miles to the Cienega, which is a lagoon formed by some of
the branches of the River Magdalena From this Cienega it bends to the west and
W.N.W., for the distance of 34 miles, to the western mouth of this celebrated river,
named Boca de Ceniza, leaving, at the distance of 8 miles to the eastward another,
named Boca de Rio Viejo, or Old River. ‘These streams form an island or Delta,
named Isla de los Gomez, which is 6 miles from north to south, and 8 from east to
west. By the two directions which the coast takes from Santa Marta, it forms a
very large bay, in the bottom of whichis the Cienega. The whole of this coast is low,
and shallow ; and from the Cienega towards the west, it forms the Isla de Salamanca,
the west point of which is formed by the Rio Viejo. The waters of the Cienega,
and those which form this island, communicate with the Magdalena by several small
channels,

The current of this great river is so powerful, that at more than 5 leagues out at
sea it gives a greenish colour to the water, resembling that over a shallow bank.
You may run along all this bay by the hand-lead for it is all clean. The west part
of the Isla de los Gomez, and the east part of the Isla Verde (Green Island), form the
Boca de Ceniza of the River Magdalena; and in the middle of this mouth there are
two cays.

Captain Chamier, R.N., has said that the waters of the Magdalena, in the first
instance, run to the N.E. “On the morning of the 17th of October, 1826, the
Snowy Mountains, bearing S.E. by S., we passed great quantities of rock-weed
bamboos, branches of trees, &c., and the water was very much discoloured; this was
decidedly the Magdalena, for there is no other river near, and we were set 10 miles
to the north and east, as shown by the chronometer and the bearings of the land.
Probably the latitude of 12° 25’ will be the limit of this outset.”

The Isla Verde stretches from east to west, 5 miles; and to the southward of
it is another, of great extent, named Sabanilla. At the S.W. end of Sabanilla,
isthe harbour of the same name, with 43, 5, and 6 fathoms water, on sand
and mud.

SABANILLA HARBOUR is situated about 7 or 8 miles to the south-westward
of the Roca de Ceniza of the Magdalena River, and is formed by the main land on the
south side, and by the islands of Sabanilla, Verde, and others on the north side. Its
entrance is between the point of Morro Hermoso, and a shoal bank, which extends
about 4 miles south-westward from the Isla Verde, and nearly 2 miles from the west
end of Sabanilla Island. The extremity of this bank has about 7 feet water on it,
and lies about 3 miles north-eastward from Morro Hermoso Point.

Directions for Sabanilla Harbour, by Joddrell Leigh, Esq., Commander of His
Majesty's Sloop, “ Ontario,” 1820 and 1821 :—*On making Sabanilla, it may be known
by aremarkable table land, lying about 2 miles to the westward of the fort. On the
east end of the table land is a square hummock, resembling a battery. Bring this
hummock to bear S.E. 3 S., and a red cliff will be seen, which steer directly for, and
you will pass to the westward of a shoal, with only 7 feet water on some parts of it,

SABANILLA HARBOUR. 35

that extends 4 miles from Isla Verde. Its bearings are the red cliff S.E. by S.;
Morro Hermoso Point 8.W. by S.; the west extremity of the land §.W.; and the
N.W. point of the island N. by E.3 E. These bearings were taken in a boat, in 7
feet water, on the edge of the bank; and at the distance of 30 yards from it, there
were 5 fathoms, increasing regularly.

“When the west extremity of the land is shut in with Morro Hermoso Point, you
will have passed the point of the shoal, and may haul up towards the fort in from
53 to 3 fathoms. The bearings at the ‘ Ontario’s’ anchorage were, the fort N.E. 3 E. ;
west point of the island N. by W. 3 W.; and Morro Hermoso Point 8.W. 4 W., at a
quarter of a mile from shore.

“When turning into this harbour, care must be taken to avoid a shoal, on which
the ‘Ontario’ tailed when in stays. It lies about a quarter of a mile from the Red
Cliff, with the following bearings :—the outer part of the island N.N.W., and the
fort E.N.E. On the inside of this bank is a reef of rocks, some of which are
above water. On the outside the depths are from 6 to 33 fathoms, and on it there
are from 33 to 2 fathoms. It is composed of sand and mud, and is, perhaps, formed
by the freshes of the small rivers throwing the mud into the current, which
setting to the westward, carries it against the rocks and there being stopped, forms
a spit, or bank.

“There is also another shoal, or oyster-bed, on which the schooners ‘ Kate’ and
‘Experiment’ lost their rudders. Its marks are the magazine in the fort, open a
little to the eastward of the guardhouse (also in the fort), and a remarkable notch in
the bottom of the bay on with a bluff point to the northward of the Custom-house.
Ships of war have no occasion for going so far up, as the anchorage is equally good a
mile below it.

“ As the wind generally blows from the N.E., ships are obliged to work up to the
anchorage. They ought not to stand inshore to less than 5 fathoms, nor to the north-
ward into less than 53, as the bank is steep-to, and on the shore side, abreast of the
Red Cliff, is the reef above mentioned.

“J have been informed that heavy gales or great freshes from the Magdalena cause
the banks to shift. During several visits to this harbour, we found the current
setting to the westward, owing perhaps to the easterly current, which from Galera to
Zamba meets the freshes from the Magdalena, causing an eddy over the outer bank
into Sabanilla Bay, which not being able to escape to the eastward, returns along the
south shore of the bay, and round the 8.W. point to sea.

“There is no regular tide at this part of the coast, but the water sometimes falls
and rises 4 or 6 feet.

“ Water of an indifferent quality may be procured here from the S.W. mouth of the
Magdalena; but the bar is so shallow, that nothing but small boats can get it. Fire-
wood may be easily obtained in any quantity, the beach near the river being nearly
covered with drift wood.”

From the Isla Verde the coast trends (8S. 58° W.) S.W. by W., for a distance of
33 miles to the Galera de Zamba, or Zamba Point; and the shore between forms a
bay of 5 or 6 miles in depth, the whole of which is shallow; for at 3 leagues from
the shore there are only 26 fathoms water, on muddy bottom. The shoals of Cascabel
and Palmarito are in it; the first lies very near the coast, in the middle ofa little
bay formed by the Morros, or hills of Damas, and of Inasco: the second is more
dangerous, for it lies at the distance of a league off shore (N. 26° W.) N.N.W. $ W.
from Morro Pelado, or Bald Hill.

The Galera de Zamba, or Zamba Point, is so low, that when there is a fresh
breeze the sea washes over the greater part of it. ‘To the west, W.N.W., and N.W.
of its western extremity, and at the distance of 2 miles from its most projecting
point, there are 4 small banks, of different sizes, with 54 fathoms water, on black

36 CARTHAGENA.

sand. Between these banks, and between them and the shore, the depths are 7, 8,
9, and 10 fathoms, on black sand. The Galera de Zamba, which projects into the sea
about 8 miles, forms on its south part an anchorage, sheltered from the breezes ; but
in taking it great caution is necessary, on account of the banks in it, and of the Isla
de Arenas, or Sandy Island, which lies in the middle of the bay of Galera de Zamba ;
therefore, every one intending to enter this anchorage, should give great attention to
the hand-lead.

At (S. 26° W.) S.8.W., distant 144 miles from the Point of Galera de Zamba, lies
the Point of Canoas, which at the water’s edge is low, but, very close to it, hilly;
between these two points the coast is of moderate height; and at about one-third from
Point Canoas there rises a hill, forming a kind of table at its top, with several bar-
rancas, or reddish coloured ravines upon it, called Bugio del Gate. On_the inter-
mediate coast there are several dangerous spots; of these the Cascajal Islet is the
first, which lies at the distance of 6 miles (S. 6° E.) 8. 3 E. from Galera de Zamba
Point, and from the coast rather more than 13 mile. (North) N. } W. from this islet,
at the distance of one mile and three-tenths, is a little bank, with 2 fathoms on it ;
and (N. 6° W.) N. 2 W., eight-tenths of a mile, is another similar to it, with 4 fathoms
on it; and there is another of equal depth at (N. 58° W.) N.W. by W. 2 W. from the
Cascajal Islet, distant nearly 2 miles, At (S. 14° W.)S. by W. from the Galera de
Zamba Point, distant nearly 7 miles, lies the West Rock of Bugio del Gato Shoal,
which extends along mile from north to south. At about N.N.E. from its north
extremity, distant half a mile, there is another, called the N.E. Rock, or Una de
Gato (Cat’s Claw); the depth on the outside of this shoal is 7, 8, Y,and up to 14
fathoms, at the distance of 24 miles. There is also at the distance of 33 miles
(N. 31° E.) N.N.E. 4 E. from Canoas Point, a rocky bank of 3 fathoms water; this
lies in the middle of Bugio del Gato Bay.

We ought to warn the navigator, that going into this bay is dangerous, more
especially by night; and if he is compelled so to do, he should not go into a less depth
than 20 fathoms.

At the distance of rather more than a mile from Point Canoas (S. 49° W.) S.W. 4 W.,
lies a shoal, called the Negrillo, of one quarter of a mile in extent; it is composed of
three rocks at a short distance from each other, in a triangular form, having from
2 to 5 feet on them.* Round and near to these rocks there are 6, 8, and 9 fathoms
water, on a bottom of rocks, small gravel, and sand; the channel between them and
the coast would be practicable, where it not for three sunken rocks, which make it
difficult to pass. From the Negrillo Shoal, the hill of La Popa at Carthagena bears
(S. 42° W.) S. 2 W., distant 72 miles; and this bearing may serve to guide you clear
of it. At (S. 50° W. ) S.W, 4 W., rather less than a mile from the southernmost
Morrito, lies the Cabeza Shoal, the least water on which is 2 feet.

CARTHAGENA.—From Point Canoas the coast trends to the eastward rather
more than a mile, and thence it bends round to the southward 3 miles, where rise
some little hills, named Los Morritos; from these the coast, which is low and covered
with mangroves, trends (S. 83°W.) 8.S.W. 2 W., 53 miles to the City of Carthagena,
which is built upon the western part of this swampy land. At about 13 mile to the
eastward of the city rises the hill of La Popa, on the summit of which there is a

clear weather this hill may be seen at the distance of 10 leagues from the quarter-deck
of a line of battle ship.

The little tongue of land on which Carthagena is built extends nearly 2 miles
(S.S.W.) S. by W..2 W. from the city; then turning round to the east, it forms with
the main land a basin, which is the anchorage or harbour, and which is as well
sheltered as the best arsenal. At one mile to the southward of the exterior point of
the little tongue is the north point of the island, called Tierra Bomba; and the
passage between the two is called Boca Grande; this is artificially shut in such a
manner that only boats, and vessels which draw very little water, can enter by it.
Yierra Bomba Jsland is about 4 miles from north to south, and its south point is the
north point of Boca Chica, which is the only entrance to the Harbour of Carthagena.
The south point of this entrance is the north point of another large island, named
Baru, and which is separated from the main land by the creek called Pasa Cabalos,
navigable by canoes only. On both points of the Boca Chica there are castles to
defend the entrance; that on the north side is called San Fernando, and that on the
south side San Joseph. This boca is rather more than 2 cables’ length wide; but
there are parts of it where the bank of shallow water, which extends off from the
south castle, narrows it one half.

This entrance first opens into a large and well sheltered bay, where there are
13 and 15 fathoms water; to the northward of this, the eastern coast of Tierra Bomba
inclines towards the main land, leaving a channel a mile in width; at the entrance
of which, and in its middle, are some shoals, which lie to the westward of an islet,
called Brujas, which is very hear to the main land. Having passed this strait you
enter into a second bay which corresponds with, or is opposite to the Boca Grande, in
which there are also 14 and 15 fathoms. To the north of this second bay there is an
entrance of less than half a mile wide, defended by other castles, and which conducts
into the harbour. This entrance has a shoal in the middle, which forms it into two
very narrow channels, but with 8 to 12 fathoms water; and the depth in the anchorage
nowhere exceeds 11 fathoms. Having described the harbour, we shall now treat of
the exterior coast and the shoals.

From Canoas Point to Boca Grande there is a great bank, the depth of water on
which diminishes gradually, and you will find 9 fathoms at about 11 miles from the
land. This bank is called the Playa Grande, and you may anchor on it, in 7 or 8
fathoms water, on a bottom of grey sand, in front of the city. Having passed the
north part of Tierra Bomba the depth increases to 20, 30, and 40 fathoms; and at
2 cables’ length from the shore there are 6 fathoms. To the westward of Tierra
Bomba, at the distance of 4 miles there is a shoal, named Salmedina, much spoken of,
on account of the great loss of ships which it has caused. This shoal, which is
little more than a mile in extent from north to south, and somewhat less from east to
