In addition to these marks, by which it may with certainty be avoided in running
from Playa Grande to Boca Chica, you ought to get into from 6 to 8 fathoms water
to the west of the city, at the distance of 3 short miles from it, and then steer
south, without inclining anything to the westward; and so soon as you inerease
the depth, keep more to the port hand, in order to close in with Tierra Bomba to the
distance of half a mile; you may run thus, or even within pistol-shot of the north
shore at the entrance of Boca Chica, avoiding the south shore, as itis foul. To enter
Boca Chica, and navigate inside the bays up to the harbour requires a pilot, and one
may generally be obtained at Boca Chica.

As the Harbour of Carthagena may be made by ships coming from the southward,
it is requisite to give some description of the South Coast, as far as the Rosario Island,
in order to connect all the information required for making the land with correctness
and security.

We have already said that the south coast of Boca Chica is the north coast of
the Island Baru. From the point of the latter, which forms the entrance of Boca
Chica, the exterior coast of it trends (8S. 353° W.) 8.8.W. 3 W., nearly 133 miles
to Baru Point; this coast is sufficiently clean, until you are as far as an islet, called
the Farallon of Perico, from which to the south it is very foul, witha reef. To the
west of this last part of the coast, that is, from Perieo Islet to the south point, are the
Islands of Rosario, of which there are four principal ones, with some small islets,
The easternmost and southernmost of these, which is also the smallest, is called
Arenas, and is distant from the Coast of Baru nearly 14 mile; but the passage is not
more than three-quarters of a mile wide, on account of the shoals and reefs, whieh
extend from both sides. West, somewhat to the north of the Island Arenas, at rather
more than 33 miles distance is the Island of Rosario; and to the northward of these
two is that which is named Isla Larga, or Long Island, which is the largest of the
group, and which, with its shallow water, islets, &c., extends out to the west further
than Rosario Island.

To the northward of the middle of Isla Larga, at the distance of rather more than
3 miles, lies the Islet Tesoro, with a reef to the west. There is a channel between
these islands, with from,16 to 25 fathoms water, on sand and rocks, from which Boea
Chica bears (N. 63° E.) N.E. by E., distant 103 miles. All these islands are very
foul, and no one should go between them unless well acquainted; but rather keep
to the westward ata sufficient distance to avoid the shallows stretching off them.
At about (S.S.W.) 8. by W. 3 W. from Rosario Isle, at the distance of 7 miles, there
isa shoal, with little water on it, named the Tortuga. The Rosario Islands are
fertile in trees, and on their south side there is shelter from the breeze. Besides the
bank of Rosario Island there are two others; one at W.N.W., distant 3} miles, and
another, S.W. by W., distant 25 miles: both consist of rocks and sand, with 6 or 7
fathoms water over them.

OBSERVATIONS AND REFLECTIONS ON THE NAVIGATION
OF THE COAST OF TERRA FIRMA, FROM THE
DRAGON’S MOUTHS TO CARTHAGENA.

From the Derrotero.

After what has been stated relative to the winds that are experienced on this
coast, there appears nothing necessary to add to the description already given, to
enable the navigator to conduct his ship in the greatest safety: in fact, there is little
else on this coast than the general breeze, or trade wind. There is nothing to fear
either from hurricanes or strong north winds: the first are absolutely unknown, and
the second, when they do at any time occur, never exceed the force of the ordinary

CAPE CODERA. 39

breeze ; and if in the rainy season, which is from May to November, there are some-
times strong southerly winds, they must be considered as squalls of short duration,
and which do but little injury, as they blow off the land. This coast, therefore,
especially as far as Cape la Vela, may be considered as a continued harbour, as far as
climate is concerned ; and it is only necessary to consult the descriptions given, to
avoid every danger upon it; for the loss of a ship upon it has very rarely indeed been
the effect of a storm.

From Cape la Vela westward, it is necessary to give some notices: for as the
breezes, especially from Cape Aguja, or rather from Point San Juan de Guia, are so
strong, that they may be considered as hard gales; and, therefore, it becomes
necessary to give some rules for making the different harbours, to prevent as much
as possible, those inadvertences, which, with winds so unmanageable, might prove of
serious consequence. There may, also, be some doubt in the making of the different
harbours, and general navigation of the coast, on account of the shifting of the wind,
which, we have said, sometimes changes to south and S.W. from June to November ;
and, therefore, the following reflections will not be considered irrelevant ; for though
they may be unnecessary, for those who are acquainted, they cannot fail of being
beneficial to those who are not so.

The principal places for commerce on this coast, and towards which vessels from
Europe, in general, direct their course, are Cumana, Barcelona, La Guayra, and Porto
Cabello; Maracaybo, Santa Marta, and Carthagena; Pampata, in the Island Mar-
garita ; and Santa Anna, in the Island of Curazoa. It being a general rule on this
coast, as well as in the whole of the Carribbean Sea, to make the land to windward
of the port of destination, as a matter of necessity, to prevent the trouble consequent
upon getting to leeward of it; we can with safety say, that being once within the
Sea of the Antilles, all those who are bound either to Margarita or Cumana, ought to:
close in with the coast, and make the land about Cape Mala Pasqua, or Cape Three
Points ; preferring the channel which Margarita forms with the main land, as stated
in the description. This route, also, appears preferable for those who are bound
to Barcelona; though it can be nowise inconvenient to pass to the northward of
Margarita.

Those bound to La Guayra from Cumana, or Barcelona, should steer a direct course
for Cape Codera, passing between the Island of Tortuga and the main land; but
those who, from Europe or any of the Antilles, are bound to that port, should navigate
to the northward of Tortuga, so as to approach the coast about the same cape, or a
little to leeward of it; taking care, if they choose to get sight of the ruck, named
El Continela, which lies to the northward of the cape. For those bound to Porto
Cabello, it is not so necessary to make Cape Codera, as any other point on the coast
to windward of their port, will answer the same purpose.

To make Cape Codera or any harbour, upon the coast to leeward of it, every one
may do it in the way most convenient to himself, or according to circumstances; that
is, he may pass through any of the straits or channels, that are formed by the islands
to the northward of the coast; and to direct him in doing this, nothing more is
necessary than to attend to the description of that which he takes.

Those bound to Maracaybo from the east, should get sight of Cape St. Roman, and
those from the westward, should make Point Espada. They may pass eituer to the
northward or southward of Curazoa, in running for Cape St. Roman ; and from that
cape they may run along by the coast until they get about 2 miles to the west of
Point Macella, from which situation the course to the bar is certain.

Should the navigation to Cape St. Roman be made outside the island, it should be
recollected that the Roques and the Islas des Aves are very dangerous on their north
sides; and to keep at a sufficient distance, especially by night, mariners must not
forget to apply to their reckoning for the night, the correction for the currents which
they experienced in the day, as deduced from the comparison of the dead reckoning

40)

with the points of departure and land-falls. ‘The due observation of this remark is of
great importance, as from what has been before stated relative to currents in this
place they require particular attention.

Those who are bound direct for Santa Marta, or Carthagena, ought unquestionably
to navigate outside all the islands, so as to make Oruba, and the land about Cape la
Vela; for, having got sight of the latter, they may with safety shape a direct course
to Point Aguja, in order to take the anchorage of Santa Marta in the manner before
described. We speak positively as to the necessity of navigating, to the northward
of all the islands; because, thus, they take the more direct course, and make the
shortest distance, as is well known to every skilful navigator.

Those, who without touching at Santa Marta, proceed on to Carthagena, will shape
a direct course from Point Aguja to the mouths of the River Magdalena, from whence,
by passing about 2 leagues to the westward of Point Zamba, and 14 to the west-
ward of Point Canoas, they may proceed on to Boca Chica, or anchor at Point Canoas,
or on the bank of Playa Grande, if they cannot effect an entrance into Boca Chica
by daylight. Calculation ought to be made, so that the distance may be proportioned
to the rate of the vessel’s sailing, or the sailing of the vessel to the distance to be
run, in order to reach Point Zamba, and thence take the Boca Chica by day. Or
anchor off Point Canoas, or on Playa Grande, in order, if possible, to avoid the
necessity of hauling the wind for the night, which will be troublesome and injurious
to the vessel and her rigging, when the breeze blows strong. But if there be no
meaus of avoiding it, you must endeavour to maintain your situation by short tacks
off and on; or, if the wind and sea will permit, let go an anchor.

When we advise a course to be shaped from point to point, along the coast, as
Points Aguja, Zamba, and Canoas, it is not only on account of shortening the distance,
awhich would be lengthened by following the various turns of the coast, but also for
the purpose of avoiding the shoals, which lie between Cape la Vela and Cape Aguja,
as noticed in the description of the anchorage off the City of la Hacha, page 31, as
well as those lying between Points Zamba and Canoas; it is strongly recommended,
not to get among the latter, with large ships.

If during the season of the breezes, it is necessary to follow the route which we
have described to Carthagena, from any place situated to the eastward of it, you
ought, in the time of the Vendavales, to steer westward from Cape la Vela, in the
parallel of 12 degrees, or rather more, for the purpose of retaining the breeze, as far
as longitude 75° 45’, or 76° 15’; and from that situation to steer south, coming up by
degrees to S.E., on getting into the region of the Vendavales ; observing also, that it
is better to make the land to the southward of Boca Chica than to the northward of
it; because, during this season, the current sets to the N.E., although in the season
of the breezes it runs to the S.W. Vessels should not run in upon the land by night,
but by day, for at such times the land is very deceiving.

In working to windward on this coast, from Carthagena to Margarita or Trinidad,
keep close by the wind, and make the boards so long as you conveniently can. The
proper time to tack ought to be decided by the daily variation of the breezes, which
at about midnight, or a little sooner, come off the shore, about E.S.E., or even 8.E.,
if it has previously rained, and the ground has been well soaked ; and from 9 to 11
in the forenoon, it gets round again to the E.N.E. At all distances from shore these
variations take place, and advantage should be taken of them in working from leeward
to windward; therefore, when at night the breeze inclines to the S.E., it will be
proper to tack, and stretch off the land until the morning, and when it gets to the
northward of east, tack and stand in towards the iand again; and if on account of
nearing the land, you cannot continue on the same tack until the breeze changes,
then you ought to work to windward along shore, by making short tacks until it
again changes to E.S.E., when you may stand out to sea. In this manner, two long
stretches may always be made, one to the N.E., the other to the S.E.; that is to say,
you may make the two within 8 points of the compass. By working to windward

FROM CARTHAGENA TO MARGARITA.

MARACAYBO, 4].

with short tacks along shore, this advantage cannot be obtained, because the breeze
always blows along the coast, unless there be a light land wind, which during the
rainy season sometimes rises in the night, and at daybreak ; but they are of short
duration, and such variations afford but little assistance.

Very small vessels cannot proceed upon this system, when the breeze is very fresh ;
which from Point Aguja to Isla Fuerte is like a heavy gale with a rough sea, which
prevents them from making any way; in these cases, it is most advisable for them to
keep in with the coast in smoother water. But in large ships, capable of resisting
these gales, or when the breeze is moderate, they ought to make long tacks, when
the wind will admit of it, in the manner before described. :

Observations by Captain Don Torquato Predrola.

On the coasts of Carthagena de Indias, of which I can speak with certainty, the
breezes do not set in before the end of November, and ordinarily with little strength,
until the middle or end of December, from which time they are powerful both day
and night ; only they frequently, but not always, moderate a little between the time
of sun-rising and 9 or 10 in the morning, when they again recover their ordinary
force. When you are very near the land, particularly if it be high, you may often
find them moderate at the dawn of day, and at sunrise veer to E.N.E. until 9 or 10
o'clock, when they again blow in their usual direction, which, on this coast, is from
N.N.E. to N.E. Of these variations, those who are acquainted with the coast, and
navigate near it, may well take advantage; and it may be better, at nightfall, to
anchor at some of the various points which offer, even for large vessels.

REMARKS ON MAKING MARACAYBO AND CARTHAGENA,
By Mr. W. C. Middlemist, Master, RN.

MARACAY3BO.—It is requisite when bound for Maracaybo to work to windward
under St. Domingo, and no ship, in my opinion, ought to attempt stretching off, till
at least as far as the Island Altevela. Easting is much sooner made under St.
Domingo than on the opposite shore; the current there setting strong to the west-
ward, at the rate of 2 knots. In the “ Helicon,” having experienced the wind much
to the northward during our passage from Jamaica, made Altavela on the 7th day at
9 in the evening, wind at E.N.E. blowing strong, but with little or no swell. Next
day at noon had made a 8.E. course, found a current of 13 miles to the westward.
On the next noon, Ist March, 1825, had made a 8.8.E. course, current 15 miles west.
At noon on the 2nd, we ‘had made a S. by E. 3 E. course, current setting due west,
49 miles; making a current of 67 miles in three days. The courses mentioned are
by reckoning, and ought to have put us in west longitude 69° 35’, instead of which
we were in 70° 45’, weathering the Monks about 10 or 12 miles. When leaving St.
Domingo, you generally find the current south-westerly, but as you come across it
gets due west. Should you fetch to leeward, it is useless to attempt working to
windward, unless you keep close in, which you may do with safety. After you have
weathered the west point of the entrance, endeavour to get sight of the weather land,
which is very low, but you will see a remarkably high peaked hill, which having got
sight of, you may steer south, running in by your soundings: it is advised to fetch
in to windward of Maracaybo, as the currents set to the westward. The land for 30
miles to the eastward is low and sandy, having nothing remarkable as a mark ; but
you may run along at the distance of 4 miles, in from 4 to 5 fathoms. To know when
you approach near to the entrance of Maracaybo, you will observe 8 or 4 hills, not
very high, the only ones you will see while running to the westward: the entrance

[CoLomBIA. ] G

42 CARTHAGENA.

is under the hills, but difficult to distinguish, unless close in. The entrance for
crossing the bar is at the west end of the island of Pazaa, to the northward of which,
for 4 or 5 miles off, is shoal water. The Castle of St. Carlos stands on the east end
of Pazaa (St. Carlos Island), and which you will see as soon as you come from the
eastward ; previously to which, you will observe a small dark fort standing outa
little to sea, apparently on the level of the shore; it is called Zaparas Castle, between
which and Carlos is an opening, and which, in all charts that I have seen, is marked
as the entrance; but this you must pass, hauling out to the northward and westward,
to avoid the shoal to the northward of Pazaa: and if you wanta pilot, make the
signal, and one will come off in a schooner-boat alongside of you, if not, anchor with
Fort Carlos bearing S.E. by 8.; the highest of the hills about south, in about 5
fatlfoms; the entrance of the bar will then bear 8.S.E. of you.

The anchorage off Maracaybo, for vessels that do not cross the bar, is in latitude
11° 1’ 30’ N., and longitude 71°40’ W., placing Fort Carlos by computation from
ditto in 10° 56’ N. latitude, and 71° 38’ 30’ W. longitude. From this anchorage, the
entrance to the bar will bear about S.S.E., known by keeping three hillocks on your
right. The bar was formerly to the eastward of the Island Pazaa, on which Fort
Carlos stands ; but owing to the continual swell setting on this shore, it has of late
been filled up ; and the entrance is now to the westward of the Island Pazaa. Even
this the pilots are obliged to examine very often, especially after a blow from the
northward. I shall leave it to the judgment of those who frequent this port, and are
unable with their vessels to cross the bar, whether it is advisable to remain at anchor
orno. In H.M.S. “ Helicon” we experienced very heavy weather, blowing hard from
the northward; the brig while at anchor was actually pitching the bowsprit under ;
a very heavy swell running on shore. We weighed and kept to windward during
the remainder of our stay here, which was several days; none of which a vessel
could lie with safety off the bar. The moon was entering her third quarter when
the breeze began, and slackened as she approached the fourth (March, 1825). The
current generally sets to the westward ; at times strong.

CARTHAGENA.—The mark to make for the Boca Chica, or Little Entrance is
Sandy Point (the northern point of entrance) midway between the Forts of San
Fernando and San José, and on with the highest part of Long Hill, on the opposite
coast, E. by N. When within + of a mile of the point, with a northerly wind, keep
close to the north shore, round the point; if the ship will lie N.E. she may shoot
round the shoal of St. José, on the north end of which there is a single post (now
in 8 feet) ; if not, it will be best to anchor as near St. Fernando as she will fetch,
(the deep channel here being only one cable wide, and steep), and warp to the
northward. ‘The ensign-staff on St. Fernando brought on between the watch-tower
north of the gate, and the embrasure next north of the watch-tower, clears the north
end of the shoal of St. José in 7 fathoms; then bear up E.S.E. in 12 fathoms, until
the Single Post comes in one with high corner of Fernando Wall, W. ; N. ; with
this mark on, run about half a mile clear of the shoals into the harbour. Ifa very
large ship, run to the E.S.E., until the same staff is on the south side of the porch of
the castle; this will clear the south side of the Knoil (which, with the staff on the
centre of the gate has only 3 fathoms); then steer N.E., for the beacon on the S.E.
end of Tierra Bomba, and pass a cable’s length to the eastward of it, keeping a N.E.
course towards the shoal of La Cruz, until the eastern magazine is open to the
westward of Fort St. Lazarus N. by W. 3 W.; this will lead between the shoals of
La Cruz to the eastward, and those of Tierra Bomba, and a spot of 5 fathoms to the
westward.

There is good anchoring ground in all the deep water of the bay and harbour.
The wind is generally from the N.W. in the day, rounding eastward to S.W. in the
morning. Notide. The currents on the coast generally set to the eastward, parti-
cularly round Galera de Zamba, to the distance of 5 or 6 leagues off shore; in a
calm, vessels are often carried from this place to Sabanilla in one day. N.B. The
flagstaff mentioned, alludes to the northern one, the other being used for signals.

THE COASTS OF NEW GRANADA, FROM
CARTHAGENA TO PORTO BELLO.

DESCRIPTION.—The coast from the River Magdalena, southward and westward,
is now attached to and forms part of the government of New Granada; the former
province of Carthagena being included in the department of the Magdalena. The
general face of the country is low towards the sea, but rising and mountainous inland;
the temperature is moist and hot, and in many parts unhealthy; it abounds with
woods, and lagoons of salt water; the shores are generally sandy, or filled with
swamps, which, from the lowness of the land in some places, the sea water inundates.
The province is well watered; the two principal rivers being the Magdalena and
Atrato; the former takes its rise in the valley of Popayan, and passing between the
great ridges of the Andes, proceeds northerly above 900 miles before it enters the sea,
By means of this noble river, a great traffic is constantly carried on with the interior
provinces, but the navigation, which is commonly performed by the means of numerous
flat-bottomed boats, is always rendered exceedingly irksome and disagreeable, both
on account of the heat and the myriads of mosquitos with which it is infested. The
Atrato has its source in the mountains of Choco, and divides the province of Darien
_ from Carthagena, and after running full 95 leagues in a northerly direction, empties
itself in the Gulf of Darien. Here it has been contemplated to form ajunction with the
Pacific Ocean, and the Canal of Rashadura has been cut for the navigation of boats,
from the River Naipi to the River Tupica, where the chain of the Andes is broken.
Both the rivers Magdalena and Atrato, abound with alligators, tortoises, and fish of
various kinds.

The shore from the Atrato to Porto Bello, is filled with marshes, and the whole
province is subjected to almost continual rains; so that the Gulf of Darien, so
advantageously situated for commerce, has no established town or settlement of con-
sequence, the climate being unhealthy, and the inland adjacent country inhabited
chiefly by a race of native savages, equally wild and ferocious, The province of
Darien, or Tierra Firma Proper, exhibits a semicircular isthmus or neck of land,
about 30 miles broad; it is generally mountainous, but the hills, which may be
considered as a continuation of the Andes, gradually decrease in height, as they
proceed northward, so that at Chagres they are estimated to be about 1200 feet above
the level of the sea.

DESCRIPTION OF THE COAST FROM CARTHAGENA TO
PORTO BELLO.

The south end of Baru and the Rosario Islands have already been described: and
it has also been noticed, that the former is separated from the main land by a narrow
channel, called Pasa Caballos, or Horses Pass. The north end of this channel opens
into the first Bay of Carthagena, and the south end of it into the Gulf of Baru, or
Bay of Barbacoas, which is formed by the Island Baru and the coast. This bay.
extends inward N.E. by E., nearly 12 miles: the points which form its mouth, are
the S.W. end of the Island Baru to the west, and Point Barbacoas on the main land
to the east. It is clean, with a depth of 9 or 10 fathoms, on fine sand and oaze; but

44 ISLES OF SAN BERNARDO.

the most general depth is from 4 to 5 fathoms. There is good shelter from the
breezes in it; and in entering, care must be taken to keep clear of the edges of the
bank, which extend from the Rosario Island, and not to forget the Tortuga Bank,
which lies (S. 42° W.) S.W. by S., distant 10 miles from Rosario Island, with 75
fathoms water on sand and rocks.

At the distance of one mile (N. 41° W.) N.W. 2 W., from Point Barbacoas, is a
bank, on which the least water is 2 fathoms: another lies 23 miles (S. 80° W.)
W.S.W. 4 W. from the same point, with from 13 to 2 fathoms on it; these are called
Barbacoas Shoals. Besides these there are two uthers, named, Atillo and Matunilla;
the first lies (N. 25° W.) N.W. by N., at the distance of 33 miles from the Point of
Barbacoas, with the depth of one foot over it, on rock; and the second at (N.E. by N.)
N.N.E. 2 E., nearly 5 miles from the same point, with very little water on it.

From Barbacoas Point, the coast trends about (S. 8° W.) S. 3° W., 153 miles to
the Fronton of Tigua; this may be known, because the highest cerro, or hill, on this
part of the coast rises on it. From this fronton, a bank with little water on it, runs
to the north somewhat westerly; and at Point Cowisario, the first and most projecting
point to the northward, its extremity extends 24 miles from shore. From the fronton,
or bluff of Tigua, to that of Boqueron, or Point San Bernardo, it is 12 miles (S. 25° W.)
S. by W.2W. To the northward and eastward of the latter point, and in the
direction of the coast, are 2 islets; the northern one named Islata de Jesus, and the
southern one Cabruna.

The Point of San Bernardo, is the S.W. point of a drowned mangrove cay; between
it and the coast there is a narrow channel, named Boqueron, frequented by canoes.

At (S. 20° BE.) §.S.E. 4 E., distant nearly 2 miles from Point St. Bernardo, lies a
rocky bank, named the Pajarito, or Little Bird Bank, the least water on which is 3
fathoms, and the greatest 45, fathoms.

ISLES OF SAN BERNARDO lie to the west of Point San Bernardo, and are
11 in number, including those of Jesus and Cabruna; but without including some
other small islets of little consideration. These islands extend to the westward,
comprising the edges of the banks, 15 miles, and from north to south, 10 miles; between
them various little channels are formed. The depth on the bank to the west and
south of these islands is very unequal; for you may instantly pass from shallow into
deep water. ‘They are low and covered with trees.

The channel, which is between the bank on the east and S.E. side of the Island
Salamanquilla and the west side of the Islet Cabruna, lies in the direction of (N.47°E.)
N. 40° E., and (S. 47° W.) S. 41° W., and is in its narrowest part three-tenths of a
mile wide, with a depth of 10 to 13 fathoms, on clay bottom, and 6 fathoms at the
edges of the steep banks. The banks have very little water upon them, and, unless
you keep in the middle of the passage, there is a great risk of grounding. The channel
is nearer to Salamanquilla than to Cabruna, for which reason you ought to keep
nearest to the former; and, in clear weather, you may see its bank, which will enable
you to pass through with less risk; but, in thick weather, the hand-lead is the only
guide.

To pass through this Salamanquilla Channel, on coming from the north, when you
have passed to the westward of the Rosario Islands, steer towards the Hill of ‘Tigua,
remembering that the shallow bank named Tortuga lies (N. 63° W.) N.W. by W. W.
from that hill, which bearing will enable you to give it a proper berth; that is, you
ought not to steer towards Tigua Hill, when in that direction, but either to the south-
ward or eastward of it; and navigate thus, until the easternmost of the San Bernardo

Islands, named Salamanguilla, bears (South) 8.3 E.: from that situation, you may

change your course to (S.S.E.) S.S.E.3E., until the Hill of Tigua bears (N.E.)
N.E.4N.; then steer (S.W.) S.W.S., keeping the hill on that bearing, and attend
to what has been previously said of this channel; keeping persons on the look-out for
the banks which run off from both sides, and which, as we have said, show plainly.

PUERTO DE CISPATA. 45

Having passed through Salamanquilla Channel, and being abreast of point San
Bernardo, you will open the great Bay of Tolu, otherwise named the Gulf of Moris-
quillo, which is formed by the Islands of San Bernardo to the north, and the Island
Fuerte to the south. The latter lies with the southernmost cay of the former bearing
(N.46° E.) N.E.3N., at the distance of 26 miles. All this gulf has deep water from
9 to 23 fathoms, on green oaze, so that you may anchor in any part of it, in the season
of light breezes, calms, and variable winds.

(S. 833° E.) S.E. 48., at the distance of nearly 13 miles from the Point of San
Bernardo, in the bottom of the gulf, is the town of Santiago de Tolu, situated close
to the sea shore; and from it the mouth of the harbour of Cispata bears (S. 63° W.)
8.W. by W., distant 13 miles, and is in latitude 9° 30’ 56” north.

The land in the vicinity of this town is plain, with savannahs, which extend to the
north, east, and south, terminated on the east by a chain of mountains, over which
there is one mount, forming two round hummocks which are called the Tetas de Tolu:
these lie 12 miles to the eastward of the town, but they are one of the marks by which
this coast is known.

In order to pass to the westward of the Islands of San Bernardo, keep at the
distance of 6 miles from the northernmost of them, called Tintipan, and do not steer
any thing to the east until the Point of San Bernardo bears (KE. by N.) E.N.E. 3 E.,
ou which course you may steer for it. Those bound to Santiago de Tolu, will find
it very convenient to enter by the Salamanquilla Channel; and when abreast of the
Point of San Bernardo, they will see the ‘letas de Tolu, with which mark they can
direct themselves to that town. Of the other hills which are seen to the southward,
the easternmost is called Santero: this lies from the Point of San Bernardo, (S. 5° W.)
south, at the distance of 21 miles, and the westernmost, named Cispata, bears
(S. 20° W.) S. by W. 4 W., 25 miles from the same point. Under this hill, and to
the northward of it, is the Harbour of Cispata: this hill is not so high as Santero.
Steer towards the valley between the hills, for the harbour.

PUERTO DE CISPATA.—The mouth of this harbour lies (S. 16° W.) 8. 3 W.,
at the distance of 174 miles from Point San Bernardo, and the Point of Zapote, which
is the east point of the harbour, in latitude 9°24’ 19"N. The west points are called
Terraplen and Balandra, between which the distance is rather more than a mile.
These western points are covered with high mangroves, which extend out into the
water: from its mouth, the harbour extends in to the distance of 7 miles (5. 64° W.)
S.W. by W.; it is sheltered from seas and winds, and the best anchorage is on the
northern shore, between the Points of Balandra and Navios; the latter point is
remarkable from its extending out to the southward. ‘The Hills of Santero and
Cispata point out the situation of this harbour: the middle and highest part of
the former lies rather more than 4 miles (8. 48° E.) 8.E. 2 E. from the fronton, or
Point of Zapote. Near this hill,and to the westward of its north part, is the village
of Santero, at the distance of 2 miles from the little bay of Zapote. The top of
Cispata Hill lies a little more than 8 miles (S. 27° 30’ W.) S. by W. 2 W. from the
same point of Zapote.

The River Sinu disembogues in the interior of Cispata Harbour : it forms almost a
semicircle towards the west and south, passing by the southern slope of the hills of
Cispata, including thus far the town of San Bernardo del Viento on the left bank, and
the villages of San Nicholas and Santa Cruz de Lorica on the right.

From Mestizos Point, which is the northernmost point of Cispata Harbour, the
coast trends (S. 81° W.) 8. 70° W., and S. 63° W: to Point Piedras, a distance of 173
miles; in the intermediate space, and on the bearings mentioned, are the Cienaga de
Venados, and Punta del Viento, between which is the place where the bank extends
farthest from the coast, 83 miles to the north, and 6% miles to the west, with a depth
of 3, 4, and 5 fathoms, on sand and rock, and also on sand and oaze.

Point Piedras forms a front in the direction of S. 40° W. and N. 40° E., a distance
of 3 miles; it is moderately high, scarped, and foul, at the water’s edge. Atits N.E.

46 ISLA FUERTE.

end, it forms a little bay, and at the distance of 2 cables’ length to the northward of
it, lies a small high rock, with some shoals half a mile to the N.W. of it, which extend
N.E. and 8.W., nearly a mile: they have on them some rocks above water, and others
which show only at low water: the depth is from 13 to 2 fathoms. Along this coast
the lead should be kept going.

The S8.W. extremity of Point Piedras is called Point Rada, from which, at the
distance of a little more than 5 miles (S. 39° W.) 8.W. by 8.;58., is Punta Broqueles,
which is low and rocky, with a reef extending about 2 cables’ length to the northward.
At ashort distance from this reef lies Baja del Toro, or Bull Shoal. Between Rada
Point and Broqueles Point, lies the Ensenada, or Bay of Rada, with a low beachy
shore: the bay is shallow, with 3+ fathoms, on oazy bottom, at the distance of eight
or nine-tenths of a mile. To the S.E. of this bay a hill is seen stretching N.E. and
S.W. with 3 peaks, the highest and largest of which lies about 5 miles south-eastward
from Broqueles Point.

ISLA FUERTE.—The N.E, end of Fuerte Island lies (S. 843° W.) W. by S.35.,
21% miles from Point Mestizos, and (N. 57° W.) N.W. by W. 2 W., 635 miles trom
the N.E. part of Point Piedras. This island is 1} mile in length from north to south,
and about three quarters of a mile from east to west; it is high in the middle, and
covered with trees and royal palms, which rise above the others. It can be approached
at its south point, called Arenas Point, only, for it is surrounded by reefs, with
various scattered rocks, some of which show themselves. On the bank outside the
reefs, and also on them, there are from 2 to 4 fathoms water, on rocks and coarse sand.
Besides these banks, which surround the island, there are two others smaller; the
one lying (8.S.W.) 8S. by W.% W., 1 mile from the island, with 5 fathoms water, on
sand; and the other (S. 28° E.) 8.E. 2 8. from Arenas Point, rather more than a mile,
with 6 fathoms on sand and gravel. The channel between this island and the main-
land has from 63 to 14 fathoms water. ‘The island may be seen from the deck at the
distance of 20 miles.

POINT BROQUELES TO THE GULF OF DARIEN.—At the distance of
about 56 miles (S. 49° W.) 8.W. 4S. from Broqueles Point, lies Punta de Caribana,
which is the northernmost point of the Gulf of Uraba, or of North Darien ; the inter-
mediate coast forms bays, trending inwards 6 miles, or somewhat less; and in this
space is the Fronton and Hill of Tortugon, which is remarkable; the Points of
Arboletes, or Little Trees, San Juan, and Sabanilla That of San Juan is high and
scarped, the others are low to the water’s edge, with beaches from point to point ; the
land in the interior, a low hilly range, which terminates near the Cerros or Hills of
Sabanilla, that lie 8.S.E. about 4 miles from the point of that name. All this coast is
shallow, so that during the time of light breezes, or of variable winds and calms, you
may anchor on it, at a greater or less distance from the shore, according to the size of
the vessel. There are no other impediments onit than a faradlon or high rock, which
lies rather more than 1$ mile (S. 39° W.) S.W. by 8.758. from Broqueles Point ;
Tortuguilla, or Tortugon Island, lies 16 miles (S. 37° W.) 8.S.W. 4 W. from that
point, and nearly west from the Fronton and Hill of Tortugon, distant rather more
than 4 miles; and the Gigantones Bank, which lies above a mile from Sabanilla
Point; being near the coast, it presents no danger, unless you go near to that point,
or that of Gigantones. The Island Tortuguilla is low, small, and covered with trees;
a little reef extends northward from it, with very little water on it.

The Point of Caribana, as we have before said, is the northernmost point of the
Gulf of Uraba. It is low, with trees, and surrounded with rocks; and is very
remarkable, because from it the coast bends to the south to form the gulf; and also
because the Cerro del Aguila is near toit. This hill is in latitude 8° 37’ 50’N.;
aud from it Cape Tiburon, which is the westernmost point that forms the Gulf of
Darien, bears (N. 84° W.) W. 3 S., distant 29 miles.

The Hill of Aguila, although of moderate height, is remarkable, from being insu-
lated in the middle of low land.

GULF OF DARIEN. 47

The shoals about Caribana Point are at the S.W. end of the general bank, which
we have mentioned as extending along the coast; and the depth of 5 fathoms on the
outer extremity lies 4 miles (N.W. by N.) N.W. 4 N. from the point. Nearly in
that direction and at a short distance from the point, there are two rocks;
one near the point partly shows itself, and the other, only a little separated
from it, has very little water on it. From the edge of the bank, in 5 fathoms, the
depth increases outward to 6 or 7, on a sandy bottom, and successively to more, so
that at the distance of 6 miles N.W. from Caribana Point, there are 10 and 11
fathoms, on oazy sand; at 11 miles, 21 fathoms, oaze ; and, at the distance of 14 miles,
32 fathoms, also on oaze. These soundings, and the bearings of Aguila Hill, may
serve to guide those bound to this gulf; noticing, that so soon as Aguila Hill bears
east, they will be clear of the shoals off Caribana Point; and may without fear run
up the Gulf of Darien nearly to Arenas Point, which lies (S. 35° W.) S.S.W. 4 W.
from that of Caribana 5} miles; all this part having a good depth of water.

GULF OF DARIEN.—This gulf has its entrance between Caribana Point on
the east, and Cape Tiburon on the west. All the eastern and southern coasts of it to
the Bay of Candelaria offer safe anchorage at all times of the year, but the rest of it
to Cape Tiburon is very wild in the time of the~breezes, and without any shelter,
except for small vessels ; but in the time of the Vendevales, or light breezes, you may
anchor in any part with safety.

The north and south points of Arenas form a low front of 2 miles in extent, bearing
from each other (S. 19° E. and N. 19° W.) S.S.E. + E. and N.N.W.i W. ‘These two
points form the western dike of the Lagoon of Aguila, which extends to the eastward
5% miles, and is 3 miles from north to south, with various low islets within it: it
begins at the southern extremity of Aguila Hill, before described.

From Arenas Point, southward, the coast trends eastward 53 miles to the Rio Salado,
forming thus a tongue of sand projecting into the sea, which, although very low, has
deep water near it, and may be coasted at less than a mile.

From the Rio Salado the coast runs south, with some inclination to the east; the
whole of it is low, with some hillocks at intervals, and on the bank off it the depth is
so regular and the bottom so clean, that it may be run along with safety by the hand
lead. From the Point, and Cerro or Hill of Cayman, which are 14 miles distant from
the Rio Salado, southward, the shores on both sides of the gulf are swampy, as far
as the principal mouth of the Rio Atrato, without showing any hill in all the space ;
and from the River Suriquilia, which is the southernmost part of the gulf, to the
north and west, may be ealled the delta of the Great Atrato, or of Darien.

The Bay of Candelaria, which is formed by the swampy land at the channel of the
river, bears from the Hill of Cayman about (8. 49° W.) 8.W. 3S. at the distance of
12 miles, For navigating all this coast of the bottom of the gulf from Point Cayman
on the east, to the Bay of Candelaria on the west, there is no other rule or guide than
the lead; nor is there any danger, for you may anchor in any part.

The principal object for entering into the Gulf of Darien, is to avail yourself of the
facility which the River Atrato: offers for conveying articles into, or bringing them
from the interior of the country; and although this river branches into the sea
by many mouths, extending overa great distance, and forming the swampy and
inundated lands that we have spoken of, yet only eight of them are navigable for
boats and launches; and of these not one offers the same advantages as the Little
Faysan, or Pheasant Branch, which discharges into the southern part of the Bay of
Candelaria: because, when anchored there, vessels will be sheltered from the sea, and
near to the channel by which their freights are to be conveyed inland.

The Coasts of the Bay of Candelaria are low and the greater part of them inun-
dated, even at low water, and covered with mangroves, reeds, and rushes; so that
no more than the N.W. point of it appears dry. ‘The mouth or entrance of the bay,
from the N.W. to the S.E., where the branch, called the Little Faysan, falls in, is
about 2 miles across: but there is a bank and shoal of sand running the whole circuit

48 GULF OF DARIEN.

of it, and extending a mile S.E., from the 8.W. point, which reduces and straighténs
the bay to scarcely a mile in breadth. From the 8.E. point this shoal extends only
1+ cable’s length; within the bay it narrows on the shore, but widens on the N.W.
side. The clear space of good anchorage is about a mile and a third in extent.

To enter this bay, great caution is necessary in the use of the lead, not to get into
less than 174 or 17 fathoms at the entrance, nor 12 within it. This caution will be
very necessary, because the sand-bank which surrounds it is so steep, that it shoals
immediately from 13 to 5 fathoms, and from 5 to beingaground. ‘Taking care to keep
in the depths just mentioned will lead through the middle of the channel, at about
4 cables’ length distance from the S.E. point. It will also be advisable to have a
person on one of the yards to look out, for the colour of the water shows both the
channel and the shallows. ‘The Little Faysan arm of the river has 3 feet on the bar;
and the tide rises 2 feet throughout the whole Gulf of Darien.

From the N.W. point of the Bay of Candelaria the coast continues low, and
covered with mangroves, in the direction of (N. 10° W.) N. by W. 3 W. to Revesa
Point, the distance being scarcely 5 miles; and thence about (W.N.W.) W.N.W. 3 W.
7 miles to the Tarena Cays. On all this coast there is a bank of shallow water,
thrown up by the mouths of the river, the largest of which is about one-third of the
distance from Revesa Point towards the Tarena Cays; and it is necessary to keep at
2 miles distance from the coast. Revesa Point, which is also called Choco Point,
forms a bight where there is good anchorage, well sheltered from the norths and
breezes; and to take it, run by the south part of the point at 13 cable distance; and
when you are abreast or to the west of it you may anchor in 13 or 14 fathoms.

On the coast to the southward of the Tarena Cays may be seen a mountain, called
the Peak of Tarena, whence rises a very lofty ridge, running to the N.W.; and of the
various peaks which it forms, the southernmost is named Candelaria, and the north-
ernmost, which is over Cape Tiburon, is named the Peak of the Cape; the peak next
to the southward of it is named Gandi.

From Tarena Cays the coast runs about (N. 2° W.) N.W.2N., a distance of
18 miles, to the Bolanderos: it is high, with various islets along it; of these, the
first, named Tutumates, is a group of three islets, very clean, and lying out about half
a mile from the shore. ‘To these follow that called Tambor, or Drum, which also lies
off the coast rather more than half a mile; although this is clean, it must be remem-
bered, that at halfa mile from its N.N.E. part there is a rocky shoal which shows
itself, and having between it and the islet a pass; but it is better always to keep
outside. To the westward of this islet the coast forms a bay, called Puerto Escondido
(Hidden Harbour), which will admit only small vessels, ‘To Tambor, follow the
Bolanderos, which is a larger islet with smaller ones to the southward of it; these
are all very clean, with sufficiently deep water around them, and they do not lie above
three quarters of a mile from the shore.

Three miles (N. 55° W.) N.W. by W.3 W. from the Great Bolandero lies the Piton
Islet, which is very clean, and about half a mile trom the coast; from thence
(N. 65° W.) W.N.W. % W., at the distance of 6 miles, is Gandi Point, forming a
beachy bay, called Tripo Gandi. From Gandi Point, about (N.N.W.) N.N.W. 2 W.,
at the distance of 12 mile, is the point of the River Gandi, which, with that named
before, forms the cove of Estola, or Gandi, in which the rivers of these names disem-
bogue: this cove is of little importance.

At (N. 16° W.) N.N.W., a little more than 63 miles from Gandi Point, is an islet,
called the Tonel, very clean, with deep water, especially on its eastern side; this lies
rather more thana mile from the coast. From this islet to Cape ‘Tiburon it is 65
miles (N. 42° W.) N.W.3 W. All this coast from the Tarena Cays to Cape Tiburon
is high and scarped, or precipitous, with deep water off it; it is very wild in the
season of the breezes, and shoukl not then be approached; but keep on the eastern
side of the gulf, where there is not only safety in anchoring, but it is easier to
beat to windward there, as there is less swell of the sea, and thus much time may
be saved.

PUNTA ESCOCES. 49

CAPE TIBURON is the N.W. boundary of the west coast of the gulf; itis rocky
and high, and projects out to the N.E. in form of an isthmus, which on the south and
west forms two little harbours. The first of these is narrow, and of little importance ;
the second is larger, and called Miel Harbour; it has good holding ground, and the
greatest depth is from 11 to 12 fathoms, on sand and clay.

(N. 62° W.) W.N.W. + W., distant 13 miles from Cape Tiburon, is the point and
peak of Carreto. Between the two points the coast formsa bay of about 24 miles
deep, called the Bay of Anachucuna; all the shore is beachy to the foot of the high
mountains, without any remarkable point. In the 8.W. part of this bay, at the
distance of 2 miles from Carreto Point, is a small harbour, called Puerto Escondido.

The point and peak of Carreto are at the eastern part of the harbour of that name ;
the western part is formed by a group of islets of various sizes and shapes; and.
between the points at the distance of a mile and a half, is the widest part; the nar-
rowest part of the mouth being only a mile. This harbour is of a semicircular form,
and runs in about a mile; the least depth of water is 34 fathoms, and the greatest
8 fathoms, on sandy bottom, but it is open to the N.E. breezes, and the seas they
raise, and has little shelter from the N.W.; therefore is only used during the season
of the calms and variable winds.

Northward from this harbour rather more than a mile, there are two little shoals
near each other, lying ina N.K. and §8.W. direction. There are 5$ fathoms water
over them on rocky bottom, and 20 to 25 fathoms close to them; with fresh breezes
the sea breaks over them.

At (N. 48° W.) N.W. by W., distant 7 miles from the point and peak of Carreto, is
the Punta Escoces, or Scot’s Point. In this line of direction are various islets of
different sizes, extending a long mile N.N.E. from the Point of Islets, which is nearly
3 miles short of Scot’s Point. ‘The land is high and scarped to the Point of Islets, but
low and beachy from thence to Punta Escoces.

PUNTA ESCOCES is the S.E. point of Carolina Bay, the great islet, named De
Oro, or Santa Catalina, being the N.W. From one point to the other the bearing is
(N. 40° W. and S. 40° E.) N.W. | W. and §.E. { E., and the distance 4 miles; and in
respect to this line the bay runs in 13 mile. In the S.E. part of this bay is Puerto
Escoces, or Escondido (Scottish or Hidden Harbour), which extends inward in that
direction nearly 3 miles, forming an excellent shelter; it has several shoals in it, as
shown in the particular plan, by which plan any vessel may take the anchorage; the
depths are 5, 6, 7, and 8 fathoms, sandy bottom.

The Isla Grande del Oro is high, and 1,8, mile to the southward of it there is a
smaller islet, named San Augustin: and in the same direction, rather more than a
cable’s length further is the Islet de Piedras, which, without doubt, takes its name
from the numerous rocks with which it is surrounded.

Between Piedras Islet to the north, the west point of the River Aglatomate to the
south, and that of San Fulgencio to the 8.W., is formed the Ensenada, or Bay of
Carolina, or Caledonia, and the Channel of Sasardi.

The Bay of Caledonia is, strictly speaking, formed by the points just mentioned:
which bear from each other (N. 26° W.) N.W. by N., and the contrary, distant a mile.
The bay is clean, with a sufficient depth of water, the greater part of its coast being
a beach, near about the middle of which is the River Aglaseniqua. The point of San
Fulgencio is projecting, scarped, and clean, and has also on its west side a little cove,
with shallow water, bordered by mangroves and cays.

Between San Fulgencio Point and the Great Oro Island, with San Augustin and
Piedras Islets, and the Mangrove Cays to the westward of them is formed the
Channel of Sasardi. The S.E. entrance from edge to edge is about 4 cables’ length
in width, with a depth of 8 to 11 fathoms, on oaze, and further in, from 7 to 9
fathoms; as also between the steep bank off Piedras Islet and the Bay of Caledonia,

50 GULF OF SAN BLAS.

he depth is from 64 to 14 fathoms. The space of sea between this bay and Port
Escoces is of a good depth ; but (S. 55° E.) S.E. by E. 3 E., somewhat less than a mile
from Piedras Islet, the sea breaks when the wind blows fresh.

These harbours are equally sheltered from the winds and seas of both seasons, and
have a good depth of water; but the Channel of Sasardi and Bay of Caledonia are
preferable, because you may either enter or sail out from them with all winds, and
with greater facility and less risk than into or out from Puerto Escoces.

The N.W. mouth of the Sasardi Channel is formed by the west point of the two
large islands and the front of Sasardi, with an opening of three quarters of a mile.
This channel has many banks, and is therefore of no utility ; neither is there any
population near it; those who wish to enter must do so with a free wind.

Between the eastern point of Great Oro Isle and the N.W. mouth of Sasardi
Channel, some reefs project out, with two islets at their extremity, which bear from
the eastern point of the Great Oro (N. 25° W.) N.W. by N., distant 2 miles, and from
the S.E. end of the large islands already mentioned, about N.E. There is a shallow
bank to the westward of the Fronton of Sasardi, at the distance of 15 mile.

The Fronton of Sasardi is projecting, round, scarped, and surrounded with reefs
near the shore. From the most salient point of this fronton the S.E. part of the Isla
de Pinos bears (N. 5° W.) N. by W., distant 2 miles: and in the intermediate space
the coast forms various small bays, the points of which are scarped, and surrounded
with reefs. Off the west part of the island is the Cienega de Navagandi, the mouth
of which is closed by reefs, and with the island forms a channel of 2 cables’ length in
width in the narrowest part, and has from 1} to 5 fathoms water.

The Isla de Pinos is high, with a hill extending along it, on which are two re-
markable points, covered with wood; it isa large mile in length, N.W. by N. and
S.E. by S., and scarcely a mile in breadth: its north, east, and south sides are high,
scarped, and bordered with reefs very near the shore. The N.E. point of this island
lies in latitude 9° 1’ 30" N., and (N. by W.) N. by W. 3 W. from its north point at the
distance of 24 miles, is the Isla de Pajaros (Bird’s Island), which is low, narrow,
and covered with brushwood, surrounded with reefs, having close to their edges 7 or
8 fathoms water, on rocky bottom. From this point commences the Archipelago of
the Malatas, composed of islands, cays, banks, and reefs, forming between them and
the main land many anchorages and well sheltered channels, secure in all weathers,
and terminating at Point San Blas. The interior of the coast is high, being a range
of hills, with remarkable peaks, shown on the chart of this part of the coast, and may
serve as marks to the various anchorages, &c.

The channels in this space are Pinos, Mosquitos, Cuiti, Zambogandi, Punta Brava,
Cocos, Rio de Monos, Ratones, Playon Grande, Puyadas, Arevalo, Mangles, Mozon,
Caobos, Holandes, Chichime, and San Blas. All are more or less free.

When a vessel is a league to the northward of Isla de Parajos, a (N.W.) course for
25 miles, and W.N.W. 40 miles, will take her clear of all those dangers, and to the
northward of the easternmost cays of the Holandes Group, at the distance of 43 or
5 miles; with these courses she will pass at the beginning 13 or 2 miles outside the
reefs, and afterwards 44 or 5 miles, but it is at the option of the navigator to pass at
a greater distance.

GULF OF SAN BLAS.—Seventeen miles to the westward of the easternmost
cays of the Holandes Group, is the Point of San Blas, in latitude 9° 34’ 36” N., and
longitude 79° 1’ 24” W. It is low, and terminates the Gulf of San Blas in the N.E.
The mouth of this gulf from the said point to the anchorage of Mandinga, is 6 miles,
north and south, and from that line as much to the west; its coasts are low, and.
covered with mangroves, which run into the sea.

From the Point of San Blas some reefs extend to the eastward to the distance
of 12 mile, with various cays; the easternmost is named Cayo Frances; from this

POINT SAN BLAS. 51

the other cays, to the number of twelve, extend to the S.W. and W,; and to the east-
ward of them are many banks and islands, being part of the Mulatas Archipelago,
and which form various channels. To go in and anchor in this gulf, whether it be
in the Bahia Inglesa, which is to the S.W. of San Blas Point, or in that of Man-
dinga, which is to the southward of it, the best and most commodious passage is by
the channels of Chichime and of San Blas.

The channel of Chichime is formed on the west by the cays off the Point of San
Bias ; on the east by the reef and group of cays of Chichime, and on the south by
another group, surrounded by reefs, which some call Cayos de Limon, or Lemon Cays.
The channel of San Blas is formed by the latter on the S.E., and those of San Blas
on the N.W. The first is 3 miles in extent between the steep edges of the banks, and
the second 12 mile.

To enter this gulf it is necessary to open the mouth of the channel of Chichime,
until the second islet (from the westward) of the Lemon Cays bears south: from
which situation steer to the south until abreast of, or rather more to the north,
than Cayo Frances; then steer (S. 50° W.) S.W. i S. through the middle of the
channel of San Blas, which is 12 mile wide between the reef of the W.S.W. Lemon
Cay, called Gallo, and the reef which extends to the southward from Cape Frances;
proceeding in this manner to the anchorage, whether it be that on the north side
of the gulf, or that in Mandinga Bay. To run for the latter, two cays, which lie to
the north of Mandinga Point, serve for a mark; of these the northernmost, named
Cabra, is distant about a mile from the said point; nearly a mile (N. 10° W.)
N. by W. § W. from Cabras Cay, there is a little sandy cay, to which a berth
ought to be given: and there is a bank of 1 and 1} fathom, lying (N. 69° W.)
W.N.W. 2 W. from Cabras Cay, at the distance of rather more than 14 mile:
between these you should pass. The anchorage of Mandinga is sheltered, and
has depth sufficient for any class of vessels. In the gulf, and extending out from
the bottom of it, 34 miles, there are various islets and cays, with banks; the
easternmost is named Maceta Cay. To which a berth must be given, if going far
into the gulf.

There is also another channel, named Canal des Holandes, which is the largest of
all those formed by the Malatas Isles; and its mouth is formed towards the east, by
the western extremity of the reefs of the Holandes Group, and those at the N.E. of
Icaros Cay; the cays are distant from each other nearly 3 miles (N. 55° E.and S. 55° W.)
N.E. g E. and 8.W. { W. The least depth in this channel is 14 fathoms, on a sandy
bottom; but at (W.N.W.) W.N.W. 3 W. from Holandes Cay above 13 mile, there is
a shoal, which extends half a mile from north to south, with 6 and 7 fathoms water,
on a bottom of rocks, on which, with a little swell, the sea breaks. This shoal may
be passed either on the east or west side, but it will always be best to pass to the
eastward of it, and near the reefs of the Holandes Group, the breakers of which serve
for marks: then steer for the east part of Icacos Cay. This cay or island is of firm
land, covered with high wood, and is so named from the abundance of the Icacos
plum-tree gowing on it. From the meridian of Icacos Cay, by the south of it, the
direction of the Holandes Channel is (W. by S.) W.S.W. 4 W., to the bottom of the
Gulf of San Blas: it is clean, with a depth of 21 to 25 fathoms water, on oaze, and a
breadth of 25 and 3 miles between groups of foul cays and reefs; but free and com-
modious to turn in, if necessary, towards the anchorages.

POINT SAN BLAS to PORTO BELLO.—At (N. 49° W.) N.W. by W., above 4
a mile from the Point of San Blas, is the northern part of its front, low, and covered.
with mangroves, and in the intermediate space is a little cay, named Piedras, and
other banks, which are joined to those off Cayo Frances. (N. 34° W.) N.W.3N.,a
; of a mile from the last named point,is a cay, named Perro, connected with the
reefs which extend in a westerly direction from Cayo Frances, and which terminates
at an island in front of a Cienaga, at the distance of 1} mile.

52 PESCADOR ISLET.

From Perro Cay the coast continues nearly 10 miles (S. 88° W.) about W. 3S. to
Cocos Point, which is the easternmost of the mouth of Escribanos Harbour: the
intermediate coast is almost alike low with ridges, and bordered with a reef, and
forming somewhat of a bay. The most visible objects on it are the Point of Mogote,
which is small, a little projecting, and has a hillock on it; that of Cerro Colorado, is
round, scarped, and projects but little; and that of Playa Grande, is round, and sur-
rounded by reefs, extending off a cable’s length,

Cocos Point advances into the sea, and from it Punta Escribanos bears (S. 80° W.)
W.S.W. 4 W., 1} mile. In the intermediate space the coast forms a bay, in the
middle of which is Escribanos Harbour, which, from its mouth, extends 3 amile to
the southward : it is very shallow, having only 1 and 13 fathom water. On the
outside of it, on both sides, there are reefs with very little water on them; and in the
channel formed by them, there are from 3% to 63 fathoms.

To the N.E. of the mouth of this harbour, lie the shoals named Escribanos: they
are two in number, and are composed of reefs with very little water on them, lying
very near to each other. That nearest to the coast hasan islet, which is distant from
Cocos Point almost 2 miles, and extends W.S.W. and E.N.E., 1 mile; the other reef
lies about W.N.W. from the said islet or rock, and extends nearly a mile from east to
west; both are steep-to, with 3 and 4 fathoms water; and on the bank are from 8s
to 12 fathoms, on a bottom of gravel and coarse sand. In the channel, which is
formed by the south-easternmost bank and Cocos Point, are from 9 to 12 fathoms,
which diminish to 6 and 5 on each side.

Escribanos Bank lies about (N.W. by W.) N.W. by W. 2 W. from the shoal of the
same name, distant 54 miles; it extends in the same direction nearly 2 miles, with
from 5 to 8 fathoms water, on rocky bottom; and about 2 cables’ length to the north-
ward of its edge are 17 and 31 fathoms. Heavy seas break over this bank, which
may serve as a guide; and when it does not, a look-out must be kept at the mast-
heads. In the channel between this bank and the Hscribanos Shoal there from 8 to
17 fathoms water, on sand, gravel, and rocks. The N.W. part of it lies 8% miles
(N. 82° W.) N.W. 3 N. from Escribanos Point.

At (N. 81° W.) W. 1.N. from Cocos Point, at the distance of 19} miles, lies Terrin
Point, and Pescador Islet; between Cocos Point and Point Quingongo, which are
distant from each other 84 miles, and on the meridian of Escribanos Bank, is the Islet
Culebra, which is two-thirds of a mile N.N.W. from Culebra Point. Continuing to
the westward you will meet the Point and Islet of Quengo. Port Escondido, which
is to the westward of this point is no more thana little Cienaga, or swamp; Points
Chaguachagua and Macolla being its most remarkable points. The mountains which
continue along this coast, from those of Darien to those of Porto Bello, are sufficiently
remarkable; that named the Cerro de gran Loma, or Cerro Gordo, being rather more
so than the rest: this lies (S. 424° W.) S.W. by S. from Culebra Islet rather more
than 7 miles, and may serve asa mark to keep clear of the Escribanos Bank and Shoal.
This hill is but little higher than the Cordillera, in which it is situated; its top is
large and extensive.

Pescador Islet lies about 2 cables’ length (N. 43° W.) N.W. % W. from Terrin
Point; this point is surrounded by reefs, which extend a cable’s length to the north,
and half a mile to the west, continuing to the §.S.W., and including three islets,
lying between that point and the N.E. point of Nombre de Dios Harbour.

Between Terrin Point, and Martin Pescador Islet, and Manzanilla Point, from
which the first bears (N. 64° W.) W.N.W. 3 W., distant above 4 miles, and the second
(N. 72° W.) W. by N., distant 5 miles, a great bay is formed, which falls in nearly
3 miles to the S.W., and to the West and N.W.., 2 miles to the bottom of the bay of
San Cristoval ; at the extreme east part of this bay, and at 13 mile (S. 49° W.) S.W.
 S., lies the west point of the harbour of Nombre de Dios, surrounded with reefs, as

GARROTE HARBOUR. 53

is also the eastern point, though from this point they extend farthest out. This
harbour is small, and the greater part of its shores have reefs and shallows; the clear
depth is 34, 38, and 44 fathoms in the mouth. The rest ot this great bay is useless in
the season of the breezes. and the reefs from the bottom of it stretch out nearly a mile
towards Point San Cristoval.

From Point San Cristoval, 2 cables’ length to the N.E. lies an islet, named Juan
del Pozo, surrounded with rocks; and about S.E. from it, distant half a mile, lies a
bank, called the Vibora. Between this bank and the islet Juan del Pozo, and
between the latter and Point San Cristoval, there are 9,10, and 13 fathoms water
and coarse sand. Point San Cristoval lies (S. 88° W.) W. 2 S., distant 35 miles from
‘ferrin Point: and also from this point the Buey Shoal lies (N. 60° W.) W.N.W.,
distant nine-tenths of a mile; between this shoal and the reefs of Terrin Point, the
depths of water are from 9 to 13 fathoms, on rocks, sand, and clay ; and 9, 12, and 14
fathoms, on bottom of the same quality, between the shoals of Buey and Vibora. The
coast between Point San Cristoval and that of Manzanilla is high.

MANZANILLA POINT is the northernmost of all the coast of Porto Bello: it is
also high, scarped, and projecting, with two hummocks on it. Near this point there
are various islets, and a shoal; the greatest, named also Manzanilla, is high and
scarped, and lies eight-tenths of a mile to the east: to the northward it has 3
farallones, of which the farthest off lies rather more than a cable’s length from it.
At §. 30° W. from the same islet there are three smaller ones, surrounded by reefs
extending N.E. and §.W.: there is also another, distant 13 cable’s length to the east ;
and finally, to the (N.N.E.) N. by E. 3 E. of the said Manzanilla Islet, distant four-
tenths of a mile, lies the islet of Martin Pescador, which extends about a cable’s
length from norti to south; all these islets are high and scarped, and between them
there are from 10 to 14 fathoms water.

Manzanilla Shoal lies N.W., four-tenths of a mile distant frem the point of the same
name: it has very little water on it, but there are 5 and 6 fathoms near it, and in the
strait which it forms with the point there are 13 fathoms water.

On this coast are two remarkable mountains, named Saxino, and Nombre de Dios,
which may serve as marks for recognizing the harbour of the last name: the first is
high, and terminates in two peaks near each other; the north-easternmost of them
bears (S. 22° E.) S.S.E. 3 E. from Terrin Point, distant nearly 7 miles. That of
Nombre de Dios lies to the south of the harbour, terminates in a peak, and bears from
Terrin Point (S.S.W.) S. by W. § W., 8 miles.

At (N. 65° W.) W.N.W. 4 W., distant 13 mile from Manzanilla Point, lies the
highest part of the islet Tambor, which is high, round, and scarped ; it is connected
by areef of 2 cables’ length, with the north part of the island Venados, or Basti-
mentos, ‘This island extends N.E. and S.W., almost a mile, forming, with the main
land, the N.E. channel of Bastimentos Harbour; the greatest extent of which,
between the reefs, is about a cable’s length, with 5 and 5% fathoms water, on sand.
This said Bastimentos Island is foul on the S.E., south, and S.W. sides; and the
latter, with the Islet Cabra, which lies west a little southerly from it, form the N.W.
channel, the least breadth of which, between the reefs, is three-tenths of a mile, with
a depth of 33 to 9 fathoms, on clay. Bastimentos Harbour is of little importance,
although sheltered, with a depth of water from 33 to 63 fathoms. All its shores are
bordered with reefs, and the ordinary anchorage is to the S.W., south, and 8.E. of
the south sandy point of Bastimentos Island.

GARROTE HARBOUR.—At (S. 51° W.) S.W. from the highest point of
Tambor Islet, at the distance of 2} miles, Jies the mouth of Garrote Harbour, formed
on the south by the main land, on the east by Great Garrote Island, and on the west
by Pelado Islet and others which follow, 14 mile to the westward, as far as Bo-
querones. The mouth of this harbour is scarcely three-tenths of a mile between the
reefs, to the west of the Great Garrote Island and Pelado Islet; its direction is from
north to south, and afterwards to S.E., with a depth of from 63 fathoms in the

54

interior of the harbour to 12 and 18 in the mouth, on clay. It is sheltered from the
seas and winds of the N.E. breeze. Between this harbour and that of Bastimentos,
rises the Hill of Garrote, of middling height, with its top terminating in a peak;
it is seven-tenths of a mile distant from the coast.

(S. by E.) 8. by E. 3 E., at the distance of 34 miles from the harbour of Garrote,
is the mountain of Capiro, or Capira, high and almost always covered with clouds.
It lies nearly east from the city of San Felipe, of Porto Bello.

BOQUERONES POINT.

At a little distance to the south of Mount Capiro, is the mountain ridge of Llorona,
stretching out east and west. ‘This is the highest of all on the coast of Porto Bello;
the eastern part of its top appears as if notched vertically, forming a peak, named
Campana, or the Bell; from which the mountain extends westward, descending
gradually to near the peak of Guanche. The appearance of this mountain is such,
that if cannot be mistaken for any other; in clear weather it may be seen at the
distance of 45 miles; but in the season of the fresh breezes, it is generally covered
with haze; and in the season of the Vendevales and variable winds, it may be seen
between 8 and 9 in the morning, and 4 and 5 in the afternoon, though during the
rest of the day it is covered with clouds.

The Levadera Shoal lies (N. 6° E.) north, seven-tenths of a mile from the north
end of Pelado Islet, and (N. 85° W.) W. 3S., at the distance of one mile from Cabra
Islet, at the mouth of Bastimentos Harbour. This shoal is of rock, with very little
water on it, steep to, with 7 or 8 fathoms close to a rock over which the sea washes.
The channels between it and the Islets Cabra and Pelado are deep, with from 14 to
17 fathoms water, on clay.

At (S. 64° W.) S.W. by W., distant 3,°, miles from the highest part of Tambor
Islet, lies the Point of Boquerones, which is projecting, high, and scarped; and from
it, upon the opposite bearing, that is (N. 64° E.) N.E. by E., are five islets, which
extend out 3 cables’ length, and are called the Boquerones. ‘The reefs and islets
which follow from Pelado to the westward, terminate here.

Boquerones Point has on the south, above a mile distant, a hill, called Casique,
terminating in a point, and of middling height, which may serve as a mark for
avoiding the Fonl Farallon, or Farallon Sucio; which rock lies (N. 33° W.) N.W.2N.,
scarcely 2 miles from Boquerones Point. The Foul Farallon lies at west end of two
groups of islets and shoals, which extend from §.W. to N.E., 63 cables’ length,
forming a channel between both, with 4 to 6 fathoms water. The north-easternmost
islet, or farallon, bears from the highest part of Tambor Islet, (N. 88° W.) W.2S.,
nearly 4 miles; in this place there are 16 to 30 fathoms water, on clay and sand;
and 16, 21, 22, and 25, between the said farallon, the islets of the coast, and the
Levadera Shoal.

(S. 69° W.) S.W. by W. 3 W., distant 3 miles from Boquerones Point, lies the
north end of the Islets of Duarte, which are four in number, and extend (S. 25° E.
and N. 25° W.) S.E. by S. and N.W. by N., six-tenths of a mile; from the northern-
most one, a reef extends a cable’s length, in the same direction. The southernmost
of these islets is separated from the Point of Duarte, which is on the mainland to the
south, a little more than 2 cables’ length; and from that of Sabanilla, which bears
N. 64° E. from it, nearly half a mile. Between the two straits, there is a depth of
from 3% fathoms on a patch near the islet, to 15 fathoms. The intermediate coast is
high and scarped, with some bays; the Point of Josef Pobre extends farthest out,
and is surrounded with rocks and reefs. Sabanilla Point has also a reef, with some
rocks.

(S. 24° W.) S. by W. 3 W., rather more than 2 miles from the northernmost part
of the Islets of Duarte, is Drake's Point, which is the N.W. point of Porto Bello ;
the intermediate coast is high and scarped, with a little harbour, called Leon, of little
importance, and bordered by reefs, which terminate in the N.N.W., ata little farallon
distant four-tenths of a mile trom its mouth.

PORTO BELLO. 59

PORTO VELO, or PORTO BELLO.—The name of this port expresses sufficiently
the excellence of the harbour for every class of vessels. The entrance, at the widest
part, which is between Drake’s Point on the north, and the islets of Buenaventura
on the south, is 1,2,0f a mile, nearly north and south ; between Iron Castle Point, and
that of Francesio, it is about half a mile wide, bearing also nearly North and South
(true). Its direction inward, from between the latter-named points, is about E. by N.,
less than 13 mile, to the mangroves at its bottom. The north shore is clean, but some
reefs and rocks, with little water on them, stretch off the south shore, to between
1 and 13 cable’s length; and in the east part of the harbour there is a bank of sand,
which advances 23 cables’ length from the mangroves towards the west; and at
(N. 26° W.) N.W. by N. from the city mole, about a cable’s length, there is a little
sand-bank, with 1 and 1} fathom water on it; the rest of the harbour is clean and
deep, diminishing gradually from 17 to 8 fathoms. Ships of the line ought to enter
this harbour by warping or towing, because there are regularly either head winds or
calms.

The best anchorage is to the N.W. of the battery of Santiago de la Gloria, in 10
or 11 fathoms, on clay and sand; but smaller vessels may go nearer to the city,
taking care to avoid the little bank already mentioned. The reefs on the south coast
continue to the W.S.W., and westward as far as the Islet of Buenaventura, the N.W.
point of which bears (8S. 55° W.) 8.W. 3 W., 3 long cables’ length from Point Cocal ;
between this islet and the point there are two smaller ones, all connected by
reefs. At (S. 37° W.) 8.S.W. 3 W., two-tenths of a mile from Drake’s Point, is the
middle of Drake’s Islet, clean all around, and has a break in the middle, which
appears to divide it into two parts. From this break in Drake’s Islet about ,°, of a
mile (W. and N. 65° W.) S. 83° W. and W.N.W. 3 W.., are comprised the south and
north extremities of the Salmedina Shoal; on the south end are some rocks covered,
over which the sea breaks; the other parts have 2 and 33 fathoms water, on rocky
bottom. ‘The water is deep all around it, and between it and Drake’s Islet there are
from 12 to 28 fathoms on clay.

Seven-tenths of a mile (South) 8. 3 E., from Drake’s Islet, and (West) W.2S.,
34 cables’ length from Point Francesio lies the Francesio Shoal, of a triangular form,
upon which are 4 or 5 fathoms water on rock. Between it and the coast there is
no passage, but in the channel between it and the Salmedina Shoal there are from
18 to 23 fathoms on clay.

This harbour is surrounded by hills, from which descend some rivulets or brooks on
both shores; at these vessels may procure water, particularly from that which disem-
bogues in the bay of, and to the west of the batteries San Fernando, on the north
side of the harbour.

Southward of Porto Velo, at the distance of a long half mile, is the Ensenada, or
Cove of Buenaventura, much bordered by reefs, and consequently of little use.

To enter Porto Velo, when approaching from the north-eastward, it is advisable to
approach the Farallones of Duarte, and from them to shape a course so as to pass at
a cable’s length to the N.W. of Drake’s Rock, so that you may pass the Salmedina in
safety ; but never try to pass between Drake’s Rock and the main, So soon as you
have passed the rock, steer to the south-eastward, so as to run up in the middle of
the harbour, or rather nearer the north than the south shore.

To enter this port from the southward, you may pass at about half a mile from the
Islet of Buenaventura, and steering towards Drake’s Rock, you will go clear of the
shoal of Francesio: then steer N.E. and East, as you perceive the harbour opening,
so that you may take mid-channel, or rather nearer to the north side, as before
directed.

FuRTHER REMARKS ON APPROACHING Porto BELLO.—Between Cape Manza~-
nilla, near Porto Bello and San Juan de Nicaragua (now Greytown) there is an
inshore current from westward to eastward. It is an eddy striking out from the

56 PORTO BELLO.

great Caribbean Current at Cape Gracias Dios, and eventually returning into it,
with a broken and divided force. The breadth of the current extends from the land
to the distance of about 30 miles in the offing ; its rate is from 1 to 2 knots; and the
direction is parallel to the curvature of the coast and capes.

The stream out of the numerous rivers entering this current seems to increase
its rapidity ; for close inshore between the rivers, the rate is seldom less than 2
knots; 6 miles off the land it runs about 1 knot, and at a greater distance the same.

Ships should never go to the southward of latitude 11° until 50 miles to the west-
ward of their intended port.

By night off Porto Bello, during the season of the breezes, should you be under sail,
be constantly on your guard against the squalls and calms prevalent in its vicinity.
The former frequently shift from the land round the compass, with torrents of rain
and gusts of wind, so as to oblige you to clew all up. Precaution must be adopted to
prevent being drifted on the Farallon Sucio, and other dangers there, over which the
current is supposed directly to set north-easterly 2 or 3 knots an hour.

INTRODUCTORY DESCRIPTION.—PANAMA. The land to the westward
of Porto Bello extends to the 8. Westward about 25 leagues, so far as the little river
Belen, which is the boundary separating the province of Panama from Veragua.
The climate is generally very hot, and during the months of August, September,
and October the heat is almost insupportable ; from October to August, the Brisas,
or trade winds, and the continual rains, to which it is then subjected, contribute to
cool the atmosphere, but render a residence there unpleasant, and, to an European,
very dangerous and unhealthy.

The soil is prolific, and produces the tropical fruits and plants in abundance.
Great part of the country is covered with forests of valuable trees ; the towns and
villages are mostly situated along the shores of the two oceans; and the land,
rising in the interior, exhibits a lofty chain of mountains, whose appearance is
abrupt and broken; their summits are generally barren and uninhabited ; they
are known to afford mines of both gold and silver, but hitherto so little has been
obtained from them, that they are, at present, abandoned, as not worth the expense
of working.

VERAGUA is about 35 leagues in length from east to west, and 25 leagues in
breadth ; like Panama it is a ragged mountainous country, inland ; covered with
vast forests, and interspersed with fertile vallies, where cattle find most luxuriant
pasturage ; but the heat of the climate, the continual rains, the frequent storms of
most terrific lightning and thunder, and the immense torrents which, during these
rainy seasons, rush with resistless impetuosity down the surrounding mountains,
render the country at these times totally impassable. The woods abound with birds,
monkeys, and other wild animals, some of which are indigenous and peculiar to
this province. There are mines of both gold and silver, but the difficulty of work-
ing them, and the immense labour of conveying the produce to be smelted, render
them, though rich, of very little practical value.
