St. Jago de Veragua, the capital of the province, is said to be a handsome town,
and is situated inland, on the banks of the river Montijo; it is surrounded by a
district where Indian corn is produced, and cattle and hogs. are numerous. The
natives produce cotton, which they dye of a peculiar purple colour, and export to
Panama and throughout Guatemala. This city is the residence of the Governor,
who has 14 villages under his jurisdiction.

The most remarkable feature of the northern shores of Veragua, is the Lagoon
of Chiriqui, which is full 40 miles long, and about 15 broad; here the singular shell
fish is procured which furnishes the purple dye before mentioned. The country
around the Lagoon is said to be very fertile, producing mangoes, the wild nutmeg,
and various sorts of spices; these were first planted by the French, who contem-
plated forming a settlement here, and such an establishment would most probably
be attended with much success, even at the present time.

A little to the westward of this Lagoon is the Point Careta, near to which is the
line of division between Veragua and Costa Rica; and this at present constitutes
the western extremity of the territory belonging to the Columbian Government.

COSTA RICA.—This province is bounded on the south-east by Veragua, on the
east by the ocean, on the north by Nicaragua, and on the west and south-west by
the Pacific ; it is, generally speaking, a mountainous country, full of woods and
deserts, thinly peopled and badly cultivated ; yet it is said to contain mines of gold
and silver, and to produce excellent cocoa. The principal town is called Cartago,
or Carthage ; its commerce consists of cattle, hides, honey, and wax. It has a few
good ports on each sea, and also some convenient bays; but these are chiefly on the
side of the Pacific. Cartago, or Carthage, is situated in the heart of the province,
between both seas ; and a trade is carried on by the natives, to Panama by land,
and to Porto Bello, Carthagena, and the Havanna by sea; the sea. port being at the
mouth of the river Matina, in latitude 10° 1’ N., and longitude 83° 7’ W.

NICARAGUA.—This is.a province of Guatemala, now distinguished by the
appellation of Centrul America. Nicaragua is situated to the northward and west-
ward of Costa Rica, extending from the Caribbean Sea to the Pacific Ocean. The
climate is generally salubrious, for though the summers are hot, and the winter
subject to rains and storms of lightning and thunder, yet they are not unpleasant
or unhealthy. The soil is fertile, and abounds with forests of valuable woods,
interspersed with fine meadow land, producing fruits and vegetables in great per-
fection. There are large breeds of cattle, goats,‘ swine, mules, and horses; with
plenty of deer, and all kinds of game, as well as birds ; but it is also the abode of
numerous snakes, scorpions, lizards, bats, and noxious insects of various kinds.
The chief products are corn, tar, wax, flax, hemp, balsams, cotton, sugar, pepper,
amber, cochineal, cocoa, turpentine, timber, and Nicaragua wood, used in dyeing ;
these, with its silver mines, constitute its principal exports: the sands of some of the
rivers furnish gold, which is often found in lumps: the population is considerable,
and the people are reported to be industrious and ingenious. Their chief commerce
is with Panama.

In this province is situated the great and important Lake of Nicaragua, which is
computed to be 95 miles long, and 37 miles broad, of a depth more than sufficient
for the navigation of the largest vessels, having a communication with the Caribbean
Sea by means of the river St. Juan, and extending, on the western side, to within
15 miles of the Pacifie Ocean. It is here the grand and long projected design of
uniting both oceans, by means of a navigable canal, will hereafter most probably
be achieved. ‘‘ Nature,” says Mr. Pinkerton, ‘has already supplied more than
half the means, and a complete passage might haye been opened at a much less
expense than the fruitless attempts made to discoyer the. north-west passages.”
But should a passage here be once opened, the force of the adjacent ocean would
soon enlarge the communication, and the projectors and completers of the under-
taking would be willingly and amply repaid for, theirlabours, by a tributary duty
on the vessels which would then pass the sound; such a design, carried into
ie could not fail to insure the thanks and applause of the whole nautical
world.

It is said that the river St. Juan is encumbered with shallows, but these might
be easily removed, and the passage adapted for ships of burthen. As it, now is,

THE COASTS OF TERRA FIRMA AND MOSQUITIA. 3

the navigation of the river St. Juan is carried on with boats, of a flat construction,
which render the passage tedious and inconvenient. Alcedo asserts, that the
river St. Juan is navigable for large vessels throughout its course to the lake, and
this is further confirmed by Estalla ; but Dr. Dancer, in his history of the ex-
pedition from Jamaica to the lake of Nicaragua, 1780, states, that at the latter end
of the dry season, March 10th, there was but little water in it, being, at that time,
full of shoals and sandy beaches, which rendered the channel dificult and dan-
gerous. There is asmall fortress erected upon the banks of the river, called by the
English, Fort St. Juan, but by the Spaniards, the Castle of our Lady ; it was
furnished with 36 cannons and a battery; level with the water is a platform,
and towards the land it is defended by a ditch and rampart, reaching to the edge
of the river, and was commonly garrisoned with 100 men. The situation is said
to be unhealthy, probably rendered so by the thick woods and stagnant marshes
which surround it. Alcedo, the author before quoted says, “it may be regarded
as the key of New Spain and Peru, for that an enemy, by possessing them-
selves of this fortress and the port of Realejo, would become the master of both
oceans.”

The Lahe of Nicaragua abounds with most excellent fish, and its shores maintain
large herds of cattle, forming a picturesque and fertile appearance; the city of
St. Leon de Nicaragua, in lat. 12° 22’, and long. 86° 40’, contains about 1200 houses,
with 4 churches, several convents, and other considerable buildings, being, during
the occupation of the Spaniards, the see of a Bishop. There is a small town of the
same name situated upon the western banks of the lake, which, from its situation,
is a place of some trade; but further north-westward is the town of Grenada,
which is now becoming more populous, and increasing in size and consequence,
on account of its proximity to the lake, and being so advantageously situated for
commercial purposes.

Whenever the proposed canal of communication shall be adopted, the lake will
offer the inestimable advantage of an internal port, well defendable by fortresses
on each side. Within the lake are several islands, and numerous excellent creeks
and harbours, where vessels might find convenience and security at all times, and
upon all occasions: in fine, this place is likely to become’ an object of great future
importance, and therefore no apology will be considered necessary for the length
of this description.

MOSQUITIA, or THE MOSQUITO SHORE.—This territory did extend to
the northward of the river St. Juan, so far as Cape Honduras, a coast nearly 150
leagues in length; but in 1820, the king of the Mosquitos granted a part of this
territory to Sir Gregor Mac Gregor, by which a line of coast, extending from 84°
40! to 85° 45’ West Longitude, and running considerably inland, has become a new
district, and known by the title of the Poyais Country.

The shores, from St. Juan to Cape Gracias a Dios, are generally low, with many
intersecting rivers ; the interior is variegated, and protected on all sides by im-
penetrable forests, extensive morasses, and inaccessible mountains; yet there are
parts of the country where the soil is extremely fertile, and where Indian corn of
the finest quality is successfully cultivated. The sugar-cane, cotton, tobacco, plan-
tains, cassava, yams, and sweet potatoes, thrive equally well.

The inhabitants of the sea coast are chiefly engaged in fishing, and a trade is
carried on for turtle, which are generally exported to Jamaica, and other islands
adjacent. The commerce usually carried on with this country, consisted chiefly
in mahogany, woods used for dying, tortoise-shells, coffee, cotton, cocoa, sarsa-
parilla, indigo, fustic, medicinal gums and balsams, cochineal, and other valuable
articles: but the native inhabitants are of so indolent a disposition, and there is
such a want of harbours fitted for any ships of burthen, that very little advantage
is now derived from any of the resources of nature, however abundant the supply,
or facile the attainment thereof; and although fishes of infinite use and interesting
variety are the tenants of their lakes and rivers, and though the neighbouring
lands abound with antelopes, deer, warree, peccary, and other quadrupeds; and
though birds of rich and varied plumage enliven every spot; yet these are per-
mitted to hold an undisturbed possession of their native haunts: for it is only
dire necessity that can induce the Mosquito Indian to interfere with either. Their
cattle are small, but fat and well flavoured; horses are numerous ; swine are

people appear to live in peace and plenty; and although exertion of any kind is
not their characteristic, yet they are mild and inoffensive, have the reputation of
virtue and morality, and never trust a man who has once deceived them, or forfeited

The most populous part of the Mosquito territory is about the environs of Cape
Gracias u Dios, and here is situated a sort of town or village, where the king usually
resides. Some settlers reside here, who have established stores for the sale of
goods, which are chiefly obtained from Jamaica.

PORTO BELLO TO CHAGRES.

At (S. 50° W.) S. W. from Drake’s Point, (the north point of the harbour of
Porto Bello) nearly 15 miles distant, is the west extremity of the Fronton of
Longarremos ; this, with the north-easternmost of the Noranjos, or Orange Isles,
which lies 4% miles (N. 66° E.) N. E. by E. from it, form a bay, into which enter
the two creeks of Minas. The creeks of this name are formed among mangroves ;
the easternmost of which runs inward, three miles to the S.S. E. ; its breadth is
very unequal, and its shores are bordered with reefs. The western creek is nar-
rower and shorter, extending to the south rather more than a mile. The Orange
Isles are low, covered with trees, and surrounded by reefs: but at the S. E. part
of them there is anchorage, with 5, 6, and 7 fathoms of water, on sand. In the
intermediate part of this coast is Punta Gorda, the most projecting point, with
several coves of little consideration. To this point the coast is high, with banks or
ridges ; and between it and Buenaventura Cove, the River Guanche disembogues.
Guanche Hill bears from Punta Gorda, (N. 82° E.) E. N. E. 2 E., at the distance
of 33 miles. From Punta Gorda to the S, W. the coast declines in height ; and
the remainder, from Punta de Rio Grande, or Rio Grande Point, and the creeks
of Minas, is low, with mangroves: the Fronton of Longarremos is also low, with
mangroves, and bordered with reefs; as are the points which form the Minas
Creeks. The reefs extend more than a cable’s length from the coast, and are steep-
to; at the distance of one-third of a mile out, there are 12 fathoms water, on clay.

From the Fronton of Longarremos, the mangroves extend to the 8. W. nearly a
mile and a half, to the Point of Manzanilla, which is also mangroves, round, and
surrounded with reefs, to the distance of more than a cable’s length ; and a little
shoal lies 3 cables’ length (N. W. by N.) N. W. 3 N. from it.

Manzanilla Harbour is formed between the islet of that name to the west, and
the main land to the east, extending in, 2short miles S .S. E. from Manzanilla Point ;
this harbour is clean, with from 3 to 63 fathoms water ; but the best anchorage for
all vessels is a little to the south of its mouth, on the east coast, in 53 fathoms water,
on sand and clay.

Five miles (S. 68° W.) S. W. by W. } W. from the Fronton of Longarremos, is
Punta del Toro, which is the westernmost point of Naos Harbour, or the Bay of
Lima ; the eastern one being the north point of Manzanilla Island, which is distant
from Zoro Point 22 miles. Toro Point is salient, high, and scarped, and bounded
by reefs, which extend outto about 2 cables’ length,* with an islet near them. This
harbour extends inward, nearly 4 miles from the middle of its mouth: its breadth is
nearly equal, though it narrows a little from two-thirds of the said distance. It is
clean to the parallel of Punta Limon, with a depth of 34 to 7 fathoms, on sand and
clay : from this last point to the south, the water is shallow. As this harbour is
exposed to winds from N.E. to N. W., round by north, it is only useful in the
season of the variable winds and calms.

From Toro Point, the coast follows W. by S., nearly 23 miles to Brujas Point,
which is of moderate height, and, like the intermediate coast, bordered with reefs,

- which extend only a short way out, but surround the islet called Mogote de
Brujas, which lies to the N. E. of the point of the same name, about 2 cables’

From Brujas Point, the coast that follows is lower than before, in the direction

CHAGRES. From Chagres Point to the west point of the Penon, on which
stands the Castle of San Lorenzo, the distance is 14 cable’s length (S. by E.)
S. by E.4 E. The Penon is scarped to the N. W. and South: and the Castle of
San Lorenzo, as we have said, is situated on it, in latitude 9° 18’ 38” N., and longi-
tude 80° 0' W. This Penon to the north, with Punta Arenas to the south, form
the mouth of the River Chagres, which, in the widest part, is little more than 2
cables’ length across, and 1} at the narrowest. To the E. §. E., at a short distance
from the Castle of San Lorenzo, is the little town or village of Chagres, composed
of huts, covered with palm leaves. The mouth of the river narrows between the
Penon and a bank which extends out from Arenas Point about half a cable’s length.
On the meridian of the Penon, there are 2} and 3 fathoms water, which depth con-
tinues, varying a little more or less, to the distance of halfa mile up the river. At
92 English fathoms, west from the Castle of San Lorenzo, is the shoal named Laja,
which extends 35 fathoms from N.E. to S. W.; itis of rock, with very little water
on it. It is very dangerous either to enter or sail out from this river, and it
can only be done by manageable vessels, which do not draw more than 12 feet ;
both these operations ought to be performed with a fair wind ; for otherwise, the
current of the river, and the various eddies which it forms from the opposition of
the Penon, Laja, and west coast, will carry the vessel on one or other of these
dangers.

From Arenas, or Sandy Point of the River Chagres, the direction of the coast is
(S. 65° W.)S. W. by W. 3 W., the distance of one mile to the Punta de Morrito,
or Little Hill Point ; and from thence (S. 38° W.) 8. S. W. # W.., a little less than
2 miles to the Point of Animas ; between which are some Red Cliffs, all the shore
being low with a beach.

At (S. 36° W.) S. S. W. 4 W., distant 2 long miles from the last mentioned
point, there is another equally low, named Point Diego, and this is the last point in-:
cluded in the surveys of Captain Fidalgo.

Remarks on the Coast near Porto BELLO and CuHacrEs, by Mr. Middlemist.

“Tn making either of the above places during the months of August, September,
and October, you must keep to the westward; the currents during these months.
setting strong to the eastward, and the wind generally from the 8. W. to N. W.,
especially in shore. In the month of July the wind is variabie, veering all round
the compass in the course of 24 hours; and if stationary, but for a few hours, turns
the current. During the above named months the current is settled to the east-
ward. Ships may water off Chagres, especially small vessels, there being several
springs falling in great quantities from the rocks, and where boats can lie in perfect
security, cutting wood while the water is filling, and that iw great loads with much
ease.

“Cuacres Roaps.—To anchor in them, the best place is in 7 fathoms, with the
Castle about S. E., and Point Brujus about N. E. $ N., when you will be about 13
mile from shore. Point Brujas is 3} miles N. E. by N. from Chagres, and has
a little bushy hillock on it, which appears like an island from the eastward or
westward.

“The only thing that can be said in favour of this anchorage is, that the bottom
is very good for holding, but such a heavy sea rolls in when the wind is from the
N. E., North, N. W., and West, that itis with the greatest risk any vessel can
ride at such times. The following remarks have been made while on the station in
1815, 16, 17 and 18, in H. M. Sloops Royalist and Beaver, at different times.

“The coast about Chagres is level and not high, neither is it remarkable ; so that

you must necessarily be at a loss to find that port on your first approach to the
coast. If bound to Chagres, endeavour to make the land near Porto Bello, where
the coast is very remarkable, being the only high land in the vicinity, and as it
projects out from 10 to 15 miles farther than the coast at Chagres, which is com-
paratively a low coast.

“Ships generally make Porto Bello first, though bound to Chagres.

“The land immediately about Porto Bello can be seen 11 or 12 leagues in clear
weather, and from the northward at that distance appears like anisland. This view
comprises all the coasts and mountains inland, from 10 miles to the westward
of Porto Bello to Point Manzanilla 10 or 12 miles eastward of that port: the wes-
tern part being high and the east low; the highest part, where there is a sudden
fall, bearing S. E. by E., will lead directly to Porto Bello, and the land will be
perceived to decline gradually down to the westward as you advance in.

“Making the land about here must only be done when the easterly winds prevail,
viz. from January to July ; during the other months, it is recommended to make
the land well to the westward of Chagres, on account of westerly winds and a strong
easterly current.

“Cuacres Harsour lies 8. W. by W., about 25 miles from Porto Bello ; it
is defended by a castle on the larboard side, which stands upon a high point or
head, and commands the entrance against shipping; but boats might get into the
harbour by night, by rowing close under the larboard shore, without being per-
ceived by the castle. In the harbour’s mouth is a rocky shoal, nearly dry, which
forms two entrances. Vessels generally enter by the eastern passage and go
out by the western: there are about 13 feet water generally, and sometimes more.
In the rainy season, the stream sets out so strong that it is dificult to enter, but
more so to get a pilot, who can seldom be procured for the space of 3 or 4 days,
in which time you may lose many opportunities of going in. The best wind
to enter with, is N. W. or W. N. W.; bring the Castle to bear S. E., and
run directly for it with all the sail you can set: this course will bring you close in
with the larboard shore, to which you must keep. As soon as you see the shoal on
your starboard bow, open the castle point on your larboard bow until you have
passed it, then steer for a low sandy point a-head of you, and hauling round it
you will be in the river.

“The coast trends E. by N. from Point Brujas 2 miles to Point del Toro, off
which there is a reef stretching E. N. E., about one-third of a mile; the soundings
are regular to it, and 5 fathoms are very near. The coast now bends in S. } E.,
forming a deep bay, in all parts of which are good anchorage. From Point del
Toro across the bay to Orange Island, is about E, N. E.; there are regular sound-
ings of 8 and 7 fathoms, and the shore all the way to Porto Bello is clear, and has
several bays and inlets, with good anchorage for small vessels.

“Porto Berto Harsour bears nearly N. E. from Orange Island, about 14
miles. Buenaventura Bay, which lies close to the southward of it, and ata dis-
tance might be mistaken by a stranger for that harbour; it is very different
on a near approach. The bay runsin §. Eastward, and the harbour E. by N.;
there is an island also, which must be kept on the starboard hand as you go
into Porto Bello: it stands in such a situation, that it forms the starboard entrance
to the harbour, and the larboard on going into.the Bay of Buenaventura: it
is not distinguishable at more than 5 or 6 miles off the mouth of the harbour, on ac-
count of the high land close behind it, both being covered with wood ; and there are
two remarkable trees, one of which, resembling an umbrella, stands on the top
of it: these trees can be observed at 6 or 7 leagues distance, and when they bear
East, or E. by §., you may find Porto Bello by steering so, as they are upon the
high point at the starboard side of the harbour. "The island is called Buenaventura,
and the bay of that name is said to be bad, having rocky bottom, and being exposed
to N. W. winds.

“In making Chagres from N. E., if running along shore, you will not perceive
the castle till you are close up with it. It would be advisable to haul in for
the land about Point Brujas, off which there is a rocky shoal running out not
more than a quarter of a mile: from this point you will see a Bluff, called
Chagres Point, upon which stands a hut. But should that be blown down, you

FROM CHAGRES TO ST. JUAN DE NICARAGUA.

From Point Diego the coast runs S. W. by W. ? W., the distance of 40 miles to
Point Rincon, having some rocky points, with sandy beaches between them, but no
danger lying off the coast; from thence, S. W. } W., 18 miles to Conception or
Gold River ; it then sweeps round about W. by S. for 32 miles to Buppan Bluff ;
about 15 miles to the eastward of the latter are some Red Cliffs. Off this part of
the coast the shore is rocky. From Buppan Bluff the coast trends N. W. by W.
for 20 miles to Coco Plum Point, between which the coast is perfectly clean all the
way to within one mile of the latter point, having from 8 to 12 fathoms within a
mile of the beach. About a mile south-eastward of Coco Plum Point is the
entrance of the River Cana, which runs south about 4 miles up toa village. From
the latter point to Cape Valiente, or Valentia Point, the course is N. W. by W., 15
miles; this part of the coast is bordered by rocks the whole distance ; between the
before mentioned points is Old Bess Point, about 4 miles from the former, west-
ward of which is Toboboo Bay, with from 3} to 6 fathoms in it; but, as the whole
of this bay is lined by a reef of rocks at a considerable distance from the shore, it
affords but little shelter.

All this coast is generally low, with the exception of some parts which rise a
little; and the water along it is so shallow, that at 3 or 4 miles from it, there are
from 20 to 40 fathoms, the bottom being mostly mud and sand. Several rivers
disembogue upon it: besides that of Chagres, there are the rivers Indios and Coclet,
which are navigable, and communicate with the interior. That of Coclet is 42
miles to the west of Chagres.

Between the river Coclet and that of Chagres, there are four remarkable moun-
tains, two of them inland, and the other two on the coast; and as they may serve
for recognizing the land, we give their marks.

4, The Sierra de Coclet: this is rather lower than the former, and bears from the

Besides these hills or mountains, there are others about 7 leagues inland, which
are well known, and celebrated for their great elevation, named the Cordillera de
Veraguas, which commence nearly south of the river Coclet, and join the Serrania
de Salamanca, nearly in the meridian of the Bocas del Toro, or Bulls’ Mouths, and
which end somewhat to the westward of the Rio de Matina. Both of these are
sufficiently elevated as to be seen in clear weather 86 leagues out at sea. At the
eastern end of the mountains of Veraguas, there is a gap, resembling a riding
saddle, which is called the Silla, or Saddle of Veraguas, and this lies on the meridian
of the river Coclet; to find which from sea, you have only to bring the Silla to
bear (South) S. 3 E., and run in for the shore. To the westward of the Silla there
is a Mount, on the very top of the Cordillera, which has the appearance of a house
or castle, and is named the Castle of Choco. This lies (S. 50° E.) S. E. by E. } E,
from the island named Escudo de Veraguas, or Shield of Veragua, so that, when the
mountain bears in that direction, you will have the island right a-head. Upon the
western part of the same mountain may be seen a remarkable peak, named the
Pan de Suerre, which derives its name from the village at its base: this may serve
as a mark for finding Matina.

The Isla del Escudo is low, but covered with cocoa and other trees, and is sur-
rounded on the east and north parts with various kays of a chalky clay, also
covered with foliage. From these hays a reef projects eastward to the distance of
half a league, and the sea breaks on it. All this island and kays are surrounded by
a shoal of sand and gravel, which extends out five miles; but. there is over it, very
near the land, a depth of 5 fathoms; and it deepens progressively outward. The
island is separated from the main land about 3 leagues; and, in case of emergency,
water may be obtained from its different rills or rivulets, though with much labour,
for it is not abundant, and is at some distance above the beach. On the south and
S. W. part of this island there is an anchorage, well sheltered from the Worths and
the breezes, or general winds. There is also anchorage on the shoal to the east ;
but it is not so commodious, because it presents no shelter from those winds, and
the bottom is rocky.

From Point Valentia, which ‘is in latitude 9° 12’ N., and longitude 81° 55’ W..,
the coast forms a great bay, which is almost inclosed or shut up with various kays
and islets, running from that point to the N. W. by W. $ W., 74 leagues to the
N. E. point of Columbus Island, which is on the western side of the Boco del Toro.
This great bay is divided into two by several kays in its interior; the eastern
part is named the Laguna de Chiriqui, and the western, Columbus Lagoon or
Admiralty Bay ; these communicate with each other, by means of various arms
and creeks having shallow water. You may enter the Lagoon of Chirigui by the
channel formed by Point Valentia and the Tiger Kays lying off it; in this channel
are but 33 fathoms water ; but in the channel, between the Ziger and Sapotilla Kays,
which lie 4 miles further to the westward, the channel is 3 miles wide with 13 and
14 fathoms water in it; within this the water again deepens to 24 or 25 fathoms ;
until you approach the narrow entrances into the Lagoon. After passing through

the narrows you will find from 20 to 22 fathoms in the middle of the Chiriqui

The entrance to Admiralty Bay is by the mouth or channel formed by Punta
Sarepta and the west point of Columbus Island ; and in this mouth, and also within
the bay, it appears that there is depth sufficient for every class of vessels. This
mouth is named the Boca del Drago, or Dragon’s Mouth, to distinguish it from
another more to the east, named Boco del Toro, or Bull’s Mouth, by which small
vessels only can enter. Within both bays the anchorage is well sheltered, and as
secure as the best harbours; but, as we have not a circumstantial description of
them, we shall content ourselves with saying, that, to enter in, or’go out, by the
Dragon’s Mouth, you ought to give a good berth to the west coast, or that of Point
Sarepta, on account of a rocky reef which runs out from it to mid-channel. -

From Point Sarepta the coast runs about N. W. by W. 3 W., 73 leagues, low
and sandy to Monkey Point; and from Monkey Point to Coaita Point, W. N. W.,
4 leagues; between which are the Monkey Hills; thence N. W.., at the distance of
20 miles, is Point Blanco, having Grape Kay to the eastward, and Salt Creek
Village to the westward. From this point the coast follows about N. W. 3 W., for
85 miles to the Parasmina Hills; this part of the coast is clean and the water
deep, the land is covered with wood the whole distance, the tops of the trees being
from 100 to 200 feet high. The three principal rivers between Point Blanco and
the above-mentioned hills, are Matina, Swarree, and Parasmina. The coast from
thence runs N. N. W. 3 W. for 32 miles to Point Arenas, or Sandy Point, which
forms the harbour of S¢. Juan. This coast is all clean and the water of a moderate
depth. The River Turtuga, near Turtle Hill, 7 leagues from St. Juan, is the only
river on this part of the coast. The River St. Juan de Nicaragua discharges its
waters by several mouths, one of which enters the harbour.

PROVINCE OF COSTA RICA.

By Mr. Henry Davy, late Master of H. M. S. Victor, 1829 and 1830.

‘Having left Chagres on the 6th of February, 1830, and being bound to the River
Matina, we steered W. by N. to W. N. W., and experienced a current running to
the S. E., from 1} to 1 mile an hour; and as we approached the land the current
increased. We met with calms, light variable winds, with showers of rain, and
found great difficulty in gaining the anchorage, the position of the river not being
known within 40 miles. On the 10th we anchored off Salt River, in 8 fathoms,
with Pumpkin Island, N. E. by’E. 3 E.; Point Blanco, East, entrance of the
river, S. by E. 3 E.; Volcano of Torre Alba, W. by S.; and Point Cartago,
N. W, by W., black sand and mud. This coast has numerous rivers, the principal
of which is the Rio Matina. Salt River, called by the natives Rio Moyne, may
be known by 3 islets near it; two to the S. E., the first of which is called Grape
Kay, and is the largest, with a little islet off its N. W. end, and a reef running
from its S. E.; Plantain Kay is one mile to the westward; and off the river is the
other, called Pumpkin Island, but the Spaniards call it Isla Cabello ; it is high and
rocky, has some tall trees on it, and is very bushy. This island is bold-to, and may
be approached on any side within a cable’s length; it is a quarter of a mile from the
main land, and the channel is clear, with a depth of 9 and 10 fathoms. A little to
the S. E. of this island is Point Blanco, which, instead of being white, is a dark
rocky point, moderately high and very woody, as indeed the whole of the coast is.
From Point Blanco, which is the outer point of the anchorage, the coast forms a deep
bend, in the furthest corner of which, 2} miles south from Pumpkin Island, is the
entrance of Salt River. This entrance, like the mouths of the other rivers, is
obstructed by a bar, on which are heavy rollers; however, there is not much
danger, provided the boat is kept end on. “After rounding the point, on the star-
board hand, the river, which is about 40 yards across and 9 feet deep, runs West,
W.S. W., and in various other directions. It has three branches, one to the
southward, called the Rio Blanco, where is a plantation of plantains and bananas,
which runs about 5 miles, and is then obstructed by trees lying across the river,
and is no longer navigable even for canoes; but the principal branch is the Chiripo,

which diverges to the N. W. and West, and formerly communicated with the

Matina, but was blocked up by order of the government; the other branch is on

the larboard side, and runs to the southward about four miles. On the starboard

side going in are 5 cane huts, used as stores to traffic with the Indians, the owners

of which are masters of small vessels, who carry on @ very lucrative trade between

this coast, North America, and Jamaica. This establishment is the only one on or

near Salt River. The entrance is in latitude 10° N. and 6° 15’ 45” West of Port

Royal, (83° 5' 22" W. of Greenwich.) The anchorage is preferable to that of

Matina, which is but a short run for the boats from Salt River; the coast trends

N. W., 9 miles to Point Cartago, which is nowise remarkable, neither is the river,

for the surf beats so violently on the whole of this coast, that the entrance is com-

pletely hid, and appears as a continuation of the same; it is therefore necessary to

look carefully for it, and, after making it out, pull boldly through the surf, bor-

rowing well on the larboard shore. On either side of the entrance is a wigwam,

generally inhabited by two or three men. After having entered the Rio Matina,

whose proper name is the Chiripo, it is 40 to 50 yards in breadth, and 1 to 2

fathoms deep; its numerous reaches vary their courses from North to West and

S. 8. E., and finally, about 14 miles from the entrance, on the starboard side, is the

small village of Matina, consisting of a few miserable huts. At this place guides

and mules can be procured ; a few soldiers are stationed here, the officer of which is

Civil and Military Governor, collects revenue, &e. A few miles above Matina, on

the same side, the river branches off to the westward; this branch is called Bar-

Billa, and runs some distance in the interior. Passing the mouth of this river, the

Chiripo continues to the mountain of the same name, which is a volcano, From

the village of Matina to the City of Cartago, or Carthage, the distance is 30
leagues, and may be travelled in 4 or 5 days. ‘The road winds in different direc-

tions, and is crossed by many rivers, particularly the Paguar and Reventason,
which must be passed in canoes. Cartago is represented as a city of huts, and
contains 18,000 inhabitants. It is situated on elevated ground, and was for-

merly the capital; earthquakes and eruptions are frequent here, particularly in the
months of May and June; it has a hot spring, and is surrounded by six volcanoes,
viz.: the Voleano of Cartago or Suerre, which is only 18 miles from the city ; Torre
Alba, which is 30; the Chiripo, Barba, Dragon, and Dulta. ‘There is snow on the
tops of some of these, particularly the Suerre. In 1822, Cartago was nearly
destroyed by an eruption from the Chiripo, and in consequence of these frequent
eruptions the houses are built low and of mud. The present capital is the City of
St. Jose, which stands 5 leagues to the northward and westward of Cartago, and its
population and appearance are the same.

“The principal trade of this province is with Jamaica; a little is carried on by
land with Panama, which is at a distance of 200 leagues; and some with the
Pacific. Punta Arena, in the Gulf of Nicoya, being about 30 leagues to the west-
ward of Cartago.

<‘ There are several mines, the most valuable is that in the mountain of Aguacati,
which is said to be a very rich gold mine, fourteen leagues from Cartago ; and I
was informed that the principal occupation of the inhabitants is to procure precious
metals: agriculture and other useful arts being entirely given up for that purpose.

< The sea coast to the southward and eastward of Matina is moderately high and
thickly covered with trees, the whole being an impenetrable wood, filled with thou-
sands of monkeys, wild hogs, and a great variety of birds; all these animals are
very numerous near the sides of the rivers, which are greatly infested with alli-
gators, some of them are very large; and in the surf of the bars there are generally
a great many sharks. In the back ground is seen a lofty range of hills, called
the Mountains of Salamanca, which stretch well to the southward; and at their
western termination commence those volcanic mountains already mentioned, and
which may be described as high peaked hills, the highest of which, on any bearing,
is Torre-Alba. This remarkable mountain is the best mark for the Rio Matina ; it
has a white top, and when visible the smoke is seen issuing from the crater; near
Matina the high land ceases, and the coast to the N. W. runs low. From Salt
River to the Rio Tortuguero, vessels may run along shore in soundings. I sounded
the whole way in a boat, and found the coast perfectly safe.”

SAN JUAN DE NICARAGUA. The harbour of St. Juan de Nicaragua

THE COASTS OF TERRA FIRMA AND MOSQUITIA. iL

was surveyed in 1832 by Mr. George Peacock, master of H.M.S. Hyacinth, and
from which plan the harbour appears to be formed by an isthmus of land on the
north, nearly 2} miles in length east and west, but in strong north winds the sea
breaks across the low western neck. The north side of this neck of land is bor-
dered by rocks and heavy breakers, and terminates to the westward in a low sandy
point called Point Arenas which has a spit running from it 14 cable’s length, on
which the sea breaks. Inside Point Arenas there is also a rocky spit running out
to the westward full half a mile, with but 8 feet on it, being about 2 cables across.

The harbour is rather difficult to make out on certain bearings, as the whole
coast in the neighbourhood is low and sandy and of uniform appearance, with
trees about 50 feet in height. In clear weather the Cartago Mountain, an extinct
volcano, 11,100 feet high, may be seen, which bears due South, distant 18 leagues
from Point Arenas, but this mountain is sometimes obscured by clouds.

The west end of the isthmus is named Punta de Arenas, and is situated in latitude
10° 58’ 30” N., and longitude 83° 45’ W. The ensenada or bay is very spacious, but
it is obstructed by a great bank with little water over it, which reduces the extent
of the anchorage to 5 cables’ length from north to south, and to 3} from east to
west. The lead is the best guide that we can recommend for entering this harbour.
Vessels within it lie securely sheltered, and have a swell only when the wind is in
the N. W. quarter, which winds are common on this coast, from September to the
end of January or beginning of February. The mouth of the River of San Juan
is S. E. by S. of Punta Arenas; and by it small vessels ascend into the Lagoon
of Nicaragua. A little to the east of Punta Arenas are some (Cacimbas) pits or
wells, where fresh water may be obtained: it may also be procured in the river.

Mr. Peacoch’s remarks on the Harbour of St. Juan de Nicaragua and coast
adjacent are as follow :—

“Vessels bound to this port should get into latitude 11° 20’ before they steer to
the westward, in order to guard against a strong S. S. E. current, which increases
as you approach the coast, running at the rate of two and three knots. Coming in
with the land on this parallel, you will first discover two high round mountains on
your starboard bow and one on your larboard; the former resembles the Monchigue
Mountains, over Cape St. Vincent in Portugal; the latter has the appearance of a
turtle, with its head to the southward. There is another mountain to the south-
ward, shelving down on its northern side, and being considerably nearer the coast,
should you fall in to the southward, will be first seen: bring the turtle-shaped
mountain to bear W. by S., and steer for it, and you will soon get sight of Point
St. Juan, which may be known by its having some naked trees on it; the land
about it is low, level, and covered with lofty trees. When Point St. Juan bears
N. W. or S. E., it has the appearance (in point of shape only) of the North
Foreland. :

“ Proceeding to the westward, you will perceive what at first sight appears to be

tion from the northern shore; its southern extremity bears from Point Arenas

DIRECTIONS FOR THE COAST OF SOUTH AMERICA,
FROM CAPE MANZANILLA TO SAN JUAN DE NICARAGUA.

By Commander William Sidney Smith, of H.M.S. Larne, 1833.*

Srasons.—On this part of the northern coast of the Isthmus of Darien the
year is divided into two seasons,—that of the breezes or trade winds and fine
weather, and that of vendayalés or rains, light breezes, variable winds, and calms.

; The months of the breezes are January, February, March, April, May, and
une.

The month of the vendayalés are July, August, September, October, November,
and December, when the trade wind seldom blows home to the land. It happens

in either season that the weather of one becomes intermingled with that of the
other.

GaLzs.—Notwithstanding hurricanes and strong gales of continuance have been
said never to blow here, his Majesty’s sloop Comus experienced a gale nearly
amounting to a hurricane, on 17th October, 18383. The barometer, in this instance,
gave a timely and suflicient indication, by falling very low indeed; which induced
the said ship to leave her anchorage at Chagres. It blew for twelve hours ex-
ceedingly hard from N. W. to S. W.. All the vessels at Panama were wrecked,
and houses blown down at Chagres and San Juan de Nicaragua.

* Extracted from that valuable periodical, the Nautical Magazine, vol. III. pp.642 and 705.

THE COASTS OF TERRA FIRMA AND MOSQUITIA. 13

NorruErs.—Fresh northers of a week’s duration, sometimes almost amounting
to a gale, are felt, particularly during winter and spring, at Chagres, but are much
more prevalent at San Juan de Nicaragua.

Except on these occasions, in both seasons, close inshore, and at a varying dis-
tance of about six miles, the land winds blow off generally during the night.

SEAsons or BreEzes.—The prevalent trades blowing home to the land by
day are more or less to the north of east: when well set in, the weather is beauti-
fully dry.

Rainy Srason.—The weather prevalent at the rainy season extends off Chagres
sometimes as far north as 13°, but generally only to 11°, or not so far. The winds
changing about, remain not six hours in any one quarter. Heavy rolling clouds of
threatening appearance are frequently discharging torrents of rain, accompanied
with a sharp squall, thunder, and dangerous lightning. A gloomy calm then suc-
ceeds ; still the barometer is little affected by any of these phenomena. From
experience I can say, there are equally dirty squalls from eastern and western
quarters, with calms between, west winds being only more prevailing.

At an offing of twenty or thirty miles from Cape Manzanilla this weather is
more particularly frequent in the vendavalés than even at Chagres, where the east
winds are not so wet as in the offing, being generally finer than the west winds, but
they are faint.

Currents, GENERAL.—It seems to be an established fact, that the great equa-
torial current from east to west in the Atlantic, entering the Caribbean Sea through
the several passages between the mouths of the Orinoco, and the Island of Marti-
nique, flows still to the westward, on the continental side, to Cape de la Vela, from
whence it inclines a point or two northerly, to pass between Cape Gracias a Dios
and Jamaica.

In the space between Cape Gracias a Dios and Cape de la Vela, offshoots and
eddies from this great current are found. This assertion is not merely grounded
on those of former navigators, or on the examination of the coast outline, but on
actual experience.

A writer worthy of great respect, Captain Machellar, R.N., has stated :—‘‘The
current between the Island of Jamaica and the Spanish Main or coast of Columbia
is not always to be depended upon as setting to the westward, as is generally
supposed ; for in crossing from Jamaica to the Main, ships have been known to
be drawn to the eastward by the current.” This circumstance must be of rare
occurrence at the northern part of the passage, and is here mentioned to make
known its possibility. I myself have made the runs across, between Jamaica and
the opposite Main, at many times and seasons, and am therefore governed by prac-
tice as well as theory in the following remarks. They necessarily extend over a
broader field than was requisite for treating on the weather, as the consideration of
currents must embrace remoter influences.

Currents between Jamaica and the opposite Main, between Capes de la Vela and
Gracias a Dios.

Ist. The local current between the south side of Jamaica, Morant Kays, and
Pedro Shoals. This is very uncertain, both in rate and direction. Its rate may be
from 0 to 1} knots per hour, and its direction either north, east, or west, according
to circumstances, whose discussion appertains to the sailing directions of that
island only.

At the Morant Kays the current is known to be variable: over the Pedro Shoals
it is supposed almost ever to run in a westerly direction. Between these two
dangers, therefore, it behoves a ship at night to be full of precaution, and not to
rely on the continuance of any current she may have ascertained, when either to
northward or southward of her then situation.

2nd. Southward of Morant Kays and Pedro Shoals, or between 17° and 15°
north latitude, the current, perhaps always, is West to N. W. by W. (true), 20 to
55 miles per day.

Among the Mosquito Shoals, equally strong and more uncertain. Between 15° N.

SAILING DIRECTIONS FOR

and a line drawn from Cape de la Vela and Gracias a Dios, including also some
Mosquito Kays, the current is W. 8. W. to N. W., 20 to 40 miles per day.

3rd. Southward of the above line, and to a distance of 30 miles from the coast,
the sets are so very changeable as to baffle all system. Sometimes no current whatever
is felt ; at other periods it may run north, south, east, or west, 35 miles a day.

Let it be borne in mind, however, that their direction is very seldom towards
the east, but generally towards the west. St. Andrew’s and the frontier rocks of
the Mosquito Bank are equally beset by changeable currents, of velocities occa-
sionally amounting to 50 miles a day.

4th. Lanp Current.—Between Cape Manzanilla, near Porto Bello, and San
Juan de Nicaragua, there is an in-shore current from westward to eastward. It is
an eddy, striking out from the great Caribbean current at Cape Gracias a Dios,
and eventually returning into it, with a broken and divided force, to the north of
Carthagena. The breadth of the current extends from the land to a distance of
about 80 miles in the offing; its rate is from one to two knots, and its direction is
parallel to the curvature of the coast and capes.

The stream out of numerous rivers entering this current seems to increase its
rapidity ; for close in-shore, between the rivers, the rate is seldom less than two
knots ; six miles off the land it runs about one knot, and at a greater distance the
same. This I lay down as its proper state.

But no established current is without its uncertainties, and the present is sub-
ject to the observation. Winds, either remote or actual, affect its direction and
velocity, to the extent of changing, neutralizing, or even reversing them entirely.
In-shore it will sometimes set two knots right upon the land; in the offing,
also, it has been experienced to vary off and on the land, and from one to two
and a half. It has been known to cease every where, or even run west for a
short while.

Most people suppose it strongest in the rainy season, and to be thrown most
upon the land, when northerly breezes prevail in the vicinity. It is, however,
quite as true, that fiery trade winds from the north-east during the fine season,
falling on the Mosquito coast, strengthen the eddy or current along the land to
its full foree, while they diminish the rate or affect the course at the outer part of
the stream.

Saizring Drrections FROM Port RoyaL To CHAGRES.

Portiany Rocx.—Though the Portland Rock lies only ten leagues from the
most frequented port of Jamaica, several situations are still assigned to it. This
causes perplexity to those shaping their course to the Main, after having caught
the sea breeze, attended with hazy weather, soon after getting clear of Port
Royal Kays. It causes still more anxiety to those striving to fetch Port Royal
from Chagres, with a scant wind.

Coursrs.—The safest position to allow Portland Rock is 17° 13’ N., 77° 10
West; a course S. by E. will pass 20 miles to windward of it. But in case the
wind should be unsteady, or the current running to westward, I would recommend
a course 8. S. E.

When with a S. S. E. course you are arrived at lat. 17° N., then alter course
to S. by W., which will carry clear of Hl Comboy. This last course is recom-
mended, as ships generally pass the position of this doubtful reef before next
morning, and are ignorant to what extent they have been set to the westward by
the current.

Arrived at 15° 30’ N., shape course for the coast, allowing each day for the
current, either according to astronomical observations, or to the information that
may be obtained from what has previously been said.

During the Season of the Breezes.

During THE BREEZES.—The best land to make is Cape Manzanilla, both on
account of its situation at a convenient short day’s run to windward of Chagres,

THE COASTS OF TERRA FIRMA AND MOSQUITIA. 15

and its appearance, of which a stranger is more readily assured than of any other
land on this coast. ;

Make Cape Manzanilla, bearing south. Should it be night before land is sighted,
run no nearer than 18 miles, then endeavour to keep thereabout until daylight,
acting according to the wind, and allowing a current to E. N. E., 1 mile per hour,

unless from the strength of the breeze, or other circumstances, you believe it
variable.

When the Cape and Farallons are distinguished at daylight, run along shore
with all convenient speed for Chagres Road, being mindful of the coast directions.

By niaut orr Porto Bretito.—Should you be under sail at night off Porto
Bello, be constantly on your guard against the squalls and calms prevalent in its
vicinity. The former frequently shift from the land round the compass, with
torrents of rain and gusts of wind, so as to oblige you to clew all up. Precautions
must be adopted to prevent being drifted on the Farallon Sucio, and other dangers
there, over which the current is supposed directly to set north-easterly two or three
knots an hour.

The land, from the rocks near Porto Bello to Chagres should not be ventured on
closer generally, at night, than 18 fathoms, for there are several low points with
reefs, as likewise the swell right on, and a strong current.

A ship, baffled in her exertions to reach Chagres, may anchor for the night in
18 or 20 fathoms between Point Toro and Chagres, and, indeed, off most parts of
the coast, either toward Porto Bello, or to the westward. But you should be sure
not to be too close to a reef. Indeed, unless the weather is entirely settled, it is
more Pradent to stand off and on, under sail, ready for the first of the sea breeze
next day.

CHAGRES. Chagres is a very difficult place to ascertain by night, even when
close in, the height, on which is the Castle, being backed at no great distance by
still higher ground. If the Castle be discerned at sun-set, and current be properly
allowed, you may expect also, until ten o’clock, to perceive and be assisted by the
lights of the village huts, in a row, at the margin of the harbour. When the village is
open of the land on either side of it, bring the lights E, by 5S. 3 S., and anchor in
10 to 12 fathoms, when you will be at 2 miles nearly from the nearest land, in
good bottom.

At that season, ships from Jamaica, under favourable circumstances, anchor at
Chagres between the third and fourth days.

During the Season of the Vendevalés.

During THE Rains. If, in the season when the trade-wind may be daily
expected to blow home, it is proper to make the land to the N. E. of Chagres, it
is necessary to pursue a contrary method during the rainy season; for now the
sea breezes may not arrive for several days, and then be faint, and insufficient to
outstem the seldom obliterated current from the west to east.

I recommend the following directions from Captain Mackellar, R. N.  ‘ Ships
should never go to the southward of lat. 11° until 50 miles to westward of their
intended port.’ Then endeayour to make the land about Escudo Island. The
westerly winds, the southerly winds often felt in the mornings, together with the
current, will set them to the eastward, thereby to gain the anchorage.

The land within Escudo is high ; that island cannot be discerned unless you are
close in-shore. [For the soundings, remarkable objects, and particulars, see Re-
marks on the Coast.] As soon as certain of being to the eastward of Escudo Island,
close the coast till within three miles, and run along at that distance from it, in
from 40 to 28 fathoms, to Chagres.

By Nieut. Whilst trying to sight the land about Escudo, should it be night
before that object is accomplished, and your position verified by it, approach no
nearer than 18 miles, on account of that island and its banks. Then keep there-
about till daylight, acting according to the wind, and allowing a current along the
land one knot. At daylight proceed south again.

16 SAILING DIRECTIONS FOR ~

When sure of your situation, in your run along the coast between Escudo and
Chagres, and night has again set in, you may either continue or anchor in from
18 to 20 fathoms. In case the squally weather should induce you to keep under
sail, every precaution must be carefully adopted to preserve the ship ten miles to
the westward of Chagres, and near to the land, in order to prevent the possibility of
being set away past it by the current, This is an important point.

DireEctions.—Captain Mackellar says, “ Should a ship find that the current
has set her to the eastward of the intended port, and light winds prevail, she should
immediately stand to the northward as far as 10° 30 or 11°, in order to meet the
north-east trade winds, and with it make good the necessary westing again.”

In September, 1833, H. M. sloop Larne was four days off Chagres, striving to
reach it ; she never got to the eastward of her port, but neither could she recover by
day the few miles she was obliged, as she conceived, to stand off during the nights,
which were without a moon.

The winds variable, with perpetual shiftings from all quarters, attended with
calms, squalls, and deluges of rain. The current N. E. by E. (true), 14 to 23 knots.
Within 5 miles of Chagres not so much northing.

The best sails to keep regularly under are —double-reefed top-sails, fore-sail,
fore-top-mast stay-sail, and reefed driver, with top-gallant sails, main-sail, and jib,
immediately a squall has ceased; and light-sail when the wind is going to be in the
least steady. The men are incessantly employed in trimming sail and sounding ;
and their clothes and bedding are universally soaked with rain water during many
days. They derive no illness therefrom at sea. The swell always rolling from the
N.E., at times suddenly makes alarmingly, as if it was going to break on a beach.
The ship, at length, anchored at night in utter darkness. She had placed herself
in a proper anchorage; but the writer of these remarks, before and since, has
frequently anchored at night, and found the ship several miles on either side of
Chagres. If not intending or unable to anchor at night, and Chagres should bear
south 5 miles, steer W. N. W., heaving deep sea-lead half-hourly, and hand-lead
constantly. Thus you will partly stem the current, and by receiving it on the lar-
board bow, be sure of only being set to the N. W. a convenient distance.

The succeeding month (October, 1833,) another man-of-war was seven days in
similar trouble, being eleven days from Jamaica to Chagres. Merchant vessels
often entirely fail to stem the current at this season, and must wait until the sea
breeze shall set in for a sufficient period, if they do not ascend to 11° N. to gather
their westing.

SAILING FROM CHAGRES.

The river Chagres imparts to the sea a yellow colour, to a distance of eight miles
from theland. The stream, after issuing’ from the harbour, and joining the sea
current, runs seldom less than one knot and a half per hour along the land to the
northward and eastward.

A ship getting under weigh from Chagres will meet with such assistance from the
current, that, notwithstanding the swell setting in, she can cast any way, and beat
off; provided the wind be not so violent as to prevent her carrying double-reefed
top-sails, jib, and courses. Thus, when the current is from W.S. W., and the
wind west, she rides with the latter two points on the starboard bow, the swell being
from N.N.E., it is desirable to cast to starboard notwithstanding : let the after-
yards and spanker be set for the larboard tack at once, and laying aback, and the
larboard head-braces a little hauled in for casting. In heaying up, port the helm,
which will be acted on by the current sufficiently long to cast her, before it will be
necessary to shift it for stern-way.

Tn light airs the current will set you close along shore, from Point Brujas Islet to
Point Toro Reefs, when you must be prepared to tow and anchor.

It is universally recommended, on all occasions, (except beating to the east-
ward during the settled time of the breezes,) that a ship leaving Chagres should
stand out to the northward four or five leagues as soon as possible, because the
winds are in general apt to fall light and variable, and the current is very strong,

THE COASTS OF TERRA FIRMA AND MOSQUITIA. 17

then setting directly on the rocks which lie off Porto Bello, and thence along the
line of coast from E. N. E. to E.S. E., and seldom less than at the rate of one and
a half to three knots per hour.

Should you be unavoidably drawn in near the land of Porto Bello, be constantly
on your guard against calms and squalls.

SAILING FROM CuaGReES TO St. JuAN DE NICARAGUA.

When you reach longitude 82°, you ought to be in latitude 11° 30’. Between
that part and Chagres, the current in fine weather is usually running to E. N. E. one
knot an hour, but it is occasionally found different.

From the above-mentioned latitude and longitude to S¢. Juan, you may be
affected by a set tothe southward, which, in fine weather, may possibly increase
to one knot and a half, after you draw within thirty miles of the land. The
navigation may be based on this information ; for although the state of the currents
cannot be possibly predicted, when the winds are not north, (see remarks on the
currents of this sea,) yet every one is still of opinion that the land should be made
twenty miles to the north of San Juan at all times and seasons.

When northerly winds set in, they are very baffling, as the swell and current,
both from the same quarter, are infinitely increased. And ships have been occa-
sionally kept many days, constantly striving to proceed in a westerly direction to
their port. In December, 1833, a ship was twelve days from Chagres to San Juan
de Nicaragua, nine of which she was off the latter place. A norther had set in
before she made the land. When she saw it in thick weather, having had no
observations previously, she run along it to find an object to verify her position by ;
she at length observed Turtle Bogue, and then hauled off to beat up. But the
ground thus lost, such was the current’s force, could not be recovered during the
above period, all which time the strength of the northerly winds disposed her,
never to anchor on the open shore at night. An easterly wind at last arrived to
carry her in. To prevent similar delays, stand in boldly fifteen or twenty miles to
northward of San Juan. The coast and the islands Paxaro Bova, and Pigeon
Kays are low ; but on the coast will be seen the hills described in the coast direc-
tions. You may approach either coast or islands to twelve fathoms, even by night.
When being thus placed in a favourable position to derive benefit from the long-
shore current, you cannot fail of arriving in a few hours. Latitude, sounding, and
good look out, must be particularly attended to in this sea.*

SAILING FROM SAN JUAN, OR CHAGRES TO JAMAICA.

Keep, in general, within thirty miles of the land, to receive the assistance of the
long-shore current from west to east. By day, during the sea breeze, you may beat
close in to eight and ten fathoms; by night, in fine weather, you may be in equally
close, if you have a knowledge of the coast, to receive the land winds, which
then set off from 10 ».m, to 8 A.m., and even to a distance of nine miles from the
land. In this respect, the shores between San Juan and Cape Blanco, and
between Escudo Island and Chagres, are more safe than the rest. After passing
Cape Manzanilla, the current commences to diminish in rapidity. The line of
kays, in a large ship, ought not to be approached within five miles, by night ;
although, by day, reference to a chart, sounding, and look out on the colour of the
bottom, may enable you to stand in higher upon a good lay.

When to the eastward of Point San Blas, and opening the Gulf of Darien,

the current to the eastward appears to have less effect, and generally draws in to
south. It is, in fact, much influenced by the prevailing winds at the different

periods of the seasons. After passing the gulf, you may see the islands of San
Bernardo, which form a cluster. The centre of them is placed by Don Fidalgo
in 9° 45’ N., which situation they occupy in the Admiralty. Chart. Captain
Machellar states them to be in 9° 27’ N., and longitude by chronometer, 75° 52! 30”
W est.

These islands are low, but very remarkable: when at the distance of ten or twelve
miles off, and bearing from East to E. by S. 3 S., several parts of them will appear
like small rocks between the islands; but at the south end of the northernmost
island there are two remarkable trees, which may be mistaken for a vessel at anchor.
These islands, like the whole of the coast, are covered with wood, and may be seen
about five leagues off.

As you proceed farther to the eastward, you will make the Rosario Islands, which
may always be known from those of San Bernardo, as they lie in a triangular form,
and are long and low.

Having passed theseislands, you may sight the hill over Carthagena called Popa,
which forms not unlike a gunner’s quoin, and has a ruined convent on its highest
part.

After you get to the eastward of Rosario Islands, you will often find a current
setting to N. W. and N. N. W. at the rate of from one to two miles and a half an
hour. The N. E, breeze often blows off this coast and half way across to Jamaica,
with great violence ; raising a very turbulent sea. Arrived in the vicinity of the
coast of Carthagena, you may stretch away to Jamaica. Some will do it without
heating so far to windward; for experience teaches that the trade almost always
draws nearly east fifty or sixty miles from the land; others make it a rule, even
though they happen previously to obtain a good lay, to work up near the shore,
as far as point Galera de Zamba, that they may be certain to go across free.

The more rapidly the strong current of the Carribbean Sea is crossed the better ;
and if a scant wind should lead a ship to leeward of the Portland Rock she will find
so strong a westerly set to contend with, that she will regret not having beaten up
higher on the side of the main.

The passage from Chagres to Port Royal is generally performed in from eight to
ten days.

ST. JUAN DE NICARAGUA TO CAPE GRACIAS A DIOS,
WITH THE ADJACENT ISLANDS.

From the harbour of San Juan of Nicaragua, the coast trends nearly north,
a distance of 82 leagues to Cape Gracias a Dios ; and is that properly named the
Mosquito Shore. It is all low land, for the high land terminates at San Juan; and
it is intersected with many rivers and lagoons, which send off a bank of soundings
about 20 leagues from the coast ; to the northward, considerably more, as there is
good ground for believing that it reaches the Serranilla. Upon this bank are
many kays and reefs, some near the coast, and others at a distance from it. On the
outside of this bank, and in front of the coast, there are various islands and banks,
whose situations are in course of examination, and in part completed, by Captain
Edward Barnett, R. N., but until they become more particularly known, there is
great risk in navigating in these parts.

Punta Gorda lies N. N. W., 10} leages from Point Arenas. The coast between
forms a bay ; the three principal rivers are Indian River, Spanish Creek, and Corn
River. The whole of this coast is so clean, and the soundings so regular, that the
lead is the only guide required in running along it. At 6 leagues N. W. of
Point Arenas, and 5 leagues S. } W. of Punta Gorda, isa remarkable round hill,
619 feet high, which serves as a good land-mark for vessels bound to the harbour of
St. Juan ; about 2 miles westward of Punta Gorda good water may be obtained
from a creek.

At 4 leagues N. E. by N. from Punta Gorda lies Monkey Point, between
which are from 4 to 5 fathoms water, clean ground ; about midway between the two

THE COASTS OF TERRA FIRMA AND MOSQUITIA. 19

points is a Kay named Pazaro ‘Bovo, between which and the shore is anchorage in
3 or 4 fathoms water. Five miles north of Punta Gorda is Rama River having 5
feet water on the bar.

About 3 leagues northward of Monkey Point are the Pigeons, and which extend
about 12 miles north and south. To the eastward of these, and without the shoal,
there is a kay, called Frenchman’s Kay, which, with the Pigeons, forms a channel,
but the passage through it is not recommended : by going outside of the kay, the
Pigeon reef will be entirely cleared, although it extends two miles from the north
part of the kays.

BLEWFIELD’S LAGOON.— On the coast at 4 miles, N. W. by N. of Pigeon
Kay, is the south point of Blewfield’s Lagoon, which is a bay extending inland nearly
10 miles ; and in the north point of it, disembogues a considerable river, named.
Escondido. From the south part of this bay or lagoon to the north one, named
Bleujield’s Point, the distance is 8 miles (N. N, E.) N. by E. 3 E.: this point is
in latitude 11° 59” N. longitude 83° 41’ W. Nearly on the line, between the two
points, is Deer Island, seyen miles in length, forming with the points two channels,
the best and principal of which is to the north, wherein during the season of the
breezes, there are 2 fathoms water ; but at that season it is dangerous, because it has
a vertical fall of 3 feet. In the season of the Vendevalés there are 23 fathoms, and
no fall. Having passed this channel or bar, you may find within the lagoon 43 to
53 fathoms water, upon clay: the anchorage is near the town on the N. E. side.
In entering this lagoon, you have only to keep along close to Blewfield’s Point,
which may be done at the distance of a stone’s throw, as it is very clean ; and the
point may be known from its being the highest land on this part of the coast.
Continue on near the north shore, for the southern side is very foul, and requires a
wide berth. It is also indispensably necessary, on entering this place, to have the
anchors ready to let go at an instant, when the current, which is moderately strong,
may render such an expedient necessary.

From Blewfield’s Point the coast runs north, inclining a little to the west, for the
distance of 21 miles, to the entrance of the Pearl Lagoon. Off this part of the coast
lies a rock called the Cayman, which is distant 6 miles from Blewfield’s Point, and
somewhat more than half a league from the nearest coast. The entrance of Pearl
Lagoon has deeper water than that of Blewfield’s, and some vessels anchor outside of
it, under shelter of the north coast, which inclines to the E. N. E. for 8 miles to
Pearl Kay Point. Off this point at the distance of 2 miles, lie the Kays, outside
of which is a shoal of 3 fathoms.

To the E. 8S. E. of Pearl Kay Point, at the distance of 28 miles is Great Corn
Island, and 73 miles N. N. E. } E. of which is Little Corn Island. To the N. E.
and North of Pearl Kay Point, within the distance of 13 miles from the coast, are
various Kays, Rocks, and Shallows, of which, at present we can give but little
account; but as there is nothing on this part of the coast to entice the Kuropean
mariner, the better way is to keep outside the whole of them, where there is a good
depth of water on the bank already noticed.

The CORN ISLANDS are two in number bearing from each other (N. N. E. } E.
and $.S. W. 3 W.,) and are 7 miles apart. The southernmost is the largest, is two
miles in length from north to south, and 2 miles in its greatest. extent from
east to west. The northern island is 14 mile from N. W. to S. E., and from east to
west, where broadest, is scarcely a mile.

The Great Corn Island has three small hills wpon it ; of which the central one is
the highest, and may be seen at the distance of 6 or 7 leagues. Its coasts are
foul, with a reef, which extends out nearly a mile from them ; but this reef has
some clear places, by which you may approach the coast, and which serve for
anchorages : of these, the two principal ones are on the west coast of the island.
The first, or northernmost, lies east and west with the central hill ; and the second
is on the S. W. part of the island, separated from the former by a reef, which
stretches out to the S. W. The first anchorage, called the Brigantines, is the most
frequented : in proceeding to it, you must not approach nearer to the coast than 2
miles, or, what will amount to the same thing, do not get into less than 10 fathoms
water, until the middle hill bears about east, and then steer for the island on that
course ; and anchor in any convenient depth, with the understanding that there are
43 fathoms at 2 cables’ length from the beach. In the south part of the S. W.

anchorage, there are three wells or holes of good water. This anchorage of the
Brigantine, which we have described, is sheltered from all winds in the N. E. and
S. E. quarters; but in the season of the norths, great vigilance is necessary, lest
you should be surprised by a gale in the anchorage.

The Little Corn Island is quite clean on its west side, and may be approached
to the distance of half a mile, under the guidance of the lead only; but from its
S. E. point to the N. W. point, it sends out a reef which extends off nearly 13 mile,
at the edge of which there are 3} fathoms water. On the west coast you may
anchor, sheltered from the breezes, in 4} fathoms water; which may be found at
half a mile from the beach.

From Pearl Kay Point already spoken of, the coast continues about north, 6
miles to Cocoa Nut Point, thence in a general direction, N. 4 W. for 82 miles to
Wawa River. Off this part of the coast on the parallel of 13° N. and longitude
83° 24’ W. is the Man of War Kay, and northward, the Great and Litile North
Creeks, the Rivers Walpasiksa, Prince Apulka, and Wounta, the depth of water at
the distance of 2 to 4 miles is 3 to 7 fathoms; but from the parallel of 13° N. to
about 14° 15’, between the coast and 82° 30’ W. we have no particulars of the navi-
gation, the former Spanish description of these parts differing so materially from the
surveys of Captain Barnett, that we do not feel justified in again issuing them until
a comparison can be made with the more recent researches.

From the River Wawa, the coast runs N. E. by N. 3 N., 13 miles to Brackman’s
Bluff, (Red Cliffs), and 6 miles further to Huesor River, thence N. by E., 15 miles
to Governor’s Point, which is known from being more salient eastward, than any
other on the coast, and thickly covered with trees. From this point the coast runs
about N. by W. $ W. a distance of 8 miles to the mouth of Sandy Bay, in which
there is so little water, that, in the season of the Breezes, it is with difficulty that
launches pass: but within is a bay, very spacious and deep. From Sandy Bay the
coast continues in the same direction for 18 miles to Guana Lagoon, and thence
N. by E., 8 miles to the Bay of Gracias a Dios.

BAY OF GRACIAS A DIOS.—This bay is formed by a tongue of land ex-
tending to the eastward more than 4 miles, and which offers a good shelter against
the winds from S. S. W. round by north, toS.S. E. The easternmost point of this
tongue of land, is that which is called Cape Gracias a Dios; and from it to the
south-westward, there is a tongue of land, which formerly constituted two islets,
named St. Pio, and the south point of it, called Sandy Point, is also the east point
of the bay. The depth of water at the entrance is 20 feet, and well within it 16
feet ; and in all parts of it there is founda soft slimy clay, and clean bottom. To
anchor in this bay, and approaching it from the north and west, you have only to
pass San Pio, and then steer for the inner part, and anchor in the number of feet
water suitable to the vessel’s draught: for all of which you have only to attend to
the lead. The only thing that requires a little care is, rounding Sandy Point. For
those coming from the south, in order to take this bay, no direction need be given.

Don Joseph del Rio reports of this bay, after visiting it in 1793, as follows :—‘“ TI
ought to make known that the anchorage at the bay of Gracias a Dios is gradually
becoming lost, for the cut of communication made by the English with the Great
River Segovia through the tongue of land which forms the bay, to convey the timber
they bring down by that river, has widened it so much, that from a narrow canal it
has become a branch of the river, bringing with it so much soil and so many trunks
of trees, as to have so much diminished the depth of the bay, that since the year
1787, there are 3 feet less water in the vicinity of Kay San Pio; and it is very
probable, that within a few years, the depth will be filled up, and ships being
obliged to anchor further out, will be deprived of the shelter that they now have ;
and which is of so great utility to those who navigate on this coast, during the
season of the Norths.”

The ‘“‘Derrotero”’ says, that “All the coast from the River Tonglas is clean: and there
are no other hays and reefs on the bank of soundings which lies along shore, than those
already noticed, and those which lie between the parallels of Governor’s Point and Cape
Gracias a Dios, called the Mosquitos and Thomas's Kays and Reefs. These, with the
coast, form a channel of four leagues in breadth, where narrowest; and although be-
tween them there are passes, with a depth of 7 fathoms or more water, it is best not to

THE COASTS OF TERRA FIRMA AND MOSQUITIA. 21

attempt them, but pass always to the west of them, that is, between them and the
coast; for there can be no risk in this pass, as the lead will be a sufficient guide
either in sailing with the wind large, or working to windward, there being 43
fathoms water at half a league from the coast, and 9 fathoms near the kays.
Therefore, by not getting into less than 4} when standing in shore, or into more
than 81 when standing to the eastward, there will not be the least cause of
anxiety. From the Bay of Gracias a Dios you may steer to the S. by E. 3 E.;
this course will lead within sight of the westernmost kay of this group, which is a
dark brown rock, visible at the distance of 5 or 6 miles. On this course you will
get from 7} to 8} fathoms, and it must be kept, without getting any thing more to
the eastward, until you reckon yourself well cleared of the most southerly kays ;
the surest guide for which will be your getting 11 fathoms water on the same
course ; and from that situation a departure may be taken.”

Having described the coast, with the kays and reefs on the bank lying to the
eastward of the shore, some observations will also be necessary respecting the
islands and shoals lying further off the land, out of soundings.

The Alburquerque, or S. S. W. kays are the most southerly and westerly of the
whole; they are three in number, all clean, on a good bank for anchorage, without
any thing more to guard against than what is actually in sight; for although there
are some rocks around them, they are too close to be of any interruption.

ST. ANDREW’S ISLAND.—The centre of this island, according to recent
surveys, is in latitude 12° 33’ N. and longitude 81° 42’ 30” W.; and the following
remarks, with directions for approaching it, are by Mr. H. Mapleton, Acting
Master of H. M.S. Arachne, in 1833.

“St. Andrew’s Island bears N. W. by N., 215 miles from Chagres. The
dangers, on approaching it from the southward, are the two Kays, lying S. S. W.
and E. 8. E. of it: the former 20 miles, and the latter 14 miles, from the south
point of the island. A good look-out being kept, they may be seen from the
mast-head 12 or 14 miles distant. On making them, shape your course so as to
pass mid-channel between them. The S. 8. W. Kays may be approached on all
sides to within a quarter of a mile, with anchorage from thence in 7 fathoms.

“The #. S, E. Kays must have a wide berth, as they cannot be approached by a
stranger to within 3 or 4 miles.

‘On making the island, which can be seen 20 or 21 miles off, it has the appear-
ance of a high perpendicular hill, running off to the eastward to a low point; a
nearer approach shows the western end of the island to be formed by two high
sugar-loaf hills running into each other, and the land to the eastward to be low and
uneven.

“Steer directly for the western point of land you see. The breakers on the
S. E. side are very heavy, and on a small sandy kay in the midst of them are two
cocoa nut trees. By steering for the southward of the island, which, as you ap-
proach, shows a high bluff point, you will avoid all danger. After rounding this
point, the west side, close to its shores, is clear of all danger. Stand on until a
house on the top of a bare hill, having the appearance of high cultivation, with two
cocoa nut trees towering over it, comes in view. Stand on until you bring this
house to bear N. by E.; you will then have the entrance of a small cove well open;
steer boldly for it, and run in until you get into white water, caused by the sandy
bottom, and at four cables’ length from the shore you will have good anchorage in
7 fathoms, sand. Quite close to the shore, on this side of the island, you will have
4, 5, and 6 fathoms; but with the exception of the sandy bottom off the cove, it is
rocky. You lie here sheltered from easterly, and open to westerly, winds.

“Tntending to make a long stay here, it would be advisable to warp into the
cove, where you will lie secure from all winds. It is about 260 feet wide, but you
have only deep water in mid-channel, about 70 feet broad. On each side of this
channel it shoals to 2 and 13 fathoms. You must be careful in taking a vessel in,
and securing her well, when in.

“The H. S. E. Kays on the Courtown Bank. From the top of the hill, where the
house before-mentioned stands, bearings were taken with an azimuth compass.
They bear E. 8. E., 14 or 15 miles from the $8. W. end of the island. The largest

of them is of considerable height out of the water, and has a great many cocoa nut

“The S. S. W. Kays bear S.S. W. from the V. W. point of the island, distant
26 miles. From information received from the turtle fishermen, who make it their
