“In running for St. Andrew’s Island at night, you must have the deep-sea lead
kept going. Shoaling your water will point out your approach to danger, and a
good look-out must be kept.”

All the shores of this island are in general rocky, the most projecting points on
the west are clean soboruco ; and all the west coast is so steep, that at half a mile
off it, there are no soundings found. The East Coast is bordered with a reef,
which makes it almost inaccessible, and which, in some places, projects out more
than a mile. The length of this island, from north to south, is 7 miles, and from
east to west, in the broadest part, 2 miles. On the west side, near the anchorage,
there are two mountains rising over the rest of the land, which is generally hilly,
without precipices, all the declivities being very gradual: these mountains may be
seen in clear weather at the distance of 10 or 12 leagues. There is neither river
nor rivulet, nor indeed any known spring on the island: the inhabitants are, there-
fore, obliged to have recourse to pits or wells, which afford only thick and brackish
water. In approaching this island, there is no necessity for having a pilot, for,
by keeping clear of the east side, which should not on any account be approached.
within 3 or 4 miles, you may freely direct yourself to any part of the west side ;
but, if you intend to anchor, steer for the south part of the island, without fear of
approaching it to half a cable’s length if necessary; and on opening West Bay,
which is formed by the western point of the island; steer towards it, and anchor in
10 fathoms, or less, on a sandy bottom: the 10 fathoms are found within 13 cable’s
length from the shore. This anchorage is well sheltered from the breezes: but, in
the time of the Norths, it will be necessary to be extremely watchful, in order. to
make sail the moment there is the slightest indication of a gale.

THE E.S. E. KAYS.—About E. by S., distant 5 leagues from the south point
of St. Andrew’s, lie three kays, called the EZ. 8. E. Kays: they are surrounded by
a reef, and a bank, called the Courtown Bank, with little depth on it; and although
there is anchorage on it for small vessels, it cannot be reached without considerable
practice in the method of proceeding to it. These kays have a ridge of rocks to
the north and N. N. E. of them, which extends 3 miles off, with 10 fathoms close
to it; and also a reef extending S. E. by E. to about the same distance, with 6 °
fathoms on its extremity.

This island is situated about 125 miles from the nearest part of the Mosquito
Coast, and 88 miles only from the edge of the Mosquito Bank; it can be seen
at the distance of 11 or 12 leagues, and is easily distinguished from the neigh-
bouring Island of St. Andrew’s by the curious outline of its abrupt and peaked
mountains, St. Andrew’s, from which it may be seen in clear weather, bears from
it S. by W. 3 W., 47 miles.

The small Island of Santa Catalina is separated from the northern end of Old Pro-
vidence by a cut or channel of from 40 to 60 yards wide, 1,800 yards long, by 1,300
in its greatest breadth, forming the northern boundary of the harbour, and affording
secure anchorage in from 2 to 34 fathoms. Both these islands are very hilly, and,
on approaching them, present a delightful variety of beautiful scenery.

Old Providence is nearly 43 miles long, and 23 in its greatest breadth, of an

irregular shape. The highest ground, which can scarcely be called a point, near
the centre of the island, rises to 1190 feet above the level of the sea; from this,
other hills, mostly wooded to their summits, diverge towards the shore and termi-
nate boldly. The island is surrounded by an extensive bank of coral and coarse
sand, stretching to the northward for 103 miles. A reef, in many parts dry, ex-
tends in a northerly direction, at a distance of three-quarters of a mile along the
eastern side, till within about 3 miles of the N. E. angle of the bank, whence it
trends west across the bank for 2} miles, having at its western extremity a small
kay, about two or three feet high, composed of coral, sand, or stones, brought there
by fishermen from the islands.

On this northern part of the reef, and three-quarters of a mile to the eastward
of the kay, H.M. Schooner Jacdaw was wrecked on the morning of the 11th of
March, 1835, which was occasioned by the inaccuracies of the Spanish plan of the
island with which she was supplied,*and the best then published. Since then very
accurate charts of the islands and kays have been completed.

This reef, binding the eastern shore of the island, extends to and terminates at a
distance of a mile and a quarter from its southern point, whence the soundings
extend in a south-western direction from 2} to 3 miles. The sea almost constantly
breaks on the reef, so that it can be discovered long before the bank is approached ;
and although the openings in the reef have a depth of from 8 to 5 fathoms water, a
passage is seldom attempted, except in small vessels. The coral rocky heads within,
to the westward of the reef are very numerous and dangerous, and some small
wooded hays are situated to the northward of the islands, ;

Drrecrions.—The island should always, if possible, be approached from the
northward, and by day, in consequence of the prevalence of N. E. winds, making
it in the parallel of 18° 32! or 13° 33’; soundings will be first got on the bank, in
from 15 to 17 fathoms, coarse coral sand; then steer W. by N.3N., keeping
along to the northward of the reef at about three-quarters of a mile distant, till the
highest peak on the island bears S. 3° E. ; then shape a course towards it, rounding
the western elbow of the reef at 13 or 2 cables’ distance, when, after a run of
about three-quarters of a mile, good anchorage may be obtained in 5, 8, or 10
fathoms, with the low hay bearing N. N. E.

If, however, intending to proceed to the anchorage off Santa Catalina, on round-
ing the reef steer S. by W. } W., nearly six miles, until Morgan’s Head transits
the highest peak on the island; then haul up 8. E. by S., and stand on till Basalt
Kay bears East, Morgan’s Head, S. E. 3 S., and anchor immediately on obtaining
soundings in 5 or 6 fathoms.

For a vessel coming from the southward and by night, the most advisable plan
would be, on making the land, to lie-to till daylight, keeping it in sight, when in
the morning the beat wp to the anchorage would not be above 6 or 7 miles, with a
certainty of a good breeze and smooth water. In working up, the clearness of the
water enables the eye to detect the shallow rocky heads, which abound within
three cables’ length of the whole edge of the bank.

Currents and Tides.—No dependence can be placed on the currents, as they vary
in strength and direction off the bank, while determining the outer eastern part of
which an almost invariable set to the N. W. was experienced.

The tides are variable; sometimes, in north-westerly breezes, rising as much as
two feet; but no greater rise or fall than 6 or 7 inches was observed during the six
weeks (in April and May) that the boats of the ship were employed surveying the
island.

The only harbour is that of Catalina, before mentioned, to enter which a pilot
is almost indispensable. The anchoring ground is good, and although open to the
winds from N. W. to S. W., the reefs in that direction form a barrier to the setting
in of a heavy sea. .

Morgan's Head is a very remarkable rock, nearly detached from the S. W.
point of Catalina Island. Ti rises 40 feet from the level of the sea, and from its
proximity to the rocks of the island is not easily distinguished till closely ap-
proached. On entering the harbour, it will be found to bear a striking resemblance
to a man’s head.

Split Hill, near the northern end of the island, is 550 feet in height, and has
the extraordinary appearance of a hill having been, by some sudden convulsion of
nature, rent in twain as far as one-third down from its summit. It is peaked on
either side of the chasm, which is about 60 feet wide and 80 feet deep.

The watering-place for ships is situated on the western shore, at 2} miles from the
anchorage in the harbour ; it can be easily recognized by being a little to the south-
ward of some white cliffs. It is the largest of four streams, issuing from one
spring, situated in the highest part of the island. The filling place, whence ex-

cellent water of a chalybeate quality was procured, is about 100 fathoms from the

mouth of the stream, and partially hid by a sandy beach, through which it forces
itself after heavy rains.

Good stock is plentiful; in fact, the soil is exceedingly productive, and nature
here appears in abundant luxuriance, affording to the animal creation the greatest
profusion, with very little cultivation. Fruits are plentiful. The cattle are gene-
rally in good order; bullocks (of 4 or 5 ewt.) sell for £3. or £4. sterling. Fowls
in abundance, 12s. per dozen. Horses are a fine breed, but rather small, at from
£3. to £4. per head. Fish abound in profusion on the banks.

Cotton is the staple export, and is cultivated more or less by every one. This,
with turtle-shell and a few hides, are the principal articles of trade. About
30,000 Ibs. of cotton, and 170 Ibs. of shell are annually taken away by the traders,
in exchange for English calicos, cloths, &c., brought from Jamaica. Cotton is
planted in June, and gathered from December to May.

In the beginning of 1835 the population, by the last census, was 342 persons,
about one half of whom were slaves. The younger part of the community employ
themselves turtling. The inhabitants are generally hospitable, but have neither
form nor observance of religious duties. Marriages are contracted by civil cere-
mony and bargain; and their only recognition of a Supreme Being is in the respect
they pay to Sunday, which is marked by a total cessation of labour, and attention
to external appearance. :

The island is under the government of the republic of New Grenada, but more
immediately so under that of St. Andrew’s, the two islands forming the ninth
canton of the republic. At Old Providence a collector and a civil magistrate reside,
who administer the government, with two assistants. Thefts and other crimes are
dealt with severely. English is the language spoken. Their flag is red, blue,
yellow, vertical in equal parts, the red being nearest the mast, with a white star of
five points in the blue division. The island is visited by the traders who frequent
the coast from Cape Gracias a Dios to San Blas, the principal of which are from
San Juan de Nicaragua.

The only town, named Isabel, stands at the northern end of the island, at the
head of Catalina Harbour, close to the channel between the two islands. Not more
than eight or nine houses remain of what was once a populous and flourishing
place. Several houses and plantations are scattered over the island, accessible only
by a sort of road that passes round the island. No one resides at Catalina ; all
the ground there capable of cultivation is laid out in plantations of corn, cotton,

RONCADOR.—The Roncador Kay, on the northernmost part of this reef, is
in latitude 13° 35’ 7” N., and longitude 80° 5’ 30” W. It is of sand and coral for-
mation, and about 6 feet above the water. From this kay the reef stretches in a
S. E. by 8. direction, about 7 miles, being 2} or 8 miles in breadth, having deep
water around it,

SERRANA. The Serrana is an extensive and dangerous reef, situated 45 miles
to the N. N. W. of Roncador Kay, between the parallels of 14° 15’ and 14° 29’ N.
latitude, and longitude 80° 7’ 30” and 80° 25' W. On its edges are several kays and
heads, with openings between them, through which the currents set very rapidly.
There is an opening on the south side of the reef called the South Channel, about
half a mile wide, with 10 fathoms at the entrance, but it is obstructed by rocky
heads, which render it such as should only be taken in cases of emergency. The
entrance to this channel is in about latitude 14° 21’ N., longitude 80° 20’ W.

QUITA SUENO.—The late surveys of these parts represent this bank as ex-
tending from the latitude of 14° 2’ to 14° 35’ N., and from longitude 81° 6’ to
81° 20° W. On the eastern part of this extent is the dangerous reef, lying about
north and south, 23 miles in length, and near the centre about 6 miles across. On
this reef there are no kays, but a sandy spot on the northern part, in latitude
14° 30’ N., and longitude 81° 7’ 30" W. ‘The eastern edge of the reef is steep-to,
having deep water, and giving no warning of approach by the lead ; on the western
side of the reef the bank is of considerable extent, having from 7 to 20 fathoms upon
it, falling suddenly into deep water: at 5 miles north of the bank there is no bottom
with 130 fathoms of line.

SERRANILLA BANE.—This bank lies between the parallels of 15° 42’ and
16° 3’ N., and the meridians of 79° 41’ and 80° 7’ W. On its eastern and southern
sides are several kays and reefs with breakers, and as the bank is steep-to quite
around, the approach to the eastern and southern sides is dangerous in dark nights.
On the bank to the N. W. of the breakers is a depth of 5 to 20 fathoms. The
Beacon Kay, on the 8. E. side of the reef, is in latitude 15° 47’ 30” N., and
longitude 79° 50’ W.

Between the Serrana and Serranilla Banks, at 25 miles true North from the
northern part of the Serana, and on the parallel of 14° 53’, the old Spanish charts
represent a rock, sometimes covered, and having from 9 to 12 fathoms around ;
but of this there has appeared no recent description, and it appears extremely
doubtful, more especially in its relative position with regard to the surrounding
banks, which have of late been accurately determined ; we therefore mention this
monitory, till its existence is confirmed and position determined, or, upon some
good authority, erased from the charts,

BAZO NUEVO, or New Shoal. The Spanish account of this shoal says, itis a
bank of about 7 miles from north to south, and 14 from east to west: all along the
east side there is a very steep reef; but on the west side the depth diminishes
gradually. On this bank, at a mile and a half from its northern extremity, there
is a sandy kay, from which, at the distance of 3 or 4 miles (W.N. W.) W.N.W.3W.,
there is anchorage ; but take care not to get into less than 10 fathoms water, for at
24 miles (W. N.W.) W.N.W. 3 W. from the hay, a rock has been found, with only
7 feet water on it: and one mile (S. by E.) S. by E. 3 E. from it, there is another,
with no more than 4 feet water. Both rocks are in 5 fathoms water; they are very
steep, and not larger than a boat.

From the remarks made on board H.M.S. Winchester, Captain the Hon. W. Weil-
lesley. The Baxo Nuevo, or New Bank, is a kind of belt of breakers, inside of
which is smooth water over a sandy bottom.

The Winchester made the east side of it, the two ends of which appear to bear

ROSALIND BANK. This bank was first reported by Captain John Arrow-
smith, of the bark Rosalind, although the old charts give a few soundings in that
neighbourhood. The Rosalind’s track across the bank, on the 18th June, 1836, was
in 16° 28’ N. latitude, and longitude 80° 28’ W. On sounding from 11] a.m. till 1
p.m., the depths varied from 15 to 10 fathoms, the least water found, the bottom
coarse corally sand. The discoloured water was seen from the mast-head, as far as
the eye could discern, to the northward and southward of the ship’s track, and the
extent of it in an eastern and western direction was about six leagues.

Captain Arrowsmith says, ‘ In giving an opinion to shipmasters taking this un-
frequented track, time may be saved, and the distance shortened by it, otherwise
lost in hauling up to sight the east end of Jamaica; but I should recommend it to
none but those well practised in night observations for latitude. In passing to the
southward of these shoals, the current frequently sets strongly towards them to the
northward, and again, in proceeding westward, at times, in the direction of the
rocks off Cape Gracias a Dios, particularly in the season of the norths, between
November and March, during which season it is extremely hazardous, for want
of clear weather, therefore it ought not to be attempted at the said period by
merchant ships. These remarks are extracted from Journals kept during twenty-
nine successive voyages.”

This bank has since been critically examined in H. M.S. Thunder, and from the

N. W. of the Serranilla Bank. The southern edge of the bank is in latitude

This shoal part begins about the parallel of 16°, and meridian of 80° 22’ 30",

sets N. W. by W. at the rate of 1 knot. The next shoal patch is on the eastern
side, in latitude 16° 20’, having 10 fathoms; and 5 miles to the north of which

Of the Kays and Reefs situated to the N. Eastward, and eastward of Cape

To commence with the most southern of which we have any particulars as to

gitude 82° 52’ 30”, and bears E. 3 S., about 19 miles from Governor’s Point. To

8 miles in extent from east to west, and 6 miles from north to south. E.3S.,

3 miles from these Kays, is the London Reef, having 13 fathoms, fine sand, to the

N. N. W. from Babel Kay, having 12 fathoms between them.

Between the Savanna Reef and Alargate Reef is the Beaufort Channel, about
5 miles wide, with 17 fathoms in it ; there is also a. channel between Logwood and Half
Moon Kays, about 2 miles wide, with 7 fathoms in it. Ata short distance north,
and around.these eefs, there are 17, 15, and 14 fathoms, shoaling gradually towards
Cape Gracias a Dios.

The next reef that we shall notice is the Maincape Reef, in form nearly similar
to the Alargate Reef, before noticed. It lies nearly on the meridian of 83°, the
northern point being in latitude 15° 17’, the south point in 15° 12’ 30,” and bearing
N.N.E., 3 E., distant 16 miles from Cape Gracias a Dios. At N. E. by E.,

14 miles from this reef, is a patch of 12 and 8 fathoms, corally ground.

The Maincape Reef and the coral patch, above alluded to, on the north, and the
Haif Moon Reef and Logwood Kay to the south, form the boundaries of the
Maincape Channel. The eastern entrance of this channel is in latitude 15° 18’,
and longitude 82° 42’, and the channel lies N. E. by E., and S. W. by W., carrying
15, 17, 15, 11, and 13 fathoms through it. Between the Maincape Reef and the
coral patch are 15 fathoms.

To the northward of the Maincape Reef, and between it and the Falsecape Reef,
to the northward, is the Falseeape Channel. This channel lies in a similar direction
to the Maincape Channel, carrying also similar depths in the parallel of 15° 24’.
The Falsecape Reef is in latitude 15° 31’, and longitude 83° 5’.

Gordo Kay. This kay isa barren rock, situated in latitude 15° 52’, and lon-
gitude 82° 24"; from the N. W. part of it, a reef extends for 2 miles, having from
Il to 15 feet on it. Just to the northward of the reef are 14 fathoms, to the
westward 9 and 7, and also 7 to the southward. At E. 3 S., 6 miles from this kay,
is the Farral Rock, on which the sea breaks, and is very dangerous; between the
rock and the kay are 7 and 16 fathoms, to the eastward are 17 and 18 fathoms.

The Eastern Pigeon is a small kay, low and covered with bushes, in latitude
15° 48’, and longitude 82° 55’. From this kay, the Western Pigeon bears N. W.
by W. 3 W., 3 miles, and is similar to the former. The Cocorocuma Kays lie
W.iS., 73 miles from the Eastern Pigeon, between which are 20, 12, and 10
fathoms. A reef, in the shape of a half moon, extends 4} miles to the northward,
and has 17 fathoms near the eastern side, 12 and 19 to the northward, and 10 and
12 to the westward. Between these reefs and the Falsecape Reef, to the south-

THE COASTS OF TERRA FIRMA AND MOSQUITIA. 29

ward, is the Cocorocuma Channel, in the parallel of 15° 35’, carrying 16, 18, and
16 fathoms through it. The S. W. Cocorocuma Kay is about 4 feet above water,
and has five cocoa-nut trees upon it.

The next dangers to the N. Westward are the Hobby Kays, very near the pa-
rallel of 16°, and meridian of 83° 7’ 30’; from these, a broken reef stretches
W. by N. 3N., for 12 miles, at the west end of which are the Caxonones Kays. The
Great Seal Kay lies 8. W. by W., 11 miles from the Hobby Kays, in latitude
15° 57’, and longitude 83° 17’, is about 4 feet above water, and has four remarkable
cocoa-nut trees upon it. The other Seal Kays lie a little to the N. Westward. At
3 miles S. E. from the Great Seal Kay is the Seal Rock, on which the sea breaks.

The Vivorilla Kays lie S. by W., nearly 6 miles from the Great Seal Kay, on one
of which is a remarkable single tree. The Seal Kays and Rock, together with the
Vivorilla Kays, are situated on a patch of shallow corally ground, which stretches
6 miles S. W. by S. from the Great Seal Kay, having 7 fathoms upon that end,
and 13 to the eastward; it thence extends 13 or 14 miles N. W. past the Vivorilla
Kays, having 5 and 7 fathoms upon it, with 19 and 20 fathoms to the southward,
23 and 25 fathoms to the westward, and to the northward, 28, 20, and 19; while to
the eastward of the Seal Kays, there are 15, 14, and 12 fathoms.

To the N. W. by N., 7 miles from the Seal Kays, and S. W. by S., 5 miles from
the Caxonones Kays, is the Carataska Shoal, very narrow from east to west, lying
N. W. by N. and 8. E. by S., about 2} miles in length. To the westward of this
shoal are 4 and 8 fathoms, between it and the Seals, 15 and 17; towards the Cazo-
nones, 14 and8; and in the channel, between the Hobby Kays and the Seals, are
19, 14, and 10 fathoms, which channel may be safely navigated in fine weather by
the largest vessels.

The Hobby Channel is to the southward of the Seals and Vivorilla Kays, between
them and the Pigeons and Cocorocuma to the southward; the fairway lying
S. W. by W. and N. E. by E., with 19 and 20 fathoms right through, muddy
bottom, decreasing gradually towards the coast.

To the southward of the parallel of 16°, and about the meridian of 83° 50’, are
some coral patches of 7 and 9 fathoms. The bank, at present sounded to the N. E.
of Cape Gracias a Dios, does not extend to the northward of 16° 30’ N., where the
depth is about 30 fathoms, and on the meridian of 83° 7’, the edge of soundings
takes aS. W. by W. 3 W. direction to the meridian of 84°, where, in the latitude

of 16° 8’, it runs to the westward towards Cape Camaron.

Throughout the bank of soundings, N. Eastward of Cape Gracias a Dios, the
bottom is pretty regular, in a depth from 12 to 20 and 30 fathoms, occasionally
more or less, chiefly of sand, shells, and coral; the shallowest water next to the
dangers enumerated, appears to be about 21 miles east of the Pigeons, and
S. W. by S., 12 miles from Gordo Kay, where there are 5 fathoms, sand and shells;
and E. S. E. from this spot, towards the meridian of 82°, and towards Gordo Kay,
there are occasionally but 1 and 2 fathoms more.

“Tt has generally been the custom of vessels leaving Jamaica, bound to the
main, even as far to the westward as Chagres, to work to windward along the
south side of Jamaica, for the purpose of weathering Portland Rock or the Morant
Kays, conceiving the former to be as far east as 77° 25’ 20” W., and in latitude
17° 7 23" N., making a channel of nearly 90 miles between it and the Morant
Kays. We passed about a quarter of a mile to the westward, but could get no
soundings with the hand lead, having too much way through the water: could
observe nothing like breakers from the mast head. After passing Portland Rock,
we stood to the south, steering for the latitude of the small island, called Roncador.
At noon the following day, May 24, 1824, found we had experienced a westerly
set of 60 miles, placing us at that distance to the westward of the island. Hauled
to the wind on the larboard tack, computing the island to bear from us E. §. E.,

30 SAILING DIRECTIONS FOR

from 17 to 20 miles. At day light on the 25th, finding the current still setting to
the westward, bore up and ran for Old Providence.

“CORN ISLANDS.—From the S$. W. anchorage, or bay of the north, or
smaller island, the course is about S. 3 W., to round the south point of the south-
ward, or Great Corn Island. This island must not be approached too close on the
N. or N. E. points, as there is a reef running off the former, and a shoal, which
commences from the middle of the E. side, stretching round the north end, and
extending some miles from the N. W. point ina S. W. direction, and a mile or two
from the N.E. Off the north end of this island there is a small 7ock, with, I
believe, a passage between it and the island, for small vessels. The south point of
this island may be approached, rounding it in 5 or 6 fathoms about 20 or 30 yards
distance, but you will shoal quickly into 3} and 8 fathoms, directly you round it
or open the S. W. bay, or anchorage, which is a large clear sandy bay of 3 fathoms
water: to the westward of this bay, the shoal extending from the N. W. point is
in a small measure a protection, as it runs S. Westerly. Butshould the wind come
on to blow hard from the westward, vessels run round the S. point into the S. E,
bay. The lat. of this bay is 12° 11’ N. long. 83° 3’ W.

“ Tn leaving this bay, it is advised to steer about S., or S. by W., till you bring
the 8. point to the northward of E., distant 5 or 6 miles; you may then, if bound to
Pearl Lagoon, haul up W. by N. 3 N., which will take you clear and into the
entrance of the lagoon, having regular soundings from 20 to 4 fathoms: in the
latter depth, we anchored in the dark, and found at daylight the entrance of Pearl
Bay Lagoon, bearing west, northerly, 6 or7 miles. Weighed and made sail for it
with a light breeze easterly. This entrance cannot be distinguished unless you are
to the southward of it, and pretty close in.

“There is no mark on the land by which you can know it, except on the N. point,
the land appears to run rather low and bushy for about a fathom or two. There is
an island, or small hay, between the Pearl Kays and Mosquitia Shore, (there was at
one time two, but severe weather has washed one away,) which do not shut in with
the N. point of the outer bay. You may run into 3 or 2} fathoms without any
danger; we carried from 4 to 3} for a distance of about 4 or 5 miles, and anchored
in 33 muddy bottom. Entrance then open and bearing west about 33 miles. This
entrance is not more than half or three-quarters of a mile wide, and leads to an
extensive lagoon of about 30 miles from north to south, and full the half of that
from east to west. At the entrance there is a bar with seven feet on it, but inside,
after an intricate navigation, you may anchor in 3 fathoms. In this lagoon fish is
to be had in plenty. The natives or inhabitants talk mostly English. From this
lagoon, the entrance of which we place in lat. 12° 23’ N. and long. 83° 39’ 40” W.,
we steered about S. 3 E., carrying regular soundings of from 4 to 17 fathoms, then
hauled up for Blewfield’s Bluff, soundings decreasing from 17 to 43 fathoms. Came
to, with the best bower in 4} hard sand, at 8 p.m. Blewfield’s Bluff W.by N. about
four or five miles. The kay between Pearl Kays and Mosquitia Shore bearing
N. E.? N., and high land in the back ground S. W. $ W.: with these bearings
on, the entrance of the lagoon will bear about W. 4 N.: take care not to shut the
kay just mentioned in with the north point of the main shore. :

“BLEWFIELD’S BLUFF we made lat. 12° 1’ 56” N. and long. 83° 42’ 15” W.
Currents variable. We experienced them strong to 8. S. W.; towards morning the
current came out to the southward.

“The distance between the entrance of Pearl Lagoon and Blewfield’s Bluff is not
more than 22 miles, the course along shore is S. 3} E. by compass; you haye
nothing to fear in running this distance, and cannot mistake the bluff, even in the
night, as it is the only land you make, and makes a complete and conspicuous bluff,
off which there is a small kay, which you may haul round in what water you please :
in the Helicon we had 3, 8} and 34, but on hauling out again to the S. E. we
deepened immediately and anchored in 4 fathoms, off shore about three-quarters or
a mile from the high land. From this again the land runs low, with now and then
a view of a hill, or high land in the back ground. After passing the southern or
small mouth of Blewfield’s Bay, you will see a kay which the natives call Pigeon
Kay, and shortly another, which they have named Frenchman’s Kay. These
appear very small, and close inshore. Off the northernmost point of the Bay of St.

THE COASTS OF TERRA FIRMA AND MOSQUITIA. 31

Juan’s, are 4 or 5 kays, or you may say, from their size, rocks ; but they extend no
distance off. . We passed them to the eastward about 1} mile, with no bottom; from
this the shore trends inwards. Off Punta Gorda we saw a single hay.

‘When bound to ST. JOHN’S, or ST. JUAN’S from the eastward, it is advised
to keep in the parallel of 11° 13’ N., and make what they call Round Hill: this
hill is by itself, close down to the water’s edge, and is easily known by having no
high land near it; it is in latitude about 11° 13 30” N. and long. about 83° 49’ W.
You will, in this parallel, or a little more to the northward, haye soundings in long.
83° 29’ W. and 35 and 40 fathoms, muddy bottom ; and by running to the westward
till you shoalen your water to 13 fathoms, then off shore about 4 or 5 miles, S¢é.
John’s Point will then bear S.S.E. 17 miles. Itis not advisable to near this
shore closer than 3 or 4 miles, as there are flats running off in some places a mile
or two. When in the above depth of 13 fathoms. you may run to the southward,
keeping the above distance off shore, and you will gradually decrease your water
to 10 fathoms, and make St. John’s Point, which is the most easterly land you will
see: it has some tall dry trees at the east extreme point ; at the same time you will
see the west end of the Island Arena, which is a low sandy point, and lies from
St. John’s Point about 8S. W. by W., 3 miles. From St. John’s Point to this, there
is a reef or flat, about half a mile off shore, which should not be approached nearer
than 6 or 7 fathoms. The lat. of the west point of Arena is 10° 56’ N. and the long.
83° 42°30" W. In making this bay from the eastward, I see no reason why you
should not haul round the island Arena, or St. John’s, giving it a berth of a mile or
1) on the N. side, and hauling close round the west, or Sandy Point, in what water
you please ; remembering that the channel is only about 200 fathoms wide, with the
deepest water on the north shore.

“From Sandy Point to the southward the land at first runs low, till you come to
Point Cartago, (Blanco Point) or a little to the northward ;_ you will then have very
high land in the back ground, with several high peaked hills rising one above the
other. The most remarkable of these is the Volcanic Mountain of Cartago, which
stands in shore and nearly by itself. We passed this mountain just at daylight,
and could plainly perceive the smoke issuing out of the crater, as the morning,
which here is seldom the case, broke uncommonly clear, but in the course of twenty
minutes there was not a top to be seen, so completely were they enveloped in clouds,
and the day turned out boisterous and rainy.

“It is advised, if bound from St. John’s to the Lagoon of Chiriqui, to keep close
along the shore, which is bold-to, as you have the advantage of the land winds,
and a strong southerly set. Should you on the contrary keep an offing of only 20
miles or less, you are liable to calms (which prevail much in this bight,) and the
set, which is generally to the S. E., will frequently sweep you past the Boca Drago,
or Dragon’s Mouth, the westernmost, best, and generally recommended channel for
this lagoon. The entrance is easily distinguished, either egming from the N. E. or
from the westward, as there are four rochs off the east point, which you leave on
your larboard hand going in: to them you may approach within half a mile,
perhaps nearer if necessary ; but in light winds, the current sets you towards them,
and between them there is no direct passage. From off the West Point a shoal
stretches to the northward some distance, between which and the point there is a
channel, but only for small vessels, and that even is very little known. The best
mark for entering this Boca is to steer for the east point ; if coming from the west-
ward, give the shoal off the west point a berth of 3} or 4 miles, and haul up for the
East Point, keeping it well open to the westward of the rocks, two of which are
seen at some distance, one of them having much the appearance of a boat with a
lug sail. You may approach pretty close to the east point, and you will open a
low sandy point, on which stand a few huts. After passing the east point, haul
right across towards a bluff woody point, to avoid a long reef stretching off from
the point on which the huts stand. You will now find most water on the starboard
shore ; but on coming in the larboard shore has the advantage. After rounding
this reef, a S. E. 4 S. course will take you as far up the lagoon as to- open Boca
del Toro, keeping the north shore on board: in mid-channel you will have deep
water, 7 and 6 fathoms. The latitude of Boca del Drago is 9° 26' N., and longitude
82°.18' W.

“From Boca del Drago we stood to the eastward, with an intention of anchoring

32 SAILING DIRECTIONS FOR
inside the Boca de Chiriqui, which is the easternmost entrance into the lagoon. Be-
tween it and Boca del Drago is that called Boca del Toro. The east point of Boca
de Chiriqui is Point Valencia. In this entrance there are several small hays or rocks,
all of which I believe are bold-to: the channel called Valencia Channel is close round
the point of that name. From this we continued standing to the eastward, and soon
raised Escudo Island.

“¢ Tsland Escudo lies in latitude 9° 6’ N., apparently about 24 or 3 miles in length,
about E. S. E. and W. N. W.: it is uninhabited, but turtles visit it at the proper
seasons. On the north side are several round rocks, covered with long green grass,
round which, and extending some distance to the northward, is a coral reef, showing
in many places just above water. This reef’ extends round to the N, W. point, from
which a fine sandy beach commences and continues along the west side, forming a
low sandy point to the S. W., from which, and between the south point, appears a
pretty large bay. The boats were sent to explore it: the water appeared deep close
to the sand, there being 6 and 7 fathoms; they found very good fresh water and in
plenty, running down close to the beach. Wood is also plentiful, and may be ob-
tained with little trouble. We passed round the south side of it in not less than 7
fathoms, at the distance of about 2 miles.

‘From this island the main land runs high in the back ground, and the course to
_Chagres is about E. by N. If coasting along this shore to the eastward during the
night, you may stand pretty close in: we stood into 11 fathoms, then steered along
shore. To know when you are to the westward of Chagres, you will observe two
very distant hillocks after having passed the high land, from which, towards
Chagres, it is rather low and even, with the exception of these hillocks. From
Chugres we shaped a course for the S..S.W. Kays, about N. W., but as the currents
are rather uncertain here, you must allow accordingly.

“The S..S. W., or S. by W. Kays, taking their name from that bearing from the
Island of St. Andrew’s, are in latitude 12° 10’ N., and longitude 81° 41’ W.: they
are two in number, bearing from each other N. N. W. 3 W., and S.S. E. 3 EB, Off
these kays is a most dangerous reef, extending from about 1 or 13 mile on the east
side, round to the northward, where it runs off 4 or 5 miles, continuing round to
W. by S. It here appeared to run west 7 or 8 miles; that is the shoal, with rocks
above water. There appeared to be a small opening on the N. W. side, but as the
day was closing rather hazy, and the wind light, we tacked and stood to the east-
ward. On the §. W. there appeared also an opening. These hays are resorted to
by turtlers, one of which was lying here at this time, apparently in the N. W.
opening, They should never be attempted but with day-light, for being very low,
if the night be ever so fine, there would be great danger of getting on the reefs
before they could be seen. Should you approach them during the night, you will
in some measure be warned of their proximity by the birds with which they abound.
If you have wind, either shorten sail or haul off, as prudence may dictate ; but I
would by no means advise navigators to approach them in the night. From these

_kays St. Andrew’s bore about N. by E. 3 E

“ST. ANDREW’S.—The south point of this island is situated in latitude 12°80'N.,
and longitude 81° 43’ 30’ W.; its length from north to south is 12 miles, and in
breadth about 3 miles. It has two harbours, one on the N. E. the other on the
S. W. side. In the latter we anchored in H. M. Sloop Helicon, and found it, though -
small, a convenient and safe anchorage, sheltered from all winds, from N. W. by W.
round by the eastward to south, which bearings are the extreme points of the har-
bour. You do not strike soundings till you have brought the north extreme on
your beam or nearly so: you will then have 7 fathoms, coral bottom, which is
plainly seen, the water being very clear. The north extreme is rather low, off
which a small reef runs to the westward: from this point the land runs high, form-
ing a hill, on which there was a flagstaff and fort; the latter more resembling a
farm-house. This hill is woody to the sea, but toward the harbour it is well culti-
vated: from this the land declines a little, (but still very woody,) and nearly in the
centre of the harbour, or a little on the starboard side, forms a conspicuous gap,
which is a good mark for running in by from the westward. From this gap the
land tapers off to the south extreme, there forming a low woody bluff. After having
gained soundings, you may shorten and run in under easy sail, till within about a
quarter of a mile of a low rocky ledge: you may then round-to and anchor, or

THE COASTS OF TERRA FIRMA AND MOSQUITIA. 33

nearer if you wish, as you have 4 and 33 fathoms close-to. From the south point
the land runs low to the sea, but inland to some height. This ledge of low land
runs into the harbour, and terminates in a rocky point forming a small cove, in
which vessels of 250 and 300 tons may enter with safety, having 2} and 3 fa-
thoms. A ship of larger tonnage may lie in this cove or basin, by letting go
an anchor in the harbour, and mooring with her stern to the rocks; the ship
Albion, of 500 tons, moored in that manner; and a merchant brig of 17 feet
hold anchored inside the basin, and delivered her cargo upon the rocks, On
the rocks which form the basin you may erect a tent, if necessary, and there
unload your vessel with ease and convenience, the water being as smooth as a
pond. Close to you there is wood and water, and fruit for the trouble of picking.
Were any vessel, whilst cruising on the Spanish or Mosquitia Coast, obliged by sick-
ness or distress to seek a harbour, she would find this a most convenient one. In
the first case, you would derive the benefit of a most healthy climate, where sickness
is never known, with a luxury of green vegetables of every description ; fish is so
plentiful, that in an hour sufficient may be caught to serve the crew. On the
other hand, a vessel might with safety enter the basin, the entrance of which is
about 10 or 12 fathoms broad, and there refit, clear her hold, and even careen if
necessary.

“This island is at present under the Columbian flag: its inhabitants consist of
about 1000, 80 or 90 of which are free, the rest slaves. The principal produce of
cotton: it likewise produces sugar cane in quantities; but the islanders only pay
attention to that on their own estates which is for their own consumption, using
the juice in the room of sugar. They have a breed of fine large cattle, with poultry
in abundance; they have also a breed of small sure-footed horses. Tobacco grows
wild, but which, owing to the little intercourse hitherto held with this island, is not
cultivated; though the islanders confess the soil is capable of producing and
bringing any thing to perfection. The grape was seen here, but our stay was
too short to permit us making many observations. The harbour on the N. E.
side is the best, and most commodious of the two, and by all accounts would be
worth examining. Sloops of war haye now and then lain here, as well as a
frigate at anchor in the N.W. harbour. ‘The island is surrounded by a coral
reef, but at the parts that we saw the danger showed itself. In approaching this
island from the southward or S. E., care must be taken not to go near to the
E. 8. E. or 8. 8. W. kays; the latter of which we have already-described. From
the E. S. E. kays there is a rocky shoal running about N. W., and by the breakers,
I think full 5 miles. This shoal runs round the kay to the eastward, and to about
3 or 4 miles E. S. E.

“On the south side there is an inlet between the breakers, which at night might
prove fatal to a vessel approaching. On the north side, and full 2 miles from the
kay, we saw the wreck of a schooner; we passed on the west side, at the distance of
about 14 mile, Sé, Andrew’s then bearing W. N. W.

“From St. Andrew’s we shaped a course for Point Bracma, or Brackman Bluff.
We struck soundings in 10 fathoms, about 25 miles to the eastward of it. We
hauled up to the northward, and ran along shore at the distance of 2 or 3 miles, in
regular soundings. From Point Bracma to the Cape Gracias a Dios the land is
very low, without a single hill or mountain, but you may run by soundings, pleasing
yourself as to depth. About 30 miles to the southward of the Cape, there are two
entrances to Bays or Lagoons ; but so narrow, that unless pointed out you will pass
them ; but, if close in, you will see the water of them over the land, from your
mast-head. ‘To the northward of these, and about 3 or 4 leagues to the southward
of the cape, is an opening, called Warner’s Sound, which makes very distinctly,
and appears to be the entrance into a very fine harbour, unless you are close-to :
you will then perceive a bar across the entrance. Hereabout, the bottom is said to
be rocky, but we anchored for a night in 3 fathoms water, blowing strong from
the eastward. In the morning weighed, but on account of an increasing breeze
from the eastward, with a swell, we could not keep sufficiently close in-shore to
observe the entrance of the bay, (which is about 2 miles broad,) and did not find
out that we had passed it, until abreast of the bay, when we tacked and stood to
the southward, rounding Arena Point close, in 2} fathoms, and anchored with the

island* bearing E. 8. E., in 2} fathoms, on mud. After passing Warner’s Sound,
keep about 1 or 14 mile from shore, and be not alarmed at getting into less than
3 fathoms, for unless you adopt this precaution you are liable to pass the entrance,
but which error is soon discovered by that part of the east side of the bay being
washed away, leaving the Island of Arena. On entering the bay, borrow on Arena

“The Mosquitia Kays are full 8 leagues E.S. E. from Arena Point and are very
dangerous. JI recommend, in working between them and the Mosquitia Shore, not
to lose sight of the latter.”

DIRECTIONS AND Description or THE Mosquitra Coast,
By Captain R. Owen, R.N.+

Carr Gracias A Dios is the N. E. extreme of the Mosquitia coast. It forms
a projecting point at the south side of the entrance of the Wanks River, (Ric
Segovia of the Spaniards.) The N. W. point of the entrance bears north-west from
the Cape, nearly three-quarters of a mile. There is a shallow bar formed in a
curve out to the north-eastward, between the points at the mouth, with only 3 or
4 feet water over it at the deepest part, which is round a dry sand bore, three-
quarters of a mile N. N. E. from the Cape. There are 2 and 3 fathoms inside.

A narrow strip of land, covered with high trees, reaches to the south-westward
from the Cupe, forming a spacious but shallow harbour, the entrance of which is
up in the bight of the bay to the south-westward, close over to the western shore.
There is a small space with two and a half and three fathoms, reaching for about
one mile beyond the entrance; the rest of the harbour has only from 8 to 12 feet,
with muddy bottom. ‘This harbour has been formed within the last century. The
English used to cut mahogany up the Wanks River, and they made a deep cut
nearly one mile and a half in length, about three miles above the mouth, into
what was at that time an open bay, with some hays on the eastern side, since
which the neck of land that now makes the eastern side of the harbour has gra-
dually formed.

The cut still remains with 12 feet water in it, but there is a bar of soft mud, that
is nearly dry, formed across the mouth.

The Bay of Cape Gracias a Dios, to the southward of the harbour, is sheltered
from N. E. by N. round by North to 8. S. W.; the soundings are very regular,
from 6 to 3 fathoms, soft muddy bottom. The best anchorage for vessels that cannot
get into the harbour is in 4 or 43 fathoms, with the entrance of the harbour bearing
N. W., and the eastern extreme of the land bearing N. E. by E.

There are a few Europeans living at a small rude village on the west shore of the
harbour, about half a mile above the mouth. They trade with the natives for
tortoise-shell, sarsaparilla, mahogany, hides, gums, and a few other articles. The
mahogany is cut up the Wanks River, where large canoes are formed roughly out
of the solid trees, and are sent to Belize and to Jamaica for sale.

The king of the Mosquitia Indians lives about forty or fifty miles up the river.
He was educated at Jamaica, but he does not appear to have benefited by any
thing that he learned there. The specimen we saw of the Mosquitia Indians at
Cape Gracias a Dios was any thing but favourable, and does not at all accord with

the account generally given of them. They were living in the most abject poverty

and wretchedness. Their huts are of the most rude and comfortless description,
much worse than any I have ever seen in Africa; they are merely a few rough
poles driven into the ground, with a roof of palmetto leaves, the sides being en-
tirely open. From their long intercourse with Europeans, I was prepared to find
them in a much more advanced state. They are not a numerous tribe, and are
said to be decreasing in number very much. They are confined principally to the
coast and the banks of the river and lagoons.

THE COASTS OF TERRA FIRMA AND MOSQUITIA. 35

THE Bank or Sounpines off the coast, between Cape Honduras and Cape
Cameron, varies in its distance off shore. Just to the eastward of the Roman River
it reaches out for 17 miles, the edge then takes a bend in to the southward, passing
on an east line about 12 miles, outside the Great and Little Rock Head, when the
breadth gradually diminishes to 5 miles off Cape Cameron. It is free from danger
for the whole extent, with deep soundings of 40 and 50 fathoms near the edge, and
from 6 to 10 fathoms close in to the beach. It is very steep-to just to the eastward
of Cape Honduras, deep soundings of 20 fathoms reaching within less than a mile
of the shore; there is, however, as little as 10 fathoms outside a few miles to the
northward, where the soundings are rather irregular.

From the Roman River to the Great Roch Head, the line of 10 fathoms is about
two miles off shore, and from thence to Cape Cameron it approaches to within a mile,
so that a vessel should not come into less than 20 fathoms during the night off this
part of the coast. The bottom is a mixture of mud and sand, except off Cape
Honduras, where it is coarse gravel, with coral near the edge.

From Cape Cameron the edge of the bank runs nearly E. by N., until about
10 miles to the eastward of the meridian of Point Patook, when it trends up
about N. E. by E., as far as the meridian of 82° 30’ West, and into the parallel of
16° 43’ N., which is the northern extreme of the Great Mosquitia Bank. The edge
is 17 miles from Point Patook, and upwards of 50 miles to the northward of the
Carataska Lagoon, whilst in the meridian of Cape Gracias a Dios, it reaches 86
miles to the northward of the Cape.

There is not any danger upon the bank to the westward of 83° 30’ W., or about
12 miles to the eastward of the meridian of the Carataska Lagoon entrance. Off
Cape Cameron the deep soundings approach very near to the shore; there are 20
fathoms within one mile and a half of the beach.

Off Black River the soundings decrease more gradually ; the line of 20 fathoms
is there about three and a half miles off shore.

Abreast of the entrance of Brewer’s Lagoon, 20 fathoms is full 7 miles out, and
off Point Patooh it reaches to the distance of 9 miles; from hence the line of 20
fathoms takes nearly an east direction as far as the Vivorilla Kays, in the meridian
of Cape False.

In beating along shore at night, between Black River and Point Patook, it
would not be adyisable to come into less than 12 fathoms; but to the eastward of
Point Patook you may stand safely into 8 fathoms all the way to Cape Gracias a
Dios. During the day you may stand close in-shore into 5 fathoms.

The soundings are very regular on this part of the bank, decreasing as you
approach the shore. Above 40 fathoms the soundings increase very suddenly to
upwards of 100 fathoms, The bottom is a mixture of sand and mud with gravel,
off Brewer’s Lagoon.

There is a coral ledge with irregular soundings from 7 to 15 fathoms, about 30
miles N. N. W. of the mouth of the Carataska Lagoon. It is 10 miles in length
from north to south, and four miles wide. The deep water soundings around it are
of soft mud and sand.

Tue Great Mosquitia Banx reaches to the north-eastward of Cape Gracias a
Dios for upwards of 130 miles.

The first danger on the bank from the north-eastward, and the one most distant
from Cape Gracias is Kay Gorda, a small isolated barren rock. It is about 70
miles north-east of the Cape. There is a small detached breaker about 5} miles
E. by 8. of Kay Gorda; it is called Farral’s Breaker. These dangers stand quite
detached ; the bank is clear for 30 miles within them. They may be avoided when
standing on to the bank from the northward, by not coming into less than 20
fathoms. There is a ledge with from 7 to 10 fathoms, reaching to the S.S. E. from
Kay Gorda for nearly 40 miles. The northern part of this ledge has corally bottom,
and the southern part has fine sand.

The Caxones of the Spaniards, called by the fishermen the Hobbies, are a cluster
of small kays and dangerous reefs, about 65 miles north of Cape Gracias, and 20
miles within the northern edge of the bank. They extend for about 12 miles

FQ

36

W.N.W. and E.S. E. The line of 20 fathoms reaches within about 4 miles of
them to the northward, which will give sufficient warning to vessels standing on
to the bank during the night.

Outside the Cazrones and of Kay Gorda, both to the northward and eastward,
the bank is quite free from danger.

There is a snug anchorage in six fathoms, under a spit of reef to the northward
of the Caxones Kays, much used by the fishermen from the Caymans and from Belize,
who come here in the season to fish for the hawk’s-bill turtle, from which tortoise-
shell is procured.

Three miles to the southward of the west end of the Caxones are the Carataska
Shoals or Reefs ; they are two small reefs, each about three-quarters of a mile long,
running about 8. S. E., with a small sandy kay, three feet above water, upon each
of the reefs.

The Seal Kays are about 4} miles 8.8. E. of the Caratasha Reefs; they are
three miles in extent in the same direction, and are situated upon a coral bank,
nearly dry. A ledge with from 7 to 10 fathoms reaches for five miles to the
8.8. E. The Great Seal Kay is at the south end of the coral bank; it is about
four feet above water, and has some cocoa nut trees growing upon it. There is a
rock nearly dry, one mile and a half S. E. by E. of the Great Seal Kay.

The Vivorillas (or Caymans of the fishermen,) are about 4 miles S. S. W. of the
Seal Kays. There are two kays about two miles apart, with trees on them, and a
coral reef between, with a few small sandy kays upon it. There is anchorage
under the west side of the reef in 7 and 8 fathoms, sheltered from the regular
breezes. A rocky ledge with irregular soundings, from 43 to 10 fathoms, runs out
for eight miles to the north-eastward of the Vivorillas, with one spot near the
west extreme and another on the north-east side having as little as 33 fathoms.
The channel between the Seal Kays and the Vivorillas is deep, with 20 fathoms.
There is also a clear channel between the Caxones and the Carataska Shoals, and
between the Carataska Shoals and the Seal Kays.

About 17 miles to the south-eastward of the Seal Kays are the Cocorocuma Kays
and Reef. The kays have some low bushes and a few cocoa nut trees upon them.
A dangerous reef runs out for five miles N. N. W. from the Kays ; it is less than
half a mile wide and steep-to all round. A small detached breaker lies about
half a mile to the westward of the north end of the reef.

The Pigeon Kays are about 4 miles to the eastward of the Cocorocumas. The
western Pigeon Kay is very small, three feet above water, with a reef running out
half a mile to the northward. The east Pigeon Kays are two in number, the same
size as the western; they are 23 miles E. S. E. of the western kay: the channel that
divides them is clear, with from 12 to 20 fathoms.

SAILING DIRECTIONS FOR

S. by W., 12 miles from Cocorocuma Kays, is a dangerous detached reef, which
we have called Allen’s Reef.* It is one mile and a half in length from N. N. W. to
§. 8. E., and has deep water, 14 to 16 fathoms, all round it.

The Cocorocuma Channel, between Allen’s Reef and the Cocorocuma Kays, is
quite clear, with from 16 to 18 fathoms, sandy bottom.

About S. by E. 4 E., 14 miles from Allen’s Reef, is another dangerous reef, very
similar in character. It is 33 miles in extent from north to south, and has from 10
to 14 fathoms round it. We have called it Barnett’s Reef.

Allen’s Channel is between Barnett’s Reef and Allen’s Reef; it is perfectly clear,
with 14 fathoms all the way between the reefs.

Barnett’s Reef is 22 miles E. by N. from Cape False, and 17} miles N. N.E.4E.
from Cape Gracias a Dios. The space between is free from danger, and the sound-
ings very regular. When beating round Cape False at night, it would be prudent
not to stand out into more than 10 fathoms.

To the E. 8. E. of Barnett’s Reef, about 16 miles distant, there is a cluster of

THE-COASTS OF TERRA FIRMA AND MOSQUITIA. 37

detached hays, with some extensive and dangerous reefs to the northward. The
reef to the north-westward, called Half-Moon Reef, is steep-to on the northern
edge ; it is more than six miles in length from east to west, and is very dangerous.
The northern edge is on the same parallel as the middle of Barnett’s Reef. Another
dangerous reef runs to the south-eastward for four miles, nearly connected with the
Half-Moon Reef at the south-east extreme. It is called the Savanna Reef. Bar-
nett’s Channel, between Half-Moon Reef and Barnett’s Reef, has from 10 to 15
fathoms across, with a bottom of sand and shells.

The kays to the southward of Half-Moon Reef are very small, standing about
three feet above the water. There is a single cocoa nut tree on the one farthest to
the southward, (Kay Bobel.)

Logwood Kay and Burn’s Kay, on the southern part of the reef, are only small
rocks, without vegetation. Half-Moon Kay is composed of sand; it is four miles
N.N.W. of Kay Bobel, and has a reef running off it to the northward for about
one mile, under which there is anchorage sheltered froin the eastward.

There is a small detached reef, called Cockburn’s Reef, about nine miles to the
southward of Kay Bobel, with deep water round it, and a small shoal, with
33 fathoms, called Hail’s Shoal, two miles and a half S. E. by S. of the kay.

To the south-west of the Savanna Reef there are three kays, detached from each
other; they are about 4 feet high, with low bushes upon two of them. There are
likewise some small dry reefs, about 5 miles to the southward of the 8. E. extreme
of the reef. This neighbourhood is too full of dangers to be ventured into by any
but small fishing vessels.

To the eastward of the Savanna Reef, about 6 miles distant, is the north-west
elbow of the Alargate Alla Reef; (keep at a distance.) This is the most dangerous
reef on the bank, it is upwards of ten miles in extent from north to south. The
eastern side forms the segment of a circle convexing to the eastward, quite steep-to,
with from 12 to 15 fathoms close to the dry reef. There is a kay off the centre of
the west side, about five feet high, detached from the reef at a distance of about two
miles; it bears nearly south from the north-west extreme of the reef. The Alargate
Alla is in the same meridian as Kay Gorda, upwards of 40 miles to the southward,
Its southern extreme is in the same parallel as Cape Gracias a Dios, about 46 miles
to the eastward. It is 42 miles within the eastern edge of the Great Mosquitia
Bank, with from 11 to 16 fathoms for the entire distance. :

All these outlying dangers, and the bank, as far as to the meridian of 82° west
longitude, were surveyed by Lieut. Barnett in the Jachdaw schooner.

The channels to the north-east of Cape Gracias a Dios are not recommended to
be used, except in cases of emergency, as none of the kays are sufficiently con-
spicuous for a landfall, and there is not any certain indication of your proximity to
the reefs even by the lead.

VESSELS BOUND To CargE Gracras from the eastward, should strike the
Great Bank about the meridian of the mouth of the Caratasha Lagoon, and beat
up in shore round Cape False ; and on leaving Cape Gracias for the eastward,
they should pass to the westward of the Vivorillas. On the north-east part of the
Great Mosquitia Bank, there is a detached knoll, about seven miles in diameter,
with from 15 to 25 fathoms. It is separated from the main bank by a channel
eight miles wide, with from 120 to 150 fathoms fine sand. We have called it
Thunder Knoll; there is deep water soundings for some miles round it, from
100 to 200 fathoms. This knoll is about seventy miles N. E. by E. from Kay
Gorda.

The north-east elbow of the Great Mosquitia Bank, to the southward of Thunder
Knoll, has from 12 to 20 fathoms. We did not quite join Lieut. Barnett’s work
to the westward, but found a bight of irregular deep soundings between 30 and
120 fathoms, running up to the northward, round the south-west corner of this
elbow, that may possibly detach it from the main bank. This will be determined
by Lieut. Barnett, who is completing the survey.

To the southward of the north-east elbow, the edge of the great bank (in the
parallel of Cape Gracias a Dios,) falls in about 30 miles to the westward, and
takes a direction nearly S. 8. W., in an undulating line, gradually nearing the

38

shore. Abreast of Cape Gracias it is 90 miles off shore ; and to the southward of
San Juan de Nicaragua it approaches to within 7 miles.

Between the parallels of 13° and 15° north latitude, (including the Mosquitia
Kays to the south-eastward of Cape Gracias, ) the bank has yet to be surveyed.

The coast to the southward of the harbour of Cape Gracias trends S. by W. for 11
miles, and then S. S. E. for 25 miles to Governor’s Point, which is a long rounding
turn in the land, beyond which the coast trends about 5.5. W., and continues in
that direction for 55 miles to the mouth of the river Wounta, or Tongula, from
whence it trends nearly south all the way to Parattee Point, to the southward of
the Pearl Kays, a distance of 67 miles. It is a low coast the whole distance, with a
sandy beach.

The first opening to the southward of the Cape is into the Guana Sound Lagoon,
about 8 miles from the harbour. the next is Sandy Kay River, about 20 miles further
to the southward. There is a small river, called Dockwara, two miles to the north-
ward of Governor’s Point, and another 15 miles to the southward, called Honeson’s
River ; these are all small rivers, with a bar of sand across the mouth, mostly im-
passable even for canoes.

There is a remarkable part of the coast, about five miles and a half from Honeson’s
River, called Brachman’s Bluff, with steep cliffs of red earth, about 35 feet high,
reaching nearly three miles along the coast ; it cannot easily be mistaken, as there
is not any thing else along the coast that at all resembles it.

The River Wava, 12} miles S.S. W. from Brackman’s Bluff, is the largest on the
coast to the northward of the Rio Grande; the water was discoloured for a con-
siderable way from the mouth. The River Wounta, or Tongula, already mentioned,
is twenty-three miles to the southward of the Wava. There are two more small
rivers, the Apulka and Walpasiksa, and some small creeks, between the Wounta and
the Rio Grande, a distance of about 36 miles.

The coast from Cape Gracias to within about 10 miles of the Rio Grande was
merely traced during a run to the southward, in the Blossom, and will require to be
more closely examined. We had from 4 to 6 fathoms, within less than 2 miles of
the coast, the whole way, except when off the Wounta River, where we had as
little as 34 fathoms, when two miles and a half off shore. The Fox Shoals are said
to be off the mouth of this river.

The first kays off the coast, to the southward of the Mosquitia Group, are the
Men-of-War Kays; they are situated about ten miles north-east of the mouth of
Rio Grande, and nearly the same distance off the nearest part of the shore; they
are very small, with trees and bushes upon them. A small low rock of shingle
stands upwards of a mile to the north-east of the kays, steep-to all round, with
9 and 10 fathoms, and a detached breaker about 1} mile to the 5. Westward.

SAILING DIRECTIONS FOR

About 8 miles to the southward of the Men-of-War Kays are two small kays,
called the Great Tyro and the Seal Kays ; and about the same distance south of the
Tyro Kay are the two King Kays.

A barren rock, about 8 feet high, lies 45 miles N.E. by N. from the Great
Tyro Kay, and another, of equal size, lies 3 miles W. S. W. of the larger Kin,
Kay. There are several rocky patches to the westward of these clusters of small
kays, but by keeping within 5 miles of the coast, there is a good channel to the
southward along-shore, until nearly down to the Pearl Kays, where it becomes in-
tricate and dangerous.

Twelve miles south of the King Kays is Askill Kay, the most northern of the
Pearl Kay Group, which extends in small clusters down to Parattee Point ; there
is deep water between the kays, but there are too many rocks and shoals to allow
of safe navigation amongst them, unless with good local knowledge.

There are some dangerous reefs and shoals to the eastward of the Pearl Kays,
reaching about 12 miles off the main land ; the most eastern is the reef off Seal Kay ;
which is about 15 miles E. N. E. from Paratiee Point.

The Pearl Kays, and the kays to the northward, are all thickly wooded, with
high trees on most of them. The trees on the Pearl Kays are from 50 to 120 feet
high, and those on the small kays to the northward from 30 to 70 feet high.

THE COASTS OF TERRA FIRMA AND MOSQUITIA. 39

A dangerous reef extends off Parattee Point for two miles.

All the kays to the southward of the Men-of-War Kays, with the bank and
coast line to the parallel of 11° 40' N., were surveyed by Lieut. Barnett, in the
Larh schooner.

At Parattee Point the coast falls in suddenly to the westward for about eight
miles to the mouth of the Pearl Kay Lagoon: the shore between is thickly wooded ;
the tops of the trees are from 100 to 140 feet high. It is very shallow for upwards
of two miles from the shore.

The Pearl Kay Lagoon is very extensive, reaching for 20 miles to the northward
of the mouth: there is a bar formed about a mile outside the mouth to the south-
eastward, with only eight feet on it at low water; it breaks, except in very fine
weather. Inside the bar there are from 2 to 4} fathoms for about three miles up,
beyond which it is very shallow. There is a rise and fall of about two feet at
the springs. High water, 1h. 45m.

About four miles within the bar to the south-westward there is an English
settlement of some extent, and another about four miles more to the westward.
The settlers came originally from Jamaica, and from the English Factory at
Black River ; they are now spread along this part of the coast of the Pearl Kay, and
at Blewfield’s Lagoons, and also at the Corn Islands, and at St. Andrew’s, and Old
Providence.

At the Lagoons and at the Corn Islands they consider themselves as living within
the Mosquitia territory, and do not acknowledge any connexion with the State of
Colombia ; whereas, at St. Andrew’s and Old Providence, they acknowledge them-
selves to belong to the State of Colombia, and have a commandant and a few
soldiers from Carthagena. The commandant resides at St. Andrew’s. Those
within the Mosquitia territory are, in fact, living asan independent race, subject only
to such laws as they have established amongst themselves.

The land projecting out to the eastward from the Pearl Kay Lagoon forms this
part of the coast into a deep bay, and affords shelter, during northerly winds, in
four or five fathoms, muddy bottom.

There is a remarkable round hill, called Cookra FTill, 98 miles S. W. 3 W. from
the bar of Pearl Kay Lagoon ; it is 587 feet high, and stands about five miles
inland. It is visible from the Great Corn Island, from whence it bears nearly west.
There is a similar hill, 14 miles to the southward, at the back of Blewfield’s Lagoon,
483 feet high. These are the only hills along the coast between Cape Gracias and
the Blewfield’s, and are very useful as landmarks, when bound to the Lagoons.

Blewfield’s Lagoon is about seven leagues south of the Pearl Kay Lagoon: the
coast between is nearly straight, with a sandy beach. There is a small ereen
mound, forming a projecting point to the southward, called False Blewfield’s, about
93 miles from the bar of the Pearl Kay Lagoon.

The Cayman Roch lies off this part of the coast, two miles from the shore, and
six miles N. 3 E. from Blevwfield’s Bluff. It is a barren rock, about 25 feet high,
with 6 and 7 fathoms close to it all round, and a clear channel, with from 3 to 6
fathoms between it and the shore.

At the entrance to Blewfield’s Lagoon, on the north side, there is a remarkable
bluff headland, forming a small peninsula, projecting to the south-westward, joined
to the main by a low narrow neck of land. This bluff is higher than any other
part ofthe coast, and makes like an island in almost every direction ; it is about
120 feet high, and is bold-to, with low steep cliffs of red clay. There is a bar
formed across the entrance into the Lagoon, off the south-west part of the bluff,
with about 13 feet at low water : there is a rise of two feet at the springs : high water
at lh. 50m. It is observed that the tide rises six inches higher in the night than
in the day. During fresh north-east winds the bar breaks heavily : it also varies
in depth, being affected by the freshes out of the river. The flood-tide only runs
for three hours. There is a rapid current out of the Lagoon after heavy rains.

When going in, keep over on the starboard hand, close along the west side of the
bluff. The best anchorage is just to the northward of the north-west point of the
bluffin 4 or 5 fathoms, muddy bottom. Above the anchorage it gets very shallow.
There is a boat channel to the northward into the Blewfield’s River, and another to

40

the westward, up to a large settlement situated under a hill, about 3} miles west
from the anchorage.

There are at this settlement between three and four hundred inhabitants. The
same race as those who are settled at the Pearl Kay Lagoon, and at the islands to
the eastward.

To anchor outside Blewfield’s in a vessel that cannot cross the bar bring the south
west point of the bluff to bear W. N. W., and stand on till the right extreme of the
bluff bears N. N. W., you will then be in 5 fathoms muddy bottom. This anchorage
is exposed to the regular breezes, but there is plenty of room to weigh, and a clear
bank to windward. There is a dangerous coral patch with as little as 8 feet water
about two miles and a half S. by E. from the south part of the bluff, and another
similar patch with as little as 6 feet, about 23 miles further to the southward, in the
same line of bearing from the bluff. Outside of these rocky patches the bank is
quite clear. Naut. Mag. Feb. 1841.

SAILING DIRECTIONS FROM

FROM GRACIAS A DIOS TO THE GULF OF HONDURAS,
WITH THE ADJACENT ISLANDS.

CAPE GRACIAS A DIOS to the WESTWARD.—From Cape Gracias a Dios
the coast runs N. W. a distance of 6 leagues, to the False Cape, which may be
known from being the highest land on this part of the coast. From the False Cape,
a bank or shoal, with very little water on it, extends about 3 miles to the N. E.;
but the soundings of the coast bank keep very regular.

From Cape False, the coast bears about W.N. W. for a distance of about 22
miles, to the Lagoon of Carataska, which is easily known by its wide mouth.
All this coast is, like the preceding, clean and with regular soundings along it: and
in navigating on it, the lead is a sufficient guide, so that you may not get into less
than 53 fathoms when standing towards the land, nor into more than 12 or 13
fathoms when standing off; by attending to these depths you will avoid falling on
the Vivorillas, which, as may be seen on the chart, lie about 12 leagues off the coast
north-eastward.

From Carataska Lagoon the coast still continues about N. W. by W. a distance
of 13 leagues to the Point and River Patook, and from it about W. 3 N., 22 miles
to the entrance of Brewer’s Lagoon thence W. by N., 18 miles to the Black River,
and 7 miles further to Cape Cameron, and the Cape River to the eastward.

BLACK RIVER is known by the mountains of Za Cruz, which are very lofty,
and are the first to be seen on all the coast, after passing Nicaragua: these moun-
tains are somewhat to the east of the mouth of the river; and on the same river
there is a summit or peak, which, from its figure, is called the Sugar Loaf. To
anchor in front of this river, bring the mouth of it to bear about south, and Cape
Cameron west, taking care not to go into less than 11 fathoms, because within that
depth there are many lost anchors, which have been left by ships forced pre-
cipitately to make sail when the Norths begin to blow.

This anchorage is an open roadstead, where, even with the winds of the breezes,
it is necessary to ride, with two-thirds of a cable out; and as soon as the wind falls
away, to heave nearly a-peak, that the anchor may not bury itself or be fouled.
When in this anchorage, in the season of the gales, that is, from October to Febru-
ary, it is necessary to pay much attention to the weather: and so soon as you see
the wind come to 8. E., and from that vere to south and S. W., the anchor should
be weighed immediately, and sail made off shore, in full confidence that a gale will
follow. In the above mentioned months, also, a cloudiness or bad appearance to-
wards the N. W. is an infallible indication of an approaching gale; nor is a swell
from the northward, that precedes the gale a considerable time, less so. At any of
the times of the gales, the loss of any ship remaining at anchor is certain; and
frequently the wind will not give time to weigh the anchor ; in which case the cable
must be slipped with a buoy on it, in order to lose no time in making sail and

GRACIAS A DIOS TO CAPE CATOCHE, &. 41

standing off shore, so that you may keep under sail until the storm is past. These
gales are very violent and raise a heavy sea ; and thus, when a vessel is very much
distressed, she has the resource of running to the bay of Gracias a Dios, and
taking shelter there at anchor, during the rough weather; and, as has been already.
stated, there is no other caution required in taking that bay, than the use of the lead.
As these gales occur generally from North, N. W., or West, it results, that ordi-
narily, the anchorage of Gracias a Dios may be considered as a port to leeward, to
which you can bear away ; in which resource, there will always be the advantage of
being to windward of Black River, when the gale ceases; because then the wind
shifts to the east, and therefore, in a short time and without trouble, the former
anchorage may be regained.

The Bar of the Black River is extremely dangerous, and boats run great risk of
upsetting on it, and the crews of being drowned, on account of the very heavy sea
which is generally on it. Therefore, either going in or coming out should be ma-
naged to take place in the calm of the morning, before the sea breeze sets in, and
after the land breeze has blown from the time it became dark ; and also thus, if the
breeze has been tolerably fresh, you can neither get in nor out; so that communi-
cation with the shore very seldom takes place, and is always troublesome and dan-
gerous.

Cape Cameron is formed by a small low tongue of land, projecting out to sea.
From this cape the coast runs S. W. 3 W., 15 miles past the Poyas River and Carib
Village, all clean. At 9 miles true south of the Carib Village is a high peak, 4000
feet high. Thence the coast runs west for 8 miles to Great Roch Head, a slight
projecting point; and after bending a little S. Westward takes a W. by N. 3 N.
direction for 15 miles to the Roman River, which discharges itself by two entrances ;
from whence to Cape Honduras or Castilla Point, is W. 3 N., 20 miles.

TRUXILLO BAY.— Point Castilla, or Cape Honduras is low, and a small bank
of sand, with little water on it, extends from the point, one quarter of a mile to the
westward. Custiila is the north point of the Bay of Truxillo, which at the entrance
is about 5 miles wide. The bay is of easy access, it having no other shoal than the
little bank off Point Castilla. On the south coast of the bay there is a very high
mountain, which may be seen 24 leagues out at sea; it is called Guaimoreto, and is
a good mark for running in by from sea; for, by bringing it to bear about S. S. E.
it will lead you clear of Point Castilla, and up to the anchorage in front of the Rio
Cristales, or Crystal River, which runs into the south side of the bay. This ancho-
rage seems preterable, not only because its contiguity to the river affords the op-
portunity of procuring water conveniently ; but also, because from this situation
Point Castilla may easily be cleared, in case of being forced to get under way by a
storm from W.5S. W., West, or W. N. W., from. which points they come on most
frequently from October or Noyember until February. With such winds it is
plain that there must be much sea in this bay: this was experienced by the ship
Maria, in December, and January, 1800, which ship having rode out one or two
of these gales at anchor, was compelled to quit it, and run for shelter into Port
Royal, in the island of Ruatan ; as her captain considered the anchorage at Truxillo
too much exposed to remain at, during the season of the Norths, which was the
season he was in it.*

To enter, or sail out of this bay no particular instructions are necessary, as there
is plenty of room for working without the least risk, only observing, not to approach
within half a mile of the Island Blanquilla or San Lucas, which lies off the south
coast about 2 miles to the westward of the bay, because it is surrounded by a shoal,
the best guide towards which is the lead; taking care not to get into less than 6
fathoms water in its vicinity, will clear every danger. This [sle¢ Blanquilla, or Kay,
lies about a mile from the coast, and you may run through the strait between with-
