Truxillo was well sheltered, and a proper place of refuge during the storms of the
winter; but it is not so, and all ships on this coast, at that season, ought to prefer
Port Royal, in Ruatan, or the harbours of Bonacca, to it.

_ BONACCA.— At the distance of 8 leagues (North) N. } W. from Point Castilla,
is the island Guanaja, or Bonacca, lying N. E. and S. W., about 3 leagues in
length; it is entirely surrounded with hays and reefs, which extend a league off
from it. On the eastern side of the island there is a very good anchorage, particu-
larly during the season of the Norths, but it will be necessary to pass between the
kays and the reefs to enter it. The best channel is to the southward, leaving on the
larboard the last southerly kay, and another kay, bearing about N. by E. from it,
on the starboard: these two kays are rather more than half a mile apart; you
ought to pass in mid-channel, and steer towards another kay, which is about two-
thirds of a mile to the west of that left on the starboard, which will then bear
about (N. 71° W.) W. N. W. 3 W. You ought always to pass between the two
last kays, which having done, nothing remains but to coast along the island to the
N. E., and anchor where convenient under shelter of the land; observing to keep
about mid-channel, between the island and the kays, in 7, 8, and 9 fathoms water,
on muddy sand. It may be necessary sometimes to run for this anchorage in
blowing weather, from North, N. W., or West, which will not permit of working
into it; in which case, it may be observed, that you may work between the three
kays before mentioned, as either of them may be approached to a cable’s length.

Directions for Bonacca, by Lieut. Smith, R.N., commanding H. M.S. Lark.

The Island of Bonacca seems to have undergone little change since its first dis- .
covery. Its magnificent forests still please the eye of the mariner, as they did 300
years since, and the scenery altogether is seldom surpassed, even in tropical regions.
The highest lands have ecohune and pine ridges, with spots of white granite here and
there visible between the trees, with bold cliffs of red and yellow ochre; making
the extremes a varied and pleasing landscape from seaward.

Jts harbours are excellent, with channels in so many directions as to be accessible
> y

for the largest ships with any wind; this is a great advantage over the harbours of

Ruatan, which cannot be entered in northers, when they are most required.

The Kays on the dry reef, forming the eastern branch, are now all covered with
cocoa nut and other trees from 40 to 80 feet high.

Pond Kay Channel will be useful with a north wind. It ean be taken by eye;
and affords good anchorage, with a well defined West Bluff, bearing W. 3 N., and
the South-west Kay, N. E., in5 or 6 fathoms, coral and sand. Thisis far preferable
to remaining under weigh during the night in bad weather. The only inhabitants
now are two men on Sheen Kay, who ran away from a man-of-war some years since.
We took one as a pilot to show where the Swift sloop-of-war struck, who soon run us
on one as bad, which I have named Lark Ridge. This extensive bank can be plainly
seen in fine weather, and breaks in bad. All the shoals inside the reefs must be
avoided by eye, in the usual way, by a person at the mast-head.

There is only one tolerable harbour on the north side, Miehael Rock Channel.
To enter, bring the-Highest Peak to bear S. E.}8. This peak is 1,200 feet high;
although somewhat difficult to make out on the south side, it never can on the
north, even when close under the land. The winds in the morning are from
E. S. E, to S$. E.; the sea breezes draw round about noon to E. N. E. and N. E.;
strong fiery gales are frequent, seldom shifting more than a point or two for some
days; and if it lulls at all, it is about daylight.

This is, probably, one of the most healthy spots in the West Indies, and certainly
has many advantages over Ruatan; not the least, is the abundant supply of excel-
lent water, which is here found in every valley. A stranger may find the spring
inside Sheen Kay, by bringing the dry sand bore between Dunbar and Peak
Rochs; the smal! stream in the east harbour will be found more convenient in the
breezes, haying smoother water, and soft mud instead of stones aud rocks. The

hawk’s bill turtle are very plentiful, and there are generally parties of Caribs
here from the main, taking them in the summer months,

Maniti are still found in the north-east bight. Several kinds of golding and
eurlew, and pie-bald pigeons are very plentiful on the S. W. Kay, and wild hogs
on the mountains. Fish may be taken at pleasure, either towing or with the seine.

The tides are much influenced by the wind; but we find it, on a calm day, to
flow, at full and change days, at 9h., rise 1} foot.

RUATAN ISLAND.—To the westward of Bonacca lies Ruatan, about E. N. E.
and W. 5. W., in which direction it is about 9 leagues in length. To the eastward
of its east point, a reef extends out to the distance of 7 miles, on which there are
several hays and islands: of these, the easternmost is called Barburata. The
distance between Barburata and Bonacca is about 10 miles, but the channel is
limited to only 7 miles, by the reefs which stretch off from both islands; and with-
out great experience, the passage of it will be attended with much danger. Al the
north coast of Ruatan is bordered by reefs, so that it may not be approached
within a league, and those not acquainted ‘with the coast, should keep at a still
greater distance. On the south coast there are some good roadsteads, but most of
them are difficult of access from the foul reefs at the entrances. ‘The principal of
all these, is that called Port Royal, on the east part of the island, and of which
mention was made, when describing the Bay of Truxillo, as being best adapted for
affording shelter during the season of the Worths. This harbour is formed by the
coast of the island on the north and west, and by some reefs and kays on the south
and east. The entrance to it is by a narrow channel, scarcely half a cable’s length
wide, clear of the reefs; but fortunately, however, this narrow part is not more
than 13 cable’s length: the east side of this channel is formed by a reef extending
from the west side of the island called S¢. George, with a fort at its east end, and
which, from its size, is easily known, and cannot be mistaken for the other hays,
which are very small. To enter this harbour, if without a good pilot it will be
necessary to mark the entrance by boats or otherwise; and it should always be
undertaken with the wind from N. E. to East, or from West to South, in order to
get within the reef. In making this island from the south, it is necessary to be
very careful of a rocky shoal lying off the western extremity of it, and which is
distant from the coast mere than 4 miles: the channel between it and the coast is
also obstructed by several other shoals; and although it has a passage for large
ships, yet, if without a pilot, you should always pass on the outside of the shoal.

The COAST from TRUXILLO BAY to TRIUNFO DE LA CRUZ.—From
the River Crystales, in the Bay of Truzillo, the coast runs W. by S., 12 miles
past Point Cameron, then bending S. W. } W., for 15 miles past Reef Point
and River. Between Point Cameron and Reef Point isa mountain; and just to
the northward of the river, a shoal of 3} and 6 fathoms runs 10 miles to the N, W.
The coast then trends a little to the northward of west for seven miles past the
entrance of another river, off which a shoal reef extends to the distance of one or
two miles; it then turns W. by 8. 45%., for 25 miles, and W. } N., 26 miles to
Triunfo dela Cruz. This coast is much exposed and dangerous, on account of the
shoals and reefs, which extend to the southward from Utilla, for which reason, if
there be no cause for keeping near to the shore, or you have not sufficient expe-
rience without risk, we strongly recommend a passage to the northward of the
Cochinos, or Hogs, and the island of Utila.

The Cochinos are two rather large islands, clean on the north side, but with
several foul hays and reefs on the south; between the islands and the kays there is
a regular anchorage.

The Island Utilla lies about W. 3 N. from the Cochinos, at the distance of 23
miles; and S. W. 3 W., 18 miles from the west end of the Island of Ruutan: the
north, south, and west coasts of it are very foul: on the east side there is a good
anchorage; but to take it, it is necessary to have a pilot. At the S. W. of the
island there is a shoal, called the Salmedina, of more than 5 miles in extent; on
account of which it will be advisable to go to the northward of Utilla, not ap-
proaching it nearer than two leagues, until you are abreast of its western points,
whence you may steer towards Point Sal.

“The Island Utilla is about seven miles long, and two and a half broad in the
widest part; with the exception of the mound near the east end, it is quite occupied
by mangrove swamps. The harbours here are superior to any on the main between
Cape Gracias and Omoa. The Hast Harbour is very secure, but having a narrow
entrance, vessels must be warped in with the wind from N. N. W. to E. 8. E.; it is
also very convenient for procuring wood and water. We were informed the well
on the north side of the harbour is never dry. It may readily be found by some
poles in the mud, where there is a lane cut through the mangrove bushes to it, and
a path across the island, A party of fishermen from Zrwzillo were salting and
drying barracouta, grouper, and market fish, &c.; much in the same way as cod
are preserved at Newfoundland.

““The only constant resident is an American on Suck Suck Kay, who has
flourishing plantain walks, and most ofthe vegetables of the country, with a good
stock of fowls; he keeps dogs for hunting the wild hogs, which are so numerous
that he killed three one morning, weighing from 150 to 200 pounds each, (in Sep-
tember, ) in excellent condition from feeding on the seeds of the wild cabbage.”

Triunfo de la Cruz, or Triumph of the Cross, is a point whence the coast rounds
to the $. W. by W., about 6 miles, and then turns to the N. W. for the space of 12
miles further to Salt Point or Punta Sal, forming a great bay well sheltered from
the breezes, and with good holding ground for vessels of every class. To the north
of Point Triumph, at the distance of half a mile, there are some islets, two. of
which are tolerably large, and may be distinguished at the distance of 2 leagues:
they are clean, and by passing at the distance of half a mile from all that is visible,
you may proceed to anchor in the eastern part of the bay, a little to the southward
of the point, in 6 or 8 fathoms, on sand.

Salt Point.—The point at which the bay terminates, is called Salt Point, and at
about half a mile to the northward of it are some high rocks called the Bishops,
forming a channel navigable for boats only. This point appears with some small
hillocks of broken ground, and to the S. W. of it is a little harbour, called Puerto
Sal, but of which we can give no details: however, off the mouth of this harbour,
and at the round of Punta Sal, vessels may anchor under shelter from the breezes,
but should not come-to in more than 12 fathoms, because in 17, 16, 15, and 14
fathoms, the bottom is of rock; and on the contrary, in less than 12, it is of
clean clay.

From Punta Sal the coast forms a bay to the South and W. N. W.., to the River
Lua, or Ulua, which is large and very deep. This river is about seven miles
W. by S. from Punta Sal, and now loads more vessels with mahogany than all the
coast of British Yucatan. In front of this river you may anchor on excellent
holding ground of clay, but without the least shelter from the Norths. About 6
miles W. by 8. from the River Lua, is another river, called the Chienlico, off which
there is also anchorage on good holding ground, but equally unsheltered from the
Norths.

PORT CABALLOS, or Cavallos, is about W. by S., at the distance of 10 miles
rom Chienlico: this harbour is formed by a low point of sand, which projects into
the sea, and to the westward of this point there is anchorage in 7, 6, or 5 fathoms,
onsand. Cavallos Harbour may be known by a round high hill, close to the sea
on the eastern coast, at about 2 leagues from the harbour. To enter this harbour
you have only to keep clear of what is visible.

From Port Cavallos to Omoa, the distance is 7 miles S. W. 3} W.; within this
space there is a small bank with very little water over it, lying north of some red
precipices or broken ground, which are seen on the coast, and at the distance of
about a league and a half from them. To keep clear of this bank, take care and
go no nearer to the coast than into the depth of 7} fathoms, until after passing the
red precipices, when you may direct your course to Omoa.

OMOA HARBOUR is formed by low land covered with mangroves, which
projects into the sea: upon this land there is a watch tower or look-out, which may

GRACIAS A DIOS TO CAPE CATOCHE, &e. 45

be seen at a considerable distance, and serves as a mark to recognize the harbour
by. Another good mark is the high land, rising from Omoa, and extending to the
westward; for from Omoa eastward, the land is all low. To enter into Omoa, we
have only to observe, that you may pass at a cable’s length from Mangrove Point,
which forms the harbour, and when you are to the westward of it, you ought to
luff to the south and east, as much as possible, approaching the south part of the
Mangrove Point ; thus gaining as much to the east as you can, until you are abreast
of the mouth of the basin, when you may anchor, and warp in.

From the anchorage of Omoa you may, in clear weather, see Cubo T'res Puntas,
or Cape Three Points, which bears about W. by N. All the land to the westward
of Omoa is very high, and upon it rise three or four peaks like sugar-loaves ; but
the coast is very low, and continues so to the Gulf of Honduras. From Omoa to
Cape Three Points, the distance is about 10 leagues, and the intermediate coast
rounds somewhat to the south, so that it forms a bight or saco, in which there is a
great beating or agitation of the sea; for which reason it is advisable not to go too
near it, but rather to steer W. N. W., to get well clear of Cape Three Points.
After running a short distance on this course, you may see, to the N. W., the
southernmost kays that lie off the eoast of Bacalar, and which are about 5 leagues
distant from Cape Three Points.

SWAN ISLANDS. According to the chart of Captain Owen, these islands are
situated in latitude 17° 25’ N., and the eastern one in longitude 83°50’ W. They
are situated on a bank of 5 fathoms, which stretches 5 miles to the westward of the
western isle, and is steep-to. The current runs to the N. W., at the rate of one to
two knots.

The Misteriosa Bank was met with by D. Tomas Nicolas de Villa, in his passage
from T'rusxillo to Batavano, in April, 1787, he having sounded in 11 fathoms on
white sand and stones. The latitude deduced from that observed at noon, places
this bank in 18° 48’ 42” N. Its longitude is 77° 29’ 24” W. of Cadiz, or 83° 46/24” W.
of Greenwich, deduced from Punta Castilla of Truzillo, (well ascertained by G. D.
Lomas Ugarte,) allowing for the errors which Villa might have made in five days’
navigation. Also on April 11th, 1805, it was sounded on by D. Josef’ Maria
Merlin, captain of a frigate called the Flecha, in his passage from Cadiz to Vera
Cruz: according to his observations, the depths of 9 and 13 fathoms were in
18° 52’ 42”, and 18° 53’ 46’ N. latitude. The longitude was deduced from the
spot where he had 16 fathoms on the eastern edge of the Serraniila.

Captain Owen has lately surveyed this bank, and found it to consist generally of
coral, sand, and rock. There is no danger on this bank, and the shoalest water, 9
fathoms, is found on its southern edge. It is 8 leagues in length N. E. by E. and
5. W. by W., narrowing at each end to a tongue, with 10 fathoms at the N. E. and
19 at the 8. W. end, then deepening suddenly : in the central part of the bank it is
nearly 7 miles wide. The current over the bank was found to set at the rate of
one to two knots per hour. The N. E. end, according to the chart, lies in latitude
18° 56’ 30” N., and longitude 83° 42’ W.; the S. W. end in 18° 44’ N., and
84° 3) W.

REMARKS ON Omoa AnD Coast TO THE WESTWARD, by Mr. G. B. Lawrence.
Extracted from the Nautical Magazine, February, 1848.

As much valuable mahogany is at present cut on the southern river of British
Honduras, and grants have been lately made by the central American Government
to the merchants at Belize for cutting on those in the State of Honduras, this part
of the coast is frequently visited by our shipping.

All vessels intending to load with mahogany from British Honduras, call at
Belize to enter at the custom house, and there having taken a pilot, proceed to
the mouths of the rivers on which the wood is cut, where the consignee has a cargo
ready waiting for shipment. Should their destination be to the rivers in the State
of Honduras, he has then to enter them also at the custom house at Omoa, and
having loaded, clear out again there, and return to Belize before their final de-
parture for England.

46

Such being the case, vessels proceeding to this part of the coast from Belize
generally prefer the channel between the main and the hays. They sometimes come
outside if bound for Omoa, but very seldom.

Making Omoa from windward. Vessels coming from the N. E. or eastward
should be careful to make the land well to the eastward, to guard against Glover's
Reef, about which the currents set in various directions. In thick dirty weather
it would be advisable to make the western part of Ruatan or the Island of Utilla,
and then shape a course a little to the northward of Point Cabello; the high
mountains to the southward of Omoa being scarcely perceptible during the seasons
of the rains, from October to March.

The Saddle Hill, a remarkable hill to the S. E. of Omoa, is, I think, the best
mark for making the harbour, as it is generally visible, being of a moderate
elevation, (1760 feet,) and not far inland.

In the dry season, from April to September or October, Omoa and Montagua
Peaks are generally clear in the mornings; these, from their great elevations and
prominent features, will assist materially in denoting the ship’s place, as the moun-
tains to the eastward of Omoa are much lower than those to the westward.

Not having extended the survey to the eastward of Omoa as far as Point Cabello,
I am unable to say whether any dangers exist between those places ; but I imagine
the only thing to be guarded against is a bank commencing at the point forming the
harbour, and extending at its greatest distance from the shore, about two miles, off
seven remarkable red cliffs, that may be easily distinguished at the distance of four
or five miles from a ship’s deck, bearing, when in one with the Saddle Hill before
mentioned, S. 37° E., distant from the entrance of Omoa 3} miles.

With these two remarkable land-marks in one, and at the distance of 3 or 3}
miles off shore, the entrance of Omoa Harbour will be seen bearing S. S. W. 3 W.,
forming a low prominent point. As the current generally sets strong in-shore to
the eastward, at the rate of 1 or 1} knot per hour, it will be advisable to close it
gradually, steering about S. W. until you observe the Castle of San Fernando
(which is very remarkable. from its large dimensions) open of the point, now
making out low and sandy, and for which you may at once haul in.

Directions, &c., for Omoa Harbour. To small vessels, drawing 11 feet water,
the harbour affords shelter from all winds, and at times for others of greater
draught, as the bar at the entrance undergoes considerable changes both in for-
mation and depth by north-westerly gales.

A few months before we surveyed it, (July, 1841,) the bridge of sand running
from the main to the point did not exist, and vessels drawing 18 feet water could
enter the harbour, or Caldera. Vessels might with safety ride out a norther close
under the sandy point, as the holding ground is good, and these gales, I am
_nformed, generally haul round to the N.E. You must in this case drop your
anchor close up to the point, within 30 or 40 fathoms of the shore: but a plan will
‘better explain.

The Castle of San Fernando is a regular fortification, capable of sustaining a
siege, it having, I was informed, wells within the walls, bomb proof casements, &c.,
evidently in the best order when in the possession of the Spaniards, but now, from
old age and want of attention, in a state of decay. The Town of Omou is at present
little better than a large village, consisting principally of huts.

Remarks on the Coast to the westward of Omoa. By reference to the chart, all
the dangers of importance will be seen exhibited at one view; the principal of
these are, the shoal of 2 feet lying between the Snake and North Seal Kays, and
the rocky knowls of 14 feet to the S. E. of Odservation Seal; these being very
small, make them more to be dreaded, especially so as the eye cannot detect their
existence.

It would be useless, in fact impossible, to say any thing of those between the
Rivers Temash and Rio Grande ; reference must be had to the General Chart, on
which the prominent hills and points are laid down, to enable the ship’s position
to be at any time determined by cross bearings or angles.

The beach, which is low and sandy, is lined with numerous cocoanut trees, parti-

_ Of the rivers which discharge thei waters between these places, the Montagua
is the most considerable, taking its rise about 12 leagues to the westward of the
city of Guatemala. The first village of importance on its banks is Gualan, situated
from the sea an average voyage of fourteen days for ‘‘ bongas.” These large barges
have much difficulty in ascending the river during the dry season, owing to the
numerous shoals and rapids that infest its beds. The first of the latter, on which
there is only 3 or 4 feet water, is met witl at the junction of the Rio Nuevo, 40 miles
from the bar.

Between the San Francesco and Hospital Bight, a communication has been
formed for canoes by means of a small canal eut through the low swainpy land,
to enable the mahogany cutters to receive supplies by this route, when the heavy
surf renders landing impracticable at the river’s mouth. On one occasion a brig
loaded in this bight, the logs having been towed through this channel from the
river.

The holding ground off the mouths of these rivers is very good, being soft olive
mud. A heavy swell generally sets in on this shore; but except in the season of
the “ norths,”’ from October to February or March, no fear of anchoring need be
apprehended.

The current invariably sets between this shore and the Seal Kays to the S. E.,
at the rate of 1 or 13 knot per hour, its acceleration being influenced by the rains.
In the bight between Cocoalee Point and the Rio Grande it is affected by the winds
as well as the rains; we generally found it setting to the N. E. one knot with the
ordinary light sea breeze from the eastward. There is also a slight rise and fall of
about one foot, also influenced by the wind, generally highest in the evenings.

The prevailing winds on this coast are the periodical land and sea breezes. The
latter usually set in about 10 a.m., and continue sometimes until late at night, but
is governed by circumstances, as during some months we found it very light, par—
ticularly so in September, when it seldom blew home to the coast.

Thunder and lightning of the worst description are constant visitors every night
during the rainy season.

The norths on the coast seldom extend to the southward of Point Placentia..
During the period of their visit the wind in the bight invariably blows off the land
from the S. W., attended with the appearance and strength of a norther. The
mountain of Trepong, south of the Dulce, being free of clouds, is considered a sure-
indication of these winds. They may be looked for at the latter end of October or-
beginning of November. The barometer would appear to be much influenced by
these winds; ours on one oecasion fell suddenly from 29.94 to 29.80, and the
thermometer down to 73°; the average temperature during the summer months
being 85°.

Of the rivers in this bight, the Sarstoon, which is the largest and deepest, has 6
feet water on its bar, and is the southern boundary of British Honduras. They all
resemble each other in appearance, their banks being low and swampy, lined with
impenetrable mangrove bushes. Mahogany is cut at the distance of a journey of
three or four days from their mouths, probably 40 or 50 miles inland. The average
height of the land from Sarstoon Hill southward, is 150 feet.

Two or three hundred Caribs have formed a settlement at Punta Gorda, whose
only occupation is raising stock for their own consumption, and at times visiting
Belize with plantains, cocoa, &c., which they exchange for wearing apparel and
other little necessaries. These people are very inoffensive and much attached to
the colonists. They hold the tenure of the land by sufferance.

In the bight between Cape Three Points and the Rio Dulce, the Ox Shoal is the
only danger to be avoided ; its limits will be seen on the chart.

The Hospital Bight affords excellent anchorage for vessels drawing 12 or 18 feet
water; the least on its bar being 14 feet. Its shores are very swampy, and lined
with mangrove bushes, rendering it, as the name implies, a most unhealthy place.

St. Thomas’s Bight forms a very safe and commodious harbour for large vessels,
and is the best place on the whole coast for watering. By keeping midway be-
tween the two shores on entering, you will avoid the banks extending off the points
on either side. A fresh water creek at the foot of the mountains on its western
shore is the watering place, off which you may anchor at the distance of one cable
in three fathoms, and large boats may pull up to the head of it, and fill their casks
with the greatest ease: the water is excellent.

About one hundred Central American fishermen live at the mouth of the Rio

Dulce, the least water on the bar of which is six feet. A few huts are also to be
met with between this and Punta Palma.

Of Omoa another navigator says,—‘‘ Having found the anchorage at Omoa much
exposed, I ascertained by soundings that we could lie in Caldera, a natural basin
formed by a sand bank stretching east and west. I got the ship warped in this snug
berth into 5 fathoms water, and lay there for five weeks. At the entrance, however,
we found only 3 fathoms, and as the sands during the northers, which are felt on
this coast, are continually shifting, it is always advisable to make good use of the
lead before taking up this berth.

“Whilst at anchor off the Bar of Dulce in 7 fathoms, I had the bar well sounded,
with the view, if possible, of sailing up the gulf, but could only find 7 feet at most,
whilst within there were from 2} to 5 fathoms.

‘With reference to currents, which often impede the navigation of these seas, as a
general rule, I should say that they change with the prevailing winds, though at
times it is difficult to assign any reason for their course.”

Tur Mono Kays. These Kays lie S. W. byS., distant 7 miles from Point
Icacos, to the westward of which there is an excellent and extensive anchorage for
any class of ships, and may be taken without a pilot. It is far more roomy and
less intricate than Port Honduras, and the remarkable range named the Seven Hills
and Rio Grande Hill prevent it ever being mistaken. When proceeding from the
eastward for the anchorage inside the Moho Kays, bring the south end of Stewart
Kay, which bears E. by N., 2 miles from Rio Grande, to bear W. $S., and run in
with this mark on until you are upwards of a mile to the westward of the South
Moho Kay, when you may haul to the northward, and anchor in 6 or 8 fathoms,
well sheltered ; observe, that one mile westward of the South Moho Kay there is a
bank, with only 2 fathoms water on it, named the Lark Bank ; you must keep to
the westward of this bank when hauling to the northward for the anchorage. There
is also a small knowl, with only 2 fathoms on it, lying one-third of a mile S. W.
from the Lark Bank; this knowl you may pass on either side; it lies W. S. W.,
14 mile from the South Moho Kay.

There is also good anchorage in 4 or 5 fathoms about three-quarters of a mile
S. by W. from Stewart Kay. When coming from the south-eastward for this
anchorage, bring the northernmost of the Seven' Hills to bear N. W. § N., and in one
with a small round Mangrove Kay ; keeping this mark on will lead you safely into 5
fathoms on the Stewart Kay Bank ; or till the south point of the Moho Kays comes
on with the West Snake, then steer W. S. W., about half a mile for the anchorage,
or until the same North Hill opens to the west of Sickle Kay, and anchor in 4
fathoms.

Porr Honpuras, lying to the westward of Point Icacos, is a good and safe har-
bour, but its entrance is impeded by several rocky heads, which renders its navi-
gation rather intricate. Point Icacos, in lat, 16° 14’ N. bears W. by N., distant 5
miles from the East Snake, which is remarkable by having trees upon it 90 feet
high, and by being the north-eastern Kay of the Snake Group. Wilson’s Kay bears
S. 3 E., two-thirds of a mile from Point Icacos ; when the north end of this Kay
bears W. by S., you must steer towards it, to avoid the foul ground that extends nearly
half a mile south-eastward of Point Icacos: keep over towards Wilson’s Kay, as the
channel here is only one-fourth of a mile wide ; and as soon as the east point of the
latter Kay bears 8. E. by S., and just touching the $. W. point of the West Snake,
steer N. W. by N., with this mark on, for about a mile, and anchorin 3} or 4
fathoms, with Point Icacos bearing E. by §. 3 S., and just touching the south point
of the Hast Snake ; here you will lie perfectly safe. Off this anchorage, a little
northward of the point, are wells of fresh water. If wishing to proceed further up

Description of the Kays, by Lieut. Smith, R.N. “Between Kay Glory and
Tobacco Kay is an unbroken mass of coral rocks, many of the heads appearing high
out of the water ; there is not a passage for the smallest boats the whole distance.
Yobacco Kay cannot well be mistaken, having a high fig tree (70 feet) near the N. E.
extreme, it is en the north side of the channel, which gradually decreases to 12 feet
due west of the Kay. Should, therefore, vessels get on this shore with northerly winds
and their constant attendant southerly currents, Victoria Channel is preferable. The
north entrance is formed by that prominent spit, named Gladden Kay Reef, outside
of this from a height of 12 feet, the kays can be plainly seen. Bring Spider Kay (the
highest and southernmost of the group) to bear W. by N. 3 N., and run in for it until
Button Wood Kay is nearly on with Gladden Kays, when the left extreme of Tarpum
Kay touching the right extreme of Rendezvous Kay will be 2 tolerable guide to the
Funk Kays. Here the channel is more intricate, but still all is plainly seen from the

~“mast-head. When abreast of Zarpum a good passage is open to windward of Chan-

nel Kay, by Steward Range, or the nearer one by Quamino Kay, should the wind
be too far to the northward, to lie through, or not sufficient time to clear it before
the sun is too low; for it must always be remembered, in navigating by eye, that
the sun should be at least 20° high, and a clear sky, or totally overcast, is better
than passing clouds, which are apt to baffle. By far the best entrance, however,
is that by the Queen Kays, having smoother water, and not less than 20 feet.
These were formerly called the Seal Kays, now altered to prevent confusion, having
others a few miles to the southward. They arelow and sandy, with a few shrubs of
bay cedar, and from their prominent position are of great assistance. In taking
this channel, bring the Little Water Kay between the southern two, bearing
W. by S. until the Queen Kays are in one : the Deep Blue Cut shows itself, which
it always does very distinctly. When through, haul up for Button Wood Kay, about
N.N. W. 4W., and get into the leading mark before described. The shortest
track is that by Hatchet Kay, but this is intricate in the vicinity of the kay.

“These kays appear to have undergone little change this last century, judging
from an old chart I met with here, published about that time ; nor have any
formed since. The hurricanes of 1813 and 1831 stripped much of the vegeta-
tion, which recovered the next season. A hurricane, in 1827, drove all the ships
on shore at Belize. These three are all that are remembered by the oldest in-
habitants.

Berizn River. ‘In May, 1839, I measured the meridian distance to Pros-
pect Plains under favourable circumstances. From this, it appears, by the wind-
ing of the river, that the first or lower falls are 26 nautic miles above the bridge.
The bank gradually increases in height to the falls, where they are 30 feet, and even
here frequently overflowed after heavy rains. The soil is extremely rich) with
partially cleared plantations, which would raise immense quantities of corn, fruit,
vegetables, and stock, if there was a demand for it. The arrow-root grown here is
very superior.

“ Large ships cannot get to town, from the intricacy of Grennel Channel, without
the aid of steamers; and the anchorage at Gof’ Kay being extremely inconvenient
for obtaining supplies, &c., we have to consider the best route coming in, as that to
the southward of the Zapotilla Kays, the worst part being in, and) approaching
Placentia Narrows. After passing the Seal Kays, hauling up to windward of
Laughing Bird Kay, the advantages of this route are—Ist. More room ; indeed,
enough for large ships to work in. 2nd. Always clear water, and: therefore every
danger seen. 38rd. No current which is strong to the south, along the main,
averaging one knot and a half and two knots, from June to December. The
greater depth of water is certainly an objection, but the stream will generally answer,

are sufficiently detached to prevent mistakes, and serve as useful land-marks,
for before losing sight of the Snake or Seal Kays, Laughing Bird and the outside

can be taken by eye, on referring to an enlarged plan. At night, strike the
bank to the southward of 16° N., and make the East Snake, if the weather is
moderately clear, bearing N.N.W. 4 W., and endeavour to be approaching
Laughing Bird Kay by daylight, and pass in through Victoria Channel, by Quamino
Kay ; from this to Belize, any sized ship may navigate by lead in the night, with
the new chart, and without a pilot.””— Nautical Mag. vol. xi. p. 731.

“ A rock, with only five feet water on it, hitherto unknown, was discovered by
H.M. surveying vessel, Lark, Lieut. Smith, in Placentia Narrows, the channel used
by all merchant vessels proceeding from Belize to the Gulf of Honduras, or the
Southern Rivers of British Yucatan.

‘¢ Its position is one mile from the reef, which forms the east side of the channel,
and one mile and one-third N. } E. (by compass) from the sand bore, when in one
with the eastern part of Scipio Kay, and 43 miles E. 38. from False Point, Placen-
tia. Vessels with a fair wind usually pass far to the westward of it; but when beating
against a head-wind, care should be taken to avoid it, as it is not larger than a ship,
and has 10 and 11 fathoms close round it.”—Nautical Mag. vol. viii. p. 719.

Description of the Eastern Edge of the Main Reefs of Yucatan, from the Zapotilla
Kays to English Kay.

ZAPOTILLA Kays. The southernmost part of these hays is in lat. 16° 5’ N., and
long. 88° 16’ W. At five miles W. S. W. of this South Kay are some dangerous
rocky heads, with only two fathoms on them in lat. 16° 3’ 30’. Therefore, when
rounding these hays, and bound to Belize, within the reefs, you ought to strike the
edge of the bank in lat. 16° N., and run in W. $5S., seven or eight miles from the
outer edge of the bank, and then steer N.N. W. } W., to make the Hast Snake
Kay, which has trees upon it 90 feet high: you may approach this kay to about
three miles, so as to make sure of your distance from it, and then a N. Easterly
course may be steered for Laughing Bird Kay.

From the Zapotilla South Kay the outer edge of the bank runs N.N.E. } E.,
82 miles, to the elbow of the reef, which is five miles S. E. by E. from the Gladden
Kay; the bank is very steep-to the whole distance, not extending more than half a
mile without the reefs, on which the sea breaks very heavily with easterly winds,

About two miles N. N. E. 3 E. from the South Kay is Nicholas Kay, which is
inhabited, and has wells of fresh water on it; between the two last-named kays are
two others, named Hunting Kay and Low Kay.

At 10 miles from the South Kay, in lat. 16° 12’ N., and long. 88° 13’ 30” W., is
Tom Owen’s Kay, which lies near the edge of the reef, and about 400 yards
southward of this kay, is a good channel, with five and six fathoms in it, and full
one-third of a mile broad, and fit for ships of any class. This channel is called
Tom Owen’s Cut: there are some bushes on two small kays on the south side of
this channel; there is also a channel a quarter of a mile north of this kay,
with five fathoms water in it; to the southward of these are other cuts through
the reef, which may be taken by the eye from aloft by those well acquainted.

Ranguana Kay is in lat. 16° 20 N., long. 88° 9’ 20” W. ; it lies 1} mile within the
edge of the bank ; between this kay and Tom Owen’s Kay, are two other good pas-
sages through the reef, with 3} fathoms in them. A small Sandy Kay, named
the North Spot, in lat. 16° 14’ 30” N.; long. 88° 11’ 50”, lies on the south side of
the southernmost of these channels: and Ranguana Kay, bearing N. W. } N.,
two miles, points out the entrance of the northernmost one. Small vessels use any
of these channels they can fetch.

From the elbow of the reef, south-eastward of Gladden Kay, the bank trends
N.N. W. 2 W., 10 miles, and then N. by W., about 10 miles to South Water Kay,
in lat. 16° 49’ N.; this kay is inhabited, and the trees upon it about 60 feet high:
water is to be had on the west side of this kay. In lat. 16° 47’, there is a channel
through the reef, named Ellen’s Cut, with 2} fathoms in it. About five miles north
of this, in lat. 16° 52’ N., is the Tobacco Kay, that cannot well be mistaken, having
a large fig tree, 70 feet high, near its north-east extreme. There is another channel
southward of this kay, named the Tobacco Kay Channel.

From the Tobacco Kay to Columbus Kay the reef trends N. by E. } E. for eight
miles, to lat. 17° N. It thence runs to the northward five miles, forming a small
elbow to Kay Glory. Between the latter kay and the Tobacco Kay is an unbroken
mass of coral rocks, many of the heads appearing high out of the water ; there is
not a passage for the smallest boats the whole distance: The channel between
Glover’s Reef and the Tobacco Kay is 11 miles wide. The breakers on the reef are
very heavy, and the soundings do not extend a quarter of a mile off, so that the lead
gives you no warning. :

From Kay Glory the reef runs N. 3 W., 14 miles to English Kay, in latitude
17° 19’ N., longitude 88° 3’ 30” W., on which is a conspicuous flagstaff, from which
signals are made to Belize. About 2} miles to the southward of the latter kay is
the Samphire Spot, which lies at the edge of the reef, haying deep water close to it ;
and 2} miles southward of the latter spot is Rendezvous Kay. About two miles within

the reef, and westward of the two latter hays, is the Middle Long Kay, extending
north and south 2} miles, off the south point of which is Negro Head, which is very
conspicuous.

Remarks made on the Passage fron Jamatca to the Bay of HonpurRas and
back, by Mr. W. C. Middlemist, Master of H. M. Sloop Helicon, in 1824.

“March 16th, 1824, took our departure, Portland Point bearing N.N.E. } E.,
and Pedro Bluff W.N.W. 4 W.., placing usin latitude 17° 41'N., longitude 77° 7’, and
by Chron. 77° 7’ W. Steered W. 3 S., with a moderate breeze, easterly ; at noon,
on the 17th, observed in 17° 43’, lat. by account, being 17° 44’. We, this 24 hours,
experienced a current westerly of 16 miles. Altered the course to W. by S.; the
wind veering from N.E. to East, the weather beautifully clear, and water re-
markably smooth. At noon, on the 18th, observed in 17° 21’ N. We, this 24
hours, had a set of 12 miles N.W. by W. 3 W. ‘The current in this longitude
(82° 9’ W.) generally sets more to the northward: in latitude of 15° to 16°, in
the same longitude, it sometimes sets nearly north, occasioned (without doubt)
by the set round Cape Gracias a Dios. Altered the course to W.S. W., var. about
7° easterly, fine clear weather and smooth water. At noon, on the 19th, observed
in 16° 33’ N. account 16° 37', experiencing a westerly set of 17 miles. Altered
the course to S. W. by W. 3 W., and at 6 p.m., observed the land about Cape
Cameron, bearing south seven or eight leagues. At 6h. 40m. lat. by the Star Sirius
16° 20’ N. At 9 altered course toW.S.W. Midnight fresh breezes and fine.
Lat. by Polar Star 16° 15’ N., altered the course to W. 3S. At 2h, a.m. observed
the land to the southward, which we supposed to be Cape Delgado. Kept a good
look-out for the Island of Bonacca, but about this time the weather got very
cloudy, with heavy rain and strong breezes. Shortened sail for convoy ; weather
very unsettled till daylight, with constant rain. At 6, on the weather clearing up,
observed the land on both sides, extremes of the Jarboard shore, the main, from
8. W. to S. E.: extremes of the islands of Bonacca and Rattan, or Ruatan, from
N. E.toW. by N. This island may be approached with safety on the north side,
on a tolerably fine night, being high, with no dangers outside of two miles. If
bound westward, and to the north of Rattan, it is advisable to get into the parallel
of from 16° 35’ to 16° 40’, and continue in that till you make the island, which on
the north side is eee endeavour to make it as early in the morning as possible, so
as to give you sufficient time for getting down to the west end of Rattan before

close of day, thereby enabling you to take a good departure for Hat Kay, if bound
northward to Belize. If bound to the bay of Omoa, you may proceed on either

side of these islands; if to the southward, and in the night, give the south end
of Bonacca a berth of about 8 or 10 miles, there being several small kays off
that end, which are surrounded by a shoal: giving it a berth of about 10 or

we observed, in 16°11’ N., the highest part, or Pumpkin Hill, as it is called,

“ From Utilla we hauled in to the S. W., steering by compass S. W. by W. 3 W.,
and soon raised Punta de Sal, which makes at first like an island; indeed you will
not be undeceived until you approach pretty near to it: you will then observe
a very low neck of land adjoining, and which attaches it to the main: behind
which, but apparently at some distance, the land is high. The coast the whole
of the way from Punta Delgado is very high in the back ground; towards the
sea it islow. Having got so far as Punta de Sal, it bearing §.5.W. about 5 miles,
double reefed our topsails, and hauled to the wind on the starboard tack: it is
preferable by far to lying-to: indeed, I would advise a vessel to stand off a
certain distance and in again, keeping good way and complete command, as the
currents hereabout sometimes differ, but generally, I believe, run to the 8. W.
However, to guard against drifting, get well hold of Punta de Sul, which is high
land, and keep sight of it the whole night. In doing so we found no set to the
westward ; and on the contrary, we fetched on standing in, some miles to the east-
ward. Off this point are two or three small kays, which you cannot well perceive
to the eastward. From this toward Omoa, the land at first is low for about 10 or
14 miles, it then rises to very high land again. Omoa lies round a very low point,
but by keeping along shore at about 2 or 24 miles, you will perceive the Castie and
Flagstaff over the low land before you are up with the point, which you may round
at the distance of halfa cable. If entering with a sea breeze, brace sharp up as you
round, and anchor in 5 or 6 fathoms muddy bottom, with good holding ground.
Should you intend to lie any time, it would save trouble by mooring at once, as the-
light winds Gr land breezes are very variable, and from a calm sets in suddenly. On
leaving this, bound to the eastward, you may suit yourself as to time of departure,
but it is preferable to get under way in the evening, and to work up close in shore:
by so doing, you will get the land breeze and be enabled to reach U¢tilla the follow~
ing morning. Should you be favoured with a moon, it is advisable to go between
these islands and the main, as the current sets strong to windward ;—but if, on the
contrary, you intend working between the islands, you will be in a good position.
We found in working through, a current to the eastward, and the third day from
Omoa we reached the island of Bonacca. The wind hanging well to the south, we
stood away to the north and east, and made the Swan Islands, they consist of two
low kays scarcely discernible of a night, let the weather be ever so fine. It is re-
commended by some, to make these tslands in your passage down to the bay, but by
so doing you gain no adyantage, but encounter a great deal of anxiety, when on the
contrary, the making of Bonacca is attended with little or no risk, being high bold
land. In the Helicon, we made, and ran through between the islands during the
night. In the same sloop we likewise hove-to, to ascertain the true position of the
Swan Kays. Wind still hanging to the §. E. stretched off to the N, E. In work-

-ing to windward, we found the current very variable, setting strong to the north-
ward and westward between the latitudes of 17° and 18° N. and in long. from 82° to
84° W. One day we had a set of upwards of 50 miles, decreasing in strength as we
went to the northward ; and when in the latitude of the Grand Cayman, and to the
eastward, we found it setting to the southward and eastward.”

Remarks from the Journals of Mr. Henry Davy, late Master of H.M.S.
Victor, 1829 and 1830.

FROM JAMAICA TO HONDURAS.

February 28th, 1829, at daylight sailed from Port Royal.* Next morning the
South Negril bore N. by E., 7 leagues distant ; steered W. S. W. until in latitude
16° 50’; keeping in that parallel we made the Jsle of Bonacca on the 3d March ;_
found its east end to be in latitude 16° 32° N.; it is mostly high land, and may be
approached without danger. Ruatan is not so high, but hummocky, and makes
like a group of little islands ; the islands off its east end, Barburat and Moratii, are
environed by reefs and kays, and in clear weather the high main land is seen to the
southward,

The Southern Four Kays are situated S. E. by E. 3 E., 40 miles from Belize, on
the south end of an extensive rocky bank, 9 leagues in length, running nearly north
and south, and is very narrow and steep-to; on its north end is a small kay, and a
little to the eastward of it isa sand patch.

The Southern Kays consist of Saddle and Half-Moon Kays, to the N. E., Long
Kay and Hat Kay, to the 8. W.; like all the other shoals in this part of the world,
the bank shows very white, and the pilots are extremely quick in perceiving shoal
water.

Saddle Kay is the northernmost, and is a small rock, with a few trees on it ; itis
called after its form, and lies well on the bank, 1} mile to the north of Half-Meon Kay.

Half-Moon Kay lies on the 8. E. extreme of the bank, and is nearly a mile long,
and covered with trees, whose tops give it a ragged appearance. The lighthouse
stands on the N. E, point of the kay, and is elevated 60 feet from the ground ; it is
painted white, with a flagstaff on its top, and in the day time is a good land mark.
It has a fixed light, which if attended to, is tolerably good. On this kay the pilots
live; there are not many, but they are steady, and appear well acquainted with the
intricate channels leading to Belize. On hoisting the signal and firing a gun or
two, they will immediately put off to the ship. Half-Moon Kay may be approached
boldly to its S. E. and south points, even to within a cable’s length, but be cautious
in nearing the northern part, where are some reefs and hidden dangers. In making
the light by night it will be necessary to lie on and off until daylight, and I re-
commend the following directions: keep the leads going, and pay great attention.
to the bearings of the light ; being on the starboard tack with the usual trade wind ;
that is, from E. N. E. to E. S. E., go about when the light bears to the southward
of W.S. W., and stand on the larboard tack no longer than to bring the light
N. by W. Half-Mcoon Kay is in latitude 17° 12’ N., longitude 37’ 10” east of
Belize (87° 29’ 57” W. of Greenwich.) The north point of Long Kay is about 24
miles from Haif-Moon Kay, being 2 to 3 miles long, and covered with small trees ;
it is on the western side of the bank, and its appearance is long and even. Hat Kay
lies 2 miles to the southward of Long Kay, and is the southernmost on the bank ; it
is very small and low, and the reef which surrounds it is shallow and dangerous,
in many places its depth being less than 6 feet, stretching 3 miles ¢o the southward
of the Kay, and thence forming a northerly sweep which terminates at Half-Moon
Kay. In standing into this bight, if for the purpose of taking shelter from a
norther, be guided by the edge of the shoals, which will be plainly seen from the
rigging ; stand towards the east end of Long Kay, within 14 cable’s length, and
anchor under Half-Moon Kay, with the lighthouse N. E. in 5 fathoms, sand, and
in anchoring veer cable quickly. There is also a temporary anchorage to the S.W.
of Hat Kay, in 5 fathoms, but only to be taken with the trade wind. Leaving
Half-Moon Kay, steer S. W. until clear of Hat Kay Reef, then steer west for
Key Bokel, leaving Glover’s Reef on the larboard hand. ‘This is the usual route
to Belize.

The north end of Glover’s Reef is indicated by two sand patches and discoloured
water ; it lies about 20 miles S. S. W. from Hulf-Moon Kay, and then trends south-

westerly to its south end, on which there are four Kays. This bank is very dangerous
on account of the strong currents which often set over it. The distance from Half-
Moon Kay to Kay Bokel is 20 miles in a circuitous route. In steering to the west-
ward you will first lift the Turneff Kays, and in a little will raise Kay Bokel, which
lies at the south end of Turneff, in latitude 17° 9’ 30". Itis a small bushy round
island, with some cocoa-nut trees on it, and surrounded a sandy beach. This kay
is the stopping place for vessels that cannot reach the Sand Bore before dark ; the
anchorage is to the W. N. W., on hard sand in 4 to 5 fathoms; running along
Turneff there is anchorage off the Third Lagoon from Kay Bokel. Kay Bokel
may be rounded by the eye and lead pretty close; then steer N. W. by N. for
English Kay, which will soon be seen, the distance being only 12 miles.

English Kay is covered with tall trees, has three houses on it, and a flagstaff, 70
feet high, where a jack is hoisted when ships are passing ; it is 13 miles from Belize,
and situated on the south side of the channel, the north side being formed by Goff’s
Kay and the Sand Bore. The Sand Bore is a patch of sand just seen at high water,
and if a vessel should come thus far without a pilot, it will be necessary to round to
and anchor. The anchorage is in 7 to 5 fathoms sand, with Goff’s Kay from N. N. W.
to North. From this place, signals may be made to the town, from which a pilot
will be sent as soon as possible. Except for small craft there is no other way to
Belize but by English Kay, and through the south channel ; the former is the most
direct, and in general use, but the pilotage is very intricate. There are three
channels, the most direct is over the flats or bar, whose depth of water is from 15
to 16 feet; the other two lead through the deep or Gireenhill’s channel, and thence
branch off to Belize ; one just to the eastward of the southern Triangle, called the
Half-Way Channel, and the other to the southward, called the Triangle Channel.
March 5th, at noon we passed over the bar in 2} fathoms, the observed latitude being
17° 23' 30” N.

The Southern Triangle consists of a cluster of small woody kays, on which a few
turtlers reside, and lies 9 miles to the southward of Belize. They are bold-to.

The harbour of Brxizx, is a very secure anchorage, and capable of holding a
number of ships of small burthen, It is formed by banks and kays, and, as before
observed, the pilotage is tedious and intricate.

The town is built on low marshy ground, and is divided by the southern branch of
the river bearing the same name, and connected by a wooden bridge ; its appearance
from the eastward is pleasing, and would lead one to expect more than can be
realized. The finest buildings form the front view; the north branch of the river
is about 3 miles from the town; its entrance is called the Haul Over. Fresh water
may be got 7 or 8 miles up, but the inhabitants preserve it in tanks.

About two cables’ length in front of the bridge is a small island, called Fort George,
which is the artillery station ; its latitude is 17° 29’ 30” N., and longitude 11° 19’ 30”
West of Port Royal, (88° 7' 7" W. of Greenwich.) Abreast of the town it is very
shallow, and boats are obliged to steer for Fort George, and when close to it, pull in
for the wharfs and river. The usual landing-place is at the bridge.

We anchored off the south end of the town, at the distance of one mile, in 3 fathoms,
muddy bottom.

Vessels leaving Belize sail or beat out of that channel, through which the wind
will most favour them, and anchor at the Sand Bore, if they have not sufficient run
for Mauger Kay. While at anchor a boat may be sent to Goff’s Kay and land.
The fish are excellent, and in great abundance. It is advisable to weigh as soon as
possible the next morning, and not to discharge the pilot until up to Mauger Kay.
The Turneff Kays, lying to the westward of the southern Four Kays Bank, corre-
spond in nature and appearance with the other kays of this coast, being low,
woody, and nearly surrounded by reefs: they form a large cluster of islands, and
the bank on which they are situated trends about N. N. E. and 8.8. W., 11 leagues,
its breadth being from 5 to 6 miles, and its nearest distance from the main reefs 5
to 7 miles. The kays form many lagoons, but they are only navigable by boats,
and abound wit turtle and fish. The channels on either side of Turneff are very
deep and clear, and vessels sailing by the western may keep the edge of the bank in
sight, and steer by it. The only anchorage on this bank besides those already

GRACIAS A DIOS TO CAPE CATOCHE, &e. 55

mentioned is to the S. W. of Mauger Kay: this kay is the northernmost on the
bank, and is the usual point of departure for vessels bound to the northward, being
in latitude 17° 87’ 15” N.

The Northern Triangles consist of four kays, situated on an extensive and very
dangerous bank, 16 leagues to the N. N.E. of Turneff’; the largest, called Long Kay,
is on the centre of the bank; there are two on the north end, and the other is on the
south. This bank is about 9 leagues in length, and great care is necessary when near
it; most ships pass to leeward.

The Currents we experienced set strong to the westward between the banks, and
when obstructed, turned to the northward, and took the direction of the coast,
running through the Yucatan Channel from 30 to 60 miles in 24 hours. The nearest
point of St. George’s Kay bears N. E. by E., 8} miles from Fort George. The kay
is in the form of a half-moon, the hollow called Irish Bay being to the westward ;
in the middle is a small islet, and the best anchorage is between it and the south
point. Halfa mile to the northward of the north point is Frenchman’s Kay. There
are about 20 houses on St. George’s Kay, and like those at Belize, they face to the
eastward, and enjoy the force of the sea breeze. The island is low and sandy, with
high cocoa-nut trees, and has a pretty appearance. The bank on which this kay
stands is only fit for small craft, and vessels that load from it anchor in a bight
formed by frontier reefs, from 2 to 3 miles to the S. E.

In the passage from Jamaica to Honduras it is not necessary to make the Swan
Islands, but as their position is well known, and no dangers in their vicinity, I think
it is most advisable to make them. From these islands steer S. W. by W., until in
latitude 16° 50’, and running on that parallel you will make the island of Bonacea.
From Bonacca you may run down to the middle of Ruatan ; however, that must
depend on time and circumstances. Bonacca is high and bold, and should a vessel
make it by night, which is very common, it will be best to shapea direct course from
thence for Half-Moon Kay. At all times of the year this route is to be preferred to
that which leads to the northward of the Four Kays Bank and Turneff, where, from
want of pilots and distinguishing marks, great danger may be incurred,

Vessels bound to Belize, the capital of British Yucatun, generally pass to the
southward of Jamaica. In so doing, it is superfluous to give a particular course to
a person possessed of a chart, as a reference to it will point out the best route to
be taken. In running down, the variation will be found from 7° to 8° E., with a
compass placed on the binnacle, and the ship’s head westerly. The strength of the
lee-current will be soonest met with by crossing the Pedro Bank, as no dangers
exist on its western part with a depth of from 7 to 20 fathoms. Between this bank
and the Swan Islands, and to the westward of them, the general set of the current
is to the N. W. and W. N. W.., varying from half a knot to 24 per hour.*

Masters of vessels, not having chronometers, should be particularly on their
guard against the effect of this current, owing to which so many ships have been
wrecked on the reefs and kays off the main coast of Yucatan ; and it is remark-
able these have frequently happened during a continuance of light winds, when the
reckonings by log have not given more than two-thirds of the whole distance
between Jamaica and this coast. During the season of the Norths it also prevails
at intervals in the same degree, when the body of the lee-set is forced towards the

Vessels bound to Honduras will frequently save time and shorten the distance, in taking a
route south of the Pedro Shoals; but this should only be attempted by the experienced, who
is confident in his position, and well-practised in night observations for latitude by stars or

a person would scarcely believe to exist in an open sea: the first occurred in
December, 1818, when, on making the western part of Rattan, the first land-fall

the latter in November, 1824, during a fresh breeze from N. N. E. The chronometer,
for the first 24 hours, gave 70° difference of longitude westing more than the log,

Former Directions advise strangers to make the Swan Islands, in order to take
fresh departure ; but the objection to this is the uncertainty, or else the loss of

has been variously given. One of the latest authorities places them in 83° 48’ W.;
but whether from celestial observations, or by chronometer from some assumed
meridian, is not stated. Spanish authorities have placed them in longitude 84° 04’,
which is generally allowed to be a little too far west. By chronometers from Port

eastern cliff, as measured by a lead-line, was found to be about 45 feet from the
surface of the sea; and the other parts, covered with small trees and bushes, did
not appear to exceed this: the southern sides are pretty clear, and there is anchor-
age off the west end. ais

Resuming the Directions from Jamaica, it is necessary to pass at a distance of
from 12 to 13 leagues to the northward of the shoals off Cape Gracias a Dios,
particularly during the season of the Norths, and then to gain the parallel of
16° 35’ or 16° 40’, in not less than a degree to the eastward of Bonacca. This track
is recommended to ship masters not possessed of chronometers. In clear weather
Sugar Loaf Hill, on the Mosquitia shore, may be seen at a great distance, and is
a good land-mark, lying about 50 miles to the eastward of Bonacca, from which
island, or Rattan, it is proper to take a departure for Half-Moon Kay.

BONACCA, (the Guanja of Columbus.) The appearance of this island is high
in the centre, and can be seen in moderately clear weather 8 or 9 leagues dis-
tant. In approaching its eastern side, you will come upon a bank in 20 fathoms,
which shoals gradually to 5, joining the reef lying off the north side. This reef
does not extend to a greater distance than 1} mile from the north point of the
island. The position of this point, as ascertained from the mean of numerous ob-
servations of the sun’s meridian altitude, I make in latitude 16° 31’ 20” N.,+ and lon-
gitude by chronometer, from the meridian of Belize, 85° 53’ W.

There is a harbour, or rather an anchorage, sheltered by the surrounding kays,
on its §. E. side, and a small one on the north side, a little to the westward of the
north point, entered by a channel through the reef; but the latter cannot with
safety be attempted without a pilot, or previously buoying the channel, and it is
«pen to northerly winds. In running down, steering W. by S. or W. by S.35.,
you will raise the Island Burburatta, or Barburat, lying W.S. W. from the north
point of Bonacca, 9 or 10 miles distant. 'To the westward of this, Moratta and the
eastern hills of Rattan will next appear.

RUATAN, or RATTAN. This island, at a few leagues’ distance in the offing,
appears in hills, and in very clear weather, the mountains on the main coast are
also seen to the southward of them. The north side of the island is bounded by 4
reef at a distance of 1 or 14 mile from the beach, with some deep channels through
it, but not of a sufficient width to be attempted by square-rigged vessels. On its
south side are several good safe harbours, but of small extent; and the only ones
frequented by shipping are New Port Royal and Calkett’s Hole; the others are
frequented by the Belize Turtlers. Since the evacuation of the island by the English,
Rattan has been uninhabited. The longitudinal position of its S$. W. point, as placed

Remarks on the Directions given to proceed to the Southern Four Kays.

From the Directions ‘formerly published, I extract the following : — ‘‘ Hay-
ing run down to the west end of Ruatan, you should take your departure
thence, in the evening, for the Southern Four Kays: the distance is 22 leagues, and
the course N. W. Continue under easy sail all night, not running more than 15 or
16 leagues till daylight, when you may make sail on the same course, and you will
soon raise the Southern Four Kays.” These instructions (which could not have
been written by a person of common experience in these seas, and, in fact, are only
a copy of the oldest extant, when vessels bound to Belize pursued a track to the
south-eastward of Bonacca and Ruatan, in order to obtain pilots) have often be-
wildered the stranger, and have been the cause of many and serious shipwrecks,
which I shall endeavour to explain. For instance, you leave the S. W. part of
Ruatan in the evening, say 6 p.M., and steer N. W. under easy sail until daylight,
running 15 leagues (and no stranger will exceed this distance through fear.) You
are now 11 or 12 hours, during night, under the influence of the current, which, if
setting to the S. W. or W.S. W., the general set here, your vessel will most as-
suredly be driven upon Glover’s Reef before daylight, the north end of it lying
in 16° 54’ or 55’. Taking the N. W. course, or N. W.2N. true, 45 miles, you
have only made 36 miles’ difference of latitude; whereas the difference of latitude
from the S. W. point of Ruatan to the north point of this reef is 39 miles, besides
allowing for the current. With a view, therefore, to safety, as well as expedition,
the object being to reach Belize the day after leaving Ruatan, I submit the following

DIRECTIONS FROM RUATAN TO THE SOUTHERN Four Kays.

During the sea-breeze season, between the months of March and November,
vessels, after passing Bonacca, ought to run down to the N. E, part of Ruatan, and
make sail at about one-third of the extent of the island from the east end, as the
reefs only lay at a distance of one to one and a half mile from the shore. You can
perceive your drift easier by keeping close in; if during a fresh breeze, 8 p.m. will
be early enough to bear away,* keeping in mind that the shorter the time you are
in running the distance, the smaller will be the drift of your ship from the direct
course. Steer N. W. by W. $ W. by compass, and you may with safety run 55 to
60 miles until daylight, when you may carry sail on the same course, to make
Half-Moon Kay. tis necessary to watch the tendency of the breeze also, which
if inclining to moderate, your sail must be increased, to make good a rate of from
6 to 7 knots an hour; and a night observation for latitude, should the horizon
permit, will apprize you of the northerly or southerly set of the current. A look-
out from the mast-head ought also to be kept after daybreak. Should a southerly
or S. W. current have prevailed during the night, the north part of Glover’s Reef
will first appear, which is easily known by two large white sandy patches: the hays
to the southward will also be in sight, if the weather be clear. On the other hand,
during a northerly or N. E. set,+ you will make the reef to the northward of Ha/f-

Half-Moon Kay is easily known from any other since the erection of the light-
house, which, being painted white, forms an excellent beacon, and has been lately
raised 10 feet higher, the lantern standing about 60 feet above the surface of the
sea. This lighthouse, so useful as a distinguishing mark on the hay, is not to be
depended upon as a light, and cannot be seen many leagues off: I therefore recom-
mend the mariner not to overrun the aforesaid distance, under the idea of seeing it
before daybreak, for fear the current should have set his ship to the northward or
southward, out of sight of it.* Should it happen that a pilot cannot be obtained
from Half-Moon Kay, shape a course to clear the pitch of Hat Kay Reef, being
careful not to get embayed in the bight of the reef with a southerly wind. From
the extremity of the reef, Hat Kay being north of you, the course is W. 3 N., 14
or 15 miles to Kay Bokell. You ean round this small kay a cable’s length off,
keeping the lead going: and during daylight anchor in 4 fathoms, bringing it to
bear about E. $. E. by compass, a quarter to half a mile distant.

Some persons, in giving instructions for Belize, have recommended a track to the
northward of Turneffe, by Maugre Kay,+ during the season of the Norths, This
advice has not been tollowed by any experienced Master in this part, and presents
several objections:—the first is, that it prevents you from obtaining a pilot, so
desirable to a stranger; and the second is, the increase of distance to English Kay.
T will here also remark, that the north winds in this sea generally blow from the
N. W. off the coast of Yucatan, and prevent an approach up the English Channel,
or even an anchorage on the Sand Bore off Goff’s Kay, without a pilot.{ Hazy
weather is common in this season, which prevents an observation for latitude, and
these low hays, and still more dangerous reefs, from being seen, until you approach
them too near. Their uniformity in appearance also renders any description useless.
Under these circumstances, and for these reasons, I would recommend no one to
take a track from Swan Islands by Maugre Kay ; and every seaman is aware that
short departures make the safest tracks; so that at all seasons the one from Bonacca
or Ruatan to Half-Moon Kay is to be preferred.

SOUTHERN FOUR KAYS.—Preyious to giving Directions from Kay Bokell,
it may not be improper to give a short description of the Southern Four Kays,
which are four in number, situated on the southern extremity of a very extensive
reef, steep-to in almost every part, with the exception of two confined anchorages :
one off Half-Moon Kay, and the other to the westward of Hat Kay. The position
of the kays, with the outline of the reefs, as placed on the Chart, (differing widely
from others) are, I presume, sufficiently well delineated for a reef, which ought
never to be approached except during daylight, and with a commanding breeze.
The latitade of the Lighthouse, from one observation only of the sun’s meridian
altitude, by a good sextant, I made 17° 12’ 45”; computing the time with this
latitude and sun’s altitude, the chronometers gave 38’ E. longitude from the meri-
dian of Belize, or 87° 31'W. ‘The rates of the watches had been previously ascer-
tained on leaving Belize, and subsequently on returning there, the elapsed time
being four days only. The mean of some observations taken on ship-board, a few
miles distant from the lighthouse, differs very little from this.

Half-Moon Kay, in its greatest extent, is scarcely three-quarters of a mile, ina
W. by N. and E. by 8. direction, with a small indented white sandy beach to the
southward of the lighthouse, from which it derives its name; and is in height from
10 to 30 feet above the level of the sea, entirely covered with trees and bushes. As

Any further description here of these hays will be unnecessary, with the excep-
tion of Hat Kay, which has been so frequently misrepresented. Before the erection
of the lighthouse, this small kay was a good mark; but from its very diminutive
size, it cannot be distinguished until a near approach to the reef. It is scarcely 100
feet in diameter, and still wears its original appearance in every direction; hence
called Sombrero by the Spaniards. It stands about three miles N. W. from the
S. E. pitch of the reef, protected on all sides from the swell of the sea: it is
covered with a small tree, called bay cedar, which lives to a great age. This may
probably account for the little encroachment made by the ocean: for its present
form and appearance are the same as when first discovered by the Spaniards.

Remarks on anchoring off Half-Moon Kay, Hat Kay, and on the East and
West Sides of Turneffe.

The anchorage off Half-Moon Kay is seldom frequented, except with a pilot on
board, and is of small extent. The next to the westward of Hat Kay is well
sheltered from the swell in sea-breezes, and convenient to anchor on for a night;
and a stranger will find less risk in stopping here, should night have overtaken
him, without a pilot, than in running to Kay Bokell, or in keeping under weigh.
You may anchor in three fathoms after rounding the pitch of the reef. The one on
the S. E. side of Turneffe is the least frequented, and only with a pilot on board
during a North. The next to the N. W. of Kay Bokell is the easiest attained in 4
fathoms, the Kay bearing from E. S. E. to $. E., a quarter to half-a-mile distant:
without this depth, the bank becomes too steep, and in-shore it shoals too suddenly.
It is advisable not to approach these anchorages except under easy sail, with a long
scope of cable ready to veer away, for fear of drifting off the bank out of
soundings. The same observation will apply in general to the Sand Bore, off Goff’s
Kay; in fact, all these anchorages are on a hard sandy bottom, interspersed with
patehes of coral, and requiring daylight to select a clear spot with a hempen cable,
where the water is clear, and the bottom visible to the eye.

TURNEFFE.— Kay Bokell is the southern extremity of this extensive range of
hays, the general direction of which is nearly N. N. E. and $. 8. W., varying in
width from 4 to 5 miles from the eastern to the western side. The hays are very
numerous, and form many lagoons, in some of which the water is deep; but the
creeks and channels leading to them do not afford more than from 4 to 8 feet in
depth. The most extensive one, called Indian Kay, lying on its east side, is sup-
posed, at some remote period, to haye been numerously peopled by the Aborigines :
broken utensils are frequently found on it; and it possesses a sufficient depth of
soil, fit for culture, rarely to be met with on any of the rest. Turneffe is surrounded
by a reef, steep-to, except on its 5. W. and 8. E. sides; the west sides are much
nearer the main reefs than the position shown in former charts. The nearest part
of Turneffe, from English Kay, is there represented to be six leagues; whereas the
true distance is only six miles, or nearly so, and the distance from the edge of
soundings on each side, which are steep-to, does not exceed four miles. Thesame
erroneous distance from Kay Bokell to English Kay, with an error of two points in
the course ““N. W. by W., 22 miles,” has been frequently given, and as often
copied even in late publications: this is surprising in a course and distance so
generally known. A ship, with a very valuable cargo on board, by so steering, got
up a small channel to the southward of Rendezvous Kay, afew years ago, and ran
aground. After getting off, and waiting for some days tor a leading wind, she was
brought out by a pilot to Belize. There is good anchorage off the opening, or
second bogue to the northward of Kay Bokell; and also off the bluff to the
N. N. W. of this hay; but in approaching them, nearly in the direct course, lie
some heads of coral rock, with only 12 to 16 feet water over them, to the north-

Directions from Kay Boxeru. to the ANCHORAGE off Gorr’s Kay, and

From Kay Bokell, English Kay bears by compass N. W., about 11* miles only,
which may be seen from the deck of a vessel in clear weather; and this angle
corresponds with its opposite one, as taken by compass from the ZLook-out on
English Kay. The difference of latitude between the two, from the mean of several
observations, only gives this distance, which corresponds nearly both with the
patent and common log.

A vessel under weigh ought to run off the edge of soundings, and with a sea-
breeze steer N. W. by N.; on this course you will make Goff’s Kay a-head, and
have the channel open between English Kay and the former. To anchor off Goff’s
Kay (commonly called the Sand Bore, ) bring it to bear about N. N. W.3 W., a
quarter of a mile distant, the Kays lying to the northward of it, a little open to the
eastward, and the north point of Long Kay well open to the southward of English
Kay, in five fathoms. You will perceive a small sandy patch to the N. E. of you, a
little above water, at a short distance: English Kay will bear S. W. } W., 14 mile
distant; and the body of Water Kay about N. W. by N., 4 miles distant. Ifa
stranger prefers an anchorage on Water Kay Spit, which is the most desirable, and
much the safest and clearest ground, he must keep nearly midway between the two
Kays, the channel being about half a mile wide here; with the lead going, you
will have 18 or 20 fathoms on entering it, avoiding a spit to the Northward and
N. W. off English Kay. The course, by compass, up the first reach of this
channel, is W. by N. 3 N. Keeping off the 8. E. part of Water Kay Spit, which
is shoal and steep-to in some parts, bringing the eastern part of this kay about
N. by E. or N. N. E., anchor in 43 fathoms, good holding ground. English Kay +
will be 8. E. of you, and further you cannot proceed without a pilot. Should the
weather be clear, the Church Spire at Belize will be seen bearing N.W., about 11
or 12 miles distant.

It is proper further to observe, that the inhabitants of Belize have lately erected
a look-out house on English Kay, with a flagstaff attached to it; and on the ap-
pearance of a vessel, a jack or ensign is hoisted, which signal is answered at the flag-
staff on the Court House at Belize, so that no vessel will remain long at. Water Kay
Spit without a pilot.

BELIZE. “The town of Belize, situated at the mouth of the river of the same
name, was so called after its first discoverer, Waillice, a noted Bucanier, who made
this the place of his retreat. The Spaniards write it Waliz, corresponding to the
English name ; but it subsequently became corrupted into Ballize, or, as it is now
called, Belize.” {

8S. E. to E.S. E.; but they got off without damage: those that commenced heaving
upon their cables, before the water fell to its ordinary level, succeeded without dis-
charging any part of their cargo; others who neglected this trial, when the gale
first began to abate, the water falling rapidly, were obliged to put out the whole of
their cargoes and stores, and with much difficulty got afloat. Another hurri-
cane occurred on June 27, 1831: a strong breeze, with heavy rain, commenced
about mid-day from the westward; it then veered to the S.S. W. about 7 P.M.
with great violence, and continued until midnight. Most of the vessels drove ;
but its greatest effect was felt some leagues north of Belize, where several small
craft and many lives were lost.

Track to the Southward of Belize, with the Names of the different Rivers within the
Possessions of the British.

The track of shipping to the southward of Belize lies between the coast and hays
to the eastward: it may be attempted by a vessel of any draught of water, with a
pilot. The hays, in most places, afford a good shelter from the eastern swell.

The regular sea-breezes generally prevail between the months of March and
September off Belize, and along the coast north of it, and frequently continue
through the night as well as the day: this may, in all probability, be owing to the
low, flat, and marshy country, as the contrary prevails south of the River Sibun,
to the southward of which, as far as the River Dulce, the interior of the country is
mountainous. Along this range of coast the land-winds succeed the sea-breezes as
regularly as in the West India Islands in the same parallel; and between the
months of June and September the land-winds are usually attended with rain,
accompanied by incessant thunder and lightning ; between the months of October
and March, the regular breezes are intercepted by winds from N.W. to S. W.,
which continue without intermission sometimes for three and four weeks, attended
with a high barometer. The names of the different rivers in British Yucatan are
Rio Honde, the south bank being the British boundary line north; to the south of
it are the New River, Northern River or Creek, River Wallice or Belize, Sibun,
Manati, Mullin’s River, North Standing Creek, Sittee River, Southern Standing
Creek, Monkey River, Deep River, Golden Stream, Middle River, Rio Grande,
Moho River, Teemarsh, Sarstoon,+ Cacollo or Cocoalee, and Rio Dulce, besides creeks
