The coast from the Rio St. Joseph to the entrance of the River Dulce, a distance
of nearly 200 miles, is navigated at all seasons of the year by the small open craft of
this country ; it is, in fact, a kind of inland navigation, scarcely to be met with on
any continent, and of the first importance to a commercial nation.

ST. GEORGE'S KAY. The south point of this hay lies from Belize Church
N. 61° E. true, about eight miles distant, and is in extent about three-quarters of
a mile. It is easily recognised at sea by the dwelling-houses built upon it; the
reef, which extends nearly north and south, lies from one to two miles from it.

The leading mark to enter the channel is Ryder’s Bluff, about two ships’ length
open of the south point of the kay, until the pitch of the reef on the starboard hand
is nearly north of you; then haul to the northward, and anchor in 18 feet water,
about half a cable’s length from the reef a-head, the point of which will then bear
about 8. E. by 8. to $. E., half a mile distant, and the south point of the kay
W. by 8. } 5.—N.B. This channel is seldom attempted without a pilot, although
these marks are sufficient to lead a vessel in, clear of danger, by a person the least
acquainted with it; yet it is not advisable for a stranger to attempt it. A small
sunken rock lies at a little distance from the western pitch of the reef, with eight or
‘nine feet water over it; and also a bunk, with 12 feet over it; a little to the S. W.
of the leading mark. Ryder’s Bluff Kay lies about 5 miles W. by N. from the
south point of St. George’s Kay ; it is somewhat higher and rounder in its ap-
pearance than the adjacent ones.

DIRECTIONS ON LEAVING BELIzE.

Vessels bound out from Belize generally carry a pilot as far as Maugre Kay ;
this is the track in the sea-breeze season ; but during north or westerly winds, a
track to the southward of Kay Bokell, and the Southern Four Kays is preferable,
provided you leave Water Kay Spit, or the Sand Bore, with a breeze sufficiently
strong to gain a good offing, before making a stretch to the northward. When the
latter track is taken, it is recommended to Masters of Ships not to attempt
passing the parallel of the Northern Triangles, in the night with an easterly wind,
as the current sets strongly over them, unless they are provided with a good
chronometer, and sure of their easting. Many vessels have been wrecked on those
reefs by this attempt, when their reckonings have placed them upwards of a degree
to windward of them.

In the sea-breeze season, when the former track is followed, it is usual to carry a
pilot as far as Maugre Kay ; and from thence to shape a course so as to go inside of
the Northern Triangles, that is with a leading breeze; but in case of the wind
veering to the northward, a stranger is placed in a situation of some danger, between
reefs on each tack, on nearing which, the lead gives him no warning, When this
occurs during night, short tacks, each way, should be made, under sufficient sail to
insure the vessel staying, with a sharp look-out, and a man at the mast-head. A
reference to the Chart will here be of service, and the distance, as shown in it,
between the reefs, will be found to differ little from the truth. After daylight,
should the wind still continue from the northward, the safest and most prudent
measure is to run theship back to the Sand Bore, or Water Kay Spit, to await a
more favourable slant. Under the circumstances which I have stated, numerous
vessels have been wrecked, after parting with their pilots on the reefs to the north-
ward of St. George’s Kay ; the general set of the current with Northerly and N. E.
winds being in this direction.

Resuming the directions to vessels after parting with their pilots off Maugre
Kay, itis recommended invariably to leave it in the evening at 6 or 8 p.m.: if

with a stiff breeze, not to attempt to run inside of the Triangles during night ;
with a sea-breeze, if it permits, keep as high as N. E., running a distance of 10
or 12 leagues, but not more; before daybreak, rather make a short tack to the
southward. At daylight keep a good look-out for the shoal water from the mast-
head: this is very necessary, as without it you are liable to run aground on the
bank to the S. W. of the South or Sandy Kay, before observing it. This is a small
sandy spot, very little above the surface of the water: off this bank the lead is no
guide, as no bottom is to be found a cable’s length from it. After sighting this part
of the bank, or probably some part further north, which is visible from the deck of
a ship before the Great Kay can be seen, you may shape a course, using your own
judgment, referring to the Chart.

NORTHERN TRIANGLES.* These extensive dangers were called by the
Spaniards El Chinchorro, or the Fishing Net (a very significant name) who appear
to have been more intimate with the danger than with their position or extent;
indeed, there is scarcely a shoal existing on which so large a proportion of vessels,
out of the number trading here, have run aground, or been wrecked upon.
These frequent losses in some degree were owing to their incorrect position
and form, as well as their being placed at too great a distance from the shore of
Ambergris on every chart formerly published, and also to the ignorance of stran-
gers, who were not aware of the strong lee-current generally setting upon them.
These reefs are steep-to in every part, with the exception of the bank in a S. W.
and south direction off the South Kay.

The current between the coast and the Triangles sets regularly with sea-breezes
nearly in the direction of the shore, about two miles an hour; and more to the
eastward, after passing the Northern Kays and Reef, the strength and direction of
which I have never found to deviate much, except during northers.

COZUMEL. This island, like most of the others off this coast, has been strangely
misplaced, and partakes of the same error, in being laid down at much too great
a distance from the shore ; the latitude of the south point, in one of the late charts,
was nearly 13 miles too far south. The position of this point I made from the
mean of observations taken on board ship at noon, when east and west of it, in
latitude 20° 16’ 45” N.; and the longitude, according to the mean of observations
by chronometers, measured from the meridian of Belize, is 86° 55’ W.+ In appear-
ance and height, a few miles distant, it resembles the other parts of the coast,
which may account for the erroneous latitude of the south point, as given by a
stranger, who no doubt had mistaken some other point on the coast for this. The
rocks off this point lie at about a mile‘distant from it, and extend to the first point
N.N. W. of it, half a mile from off-shore ; from hence, and all along the west side;
it is clear of dangers, and can be approached within a quarter of a mile. This side
of the island is distant about 9 or 10 miles from the coast, with a clear channel
between them. The lee-current, or indraught, will sometimes set your ship, with
moderate winds, into this channel: should this occur to a stranger, he need be
under no apprehension even during night, with a look-out, as the current, setting
strongly in the direction of the coast, will favour him much in getting through
during sea-breezes. There is good clear anchorage off the north side, well-sheltered
from the eastern swell ; with this swell, in the sea-breeze season, there are strong
ripplings or overfalls to the northward of the rocks off the north point of the
island, occasioned by the current and swell striking or meeting the edge of sound-
ings: this appearance has often been mistaken for a reef, though the rocks do not
extend above two miles from the point. On its eastern shores are the remains of
some stone buildings, supposed to have existed before the landing of Cortez.’ This
island is uninhabited.

To the N. N. E. of the island lies a bank, over which I passed and sounded upon,
on the 8th of August, 1823: the current at the time was setting strongly to the
northward, and during the previous 24 hours had set N. 18° E., 63 miles, by the

The Kays and Coast of Yucatan, from English Kay to Cape Catoche.

Gorr’s Kay bears from English Kay N. by E.} E., distant 13 mile, between
which is the deep water channel leading to Belize. N. by W.} W. from Goff’s Kay,
distant 12 miles, is St. George’s Kay, hetween which the Water Kay and Drowned
Kays extend nearly 9 miles in the same direction.

Sr. Grorer’s Kay, which may be easily known by the houses upon it, lies
W.35S., 14 miles from the north end of Turneffe ; the reef then runs N. by E. 3 E.,
36 miles to Reef Point, the N. E. point of Ambergris Kay ; about 6 miles south
from the south point of this kay is the north end of Corker Kay, extending south
about 43 miles ; at about one-third from the south end of this kay are two wells of
good water. The next kay to the southward is Chapel Kay, about two miles in
length north and south, and about two miles southward of the latter is Long Kay,
extending nearly north and south about two miles.

At 33 miles N. N. W. from Reef Point there is a small channel with 2} feet
water in it, which separates the north point of Ambergris Kay from the main
land of Yucatan. Off Reef Point a reef commences, and reaches near a mile and
a half from the shore, and runs along the shore to the northward, decreasing gra-
dually at five leagues northward of the point; it is not more than one-third of a
mile wide, and thus continues to latitude 19¢ 2’ N.

AMBERGRIS Kay is about 19 miles long, running N. N. E. and S. S. W., and
about three miles broad ; the coast from the north end of this kay to Hervero or
Smith’s Point runs N. by E. for 70 miles, and ten miles north of the latter is Point
Fuper ; these two points form the north and south points of Spiritu or Shamrock
Bay, which is an inlet of the sea about ten miles wide, with a reef across its en-
trance, with some openings in it that will admit of small vessels.

About nine miles north of Point Fuper is Point Nojou, or Bird Point, at. the
southern entrance of Ascension Bay, and ten miles north of the latter point is Point
Nichaabin, or Allen’s Point, at the northern part of the bay, between which is a
bank running the whole distance, with from 12 to 23 fathoms on it ; within this are
a number of kays and reefs stretching nearly across the entrance of the bay, leaving
a few passages between them for boats or small vessels.

From Point Nichaabin the bank continues to run to the northward for about
seven miles, with ten fathoms on it, and runs out nearly two miles from the land,
when it terminates at Boca de Pail, or Blossoms Point, where a reef of rocks com-
mences skirting the shore as far north as latitude 20° 0’ N.

Yuan or Kitpripe Cuirrs lie N. 3 W., 23 miles from Nichaabin, and are very
remarkable, being the only cliffs on the coast ; they extend nearly three miles to
the northward. On this cliff is a emarkable stone building, resembling the turret
of a castle, and stands about 80 feet high, and serves for a good landmark ; its lat.
is in 20° 12’ N., long. 87° 26’ West.

From Yuan Cliffs to Hut Point the land trends nearly N. E. by N., 40 miles,
bordered by a reet which lies close in, the channel between this part and Cozumel
being only nine miles wide. Abreast of the N. W. part of the island, on the main
land, are two remarkable square stone buildings in ruins, situated at the distance of
four and five leagues 8. W. by S. from Hut Point.

Hut Point is in lat. 20° 43’ N.; the coast then trends N. N. E. for 22 miles to
Point Nisue, the south point of Cancon Island; this part of the coast is bordered
by a reef at the distance of a mile from the shore, with openings through it for
boats, but the bank of soundings extends from two to three miles from the land,

with from 18 to 23 fathoms on it. Here the Great Bank of Yucatan may be said
to commence.

Cancon Isianp is seven miles in length and very narrow, running N. 3 E. and
S. 3 W., between which and the main is a lagoon, with only about three feet water
in it; there is a narrow passage into the lagoon at the south end of the island; off
this point of the island is a reef extending above half a mile; the current here runs
very strong to the northward, often causing strong ripplings. The island is bold-to
all along the east side; near the north end of the island are wells of fresh water, to
the southward of which are some remarkable sand-hills.

Maver or Woman’s Isuanp. The S. E. point of this island lies N. N. E.,
four miles from the north end of Cancon ; it thence extends four miles N. W. by N.,
and is about half a mile broad. On the S. E. end of this island is a turret, ren-
dered very conspicuous from there being no trees near it; it lies in lat. 21° 1220’ N.
There is very good shelter in the harbour between this and Cancon, with the turret
bearing E. S. E., about three miles, in three or four fathoms, carefully avoiding by
eye the Becket Rock which lies in mid-channel, and the sand-bores on the west
side. This is a very good harbour with northerly winds. The Becket Rock dries
about two feet at low water. There is a passage for vessels within Maugre Island,
with twelve feet water in it for eight miles, where there is an outlet to the south-
ward of Blanquilla, with five fathoms water in it. From the north point of Maugre
Island a reef of rocks extends N. by W., three miles, the largest of which is nearest
the island, and named Anvil Rock. From the middle of Maugre Island the
bank of soundings extends to the eastward 10 miles, with from 9 to 20 fathoms
on it.

MauveGre Harzsovur. When bound into this harbour, pass one mile to the
southward of the south end of the island, and bring the north extreme of the white
sand cliffs, which you will see on the main land, to bear W. by N., and run in
that direction until nearly midway between the white cliffs before mentioned and
the end of the Island, or when the north end of the Island and Anvil Rock bears
N. 3 W.; you may then haul up for it, and anchor in 4 or 3} fathoms, with the
south end of the Island bearing E. by S. or E. S. E., well sheltered. By steering
the above-mentioned courses you will avoid the coral patches, which lie west, 13
mile from the south point of the island, and also the bank, which runs N. N. W.
from these patches, with only 10, 11, and 12 feet on it. Northward of this bank
there are from 33 to 4} fathoms for five miles within the island and reef, all the
way to the outlet, three miles N. N. W. of Anvil Rock.

Contoy. N. by W. 3 W., 12 miles from the north end of Maugre Island, lies
the south end of Contoy ; it thence extends N. by W. } W.., five miles, and is very
narrow. A reef of rocks, always above water, runs off from the south end of the
island S. by E., for six or seven miles, and a spit runs off from the north end
N. by W., for three miles, having from 23 to 34 fathoms on it. There is very good
anchorage to the westward of this spit, in four or five fathoms, clear sand, which
may be safely taken from March to October: there is a sand hill near the south
end 27 feet high. The north end of the island is formed of low black rocks ; there
are some trees near this 35 feet high, and also some rounding hillocks, from 60 to
80 feet high. The north point of Contoy is in lat. 21° 32’ N., long. 86° 49’ W.,
and is generally mistaken for Cape Catoche, which lies 16 miles W. 3 N. from it.
About eight miles westward of Contoy, on the main, is a large stone building like a
church, which, although in ruins, has stood, and probably will stand for ages, as a
conspicuous landmark tor this celebrated Cape.

Remarks and Rerrections on NayieatTine off the Coast between CarTHa-
GENA and Cark CatocuEr, and generally in Navigating from LEEWARD to
WINDWARD in the CARIBBEAN SEA.—(From the Derrotero.)

We have said, that between Carthagena and Nicaragua, there is a change of
wind, which comes from the westward in the months from July to January, and
which does not extend out further than the parallel of 123° or 18° of latitude. We
have also said, that, in general, the currents on this coast follow the direction of the

{Parr IV.] K

66

winds; and we have also inculcated the necessity there is of making a land-fall at
some part to windward of your port of destination, in all places where the wind
blows constantly from a determined point of the horizon. Therefore, bearing all
this in remembrance, it will naturally occur to your consideration, that in order to
navigate from Carthagena to any part of the coast situated to the westward, in the
season of the breezes, it is only necessary to shape a direct course, and without more
care than is requisite to allow for any errors in the run, by keeping sufficiently to
windward. Also in getting from Carthagena to the westward in the season of
the Vendavalés, or rainy season, it will be requisite to run up to the parallel of
123° or 13° of latitude, in order to fall in with the breezes, so that with them you
may run down the necessary longitude; when this is done, shape a course to
the southward to make the port of destination, but take care to make your land-
fall to windward of it; that is, further to the westward. This advice contains all
that can be said on this head, without descending to a minute detail, which is not
necessary ; we shall therefore only add, that in general practice, it will be sufficient
to make the longitude of the Escudo de Veragua, in order to make the west point of
Porto Bello, and to enter that harbour with safety.

These observations will also apply to the case of those making a passage from the
westward to Carthagena: thus, during the season of the Vendavalés, or rainy
season, a direct course ought to be made; so in the time of the breezes it will be
necessary to increase the latitude, even though in higher parallels winds decidedly
free may not be met with, yet, however, winds from the N. W. quarter may be
taken advantage of, which, at that season, are frequent off the Mosquitia Coast ;
to this may be added, that further out from the proximities of that coast, the breezes
diminish in force, and the currents in strength. We may here remark, that, on the
meridian of Hseudo de Veragua, and in the vicinity of that island, the NMorths from
the Mosquitia Coast are felt, and in such force sometimes as to render it necessary
to lie-to: hence arises the knowledge, that if with the breezes a ship takes the star-
board tack, whether sailing from Darien, or Porto Bello, it will conduct her into
parallels, where the winds from the N. W. quarter are more frequent, and with
which, on the larboard tack, the harbour of Carthagena may be reached with con-
venience, and inashort time. It certainly does not appear correct to prescribe
rules in cases that have not been as yet sufficiently experienced ; but we are fully
persuaded that such is the practice which ought to be followed, and so perseveringly,
that, -as we think, the starboard tack should be prolonged even to the length
of getting into soundings off the Mosquitia Coast, for ascertaining your situation
on it; whence, by taking a departure thence, and making for the island of Sé.
Andrew, or of Providence, you may, from either of them, fetch Carthagena on one
board ; or even, if that could not be done in one stretch, it may be accomplished in
avery few days. We know that this was done by Captain Don Manuel de Castillo,
who, having the brigantine Alerta under his command dismasted, in January, 1805,
while employed in an expedition for the purpose of ascertaining the exact positions
of the frontier shoals off the Mosquitia Coast, got up to the island of St. Catalina.
He there raised a jury-mast in lieu of his main-mast, sailed again in the beginning of
February, and made the Rosario Islands on the 8th of the same month ; so that he
made the passage in less than eight days, and this being done in the month of
February, shows clearly that the winds are sufficiently free for shaping a course.

SAILING DIRECTIONS FROM

We have nothing further to add to what we have already said in the description
of this coast, and therefore shall only say that to make St. Juan de Nicaragua, it
is necessary to be very sure of your latitude, and that, at all seasons, it is better to
make the land to the north, than to the south of it.

With respect to the Mosquitia Coast, and its frontier sea, we shall observe, that
prudence advises the navigator not to risk himself in the tract comprized between
the parallels of the south end of Providence and St. Catalina, and the north ex-
tremity of the Baxo Nuevo, or New Shoal; and also between the eastern meridian
of that shoal, and the western meridian of the Mosquitia Kays; because there are
within these limits many shoals, and there would be great risk of falling in with
some of them.

Those who sail from Carthagena, will always be able to pass to windward of the
eastern banks ; but those from parts further to the westward, who have to navigate
to the northward, for instance, those who sail from Darien, or Porto Bello, will be

GRACIAS A DIOS TO CAPE CATOCHE, &c. 67

obliged to proceed by the channel of the coast, to double Cape Gracias a Dios, and
get to the westward of the Vivorillus, whence they will be able to shape the courses
necessary to make Cuba. The navigation of this channel is perfectly safe, as we
have before said, for the lead is an infallible guide through it, in all weathers and
under all cireumstances.

From what has been said, it may be deduced, that in proceeding to any point on
the Mosquitia Coast, you should avoid getting among the frontier shoals of it; and
to go to it, it is necessary to proceed either by the south or north, as may best suit
for the point of destination and situation of the ship. To go to it by the south, you
ought to get soundings off it, in the parallel of the Corn Islands, a little more or
less; and having once ascertained your situation on the soundings, you have only
to direct yourself on them to your point of destination, bearing in mind what has
been pointed out in the description.

To go to this coast by the north, it is necessary to approach the shore of Black
River, by the meridian of Brewer’s Lagoon, in order to be clear of the Caxones and
Vivorillas, which, being steep-to, are very dangerous. To make the land-fall with
certainty, it is advisable to get a sight of the Swan Islands ; and from thence, with
a south course, you will fetch the coast on the meridian just mentioned. In making
the coast, whether the Swan Islands have or have not been seen, if you are satisfied
as to your longitude, and are certain of being to the westward of the Cazones and
Vivorillas, you have nothing more to attend to than the lead ; for as we have shown
in the description of this coast, it has such regular soundings, and the depth of water
decreases so gradually, that it is impossible, if the lead. be kept going, to be lost
from touching the ground unexpectedly. Being once on soundings, you have only
to place yourself in a suitable depth for running eastward, for doubling Cape
Gracias a Dios in the manner that we have stated in the description, to which we
have nothing to add.

If you are bound to the Black River, it will be also proper to make the Swan
Tslands, and to steer thence S.S. W. The currents on this coast are very uncertain,
though generally with the breeze they set to the N. W., and therefore you some-
times cannot make the land at the desired point; but the difference cannot be great,
so that the error may be easily corrected. Those who visit this coast, at the first
time, may be in doubt as to the exact part of it on which they find themselves,
from not knowing the land; but there can be no reason for doubt, because the
land from Brewer’s Lagoon to the eastward is all low, and, on the contrary, to the
westward it is very high.

In navigating to the westward for Porto Caballo, Omoa, or the Gulf of Honduras,
it is necessary to pass to the southward of Ruatan, or Rattan, and to the northward
of Utilla ; and having got sight of the latter, to steer in for the land about Point
Sal, as we have said in the description, in order to run along the coast from it to
the port of destination; but great attention must be paid to the state of the
weather in the season of the storms, so as to proportion it in such a manner as to
have the steady breeze to sail from Ruatan to Porto Caballo or Omoa.

If these precautions are necessary for entering the gulf, they are equally so for
going out of it; and this navigation ought to be made by taking the utmost ad-
vantage of the land-breeze, and by working to windward with the regular breeze
as far as Omoa or Port Cavallo. From Omoa, if it be in the season of the regular
breezes, that is, from March to the end of August, you ought to work to windward
in the proximity of the coast, as far as the meridian of Barburata, managing so
as to stand off shore about 8 or 9 leagues, in order to tack and stand in shore
about noon, which is the hour the sea breeze sets in, and keep on until the be-
ginning of the night; about this time the land wind blows, and affords an oppor-
tunity of again standing off shore. By this mode, both tacks are made within
eight points or less, with evident advantage. Great care ought to be taken in this
navigation, but which we need hardly remark, as a bare inspection of the chart
will show the necessity of it. In the season of the Norths, when you think the
weather settled, you ought to leave Omoa ata time so as to reach Ruatan while
the weather is good. In this season the land winds blow during the whole of
the night, and the greater part of the day, and will admit of courses being steered
to the eastward ; but, in the first place, you ought to steer to the N. E., for the

from N.E. to North, to continue on the starboard tack to the westward; but
you must change the tack to E.S. E. or East, that you may not approximate
too much to the Chincorra, or the island of Cozumel, which might prove dan-
gerous.

If bound to the River Belize, on the coast of Bacalar, it will be necessary to
enter, either by what is called the South Channel, or by that of English Kay; the
first is the best for large ships, because it has the deepest water, although it is the
longest. By whichever of these channels you may intend to enter, when approach-
ing from the open sea, it is advisable to get sight of Ruatan first, in order to take a
fresh departure, and thereby ensure a correct land fall.

To conclude this subject, we shall say something of the route, which it is ad-
visable to pursue from the western meridian of Cuba to any point on the coasts of the
Caribbean Sea. That which has hitherto been generally followed, was to run out
by the Gulf or Strait of Florida, and steer for high parallels of latitude, in order to
gain sufficient longitude; then to run down to the south, and make the land at the
Lesser or Greater Antilles, or the coast of Cumana and Caraccas, in the same manner
as vessels coming from Europe. This navigation is undoubtedly very good and well
considered, but it has been taken so, generally, without meditating on the advan-
tages of the navigation within the Caribbean Sea, not only for shortening the dis-
tance, but also for its safety.

To proceed to the subject with certainty, it is necessary to remember, that in
the season of the Norths, there is much facility in navigating to the eastward by
the south side of Cuba, Hayti or St. Domingo, and Porto Rico ; and, as pointed
out, you will not run so much risk in pursuing this route as you would going by the
North, in passing through the Gulf’ of Florida; for although within this channel,
with skilful navigation, there is no great risk, still before entering-there will be,
if the wind is such as to make the coast of Cuba a lee shore, which is a navigation
exceedingly dangerous and exposed. With such winds also, the navigation of
the Gulf of Florida is much obstructed ; while on the contrary, that within the
Caribbean Sea is facilitated and shortened; adding to this the increased distance
by the first route, renders it extremely probable, that much shorter passages may
be effected by the second. It is true, that to the eastward of the eastern meridian
of Cuba, the Norths are neither frequent nor lasting, and therefore cannot be much
calculated on; all the longitude that remains to the meridian of your destination,
must be gained on a bow-line; but if your vessel sails moderately well, by availing
yourself of the daily variations of the breeze, you may make very advantageous
boards’ or tacks, and by working between the parallels of 15° and 16°, where the
currents have little or no effect, the longitude required may be gained with much
facility.

From March to June is the time when it is advisable to run out by the Gulf of
Florida ; for in these months the breezes are very strong, especially on the coast of
Terra Firma, from St. Juan de Guia to leeward, and however well a ship may be
equipped, some damage must be expected.

In the other months, during which the breezes are moderate or manageable, the
land winds more fresh and certain, and the currents very weak, the navigation
within seems preferable; because by keeping along near the main land, the
hurricanes will be avoided ; which circumstance alone is enough to induce one to
take this determination ; but, in this case, it is necessary, so soon as you can pass
to windward of the frontier shoals of the Mosquitia shore, to stretch across towards
the main land, and navigate to windward along by it.

From what has been stated, it results that, in the time of the moderate breezes and
of the Norths, that is, from July to March, it is advisable to preter the route within :

and in that of the strong breezes, or from March to June, the route without; by
running through the Gulf of Florida.

In order to illustrate this subject by practical example, we will cite the inner route
performed by Don Josef Primo de Ribera, a Lieutenant of the Spanish Navy, who
commanded a merchant ship from Vera Cruz to La Guayra, in January, 1803 ; and
the route without, made in March, 1795, by a squadron under the command of
Lieut. Gen. Don Gabriel de Aristizabal, which presents a fair comparison, and will
serve as a guide to those who hereafter may take the same route.

Don Josef Primo de Ribera sailed from Vera Cruz on the 30th of December, 1803,
and at night, on the 7th of January following, he found himself 10 miles to the
westward of Cape Corrientes, in the island of Cuba; from this point he continued
working to windward on both tacks, and taking advantage of the variations of the
breeze until the 10th, when a North wind set in, with which he shaped a course,
and passed to the southward of the Bivora Bank, or Pedro Shoals, having pre-
viously made the Great Cayman. On the evening of the 11th, the North wind
terminated, and he was then in latitude 16° 3’ N., and longitude 78° 17’ W. from
Greenwich. Until the 19th, he worked to windward between the parallels of
16° and 17°, on which day, having obtained good observations for the longitude,
which placed him in 74° 40’, he determined upon crossing over to the main coast,
which he did; and at the close of day on the 22d, got sight of the (Sterra Nevada)
snowy mountains of Santa Martha, bearing 8. 19° W. (true), and on the fol-
lowing day he was off Cape la Vela. Thence he persevered in working to windward ;
but being unable to get through the channel between Orua and the coast of Pa-
raguana, he passed on the outside, and stretched well off, to avoid the currents in the
vicinity of that strait; he then succeeded in fetching, on the other tack, in be-
tween Orua and Curazao, and then continued beating up, between these islands
and the main land, to La Guayra, which was his port of destination, and in which
he anchored on the 4th of February, at eight o’clock in the morning: thus making
his passage from Cape Corrientes in 27 days.

The Squadron of General Aristizabal sailed from Havanna on the 27th of
February, 1795. On the 5th of March, they found themselves clear of the Gulf
of Florida, and continued between the parallels of 28° and 29°, until the 14th
of the same month ; when finding they were in longitude 60° 17’ west of Greenwich
they began to run down the latitude on about aS. S. E. course, until the 21st,
when being in latitude 19° and longitude 54° 17’, the course was altered to
S.S. W., with which, on the 27th, they were in latitude 11°, and longitude 57° 17’,
from whence they steered west, and anchored at Trinidad, on the 29th of March,
having performed the voyage in 30 days.

By these reflections, we do not pretend to persuade navigators that the route
within the Caribbean Sea is the shortest; but our object is to awaken attention to
the subject; which, as it has been hitherto doubtful, may, by successive practical
experience, be satisfactorily illustrated.

THE COAST OF THE GULF OF MEXICO, FROM CAPE
CATOCHE, TO THE BAY OF SAN BERNARDO.

The MEXICAN BAY, or GULF of MEXICO, is an immense GULF, sur-
rounded or shut up on all parts, except on the south-east. The island of Cuba,
which advances considerably to the west, forms with this opening two strazts or
passages ; one on the south with Cape Catoche, by which a communication 1s
opened between the Gulf and the Caribbean Sea; and the other on the east with
the south coast of Florida, through which it communicates with the Atlantic
Ocean ; so that these are the only two passages leading in to the Mexican Gulf.
That to the east, which is called the Bahama Channel, or Gulf of Florida, we have
already treated with sufficient detail to render the navigation of it secure, in the
Second Part of this work. Of the southern passage. but little requires to be said,

CAPE CATOCHE* has two islets along its shore, which extend off scarcely a
mile from it, and form, with Jolvas Island, two mouths, which are called Jonjon
and Nueva, fit only for canoes. From the said Cape to the westward, the coast
bends somewhat to the southward, for a distance 18 miles, to the west end of
Jolvas Island, which forms the Bocas, or Mouths of Conil. This eoast is foul, for a
rocky bank, with little water on it, extends off 23 miles; and on the meridian of
Cape Catoche, which is situated in latitude 21° 35’ 40” N., and longitude 87° 6’ W.,
are several shoals or ridges, which extend as far north as 21° 45’ N., having from
2% to 3% fathoms upon them, the outer one having 33, called the Green Ridge. Be-
tween the Island of Jolas and the coast a lake is formed, which is obstructed by
various islets and grassy spots, and is fit for small canoes only. Six miles north of
the western end of the Island of Jolvas is the Privateer Shoal, of two fathoms.

From the Bocas of Conil, the coast trends W. } N., 33 miles to the meridian of
88° W., thence W. by 8. 3 S., 35 miles to Jungle Point, whence it follows S. W.
by W. 3 W., for 23 miles to the meridian of 89°, turning W. 3S. for 12 miles;
thence W. by S. 3 S., 35 miles; and S. W. by W. 3 W., 16 miles, past Sisal to
Point Piedras, and 8. W., 17 miles to Point Palma, on the parallel of 21°, and
meridian of 90° 21’. The whole of this north coast of Yucatan is low and sandy,
with a few hills and clumps of trees near the coast; the approach to it is clean,
having, to the westward of Jolvas Island, as far as Sisul, not less than 3 or
23 fathoms, within two miles of the shore.

From Jungle Point, which has some trees upon it, 170 feet high, at the distance
of 46 miles, is the Vigia, or Look-out of Ygil; in the intermediate space are the
Bocas of Silan, and the Vigias of Silan, Santa Clara, and Telchaac; at the first and
last, water may be procured.

From the Vigia of Ygil to Mount Note-perderas, (do not lose yourself,) at the
foot of which is Point Piedras ; on the intermediate coast are the Vigias of Chujulu,
Chuburna, and, finally, the Castle of Sisal. All this coast from Cape Catoche, is
very low, with shallow water, and without any more remarkable objects than
Monte Cuyo, at the River Lagartos, which is a heap of stones, raised by the Indians
for a mark, and is known by its resemblance to the figure of a hat; and the little
woody hills of Angostura, Yaleopo, and Puerto de Mar, which are situated between
the Vigia of the River Lagartos, and the Monte Cuyo. Neither of these Vigias, nor
the Monte Cuyo, nor the Castle of Sisal, can be seen farther off the shore than
from the depth of 53 fathoms water. From the Cuyo to Chuburna, you may anchor
without risk, in from four fathoms outward, but not nearer the land, on account of
various stones, shoals, and banks of sand, and rocks, very difficult to be ascertained
by the lead, because they are covered with a coat of sand ; besides the depth suddenly
diminishes upon them, and therefore there is great danger of getting aground, and
of being lost.

These Vigias, or Look-outs, are no more than towers of wood, in which watchmen
are placed to dicover vessels. The Castle of Sisal is built close to the edge of the
sea; and near it there is a town, with the houses covered with thatch, and ware-
houses to deposit articles of merchandize brought hither in coasting vessels, to be
conveyed to Merida, and other inland parts of this province; and also for articles

Upon Point Piedras, as before said, there is a little Mount, named Note-perderas,
which served for a.good mark to know it by, and which might formerly be seen
from the Sisal Bank, or at 14 miles distant ; but the trees are now decaying, and
are hardly to be distinguished. From this point the coast rounds about to the
S. Westward for the distance of 17 miles, to Point Palma, and forms the N. W.
front of the Peninsula of Yucatan ; this coast, as well as the preceding, may be seen
well from the depth of 5} fathoms, and is commonly called the Palmares, because,
among the wood, with which it is covered, many Palmitos are seen, though there
are none on the other parts of this coast of which we are speaking; and no one
ought to anchor on it, for the bottom is of stones, covered with a thin coat of sand,
which deceives the lead. Three miles to the southward of Point Palma are some
trees, about 90 feet high.

From POINT PALMA the coast continues to the South, a distance of 30
miles, to Las Bocas, or the Mouths, which are two little inlets or entrances
in the coast, in front of which, and very near to them, are two very little
islets. From the Bocas the coast continues to the south, inclining somewhat
to the west, a distance of 15 miles, to Jaina, which is another inlet of the
coast, forming the mouth of a river, in front of which is another little islet;
and midway between the Bocas and Jaina there is another little islet, called Isle
de Piedras.

From Jaina the coast continues with some inclination to the west, a distance of
21 miles to the River of St. Francisco, which is 4} miles to the N. Eastward of
Campeche, and which is the principal, and only point of commerce on this coast.

The coast between Point Palma and the River St. Francisco, cannot be seen
beyond three or four fathoms depth of water; and then it appears to the view, with
various breaks, like very low kays; all of it is remarkably shallow and clean, so
that with the lead in hand there is not the least risk on the whole of it.

From the River of St. Francisco, the coast continues to the (S. W.) 8. W. 2S., a
distance of 12 miles, to Point Morros, on which the first thing descried is the Castle
of San Josef, afterwards the City of Campeche ; to it follows the Castle of St. Miguel,
next to it the Town of Lerma; and after it a point of the coast projecting somewhat
into the sea, called Point Martin, and the next to it is Point Morros. All this
front of the coast, which forms the anchorage of Campeche, may be plainly seen
from the depth of 43 fathoms; for it is so shallow, that 33 fathoms will be found
at 15 miles from the land, and 2} fathoms at four miles fromit. Consequently this
anchorage needs no pilot, nor any particular advice for taking it; for when you
get in the depth suitable for the vessel’s draught of water, you may drop your
anchor, as if in the midst of the ocean. Hence results great labour in loading and
discharging cargoes ; for even those vessels that can approach nearest to the land,
remain at four miles distance from it; and to diminish this labour, and to manage
so that the lighters, or launches, may go to, and return from the shore under sail,
they anchor to the west of the tower. In this anchorage, although open to the
winds from North and N. W., which, in their season, blow with great force, there is
nothing to fear, for they do not raise any sea of consequence, and therefore vessels
remain at anchor with sufficient security.

Off Point Morros, about west, and a little more tothe south, the depth is rather
greater, as according to report there are 33 fathoms at a league from the land ;
this information, if not positive, is at least probable, and those whose object is to
keep so close to the shore as is practicable for the purpose of wooding and
watering, should endeavour to reach this part of the anchorage, near which, a
little to the south, is the Town of Champoton, where both articles may be easily
procured.

From POINT MORROS the coast trends (S. 25° W.) S. by W. 3 W., a distance
of 36 miles, to the north point of Javenal, from which the coast begins to round
itself to (S. 60° W.) S. W. 3 W. for a distance of 61 miles to Point Xicalango,
which is the western extremity of the Lagoon of Terminos. This lagoon is a great
bay, whose mouth is about 36 miles wide, and is about 25 miles deep ; between the
two points which form the mouth, are two islands, which shelter it; the western-

THE SouNDINGS OR BAanx or CAMPECHE.

The Bank of Campeche, is a great shoal, which extends from the north coast of
Yucatan, almost as far as the 24th degree of latitude, and from the coast of Cam-
peche, westward, as far as the meridian of the River Chiltepec. The depths, as well as
the quality of the soundings on it, are so very irregular, as to render it impossible
to ascertain your situation on it by the lead; a single glance at the chart will verify
this assertion. Nevertheless, the soundings from the depth of 18 fathoms towards
the shore, are sufficiently regular for navigating thereby in safety ; for having
caught that depth, which will be found at 10 or 12 leagues trom the coast, it follows
the direction of the land as far as N. W. of Point Piedras, where it suddenly

decreases two fathoms. A similar regularity is remarked in all the soundings,
from the depth of 18 fathoms to 4, in all of which there will be found the same
diminution at the N. W. of Point Piedras, caused, no doubt, by a spit or ledge of
rocks that stretches off from the point, for the soundings in that direction are always
upon flat stones. From four fathoms to the shore, on all that part of the coast
comprehended between the Cuyo at the River Lagarios and the Vigia, or Look-out
Tower of Chuburna, we have already said that there are various stones, and shoals
most dangerous to navigation.

The quality of the bottom, from 18 fathoms towards the shore, is not marked by
any degree of regularity ; for sometimes it is grey sand, with gravel; at others,
gravel only ; and at others, sand with shells and coral: thus it alternates until to
the N. W. of Point Piedras, where, as we have said, the soundings are on stones
or rocks. This is, however, a very good mark for knowing a vessel’s situation by,
so as to shape a course with security to pass between the Triangles and the Baja
Nuevo, or New Shoal, which is the channel that ought to be preferred for running
off the bank on its west side, as will be presently explained. But a still better
guide for ascertaining the ship’s position, is by the course which is necessary to
steer, in order to preserve the depth of 18 fathoms; for, if you keep in that depth,
steering W. by S., it is a proof of being between the meridians of the Cuyo of
Lagartos and Point Piedras, but if on that course the depth be augmented, and it
becomes necessary to change it to W. S. W. and S. W., itis a proof that you have
passed the meridian of Point Piedras, and that you are off the N. W. front of the
coast, or between Point Piedras and Point Palma; and, finally, if in order to
keep in the same depth, it becomes necessary to steer south, there can be no doubt
of having passed, or at least are abreast of, or on the parallel of, Palma.
What has been just said of the depth of 18 fathoms applies also to any smaller depth
on this coast.

But respecting the rest of the soundings from 18 to 20 fathoms, into greater
depths, there is no regularity whatever, either in the depth of water or quality of
the bottom, especially towards the north part of the bank; and this necessarily
follows, for it is sown with shoals most dangerous to navigation, of which we shall
speak in regular order.

The SISAL SHOAL was sought for and found by Captain Don Ciriaco de Cevallos
on quitting the anchorage at Sisal. This officer says, that the least water on it is
two fathoms, according to the traditionary account of the people of the country ;
but he found no less than 17 feet, very closely surrounded on all sides, by 6, 8, and
9 fathoms. Between it and the contiguous shore there is a channel 12 miles wide,
fit for the largest vessels. It is true, when we found 17 feet, we were ignorant of
the state of the tide, which at that time rose from 8 to 4 feet at high water. From
this shoal, or rather depth of 17 feet, Mount Note-perderas (, you shall not lose your-
self) bears 8. 7° E., true, distant 14 miles; and this is the best mark for avoiding it,
either in passing to the northward or southward.

The ALACRAN or ALACRANES.—This shoal extends 14 miles from north to
south, and 11 from east to west. There are near its southern part three islands,
called Perez, Chicha, and Pajaros, with various banks and reefs, more or less above
the surface of the water. On the south side there is a harbour formed between the
reefs, which extend to the south and east from Perez, and those which stretch off
from Pajaros, about a mile to W.S. W. This harbour is secure, and very well
sheltered, having at its mouth from 23 to 6} fathoms, and farther in, from 23 to 7
fathoms. The best anchorage is to the eastward of the middle of Perez, in 6.
fathoms water, on sand and shells, having to the south a rocky bank extending from
the S. W. end of that island, about six cables’ length towards the East and E. S. E.
This Harbour is frequented only by the people of Campeche, who repair thither to
make oil from the fish with which it abounds. By all others this shoal ought to be
carefully avoided: therefore no one should sail from east to west, in the depth of
26 fathoms or more, in its neighbourhood, but should always pass in 18 to 20
fathoms.

The situation given of Port Alacran by Captain Barnett is lat. 22° 23! N., and
long. 89° 40’ W.

The ARCAS are three islets which may be seen at the distance of five miles:

they are the southernmost upon the western edge of these soundings, and lie

the said island (N. W. by W.) N. W. by W. 3 W., rather more than four-tenths of
a mile; and which forms the true channel between that and the western Arca, of
two cables’ length in breadth.

The westernmost island has reefs extending to W. N. W. and W.S. W.,; and at
2 and 1} cable’s length from the north point of the large island, there are three foul
reefs extending westward, the farthest of which is distant 4 cables’ length from the
point.

The S. E. Arca is surrounded by a reef, which is separated from it by a space of
about a cable’s length : this island, with the reefs at the S. E. part of the large one,
form a channel scarcely two cables’ length wide, with a depth of 5 to 15 fathoms,
on sand, stone, and gravel ; by which an entrance to the anchorage may be effected,
in case of necessity, according to the situation of the vessel.

This anchorage is very superior in northerly gales to that of Campeche, and as
there is a sufficient depth of water in it for ships of any class, those who are able to
take advantage of it under such circumstances will find themselves well sheltered
and secure.

OBISPO.—At (N. 40° W.) N. W. 3 W. from the Arcas, distant 7 leagues, there
is a shoal of small extent, called El Obispo, or the Bishop, which is a flat rock with
42 fathoms water on it, and so steep, that 25 fathoms are found close to it; and this
causes the sea to break on it with great violence, therefore it ought at all times to
be given a wide berth.

PLACER NUEVO.—(N. 80° E.) E. N. E. 4 E. from the Obispo, distant 5
leagues, there is a rocky shoal with nine fathoms water oyer it, called the Placer
Nuevo, or New Shoal, of which equal caution must be taken to steer clear of;
and also of a Rocky Head or Cabeza de Piedra, which lies 133 miles 8. W. of the
Arcas, with only one fathom over it.

The TRIANGLE lies 24 miles to the northward of the Obispo: this is composed
of three small islands, of which the two eastern ones are a little more than two
miles distant from each other, but they are connected by reefs. The westernmost
bears from the largest, which is also the easternmost, (N. 75° W.) W. 3 N., distant
rather more than eight miles, and between the former and the middle one there is a
channel six miles wide, with 17 to 30 fathoms water, on sand, gravel, and rock.

From the easternmost island, which has a small islet close to it, a reef extends,
first to the N. N. E. and then to N. W., forming an arch or bow, the end of which
is nearly two miles from the island. The western island has also a reef, extending
a short distance to the north and east.

The soundings in the vicinity of the Triangle are 18 fathoms, on fine sand, at two
miles E. by S. from the larger island; 23 fathoms, on sand, grayel, and rock, at
seven-tenths of a mile; 26 fathoms, sand and clay, at nine-tenths of a mile to the
S. E.; 18 fathoms, gravel, at two cables’ length to the south ; and 19 fathoms from
three to six-tenths of a mile to the south of the reefs which connect the eastern
island to the middle one. To the W.S. W. of the middle island there are 19 fathoms,
on sand and gravel.

BAJA NUEVO, or the New Shoal, is a head of sand, which shows at low water,
with several rocks or stones, which also show a little ; the sea breaks upon it with
ordinary breezes, and it is so steep that there are 25 fathoms at half a mile from its
western head ; and all round it at 13 mile distance there are from 18 to 23 fathoms,

ISLA DE ARENAS.—This island was surveyed by Don Ciriaco de Cevallos, in

ISLAND BERMEJA,—This island, which is placed in all the old charts, is of very
doubtful existence ; the lieutenants of the Spanish navy, Don Miguel Alderete, and
Don Andres Valderrama, in their searches for the Negrillo did not see it: the same
happened to Don Ciriaco de Cevallos, in July, 1804, who purposely searched for it ;
therefore we believe its existence is not true. Nevertheless, we have placed it in
the chart, in latitude 22° 33’, and longitude 85° 5’ west of Cadiz, or 91° 22’ west
of Greenwich, until more elaborate surveys decide whether it exists or not.

The NEGRILLO is a shoal spoken of by all who navigate in these seas, but no
one has been able to give the true situation of it. In the ship of the line San
Julian, commanded by Don Juan Joaquin Moreno, the deposition of the gunner,
Don Manuel Sandoval, was taken, in which he said that, being in the ship of the
line, Buen Consejo, commanded by Don Joaquin Olivares, on his passage from Vera
Cruz to the Havanna, and on the ninth day after sailing from the port, at about
2 p.m., they saw breakers, and that having sent a boat, in which the deponent was
bow-man, to examine the spot, they discovered a rock of about lialf a boat’s length
in extent, and that he held on it with a boat-hook, while others sounded over the
stern with 120 fathoms without finding bottom, and, though they repeated this
with equal diligence, all around the rock, they found the same results. There were
not more than two or three feet water over the rock, and he heard the officers and
pilots of the ship say that it must have been the Negrillo Shoal.

The principal object of the expedition of Alderete and Valderrama, in 1775, was
to search for this shoal, but they were unable to find it, although they eruized for it
in all directions, in the space assigned to it by the old charts. But from the decla-
ration of a seaman who had navigated in the Gulf of Mexico many years, taken at
Vera Cruz, by Don Tomas Ugarte, who says, that going in a private brig, and
having observed, and passed to the westward in the afternoon, they sailed N. W.,
30 or 40 miles, and then lay-to; two hours before day-break, to avoid, as he heard
the captain say, crossing the parallel of the Wegrillo in the dark. At day-light they
found themselves in a channel, formed by two shoals, of about a cable’s length
wide, and without soundings, which the captain said were the N egrillo. From this
information, laying it down in the chart, and allowing the same distance as for the
Alacran, the result is, that the shoal must be in latitude 23° 2’, and longitude
83° 53’ west of Cadiz, (90° 10' west of Greenwich, ) a position certainly out of the
tracks in which Alderete and Valderrama cruized for it; and consequently we are
not surprised at their not finding it.

There is another very confused account of an extensive shoal which was discovered
in the year 1768, in the Calandru Poder de Dios, by the pilot Juan de Hita
Salazar, whose journal was examined at the Havanna hy command of Don Juan
Antonio de la Colina; from this nothing more can be deduced, than that the vessel
sailed from the eastern end of the Campeche Bank, on courses in the N, E, quarter
for the Havanna. On the third day she was in latitude 24° 2’, and about 38
leagues W. by S. from the Tortugas; and then steered on courses in the S. E.
quarter, to make the land of Cuba; at 3 p.m. finding himself on the Campeche
soundings, in 32 fathoms, he steered N. N. E., and increased the depth until noon
on the sixth day, when he observed in latitude 23° 15’, and had 46 fathoms water.
He then steered N. E. with light winds, keeping the same depth until 1h. 30m,
P.M. when he suddenly shoaled to 13 fathoms, on rocky bottom; here he anchored,

and stood N. E. with the lead constantly going: in a short time he got into 54

sand. He then steered eastward to get clear of the shoal, which he conjectured
must be the Negrillo, and in two hours had the depth of 48 fathoms, on sandy

was 23° 28’. From this noon until day-break on the following morning, the depths
were irregular, from 35 to 43 fathoms, on rocky bottom, and then upon sand, with
an increasing depth, so that at noon, on observing in latitude 23° 46’, he had 68
fathoms; and with a N. N. E. course, he preserved the same depth till midnight,
when he found 35 fathoms, on rocky bottom, on which he continued until daylight,
when he had a greater depth, on sandy bottom; as he proceeded the depth in-
creased, and at noon observed in 24° 3’, when he had 106 fathoms on sand, whence
he shaped a course for the Tortugas Soundings, on which he entered without any
new difference in the reckoning.

From all this ambiguous relation, we can only make out, that the soundings
which this vessel ran over, were from the meridian of the Alacranes to the east-
ward; that the edge of the bank extends to 24 degrees of latitude, and that there
are many shoals on it, but very little known, which are very dangerous to navi-
gation.

Since this part of the present work was written, Captain Don Ciriaco Cevallos
has transmitted a declaration made by Don Domingo Casals, Captain of the schooner
Villabonesa, who saw it on Nov. 14th, 1806, at 3 p.m., in latitude 23° 25’, deduced
from the latitude at noon, from a good observation, and longitude 89° 56’ 34” W. of
Greenwich, as deduced from the points of departure from the Campeche Soundings,
and the making of Vera Cruz. He says this shoal is no more than a rock, of a
quarter of a cable in extent, N. E. and S$. W., over which the sea washes, except at
the two extremities, which show a little. These could not be seen before getting
within a cable and a half of them; and within a cable’s length of them, there was
no bottom at 70 fathoms.

Besides these shoals, which are known on the oldest charts, others have been more
recently discovered ; of which we have the following notices.

Don Sebastian Roderiguez de Arias, a Lieutenant of the Spanish royal navy,
Commander of the brig Argus, in a passage from Vera Cruz to the Havanna, on the
llth of July, 1818, at 2 p.m., being in latitude 24° 2’, and longitude 89° 43’ west
from Greenwich, discovered on his beam a breaker, that appeared from his vessel to
be a little shoal of about 14 cable’s length over in all directions; in the middle of
which, over a space of 12 or 15 fathoms, the sea broke very high, although it was
otherwise very smooth, and but very little wind.

At noon he had observed in latitude 24° 4’, and at 5 p.m. the longitude by lunar
distances, was 89° 55’, both good observations; which reduced to the hour, gives
the position of the shoal in latitude 24° 3’ 80’, and longitude 89° 41’ west from
Greenwich. This appears to be the same shoal that was seen on Noy. 19th; 1800,
by Don Narciso Riera, Captain of the merchant schooner Catalina, in his passage
from Campeche to New Orleans; but as his longitude was deduced from dead
reckoning, we placed more confidence in the position assigned to it by Arias; never-
theless, navigators sailing on or near this parallel, ought to do it with caution, lest
the two dangers should really exist.

Don Manuel Bozo, Pilot of the Spanish bombard, Nuestra Senora del Carmen,
in a passage from Vera Cruz and Terminos Lagoon, towards the Havanna, on
December the 8th, 1817, at day break saw a breaker or rock, off the starboard
gangway ; the sea being very smooth, and the wind light from the eastward, there
was no doubt of its being a shoal, which he estimated at 2 or 3 cables’ length extent,
stretching N. E. and §. W.; and on its ends he saw two insulated rocks of about
three feet in height. His distance from it was 3 or 3} cables’ length, in which position
he sounded, but found no bottom at 64 fathoms; and although he thought to
examine it with his boat, it was impracticable on account of the great breakers in

On correcting his reckoning for 6 a.m., the hour on which he saw it, he found it

This shoal appears to be distinct from the former, although its latitude is so nearly
the same: the short time between his sailing from the Vigia of Churula and his
getting on the Tortugas Bank, when he found no more than 18 miles of error in his
longitude by dead reckoning, proves that its situation as to longitude cannot be far
from correct. Besides, the configuration and circumstances of the shoal as de-

manuscript, show a danger, with the word doubtful, very near the position of this
last shoal; which also tends to confirm the belief of its existence.

These are the shoals, which, down to the present time, have been known as exist-
ing on the Campeche Bank of soundings. He who navigates on it, in 18 fa-
thoms, will go clear of the Alacranes, and Sisal shoals, and in a safe track for
passing through the channels formed by those on the western edge. Of all these
channels, the best is between the Triangle and the New Shoal; because it is the
clearest ; and therefore as such, we recommend it to be used. The soundings which
conduct the mariner through the middle of it, and clear of the shoals which form it
on each side are tolerably regular, although with little variations, for from being
N. W. from Point Piedras, in latitude 21° 40’, and having between 20 and 25
fathoms water, on fine sand; if the course be continued between W.S. W. and
W. by 8., 18, 22, and 25 fathoms will be found, on fine white sand: and still con-
tinuing to the westward in latitude 21° 20’ there will be found 30, 42, 55, and 73
fathoms, on mud, and soft oaze; and at a little distance from the latter depth, you
will be off the western edge of the bank, and clear of the rocks.

In the first charts that were published by the Hydrographical Directory, and in
the first edition of the Derrotero, it is said, ‘‘ about the middle of this channel there
is a bank with 26 fathoms water, on hard sand and gravel, having a patch of rock
of 9 fathoms, which generally created some alarm to those who sounded on it, from
exciting a suspicion of being near to some of the shoals.”’ According to the latest
soundings, and survey made in this passage, a bank of 24 fathoms, gravel, is placed
in latitude 21° 26’ 30”, and on the meridian of the Baja Nuevo, New shoal, without
noticing the above quoted shoal, which perhaps may exist. The chart published in
1799, places it in 21° 20’ North latitude, and 85° 27’ longitude West from Cadiz,
(91° 44’ W. from Greenwich.)

The preceding account of, and directions for the dangers on the Bank of Cam-
peche, ave from the original Spanish Surveys ; but we shall here introduce what mo-
dern accounts we have of the dangers, that the mariner may have the benefit of
later and more competent experience.

The position of the Sisal Shoal, has been thoroughly surveyed by Captain Barnett,
R. N., from which it appears, that it was previously laid down in the charts a mile
and a half too far to the northward, and three miles and a half to the westward
of its real position. The centre of this bank lies in latitude 21° 20’ 44”, and longi-
tude 90° 9’ 36” W.., in a direction of N. 31° W. (true), 124 miles from Sisal Castle ;
the least water in it is 9 feet, and it is about three-quarters of a mile ina N. N. W.
and S.§. E. direction and in the channel, between it and the shore, is not more
than 7 fathoms, with tolerably regular soundings. The celebrated Mount Note-
perderas, the Spaniard’s mark for keeping clear of the Sisal Shoal, is becoming in-
distinct, in consequence of the trees on it falling, from the ravages of insects.

The MADAGASCAR SHOAL was likewise surveyed by Captain Barnett. It
is a most dangerous, narrow coral ledge, lying in a direction nearly Hast and West,
about a mile and a quarter long, covered with dark grass, and having in one part,
on its western end, only 9 feet. The latitude and longitude of its two extremes are
as follows: East end, lat. 21° 26’ 6” N., long. 90° 17’ 30” W., West end, lat. 21°

DESCRIPTION OF ALACRAN.

From the survey of Don Ciriaco de Cevallos, in 1802, we supposed the port
of Alacran capable of admitting small craft only. It is true a vessel drawing
eleven feet may pass over the rocky heads between Perez and the South spit, which
makes the entrance intricate ; still, with the wind to the south of east, which is gene-
rally in the morning, or rather before noon, a vessel drawing eighteen feet may
sailin. It is one of those harbours which can only be taken by eye, and from aloft
every shoal may be plainly seen. A vessel entering should pass close to the South
Spit, and run N. 3 W., until within a cable’s length of Perez Spit ; then haul close
round it, keeping in the blue water, and anchor with the huts W. by N. one-fourth
of a mile. he white water on Perez Spit can be plainly traced from the island,
coming in from the westward, with the huts bearing N. and N.W.by N. ‘There
are heads with sixteen feet water over them, a quarter of a mile off from the reef x
therefore the eastern extreme of Perez Spit should not be brought to bear to the
eastward of N. E. by E;

Alacran affords a very secure harbour, the dry reefs protecting it as effectually
as would the land. The outside anchorage, two cables’ length north of the South
Spit, in six fathoms and a. half, coral sand, is very safe, with all but westerly winds,
which are rare, and give timely warning.

The tide, if it can be so called, is very remarkable. It was new moon on the
25th of March, about three in the afternoon. On the following day the tide fell
from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. 73 inches, and the next day 13 inches, the wind being from
E. N. E. to E. S. E., moderate. Again, on the 26th of April, two days after the
new moon, wind in the same direction, rather less ; it fell 26 inches from 7 a.m. to
6 p.m. This was a very unusual tide, and several reefs were quite dry that were not
seen before above water. We may suppose this rising of the waters in the morning
to have been occasioned by the land and sea wind, (the few inches are scarcely
worth noticing,) the mean height being about noon. On the plan, therefore, there
may be sometimes a foot more or less than there shown. The fishermen we found
on our second visit, were supplied with water from the main land, astrong proof that
it cannot be procured at Alacran. ;

The main reef forms a regular segment, convexing to the N. E., its base or ex-
treme length tending N. W. by N., fourteen miles. The lead does not give suf-
ficient warning of approach; the abrupt descent from 20 fathoms to dry rocks is
very remarkable, as are the shelves on the west side from 7 to 24 fathoms in a ship’s
length. The nature of the deep water soundings is yery fine sand ; that called grey,
white, and yellow, is much of the same kind; a horn-protracter laid on white paper
will give the exact tint. This will be found the predominant colour on the ground
of Campeche Bank. To the eastward of Alacranes there is no appearance of sound-
ings, with a constant current to the N. W., from one to one and a half knot per
hour. The dry sand bores were conveniently situated for our work. Three of the
same stars as were observed at Pajores make the high north bore in lat. 22° 32’ 15’ N,
These sand bores soon get covered with grass, samphire, and various kinds of herbs,
when above water. The first formation of all is branches of dead coral. These we
found by digging to the level of high water mark, and probably is the reason the
Alacran does not contain fresh water. Fish of all kinds are very abundant. Turtle
are also plentiful.

Kay Arenas, lying in lat. 22° 7 N +» long. 91° 24’ W. Commander Barnett

observes, that ‘‘the Arenas shoals, instead of being upwards of nine miles, as de-

These Kays are composed of a mass of coral heads, usually termed brain stones.
The windward side is formed entirely of this coral, but the others are intermixed
with fine and coarse sand. The deposit of the boobies, and other birds, has raised
this mass to a height of eleven feet above the ocean; and on the southern extreme
a beacon of stones has been erected, the top of which is twenty feet above the sea.
Equal altitudes, two days from Alacran, gave meridian distance 6! 51/5 West,
and stars, north and south, 27° 7/10" N. Instead of a spacious bay, (as in the Ad-
miralty chart,) we found the anchorage a miserable cove, in which there is scarcely
room for three small vessels, and by no means a pleasant place to be caught in with
a westerly wind. A vessel should anchor under the windward reef, in 6 or 7
fathoms, in preference to this cove, and she will have sufficient room to get under
way, should the wind come from that quarter. Light variable southerly winds and
calms generally precede them. We had a regular norther on the 18th of April; a
sure indication of which is the rising of the barometer. In this instance it amounted
to 0 in 40, a great rise for this climate. The gale lasted two days, but we rode it
out very well, in comparatively smooth water, under the windward reef.

The channels between the reefs are distinctly seen from aloft. Should the weather
be dark, however, it is not so; then run with the extreme west end of Kay Arenas,
bearing N. N. W. 3 W., until it subtends an angle of 85° with the easternmost or
Stoney Kay ; or when it bears N. E. by E., then haul up and choose your ancho-
rage in 10, 7, or 5 fathoms; observing, close under the reef, there is more shelter
from S. E. winds, which at times throw in a heavy swell. Should the wind be at
North, or N. E. run with west end of Kay Arenas, 8. W. by S., until Stoney Kay

subtends an angle of 95°; or when it bears S. E. by E. 3 E., then proceed as before.

The tides here are precisely the same as at Alacran. It was full moon on the 9th
of April, about eight in the evening. The same careful man at the tide pole, on the
10th observed it to fall from 8h. a.m. to 6h. p.m. seven inches, and on the following
day, from 6 to 6, twelve inches. Wind from E. N. E. to S. E. by E. If this is not
caused by the wind, it is a regular 12 hours’ tide. High water, full and change,
about 5 a.m., the fall being about an inch per hour.

Fish and birds are of much the same kind as at Alacran. Seals are also found
here of the smooth-haired kind of North America, a distinct species from the fur
seals of the South seas. We killed several, and got about 12 gallons of good oil from
each. This Kay, the Sarranilla, and Baxa Nueva, to the southward of the Pedro
bank, are scarcely ever visited by fishermen, and are the only ones we found seals on.
It is worthy of remark, we had but one shower of rain in the two months, March
and April. Abridged from the Naut. Mag. December, 1838.

Remarks on Campeche, by Mr, H. Davy, R.N.

CamprcuE.—The land about Campeche is hilly, and that to the southward
moderately high. In running for the anchorage, you will first make Fort S¢.
Michael, which is a white building on the top of a hill, some distance to the south-
ward of the town; and on steering in to the eastward, will soon raise several forts,
the town and village of Zerma. The latitude will afford the necessary information
for closing the land. The soundings are regular and shallow, while any of the dis-
tinguishing marks are visible. ‘The town of Cumpeche is the principal sea port in
the province of Yucatan, of which Merida is the capital; it is of moderate size,
with extensive suburbs, and like Vera Cruz is walled round. The town is well
built, and very clean, with a good market, which is well supplied with every kind
of provisions, all of which are much cheaper than at Vera Cruz. There is a very
fine pier, but the water is shallow, and will scarcely admit boats to approach it.
To the northward of the town, just without the walls, are the large suburbs of
Guadaloupe and San Francisco, at the extremity of which are two forts; Fort San
Jose, which stands on the summit of a hill, and Fort St. Mathias, lower down.
The suburb to the southward of the town is called San Roman, which is commanded
by many forts. To the 8. W. is Fort St, Michael, already mentioned, and just

80 SAILING DIRECTIONS FROM

under it is Fort Sun Ferdinand; beyond this is the village of Zerma. Campeche is
a good place to get stock.

During our stay on this coast, we had several tornadoes, some of them very
strong, and at times they would come on successively for three or four days; how-
ever, they gave sufficient warning ; the early part of the day was generally very
fine and clear ; about two o’clock it would begin to look cloudy to windward, which
appearance would increase, and about four or five blow most furiously ; sometimes
with heavy rain and a dark cloudy sky. We generally shortened all sail. These
tornadoes were mostly off the land, but would veer about a good deal, and at times
last several hours.

Remarks on the Navigarion of the Guur or Mexico,
by Mr. H. Davy, Master, R.N.

SHIPS BOUND oO Camprcue, Laguna, or Vera Cruz, after reaching the Cam-
peche Bank, will find the shortest route to Mexico the safest, as the dangers in the
neighbourhood of the Sisal Shoals have been most satisfactorily surveyed. .

Vessels intending to take this way may run down the north coast of Yucatan,
sighting the Vigias or Telegraphs, and keeping outside of five fathoms ; they should
be careful of the soundings in approaching the Castle of Sisal, between which and
the shoal they should go no nearer the shore than four fathoms, or to the shoal
than six fathoms. Having cleared the channel, either the north or south one, a
west course will clear all dangers. The other passages on the Campeche Bank are
also perfectly safe. During the season of the norths it will be prudent, more par-
ticularly for large ships, to go outside of all the shoals, and frequently very quick
passages are made by so doing. Ships leaving Vera Cruz at this time should push
up to the northward as fast as possible, and having attained a good position, the
north becomes the best wind that can blow.

Maxine or Vera Cruz.—Few countries possess such advantages for seamen
as Mexico, in its magnificent and well-defined mountains. These unerring guides
to the navigator are visible in clear weather at great distances from the land, and
when first seen, excite his surprise and admiration ; they must particularly interest
him, as a reference to the chart is sufficient to direct him to an anchorage. The
appearance of the land is a mountainous ridge, of which Orizaba, Perote, and
Villa Rica form the grand elevations. Orizaba, the giant of the chain, is a conical
mountain, whose apex is capped in perpetual snow ; it is estimated at 18,000 feet
above the sea, 60 miles inland, and may be seen from seaward at the distance of
120. One-half of this majestic mountain, with its beautiful white top, appears
above the ridge, with Perote to the right, and Villa Rica on the left. The Cofre
de Perote, of a little less height, is 80 miles to the northward ; it isan immense
mass of mountain, with a small indent at its summit, and snow is very seldom seen
onit. The other high lands are the lesser hills in the vicinity of Point Delgada ;
and at about 10 leagues south-eastward of Vera Cruz are the mountains of San
Martin, of which the voleano of Tuxtla is the highest. On the parallel of Vera
Cruz, or having been driven to the southward, Twatla will be easily made out.
Should the high lands be hidden, which is frequently the case, particularly in the
months of February, March, and April, it will be necessary to pay strict attention
to the lead ; shoaling the water will give notice of approaching the shoals off Anton
Lizardo. The immediate sea coast, from Point Gorda to a considerable distance
southward, is low and sterile, with small sand-hills partially covered with verdure.
Over Point Mocambo is a little dark hill forming a saddle, and close by, near

another hill, is a single tree; these are excellent marks for Sacrificios, and will
often be seen before the Castle or City.

ANCHORAGE AT Sacriricros.—Steering in towards the shoals, and havin
made out the City, Castle, &e., it will be necessary to determine by the direction
of the wind which way to approach the anchorage. The channels between the
Gallega and Blanquilla’ Reefs, between Isle Verde and Pajaros, are those most in
use: I have piloted ships through each of them, and found them equally clear and
safe for any class of ships. In making the reefs, Isle'Verde, which at all times
shows very white, will first present itself, and if it be decided to go south of the

CAPE CATOCHE TO THE BAY OF SAN BERNARDO. 81
shoals, steer for it, leaving it at any convenient distance to starboard, also Pajaros,
and approach Sucrificios boldly ; at 100 yards from its reef are 8 and 7 fathoms
water ; round the south point at that distance, and anchor close up under the lee
of the reefs, the nearer the better, as a hawser will always steady the ship astern.
The bottom is excellent holding ground, and in the north there is greater protection
and smoother water.

The deepest water is in a line between the south point of the island and Point
Mocambo : within a cable’s length of the point are 10 fathoms, thence 10 to near
mid-channel, when the city will be shut in by Point Hornos, from this 9, 8, and a
gradual decrease to 5 and 4 fathoms towards Mocambo ; from this line of soundings
the water shoalens to 8, 7, and 6 fathoms throughout the anchorage. This space is
perfectly clear, and the largest class of ships may work in or out, observing to
tack at the first cast in 5 fathoms. Even inshore of this the bottom has a gradual
ascent, the water being 5, 4, 3, and so on. At this time there are 22 vessels safely
moored here, and it isa much more secure place than usually considered. At all
times, either with the trade wind or during the northers, a heavy swell sets in
towards Point Mocambo, and more or less on the whole coast of the main land.

The Island of Sacrificios lies S. E. by E. 3 E., 3 miles from the city, and is
now a very low barren spot; the high cane trees have within the last few years
been all cut down.

Other anchorages.—The anchorage at Isle Verde is very good, and during the
fine season temporary stopping places can be found under the lee of any of the
reefs, and on the coast between Sacrificios and Anton Lizardo. If night, calms, or
other causes should prevent reaching the port, I would recommend bringing up, if
possible, which is much preferable to risk being driven about by uncertain cur-
rents,

Currents and tides.—The rise and fall here is from 2 feet 9 inches to 4 feet 3
inches ; it mostly occurs once in 24 hours, and causes no perceptible stream.

The currents appear to be driven from whichever point the wind blows ; inshore
it is northerly or southerly along the coast from one-half to two knots, according
to the strength or duration of the breeze. In the north the current is generally
strong to the southward, and turns again northerly as soon as it is over. I have
known it change its direction within an hour after the wind, and at times it appears
almost simultaneous. They are also much stronger near Vera Cruz and at the °
bottom of the gulf than farther to the northward.

Winds.—Throughout the year, except during the season of the norths, which is
from October to March, there are no winds higher than N° 6;* calms, light
land airs, and moderate sea breezes prevail. During the north monsoon, which in
some years may be a month earlier or later, the winds are to the south-eastward
between the norths.

Anchorage at Anton Lizardo, by Mr. Davies, Master of H.M.S. Edinburgh.

Ships coming in from the northward must not approach the western side of the
outer reefs nearer than 27 fathoms until within six miles of the land. They should
then pass the inner reefs in 16 to 18 fathoms, and endeavour as soon as possible to
get sight of the Isle Blanquilla. This island, which forms the western entrance, is
of sand, and so low, that from the northward it is not easily distinguishable from
the main. The low Point del Collol cannot be mistaken, as it is the south point of
the anchorage, and when it bears S. 40° E., Blanguilla will be seen open of the
point. Approach the island no nearer than three-quarters of a mile while to the
N. W. of it, until it bears E. by N. 3 N., when Medio Island will be on with it;
and when Medio opens to the southward, haul up E. S. E., passing Blanquilla at
two cables’ distance, which must not be brought to the westward of W. by N.
until you are three-quarters of a mile to the eastward of it, then haul more to the
northward, and anchor where conyenient, in 8, 10, 12, or 14 fathoms, good holding
ground.

The reefs to the northward are all visible, particularly at low water, and of them-

Should the wind be from the eastward and working in, be careful, in standing
towards the shore, to tack immediately at the first cast in 9 fathoms : the shore is

the largest ship may be safely worked in. Should night be coming on, and pre-

Anton Lizardo is undoubtedly the most capacious, sheltered, and safest anchorage
on the Mexican coast; its great drawbacks are, want of supplies, no water, and
distance from the city, which is 15 miles; fish are abundant. ;
